title: Basic Nursing Care — Safety, Comfort & Physical Needs (Set 2)
subtitle: Skin, nutrition/hydration, elimination, mobility, oxygen, glucose & emergency basics
scenario: Meeting clients' basic physical needs safely: skin integrity, nutrition and hydration, elimination, mobility, oxygen, blood glucose, and recognizing changes to report.

steps.q: To prevent pressure injuries in a client who is immobile, the technician should reposition the client at least every:

opts.text: 2 hours
opts.rat: Repositioning at least every 2 hours relieves pressure over bony prominences and helps prevent pressure injuries.

opts.text: 8 hours
opts.rat: Eight hours is far too long; tissue damage can begin within a couple of hours.

opts.text: 12 hours
opts.rat: This interval greatly increases pressure-injury risk.

opts.text: 24 hours
opts.rat: Once daily repositioning is grossly inadequate.

steps.q: A client is eating in the dayroom, suddenly clutches the throat, and cannot speak, cough, or breathe. The technician should:

opts.text: Offer the client a glass of water
opts.rat: Giving fluids to a choking person can worsen airway obstruction.

opts.text: Perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver)
opts.rat: A conscious, choking adult with a complete obstruction (no air movement) needs immediate abdominal thrusts.

opts.text: Wait to see if the client can clear it alone
opts.rat: Complete obstruction is a life threat; waiting risks death.

opts.text: Lay the client flat and elevate the legs
opts.rat: This does not relieve an airway obstruction.

steps.q: A client on insulin becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and confused. The technician suspects hypoglycemia and, if the client is awake and able to swallow, should:

opts.text: Withhold all food until the next meal
opts.rat: Withholding carbohydrate worsens hypoglycemia and endangers the client.

opts.text: Encourage the client to exercise
opts.rat: Activity lowers glucose further, worsening hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Give a fast-acting carbohydrate such as juice, then notify the nurse
opts.rat: Awake, hypoglycemic clients who can swallow should receive a fast-acting carbohydrate, followed by prompt reporting and reassessment.

opts.text: Give a large dose of the client's insulin
opts.rat: Insulin further lowers glucose and could be fatal.

steps.q: Which findings BEST indicate that a client may be dehydrated?

opts.text: Moist mucous membranes and large urine output
opts.rat: These are signs of adequate hydration.

opts.text: Bounding pulse and elevated blood pressure
opts.rat: Dehydration more often produces a weak, rapid pulse and low blood pressure.

opts.text: Weight gain and edema
opts.rat: These suggest fluid overload, not dehydration.

opts.text: Dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output, and poor skin turgor
opts.rat: Dry mucous membranes, low urine output, and poor skin turgor are classic signs of dehydration.

steps.q: When recording intake and output (I&O), which is counted as OUTPUT?

opts.text: Urine and emesis (vomit)
opts.rat: Output includes measurable fluid losses such as urine, emesis, and drainage.

opts.text: Gelatin and ice chips consumed
opts.rat: Gelatin and ice chips are counted as intake.

opts.text: Water taken with medications
opts.rat: Fluids taken by mouth are intake.

opts.text: Soup at lunch
opts.rat: Liquid foods count as intake.

steps.q: Using proper body mechanics when helping to transfer a client, the technician should:

opts.text: Bend at the waist and keep the knees straight
opts.rat: Bending at the waist strains the back and risks injury.

opts.text: Bend the knees, keep the back straight, and hold the client close
opts.rat: Bending the knees, keeping the back straight, using the legs, and keeping the load close protect the back during transfers.

opts.text: Twist the spine while lifting to save time
opts.rat: Twisting while lifting is a common cause of back injury.

opts.text: Hold the client as far from the body as possible
opts.rat: Holding the load away from the body increases strain and instability.

steps.q: A client is receiving oxygen therapy. An important safety measure is to:

opts.text: Allow smoking near the oxygen source
opts.rat: Oxygen supports combustion; smoking or open flames near it can cause fire.

opts.text: Store the tank lying loose on the floor
opts.rat: Tanks must be secured to prevent falls/damage; this is a safety hazard.

opts.text: Keep the oxygen away from open flames and post 'no smoking' signage
opts.rat: Because oxygen supports combustion, ignition sources and smoking must be kept away and warning signage posted.

opts.text: Use petroleum jelly around the nares
opts.rat: Petroleum products near oxygen are flammable; water-based products are used.

steps.q: A pulse oximeter reads 84%, but the client is talking comfortably with warm, pink skin. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Document the value and take no further action
opts.rat: An abnormal reading must be verified and acted on, not simply recorded.

opts.text: Immediately remove all clothing
opts.rat: This does not address the measurement or the client's status.

opts.text: Tell the client to hold their breath
opts.rat: This would worsen oxygenation and is inappropriate.

opts.text: Check probe placement and perfusion, then reassess and report
opts.rat: Poor probe placement, movement, cold digits, or nail polish can cause false low readings; confirm the reading, then report a true low value.

steps.q: To help prevent constipation in a client, the technician should encourage:

opts.text: Adequate fluids, dietary fiber, and physical activity as tolerated
opts.rat: Fluids, fiber, and activity support normal bowel elimination and help prevent constipation.

opts.text: Decreased fluids and bed rest
opts.rat: Low fluids and inactivity promote constipation.

opts.text: A low-fiber diet
opts.rat: Low fiber contributes to constipation.

opts.text: Routinely ignoring the urge to defecate
opts.rat: Suppressing the urge worsens constipation.

steps.q: To reduce aspiration risk, a client who has just finished eating should be kept:

opts.text: Lying flat immediately
opts.rat: Lying flat after meals increases reflux and aspiration risk.

opts.text: Upright (sitting) for about 30–60 minutes after the meal
opts.rat: Remaining upright after eating reduces reflux and aspiration risk.

opts.text: In the Trendelenburg (head-down) position
opts.rat: Head-down positioning increases aspiration risk.

opts.text: Turned face-down
opts.rat: Prone positioning after meals is unsafe and inappropriate.

steps.q: The MOST reliable indicator of a client's pain is:

opts.text: The technician's personal judgment of how much it 'should' hurt
opts.rat: Staff assumptions are unreliable and can lead to undertreatment.

opts.text: Whether the diagnosis 'usually' causes pain
opts.rat: Diagnosis-based assumptions do not replace the client's report.

opts.text: The client's own self-report of pain
opts.rat: Pain is subjective; the client's self-report is the most reliable indicator when they can communicate.

opts.text: The presence of visible bleeding only
opts.rat: Pain can be severe without visible injury; absence of bleeding does not rule it out.

steps.q: During a skin check, the technician notes an area of redness over the sacrum that does not turn white (blanch) when pressed. The technician should:

opts.text: Massage the reddened area vigorously
opts.rat: Vigorous massage of compromised skin can cause further tissue damage.

opts.text: Ignore it since the skin is intact
opts.rat: Intact but non-blanching redness is an early pressure injury requiring action.

opts.text: Apply a heating pad to the area
opts.rat: Heat is not indicated and could worsen tissue injury.

opts.text: Report and document it and relieve pressure on the area
opts.rat: Non-blanching redness is an early (stage 1) pressure injury; it must be reported/documented and pressure relieved.

steps.q: A client uses a cane for balance after a left-leg weakness. The technician teaches the client to hold the cane:

opts.text: On the strong (right) side, moving cane and weak leg together
opts.rat: The cane is held on the stronger side; the cane and the weaker leg advance together for support and stability.

opts.text: On the weak (left) side
opts.rat: Holding the cane on the weak side does not provide effective support.

opts.text: In whichever hand is dominant regardless of weakness
opts.rat: Cane placement is based on the affected side, not hand dominance.

opts.text: Above the head for balance
opts.rat: This is unsafe and provides no support.

steps.q: For a client with an indwelling urinary catheter, the drainage bag should always be positioned:

opts.text: Above the level of the bladder
opts.rat: Raising the bag above the bladder allows urine to flow back, increasing infection risk.

opts.text: Below the level of the bladder without touching the floor
opts.rat: Keeping the bag below the bladder promotes gravity drainage and prevents backflow; it should not rest on the floor (contamination).

opts.text: Clipped to the bed rail at chest height
opts.rat: This places the bag above the bladder, risking backflow.

opts.text: Resting on the client's abdomen
opts.rat: This is above the bladder and promotes backflow.

steps.q: Which measure BEST promotes sleep for a client with insomnia on the unit?

opts.text: Offer coffee in the evening
opts.rat: Caffeine is a stimulant that impairs sleep.

opts.text: Encourage a long daytime nap
opts.rat: Long daytime naps can worsen nighttime insomnia.

opts.text: Maintain a consistent bedtime routine and reduce evening noise/light/caffeine
opts.rat: Good sleep hygiene—consistent routine, reduced stimulation and caffeine—supports natural sleep.

opts.text: Keep the lights and television on all night
opts.rat: Light and noise disrupt sleep.

steps.q: A client refuses to eat and has lost weight. The technician's BEST action is to:

opts.text: Force the client to eat
opts.rat: Forcing food violates rights and can cause aspiration or injury.

opts.text: Ignore the weight loss
opts.rat: Unaddressed weight loss can lead to serious complications.

opts.text: Remove all food and fluids
opts.rat: Withholding nutrition and hydration is harmful.

opts.text: Document intake/weight, offer preferred foods, and report the poor intake to the nurse
opts.rat: Monitoring and documenting intake/weight, offering acceptable foods, and reporting decline allow the team to intervene appropriately.

steps.q: The BEST way to reduce the need for physical restraints is to:

opts.text: Use frequent observation, meet needs proactively, and provide activity/orientation
opts.rat: Least-restrictive care uses monitoring, meeting needs (toileting, comfort, activity), and orientation to reduce agitation and restraint use.

opts.text: Apply restraints early on all confused clients
opts.rat: Routine restraint is restrictive and increases injury risk; it is not preventive care.

opts.text: Isolate clients in locked rooms
opts.rat: Seclusion is itself a restrictive intervention, not a restraint-reduction strategy.

opts.text: Sedate all restless clients
opts.rat: Chemical restraint for convenience is inappropriate and regulated.

steps.q: When a client has a fever, an appropriate basic nursing measure is to:

opts.text: Cover the client with heavy blankets to sweat it out
opts.rat: Excessive covering traps heat and can raise temperature further.

opts.text: Encourage fluids, provide light clothing/covers, and report the fever
opts.rat: Promoting fluids, avoiding overheating, and reporting the fever support the client and allow ordered treatment.

opts.text: Restrict all fluids
opts.rat: Fever increases fluid needs; restricting fluids risks dehydration.

opts.text: Give aspirin without an order
opts.rat: Administering medication without an order is outside protocol and unsafe.

steps.q: The technician assists a client who has been on bed rest to stand, and the client reports dizziness. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Encourage the client to walk quickly to 'shake it off'
opts.rat: Walking while dizzy risks a fall.

opts.text: Leave the client standing alone to adjust
opts.rat: Leaving a dizzy client unsupported risks injury.

opts.text: Help the client sit or lie back down and rise slowly, then reassess
opts.rat: Dizziness on standing suggests orthostatic changes; returning the client to a safe position and changing position slowly prevents falls.

opts.text: Give caffeine to raise the blood pressure
opts.rat: Caffeine is not an appropriate intervention for positional dizziness.

steps.q: Which change should the technician report to the nurse IMMEDIATELY?

opts.text: A client who slept well and ate breakfast
opts.rat: This is a normal, reassuring finding.

opts.text: A client requesting a second helping at lunch
opts.rat: This is not an urgent clinical concern.

opts.text: A client watching television in the dayroom
opts.rat: This is normal activity, not a change to escalate.

opts.text: New confusion, chest pain, or difficulty breathing
opts.rat: Acute changes such as new confusion, chest pain, or respiratory distress are potential emergencies requiring immediate reporting.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Medication Administration (Set 3)
subtitle: Rights of med admin, identification, routes, safety, refusals & basic calculations
scenario: Administering medications safely: the rights of medication administration, correct identification, routes, handling refusals and reactions, and basic dosage calculations.

steps.q: Which set BEST represents the classic 'rights' of medication administration?

opts.text: Right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time
opts.rat: The core rights are right patient, drug, dose, route, and time (with right documentation and right reason added); they prevent medication errors.

opts.text: Right color, right smell, right size, right shape, right price
opts.rat: These are not the rights of medication administration.

opts.text: Right room, right bed, right meal, right blanket, right TV
opts.rat: These are unrelated to safe medication administration.

opts.text: Right mood, right weather, right day of week
opts.rat: These are irrelevant to medication safety.

steps.q: Before giving a medication, the technician should verify the client's identity using:

opts.text: The room number only
opts.rat: Room/bed numbers change and are not reliable identifiers.

opts.text: Two identifiers, such as name and date of birth
opts.rat: Using two identifiers (e.g., name and date of birth) confirms the right patient and prevents errors.

opts.text: Whoever answers to the name called out
opts.rat: Responding to a name is unreliable, especially with confused clients.

opts.text: The client's meal tray
opts.rat: A meal tray is not a valid identifier.

steps.q: Before administering any medication, the technician must always check the client's:

opts.text: Favorite color
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to medication safety.

opts.text: Shoe size
opts.rat: This has nothing to do with medication administration.

opts.text: Allergies
opts.rat: Checking allergies before every medication prevents potentially life-threatening allergic reactions.

opts.text: Television preferences
opts.rat: This is unrelated to medication safety.

steps.q: When should the technician document that a medication was given?

opts.text: Before preparing it, to save time
opts.rat: Charting before giving risks documenting a dose that was never taken.

opts.text: At the end of the week
opts.rat: Delayed documentation is inaccurate and unsafe.

opts.text: Only if the client asks
opts.rat: Documentation is required regardless of client request.

opts.text: Immediately after the client takes it
opts.rat: Medications are documented right after administration—never before—to keep the record accurate and prevent double-dosing.

steps.q: A client refuses their prescribed medication. The technician should:

opts.text: Respect the refusal, then document it and notify the nurse
opts.rat: A client may refuse medication; the technician documents the refusal and reports it so the team can follow up.

opts.text: Force the medication into the client's mouth
opts.rat: Forcing medication violates the client's rights and is unsafe.

opts.text: Hide the medication in food without telling anyone
opts.rat: Covertly medicating a client is a rights violation.

opts.text: Give a double dose next time
opts.rat: Doubling a dose is dangerous and never appropriate for a missed dose.

steps.q: The technician observes a client hiding a pill in the side of the mouth ('cheeking'). The BEST action is to:

opts.text: Ignore it if the client seems calm
opts.rat: Cheeking risks a missed dose or later overdose and must be addressed.

opts.text: Check the mouth to confirm the pill was swallowed and report cheeking to the nurse
opts.rat: Checking the mouth ensures the dose was taken; reporting cheeking allows the team to prevent hoarding or overdose.

opts.text: Let the client save the pill for later
opts.rat: Allowing hoarding is unsafe and can lead to overdose.

opts.text: Give another pill immediately without checking
opts.rat: Giving more without verifying risks a double dose.

steps.q: A client has difficulty swallowing pills. The technician knows that which type of tablet should NOT be crushed?

opts.text: Any tablet, since crushing is always safe
opts.rat: Not all tablets are safe to crush; some must be given whole.

opts.text: Only chewable vitamins
opts.rat: Chewables are meant to be chewed; the concern is enteric-coated/extended-release forms.

opts.text: Enteric-coated or extended-release tablets
opts.rat: Crushing enteric-coated or extended/sustained-release tablets destroys their design and can cause overdose or irritation; check before crushing any medication.

opts.text: Plain, immediate-release scored tablets
opts.rat: These are generally safe to crush/split; the hazard is coated or extended-release forms.

steps.q: A sublingual medication should be administered by having the client:

opts.text: Swallow it whole with a full glass of water
opts.rat: Swallowing defeats sublingual absorption.

opts.text: Chew it thoroughly and spit it out
opts.rat: This is not how sublingual medication works.

opts.text: Crush it into their food
opts.rat: This is not the correct sublingual route.

opts.text: Place it under the tongue and let it dissolve
opts.rat: Sublingual medications are placed under the tongue to dissolve and absorb through the mucosa; they should not be swallowed.

steps.q: After preparing medications, the technician should NEVER:

opts.text: Leave the medication unattended at the bedside for the client to take later
opts.rat: Leaving medications unattended risks the wrong person taking them, missed or hoarded doses; the technician stays until the dose is taken.

opts.text: Stay with the client while they take the dose
opts.rat: Staying to confirm the dose is taken is correct practice.

opts.text: Verify the client's identity first
opts.rat: Verifying identity is required, not prohibited.

opts.text: Document after administration
opts.rat: Documenting after administration is correct.

steps.q: A PRN medication is one that is given:

opts.text: On a fixed schedule regardless of need
opts.rat: That describes scheduled, not PRN, medication.

opts.text: As needed, after assessing that the client meets the criteria for it
opts.rat: PRN ('as needed') medications are given based on assessed need within the ordered parameters, and the reason and response are documented.

opts.text: Only once in a lifetime
opts.rat: PRN refers to as-needed dosing, not a one-time-ever rule.

opts.text: Without any assessment or documentation
opts.rat: PRN doses require assessment and documentation of reason and effect.

steps.q: The technician should verify a medication against the medication administration record (MAR):

opts.text: Never; checking once from memory is enough
opts.rat: Relying on memory increases the risk of error.

opts.text: Only after the client has taken it
opts.rat: Verification must occur before administration.

opts.text: Three times before administering it
opts.rat: The standard safety practice is to check the medication against the MAR three times before giving it.

opts.text: Only when a supervisor is watching
opts.rat: Verification is always required, not only when observed.

steps.q: A physician orders 500 mg of a medication. The tablets on hand are 250 mg each. How many tablets should the technician give?

opts.text: 1 tablet
opts.rat: One 250 mg tablet provides only 250 mg, half the ordered dose.

opts.text: 4 tablets
opts.rat: Four tablets would be 1,000 mg, double the ordered dose.

opts.text: Half a tablet
opts.rat: Half a tablet is 125 mg, far below the ordered dose.

opts.text: 2 tablets
opts.rat: Using desired ÷ have: 500 mg ÷ 250 mg = 2 tablets.

steps.q: A medication is ordered as 125 mg. The scored tablets available are 250 mg each. The technician should give:

opts.text: One-half (½) tablet
opts.rat: 125 mg ÷ 250 mg = 0.5, so half of a scored (splittable) tablet provides the ordered dose.

opts.text: 2 tablets
opts.rat: Two tablets would be 500 mg, four times the ordered dose.

opts.text: 3 tablets
opts.rat: This greatly exceeds the ordered dose.

opts.text: 1 whole tablet
opts.rat: One whole 250 mg tablet is double the ordered 125 mg.

steps.q: An oral liquid is ordered as 250 mg. The bottle is labeled 125 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the technician give?

opts.text: 2.5 mL
opts.rat: 2.5 mL would provide only about 62.5 mg.

opts.text: 10 mL
opts.rat: 250 mg ÷ 125 mg = 2, and 2 × 5 mL = 10 mL delivers the ordered 250 mg.

opts.text: 5 mL
opts.rat: 5 mL provides 125 mg, half the ordered dose.

opts.text: 20 mL
opts.rat: 20 mL would deliver 500 mg, double the ordered dose.

steps.q: The technician should question or clarify a medication order when:

opts.text: It is written clearly and matches the client's care
opts.rat: A clear, appropriate order does not require clarification.

opts.text: The client simply prefers a different color pill
opts.rat: Color preference is not a reason to change an order.

opts.text: The order is unclear, incomplete, or appears unsafe
opts.rat: An unclear, incomplete, or seemingly unsafe order must be clarified with the prescriber before administering—never guessed.

opts.text: Never; all orders are given exactly as written no matter what
opts.rat: Unsafe or unclear orders must be questioned to protect the client.

steps.q: The technician should administer only medications that they:

opts.text: Found already poured by an unknown coworker
opts.rat: Giving a dose prepared by someone else risks errors you cannot verify.

opts.text: Discovered loose on the counter
opts.rat: Unlabeled, loose medication cannot be verified and must not be given.

opts.text: Guessed at from an unlabeled cup
opts.rat: Unlabeled medication must never be administered.

opts.text: Personally prepared and can verify
opts.rat: A person should give only medications they prepared themselves, so they can verify the drug, dose, and integrity; never give a dose drawn up by someone else.

steps.q: Controlled substances (e.g., certain sedatives) require the technician to:

opts.text: Follow secure storage and accurate counting/documentation per policy
opts.rat: Controlled substances require locked storage, accurate counts (often verified by two staff), and precise documentation of every dose and any waste.

opts.text: Store them loose in an open drawer
opts.rat: Controlled substances must be secured, not left openly accessible.

opts.text: Skip documentation to save time
opts.rat: Documentation of controlled substances is mandatory.

opts.text: Give them to any client who asks
opts.rat: They are given only per order to the correct client, with strict accountability.

steps.q: Some medications have 'hold parameters' (e.g., hold a blood-pressure drug if systolic BP is below a set value). This means the technician should:

opts.text: Give the medication regardless of the vital signs
opts.rat: Ignoring hold parameters can seriously harm the client.

opts.text: Check the relevant vital sign before giving and hold/report if it is outside the parameter
opts.rat: Hold parameters require checking the specified vital sign first and withholding the dose (and notifying the nurse) if the value falls outside the safe range.

opts.text: Double the dose if the vital sign is abnormal
opts.rat: Doubling a dose is never an appropriate response to a hold parameter.

opts.text: Ignore the parameter entirely
opts.rat: Hold parameters exist for safety and must be followed.

steps.q: Shortly after receiving a medication, a client develops hives, swelling, and difficulty breathing. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Give another dose of the same medication
opts.rat: Re-administering the suspected allergen could be fatal.

opts.text: Wait an hour to see if it worsens
opts.rat: Delaying care during a possible anaphylactic reaction is dangerous.

opts.text: Recognize a possible allergic/anaphylactic reaction and get help immediately
opts.rat: Hives, swelling, and breathing difficulty suggest a severe allergic reaction; this is an emergency requiring immediate help and rapid escalation.

opts.text: Document it at the end of the shift and take no other action
opts.rat: This is an emergency needing immediate intervention, not delayed charting.

steps.q: Which is an appropriate site for an intramuscular (IM) injection?

opts.text: The center of the abdomen
opts.rat: The abdomen is used for subcutaneous injections (e.g., insulin/heparin), not IM.

opts.text: The palm of the hand
opts.rat: The palm is not an injection site.

opts.text: The bottom of the foot
opts.rat: The sole of the foot is not an IM injection site.

opts.text: The ventrogluteal or deltoid muscle
opts.rat: The ventrogluteal site (and the deltoid for small volumes) are appropriate, well-established IM injection sites.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Infection Control & Precautions (Set 4)
subtitle: Hand hygiene, standard & transmission-based precautions, PPE, sharps & isolation
scenario: Preventing the spread of infection through hand hygiene, standard and transmission-based precautions, personal protective equipment, safe sharps handling, and supportive isolation care.

steps.q: The SINGLE most effective way to prevent the spread of infection is:

opts.text: Hand hygiene
opts.rat: Proper hand hygiene is the single most effective measure to prevent the transmission of infection.

opts.text: Wearing a gown at all times
opts.rat: Gowns are used situationally; hand hygiene is the foundational measure.

opts.text: Keeping the lights dim
opts.rat: Lighting has no effect on infection transmission.

opts.text: Playing soft music
opts.rat: This is unrelated to infection control.

steps.q: Standard precautions should be used:

opts.text: Only for clients known to have an infection
opts.rat: Standard precautions apply to everyone, since infection status is not always known.

opts.text: With every client, treating all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
opts.rat: Standard precautions apply to all clients and treat blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, regardless of diagnosis.

opts.text: Only during flu season
opts.rat: Standard precautions are used year-round with all clients.

opts.text: Only in the emergency department
opts.rat: They apply in all care settings.

steps.q: When should the technician perform hand hygiene?

opts.text: Only at the start of the shift
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is required at many points, not just once per shift.

opts.text: Only if the hands look dirty
opts.rat: Hands can carry pathogens even when they appear clean.

opts.text: Before and after client contact and after removing gloves
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is performed before and after client contact, after contact with body fluids, and after removing gloves, among other moments.

opts.text: Only after using the restroom
opts.rat: That is one of many required times, not the only one.

steps.q: When hands are visibly soiled, the technician should clean them with:

opts.text: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer only
opts.rat: Alcohol sanitizer does not remove visible soil and does not kill certain spores.

opts.text: A dry paper towel alone
opts.rat: Wiping does not disinfect soiled hands.

opts.text: Lotion
opts.rat: Lotion does not clean or disinfect the hands.

opts.text: Soap and water
opts.rat: Visibly soiled hands must be washed with soap and water; alcohol-based sanitizer is not sufficient for visible soil.

steps.q: The correct order for REMOVING personal protective equipment (PPE) generally begins with:

opts.text: Removing the gloves first (the most contaminated item)
opts.rat: Gloves are removed first because they are the most contaminated, followed by goggles/face shield, gown, then mask, with hand hygiene afterward.

opts.text: Removing the mask first
opts.rat: The mask/respirator is removed last, after leaving the room.

opts.text: Removing the gown before the gloves
opts.rat: Gloves come off before the gown to avoid contaminating the hands.

opts.text: There is no particular order
opts.rat: There is a specific sequence to prevent self-contamination.

steps.q: A client has a wound infected with MRSA. Which type of transmission-based precaution is required?

opts.text: No extra precautions
opts.rat: MRSA requires contact precautions beyond standard precautions.

opts.text: Contact precautions (gown and gloves)
opts.rat: MRSA and similar organisms spread by contact require contact precautions—gown and gloves—plus dedicated or disinfected equipment.

opts.text: Airborne precautions with an N95
opts.rat: MRSA wound infection spreads by contact, not the airborne route.

opts.text: Only a surgical mask
opts.rat: A mask alone does not address contact transmission.

steps.q: Which precaution is required for a client with active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB)?

opts.text: Contact precautions only
opts.rat: TB is airborne, not primarily contact-spread.

opts.text: No precautions beyond standard
opts.rat: Active TB requires airborne precautions.

opts.text: Airborne precautions with an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
opts.rat: TB spreads via airborne droplet nuclei, requiring airborne precautions: an N95 (fit-tested) respirator and a negative-pressure room with the door closed.

opts.text: A cloth face covering is sufficient
opts.rat: A cloth covering does not filter airborne droplet nuclei; an N95 is required.

steps.q: Droplet precautions (e.g., for influenza) require the technician to:

opts.text: Wear an N95 and use a negative-pressure room
opts.rat: That is airborne precautions, more than droplet precautions require.

opts.text: Use no protective equipment at all
opts.rat: A mask is needed for droplet precautions.

opts.text: Wear only gloves
opts.rat: Gloves alone do not protect against droplet spread; a mask is required.

opts.text: Wear a surgical mask when within close range of the client
opts.rat: Droplet precautions require a surgical mask when in close proximity, since droplets travel short distances through the air.

steps.q: For a client with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), the technician should perform hand hygiene by:

opts.text: Washing with soap and water rather than relying on alcohol sanitizer
opts.rat: C. diff spores are not reliably killed by alcohol sanitizer; hands must be washed with soap and water, and contact precautions are used.

opts.text: Using alcohol-based sanitizer only
opts.rat: Alcohol sanitizer does not kill C. diff spores.

opts.text: Skipping hand hygiene if gloves were worn
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is still required after removing gloves.

opts.text: Wiping hands on a towel only
opts.rat: This does not remove spores.

steps.q: After giving an injection, the technician should dispose of the needle by:

opts.text: Recapping it and putting it in the trash
opts.rat: Recapping increases needlestick risk and the regular trash is unsafe for sharps.

opts.text: Placing it uncapped into a puncture-resistant sharps container
opts.rat: Needles are placed directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container without recapping, to prevent needlestick injury.

opts.text: Bending the needle and pocketing it
opts.rat: This is extremely unsafe and prohibited.

opts.text: Leaving it on the bedside table
opts.rat: Leaving a sharp exposed endangers clients and staff.

steps.q: To prevent a needlestick injury, the technician should:

opts.text: Always recap needles with two hands
opts.rat: Two-handed recapping greatly increases injury risk.

opts.text: Carry used needles in a pocket
opts.rat: This is extremely dangerous.

opts.text: Never recap a used needle by hand
opts.rat: Recapping used needles by hand is a leading cause of needlestick injuries and should be avoided; sharps go directly into the container.

opts.text: Hand used needles to a coworker
opts.rat: Passing exposed sharps risks injury; they go into the sharps container.

steps.q: When handling soiled linens, the technician should:

opts.text: Shake them out to loosen debris
opts.rat: Shaking linens spreads microorganisms into the air.

opts.text: Hug them against the uniform
opts.rat: Holding soiled linens against the body contaminates the uniform.

opts.text: Place them on the floor first
opts.rat: The floor is contaminated and this spreads organisms.

opts.text: Hold them away from the body and avoid shaking them
opts.rat: Soiled linens are held away from the uniform and not shaken, to avoid dispersing microorganisms into the air and onto the technician.

steps.q: Respiratory hygiene / cough etiquette includes teaching clients to:

opts.text: Cover coughs/sneezes and perform hand hygiene afterward
opts.rat: Covering coughs and sneezes (with a tissue or the elbow) and cleaning the hands afterward reduces the spread of respiratory infections.

opts.text: Cough openly into the air near others
opts.rat: Uncovered coughing spreads respiratory droplets.

opts.text: Never wash hands after coughing
opts.rat: Hand hygiene after coughing is part of respiratory etiquette.

opts.text: Share used tissues
opts.rat: Sharing tissues spreads infection.

steps.q: A client in isolation for an infection becomes tearful and says they feel lonely and 'like a leper.' The technician should:

opts.text: Avoid the room to save time
opts.rat: Avoiding the client worsens isolation and neglects care.

opts.text: Provide emotional support and regular interaction while maintaining precautions
opts.rat: Isolation can cause loneliness and low mood; the technician should offer psychosocial support and frequent, warm interaction while following precautions.

opts.text: Tell the client to stop complaining
opts.rat: This is dismissive and non-therapeutic.

opts.text: Remove the precautions to make the client feel better
opts.rat: Precautions must be maintained for safety; support is provided within them.

steps.q: Which finding suggests a client may have a localized infection that the technician should report?

opts.text: Pink, intact, cool skin
opts.rat: This describes healthy skin, not infection.

opts.text: A normal temperature and no drainage
opts.rat: These are reassuring findings, not signs of infection.

opts.text: Redness, warmth, swelling, and purulent (pus) drainage at a site
opts.rat: Redness, warmth, swelling, and purulent drainage are classic signs of a localized infection and should be reported.

opts.text: A well-healed, dry scar
opts.rat: A healed scar is not a sign of active infection.

steps.q: Gloves should be changed:

opts.text: Only once per shift
opts.rat: Wearing the same gloves all shift spreads contamination.

opts.text: Never, if they still look intact
opts.rat: Gloves are changed regardless of appearance to prevent cross-contamination.

opts.text: Only when visibly torn
opts.rat: Gloves are changed between clients/tasks, not only when torn.

opts.text: Between clients and between tasks (e.g., dirty to clean) on the same client
opts.rat: Gloves are changed between clients and between a contaminated and a clean task on the same client, with hand hygiene in between.

steps.q: An immunocompromised (e.g., very low white-blood-cell count) client may need protective (reverse) isolation, which is intended to:

opts.text: Protect the client from organisms carried by others
opts.rat: Protective (reverse) isolation shields a highly susceptible, immunocompromised client from pathogens that visitors and staff may carry.

opts.text: Protect staff from the client
opts.rat: That is the purpose of standard/transmission-based precautions, not protective isolation.

opts.text: Punish the client
opts.rat: Isolation is never punitive.

opts.text: Save money on supplies
opts.rat: This is unrelated to the purpose of protective isolation.

steps.q: The 'chain of infection' can be interrupted by the technician when they:

opts.text: Encourage sharing of personal items between clients
opts.rat: Sharing items promotes, rather than blocks, transmission.

opts.text: Perform hand hygiene and follow precautions to block transmission
opts.rat: Breaking any link in the chain of infection—most readily the mode of transmission, via hand hygiene and precautions—prevents spread.

opts.text: Skip cleaning shared equipment
opts.rat: Not cleaning equipment allows transmission to continue.

opts.text: Reuse disposable supplies between clients
opts.rat: Reusing single-use supplies spreads infection.

steps.q: When a small blood spill occurs on a surface, the technician should:

opts.text: Leave it for the next shift
opts.rat: Blood spills must be cleaned promptly for safety.

opts.text: Wipe it with a bare hand
opts.rat: Bare-handed contact with blood is unsafe; gloves are required.

opts.text: Wear gloves and clean/disinfect the spill per facility policy
opts.rat: Blood spills are cleaned while wearing gloves and disinfected with an appropriate agent per policy, treating the blood as potentially infectious.

opts.text: Cover it with a blanket
opts.rat: Covering does not clean or disinfect the spill.

steps.q: To reduce the risk of transmitting infection, the technician should:

opts.text: Wear long artificial nails for direct care
opts.rat: Artificial/long nails harbor more microorganisms and are discouraged in direct care.

opts.text: Skip hand hygiene if wearing rings
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is always required; rings can harbor organisms.

opts.text: Avoid changing gloves to save supplies
opts.rat: Not changing gloves spreads infection.

opts.text: Keep fingernails short and avoid artificial nails when giving direct care
opts.rat: Short natural nails (avoiding artificial nails) harbor fewer organisms and support effective hand hygiene during direct client care.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Nutrition, Feeding & Therapeutic Diets (Set 5)
subtitle: Dysphagia & feeding technique, therapeutic diets, hydration, tube feeding & food-drug safety
scenario: Supporting nutrition and hydration: safe feeding technique, therapeutic diets, tube-feeding basics, and food-medication safety.

steps.q: A client with dysphagia is often ordered thickened liquids because:

opts.text: Thin liquids are harder to control and increase aspiration risk
opts.rat: Thin liquids move quickly and are difficult to control with dysphagia; thickening them slows flow and reduces aspiration risk.

opts.text: Thickened liquids taste better to everyone
opts.rat: The reason is safety (aspiration prevention), not taste.

opts.text: Thin liquids are always safest in dysphagia
opts.rat: Thin liquids are typically the highest aspiration risk in dysphagia.

opts.text: It has nothing to do with swallowing
opts.rat: Thickening is specifically a swallowing-safety measure.

steps.q: When feeding a client at risk for aspiration, the technician should:

opts.text: Feed the client quickly while lying flat
opts.rat: Lying flat and rushing greatly increase aspiration risk.

opts.text: Position upright, give small bites, and avoid rushing
opts.rat: Sitting the client upright, offering small bites/sips, allowing time, and minimizing talking while eating reduce aspiration risk.

opts.text: Give large mouthfuls to finish faster
opts.rat: Large bites increase choking and aspiration risk.

opts.text: Encourage talking and laughing during bites
opts.rat: Talking while swallowing increases aspiration risk.

steps.q: When assisting a client who needs help eating, the technician should:

opts.text: Rush the client to finish for the next task
opts.rat: Rushing risks choking and reduces intake and dignity.

opts.text: Feed the next bite before the client has swallowed
opts.rat: Giving the next bite too soon risks choking/aspiration.

opts.text: Allow adequate time, offer choices, and respect the client's pace
opts.rat: Patient, unhurried feeding with choices and respect for the client's pace supports intake and dignity.

opts.text: Force-feed if the client is slow
opts.rat: Force-feeding is unsafe and violates the client's rights.

steps.q: An order for 'NPO' means the client should:

opts.text: Eat a normal diet
opts.rat: NPO is the opposite of a normal diet.

opts.text: Drink extra fluids
opts.rat: NPO means no fluids by mouth.

opts.text: Eat only dessert
opts.rat: NPO permits nothing by mouth.

opts.text: Have nothing by mouth (no food or fluids)
opts.rat: NPO (nil per os) means nothing by mouth—no food or fluids—until the order is changed.

steps.q: Which item is allowed on a CLEAR liquid diet?

opts.text: Apple juice, broth, and plain gelatin
opts.rat: A clear liquid diet includes see-through liquids such as clear juices, broth, plain gelatin, and tea.

opts.text: A cheeseburger
opts.rat: Solid food is not part of a clear liquid diet.

opts.text: Whole milk
opts.rat: Milk is opaque and belongs to a full liquid diet, not clear liquids.

opts.text: Mashed potatoes
opts.rat: This is a solid/pureed food, not a clear liquid.

steps.q: A consistent-carbohydrate diet is used primarily for clients with:

opts.text: A broken arm
opts.rat: This diet is not indicated for fractures.

opts.text: Diabetes, to help manage blood glucose
opts.rat: A consistent-carbohydrate diet keeps carbohydrate intake steady across meals to help manage blood glucose in diabetes.

opts.text: Normal healthy adults with no condition
opts.rat: It is a therapeutic diet for glucose management, not a general diet.

opts.text: A simple cold
opts.rat: It is not prescribed for a cold.

steps.q: A client on a low-sodium diet should be taught to avoid:

opts.text: Fresh fruits and vegetables
opts.rat: Fresh produce is generally low in sodium and encouraged.

opts.text: Plain water
opts.rat: Water is not restricted for sodium content.

opts.text: Processed, canned, and cured foods and added table salt
opts.rat: Processed, canned, and cured foods are high in sodium; a low-sodium diet limits these and added salt, often for heart failure or hypertension.

opts.text: Home-cooked food without added salt
opts.rat: Unsalted home cooking is appropriate on a low-sodium diet.

steps.q: To help relieve and prevent constipation, a client is encouraged to eat a diet high in:

opts.text: Only refined white bread
opts.rat: Low-fiber refined foods contribute to constipation.

opts.text: No fiber at all
opts.rat: Removing fiber worsens constipation.

opts.text: Only cheese
opts.rat: A cheese-only diet is low in fiber and can worsen constipation.

opts.text: Fiber, along with adequate fluids
opts.rat: A high-fiber diet with adequate fluids and activity promotes normal bowel elimination and helps prevent constipation.

steps.q: The technician records how much a client ate at each meal because:

opts.text: Intake is monitored to track nutrition and identify problems early
opts.rat: Documenting the percentage/amount eaten helps the team monitor nutrition and catch declining intake early.

opts.text: It is unnecessary busywork
opts.rat: Intake documentation directly informs nutritional care.

opts.text: Only to fill out paperwork for fun
opts.rat: It serves a real clinical purpose.

opts.text: It should be guessed without looking
opts.rat: Intake should be observed and recorded accurately, not guessed.

steps.q: Which finding indicates a client is likely well hydrated?

opts.text: Very dark, scant urine
opts.rat: Dark, scant urine suggests dehydration, not good hydration.

opts.text: Pale-yellow urine and adequate urine output
opts.rat: Pale-yellow urine and adequate output suggest good hydration; dark, scant urine suggests dehydration.

opts.text: Dry, cracked lips and no urine for many hours
opts.rat: These are signs of dehydration.

opts.text: Sunken eyes and poor skin turgor
opts.rat: These indicate dehydration.

steps.q: When caring for a client receiving a tube (enteral) feeding, the technician should keep the head of the bed:

opts.text: Flat, with the client lying supine
opts.rat: Lying flat increases reflux and aspiration risk during tube feeding.

opts.text: In a head-down position
opts.rat: Head-down positioning increases aspiration risk.

opts.text: Elevated (at least about 30–45 degrees) during and after the feeding
opts.rat: Keeping the head of the bed elevated during and after tube feedings reduces reflux and aspiration risk.

opts.text: Turned face-down
opts.rat: Prone positioning is unsafe for tube feeding.

steps.q: A client's dietary restrictions include their cultural and religious food practices. The technician should:

opts.text: Ignore the preferences and serve anything
opts.rat: Disregarding these practices is disrespectful and may violate the client's beliefs.

opts.text: Tell the client their beliefs do not matter
opts.rat: This is disrespectful and non-therapeutic.

opts.text: Force the client to eat restricted foods
opts.rat: Forcing restricted foods violates the client's rights and beliefs.

opts.text: Respect and accommodate the client's cultural/religious food preferences
opts.rat: Honoring cultural and religious dietary practices respects the client and supports their intake and dignity.

steps.q: A significant unintended change in a client's weight should be:

opts.text: Reported, as it may signal a nutritional or medical problem
opts.rat: Notable weight loss or gain can indicate nutritional deficits, fluid shifts, or illness and should be reported for evaluation.

opts.text: Ignored unless the client complains
opts.rat: Weight changes are monitored proactively, not only on complaint.

opts.text: Kept secret from the nurse
opts.rat: Findings must be communicated to the team.

opts.text: Assumed to be unimportant
opts.rat: Weight changes can be clinically important.

steps.q: Which findings may indicate malnutrition in a client?

opts.text: Steady weight and good energy
opts.rat: These are signs of adequate nutrition.

opts.text: Unintended weight loss, muscle wasting, and poor wound healing
opts.rat: Weight loss, muscle wasting, fatigue, and poor wound healing are signs of malnutrition that warrant reporting.

opts.text: Rapid wound healing and strong muscles
opts.rat: These reflect good, not poor, nutrition.

opts.text: Excellent appetite with stable weight
opts.rat: This is reassuring, not a sign of malnutrition.

steps.q: A client taking warfarin (a blood thinner) is taught to keep intake of which nutrient CONSISTENT?

opts.text: Vitamin C from citrus only
opts.rat: Vitamin C is not the key interacting nutrient for warfarin.

opts.text: Table salt
opts.rat: Sodium is not the warfarin-interaction concern.

opts.text: Vitamin K (found in green leafy vegetables)
opts.rat: Vitamin K affects warfarin's action; clients keep vitamin K intake (leafy greens) consistent rather than suddenly increasing or decreasing it.

opts.text: Caffeine
opts.rat: Caffeine is not the vitamin that interacts with warfarin.

steps.q: Grapefruit juice is a concern with certain medications because it can:

opts.text: Have no effect on any medication ever
opts.rat: Grapefruit juice interacts with a number of medications.

opts.text: Cure the underlying illness
opts.rat: It does not treat the illness; it can cause interactions.

opts.text: Replace the need for medication
opts.rat: It does not replace medication.

opts.text: Alter how some medications are metabolized, changing their levels
opts.rat: Grapefruit juice can interfere with the metabolism of certain medications, raising drug levels and the risk of adverse effects; clients should check with the prescriber/pharmacist.

steps.q: When serving a meal to a client with visual impairment, a helpful technique is to:

opts.text: Describe the location of foods using a clock-face reference
opts.rat: Describing plate contents by clock positions (e.g., 'potatoes at 6 o'clock') helps a client with visual impairment eat independently.

opts.text: Say nothing and let the client guess
opts.rat: Leaving the client to guess reduces independence and intake.

opts.text: Remove the plate before they finish
opts.rat: Removing food early reduces intake and dignity.

opts.text: Feed them without asking
opts.rat: Assuming the client cannot self-feed removes autonomy; offer assistance based on need and preference.

steps.q: To encourage adequate fluid intake in a client at risk for dehydration, the technician should:

opts.text: Restrict all fluids
opts.rat: Restricting fluids worsens dehydration risk.

opts.text: Offer preferred fluids frequently and keep them within reach
opts.rat: Frequently offering preferred, accessible fluids helps maintain hydration, especially in older or cognitively impaired clients.

opts.text: Only offer fluids once per day
opts.rat: Infrequent offering is inadequate for hydration.

opts.text: Place fluids out of the client's reach
opts.rat: Out-of-reach fluids discourage intake.

steps.q: A client on a mechanically altered (pureed) diet is served this texture because they:

opts.text: Simply prefer baby food
opts.rat: The diet is prescribed for swallowing/chewing safety, not mere preference.

opts.text: Need extra crunchy foods
opts.rat: Crunchy foods would be unsafe for these clients.

opts.text: Have difficulty chewing or swallowing regular-texture food safely
opts.rat: Pureed/mechanically altered diets are ordered when a client cannot safely chew or swallow regular textures, reducing choking/aspiration risk.

opts.text: Are being punished
opts.rat: Diet textures are for safety, never punishment.

steps.q: To help prevent choking during meals, the technician should:

opts.text: Leave clients who are at risk to eat alone
opts.rat: At-risk clients need supervision during meals.

opts.text: Serve large chunks of tough food to at-risk clients
opts.rat: Large, tough pieces increase choking risk.

opts.text: Have clients eat quickly while lying down
opts.rat: Eating fast while reclined increases choking and aspiration risk.

opts.text: Supervise at-risk clients, ensure proper positioning, and watch for distress
opts.rat: Supervising at-risk clients, positioning them upright, providing appropriate food textures, and watching for signs of distress help prevent choking.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Elimination: Urinary, Bowel, Catheter & Ostomy (Set 6)
subtitle: Catheter care & CAUTI prevention, UTI signs, I&O, urinary retention, incontinence, ostomy care, impaction/diarrhea & safe toileting
scenario: Supporting safe, dignified urinary and bowel elimination—caring for indwelling catheters and ostomies, recognizing infection and retention, managing incontinence, diarrhea, and impaction, and assisting clients to toilet safely while using standard precautions.

steps.q: To help prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) in a client with an indwelling urinary catheter, the technician should:

opts.text: Keep the drainage system closed, provide routine perineal and catheter care, and keep the tubing free of kinks
opts.rat: Maintaining a closed drainage system, performing routine perineal/catheter hygiene, and keeping tubing unobstructed help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infections.

opts.text: Open the drainage system frequently to check it
opts.rat: Breaking the closed system introduces bacteria and raises infection risk.

opts.text: Rest the drainage bag on the floor
opts.rat: The bag should be kept off the floor to avoid contamination.

opts.text: Allow the tubing to become kinked or looped below the bag
opts.rat: Kinks and dependent loops obstruct flow and can promote infection; tubing should drain freely.

steps.q: Which findings should the technician report as possible signs of a urinary tract infection (UTI)?

opts.text: Clear, pale-yellow urine with no odor
opts.rat: Clear, pale urine without odor is a normal finding, not a sign of infection.

opts.text: Cloudy or foul-smelling urine, burning, urgency or frequency, fever, or new confusion in an older adult
opts.rat: Cloudy/foul-smelling urine, burning, urgency/frequency, fever, or new-onset confusion in an older adult can indicate a UTI and should be reported for assessment.

opts.text: A normal, regular voiding pattern
opts.rat: A normal voiding pattern is not a sign of infection.

opts.text: The client stating they feel completely well
opts.rat: Feeling well is not a warning sign; the concern is the symptoms of infection.

steps.q: When emptying an indwelling catheter's drainage bag, the technician should:

opts.text: Let the drain spout touch the sides of the measuring container
opts.rat: Touching the spout to the container contaminates it and the closed system.

opts.text: Skip measuring the amount
opts.rat: Output should be measured and recorded, not skipped.

opts.text: Use clean technique, avoid touching the spout to the container, and measure and record the output
opts.rat: Emptying the bag with clean technique, keeping the drain spout from touching the container, and measuring/recording the output protects the closed system and provides accurate data.

opts.text: Empty it directly onto the floor
opts.rat: Emptying onto the floor is unsanitary and does not allow measurement.

steps.q: Monitoring a client's 'intake and output' (I&O) means the technician records:

opts.text: Only the meals the client eats
opts.rat: I&O includes fluids in and out, not just meals.

opts.text: Only the client's weight
opts.rat: Weight is a separate measure; I&O tracks fluids in and out.

opts.text: Only how many times the client walks
opts.rat: Activity is not part of I&O.

opts.text: Fluids taken in (drinks, IV as applicable) and fluids put out (urine, emesis, drainage)
opts.rat: Intake and output records fluids the client takes in and fluids they put out, helping monitor hydration and kidney/bladder function.

steps.q: A client has not voided for many hours, reports lower abdominal discomfort, and the lower abdomen feels firm and rounded. The technician should:

opts.text: Suspect urinary retention (possible bladder distension) and report it
opts.rat: Not voiding for a prolonged time with lower abdominal fullness and a firm, rounded lower abdomen suggests urinary retention with bladder distension, which should be reported for prompt assessment.

opts.text: Assume it is normal and do nothing
opts.rat: These findings are not normal and should not be ignored.

opts.text: Restrict the client's fluids further
opts.rat: Restricting fluids does not address retention and can cause other problems.

opts.text: Encourage the client to hold it longer
opts.rat: Encouraging further retention could worsen bladder distension.

steps.q: Appropriate care for a client with urinary incontinence includes:

opts.text: Leaving the skin damp to save time
opts.rat: Damp skin breaks down quickly; skin must be kept clean and dry.

opts.text: Keeping the skin clean and dry, protecting the skin, maintaining dignity, and offering scheduled toileting
opts.rat: Good incontinence care keeps the skin clean, dry, and protected to prevent breakdown, preserves the client's dignity, and offers scheduled toileting to promote continence and comfort.

opts.text: Restricting all fluids to reduce accidents
opts.rat: Fluid restriction can cause dehydration and concentrated urine; it is not the answer to incontinence.

opts.text: Making the client feel ashamed to discourage it
opts.rat: Shaming is harmful and disrespectful; care should protect dignity.

steps.q: When a urine specimen is needed from a client with an indwelling catheter, the technician should:

opts.text: Pour it out of the bottom of the drainage bag
opts.rat: Urine that has sat in the drainage bag is not a fresh, reliable specimen and is not the correct source.

opts.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to collect it
opts.rat: Disconnecting breaks the closed system and raises infection risk; specimens are taken from the sampling port.

opts.text: Collect it from the designated sampling port using clean technique (not from the drainage bag)
opts.rat: A catheter urine specimen is obtained from the designated sampling port using clean technique, keeping the system closed—not from the drainage bag. (Confirm the exact facility procedure with faculty.)

opts.text: Ask the client to void around the catheter into a cup
opts.rat: This does not provide a valid catheter specimen and is not the correct method.

steps.q: A healthy ostomy stoma normally appears:

opts.text: Pale white and dry
opts.rat: A pale, dry stoma is not the expected healthy appearance and may indicate a problem.

opts.text: Black and hard
opts.rat: A black stoma suggests compromised blood supply and must be reported urgently.

opts.text: Bright yellow
opts.rat: A healthy stoma is not yellow; it is pink to red and moist.

opts.text: Pink to red and moist
opts.rat: A healthy stoma is pink to red and moist, reflecting good blood supply.

steps.q: Which change in a client's stoma should the technician report promptly?

opts.text: A stoma that looks dark, dusky, purple, or black
opts.rat: A dark, dusky, purple, or black stoma can indicate impaired blood supply to the tissue and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: A stoma that remains pink and moist
opts.rat: A pink, moist stoma is the expected healthy appearance, not a concern.

opts.text: The pouch collecting normal output
opts.rat: Normal output collecting in the pouch is expected.

opts.text: Intact, healthy skin around the stoma
opts.rat: Healthy peristomal skin is a good finding, not something to report as a problem.

steps.q: To protect the skin around a client's ostomy (peristomal skin), the technician should:

opts.text: Leave stool in contact with the skin for long periods
opts.rat: Prolonged contact with stool irritates and breaks down peristomal skin.

opts.text: Keep the peristomal skin clean and dry and ensure the appliance fits well without leaking
opts.rat: Keeping the skin around the stoma clean and dry and ensuring a well-fitting, non-leaking appliance protects the skin from breakdown.

opts.text: Use a pouch that is clearly too large and leaks
opts.rat: A poorly fitting, leaking appliance exposes skin to output and causes breakdown.

opts.text: Scrub the skin vigorously with harsh products
opts.rat: Harsh scrubbing damages the skin; gentle cleansing is appropriate.

steps.q: An ostomy pouch should generally be emptied:

opts.text: Only once it is completely full and overflowing
opts.rat: Waiting until it overflows causes leaks and skin problems.

opts.text: Never—it should be left until the whole appliance is changed
opts.rat: The pouch is emptied regularly between appliance changes.

opts.text: Before it becomes too full (commonly when about one-third to one-half full) to prevent leakage and the weight pulling it loose
opts.rat: Emptying the pouch before it gets too full (often described as about one-third to one-half full) helps prevent leakage and keeps the weight from loosening the seal. (Confirm the specific guideline with faculty/policy.)

opts.text: Only when the client complains of pain
opts.rat: Routine emptying is based on fullness, not waiting for pain.

steps.q: Because normal bowel patterns vary from person to person, the technician should:

opts.text: Expect every client to have a bowel movement at the exact same frequency
opts.rat: Bowel patterns vary; there is no single 'normal' frequency for everyone.

opts.text: Assume any pattern is fine and never report changes
opts.rat: Significant changes from a client's usual pattern should be reported.

opts.text: Only track bowel movements if the client asks
opts.rat: Monitoring elimination is part of routine care, not only on request.

opts.text: Know each client's usual pattern and report significant changes from their baseline
opts.rat: Knowing the client's usual bowel pattern lets the technician recognize and report meaningful changes (such as new constipation or diarrhea) from their baseline.

steps.q: Which pattern may indicate a fecal impaction that should be reported?

opts.text: No formed bowel movement for a prolonged period, then leakage of liquid stool, with abdominal discomfort or distension
opts.rat: A fecal impaction can cause no formed stool for a prolonged time, then seepage of liquid stool around the mass, along with abdominal discomfort/distension. It should be reported.

opts.text: A soft, formed daily bowel movement
opts.rat: A soft, regular bowel movement is normal, not a sign of impaction.

opts.text: The client passing normal gas comfortably
opts.rat: Passing gas comfortably is not a warning sign.

opts.text: A predictable, comfortable elimination routine
opts.rat: A comfortable, predictable routine is a healthy pattern.

steps.q: For a client with diarrhea, appropriate priorities include:

opts.text: Ignoring skin care around the perineal area
opts.rat: Diarrhea irritates skin; protecting the skin is a priority.

opts.text: Protecting the skin, monitoring hydration, following any infection-control precautions, and reporting the diarrhea
opts.rat: Diarrhea care focuses on protecting perineal skin, watching for dehydration, using indicated infection-control precautions, and reporting so the cause can be addressed.

opts.text: Withholding all fluids
opts.rat: Withholding fluids risks dehydration; hydration must be monitored and supported per the plan.

opts.text: Assuming it is never contagious
opts.rat: Some causes of diarrhea are contagious; appropriate precautions should be followed.

steps.q: To promote normal bowel and bladder elimination, the technician can:

opts.text: Rush the client and deny privacy
opts.rat: Rushing and lack of privacy inhibit normal elimination.

opts.text: Discourage the client from using the toilet
opts.rat: Supporting timely toileting promotes elimination, not discouraging it.

opts.text: Provide privacy, respond promptly to toileting needs, assist to a normal (upright) position when possible, and support a routine
opts.rat: Privacy, prompt response to the urge, a normal upright toileting position when possible, and a consistent routine all support normal elimination.

opts.text: Keep the client lying flat for all elimination
opts.rat: A flat position makes elimination harder; an upright/seated position is more natural when possible.

steps.q: When providing perineal care (or teaching a client), to help prevent urinary infection the technician should wipe:

opts.text: From back to front
opts.rat: Wiping back to front can move bacteria from the anal area toward the urethra, increasing infection risk.

opts.text: In any direction, as it makes no difference
opts.rat: Direction matters; front to back reduces contamination risk.

opts.text: In a circular scrubbing motion repeatedly over the same area
opts.rat: Repeated scrubbing over the same area does not follow clean-to-dirty principles and can irritate skin.

opts.text: From front to back (clean to dirty)
opts.rat: Wiping from front to back moves from the cleaner urethral area toward the anal area, reducing the risk of introducing bacteria to the urinary tract.

steps.q: A bladder or bowel training program is intended to:

opts.text: Help the client establish a regular, predictable elimination routine and improve continence
opts.rat: Bladder/bowel training uses scheduled toileting and routine to help the client achieve more regular, predictable elimination and improved continence.

opts.text: Punish the client for incontinence
opts.rat: Training is supportive, never punitive.

opts.text: Eliminate the client's need for any fluids
opts.rat: Adequate fluids remain important; training does not remove that need.

opts.text: Keep the client in bed at all times
opts.rat: Training promotes routine toileting, not staying in bed.

steps.q: If the technician notices blood in a client's urine or stool, the appropriate action is to:

opts.text: Assume it is nothing and discard it
opts.rat: Blood in urine or stool can be significant and should not be dismissed or discarded without reporting.

opts.text: Report it to the nurse and document the finding
opts.rat: Blood in the urine or stool is an abnormal finding that should be reported to the nurse and documented objectively for follow-up.

opts.text: Tell the client to keep it private
opts.rat: This finding needs to be reported, not concealed.

opts.text: Wait several days to see if it happens again
opts.rat: Delaying could miss a serious problem; it should be reported promptly.

steps.q: When assisting a client to the toilet or a bedside commode, safety measures include:

opts.text: Leaving the client alone with the call light out of reach
opts.rat: The call light must be within reach and fall precautions maintained for safety.

opts.text: Rushing the client without any support
opts.rat: Rushing and lack of support increase fall risk.

opts.text: Keeping the call light within reach, ensuring privacy, and providing fall precautions and appropriate assistance
opts.rat: Safe toileting includes keeping the call light within reach, providing privacy, and using fall precautions and appropriate physical assistance based on the client's needs.

opts.text: Removing all grab bars and supports
opts.rat: Grab bars and supports help prevent falls and should be available.

steps.q: Throughout all elimination care, the technician must always:

opts.text: Discuss the client's elimination openly in public areas
opts.rat: Elimination is private; discussing it publicly violates dignity and confidentiality.

opts.text: Skip hand hygiene to save time
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is essential to prevent the spread of infection.

opts.text: Work without gloves when handling body fluids
opts.rat: Gloves are part of standard precautions when handling body fluids.

opts.text: Maintain the client's privacy and dignity and use standard precautions (gloves and hand hygiene)
opts.rat: Elimination care must always protect the client's privacy and dignity and follow standard precautions—gloves and thorough hand hygiene—to prevent infection.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (elimination). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Procedural specifics—catheter urine-specimen collection from the sampling port and the ostomy pouch-emptying guideline (about one-third to one-half full)—follow facility policy and are marked for faculty confirmation. No specific numeric thresholds (e.g., urine-output values) are asserted. Pending faculty review. Complements catheter drainage-bag positioning and constipation-prevention items already covered in Sets 2 and 5.
referenceNote: Cross-reference: catheter bag position (bnc-core-02), constipation prevention/fiber diet (bnc-core-02, bnc-core-05).

title: Basic Nursing Care — Mobility, Positioning, Transfers & ROM (Set 7)
subtitle: Complications of immobility, range of motion & contractures, safe transfers, gait belts & mechanical lifts, wheelchair/walker safety, positioning & DVT recognition
scenario: Keeping clients safely mobile—preventing the complications of immobility, performing range-of-motion, positioning clients correctly, transferring and ambulating them safely with belts, lifts, and assistive devices, and recognizing problems such as deep vein thrombosis.

steps.q: Prolonged immobility can lead to which serious complications the technician should help prevent?

opts.text: Blood clots (DVT), pneumonia, muscle wasting, and joint contractures
opts.rat: Immobility increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis, respiratory problems like pneumonia, loss of muscle strength, and contractures, among other complications—so promoting safe movement matters.

opts.text: Improved circulation and lung function
opts.rat: Immobility tends to impair, not improve, circulation and lung function.

opts.text: Stronger muscles and joints
opts.rat: Immobility leads to muscle weakening and stiff joints, not strengthening.

opts.text: No effect on the body at all
opts.rat: Immobility has many harmful effects on nearly every body system.

steps.q: 'Passive' range-of-motion exercises are:

opts.text: Movements the client does entirely on their own
opts.rat: When the client does the movement themselves, it is active range-of-motion.

opts.text: Movements the technician or caregiver performs for a client who cannot move the joint themselves
opts.rat: Passive range-of-motion is performed by the caregiver for a client who cannot move the joint on their own, helping maintain joint flexibility.

opts.text: Only done during physical therapy sessions
opts.rat: Passive ROM can be part of routine care, not only formal therapy.

opts.text: A type of medication
opts.rat: Range-of-motion is a physical exercise, not a medication.

steps.q: 'Active' range-of-motion means:

opts.text: The technician moves the joints while the client stays still
opts.rat: That describes passive range-of-motion, not active.

opts.text: The joints are never moved
opts.rat: Range-of-motion involves moving the joints; active means the client does it.

opts.text: The client performs the joint movements themselves
opts.rat: In active range-of-motion the client moves their own joints, which helps maintain both mobility and strength.

opts.text: Movement is done only with a machine
opts.rat: Active ROM is performed by the client, not by a machine.

steps.q: When performing range-of-motion exercises, the technician should:

opts.text: Force each joint well past the point of resistance
opts.rat: Forcing past resistance can injure the joint; movement should be gentle.

opts.text: Move quickly and jerkily to finish fast
opts.rat: Fast, jerky movements can cause injury; ROM is done slowly and smoothly.

opts.text: Continue even when the client reports sharp pain
opts.rat: Sharp pain is a signal to stop; ROM should not be pushed into pain.

opts.text: Move each joint slowly and gently to the point of resistance, without forcing past pain
opts.rat: Range-of-motion is performed slowly and gently, moving each joint to the point of resistance but not forcing beyond it or into pain.

steps.q: The main purpose of range-of-motion exercises is to:

opts.text: Maintain joint mobility and prevent contractures and stiffness
opts.rat: Range-of-motion keeps joints flexible, maintains mobility, and helps prevent contractures and stiffness caused by immobility.

opts.text: Replace the client's need for any repositioning
opts.rat: ROM does not replace repositioning; both are part of care.

opts.text: Cure underlying diseases
opts.rat: ROM maintains function; it does not cure underlying disease.

opts.text: Increase the client's blood pressure
opts.rat: Raising blood pressure is not the purpose of ROM.

steps.q: A 'contracture' is:

opts.text: A temporary muscle cramp that resolves in minutes
opts.rat: A contracture is not a brief cramp; it is a lasting shortening of tissue.

opts.text: A permanent shortening and tightening of a muscle or joint from lack of movement
opts.rat: A contracture is a permanent tightening/shortening of muscle, tendon, or joint tissue that can result from prolonged immobility; preventing it is a key reason for ROM and positioning.

opts.text: A type of skin rash
opts.rat: A contracture affects muscle/joint tissue, not the skin as a rash.

opts.text: A normal, healthy joint
opts.rat: A contracture is an abnormal, restricting condition, not a healthy joint.

steps.q: A gait (transfer) belt is used during ambulation or transfers to:

opts.text: Restrain the client to the bed
opts.rat: A gait belt is a support/safety aid for movement, not a restraint device.

opts.text: Replace the need for the technician to be present
opts.rat: The belt is used by the technician who stays with the client; it does not replace their presence.

opts.text: Give the technician a secure hold to steady and support the client and help prevent falls
opts.rat: A gait belt around the client's waist gives the technician a secure grip to steady and support the client during transfers and ambulation, reducing fall risk.

opts.text: Measure the client's waist for clothing
opts.rat: A gait belt is a mobility safety aid, not a measuring tool.

steps.q: When ambulating a client who has one-sided (e.g., left-leg) weakness, the technician generally positions themselves:

opts.text: Far away, out of reach
opts.rat: Staying out of reach would prevent the technician from supporting or catching the client.

opts.text: Directly in front, blocking the client's path
opts.rat: Standing directly in front blocks movement and does not support the weak side.

opts.text: Behind and to the side of the client's stronger side only
opts.rat: The technician generally supports the weaker side to guard against a fall toward it.

opts.text: On the client's weaker (affected) side, using a gait belt, to support and guard them
opts.rat: The technician typically stands on the client's weaker/affected side (slightly behind), using a gait belt, so they can support and guard the client if the weak side gives way. (Confirm the exact technique with faculty.)

steps.q: Before transferring a client into or out of a wheelchair, the technician must FIRST:

opts.text: Lock the wheelchair brakes and move the footrests out of the way
opts.rat: Locking the brakes keeps the wheelchair from rolling, and moving the footrests aside prevents tripping and injury—both essential before a transfer.

opts.text: Leave the brakes unlocked so the chair can move freely
opts.rat: An unlocked chair can roll away during transfer, causing a fall.

opts.text: Leave the footrests down and in the way
opts.rat: Footrests left down are a trip/injury hazard during transfer.

opts.text: Remove the client's non-skid footwear
opts.rat: Non-skid footwear should be on for safe transfers, not removed.

steps.q: For a client who is heavy or fully dependent and cannot bear weight, the safest way to move them is to:

opts.text: Lift the client alone as quickly as possible
opts.rat: Lifting a dependent client alone risks injury to both the client and the technician.

opts.text: Use a mechanical lift and/or get adequate help, following safe-handling policy
opts.rat: Dependent clients who cannot bear weight should be moved with a mechanical lift and/or sufficient staff, following safe patient-handling policy, to protect the client and staff from injury.

opts.text: Drag the client by the arms
opts.rat: Dragging by the arms can injure the client's shoulders and skin and is unsafe.

opts.text: Have the client transfer with no assistance
opts.rat: A fully dependent client cannot safely transfer without assistance.

steps.q: When a client who has been lying down is going to stand, the technician should first:

opts.text: Have them jump straight up to standing
opts.rat: Standing up suddenly can cause a drop in blood pressure and dizziness.

opts.text: Keep them lying flat and pull them upright quickly
opts.rat: A quick move from flat to standing risks orthostatic dizziness and injury.

opts.text: Let them sit and dangle their legs at the bedside briefly before standing, to prevent dizziness
opts.rat: Allowing the client to sit and dangle their legs for a short time lets blood pressure adjust and reduces dizziness from orthostatic (postural) hypotension before standing.

opts.text: Have them stand and immediately walk quickly
opts.rat: Standing and rushing to walk increases the risk of a fall from dizziness.

steps.q: Correct use of a standard walker involves the client:

opts.text: Placing the walker far ahead and lunging toward it
opts.rat: Reaching too far and lunging is unstable and increases fall risk.

opts.text: Lifting the walker overhead between steps
opts.rat: The walker is used at ground level for support, not lifted overhead.

opts.text: Leaning the whole body weight backward away from the walker
opts.rat: Leaning backward away from the walker is unstable and unsafe.

opts.text: Moving the walker a short distance forward, then stepping toward it while all legs/tips are stable on the ground
opts.rat: The client advances the walker a short, controlled distance with all tips on the ground for stability, then steps toward it—keeping support throughout. (Confirm the specific gait technique with faculty.)

steps.q: Having a client wear non-skid (non-slip) footwear during ambulation primarily helps to:

opts.text: Prevent slips and falls
opts.rat: Non-skid footwear improves traction on the floor, helping prevent slips and falls during walking and transfers.

opts.text: Improve the client's appearance only
opts.rat: The purpose is safety/traction, not appearance.

opts.text: Make the client walk faster
opts.rat: The goal is safe footing, not increased speed.

opts.text: Replace the need for any assistance
opts.rat: Footwear supports safety but does not replace needed assistance.

steps.q: To help prevent footdrop in a client on prolonged bed rest, the technician can:

opts.text: Leave the feet unsupported and pointed downward
opts.rat: Leaving the feet pointed down (plantar flexed) unsupported contributes to footdrop.

opts.text: Support the feet in a neutral position (for example, with a footboard or supportive device) and use ROM
opts.rat: Keeping the feet supported in a neutral position—such as with a footboard or approved device—along with range-of-motion helps prevent footdrop. (Confirm the specific device/method with faculty.)

opts.text: Keep heavy bedding pressing the toes downward
opts.rat: Heavy bedding pushing the toes down promotes, rather than prevents, footdrop.

opts.text: Avoid moving the ankles at all
opts.rat: Ankle range-of-motion helps prevent footdrop; immobilizing the ankles does not.

steps.q: To keep a client in proper body alignment while in bed, the technician:

opts.text: Twists the client's spine and limbs into awkward positions
opts.rat: Awkward, twisted positions strain the body and can cause harm.

opts.text: Leaves the client in one position indefinitely
opts.rat: Clients need repositioning; staying in one position too long causes complications.

opts.text: Uses pillows and supports to maintain natural alignment and prevent strain
opts.rat: Pillows and supportive devices help keep the head, spine, and limbs in natural alignment, preventing strain, deformity, and pressure.
