opts.text: Removes all support so the client lies completely flat and rigid
opts.rat: Supports are used to maintain comfortable, natural alignment, not removed.

steps.q: When transferring a client with one-sided weakness from bed to a chair, it is generally best to position the chair:

opts.text: Far from the bed so the client walks a long way
opts.rat: The chair should be close to allow a short, safe transfer.

opts.text: Behind the client where they cannot see it
opts.rat: The client should be able to see and reach the chair for a safe transfer.

opts.text: So the client must pivot toward their weaker side
opts.rat: Moving toward the weaker side is less stable; leading with the stronger side is safer.

opts.text: On the client's stronger (unaffected) side, so they move toward their stronger side
opts.rat: Placing the chair on the client's stronger side lets them lead and bear weight with the unaffected side, making the transfer safer and more stable. (Confirm technique with faculty.)

steps.q: Which finding in a client's leg should the technician report as a possible blood clot (deep vein thrombosis)?

opts.text: New swelling, redness, warmth, or pain in the calf or leg
opts.rat: New unilateral swelling, redness, warmth, or pain/tenderness in the calf or leg can indicate a deep vein thrombosis and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: Both legs looking their normal size and color
opts.rat: Normal, symmetric legs are not a warning sign.

opts.text: The client walking comfortably
opts.rat: Comfortable walking is not a sign of a clot.

opts.text: Cool, pink, comfortable feet
opts.rat: Warm, painful swelling—not cool, comfortable feet—is the concern for DVT.

steps.q: If the technician suspects a client has a deep vein thrombosis (a swollen, warm, painful calf), they should:

opts.text: Vigorously massage or rub the area to improve circulation
opts.rat: Massaging or rubbing a suspected clot is dangerous—it could dislodge the clot. This must be avoided.

opts.text: Report it promptly and NOT massage or rub the area
opts.rat: A suspected DVT should be reported promptly, and the area must not be massaged or rubbed, because that could dislodge the clot.

opts.text: Have the client vigorously exercise the leg
opts.rat: Vigorous activity on a suspected clot is unsafe; report and follow direction instead.

opts.text: Ignore it unless the client complains repeatedly
opts.rat: A suspected DVT is potentially serious and should be reported promptly, not ignored.

steps.q: Encouraging appropriate activity and early mobility (as allowed) benefits the client by:

opts.text: Increasing the risk of every complication
opts.rat: Appropriate mobility reduces, rather than increases, complications of immobility.

opts.text: Weakening the muscles and lungs
opts.rat: Activity strengthens muscles and supports lung function.

opts.text: Improving circulation, breathing, and digestion and helping prevent complications of immobility
opts.rat: Appropriate activity and early mobility improve circulation, respiratory function, and digestion, and help prevent clots, pneumonia, constipation, and muscle loss.

opts.text: Having no benefit for the client
opts.rat: Mobility has many well-established benefits.

steps.q: During all transfers and mobility assistance, the technician should:

opts.text: Attempt every move alone to prove independence
opts.rat: Working beyond safe limits alone risks injury; getting help is safer.

opts.text: Ignore the client's abilities and limits
opts.rat: Care must be based on the client's specific abilities and limits.

opts.text: Skip safety checks to save time
opts.rat: Skipping safety checks (brakes, footwear, help) endangers the client and technician.

opts.text: Use safe technique, assess the client's ability, get help when needed, and protect both the client's and their own safety
opts.rat: Safe mobility care means using proper technique, assessing what the client can do, obtaining help or equipment when needed, and protecting both the client's and the technician's safety.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (mobility, positioning, transfers & range of motion). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Technique specifics—standing on the weaker side during ambulation, walker gait, footboard/footdrop prevention, and chair placement on the stronger side for transfers—follow facility policy and are marked for faculty confirmation. No specific numeric values are asserted. Complements body-mechanics, cane use, and pressure-injury repositioning items already covered in Set 2. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Skin Integrity, Wound Care & Pressure-Injury Staging (Set 8)
subtitle: Pressure-injury risk & staging (1–4/unstageable), friction & shear, prevention, wound-infection signs, drainage types & dressing care
scenario: Protecting skin integrity and supporting wound healing—recognizing pressure-injury risk and stages, preventing breakdown from pressure, friction, shear, and moisture, observing wounds and dressings, and reporting changes early.

steps.q: Pressure injuries most commonly develop over:

opts.text: Bony prominences such as the sacrum (tailbone), heels, hips, and elbows
opts.rat: Pressure injuries form where bone is close to the skin and pressure is concentrated—commonly the sacrum, heels, hips (trochanters), elbows, and back of the head.

opts.text: The center of the palms only
opts.rat: The palms are not typical pressure-injury sites; bony prominences are.

opts.text: Well-padded, muscular areas away from bone
opts.rat: Well-padded areas are at lower risk; pressure injuries concentrate over bony prominences.

opts.text: Only areas covered by clothing
opts.rat: Location relates to pressure over bone, not simply to clothing coverage.

steps.q: Which combination increases a client's risk for a pressure injury?

opts.text: Frequent movement, dry intact skin, and good nutrition
opts.rat: These are protective factors, not risks.

opts.text: Immobility, moisture (such as incontinence), poor nutrition, and friction or shear
opts.rat: Immobility, excess moisture, poor nutrition/hydration, and friction or shear all raise the risk of pressure injury, especially in combination.

opts.text: Regular repositioning and a pressure-redistributing surface
opts.rat: These reduce risk rather than increase it.

opts.text: Being young, active, and well-hydrated
opts.rat: These lower risk; the concern is immobility, moisture, and poor nutrition.

steps.q: A Stage 1 pressure injury is characterized by:

opts.text: Exposed muscle and bone
opts.rat: Exposed muscle or bone describes a Stage 4 injury, not Stage 1.

opts.text: A deep crater with visible fatty tissue
opts.rat: A deep crater into fatty tissue describes Stage 3, not Stage 1.

opts.text: Intact skin with an area of non-blanchable redness (redness that does not turn white when pressed)
opts.rat: In a Stage 1 pressure injury the skin is still intact but shows persistent, non-blanchable redness—an early warning sign that pressure must be relieved. (Confirm staging definitions with faculty.)

opts.text: A shallow open sore or blister
opts.rat: A shallow open area or blister describes Stage 2; Stage 1 skin is intact.

steps.q: A Stage 2 pressure injury involves:

opts.text: Intact skin with only redness
opts.rat: Intact skin with redness is Stage 1; Stage 2 has some skin loss.

opts.text: Full-thickness loss down to muscle or bone
opts.rat: Loss to muscle or bone is Stage 4, not Stage 2.

opts.text: A wound base completely covered by slough or eschar
opts.rat: A base obscured by slough/eschar is 'unstageable,' not Stage 2.

opts.text: Partial-thickness skin loss—a shallow open area or an intact/ruptured blister
opts.rat: A Stage 2 pressure injury shows partial-thickness skin loss, such as a shallow open sore or a blister (intact or ruptured), without deeper tissue exposed. (Confirm staging definitions with faculty.)

steps.q: A pressure injury that extends into the fatty (subcutaneous) tissue—sometimes with a crater—but does NOT expose muscle, tendon, or bone is:

opts.text: Stage 3
opts.rat: A Stage 3 pressure injury is full-thickness loss extending into subcutaneous fat, which may look like a crater, but without exposed muscle, tendon, or bone. (Confirm staging definitions with faculty.)

opts.text: Stage 1
opts.rat: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable redness—far less severe.

opts.text: Stage 2
opts.rat: Stage 2 is only partial-thickness loss, not into the fatty tissue.

opts.text: A normal healing wound
opts.rat: This describes a specific pressure-injury stage, not normal healing.

steps.q: A pressure injury that extends through the tissue to expose muscle, tendon, or bone is:

opts.text: Stage 1
opts.rat: Stage 1 involves intact skin only.

opts.text: Stage 4
opts.rat: A Stage 4 pressure injury is the deepest—full-thickness loss with exposed muscle, tendon, or bone—and carries a high risk of serious complications. (Confirm staging definitions with faculty.)

opts.text: Stage 2
opts.rat: Stage 2 is shallow, partial-thickness loss, not exposure of muscle or bone.

opts.text: A Stage 1 that is healing
opts.rat: Exposed muscle/bone is the most severe stage, not a healing Stage 1.

steps.q: When the base of a pressure injury is completely covered by slough or eschar so its true depth cannot be determined, it is termed:

opts.text: Stage 1
opts.rat: Stage 1 has intact skin and is clearly assessable; it is not obscured.

opts.text: Fully healed
opts.rat: A wound covered in slough/eschar is not healed.

opts.text: Unstageable
opts.rat: When slough or eschar covers the base so the depth cannot be seen, the injury is 'unstageable' until the base is visible. (Confirm staging definitions with faculty.)

opts.text: Stage 2
opts.rat: Stage 2 is a visible, shallow partial-thickness wound; an obscured base is unstageable.

steps.q: 'Shear' injury to the skin occurs when:

opts.text: The skin is kept clean and dry
opts.rat: Clean, dry skin is protective, not a cause of shear.

opts.text: The client drinks plenty of fluids
opts.rat: Hydration supports skin health and is unrelated to shear.

opts.text: The client is repositioned frequently
opts.rat: Frequent repositioning helps prevent injury; shear is a mechanical force.

opts.text: Layers of skin and deeper tissue slide against each other—for example, when a client slides down in bed
opts.rat: Shear happens when the skin stays in place while deeper tissue slides (as when a client slides down in a raised bed), damaging blood vessels and tissue. (Confirm the concept with faculty.)

steps.q: To reduce friction and shear when moving a client up in bed, the technician should:

opts.text: Lift the client using a draw sheet with adequate help, rather than dragging them across the sheets
opts.rat: Using a draw sheet and enough help to lift (not drag) the client reduces friction and shear on the skin, protecting against breakdown.

opts.text: Drag the client by the arms across the bed
opts.rat: Dragging causes friction and shear and can injure the skin and shoulders.

opts.text: Pull the client by the ankles
opts.rat: Pulling by the ankles causes friction/shear and is unsafe.

opts.text: Leave the client sliding down in a high-Fowler's position
opts.rat: Letting the client slide down increases shear; they should be repositioned properly.

steps.q: A good practice to protect the heels of an at-risk, bedbound client is to:

opts.text: Press the heels firmly against the mattress at all times
opts.rat: Constant pressure on the heels against the mattress promotes breakdown.

opts.text: Offload ('float') the heels—for example, place a pillow under the calves so the heels are off the mattress
opts.rat: Floating the heels by supporting the lower legs on a pillow keeps pressure off the heels, a common and vulnerable pressure-injury site. (Confirm the specific method/device with faculty.)

opts.text: Massage the heels vigorously each hour
opts.rat: Vigorous massage of at-risk skin can worsen tissue damage and is not recommended.

opts.text: Ignore the heels since they rarely break down
opts.rat: Heels are among the most common pressure-injury sites and need protection.

steps.q: For a client who is incontinent, protecting the skin from moisture-associated damage includes:

opts.text: Leaving the skin wet to avoid friction
opts.rat: Wet skin breaks down more easily; it should be cleansed and kept dry.

opts.text: Scrubbing the skin hard with harsh soap
opts.rat: Harsh scrubbing damages fragile skin; gentle cleansing is appropriate.

opts.text: Cleansing gently and promptly, keeping the skin dry, and applying a barrier product as indicated
opts.rat: Prompt gentle cleansing, keeping the skin dry, and using a moisture-barrier product as indicated protect the skin from breakdown caused by prolonged moisture.

opts.text: Applying heat to dry the skin quickly
opts.rat: Applying heat can burn or further damage fragile skin.

steps.q: Current best practice regarding a reddened area over a bony prominence is to:

opts.text: Massage and rub the reddened area to increase blood flow
opts.rat: Massaging reddened skin over a bony prominence is no longer recommended—it can worsen underlying tissue damage.

opts.text: Apply firm continuous pressure to the area
opts.rat: Continuous pressure worsens the injury; pressure must be relieved.

opts.text: Leave the client in that position to avoid disturbing the skin
opts.rat: Leaving the client on the reddened area continues the pressure that caused it.

opts.text: Relieve the pressure (reposition), protect the area, and report it—do NOT massage the reddened area
opts.rat: The area should have pressure relieved by repositioning, be protected, and be reported. Massaging reddened skin over a bony prominence is contraindicated in current practice. (Confirm current guidance with faculty.)

steps.q: Adequate nutrition and hydration support skin integrity and wound healing because:

opts.text: Protein, calories, and fluids are needed to build and repair tissue and heal wounds
opts.rat: The body needs adequate protein, calories, fluids, and nutrients to maintain skin and repair tissue; poor nutrition and dehydration impair healing and increase breakdown risk.

opts.text: Food and fluids have no effect on the skin
opts.rat: Nutrition and hydration strongly affect skin health and healing.

opts.text: Only water matters; nutrients are irrelevant
opts.rat: Both adequate nutrients (especially protein) and fluids matter.

opts.text: Eating less speeds wound healing
opts.rat: Undernutrition slows healing; adequate intake supports it.

steps.q: Which findings around a wound should the technician report as possible signs of infection?

opts.text: Gradually shrinking size and new healthy tissue
opts.rat: Shrinking size and healthy new tissue are signs of healing, not infection.

opts.text: Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus (purulent drainage), foul odor, or fever
opts.rat: Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, purulent (pus) drainage, foul odor, increased pain, or fever suggest possible wound infection and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: Clean, dry, intact surrounding skin
opts.rat: Clean, intact surrounding skin is a good sign, not infection.

opts.text: Decreasing drainage over time
opts.rat: Decreasing drainage generally indicates improvement.

steps.q: Clear, watery drainage from a wound is described as 'serous.' Drainage that is bloody is described as:

opts.text: Purulent
opts.rat: Purulent drainage is thick pus, often a sign of infection—not simply bloody.

opts.text: Serous
opts.rat: Serous is the clear, watery drainage already described, not bloody drainage.

opts.text: Sanguineous
opts.rat: Bloody drainage is 'sanguineous'; a mix of blood-tinged, watery drainage is 'serosanguineous.' (Confirm drainage terminology with faculty.)

opts.text: Intact
opts.rat: 'Intact' is not a type of drainage.

steps.q: If a client's wound dressing becomes saturated with drainage or comes loose, the technician should:

opts.text: Ignore it until the next scheduled dressing change
opts.rat: A saturated or loose dressing needs attention, not waiting until the next scheduled change.

opts.text: Remove the dressing and leave the wound open to air without direction
opts.rat: Removing the dressing without an order can disrupt healing and the sterile field.

opts.text: Throw extra tape over it and say nothing
opts.rat: Simply taping over it without reporting does not address the underlying issue.

opts.text: Reinforce or report it per facility policy and notify the nurse
opts.rat: A saturated or loosened dressing should be handled per policy—reinforcing and/or reporting—and the nurse notified, since increased drainage may also signal a change needing assessment.

steps.q: When wound care or a dressing change is ordered, the technician should:

opts.text: Follow the ordered technique (clean or sterile as specified) and not change or remove dressings on their own initiative outside the orders/scope
opts.rat: Wound care follows the specific order and technique (clean or sterile as directed) and stays within scope; the technician does not independently alter, remove, or perform wound care beyond what is ordered and authorized.

opts.text: Use whatever technique is fastest, ignoring the order
opts.rat: The ordered technique must be followed to protect the wound and prevent infection.

opts.text: Perform any wound procedure regardless of scope or training
opts.rat: Wound procedures must be within the technician's scope and competence.

opts.text: Reuse old dressing supplies to save time
opts.rat: Reusing dressings/supplies breaks infection-control principles.

steps.q: Routine skin inspection for a client at risk of breakdown should:

opts.text: Be done only once on admission and never again
opts.rat: Skin must be inspected regularly, not just once.

opts.text: Occur regularly, with special attention to bony prominences, and any early changes reported
opts.rat: At-risk clients need regular skin inspection—especially over bony prominences—so early changes (like non-blanchable redness) are caught and reported before they worsen.

opts.text: Only happen if the client complains of pain
opts.rat: Many at-risk clients cannot report skin problems; inspection must be proactive.

opts.text: Focus only on areas the client points out
opts.rat: Inspection should be systematic, especially over vulnerable bony areas.

steps.q: Because older adults often have thin, fragile skin, to help prevent skin tears the technician should:

opts.text: Handle limbs roughly to move quickly
opts.rat: Rough handling can tear fragile skin.

opts.text: Drag the client across rough surfaces
opts.rat: Dragging causes friction and skin tears.

opts.text: Handle the skin gently, avoid friction, and be careful with tape and adhesives
opts.rat: Gentle handling, minimizing friction, careful transfers, and cautious use of tape/adhesives help prevent skin tears in fragile, aging skin.

opts.text: Apply and rip off strong adhesive tape frequently
opts.rat: Aggressive adhesive use and removal can tear fragile skin.

steps.q: The overall goal of skin and wound care is to:

opts.text: Keep dressings on as long as possible regardless of condition
opts.rat: Dressings are managed based on the wound and orders, not left indefinitely.

opts.text: Focus only on wounds after they form
opts.rat: Prevention of breakdown is as important as treating existing wounds.

opts.text: Limit the client's movement to protect the skin
opts.rat: Appropriate movement and repositioning protect the skin; immobility harms it.

opts.text: Maintain skin integrity, prevent breakdown, promote healing of existing wounds, and report changes early
opts.rat: The aim is to keep skin intact, prevent pressure and moisture damage, support healing of any wounds, and report changes early so problems are addressed promptly.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (skin integrity & wound care). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Pressure-injury staging definitions (Stages 1–4 and 'unstageable'), the friction/shear concept, and wound-drainage terminology (serous/sanguineous/serosanguineous/purulent) are stated at an introductory level and marked for faculty confirmation against the current pressure-injury staging system. Current practice that reddened bony prominences are NOT massaged is included and flagged. No specific repositioning intervals or numeric values are asserted (repositioning timing is covered in Set 2). Complements pressure-injury repositioning/redness (bnc-core-02), MRSA/precautions (bnc-core-04), and peristomal skin (bnc-core-06). Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Oxygenation & Respiratory Care Basics (Set 9)
subtitle: Positioning for breathing, early vs late signs of hypoxia, oxygen delivery devices & safety, nasal-cannula skin care, pulse oximetry, incentive spirometry, pursed-lip breathing, secretion clearance and when to report respiratory distress
scenario: Supporting clients' oxygenation and breathing safely: positioning, recognizing hypoxia early, using oxygen equipment safely, basic pulmonary hygiene, and knowing which respiratory changes to report to the licensed nurse.

steps.q: A client is short of breath. Which position best promotes lung expansion and easier breathing?

opts.text: High-Fowler's (sitting upright)
opts.rat: Sitting upright lowers the diaphragm and allows fuller lung expansion, easing the work of breathing for a dyspneic client.

opts.text: Flat on the back (supine)
opts.rat: Lying flat lets abdominal organs press on the diaphragm and worsens shortness of breath.

opts.text: Trendelenburg (head lower than feet)
opts.rat: Head-down positioning increases pressure on the diaphragm and worsens breathing.

opts.text: Prone (lying face-down)
opts.rat: This is not a routine comfort position for a dyspneic client and can restrict chest movement.

steps.q: Which finding is usually the EARLIEST sign that a client is not getting enough oxygen?

opts.text: Restlessness, anxiety, or a change in behavior
opts.rat: The brain is very sensitive to low oxygen, so restlessness, anxiety, or confusion are often the earliest signs of hypoxia.

opts.text: Bluish lips and nail beds (cyanosis)
opts.rat: Cyanosis is a late sign; oxygen is already significantly low by the time it appears.

opts.text: Clubbing of the fingertips
opts.rat: Clubbing reflects chronic long-term low oxygen, not an acute early change.

opts.text: A drop in body temperature
opts.rat: Temperature change is not a reliable early indicator of hypoxia.

steps.q: Bluish discoloration of the lips and nail beds (cyanosis) is best described as:

opts.text: A late sign of inadequate oxygenation that should be reported promptly
opts.rat: Cyanosis appears after oxygenation has already fallen substantially; it is a late warning sign and needs prompt reporting.

opts.text: A normal finding in most clients
opts.rat: Cyanosis is never a normal expected finding.

opts.text: The first sign of low oxygen
opts.rat: Restlessness and anxiety typically appear before cyanosis; cyanosis is late.

opts.text: A sign the client has too much oxygen
opts.rat: Cyanosis indicates too little oxygen reaching the tissues, not too much.

steps.q: A pulse oximeter is used to measure:

opts.text: The percentage of oxygen saturation in the blood
opts.rat: A pulse oximeter noninvasively estimates the oxygen saturation of the blood (SpO2).

opts.text: The client's blood pressure
opts.rat: Blood pressure is measured with a cuff and sphygmomanometer, not a pulse oximeter.

opts.text: The blood glucose level
opts.rat: Glucose is measured with a glucometer, not a pulse oximeter.

opts.text: The amount of oxygen in the room air
opts.rat: A pulse oximeter reads the client's saturation, not environmental oxygen.

steps.q: To obtain an accurate pulse-oximeter reading on a client's finger, the technician should:

opts.text: Make sure the finger is warm and remove dark nail polish or artificial nails if present
opts.rat: Poor circulation from a cold finger and light-blocking nail polish or artificial nails can cause a falsely low or unreliable reading.

opts.text: Place the probe on a cold, cyanotic finger for the truest value
opts.rat: Cold, poorly perfused fingers give inaccurate readings.

opts.text: Have the client hold their breath during the reading
opts.rat: Breath-holding is unnecessary and can alter the reading.

opts.text: Tape the probe on tightly enough to blanch the fingertip
opts.rat: Excessive pressure impairs blood flow and produces an inaccurate reading.

steps.q: Because oxygen strongly supports combustion, the MOST important safety rule where oxygen is in use is:

opts.text: No smoking or open flames, and post 'Oxygen in Use' precautions
opts.rat: Oxygen makes fires ignite and spread more easily, so eliminating smoking, sparks, and open flames is the priority safety measure.

opts.text: Keep the oxygen tubing tightly coiled under the blanket
opts.rat: Tubing hidden under bedding can kink and can trap heat; it is not the key fire-safety rule.

opts.text: Apply a petroleum-based lubricant to the client's lips and nose
opts.rat: Petroleum (oil-based) products are flammable and should be avoided around oxygen; water-based products are used instead.

opts.text: Turn the oxygen off whenever staff leave the room
opts.rat: Oxygen is a prescribed therapy and is not turned off without an order.

steps.q: A client wearing a nasal cannula reports soreness behind the ears and dryness of the nose. The technician should:

opts.text: Pad the tubing behind the ears and provide water-based lubricant to the nares
opts.rat: Padding pressure points and using a water-soluble moisturizer relieve skin breakdown and dryness without introducing a flammable oil-based product.

opts.text: Apply petroleum jelly generously inside both nostrils
opts.rat: Oil-based products are a fire hazard around oxygen and can be aspirated; use water-based products.

opts.text: Remove the oxygen until the skin heals
opts.rat: Oxygen is a prescribed therapy and is not discontinued without an order.

opts.text: Tighten the cannula strap firmly to stop the movement
opts.rat: Tightening increases pressure and worsens skin breakdown.

steps.q: A low-flow nasal cannula is generally used to deliver oxygen at approximately:

opts.text: 1 to 6 liters per minute
opts.rat: A standard low-flow nasal cannula commonly delivers oxygen in the 1–6 L/min range; higher rates dry the nares and are uncomfortable.

opts.text: 15 to 20 liters per minute
opts.rat: These very high flows are not delivered through a standard nasal cannula.

opts.text: 0 liters per minute
opts.rat: Zero flow would deliver no supplemental oxygen.

opts.text: Any rate the client prefers
opts.rat: Oxygen flow is set to the prescribed rate, not client preference.

steps.q: Compared with a nasal cannula, a simple face mask generally:

opts.text: Delivers a higher concentration of oxygen
opts.rat: A simple mask covers the nose and mouth and delivers a higher oxygen concentration than a low-flow nasal cannula.

opts.text: Delivers less oxygen than a cannula
opts.rat: A mask delivers more, not less, oxygen than a low-flow cannula.

opts.text: Allows the client to eat easily while wearing it
opts.rat: A mask must be removed to eat, unlike a nasal cannula.

opts.text: Is used only during sleep
opts.rat: Mask use is based on oxygen need, not the time of day.

steps.q: The normal resting respiratory rate for an adult is about:

opts.text: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
opts.rat: A normal adult resting respiratory rate is approximately 12–20 breaths per minute.

opts.text: 4 to 8 breaths per minute
opts.rat: This is abnormally slow (bradypnea) for a resting adult and should be reported.

opts.text: 30 to 40 breaths per minute
opts.rat: This is abnormally fast (tachypnea) for a resting adult and should be reported.

opts.text: 60 to 80 breaths per minute
opts.rat: This far exceeds a normal adult rate.

steps.q: Which observation most clearly indicates a client is in respiratory distress and should be reported to the nurse immediately?

opts.text: Use of neck and shoulder (accessory) muscles, nasal flaring, and rapid labored breathing
opts.rat: Accessory-muscle use, nasal flaring, and rapid labored breathing are hallmark signs of increased work of breathing and respiratory distress.

opts.text: Even, quiet breathing at rest
opts.rat: This describes normal, unlabored breathing.

opts.text: Speaking in full sentences without pausing for breath
opts.rat: Being able to speak in full sentences suggests the client is not in acute distress.

opts.text: A regular respiratory rate of 16 per minute
opts.rat: This is within the normal adult range.

steps.q: The main purpose of teaching a client to use an incentive spirometer is to:

opts.text: Encourage slow, deep breaths that expand the lungs and help prevent atelectasis
opts.rat: The incentive spirometer promotes sustained deep inhalation, which re-expands alveoli and helps prevent atelectasis, especially after immobility or surgery.

opts.text: Measure the client's blood oxygen level
opts.rat: Oxygen saturation is measured with a pulse oximeter, not an incentive spirometer.

opts.text: Deliver aerosolized medication to the lungs
opts.rat: Medication is delivered by a nebulizer or inhaler, not an incentive spirometer.

opts.text: Strengthen the client's cough by forcing rapid exhalation
opts.rat: The device emphasizes slow, deep inhalation, not forced exhalation.

steps.q: When coaching a client to use an incentive spirometer, the technician should instruct the client to:

opts.text: Seal the lips around the mouthpiece and inhale slowly and deeply, then hold briefly
opts.rat: A slow, deep inhalation with a brief breath-hold maximizes lung expansion, which is the goal of the device.

opts.text: Blow out into the device as hard and fast as possible
opts.rat: The incentive spirometer is used on inhalation, not forceful exhalation.

opts.text: Take rapid shallow breaths for one minute
opts.rat: Rapid shallow breathing does not expand the alveoli effectively.

opts.text: Use it only when short of breath
opts.rat: It is used regularly on a schedule to prevent complications, not only during distress.

steps.q: Pursed-lip breathing is often taught to clients with chronic lung disease because it:

opts.text: Slows and prolongs exhalation, helping keep airways open and reduce trapped air
opts.rat: Exhaling slowly against pursed lips creates slight back-pressure that keeps small airways open longer, improving air emptying and easing dyspnea.

opts.text: Forces the client to breathe faster
opts.rat: Pursed-lip breathing slows the breathing rate rather than speeding it up.

opts.text: Increases carbon dioxide in the lungs
opts.rat: It helps the client exhale trapped air more effectively, aiding CO2 removal.

opts.text: Replaces the need for prescribed oxygen
opts.rat: It is a breathing technique, not a substitute for prescribed oxygen therapy.

steps.q: To help a client mobilize and clear lung secretions, the technician can encourage the client to:

opts.text: Turn, cough, and deep-breathe regularly and stay well hydrated as allowed
opts.rat: Position changes, coughing, deep breathing, and adequate fluids help loosen and clear secretions and prevent pooling in the lungs.

opts.text: Lie still and breathe as shallowly as possible
opts.rat: Immobility and shallow breathing allow secretions to pool and increase the risk of atelectasis and infection.

opts.text: Avoid all fluids to keep secretions from forming
opts.rat: Adequate hydration thins secretions and makes them easier to clear; restricting fluids thickens them.

opts.text: Suppress every cough with medication
opts.rat: A productive cough clears secretions and should generally be encouraged, not suppressed.

steps.q: A client receiving oxygen becomes newly confused and restless. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Check the client and oxygen equipment and report the change to the nurse, as this may signal hypoxia
opts.rat: New confusion and restlessness can be early signs of hypoxia; the technician assesses the client and equipment and promptly reports so oxygenation can be evaluated.

opts.text: Assume the client is seeking attention and ignore it
opts.rat: Dismissing a new mental-status change could miss dangerous hypoxia.

opts.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate independently
opts.rat: Oxygen flow is changed only per order; the technician does not adjust it independently.

opts.text: Apply wrist restraints to keep the client still
opts.rat: Restraints do not address the cause and are never a first response to a mental-status change.

steps.q: Oxygen is considered a medication. This means the technician should:

opts.text: Administer it at the prescribed flow rate and delivery device, and report changes rather than adjusting it independently
opts.rat: Because oxygen is a prescribed therapy, it is given as ordered; changes in the client's status are reported so the licensed team can adjust the order.

opts.text: Change the flow rate whenever the client feels short of breath
opts.rat: Adjusting flow without an order exceeds scope; report the client's status instead.

opts.text: Discontinue it once the client says they feel better
opts.rat: Oxygen is stopped only per order, not on the client's say-so.

opts.text: Share one client's oxygen setup with another client
opts.rat: Equipment and prescribed settings are individual and are never shared between clients.

steps.q: Humidification is often added to oxygen therapy mainly to:

opts.text: Add moisture that helps prevent drying of the airways and nasal passages
opts.rat: Supplemental oxygen is dry; adding humidity reduces drying, cracking, and irritation of the nose and airways.

opts.text: Increase the percentage of oxygen delivered
opts.rat: Humidification adds moisture; it does not raise the oxygen concentration.

opts.text: Sterilize the air the client breathes
opts.rat: Humidifiers moisten air; they do not sterilize it.

opts.text: Replace the need for the client to drink fluids
opts.rat: Airway humidity does not substitute for systemic hydration.

steps.q: When assisting the nurse with oral suctioning of secretions, a key safety principle is to:

opts.text: Apply suction only while withdrawing the catheter and keep each suctioning pass brief
opts.rat: Suctioning only on withdrawal and limiting the duration of each pass reduce mucosal trauma and prevent lowering the client's oxygen level.

opts.text: Apply continuous suction for a full minute at a time
opts.rat: Prolonged suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions and traumatizes tissue.

opts.text: Insert the catheter while actively suctioning
opts.rat: Suctioning on insertion damages mucosa; suction is applied on withdrawal.

opts.text: Reuse the same suction catheter between clients without cleaning
opts.rat: This breaks infection-control principles and can transmit organisms.

steps.q: Which set of changes should the technician report to the licensed nurse as possible worsening of a client's breathing?

opts.text: Faster, more labored breathing with restlessness and a lower pulse-oximeter reading
opts.rat: Rising respiratory rate and effort, new restlessness, and a falling SpO2 together suggest deteriorating oxygenation and need prompt reporting.

opts.text: Even breathing, calm behavior, and a stable oxygen reading
opts.rat: These are reassuring, stable findings.

opts.text: The client comfortably reading a book
opts.rat: This indicates the client is not in distress.

opts.text: A respiratory rate of 14 with pink, warm skin
opts.rat: This is within normal limits with good perfusion.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (oxygenation & respiratory care). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Numeric values stated here—normal adult respiratory rate (~12–20/min), low-flow nasal-cannula range (~1–6 L/min), and the general expectation of a normal pulse-oximeter reading—are common reference figures and are marked for faculty confirmation against current facility standards. Oxygen is treated as a prescribed medication administered at the ordered rate/device, consistent with LPT scope; the technician reports changes rather than adjusting flow. Fire-safety (no smoking/open flame, avoid oil-based products near oxygen) and suctioning-on-withdrawal principles are stated at an introductory level. Complements oxygen-safety and pulse-oximetry basics (bnc-core-02) and emergency/choking care (planned BNC-10). No medication doses are asserted. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Emergency Care Basics (BLS, Choking, Seizure, Shock & First Aid) (Set 10)
subtitle: Recognizing an emergency and activating help, responder priorities and scope, choking response, seizure safety, fainting and shock, bleeding and burns, chest-pain and stroke recognition, and basic first-aid principles for the psychiatric technician
scenario: Responding safely to common emergencies within the technician's scope: recognizing the problem, calling for help, protecting the client from harm, and providing basic first aid until licensed help arrives.

steps.q: The technician finds a client collapsed and unresponsive. The FIRST action is to:

opts.text: Check responsiveness and immediately call for help/activate the emergency response
opts.rat: Confirming unresponsiveness and getting help started right away brings the resources and licensed staff needed for a possible arrest.

opts.text: Leave to find the client's chart first
opts.rat: Retrieving the chart delays help; summoning assistance comes first.

opts.text: Give the client food or water
opts.rat: Nothing is given by mouth to an unresponsive person; it risks choking/aspiration.

opts.text: Wait a few minutes to see if the client wakes up
opts.rat: Waiting wastes critical time in a potential emergency.

steps.q: In any emergency, the technician's role is best described as:

opts.text: Recognize the emergency, summon help, provide basic first aid within training, and report—without acting beyond one's scope
opts.rat: The technician recognizes, calls for help, and gives basic first aid they are trained for, while leaving advanced interventions to licensed staff.

opts.text: Independently perform advanced medical procedures
opts.rat: Advanced procedures exceed the technician's scope and are performed by licensed clinicians.

opts.text: Do nothing until a physician personally arrives
opts.rat: Basic life-saving first aid and calling for help should begin immediately.

opts.text: Diagnose the medical condition before acting
opts.rat: Diagnosing is outside scope; the priority is safety, help, and basic first aid.

steps.q: A client is coughing forcefully after food 'went down the wrong way' but can still cough and speak. The technician should:

opts.text: Encourage the client to keep coughing and stay with them, ready to act if the airway becomes blocked
opts.rat: A strong cough means air is still moving; forceful coughing is the most effective way to clear a partial obstruction, so it should be encouraged.

opts.text: Immediately begin abdominal thrusts
opts.rat: Abdominal thrusts are for a complete obstruction (cannot cough, speak, or breathe), not effective coughing.

opts.text: Slap the client hard on the back repeatedly
opts.rat: With effective coughing, interfering can worsen the situation; let the client clear it.

opts.text: Give the client a large drink of water
opts.rat: Fluids can worsen an airway problem and are not the response to coughing on food.

steps.q: A choking client who could not breathe becomes unresponsive and slumps to the floor. The technician should:

opts.text: Call for help/activate emergency response and begin CPR as trained
opts.rat: When a choking victim becomes unresponsive, emergency help is activated and CPR is started per BLS training.

opts.text: Sit the client back up and offer water
opts.rat: An unresponsive client is not given anything by mouth; CPR and help are needed.

opts.text: Do nothing until the choking resolves on its own
opts.rat: An unresponsive choking victim needs immediate action, not waiting.

opts.text: Place the client in a chair and leave to document
opts.rat: Leaving delays life-saving care; help and CPR come first.

steps.q: A client begins having a generalized seizure while standing. The technician's priority is to:

opts.text: Ease the client to the floor and protect them from injury, clearing nearby hazards
opts.rat: Preventing injury—lowering the client and moving hazardous objects away—is the priority during an active seizure.

opts.text: Hold the client's limbs still to stop the movements
opts.rat: Restraining a seizing client can cause injury and does not stop the seizure.

opts.text: Place a padded object between the teeth
opts.rat: Nothing is placed in the mouth; it can break teeth or block the airway.

opts.text: Lift the client into bed immediately
opts.rat: Lifting during a seizure risks injury to client and staff; protect them where they are.

steps.q: During a seizure, the technician should NEVER:

opts.text: Put fingers or objects into the client's mouth
opts.rat: Placing anything in the mouth can cause broken teeth, bites, or airway obstruction and is never done.

opts.text: Note the time the seizure started
opts.rat: Timing the seizure is helpful and appropriate.

opts.text: Move nearby furniture away from the client
opts.rat: Clearing hazards protects the client and is appropriate.

opts.text: Loosen tight clothing around the neck
opts.rat: Loosening restrictive clothing is a safe, helpful action.

steps.q: As a seizure ends and the client is drowsy and confused (postictal), the technician should:

opts.text: Turn the client onto their side, keep the airway clear, stay with them, and allow rest while reorienting
opts.rat: Side-lying helps drain secretions and protect the airway; staying present and reorienting supports the recovering client.

opts.text: Immediately make the client stand and walk
opts.rat: The postictal client is confused and at risk of falling; forcing activity is unsafe.

opts.text: Leave the client alone to 'sleep it off'
opts.rat: The client should be monitored, not left unattended, during recovery.

opts.text: Give a large meal right away
opts.rat: A confused, drowsy client is at aspiration risk; feeding is not the immediate priority.

steps.q: Which seizure situation most clearly requires activating emergency medical help?

opts.text: A seizure that is unusually prolonged, repeats without recovery, or is accompanied by breathing difficulty or injury
opts.rat: Prolonged or repeated seizures, trouble breathing, or injury are red flags requiring emergency response.

opts.text: A brief seizure in a client with a known seizure disorder who recovers as expected
opts.rat: A typical, brief seizure with normal recovery in a known-disorder client is monitored and reported per policy, not necessarily an emergency call.

opts.text: The client feeling tired afterward
opts.rat: Postictal fatigue is expected and not by itself an emergency.

opts.text: The client wanting to rest quietly
opts.rat: Wanting rest after a seizure is normal.

steps.q: A client says they feel dizzy and about to faint. The technician should:

opts.text: Help the client sit or lie down safely to prevent a fall, and stay with them
opts.rat: Getting the client safely down prevents fall injury; staying with them allows monitoring and further help if needed.

opts.text: Tell the client to keep walking to shake it off
opts.rat: Continuing to walk risks a fall if the client faints.

opts.text: Leave to get a snack from another room
opts.rat: The client should not be left alone when at risk of fainting.

opts.text: Have the client stand very still with locked knees
opts.rat: Standing still with locked knees can worsen fainting.

steps.q: Which set of findings suggests a client may be going into shock?

opts.text: Pale, cool, clammy skin; a rapid, weak pulse; and restlessness
opts.rat: Reduced perfusion in shock typically causes pale, cool, clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, and restlessness or altered mental status.

opts.text: Warm, dry, pink skin with a calm, strong pulse
opts.rat: These are signs of good perfusion, not shock.

opts.text: Slow, deep, comfortable breathing at rest
opts.rat: This describes normal breathing, not shock.

opts.text: Rosy cheeks and steady energy
opts.rat: These are reassuring findings, not indicators of shock.

steps.q: While waiting for help for a client showing signs of shock, the technician should:

opts.text: Keep the client lying down and warm, avoid food or drink, and monitor while help is on the way
opts.rat: Lying down, preventing heat loss, and withholding oral intake are safe supportive measures until licensed help arrives.

opts.text: Give the client a large meal to boost energy
opts.rat: Oral intake is withheld; a client in shock may need procedures and is at aspiration risk.

opts.text: Have the client sit upright and walk around
opts.rat: Activity can worsen shock; the client should rest lying down.

opts.text: Leave the client alone to get warm blankets from another building
opts.rat: The client should not be left alone; call for help to bring supplies.

steps.q: A client has heavy bleeding from a cut on the forearm. The technician should first:

opts.text: Apply firm, direct pressure over the wound with a clean cloth or dressing and call for help
opts.rat: Direct pressure is the first and most effective way to control external bleeding while summoning help.

opts.text: Wipe the blood away repeatedly to watch the wound
opts.rat: Repeated wiping disrupts clotting; steady direct pressure is needed.

opts.text: Apply a tight tourniquet as the first step
opts.rat: Direct pressure is the first-line measure; a tourniquet is a last resort for uncontrolled limb hemorrhage.

opts.text: Leave to find antiseptic before doing anything
opts.rat: Controlling bleeding with direct pressure comes before cleaning supplies.

steps.q: Appropriate first aid for a minor thermal burn (small, superficial) is to:

opts.text: Cool the area with cool (not ice-cold) running water and cover loosely with a clean dressing
opts.rat: Cool running water limits tissue damage; a clean, loose covering protects the area. Ice and greasy substances are avoided.

opts.text: Apply butter or oily ointment to the burn
opts.rat: Greasy substances trap heat and increase infection risk; they should not be used.

opts.text: Pack the burn in ice for a long period
opts.rat: Ice can worsen tissue injury; cool (not ice-cold) water is preferred.

opts.text: Break any blisters that form
opts.rat: Blisters are left intact to protect underlying tissue and reduce infection risk.

steps.q: A client has fallen and may have injured the neck or back. The technician should:

opts.text: Avoid moving the client unnecessarily, keep them still, and call for help
opts.rat: If a spinal injury is possible, unnecessary movement can worsen harm; the client is kept still while help is summoned.

opts.text: Quickly sit the client up and move them to a chair
opts.rat: Moving a possible spinal injury can cause further damage.

opts.text: Have the client stand and walk to test for injury
opts.rat: Testing by walking is unsafe with a possible spinal injury.

opts.text: Roll the client repeatedly to inspect the back
opts.rat: Repeated movement risks worsening a spinal injury; assessment is done by licensed staff.

steps.q: A client suddenly reports crushing chest pain and looks pale and sweaty. The technician should:

opts.text: Activate the emergency response, keep the client calm and resting, stay with them, and report immediately
opts.rat: Chest pain with pallor and sweating may signal a heart attack; activating help, keeping the client at rest, and staying present are appropriate immediate actions.

opts.text: Tell the client to walk it off in the hallway
opts.rat: Exertion can worsen a cardiac event; the client should rest while help is summoned.

opts.text: Leave the client alone and check back in an hour
opts.rat: Delaying and leaving a client with possible cardiac symptoms is dangerous.

opts.text: Independently give a heart medication from the cart
opts.rat: Administering medication in this situation is outside scope; report and get licensed help.

steps.q: The technician notices a client with a sudden facial droop, one-sided arm weakness, and slurred speech. These are warning signs of a possible stroke, so the technician should:

opts.text: Recognize the signs and get emergency help immediately, noting the time symptoms began
opts.rat: Facial droop, arm weakness, and speech difficulty are classic stroke warning signs; fast recognition and activating help—along with noting symptom-onset time—are critical.

opts.text: Assume the client is just tired and wait until morning
opts.rat: Delaying care for stroke signs can lead to serious, permanent harm.

opts.text: Give the client a large drink to help the speech
opts.rat: Oral intake risks aspiration in possible stroke; getting help is the priority.

opts.text: Have the client exercise the weak arm vigorously
opts.rat: Exercise does not address a stroke; emergency evaluation is needed.

steps.q: Appropriate first aid for a client with a nosebleed (no injury suspected) is to have the client:

opts.text: Sit up and lean slightly forward while pinching the soft part of the nose
opts.rat: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat, and pinching the soft part of the nose applies pressure to stop the bleeding.

opts.text: Tilt the head far back and swallow the blood
opts.rat: Tilting back lets blood drain into the throat, which can cause choking or nausea.

opts.text: Lie flat on the back
opts.rat: Lying flat also allows blood to flow into the throat.

opts.text: Blow the nose forcefully to clear it
opts.rat: Forceful blowing can restart or worsen the bleeding.

steps.q: If a client is known or suspected to have swallowed a poison or overdosed, the technician should:

opts.text: Get help immediately and follow facility policy/poison-control guidance; do not make the client vomit unless directed
opts.rat: Rapid help and expert guidance (facility policy/poison control) direct safe care; inducing vomiting can be harmful and is only done if specifically directed.

opts.text: Automatically make the client vomit right away
opts.rat: Inducing vomiting can cause additional harm and is not done unless directed by proper guidance.

opts.text: Wait and watch for several hours before telling anyone
opts.rat: Delaying reporting a possible poisoning is dangerous.

opts.text: Give the client a large meal to dilute the poison
opts.rat: Giving food/fluids without guidance can be harmful; follow expert direction.

steps.q: Before approaching any emergency scene, the technician should FIRST make sure that:

opts.text: The scene is safe for the responder and the client
opts.rat: Ensuring scene safety first prevents the responder from becoming a second victim and protects the client from further harm.

opts.text: All paperwork is completed
opts.rat: Documentation follows the response; safety comes first.

opts.text: A supervisor has given written permission
opts.rat: Emergencies require immediate action; safety and help cannot wait for written permission.

opts.text: The client's family has been billed
opts.rat: Billing is irrelevant to the immediate emergency response.

steps.q: After any emergency response, an important responsibility of the technician is to:

opts.text: Accurately report and document what happened and the actions taken
opts.rat: Clear, accurate reporting and documentation ensure continuity of care and an accurate record of the event and interventions.

opts.text: Avoid telling anyone to keep the record simple
opts.rat: Concealing or omitting events is unsafe and improper; accurate reporting is required.

opts.text: Change the facts to make the response look smoother
opts.rat: Falsifying records is unethical and illegal.

opts.text: Document only if the outcome was good
opts.rat: All emergencies are documented regardless of outcome.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (emergency care & first aid). Written from standard psychiatric-technician, nursing, and basic first-aid references at an introductory level. General first-aid principles are stated conceptually: activate emergency help early, ensure scene safety, control external bleeding with direct pressure, protect (do not restrain) a seizing client and never place objects in the mouth, position a postictal client on the side, cool minor burns with cool running water, lean forward for a nosebleed, and follow poison-control/facility guidance for ingestions. Specific CPR/BLS parameters (compression rate/depth, breath ratios) are intentionally NOT asserted and follow the technician's current BLS certification; choking-response mechanics complement bnc-core-02 and choking prevention in bnc-core-05. Recognition items for possible heart attack and stroke are introductory and marked for faculty confirmation. No numeric values are asserted. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Diabetes Care Basics (Glucose Monitoring, Insulin & Hypo/Hyperglycemia) (Set 11)
subtitle: Recognizing and responding to hypoglycemia vs hyperglycemia, the rule of 15, blood-glucose monitoring technique, insulin as a high-alert medication (storage, site rotation, rapid vs long-acting concept), diet and activity effects, diabetic foot care, and when to report
scenario: Supporting clients with diabetes: monitoring blood glucose, recognizing and responding to low and high blood sugar, handling insulin safely within scope, and reinforcing diet, activity, and foot-care basics while knowing what to report.

steps.q: Diabetes mellitus is best described as a condition in which:

opts.text: The body cannot properly produce or use insulin, leading to high blood glucose
opts.rat: In diabetes, insufficient insulin or the body's poor use of it leaves glucose elevated in the blood.

opts.text: Blood glucose is always dangerously low
opts.rat: Diabetes is characterized by high blood glucose; lows occur mainly as a treatment complication.

opts.text: The body makes too much insulin on purpose
opts.rat: The core problem is inadequate insulin production or action, not intentional excess.

opts.text: Glucose is completely absent from the blood
opts.rat: Glucose is present—typically elevated—not absent.

steps.q: Which set of signs is most typical of HYPOglycemia (low blood glucose)?

opts.text: Shakiness, sweating, rapid heartbeat, hunger, and confusion coming on quickly
opts.rat: Low blood glucose triggers rapid adrenergic and neurologic signs—shakiness, sweating, palpitations, hunger, and confusion.

opts.text: Gradual increased thirst and frequent urination over hours
opts.rat: Increased thirst and urination developing gradually point to hyperglycemia.

opts.text: Slowly worsening blurred vision over days
opts.rat: A gradual course fits high, not low, blood glucose.

opts.text: No symptoms at all, ever
opts.rat: Hypoglycemia usually produces noticeable, rapid symptoms.

steps.q: Which set of signs is most typical of HYPERglycemia (high blood glucose)?

opts.text: Increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurred vision developing gradually
opts.rat: High blood glucose classically causes increased thirst, urination, fatigue, and blurred vision, usually developing more gradually than hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Sudden shakiness, sweating, and rapid confusion
opts.rat: These rapid adrenergic signs point to hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Immediate loss of consciousness within seconds
opts.rat: This is not the typical presentation of gradual hyperglycemia.

opts.text: Cold, clammy skin with intense hunger
opts.rat: Cold, clammy skin with hunger is more consistent with hypoglycemia.

steps.q: Compared with hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia is important to treat promptly because it:

opts.text: Comes on rapidly and can quickly become a dangerous emergency
opts.rat: Low blood glucose can worsen within minutes to loss of consciousness or seizure, so it needs quick treatment.

opts.text: Always develops slowly over several days
opts.rat: A slow course describes hyperglycemia; hypoglycemia is rapid.

opts.text: Is never a safety concern
opts.rat: Hypoglycemia is a serious safety concern requiring prompt action.

opts.text: Can safely be ignored until the next scheduled meal
opts.rat: Waiting can allow hypoglycemia to become life-threatening.

steps.q: A conscious client who can swallow shows signs of hypoglycemia. Following the commonly taught 'rule of 15,' the technician should give:

opts.text: About 15 grams of a fast-acting carbohydrate (such as juice or glucose tablets), then recheck in about 15 minutes
opts.rat: The rule of 15 gives roughly 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and rechecks in about 15 minutes, repeating if still low—per facility parameters.

opts.text: A high-fat food such as cheese or peanut butter first
opts.rat: Fat slows glucose absorption; a fast-acting carbohydrate is needed first for a low.

opts.text: Nothing, and simply wait for it to pass
opts.rat: Untreated hypoglycemia can worsen quickly; a fast-acting carbohydrate is given.

opts.text: A dose of insulin to balance things out
opts.rat: Insulin would lower glucose further and is dangerous during hypoglycemia.

steps.q: After treating a low with a fast-acting carbohydrate and the recheck shows the glucose has recovered, a helpful next step (per facility policy) is to:

opts.text: Provide a longer-acting snack or the next meal to help keep the glucose stable
opts.rat: Following recovery with a snack or meal containing protein/complex carbohydrate helps prevent the glucose from dropping again.

opts.text: Give another large dose of fast-acting sugar anyway
opts.rat: Once recovered, more fast sugar risks overshooting; a sustaining snack/meal is appropriate.

opts.text: Have the client skip the next meal
opts.rat: Skipping the meal could cause the glucose to fall again.

opts.text: Encourage vigorous exercise right away
opts.rat: Exercise can further lower glucose and is not appropriate immediately after a low.

steps.q: A client with diabetes is found unresponsive and cannot swallow. The technician should:

opts.text: Give nothing by mouth, call for help/activate emergency response immediately
opts.rat: An unresponsive client cannot safely swallow; oral glucose would cause choking, so emergency help is summoned (glucagon or IV treatment is given by licensed staff).

opts.text: Pour juice into the client's mouth to raise the sugar
opts.rat: Giving oral fluids to an unresponsive client risks aspiration and choking.

opts.text: Wait to see if the client wakes up on their own
opts.rat: This is an emergency; help must be summoned right away.

opts.text: Administer insulin to be safe
opts.rat: Insulin would be dangerous and is never given for a suspected low.

steps.q: When obtaining a capillary blood glucose sample, a good technique is to:

opts.text: Clean the site, use the side of the fingertip, and obtain an adequate drop of blood
opts.rat: Cleaning the site, lancing the less-sensitive side of the fingertip, and getting an adequate drop yield a reliable, less painful sample.

opts.text: Squeeze the fingertip very hard to force out blood
opts.rat: Excessive squeezing can dilute the sample with tissue fluid and cause inaccurate results.

opts.text: Reuse the same lancet on several clients
opts.rat: Lancets are single-use per client; reuse violates infection control.

opts.text: Use the very center pad of the fingertip every time
opts.rat: The central pad is more sensitive; the side of the fingertip is preferred.

steps.q: Blood glucose checks and insulin are typically scheduled:

opts.text: According to the provider's orders, often around meals and bedtime
opts.rat: Monitoring and insulin timing follow the individualized order, frequently coordinated with meals and bedtime.

opts.text: Whenever the technician happens to have time
opts.rat: Timing follows the order, not staff convenience, because it is coordinated with food and insulin action.

opts.text: Only once a week regardless of the order
opts.rat: Frequency is set by the order and the client's needs, not an arbitrary weekly schedule.

opts.text: Only when the client feels unwell
opts.rat: Scheduled monitoring occurs per order, not solely when symptoms appear.

steps.q: Insulin is considered a 'high-alert' medication. This means the technician should:

opts.text: Handle and administer it only as ordered and within scope, verifying carefully because errors can cause serious harm
opts.rat: High-alert drugs like insulin carry a high risk of serious harm if given incorrectly, so careful verification and adherence to the order and scope are essential.

opts.text: Give extra doses freely if the client seems high
opts.rat: Insulin is given only as ordered; independent extra dosing is dangerous.

opts.text: Treat it casually like any low-risk product
opts.rat: Insulin requires heightened caution, not casual handling.

opts.text: Share one client's insulin pen among several clients
opts.rat: Insulin pens/supplies are single-client; sharing is unsafe and prohibited.

steps.q: Rotating insulin injection sites is important mainly to:

opts.text: Prevent tissue changes (such as lipohypertrophy) that can affect insulin absorption
opts.rat: Repeated injections in one spot cause fatty lumps or tissue changes that impair absorption; rotating sites keeps absorption consistent.

opts.text: Make the injection hurt more each time
opts.rat: Rotation is for tissue health and absorption, not to increase pain.

opts.text: Allow the client to skip cleaning the skin
opts.rat: Site rotation does not replace proper skin preparation.

opts.text: Let staff use a larger needle
opts.rat: Needle size is unrelated to the purpose of site rotation.

steps.q: Which statement about types of insulin is most accurate at a basic level?

opts.text: Rapid-acting insulin works quickly and is timed with food, while long-acting insulin provides a steadier baseline effect
opts.rat: Rapid-acting insulin covers meals and acts quickly; long-acting insulin gives a more even, background effect over a longer period.

opts.text: All insulins act at exactly the same speed
opts.rat: Insulins differ in onset, peak, and duration; they are not all the same.

opts.text: Long-acting insulin is meant to fix a sudden low
opts.rat: A sudden low is treated with fast-acting carbohydrate, not long-acting insulin.

opts.text: Rapid-acting insulin should be given long before any food is available
opts.rat: Rapid-acting insulin is timed closely with food to avoid causing a low.

steps.q: Regarding insulin storage, a generally correct practice is to:

opts.text: Keep spare insulin refrigerated and protect it from freezing and extreme heat, following the manufacturer's guidance
opts.rat: Insulin is kept cool but not frozen; extreme temperatures degrade it. In-use handling follows manufacturer and facility guidance.

opts.text: Store all insulin in the freezer
opts.rat: Freezing damages insulin and it should not be used if frozen.

opts.text: Leave insulin in a hot car or sunny windowsill
opts.rat: Extreme heat and direct sun degrade insulin.

opts.text: Use insulin that looks abnormally clumped or discolored
opts.rat: Insulin that looks abnormal should not be used; it may be degraded.

steps.q: A client received their insulin but then refuses to eat the meal. The technician should recognize that this:

opts.text: Increases the risk of hypoglycemia, so the technician should monitor closely and report promptly
opts.rat: Insulin given without the expected food can drop the glucose too low; close monitoring and prompt reporting allow timely action.

opts.text: Has no effect on blood glucose
opts.rat: Insulin without food commonly leads to hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Means the client should get more insulin
opts.rat: More insulin would worsen the risk of a low.

opts.text: Should simply be ignored
opts.rat: This is a setup for hypoglycemia and must be monitored and reported.

steps.q: Physical activity or exercise in a client taking insulin generally:

opts.text: Can lower blood glucose, so the technician should watch for signs of hypoglycemia
opts.rat: Exercise increases glucose use and can cause a low, so monitoring for hypoglycemia around activity is important.

opts.text: Always raises blood glucose to dangerous highs
opts.rat: Activity typically lowers, not raises, blood glucose.

opts.text: Has no relationship to blood glucose
opts.rat: Exercise clearly affects glucose levels.

opts.text: Eliminates the need for any monitoring
opts.rat: Activity increases the need for monitoring because of hypoglycemia risk.

steps.q: Reinforcing diabetic foot care, the technician teaches the client to:

opts.text: Inspect the feet daily, wear proper footwear, and report any sores or breaks in the skin promptly
opts.rat: Reduced sensation and slower healing in diabetes make daily foot inspection, good footwear, and early reporting of sores essential to prevent serious complications.

opts.text: Walk barefoot often to toughen the feet
opts.rat: Going barefoot risks unnoticed injuries, which are dangerous in diabetes.

opts.text: Ignore small sores since they always heal fast
opts.rat: Diabetic wounds heal slowly and can worsen; sores are reported promptly.

opts.text: Soak the feet in very hot water daily
opts.rat: Reduced sensation makes hot water a burn risk; this is unsafe.

steps.q: Coordinating meals for a client on insulin is important because:

opts.text: Food intake and insulin need to be balanced so the glucose does not go too high or too low
opts.rat: Insulin lowers glucose, and food raises it; timing and consistency help keep the client's glucose in a safe range.

opts.text: Meal timing has no effect when insulin is used
opts.rat: Meal timing is closely tied to insulin action and glucose control.

opts.text: The client should eat as little as possible after insulin
opts.rat: Skimping on food after insulin risks hypoglycemia; balanced intake is the goal.

opts.text: Only the type of food matters, never the timing
opts.rat: Both type and timing of food matter with insulin.

steps.q: Which blood-glucose situation should the technician report to the nurse promptly?

opts.text: A reading that is very high or very low, or any change in the client's level of consciousness
opts.rat: Extremes of glucose and any change in alertness signal potential emergencies that require prompt reporting and licensed evaluation.

opts.text: A reading that is within the client's ordered target range
opts.rat: An in-target reading is expected and not an urgent report.

opts.text: The client eating a normal, balanced meal
opts.rat: A normal meal is routine, not a concern to report.

opts.text: The client feeling well and alert
opts.rat: Feeling well and alert is reassuring, not a red flag.

steps.q: Untreated, significantly high blood glucose over time can:

opts.text: Lead to serious complications, so persistent highs and related symptoms should be reported
opts.rat: Sustained hyperglycemia can progress to serious acute and long-term complications, so persistent highs and symptoms are reported for evaluation.

opts.text: Always resolve on its own with no risk
opts.rat: Persistent hyperglycemia carries real risks and should not be assumed to self-resolve.

opts.text: Improve the client's health
opts.rat: High glucose harms health; it does not improve it.

opts.text: Be safely ignored indefinitely
opts.rat: Ignoring persistent highs is dangerous; they are reported.

steps.q: A client on insulin suddenly becomes shaky, sweaty, and confused, and can still swallow safely. A glucometer is not immediately at hand. The safest action is to:

opts.text: Treat for hypoglycemia by giving a fast-acting carbohydrate and get help/check glucose, since a rapid low is the immediate danger
opts.rat: These are classic hypoglycemia signs; because a low can become life-threatening within minutes, giving fast-acting carbohydrate to a client who can swallow while summoning help and checking glucose is the safest response.

opts.text: Give insulin in case the glucose is high
opts.rat: The picture strongly suggests a low; insulin could be fatal.

opts.text: Do nothing until a reading is available, no matter how long that takes
opts.rat: Delaying treatment of a likely severe low is dangerous; treat and get help while arranging a check.

opts.text: Have the client lie down and withhold all food and fluids
opts.rat: A conscious client with hypoglycemia signs who can swallow needs fast-acting carbohydrate, not withholding.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (diabetes care basics). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Recognition of hypoglycemia vs hyperglycemia, the rapid/emergent nature of lows, the commonly taught 'rule of 15' (~15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in ~15 minutes), no-oral-intake for an unresponsive client, capillary blood-glucose technique, insulin as a high-alert medication (storage, single-client use, site rotation, rapid- vs long-acting concept), diet/activity effects, and diabetic foot care are stated at an introductory level and marked for faculty confirmation against current standards. Specific glucose target/threshold numbers and insulin onset/peak/duration times are intentionally NOT asserted (they follow provider orders, facility parameters, and product labeling). Insulin administration is performed only as ordered and within the technician's scope. Builds on the hypoglycemia-recognition item in bnc-core-02. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Fluid & Electrolyte Basics and IV Observation (Set 12)
subtitle: Fluid balance and overload, daily weights and accurate I&O, at-risk clients, electrolyte function and imbalance warning signs, and observing an IV site safely within scope (recognizing problems, reporting, never adjusting the rate)
scenario: Helping keep clients in safe fluid and electrolyte balance: monitoring intake/output and weight, recognizing dehydration, fluid overload, and electrolyte-imbalance warning signs, and observing an IV site while leaving IV therapy to licensed staff.

steps.q: Why is fluid balance important to monitor?

opts.text: Both too little fluid (dehydration) and too much fluid (overload) can harm the body and must be recognized
opts.rat: The body works best in balance; monitoring catches both dehydration and fluid overload, each of which is dangerous.

opts.text: Only dehydration is ever a problem
opts.rat: Fluid overload is also harmful; both extremes matter.

opts.text: Only fluid overload is ever a problem
opts.rat: Dehydration is equally important to recognize.

opts.text: Fluid balance has no effect on health
opts.rat: Fluid balance is essential to circulation, organ function, and safety.

steps.q: Which findings suggest possible FLUID OVERLOAD?

opts.text: Swelling (edema), sudden weight gain, puffiness, and shortness of breath
opts.rat: Excess fluid collects in tissues and the lungs, producing edema, rapid weight gain, and breathing difficulty.

opts.text: Dry mouth, sunken eyes, and very dark urine
opts.rat: These point to dehydration, not overload.

opts.text: Strong thirst with poor skin turgor
opts.rat: Thirst and poor turgor suggest dehydration.

opts.text: Weight loss with concentrated urine
opts.rat: Weight loss and concentrated urine suggest fluid deficit, not overload.

steps.q: Daily weights are a valuable way to track fluid status because:

opts.text: A rapid change in weight often reflects a change in body fluid, so weights are taken consistently (same time, scale, and clothing)
opts.rat: Short-term weight changes largely reflect fluid gain or loss; consistent technique makes the trend reliable.

opts.text: Weight has nothing to do with fluid balance
opts.rat: Rapid weight changes are closely tied to fluid shifts.

opts.text: Weighing at random times gives the best data
opts.rat: Inconsistent timing/technique makes the trend unreliable.

opts.text: Only monthly weights matter for fluid status
opts.rat: Fluid changes can occur quickly, so daily weights are used when monitoring fluid status.

steps.q: When keeping intake and output (I&O) records, the technician should:

opts.text: Measure and record all intake and output accurately rather than estimating
opts.rat: Accurate measurement makes I&O useful for detecting fluid imbalance; guessing undermines its value.

opts.text: Estimate the amounts to save time
opts.rat: Estimating reduces accuracy and can mask a developing imbalance.

opts.text: Record only what the client drinks, never output
opts.rat: Both intake and output must be recorded for a complete picture.

opts.text: Record intake only at the end of the week
opts.rat: I&O is recorded in real time so trends are accurate and timely.

steps.q: Which client is at the GREATEST risk for a fluid or electrolyte imbalance?

opts.text: An older adult with vomiting and diarrhea who depends on others to bring fluids
opts.rat: Fluid losses from vomiting/diarrhea plus limited ability to obtain fluids and age-related factors greatly increase imbalance risk.

opts.text: A healthy adult drinking normally
opts.rat: Normal intake and no losses make imbalance unlikely.

opts.text: A client eating and drinking well with no losses
opts.rat: Good intake without losses is low risk.

opts.text: A client with stable weight and normal output
opts.rat: Stable weight and output suggest balance, not risk.

steps.q: A client has had several episodes of vomiting and diarrhea. The technician should recognize that this can cause loss of:

opts.text: Both fluids and electrolytes, so the client should be monitored and the losses reported
opts.rat: Vomiting and diarrhea remove water and electrolytes; monitoring and reporting allow timely correction and prevent complications.

opts.text: Nothing of importance to the body
opts.rat: These losses can quickly cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

opts.text: Only calories, not fluids
opts.rat: Significant fluid and electrolyte loss occurs, not just calories.

opts.text: Only fat stores
opts.rat: The concern is fluid and electrolyte loss, not fat.

steps.q: Electrolytes (such as sodium and potassium) are important because they:

opts.text: Help the heart, muscles, and nerves function properly
opts.rat: Electrolytes are essential minerals that support normal heart rhythm, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling.

opts.text: Have no role in body function
opts.rat: Electrolytes are vital to many body processes.

opts.text: Only affect the color of the skin
opts.rat: Their role is far broader—heart, muscle, and nerve function.

opts.text: Are only important during exercise
opts.rat: Electrolyte balance matters at all times, not only during exercise.

steps.q: Why is a significant potassium imbalance particularly concerning?

opts.text: It can affect the heart's rhythm, so related symptoms should be reported promptly
opts.rat: Potassium strongly influences cardiac rhythm; imbalances can cause dangerous arrhythmias, making prompt reporting important.

opts.text: It only changes the taste of food
opts.rat: Potassium's key concern is its effect on the heart and muscles, not taste.

opts.text: It has no effect on the body
opts.rat: Potassium is critical to heart and muscle function.

opts.text: It only matters in children
opts.rat: Potassium balance matters across all ages.

steps.q: Which findings could signal an electrolyte imbalance the technician should report?

opts.text: New muscle weakness or cramps, confusion, an irregular pulse, or a change in alertness
opts.rat: Electrolyte imbalances commonly affect muscles, nerves, and the heart, producing weakness/cramps, confusion, irregular pulse, or altered alertness.

opts.text: Normal strength, clear thinking, and a regular pulse
opts.rat: These are reassuring, normal findings.

opts.text: A calm client resting comfortably
opts.rat: This is not a warning sign.

opts.text: Steady mood and usual activity level
opts.rat: Baseline stability is not a concern to report.

steps.q: When the technician notices possible signs of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance, the appropriate action is to:

opts.text: Recognize the signs and report them to the nurse for evaluation
opts.rat: The technician observes and reports; evaluating and treating imbalances is done by licensed staff.

opts.text: Diagnose the specific imbalance and start treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosing and treating are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Give the client extra electrolyte pills independently
opts.rat: Administering supplements without an order is outside scope and unsafe.

opts.text: Ignore the signs unless the client complains loudly
opts.rat: Signs are reported when noticed, not only when the client complains.

steps.q: Regarding a client's IV (intravenous) therapy, the psychiatric technician's role is generally to:

opts.text: Observe the IV site and the client and report concerns—not to start the IV, regulate the rate, or give IV medications
opts.rat: Within scope, the technician monitors and reports; starting, adjusting, and medicating IVs are done by licensed staff.

opts.text: Independently start and program the IV pump
opts.rat: Starting and programming IV therapy is outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Adjust the IV flow rate as they see fit
opts.rat: Only licensed staff set/adjust the IV rate per order.

opts.text: Push medications into the IV line
opts.rat: Administering IV medications is outside the technician's scope.

steps.q: While observing an IV site, which finding should the technician report as a possible problem?

opts.text: Redness, swelling, warmth or coolness, pain, or fluid leaking around the site
opts.rat: These can indicate infiltration, phlebitis, or infection at the IV site and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: A clean, dry site with no redness or swelling
opts.rat: A normal-looking site is not a concern.

opts.text: The client resting comfortably with no complaints
opts.rat: No complaints and comfort are reassuring, not a problem.

opts.text: Intact, well-secured tubing
opts.rat: Properly secured tubing is expected, not a concern.

steps.q: A client says the IV site is burning and painful. The technician should:

opts.text: Notify the nurse promptly and not adjust the IV themselves
opts.rat: Pain/burning may signal a site problem; the technician reports it right away and leaves any IV adjustment to licensed staff.

opts.text: Speed up the IV to flush the discomfort away
opts.rat: Changing the IV rate is outside scope and could worsen harm.

opts.text: Ignore it since IVs are 'supposed to' hurt
opts.rat: Burning pain is not normal and should be reported.

opts.text: Remove the IV independently
opts.rat: Discontinuing an IV is done by licensed staff, not the technician, and it should first be reported.

steps.q: To help keep a client's IV functioning safely, the technician can:

opts.text: Keep the site dry, avoid kinks in the tubing, and prevent the client from pulling on the line
opts.rat: These simple protective measures help maintain the IV without adjusting the therapy itself.

opts.text: Let the tubing kink under the client's body
