opts.rat: Kinked tubing interrupts flow and should be avoided.

opts.text: Encourage the client to tug on the line for comfort
opts.rat: Pulling on the line can dislodge the IV and cause injury.

opts.text: Soak the IV dressing during bathing
opts.rat: Keeping the site dry helps prevent infection and dressing failure.

steps.q: Which IV-related situation should the technician report to the nurse?

opts.text: The IV pump is alarming, the bag is empty, the drip has stopped, or the line has become disconnected
opts.rat: These indicate the IV needs attention from licensed staff and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: The IV is running as ordered with a comfortable client
opts.rat: Normal function with a comfortable client is not a concern.

opts.text: The dressing is clean, dry, and intact
opts.rat: An intact dressing is expected, not a problem.

opts.text: The client is resting quietly
opts.rat: Restful comfort is not a reportable IV problem.

steps.q: When helping a client with an IV move or transfer, the technician should:

opts.text: Protect the site and tubing so the IV is not pulled or dislodged
opts.rat: Supporting the arm and managing the tubing during movement prevents dislodging the IV and causing injury.

opts.text: Let the tubing catch on the bed rails during the transfer
opts.rat: Snagging the tubing can dislodge the IV; it should be managed carefully.

opts.text: Pull the client by the IV arm
opts.rat: Pulling on the IV arm risks dislodging the line and injuring the client.

opts.text: Disconnect the IV to make moving easier
opts.rat: Disconnecting the IV is outside scope and risks contamination and interruption of therapy.

steps.q: Regarding oral fluids, the technician should:

opts.text: Encourage or restrict fluids according to the client's care plan and orders
opts.rat: Some clients need encouragement to drink while others are on fluid restriction; the technician follows the individualized order.

opts.text: Always push maximum fluids on every client
opts.rat: Some clients are on fluid restriction; more is not always better.

opts.text: Always restrict fluids for every client
opts.rat: Many clients need adequate or increased intake; restriction is order-specific.

opts.text: Ignore the care plan and let the client decide entirely
opts.rat: Intake is guided by the care plan, especially when a restriction or goal exists.

steps.q: A client on daily weights has a notable weight gain since yesterday. The technician should:

opts.text: Report the change to the nurse, since a rapid gain may indicate fluid retention
opts.rat: A sudden weight increase can reflect fluid retention/overload and should be reported for evaluation.

opts.text: Assume the scale is wrong and ignore it
opts.rat: Rather than dismissing it, the technician verifies technique and reports the change.

opts.text: Restrict the client's food to reverse the gain
opts.rat: Restricting food is not the response; the change is reported for evaluation.

opts.text: Wait a week before mentioning it
opts.rat: A rapid change is reported promptly, not after a week.

steps.q: A client with dehydration signs who is allowed oral fluids would benefit MOST from the technician:

opts.text: Offering fluids frequently within the care plan and monitoring intake and output
opts.rat: Regularly offering permitted fluids and tracking I&O supports rehydration and detects whether balance is improving.

opts.text: Withholding fluids until the next meal
opts.rat: Withholding fluids worsens dehydration.

opts.text: Waiting for the client to ask before offering anything
opts.rat: At-risk clients may not ask; the technician offers fluids proactively within the plan.

opts.text: Giving only dry foods
opts.rat: Dry foods do not address the fluid deficit.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in fluid, electrolyte, and IV care is to:

opts.text: Monitor I&O and weights, recognize dehydration/overload/imbalance signs, observe the IV site, and report—leaving IV therapy management to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician's contributions are monitoring, recognition, observation, and reporting; managing IV therapy is done by licensed staff.

opts.text: Independently manage all IV therapy and fluid orders
opts.rat: Managing IV therapy and writing fluid orders are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Diagnose and treat electrolyte imbalances
opts.rat: Diagnosis and treatment are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Ignore fluid status since it is not important
opts.rat: Fluid and electrolyte status is important and is actively monitored and reported.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (fluid and electrolyte basics and IV observation). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Fluid balance/overload signs, daily-weight and accurate-I&O monitoring, at-risk clients, the general role of electrolytes (heart/muscle/nerve function), potassium's effect on cardiac rhythm, and warning signs of imbalance are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation. Specific electrolyte reference values and IV flow rates/calculations are intentionally NOT asserted. IV content reflects the technician's scope: observe the site and client and report problems (redness/swelling/pain/leaking, pump alarms, empty bag, disconnection), while starting, regulating, medicating, or discontinuing IV therapy is performed by licensed staff. Builds on dehydration/I&O items in bnc-core-02/06 and fluid-encouragement/low-sodium items in bnc-core-05. Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Specimen Collection & Diagnostic Prep (Set 13)
subtitle: Correct client identification and specimen labeling, clean-catch/midstream urine, 24-hour urine, stool and sputum collection technique, safe handling and timing, culture-before-antibiotics, requisition matching, documentation, and preparing clients for diagnostic tests and procedures
scenario: Collecting specimens accurately and safely and preparing clients for diagnostic tests: verifying identity, using correct technique for each specimen type, handling and labeling properly, and supporting test preparation within the technician's scope.

steps.q: Before collecting any specimen, the technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Verify the client's identity using two identifiers
opts.rat: Confirming identity with two identifiers ensures the specimen is collected from and labeled for the correct client, preventing dangerous mix-ups.

opts.text: Label the container after the client has left
opts.rat: Specimens are labeled at the bedside for the correct client, not later from memory.

opts.text: Collect first and identify the client afterward
opts.rat: Identity must be confirmed before collection to avoid errors.

opts.text: Skip identification if the unit is familiar
opts.rat: Identity is always verified, regardless of familiarity.

steps.q: Specimen containers should be labeled:

opts.text: Accurately at the bedside, matching the client and the requisition, before leaving the room
opts.rat: Labeling at the bedside against the client and order prevents mislabeling, a serious safety error.

opts.text: Later at the nurses' station from memory
opts.rat: Labeling away from the bedside risks mix-ups; it is done at the point of collection.

opts.text: Only if the lab requests it
opts.rat: All specimens are labeled correctly as a standard safety practice.

opts.text: With just the room number
opts.rat: Proper labeling uses client identifiers, not only a room number.

steps.q: A clean-catch (midstream) urine specimen is collected by having the client:

opts.text: Clean the area, begin voiding, then catch urine midstream in a sterile container
opts.rat: Cleaning first and catching the middle of the stream reduces contamination and yields a more accurate result.

opts.text: Collect the very first drops of urine without cleaning
opts.rat: The first stream and an uncleaned area increase contamination; midstream after cleaning is preferred.

opts.text: Urinate into the toilet and scoop from the bowl
opts.rat: Toilet water contaminates the specimen; a sterile container is used.

opts.text: Use any nearby cup without cleaning
opts.rat: A clean-catch requires cleaning and a sterile container to limit contamination.

steps.q: For a 24-hour urine collection, the technician should:

opts.text: Discard the first void to start timing, then collect all urine for 24 hours—including the final void—storing per policy
opts.rat: The collection begins with an empty bladder (first void discarded) and captures all urine over the full period, ending with a final void, kept per storage requirements.

opts.text: Save the first void and stop collecting after one or two samples
opts.rat: The first void is discarded to mark the start, and all urine for the full 24 hours is collected.

opts.text: Collect only urine that appears abnormal
opts.rat: All urine over 24 hours is collected, not selectively.

opts.text: Leave the container at room temperature and open to air regardless of policy
opts.rat: Storage (often refrigerated/on ice) follows policy; ignoring it can invalidate the test.

steps.q: If any urine is accidentally discarded during a 24-hour collection, the technician should:

opts.text: Report it, because a missed sample can invalidate the test and it may need to restart
opts.rat: Completeness is essential; a missed void compromises accuracy, so it is reported and the collection may be restarted per policy.

opts.text: Say nothing and send the incomplete collection
opts.rat: An incomplete collection gives inaccurate results; it must be reported.

opts.text: Add extra water to make up the volume
opts.rat: Adding water falsifies the specimen and is never done.

opts.text: Guess how much was lost and note it
opts.rat: Guessing does not fix a compromised collection; report it.

steps.q: When collecting a stool specimen, the technician should ensure the sample is NOT contaminated with:

opts.text: Urine, toilet water, or toilet paper
opts.rat: Contamination with urine, toilet water, or paper can affect stool test results, so the sample is collected to avoid them.

opts.text: The correct labeling
opts.rat: Proper labeling is required, not something to avoid.

opts.text: A clean collection container
opts.rat: A clean container is used; it is not a contaminant.

opts.text: The client's identification
opts.rat: Client identification is necessary, not a contaminant.

steps.q: A sputum specimen for the lab is best obtained by having the client:

opts.text: Take deep breaths and cough deeply to bring up secretions from the lungs, ideally in the early morning
opts.rat: A deep cough produces true lower-airway sputum rather than saliva, and early-morning samples tend to be more concentrated.

opts.text: Spit ordinary saliva into the cup
opts.rat: Saliva is not sputum; a deep cough is needed for a valid specimen.

opts.text: Provide the sample right after brushing with mouthwash mid-day
opts.rat: Timing and technique matter; a deep morning cough is preferred, and saliva/mouthwash residue is not the target.

opts.text: Clear the throat lightly without coughing
opts.rat: Throat clearing yields saliva, not deep-airway sputum.

steps.q: After a specimen is collected, it should generally be:

opts.text: Sent to the lab promptly or stored as required, not left sitting out
opts.rat: Timely transport or correct storage preserves specimen integrity; delays and improper storage can alter results.

opts.text: Left on the counter for several hours
opts.rat: Leaving specimens out can degrade them and invalidate results.

opts.text: Kept in the client's room overnight
opts.rat: Specimens are transported or stored properly, not kept casually in the room.

opts.text: Discarded and recollected only if the lab complains
opts.rat: Proper handling is done from the start, not after a complaint.

steps.q: When handling any specimen, the technician should use:

opts.text: Standard precautions—gloves, hand hygiene, and a properly closed container
opts.rat: Body-fluid specimens are treated as potentially infectious; standard precautions and secure containment protect staff and others.

opts.text: Bare hands to feel the specimen's temperature
opts.rat: Touching specimens without gloves risks exposure to infectious material.

opts.text: An open, uncovered cup for transport
opts.rat: Specimens are transported in closed containers to prevent spills and exposure.

opts.text: No precautions if the client 'looks healthy'
opts.rat: Standard precautions apply to all specimens regardless of appearance.

steps.q: For a culture specimen (to identify infection), a general principle is that it is best obtained:

opts.text: Using clean/sterile technique and, when possible, before antibiotics are started
opts.rat: Sterile technique prevents contamination, and collecting before antibiotics improves the chance of identifying the organism.

opts.text: After several days of antibiotics for best results
opts.rat: Antibiotics can suppress the organism, making it harder to identify; culture is ideally obtained before starting them.

opts.text: With deliberately contaminated technique
opts.rat: Contamination invalidates a culture; sterile technique is used.

opts.text: Only from a different client for comparison
opts.rat: The specimen must come from the correct client being evaluated.

steps.q: The requisition (test order) that accompanies a specimen should:

opts.text: Match the specimen and the client so the correct test is performed on the right sample
opts.rat: Matching the requisition to the labeled specimen and client ensures the intended test is run on the right sample.

opts.text: Be for any client to save paperwork
opts.rat: The requisition must correspond to the specific client and specimen.

opts.text: Be left blank and filled in by the lab
opts.rat: Required information is provided accurately, not left blank.

opts.text: List a different test than the one ordered
opts.rat: The requisition reflects the actual order to avoid errors.

steps.q: After collecting a specimen, the technician should document:

opts.text: The type of specimen, the date/time collected, its appearance if relevant, and that it was sent to the lab
opts.rat: Clear documentation supports accurate results interpretation and continuity of care.

opts.text: Nothing, since the lab keeps its own records
opts.rat: Collection is documented in the client's record, not left solely to the lab.

opts.text: Only the client's room number
opts.rat: Documentation includes specimen details, not just a room number.

opts.text: A guess about the test result
opts.rat: The technician documents the collection, not a guessed result.

steps.q: Some blood tests or procedures require the client to fast beforehand. The technician should:

opts.text: Follow the specific fasting/NPO order and verify the client has been prepared as directed
opts.rat: Fasting requirements vary by test; following the exact order and confirming preparation ensures valid results and safety.

opts.text: Decide on their own how long the client should fast
opts.rat: Fasting duration follows the order, not the technician's independent decision.

opts.text: Let the client eat freely regardless of the order
opts.rat: Ignoring an NPO order can invalidate the test or create risk.

opts.text: Assume fasting is never needed
opts.rat: Certain tests do require fasting; the order is followed.

steps.q: When a client is scheduled for a diagnostic procedure, part of preparation is to:

opts.text: Reinforce simple explanations, ensure ordered prep is done, support comfort, and confirm required consent was obtained by the appropriate staff
opts.rat: Preparing the client includes reinforcing teaching, completing ordered prep, comfort measures, and confirming that the proper consent process was handled by licensed staff.

opts.text: Obtain the client's informed consent for the procedure independently
opts.rat: Obtaining informed consent for a procedure is the responsibility of the provider performing it, not the technician.

opts.text: Skip preparation to save time
opts.rat: Proper preparation is important for safety and accurate results.

opts.text: Tell the client nothing to avoid worrying them
opts.rat: Appropriate, honest preparation reduces anxiety and supports cooperation.

steps.q: Teaching a client to collect their own specimen correctly is important because:

opts.text: Proper technique reduces contamination and gives more accurate results
opts.rat: Clear instructions help the client collect a valid, uncontaminated specimen, improving accuracy.

opts.text: It does not matter how the client collects it
opts.rat: Technique strongly affects the accuracy of the result.

opts.text: Contaminated specimens give the best results
opts.rat: Contamination reduces accuracy; clean technique is needed.

opts.text: Instructions confuse clients and should be skipped
opts.rat: Clear instructions help, not hinder, correct collection.

steps.q: Two client identifiers used to confirm identity before collection could be:

opts.text: The client's full name and date of birth (per facility policy)
opts.rat: Using two approved identifiers such as name and date of birth reliably confirms the correct client.

opts.text: The room number alone
opts.rat: A room number is not an acceptable client identifier by itself.

opts.text: Whoever is in the bed at the time
opts.rat: Assuming based on bed position risks a serious mix-up.

opts.text: The staff member's own name
opts.rat: Identifiers must belong to the client, not the staff.

steps.q: If the technician notices a specimen looks unusual (for example, urine that is very cloudy or bloody), they should:

opts.text: Document the appearance objectively and report it to the nurse
opts.rat: Objective documentation and reporting of an abnormal appearance support timely evaluation.

opts.text: Diagnose the cause and begin treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosing and treating are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Discard it so no one worries
opts.rat: Discarding an abnormal specimen removes important information; it is reported.

opts.text: Ignore it as unimportant
opts.rat: Unusual findings are documented and reported, not ignored.

steps.q: When transporting a client for a diagnostic test, the technician should:

opts.text: Confirm the correct client and test, ensure safety and comfort during transport, and follow any ordered preparation
opts.rat: Verifying identity and the test, transporting safely, and ensuring prep is complete prevent errors and support the client.

opts.text: Take whoever is ready without checking the order
opts.rat: Transporting the wrong client or for the wrong test is a serious error.

opts.text: Ignore the client's comfort and safety
opts.rat: Comfort and safety during transport are part of good care.

opts.text: Skip verifying the test that is scheduled
opts.rat: The scheduled test and client are verified before transport.

steps.q: Collecting the correct specimen at the correct time (for example, a timed sample) matters because:

opts.text: Some tests depend on specific timing, and errors can produce inaccurate or unusable results
opts.rat: Timed and correctly typed specimens are essential for accurate results; wrong timing or type can invalidate the test.

opts.text: Timing never affects test results
opts.rat: Timing is critical for many tests.

opts.text: Any specimen at any time is equally valid
opts.rat: The correct type and timing are required for validity.

opts.text: The lab prefers surprises
opts.rat: Accuracy depends on following the ordered type and timing.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in specimen collection and diagnostic prep is to:

opts.text: Collect specimens correctly within scope, verify identity, label and handle them properly, prepare and support clients, and report—leaving diagnosis and consent for procedures to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician collects accurately, safeguards identity and handling, prepares clients, and reports, while diagnosis and procedure consent belong to licensed providers.

opts.text: Interpret and diagnose the test results
opts.rat: Interpreting and diagnosing are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Obtain informed consent for invasive procedures
opts.rat: Informed consent for a procedure is obtained by the provider performing it.

opts.text: Skip labeling and handling standards when busy
opts.rat: Labeling and handling standards are always followed to ensure safety and accuracy.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (specimen collection and diagnostic preparation). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Practices are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: two-identifier verification and bedside labeling; clean-catch/midstream urine; 24-hour urine collection (discard first void, collect all urine including the final void, store per policy, restart if a sample is lost); avoiding contamination of stool specimens; deep-cough (ideally early-morning) sputum vs saliva; prompt transport/proper storage; standard precautions; culture using sterile technique ideally before antibiotics; requisition matching; documentation; fasting/NPO per order; and diagnostic-procedure preparation. Consistent with the technician's scope: collect, handle, prepare, and report, while diagnosis and obtaining informed consent for procedures are performed by licensed staff. No specific fasting durations, storage temperatures, or reference values are asserted. Builds on NPO (bnc-core-05), catheter urine specimen and blood-in-urine reporting (bnc-core-06), and capillary blood glucose (bnc-core-11). Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Perioperative & Pre/Post-Procedure Care Basics (Set 14)
subtitle: Preoperative preparation and checklist, pre-op teaching (deep breathing, coughing, leg exercises, early ambulation), NPO/aspiration rationale, post-anesthesia airway and monitoring priorities, positioning, complication prevention (atelectasis, DVT), wound/dressing and pain observation, and reporting within scope
scenario: Assisting with care before and after a surgery or procedure: preparing the client, reinforcing pre-op teaching, keeping the recovering client safe (airway, positioning, safety), watching for complications, and reporting to the nurse—while procedures and consent remain with licensed staff.

steps.q: The overall purpose of preoperative preparation is to:

opts.text: Prepare the client physically and psychologically and ensure ordered pre-op steps are completed
opts.rat: Good pre-op care readies the client's body and mind and confirms that required preparations and orders are carried out for a safe procedure.

opts.text: Rush the client to surgery without any preparation
opts.rat: Skipping preparation increases risk; pre-op steps are important for safety.

opts.text: Hide all information from the client
opts.rat: Appropriate teaching and reassurance are part of pre-op care.

opts.text: Complete billing before anything else
opts.rat: Clinical preparation and safety, not billing, are the focus of pre-op care.

steps.q: Why is a client kept NPO (nothing by mouth) before surgery with anesthesia?

opts.text: To reduce the risk of aspiration (stomach contents entering the lungs) during anesthesia
opts.rat: An empty stomach lowers the chance of vomiting and aspirating during anesthesia, a serious complication.

opts.text: To punish the client
opts.rat: NPO is a safety measure, never punishment.

opts.text: Because food has no effect on anesthesia safety
opts.rat: Food in the stomach raises aspiration risk under anesthesia.

opts.text: To save money on meals
opts.rat: NPO is for aspiration prevention, not cost.

steps.q: Confirming that informed consent for the surgery has been obtained is:

opts.text: Verified as present on the chart before the procedure, with the consent itself obtained by the provider performing it
opts.rat: The technician can confirm the signed consent is in place, but obtaining informed consent is the responsibility of the provider doing the procedure.

opts.text: Obtained independently by the technician
opts.rat: Obtaining informed consent for a procedure is the provider's responsibility, not the technician's.

opts.text: Unnecessary for surgery
opts.rat: Informed consent is required before a surgical procedure.

opts.text: Something to skip if the unit is busy
opts.rat: Consent verification is essential and not skipped.

steps.q: A typical preoperative checklist item the technician may help with is:

opts.text: Ensuring the ID band is on and removing items like jewelry and dentures per policy
opts.rat: Confirming identification and removing jewelry, dentures, and similar items (per policy) are standard pre-op safety steps.

opts.text: Leaving all jewelry and dentures in place for surgery
opts.rat: These are typically removed before surgery for safety per policy.

opts.text: Removing the client's ID band
opts.rat: The ID band is kept on to verify identity, not removed.

opts.text: Feeding the client a large meal just before surgery
opts.rat: The client is NPO before surgery, not fed a large meal.

steps.q: Pre-op teaching often includes showing the client how to deep-breathe, cough, and do leg exercises because these help:

opts.text: Prevent post-operative complications such as lung problems and blood clots
opts.rat: Deep breathing/coughing help prevent atelectasis and pneumonia, and leg exercises/early movement help prevent blood clots after surgery.

opts.text: Make the surgery take longer
opts.rat: These measures aid recovery; they do not affect surgery length.

opts.text: Replace the need for the surgery
opts.rat: They support recovery, not replace the procedure.

opts.text: Have no effect on recovery
opts.rat: They meaningfully reduce common post-op complications.

steps.q: A client is visibly anxious before surgery and has questions. The technician should:

opts.text: Provide reassurance, allow the client to express concerns, and notify the nurse of questions needing answers
opts.rat: Emotional support and routing clinical questions to the nurse address the client's psychological preparation appropriately.

opts.text: Tell the client their feelings do not matter
opts.rat: Dismissing feelings is nontherapeutic; support is part of pre-op care.

opts.text: Ignore the client's questions entirely
opts.rat: Questions are acknowledged and routed to the nurse as needed.

opts.text: Give detailed medical answers beyond their scope
opts.rat: Clinical questions beyond scope are referred to the nurse or provider.

steps.q: Obtaining baseline vital signs before surgery is important because they:

opts.text: Provide a comparison point to help detect changes after the procedure
opts.rat: Baseline vitals let the team recognize post-op changes that may signal a problem.

opts.text: Are never needed for surgery
opts.rat: Baseline vitals are a standard, important part of pre-op assessment.

opts.text: Only matter for billing
opts.rat: They are clinically important for detecting change, not administrative.

opts.text: Should be skipped to save time
opts.rat: Baseline vitals are obtained, not skipped.

steps.q: Immediately after anesthesia, the HIGHEST priority in monitoring the recovering client is:

opts.text: Airway and breathing, along with level of consciousness and vital signs
opts.rat: After anesthesia, protecting the airway and ensuring adequate breathing are the top priorities, with close monitoring of consciousness and vitals.

opts.text: Whether the client's TV is working
opts.rat: Comfort items are minor compared with airway and breathing.

opts.text: The client's meal preferences
opts.rat: Meal preferences are not the immediate post-anesthesia priority.

opts.text: The color of the client's gown
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to post-anesthesia safety.

steps.q: A client who is still drowsy and not fully awake after anesthesia is best positioned:

opts.text: On their side (or as ordered) to help keep the airway clear and reduce aspiration risk
opts.rat: Side-lying helps secretions or vomit drain away and protects the airway in a client who is not fully alert.

opts.text: Flat on the back and left unmonitored
opts.rat: A not-fully-awake client on their back is at aspiration risk and needs monitoring; side-lying is safer.

opts.text: Sitting fully upright and made to walk immediately
opts.rat: A drowsy post-anesthesia client is at fall risk; immediate walking is unsafe.

opts.text: Face-down with the face pressed into the pillow
opts.rat: This can obstruct the airway and is unsafe.

steps.q: Which post-operative finding should the technician report to the nurse promptly?

opts.text: Increasing bleeding, a drop or change in vital signs, decreasing responsiveness, or difficulty breathing
opts.rat: These can indicate serious post-op complications (hemorrhage, shock, respiratory or neurological problems) requiring immediate attention.

opts.text: The client resting comfortably with stable vitals
opts.rat: This is reassuring, not a concern to report urgently.

opts.text: A clean, dry, intact dressing
opts.rat: An intact dressing is an expected, normal finding.

opts.text: The client asking for a blanket
opts.rat: A routine comfort request is not a complication.

steps.q: To help prevent lung complications (such as atelectasis) after surgery, the technician should encourage the client to:

opts.text: Deep-breathe and cough regularly and use the incentive spirometer as taught
opts.rat: Regular deep breathing, coughing, and incentive spirometry re-expand the lungs and help prevent post-op atelectasis and pneumonia.

opts.text: Lie still and breathe as shallowly as possible
opts.rat: Shallow breathing and immobility promote atelectasis.

opts.text: Avoid all movement for several days
opts.rat: Prolonged immobility increases complications; movement and breathing exercises help.

opts.text: Hold the breath as long as possible repeatedly
opts.rat: This is not the recommended technique; deep breathing and spirometry are.

steps.q: To help prevent blood clots (such as deep vein thrombosis) after surgery, a helpful measure is:

opts.text: Encouraging early movement/ambulation and leg exercises as ordered
opts.rat: Movement and leg exercises promote circulation and help prevent clots from forming during post-op recovery.

opts.text: Keeping the client completely immobile for as long as possible
opts.rat: Immobility increases clot risk; movement helps prevent it.

opts.text: Massaging the legs vigorously to break up any clots
opts.rat: Vigorously massaging the legs is unsafe and could dislodge a clot; it is not done.

opts.text: Restricting all leg motion indefinitely
opts.rat: Restricting motion raises clot risk; gentle activity is encouraged as ordered.

steps.q: When observing a post-operative surgical dressing, the technician should:

opts.text: Check for bleeding or increasing drainage and report changes, without removing the initial dressing unless directed
opts.rat: Monitoring the dressing for bleeding/drainage and reporting changes is within scope; the first surgical dressing is usually changed by licensed staff or per order.

opts.text: Remove the surgical dressing to look at the incision out of curiosity
opts.rat: The initial dressing is not removed casually; doing so risks contamination and bleeding.

opts.text: Ignore any drainage that appears
opts.rat: Drainage changes are observed and reported, not ignored.

opts.text: Reinforce the dressing and never tell anyone
opts.rat: Changes are reported to the nurse, not concealed.

steps.q: Regarding post-operative pain, the technician should:

opts.text: Ask about and observe for pain, provide comfort measures within scope, and report it to the nurse for management
opts.rat: Recognizing and reporting pain and offering comfort measures support the client while the nurse manages medication and treatment.

opts.text: Assume post-op clients never have pain
opts.rat: Post-op pain is common and should be assessed and reported.

opts.text: Tell the client to simply ignore the pain
opts.rat: Dismissing pain is nontherapeutic; it is reported for management.

opts.text: Independently administer additional pain medication
opts.rat: Medication administration follows orders and scope; pain is reported to the nurse.

steps.q: A post-operative client becomes nauseated and begins to vomit. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Position the client to protect the airway (such as turning the head or side-lying) and report to the nurse
opts.rat: Protecting the airway prevents aspiration during vomiting; reporting allows treatment of the nausea.

opts.text: Lay the drowsy client flat on their back and leave
opts.rat: Flat positioning during vomiting risks aspiration, especially if the client is drowsy.

opts.text: Give the client a large drink of water immediately
opts.rat: Giving fluids during active vomiting can worsen aspiration risk.

opts.text: Ignore it and continue other tasks
opts.rat: Vomiting post-op requires airway protection and reporting, not ignoring.

steps.q: Monitoring urinary output after surgery is important because:

opts.text: Inability to void or low output can signal a problem and should be reported
opts.rat: Post-op clients may have difficulty voiding; tracking output and reporting problems supports timely intervention.

opts.text: Urinary output has no relevance after surgery
opts.rat: Output is an important indicator of recovery and fluid status.

opts.text: Output is only tracked before surgery
opts.rat: Post-op output is monitored as part of recovery.

opts.text: The client should be discouraged from voiding
opts.rat: Voiding is encouraged as able; inability to void is reported.

steps.q: Because a client recovering from anesthesia may be drowsy or unsteady, the technician should:

opts.text: Take fall-prevention measures—assist with movement and use safety measures per policy
opts.rat: Post-anesthesia drowsiness and dizziness increase fall risk, so assistance and safety measures protect the client.

opts.text: Let the client get up and walk alone right away
opts.rat: Unassisted early ambulation after anesthesia risks falls.

opts.text: Assume the client is steady and needs no help
opts.rat: Recovering clients are often unsteady and need assistance.

opts.text: Leave the drowsy client unmonitored on a high surface
opts.rat: This is unsafe; monitoring and fall precautions are needed.

steps.q: To reduce infection risk in a post-operative client, the technician should:

opts.text: Perform hand hygiene and follow wound-care and precaution orders
opts.rat: Hand hygiene and following ordered wound-care/precautions are key to preventing surgical-site and other infections.

opts.text: Skip hand hygiene to save time
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is essential to infection prevention.

opts.text: Touch the wound with bare, unwashed hands
opts.rat: This introduces infection risk and violates infection-control principles.

opts.text: Ignore ordered precautions
opts.rat: Ordered precautions are followed to protect the client.

steps.q: Which is an early sign the technician should report as a possible post-operative complication?

opts.text: A rising pulse with a falling blood pressure and increasing restlessness
opts.rat: These together can indicate developing bleeding or shock after surgery and require prompt reporting.

opts.text: Stable vital signs and a comfortable, alert client
opts.rat: These are reassuring, expected findings.

opts.text: The client sipping ordered fluids without difficulty
opts.rat: Tolerating ordered fluids is a good sign, not a complication.

opts.text: The client dozing comfortably with normal breathing
opts.rat: Comfortable rest with normal breathing is reassuring.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in perioperative care is to:

opts.text: Assist with preparation, support the client, monitor and provide basic care, watch for complications, and report—while procedures, consent, and medical management belong to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician prepares, supports, monitors, and reports within scope, while surgery, consent, and clinical management are handled by licensed providers and nurses.

opts.text: Perform the surgical procedure
opts.rat: Performing procedures is far outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Obtain surgical informed consent independently
opts.rat: Consent for a procedure is obtained by the provider performing it.

opts.text: Manage anesthesia and prescribe medications
opts.rat: Anesthesia and prescribing are outside the technician's scope.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (perioperative and pre/post-procedure care). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Concepts are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: pre-op preparation and checklist (ID band, removing jewelry/dentures per policy), NPO/aspiration rationale, verifying (not obtaining) consent, pre-op teaching (deep breathing, coughing, leg exercises, early ambulation), baseline vitals; and post-anesthesia priorities (airway/breathing/consciousness), side-lying positioning for the not-fully-awake client, complication recognition (bleeding/shock, respiratory), atelectasis and DVT prevention, dressing/pain/nausea/output monitoring, infection prevention, and fall precautions. Roles reflect the technician's scope: assist, support, monitor, and report, while procedures, consent, anesthesia, and prescribing belong to licensed staff. No specific NPO durations, vital-sign values, or medication details are asserted. Builds on NPO (bnc-core-05), incentive spirometry (bnc-core-09), ambulation/gait belt (bnc-core-07), and procedure prep/consent (bnc-core-13). Pending faculty review.

title: Basic Nursing Care — Documentation, SBAR Reporting & Delegation Basics (Set 15)
subtitle: Purposes and qualities of good documentation, timing and integrity of chart entries, the SBAR communication format, safe shift handoff, the delegation process and the 'rights' of delegation, accepting/clarifying delegated tasks within scope, and reporting back
scenario: Communicating and documenting safely: recording care accurately and on time, using SBAR to report clearly, handing off at shift change, and working within delegation and scope while reporting results back to the nurse.

steps.q: A primary purpose of documentation in the client's record is to:

opts.text: Communicate care to the team, provide a legal record, and support continuity of care
opts.rat: The record shares information among caregivers, serves as a legal document, and lets care continue safely across shifts.

opts.text: Serve only as optional busywork
opts.rat: Documentation is essential to communication, safety, and the legal record, not busywork.

opts.text: Provide entertainment for staff
opts.rat: Documentation has clinical and legal purposes, not entertainment.

opts.text: Replace all verbal communication permanently
opts.rat: Documentation complements—rather than replaces—necessary verbal communication such as reports and handoffs.

steps.q: Good documentation should be:

opts.text: Accurate, factual, objective, timely, legible, and complete
opts.rat: These qualities make the record trustworthy and useful for safe, continuous care.

opts.text: Vague, delayed, and based on opinion
opts.rat: Vague, delayed, opinion-based notes undermine safety and accuracy.

opts.text: Written illegibly to save time
opts.rat: Illegible entries can cause errors; documentation must be legible.

opts.text: Exaggerated to make a point
opts.rat: Exaggeration falsifies the record; documentation is factual.

steps.q: When should care be documented?

opts.text: Promptly after the care is provided—never charted in advance
opts.rat: Charting soon after care keeps the record accurate; documenting care before it is done is falsification and dangerous.

opts.text: Before the care is actually given, to save time
opts.rat: Charting ahead is falsification; care is documented after it is performed.

opts.text: Several days later from memory
opts.rat: Delayed charting is inaccurate; documentation should be timely.

opts.text: Only at the end of the month
opts.rat: Care is documented promptly, not batched far later.

steps.q: To maintain the integrity of a paper chart, the technician should:

opts.text: Avoid leaving blank lines or gaps that others could fill in later
opts.rat: Blank spaces can be altered or added to; keeping entries continuous protects the record's integrity.

opts.text: Leave large blank areas between entries
opts.rat: Gaps invite tampering and are avoided.

opts.text: Use white-out to remove mistakes
opts.rat: Correction fluid is never used; errors are corrected per policy (for example, a single line through).

opts.text: Write entries for other staff members
opts.rat: Each caregiver documents their own care, not others'.

steps.q: The SBAR communication format stands for:

opts.text: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
opts.rat: SBAR is a structured way to organize a report: Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation.

opts.text: Start, Begin, Act, Rest
opts.rat: This is not what SBAR stands for.

opts.text: Safety, Billing, Admission, Records
opts.rat: These are not the SBAR components.

opts.text: Sign, Behave, Ask, Report
opts.rat: This is not the SBAR format.

steps.q: In SBAR, the 'Situation' is:

opts.text: A brief statement of the current problem or reason for the report
opts.rat: The Situation concisely states what is happening right now that prompted the communication.

opts.text: The client's entire life history
opts.rat: Detailed history belongs to Background; Situation is the current problem.

opts.text: The recommendation for what to do
opts.rat: That is the Recommendation, not the Situation.

opts.text: The client's insurance details
opts.rat: Administrative details are not the Situation.

steps.q: In SBAR, the 'Background' provides:

opts.text: Relevant history and context related to the current situation
opts.rat: Background gives the pertinent history and context needed to understand the situation.

opts.text: The final decision about treatment
opts.rat: Decisions/requests are the Recommendation, not Background.

opts.text: Only the client's favorite foods
opts.rat: Preferences unrelated to the issue are not relevant background.

opts.text: The technician's personal opinions about coworkers
opts.rat: Personal opinions are not part of a professional SBAR report.

steps.q: In SBAR, the 'Assessment' (within the technician's scope) includes:

opts.text: The technician's relevant observations and what they think the concern is
opts.rat: The Assessment shares pertinent observations and the reporter's read of the situation, within their scope.

opts.text: A formal medical diagnosis
opts.rat: Diagnosing is outside the technician's scope; they report observations and concerns.

opts.text: Nothing at all
opts.rat: The Assessment does convey observations and the reason for concern.

opts.text: The billing code for the visit
opts.rat: Billing is not part of the SBAR assessment.

steps.q: In SBAR, the 'Recommendation' is:

opts.text: What the reporter is requesting or suggesting be done next
opts.rat: The Recommendation states what the reporter needs—for example, asking the nurse to assess the client or give direction.

opts.text: A restatement of the client's birthdate
opts.rat: That is not the Recommendation.

opts.text: The client's meal order
opts.rat: A meal order is not the SBAR recommendation.

opts.text: The weather report
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to SBAR.

steps.q: The main benefit of using SBAR is that it:

opts.text: Organizes communication so it is clear and complete, helping reduce errors
opts.rat: A structured format ensures important information is conveyed clearly and completely, improving safety.

opts.text: Makes reports longer and more confusing
opts.rat: SBAR streamlines and clarifies communication.

opts.text: Lets staff leave out important information
opts.rat: SBAR is designed to include the key information, not omit it.

opts.text: Replaces the need to document
opts.rat: SBAR structures verbal reporting; documentation is still required.

steps.q: A good shift handoff (end-of-shift report) provides:

opts.text: Organized, accurate, relevant information so the next caregiver can safely continue care
opts.rat: A clear, accurate handoff of the pertinent information supports safe continuity of care between shifts.

opts.text: Only gossip about the clients
opts.rat: Handoff is professional and clinical, not gossip.

opts.text: As little information as possible
opts.rat: Withholding relevant information endangers continuity and safety.

opts.text: Made-up details to fill time
opts.rat: Handoff must be accurate; fabrication is unsafe.

steps.q: When the technician needs to report a change in a client's condition to the nurse, the communication should be:

opts.text: Prompt, clear, and organized (for example, using SBAR)
opts.rat: Timely, well-organized reporting—such as SBAR—helps the nurse understand and act on the concern quickly.

opts.text: Delayed and disorganized
opts.rat: Delay and disorganization can lead to missed or mishandled problems.

opts.text: Left as a vague hint
opts.rat: Vague reporting risks the concern being missed.

opts.text: Skipped entirely if the technician is busy
opts.rat: Changes in condition are always reported, regardless of workload.

steps.q: Delegation in nursing refers to:

opts.text: A licensed nurse assigning a task to the technician to perform within the technician's training and scope
opts.rat: The nurse delegates appropriate tasks that the technician is trained and permitted to perform.

opts.text: The technician assigning tasks to the nurse
opts.rat: Delegation flows from the licensed nurse to the technician, not the reverse.

opts.text: Clients deciding staff assignments
opts.rat: Delegation is a professional nursing responsibility, not decided by clients.

opts.text: Performing any task regardless of training
opts.rat: Delegated tasks must be within the technician's training and scope.

steps.q: The commonly taught 'rights of delegation' include the right:

opts.text: Task, circumstances, person, direction/communication, and supervision
opts.rat: These 'five rights' guide safe delegation: the right task, under the right circumstances, to the right person, with clear direction and appropriate supervision.

opts.text: Color, size, weight, and shape
opts.rat: These are not the rights of delegation.

opts.text: Speed, secrecy, and shortcuts
opts.rat: These are unsafe and are not delegation principles.

opts.text: Cost, brand, and packaging
opts.rat: These are unrelated to delegation.

steps.q: Before accepting a delegated task, the technician should ensure that it:

opts.text: Is within their training, scope, and competence—and clarify with the nurse if unsure
opts.rat: Accepting only tasks one is trained and permitted to do, and clarifying uncertainty, keeps clients safe.

opts.text: Is accepted without any thought
opts.rat: The technician confirms the task is appropriate before accepting.

opts.text: Is performed even if clearly beyond scope
opts.rat: Tasks outside scope are not performed; the technician clarifies or declines.

opts.text: Is done secretly without reporting results
opts.rat: Results are reported back; secrecy is not appropriate.

steps.q: If a nurse delegates a task that is unsafe or outside the technician's scope, the technician should:

opts.text: Respectfully clarify or decline and inform the nurse, rather than performing it
opts.rat: The technician does not perform tasks beyond scope or that are unsafe; clarifying or declining and communicating protects the client.

opts.text: Perform it anyway to avoid conflict
opts.rat: Performing an unsafe or out-of-scope task endangers the client and the technician.

opts.text: Do it and hide any problems
opts.rat: Concealing problems is unsafe and improper.

opts.text: Delegate it to a client
opts.rat: Tasks are not delegated to clients.

steps.q: After completing a delegated task, the technician should:

opts.text: Report the outcome and any relevant observations back to the delegating nurse and document as required
opts.rat: Reporting results and observations back closes the loop, lets the nurse follow up, and keeps the record accurate.

opts.text: Say nothing, since the task is finished
opts.rat: The nurse needs the results to continue safe care; report back.

opts.text: Only report if something went wrong
opts.rat: Outcomes are reported whether or not a problem occurred.

opts.text: Report to a different client instead
opts.rat: Results go to the delegating nurse, not to another client.

steps.q: Which type of responsibility generally CANNOT be delegated to the technician?

opts.text: Professional nursing judgment such as client assessment, evaluation, and teaching
opts.rat: Higher-level nursing judgment—assessment, evaluation, and teaching—remains with the licensed nurse and is not delegated to the technician.

opts.text: A routine task within the technician's training
opts.rat: Routine tasks within training are appropriately delegated.

opts.text: Assisting a client with hygiene as trained
opts.rat: This is an appropriate delegated task within scope.

opts.text: Reporting observations to the nurse
opts.rat: Reporting observations is part of the technician's role, not something that cannot be delegated.

steps.q: When giving or receiving a verbal report, information about the client should be shared:

opts.text: Only with those involved in the client's care and in a private, professional manner
opts.rat: Client information is shared on a need-to-know basis and kept confidential, consistent with privacy requirements.

opts.text: Loudly in a public hallway
opts.rat: Discussing client information where others can overhear breaches confidentiality.

opts.text: With anyone who is curious
opts.rat: Information is limited to those involved in care, not the merely curious.

opts.text: On social media for efficiency
opts.rat: Sharing client information on social media violates confidentiality.

steps.q: Overall, effective communication and delegation practice for the technician means:

opts.text: Documenting accurately and on time, reporting clearly (e.g., SBAR) and handing off safely, and working within delegation/scope while reporting results back
opts.rat: Accurate documentation, structured reporting and handoff, and working within scope with report-back together support safe, coordinated care.

opts.text: Charting in advance and reporting vaguely
opts.rat: Advance charting and vague reports are unsafe and improper.

opts.text: Performing any delegated task regardless of scope and never reporting back
opts.rat: Tasks must be within scope, and results are reported back.

opts.text: Keeping information from the care team
opts.rat: Relevant information is communicated to the team for safe care.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (documentation, reporting, and delegation basics). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Concepts are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: purposes and qualities of documentation; timely, integrity-preserving charting (documenting after care, avoiding blank gaps, no correction fluid); the SBAR format (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) and its components; safe shift handoff; delegation as a nurse-to-technician process; the 'five rights' of delegation (task, circumstances, person, direction/communication, supervision); accepting only in-scope tasks and clarifying/declining unsafe ones; reporting results back; and that professional nursing judgment (assessment, evaluation, teaching) is not delegated to the technician. Confidentiality in reporting is consistent with privacy requirements. Complements documentation-quality/error-correction items in legal-core-01/02, scope/delegation/accountability items in legal-core-03/04, objective documentation in mh-core-20, and the many 'report to the nurse' items across the BNC sets. No specific numbers, doses, or lab values are asserted. Pending faculty review.

title: Acute Ischemic Stroke
subtitle: 64 y/o female, in the alteplase window
nursesNote: 0712 - 64 y/o female brought in by EMS after sudden onset of right-sided facial droop, right arm weakness, and slurred speech witnessed by spouse at 0635. Last known well 0630. NIHSS at triage: 14 (moderate). Spouse denies recent surgery, head trauma, GI bleed, or anticoagulant use. CT head without contrast at 0745 - no hemorrhage, no early ischemic changes. Neurology at bedside; client is being evaluated for IV alteplase pending BP control.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) cues that BEST establish this client as a candidate for IV alteplase.

opts.text: Last known well at 0630 (within the 4.5-hour window)
opts.rat: The IV alteplase window is up to 4.5 hours from LAST KNOWN WELL - not from symptom discovery or ED arrival. This single data point is the gatekeeper for thrombolysis (AHA/ASA 2019).

opts.text: Non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage and no early ischemic changes
opts.rat: A negative head CT excludes intracerebral hemorrhage - the mandatory prerequisite for alteplase. Absence of early ischemic changes does NOT rule out infarct (often invisible <6h).

opts.text: NIHSS 14 (moderate stroke severity)
opts.rat: NIHSS quantifies severity; scores 5-25 derive the greatest benefit from thrombolysis. A 14 supports treatment in an otherwise eligible candidate.

opts.text: BP 204/112 mmHg
opts.rat: Currently EXCLUDES alteplase until lowered to <185/110. This is a barrier to address, not an eligibility cue.

opts.text: Slurred speech (dysarthria)
opts.rat: Confirms stroke but does not specifically establish thrombolytic candidacy - time window, CT, and severity do.

opts.text: Glucose 142 mg/dL
opts.rat: Mildly elevated but rules OUT hypoglycemia mimic. Does not, by itself, establish candidacy.

opts.text: INR 1.0, platelets 245 K/uL
opts.rat: Supportive normal coags - but normal labs are not 'cues' to recognize.

opts.text: NKDA per spouse
opts.rat: Background safety data, not a clinical cue for thrombolysis.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly link the cues to underlying pathophysiology.

opts.text: Focal deficits arise from arterial occlusion creating an irreversibly infarcted core surrounded by a salvageable penumbra
opts.rat: The core infarcts within minutes; the penumbra remains viable for hours if reperfusion occurs (Lewis Med-Surg 11e, p. 1395).

opts.text: The elevated BP is largely a compensatory response to maintain cerebral perfusion to the penumbra
opts.rat: Cerebral autoregulation is impaired in the penumbra, making perfusion pressure-dependent.

opts.text: Aggressive BP lowering before reperfusion can extend the infarct by reducing penumbral perfusion
opts.rat: Overshoot lowering converts salvageable penumbra to infarcted tissue (AHA/ASA 2019).

opts.text: The 4.5-hour alteplase window starts from the time of ED arrival
opts.rat: Incorrect - starts from LAST KNOWN WELL.

opts.text: Alteplase reverses damage already completed in the infarct core
opts.rat: Alteplase only salvages the penumbra; the core infarct is irreversible.

opts.text: A negative head CT definitively rules out acute ischemic stroke
opts.rat: CT is sensitive for hemorrhage; acute ischemia is often invisible for 6-24 hours.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Acute ischemic stroke - large-vessel (likely left MCA) territory
opts.rat: Sudden contralateral focal deficits, NIHSS 14, witnessed onset, and CT excluding bleed make AIS overwhelmingly most likely.

opts.text: Hemorrhagic stroke (intracerebral hemorrhage)
opts.rat: Always in the differential, but the negative non-contrast CT effectively excludes acute hemorrhage now.

opts.text: Stroke mimic - hypoglycemia
opts.rat: Always assessed early because rapidly reversible, but ruled out here by glucose 142.

opts.text: Stroke mimic - complex migraine or Todd's paralysis
opts.rat: Possible but no headache aura history, no witnessed seizure, deficits persistent.

opts.text: Conversion (functional) disorder
opts.rat: Least likely: deficits follow a clear vascular distribution. Diagnosis of exclusion.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) MOST time-critical interventions for the alteplase pathway in the first hour.

opts.text: Administer IV labetalol per stroke protocol to lower BP to <185/110 prior to alteplase
opts.rat: Alteplase is contraindicated above this threshold; controlling BP is the immediate gateway to thrombolysis.

opts.text: Administer alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (10% bolus, 90% infusion over 60 min) once eligible
opts.rat: Standard adult dose for AIS within 4.5 hours of last known well; max total 90 mg. Door-to-needle goal <=45 min.

opts.text: Initiate continuous cardiac/BP monitoring with q15-min neuro checks
opts.rat: Mandatory safety baseline for detecting hemorrhagic conversion or angioedema during and after the infusion.

opts.text: Administer aspirin 325 mg PO immediately
opts.rat: Antiplatelets must be HELD for 24 hours after alteplase to avoid hemorrhagic conversion.

opts.text: Bolus 1 L of 0.9% normal saline wide open
opts.rat: No evidence of hypovolemia; would worsen severe HTN.

opts.text: Administer clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose now
opts.rat: Antiplatelet loading is contraindicated peri-thrombolysis - markedly increases ICH risk.

opts.text: Give sublingual nifedipine for rapid BP drop
opts.rat: Causes precipitous, uncontrolled hypotension that can extend the infarct.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Place client on continuous cardiac/BP monitoring and initiate q15-min neuro checks
opts.rat: FIRST - establishes the safety baseline before any intervention.

opts.text: Administer IV labetalol per protocol to bring BP <185/110
opts.rat: SECOND - alteplase is contraindicated above this threshold.

opts.text: Confirm all alteplase inclusion/exclusion criteria with the neurologist and obtain informed consent
opts.rat: THIRD - final eligibility check immediately before the bolus.

opts.text: Administer alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (10% bolus, then 90% infusion over 60 minutes)
opts.rat: FOURTH - door-to-needle goal <=45 minutes per AHA/ASA.

opts.text: Transfer to the Neuro ICU for ongoing post-thrombolysis monitoring
opts.rat: LAST - ICU-level monitoring is required for at least the first 24 hours.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After 24 hours of post-alteplase care, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: NIHSS improved from 14 to 6 at 24 hours post-alteplase
opts.rat: A reduction of >=4 points on NIHSS is clinically meaningful and reflects successful reperfusion of the penumbra.

opts.text: BP controlled at 162/88 mmHg throughout the alteplase infusion
opts.rat: Maintaining BP <180/105 during and 24 hours post-alteplase is the AHA/ASA target.

opts.text: Client passes the bedside dysphagia screen and tolerates small sips of water
opts.rat: Permits safe oral intake and PO meds; signals adequate bulbar function.

opts.text: Sudden severe headache, nausea, and vomiting 4 hours after alteplase infusion
opts.rat: Classic presentation of symptomatic ICH post-thrombolysis. STOP infusion if running, stat CT, notify provider.

opts.text: Right-sided facial droop resolved; only mild residual right hand weakness
opts.rat: Resolution of major focal deficits reflects successful reperfusion.

opts.text: Tongue and lip swelling noted 30 minutes into the alteplase infusion
opts.rat: Orolingual angioedema (1-5%, higher on ACE inhibitors). Stop infusion and protect the airway.

opts.text: No bleeding from IV sites, gums, or urinary catheter; no new bruising
opts.rat: Absence of systemic bleeding is positive given alteplase's systemic fibrinolytic effect.

opts.text: NIHSS unchanged at 14 with no new deficits at 24 hours
opts.rat: Stability, not improvement. Lack of NIHSS reduction suggests failed reperfusion - consider thrombectomy evaluation.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Acute ST-Elevation MI (STEMI)
subtitle: 58 y/o male, anterior wall infarct, door-to-balloon clock running
nursesNote: 1430 - 58 y/o male presents to ED via private vehicle with sudden onset crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to left jaw and arm, started 45 minutes ago while mowing the lawn. Pain 9/10, diaphoretic, nauseated, anxious. PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia, 30 pack-year smoker, father died of MI at 56. Currently on lisinopril and atorvastatin (compliance unclear). Initial 12-lead ECG shows 3-mm ST elevation in leads V1-V4 with reciprocal depression in II, III, aVF. Cath lab activated; cardiologist en route. Patient is alert, oriented x4, denies prior cardiac history.

patient.name: R. Petrov
patient.admitDate: Today, 1430

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) cues that BEST establish this client as having an acute STEMI requiring emergent reperfusion.

opts.text: 3-mm ST elevation in V1-V4 with reciprocal depression in II, III, aVF
opts.rat: ST elevation >=1 mm in two or more contiguous leads is the diagnostic ECG criterion for STEMI. V1-V4 localizes to the anterior wall (LAD distribution). Reciprocal changes confirm a true infarct (AHA/ACC 2022).

opts.text: Troponin I rising from 0.18 to 12.4 ng/mL over 3 hours
opts.rat: A rising troponin pattern with values >99th percentile confirms acute myocardial injury. The trajectory matters more than a single value (4th Universal Definition of MI).

opts.text: Crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to left jaw and arm with diaphoresis
opts.rat: Classic anginal equivalent presentation. Combined with diaphoresis and nausea, this triad is highly specific for acute coronary syndrome in a 58-year-old male with risk factors.

opts.text: BP 162/96 on arrival
opts.rat: Hypertension is a contributing risk factor and a current finding, but it does not by itself ESTABLISH the STEMI diagnosis. The ECG, troponin, and presentation do.

opts.text: Glucose 168 mg/dL
opts.rat: Mildly elevated, likely stress hyperglycemia from catecholamine surge. Not a defining cue for STEMI.

opts.text: 30 pack-year smoking history
opts.rat: A risk FACTOR, not a current clinical cue. History informs probability but does not establish acute infarction.

opts.text: Father died of MI at 56
opts.rat: Family history is a risk factor, not a presenting cue.

opts.text: Patient alert and oriented x4
opts.rat: Reassuring (no cardiogenic shock yet) but a normal finding - not a cue OF the infarct.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly link the cues to the underlying pathophysiology.

opts.text: ST elevation in V1-V4 indicates transmural ischemia of the anterior LV wall, most likely from acute occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery
opts.rat: V1-V4 are the precordial leads overlying the anterior wall; the LAD supplies this territory. Anterior MIs carry the highest mortality because the LAD perfuses the largest LV mass (Lewis Med-Surg 11e, p. 743).

opts.text: Rising troponin reflects myocyte necrosis as ischemic cardiomyocytes die and release contractile proteins into the bloodstream
opts.rat: Troponin I is released only when myocardial cells die. The rate of rise correlates with infarct size. Peak typically occurs at 12-24 hours.

opts.text: Time is muscle: every minute of LAD occlusion expands the infarct - the door-to-balloon goal is <=90 minutes for primary PCI
opts.rat: Salvageable myocardium decreases exponentially with time. Primary PCI within 90 minutes is the standard of care; if PCI is unavailable within 120 min, fibrinolytics are indicated (AHA/ACC 2022 STEMI guidelines).

opts.text: ST elevation reflects subendocardial ischemia only, not full-thickness damage
opts.rat: Backwards. ST DEPRESSION reflects subendocardial (NSTEMI) ischemia; ST ELEVATION indicates transmural (full-thickness) injury.

opts.text: Troponin elevation always represents acute coronary syndrome
opts.rat: Troponin can also rise in PE, sepsis, myocarditis, renal failure, and severe HF. The clinical context plus ECG plus rising trajectory is what makes the diagnosis.

opts.text: Reciprocal ST depressions in inferior leads suggest a separate inferior infarct
opts.rat: Reciprocal changes are mirror-image findings from the SAME infarct viewed from opposite leads - they CONFIRM the anterior STEMI rather than indicating a second event.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the differentials from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Acute anterior STEMI from LAD occlusion (Type 1 MI)
opts.rat: Classic presentation, diagnostic ECG, rising troponin, multiple risk factors. Type 1 = atherosclerotic plaque rupture with thrombus.

opts.text: NSTEMI / Unstable angina
opts.rat: Same disease spectrum but ECG would show ST depression or T-wave inversion, not ST elevation. The 3-mm ST elevation rules this in as STEMI specifically.

opts.text: Acute pericarditis
opts.rat: Can cause chest pain and ST elevation but typically diffuse (not localized to V1-V4), pleuritic, positional, with PR depression. Troponin usually only mildly elevated.

opts.text: Aortic dissection
opts.rat: Tearing chest pain radiating to back; BP differential between arms; widened mediastinum. Important to consider before thrombolytics, but presentation here favors STEMI.

opts.text: Pulmonary embolism
opts.rat: Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, S1Q3T3 pattern. Troponin can rise but ST elevation in V1-V4 is not the typical pattern.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) MOST time-critical interventions for this client in the first hour.

opts.text: Activate cath lab and prepare for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact
opts.rat: Primary PCI is the gold-standard reperfusion therapy for STEMI when available within 90 min. Each 30-minute delay increases 1-year mortality by ~7.5% (AHA/ACC 2022).

opts.text: Administer dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin 325 mg chewed PLUS a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., ticagrelor or clopidogrel)
opts.rat: DAPT is a class I recommendation pre-PCI. Aspirin chewed (not swallowed) gives faster absorption. Reduces stent thrombosis and reinfarction.

opts.text: Place on continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator at bedside
opts.rat: Anterior STEMI carries the highest risk of malignant ventricular dysrhythmias (VF/VT) and cardiogenic shock. Defibrillator must be immediately available.

opts.text: Administer fibrinolytic (alteplase) immediately while awaiting cath lab
opts.rat: Fibrinolytics are reserved for when PCI is NOT available within 120 minutes. With cath lab activated and cardiologist en route, primary PCI is the better choice.

opts.text: Give nifedipine sublingually for BP control
opts.rat: CONTRAINDICATED in ACS - causes reflex tachycardia and increases myocardial oxygen demand, worsening ischemia.

opts.text: Administer IV beta-blocker (metoprolol) within the first hour while BP is 162/96
opts.rat: IV beta-blockers within the first 24 hours INCREASE risk of cardiogenic shock per the COMMIT trial. Oral beta-blockers can be started later if hemodynamically stable. Not a first-hour priority.

opts.text: Administer IV morphine for chest pain refractory to nitroglycerin
opts.rat: Morphine is no longer a first-line MONA component - associated with worse outcomes (CRUSADE registry). Reserved for pain unresponsive to nitrates. Not a first-hour priority.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Apply oxygen if SpO2 <90%, place on continuous cardiac monitor with defibrillator at bedside
opts.rat: FIRST - establishes safety baseline. ABCs and monitoring for the most likely killer (VF) come before any drug. Note: routine O2 in non-hypoxic ACS is no longer recommended.

opts.text: Establish two large-bore IV lines and draw cardiac biomarkers, CBC, BMP, coags, type and screen
opts.rat: SECOND - access is required for medications and contrast; labs guide PCI safety (renal function, coags, platelets).

opts.text: Administer aspirin 325 mg chewed and the prescribed P2Y12 loading dose
opts.rat: THIRD - DAPT is class I and time-sensitive for plaque stabilization and reducing peri-PCI thrombosis.

opts.text: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin q5 min x 3 for chest pain (if SBP >90)
opts.rat: FOURTH - reduces preload and coronary vasospasm. Hold if SBP drops or right ventricular infarct is suspected.

opts.text: Transport to cath lab for primary PCI; provide handoff (SBAR) to interventional team
opts.rat: LAST in this sequence - the goal of all prior steps. Door-to-balloon time clock is running; everything else has been done to make this as safe as possible.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After successful PCI with stent placement to the LAD, classify each post-procedure finding.

opts.text: Chest pain resolved post-PCI; client rates pain 0/10
opts.rat: Resolution of ischemic pain after reperfusion is the most reliable bedside marker of successful PCI.

opts.text: ST elevation in V1-V4 has decreased by >50% on post-PCI ECG
opts.rat: ST resolution >50% within 60-90 min of reperfusion correlates with successful epicardial AND microvascular reperfusion - a positive prognostic marker.

opts.text: Troponin I peaks at 88 ng/mL at 18 hours, then begins downtrending
opts.rat: A predictable peak-and-fall pattern is EXPECTED after reperfusion - troponin keeps rising even after the artery is open as damaged cells finish releasing contents. The downtrend signals stabilization.

opts.text: New onset of frequent PVCs and a 12-beat run of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia 30 min post-PCI
opts.rat: Reperfusion arrhythmias can occur but sustained or symptomatic VT is dangerous - notify provider, ensure defibrillator at bedside, check electrolytes (especially K+ and Mg), assess for ongoing ischemia.

opts.text: BP 110/70, HR 78, SpO2 98% on room air, lungs clear bilaterally
opts.rat: Hemodynamic stability with adequate perfusion suggests preserved LV function and absence of cardiogenic shock - the most feared early complication of anterior MI.

opts.text: New holosystolic murmur at the apex with sudden-onset dyspnea and pink frothy sputum 8 hours post-PCI
opts.rat: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture or LV remodeling causing flash pulmonary edema - a mechanical complication requiring emergent echo and possible surgery.

opts.text: Femoral access site soft, no hematoma, distal pulses 2+ bilaterally
opts.rat: No bleeding or vascular complication from the PCI access site - an important safety check given antiplatelet load and heparin exposure.

opts.text: Persistent chest pressure 4/10 unchanged from pre-PCI; ECG ST elevation persists
opts.rat: Failed reperfusion (no-reflow phenomenon, failed stent, or wrong vessel). Requires immediate notification of cardiology - may need rescue PCI or CABG. Lack of improvement is itself a critical finding.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Acute Pulmonary Embolism
subtitle: 62 y/o female, post-op day 5 hip arthroplasty, sudden dyspnea
nursesNote: 0815 - 62 y/o female POD#5 right total hip arthroplasty, otherwise recovering well, suddenly developed acute shortness of breath while ambulating to the bathroom. Reports sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsens with inspiration. Anxious, diaphoretic, stating 'I feel like I cannot catch my breath.' Right calf tender and slightly swollen with positive Homans sign noted. PMH: obesity (BMI 34), HTN, oral contraceptive use until 1 year ago. SCDs were ordered but client reports inconsistent use overnight. Lovenox prophylaxis given on schedule. STAT CT pulmonary angiogram ordered; troponin and BNP drawn; cardiology consulted. Client A&Ox4, no prior cardiac history, no leg cast, no recent travel.

patient.name: L. Henderson
patient.admitDate: POD#5 hip arthroplasty

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) cues that BEST establish high clinical suspicion for acute pulmonary embolism in this client.

opts.text: Sudden-onset dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain in a post-op patient with unilateral calf tenderness and swelling
opts.rat: Classic PE triad. Post-op immobility is a major Virchow's triad risk factor. Unilateral calf findings strongly suggest DVT as the embolic source (Wells criteria: 3 points for clinical signs of DVT).

opts.text: Progressive hypotension and tachycardia (BP 108/68 -> 88/54, HR 118 -> 132) with hypoxemia despite supplemental oxygen
opts.rat: Hemodynamic instability defines MASSIVE (high-risk) PE - mortality approaches 50% without rapid intervention. RV failure causes obstructive shock. This single finding upgrades treatment to thrombolytics or embolectomy.

opts.text: ABG showing acute respiratory alkalosis with severe hypoxemia (PaO2 58, PaCO2 28, pH 7.48)
opts.rat: The PE-classic ABG: hyperventilation drops CO2 (alkalosis) but the V/Q mismatch from clot prevents oxygen uptake (hypoxemia). PaO2 <60 = respiratory failure threshold.

opts.text: BMI 34 (obesity)
opts.rat: A risk FACTOR for VTE but not a current clinical cue establishing acute PE. History informs probability; current findings establish diagnosis.

opts.text: Prior oral contraceptive use (stopped 1 year ago)
opts.rat: Hormonal therapy is a historical risk factor. Discontinued 1 year ago, so contributes minimally to current event.

opts.text: D-dimer 4,820 ng/mL
opts.rat: Elevated D-dimer is SUPPORTIVE but extremely non-specific - elevated in surgery, infection, malignancy, pregnancy. Useful only when NEGATIVE to rule out PE in low-probability patients. The clinical picture and CTPA establish the diagnosis, not the D-dimer.

opts.text: Lovenox prophylaxis given on schedule
opts.rat: Medication compliance is reassuring history but does not establish or rule out PE - prophylactic doses can fail, especially with inconsistent SCD use.

opts.text: A&Ox4 with no prior cardiac history
opts.rat: Reassuring (no AMS yet) but a normal finding - not a CUE of PE.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly link the cues to the underlying pathophysiology.

opts.text: A clot from the deep veins of the leg traveled through the IVC and right heart, lodging in a pulmonary artery and creating a V/Q mismatch (ventilation without perfusion)
opts.rat: Classic embolic pathway. The clot blocks pulmonary artery flow, so alveoli ventilate but cannot exchange gas - explains hypoxemia despite normal lung mechanics (Lewis Med-Surg 11e, p. 561).

opts.text: Acute pulmonary artery obstruction increases right ventricular afterload, causing RV strain and eventually obstructive shock with hypotension and lactic acidosis
opts.rat: The RV is thin-walled and tolerates acute afterload poorly. Elevated troponin and BNP here confirm RV strain. Hypotension and rising lactate signal the transition to massive PE.

opts.text: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 (respiratory alkalosis), but ventilation cannot correct the hypoxemia caused by the V/Q mismatch
opts.rat: The patient breathes faster trying to compensate, blowing off CO2 - but no amount of ventilation overcomes blocked perfusion. This is why PE patients often need anticoagulation/thrombolysis, not just oxygen.

opts.text: The hypoxemia is best explained by alveolar hypoventilation from chest pain
opts.rat: Splinting from pain reduces tidal volume, but the primary mechanism here is V/Q mismatch from arterial obstruction - hence the very high A-a gradient.

opts.text: Aggressive IV fluid bolus will improve hemodynamics by increasing RV preload
opts.rat: DANGEROUS. Excessive fluid worsens RV distension and septal bowing into the LV, dropping cardiac output further. Modest fluids (~500 mL) only if hypovolemic; vasopressors are preferred for shock.

opts.text: A normal chest X-ray rules out PE
opts.rat: Chest X-ray is often NORMAL or shows nonspecific findings in PE. Definitive diagnosis is by CT pulmonary angiogram (or V/Q scan if CT contraindicated).

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the differentials from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability
opts.rat: Post-op immobility, unilateral calf signs, sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, classic ABG, troponin/BNP rise, and now hypotension - textbook massive PE.

opts.text: Submassive PE (intermediate-risk) with RV strain
opts.rat: Same disease spectrum without the hypotension. The patient has now progressed past this category as BP dropped to 88/54.

opts.text: Acute MI / STEMI
opts.rat: Troponin is elevated and chest pain is present, but pleuritic quality, hypoxemia, and unilateral calf signs point away from primary cardiac event. Worth considering and ruling out with ECG.

opts.text: Pneumothorax
opts.rat: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain fit, but no trauma history and absent breath sounds would be expected. CXR rules in/out quickly.

opts.text: Acute MI from contrast nephropathy
opts.rat: No contrast given yet (CTPA pending). Distractor.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) MOST time-critical interventions for this hemodynamically unstable PE.

opts.text: Apply high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask, target SpO2 >=94%
opts.rat: Refractory hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch demands maximal oxygen delivery. ABCs - oxygenation comes first.

opts.text: Initiate IV unfractionated heparin per weight-based protocol (bolus + infusion)
opts.rat: Therapeutic anticoagulation must start immediately when PE suspicion is high - delaying for confirmatory imaging is dangerous. UFH is preferred over LMWH in unstable patients because it is reversible if thrombolysis is given (CHEST guidelines).

opts.text: Prepare for systemic thrombolytic therapy (alteplase) and notify provider that BP is 88/54 with rising lactate
opts.rat: Massive PE with hemodynamic instability is a class I indication for thrombolytics. The 'tPA for stroke is 90 min, tPA for PE is hours' rule applies. Alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours is standard.

opts.text: Administer 2 L of 0.9% NS bolus wide open to raise BP
opts.rat: Excessive fluid worsens RV distension and drops cardiac output. Limit to ~500 mL if hypovolemic; use norepinephrine for shock.

opts.text: Position the client flat (Trendelenburg) to improve venous return
opts.rat: Trendelenburg worsens dyspnea and is contraindicated in respiratory distress. Semi-Fowler's or position of comfort is preferred.

opts.text: Hold all anticoagulation until CTPA confirms PE
opts.rat: DANGEROUS. With high clinical suspicion and instability, anticoagulation is started empirically. Each hour of delay increases mortality.

opts.text: Administer aspirin 325 mg PO and prepare for cardiac catheterization
