steps.inst: Select ALL findings that are clinically significant cues requiring immediate nursing attention.

opts.text: Day 7 of high fever unresponsive to antipyretics in a previously healthy 4-year-old with no clear localizing source
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — fever ≥5 days is the cardinal criterion for Kawasaki Disease diagnosis. Prolonged unexplained fever in pediatric practice is one of the longest considered DDx — KD always on the list. Once 5 days reached without source, KD workup activated.

opts.text: Bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctivitis with perilimbal sparing — classic KD feature
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — 1 of 5 classic criteria. 'Non-purulent' is key (purulent suggests infection); 'perilimbal sparing' (clear ring around iris) is a classic KD finding. Other criteria need to be checked systematically.

opts.text: Strawberry tongue + cracked red lips + diffuse oral/pharyngeal injection (no exudate, no Koplik spots)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — oral changes — 1 of 5 classic criteria. The combination of strawberry tongue + cracked lips is characteristic. Distinguish from scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, strep+) and measles (Koplik spots, conjunctivitis with light sensitivity, no live vaccines).

opts.text: Polymorphous truncal rash spreading to extremities (maculopapular, not vesicular)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — rash — 1 of 5 classic criteria. 'Polymorphous' means it can take many forms — morbilliform, scarlatiniform, urticarial — but NOT vesicular (which would suggest viral exanthem like varicella). No bullae, no target lesions (rules out SJS/erythema multiforme).

opts.text: Extremity changes: reddened, edematous hands and feet earlier in week; NOW periungual desquamation of fingertips beginning today (Day 7+) — late finding
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — extremity changes — 1 of 5 classic criteria. Desquamation is a LATE finding (Week 2+) — when it appears, often clinches the diagnosis retrospectively. Patient is presenting with the constellation appearing in this order over the week.

opts.text: Unilateral L cervical lymphadenopathy 2 cm, tender
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — adenopathy — 1 of 5 classic criteria. Often the MOST VARIABLE criterion (can be absent in classic KD). Unilateral, >1.5 cm, often firm, sometimes tender. Distinguish from infectious lymphadenitis (suppurative, with overlying redness — would have positive culture or response to antibiotics).

opts.text: Echocardiogram: mildly DILATED left main coronary artery z-score +2.4 (normal <2.0)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — coronary involvement raises urgency. Z-score 2.0–2.5 is dilated (borderline); 2.5–5.0 small aneurysm; 5.0–10.0 medium; >10.0 giant. Treatment with IVIG within Day 10 of illness substantially reduces progression risk (~25% to ~5% aneurysm rate).

opts.text: Inflammatory markers markedly elevated: CRP 18.4, ESR 88, WBC 18.6, platelets 614, albumin 2.8 — KD lab pattern
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — supports KD diagnosis. Characteristic KD pattern: WBC ↑, platelets ↑ in Week 2 (often 600K–1M+), CRP ↑↑, ESR ↑↑, albumin ↓, mild hepatitis pattern. No single lab confirms KD (clinical diagnosis), but lab profile supports.

opts.text: Sterile pyuria (WBC 12/hpf, LE positive, nitrites negative, urine culture growing nothing) — characteristic of KD
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — supportive finding. Sterile pyuria reflects urethritis-like inflammation common in KD; rules out UTI as alternative fever source. Useful for ruling in/out.

opts.text: Infection workup NEGATIVE (strep neg, viral panel neg, blood cx neg at 24 hr, SARS-CoV-2 PCR neg)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — rules out the most important alternative diagnoses. KD is a CLINICAL diagnosis (no single confirming test); ruling out mimics is part of the workup. SARS-CoV-2 PCR negative + no prior COVID history is important to rule out MIS-C (the most relevant modern mimic).

opts.text: Weight 17.8 kg — needed for ALL pediatric medication dosing (every dose is mg/kg)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — pediatric dosing principle. Weight is the dosing weight for IVIG (2 g/kg = 35.6 g), ASA (80 mg/kg/day = 360 mg q6h initially), and maintenance fluids (Holliday-Segar). Confirm and document admission weight; recheck if rapid weight change concern.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA
opts.rat: Reassuring — no drug allergies. Document and proceed. Helpful given the IVIG and ASA being initiated.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate linkages between cues and underlying pathophysiology / management.

opts.text: KAWASAKI DISEASE is an ACUTE MEDIUM-VESSEL VASCULITIS of childhood; preferentially affects coronary arteries; cause unknown (likely infectious trigger in genetically predisposed children); peak age 6 months to 5 years; classic diagnosis requires FEVER ≥5 days + 4 of 5 principal criteria (or fever + 3 criteria + coronary findings on echo)
opts.rat: CORRECT — disease definition. The peak age and clinical-diagnosis nature are high-yield. Older or younger atypical-age cases exist (INCOMPLETE KD) with similar treatment based on fewer criteria + supportive labs/echo.

opts.text: Untreated KD has ~25% risk of CORONARY ARTERY ANEURYSM, with subsequent thrombosis, infarction, sudden death; treatment with IVIG WITHIN DAY 10 of illness reduces aneurysm rate to ~5%; treatment after Day 10 still beneficial but lower efficacy
opts.rat: CORRECT — drives the urgency of diagnosis and treatment. Day 7 (today) is within the optimal window. IVIG mechanism is unclear but thought to modulate immune response. Repeat echocardiogram at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks to detect aneurysms.

opts.text: IVIG dose for KD is 2 g/kg IV over 10–12 hours as a SINGLE infusion; premedicate with acetaminophen + diphenhydramine; monitor for rate-related infusion reactions (chest tightness, dyspnea, flushing, headache, back pain, fever, rash); slow or pause if symptoms
opts.rat: CORRECT — IVIG administration high-yield. Slow rate initially, advance gradually. Most reactions are rate-related and resolve with slowing. Severe reactions are rare. Monitor vitals frequently during infusion.

opts.text: ASPIRIN in KD: HIGH-DOSE 80 mg/kg/day divided q6h x 48 hr after fever resolution (anti-inflammatory dose), then TRANSITION to LOW-DOSE 3–5 mg/kg PO once daily (antiplatelet dose) for at least 6–8 weeks until labs normal and echo clear; longer if persistent coronary involvement
opts.rat: CORRECT — KD is one of the few PEDIATRIC indications for aspirin. High dose for anti-inflammatory effect during acute phase; transition to low antiplatelet dose for coronary protection during convalescent phase. Reye syndrome theoretical concern has not been substantiated in KD.

opts.text: PEDIATRIC ASPIRIN GENERAL RULE: AVOID in children with viral illness due to RISK OF REYE SYNDROME (encephalopathy + fatty liver after viral illness — influenza, varicella); KD is one of the very few pediatric ASA INDICATIONS; other rare ones include rheumatic fever, certain cardiac conditions, post-Fontan procedure
opts.rat: CORRECT — high-yield nursing teaching. Parents should NEVER give ASA to a child with viral illness. KD-treatment ASA is an exception under medical guidance; verify with family the rationale and the timing of low-dose transition. Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines important for ASA-treated children (prevent triggers).

opts.text: IVIG passive antibodies interfere with attenuated LIVE VIRUS VACCINES (MMR, varicella) for ~11 MONTHS; defer those vaccines for 11 months after IVIG; INACTIVATED vaccines (flu shot — NOT FluMist nasal which is live, DTaP, IPV, pneumococcal, Hib, hepatitis) continue on schedule
opts.rat: CORRECT — important family education and EMR documentation. Document the IVIG date and the 'no live vaccines' end date in EMR; notify PCP and school. The inactivated flu shot is recommended in ASA-treated children to reduce flu risk and theoretical Reye risk.

opts.text: Maintenance IV fluid calculation for pediatrics — HOLLIDAY-SEGAR 4-2-1 rule: 4 mL/kg/hr for first 10 kg + 2 mL/kg/hr for next 10 kg + 1 mL/kg/hr beyond; for this 17.8 kg child = 40 + 15.6 = 55.6 ≈ 56 mL/hr
opts.rat: CORRECT — pediatric fluid foundation. D5 1/2 NS is standard maintenance; D5 NS is acceptable per recent AAP guidance (isotonic preferred to prevent hyponatremia); avoid hypotonic in acutely ill children. Reassess as PO intake improves; do not over-resuscitate.

opts.text: PERSISTENT FEVER >36 hr after IVIG completion = IVIG REFRACTORY (10–20% of cases); options for treatment: SECOND DOSE IVIG (2 g/kg), or IV METHYLPREDNISOLONE pulse (30 mg/kg x 3 days), or INFLIXIMAB (anti-TNFα); pediatric rheumatology / cardiology consultation
opts.rat: CORRECT — escalation pathway. Refractory KD has higher coronary aneurysm risk; aggressive escalation justified. Track fever curve during and after IVIG; rapid involvement of subspecialty teams.

opts.text: Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO q6h continues alongside high-dose aspirin for combined anti-inflammatory and fever control
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — NSAIDs (ibuprofen) AVOIDED in KD treatment because they INTERFERE with the antiplatelet effect of aspirin (especially when transitioning to low-dose ASA). Acetaminophen is the appropriate antipyretic; NSAIDs HELD during ASA therapy.

opts.text: MMR booster vaccine should be given before discharge to maximize protection before the IVIG-induced 11-month deferral period passes
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — exactly backward. IVIG INTERFERES with live virus vaccines for ~11 months; giving MMR right after IVIG would render the vaccine INEFFECTIVE (no immune response generated). Defer live vaccines 11 months; document deferral; PCP plans re-vaccination.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Rank nursing concerns from highest to lowest priority
steps.inst: Rank these nursing concerns from #1 (HIGHEST priority) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Risk for Coronary Artery Aneurysm / Cardiac Complications r/t Kawasaki vasculitis with current LMCA z-score +2.4; need urgent IVIG treatment within Day 10 of illness
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. The whole point of treatment is preventing this. IVIG within Day 10 reduces aneurysm rate from ~25% to ~5%. Serial echocardiography at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks tracks evolution. ASA antiplatelet effect protects coronary thrombosis.

opts.text: Risk for IVIG Infusion Reaction r/t the prolonged infusion of a blood product (immunoglobulin) over 10–12 hours
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Most reactions are rate-related and manageable (slow or pause infusion). Severe anaphylaxis-like reactions are rare. Premedicate; monitor vitals frequently (q15 min early, q30 min, then q1h); be alert for chest tightness, dyspnea, flushing, headache, back pain, fever, rash.

opts.text: Pain / Comfort / Hydration r/t cracked lips, oral pain, sore mouth → refusing PO → dehydration
opts.rat: #3 — Significant. Mild dehydration on admission; oral pain from KD inflammation. Lubricant ointment for lips; cool soft preferred foods (popsicles, smoothies); IV fluids during the acute phase; acetaminophen for pain. Resolves as inflammation responds to treatment.

opts.text: Family Distress / Caregiver Knowledge Deficit r/t new diagnosis, complex treatment regimen, prolonged follow-up requirements, and fear
opts.rat: #4 — Important. Parents need clear education on: what KD is, why ASA in this case, watching for warning signs (chest pain, severe abdominal pain, syncope, unusual fatigue), follow-up echo schedule, vaccine deferral, normal activity guidance. Child Life for age-appropriate explanation to the child.

opts.text: Risk for Vaccine Mismanagement r/t IVIG interference with live virus vaccines for 11 months
opts.rat: #5 — Important but lowest in immediate stack. Document IVIG date and live-vaccine-defer end date in EMR; notify PCP and school; inactivated vaccines (flu — NOT live nasal FluMist) continue on schedule. Plan re-vaccination timing with PCP.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH intervention, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this client at this moment.

opts.text: IVIG 2 g/kg IV (35.6 g for 17.8 kg) over 10–12 hours via PIV; premedicate with acetaminophen + diphenhydramine 30 min before; monitor vitals q15 min x 1 hr, then q30 min x 2 hr, then q1h
opts.rat: Core treatment of KD; reduces aneurysm rate from ~25% to ~5% when given within Day 10. Slow rate initially; advance gradually; monitor for infusion reactions (slow/pause if symptoms; can usually restart at lower rate).

opts.text: HIGH-DOSE ASPIRIN 80 mg/kg/day divided q6h (= 360 mg PO q6h for 17.8 kg) x 48 hr after fever resolution, then transition to LOW-DOSE 3–5 mg/kg once daily for at least 6–8 weeks until labs normal and echo clear
opts.rat: KD is one of the few PEDIATRIC ASA indications. Anti-inflammatory dose during acute phase; antiplatelet dose for coronary protection in convalescent phase. Hold NSAIDs (interfere with antiplatelet effect).

opts.text: Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO q6h scheduled for additional anti-inflammatory effect alongside the aspirin
opts.rat: ⚠️ HOLD NSAIDs while on ASA in KD — they interfere with the antiplatelet effect of aspirin (especially during low-dose transition). Use ACETAMINOPHEN for fever and pain. NSAIDs may resume after ASA discontinuation.

opts.text: Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO q4–6h PRN fever and discomfort; cool compresses; lubricant ointment to cracked lips; bicarbonate mouth rinse
opts.rat: Comfort and supportive care during the acute phase. Acetaminophen is safe with ASA (different mechanism, no antiplatelet interference). Oral care eases the discomfort that's limiting PO intake.

opts.text: Maintenance D5 1/2 NS at 56 mL/hr (Holliday-Segar 4-2-1 calculation for 17.8 kg = 56 mL/hr); reassess as PO improves; encourage cool soft preferred foods (popsicles, smoothies, applesauce)
opts.rat: Pediatric maintenance fluids during the inflammatory phase + mild dehydration. Cool soft foods bypass oral pain. Reassess fluid needs as PO improves; do not over-resuscitate.

opts.text: Echocardiogram NOW (baseline), repeat at 2 WEEKS, repeat at 6–8 WEEKS; pediatric cardiology consultation; longer surveillance if coronary abnormalities persist
opts.rat: Standard KD surveillance. Baseline at diagnosis; 2-week and 6-8 week follow-up are routine. Coronary abnormalities at any visit prompt longer surveillance and possibly continued antiplatelet therapy.

opts.text: Give MMR booster vaccine BEFORE discharge to maximize protection before the IVIG-induced deferral period
opts.rat: ⚠️ Exactly backward. IVIG INTERFERES with live virus vaccines for ~11 months; MMR given right after IVIG would be ineffective. DEFER live vaccines (MMR, varicella, FluMist nasal) for 11 months; inactivated vaccines (flu shot, DTaP, IPV, pneumococcal, Hib) continue on schedule.

opts.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring during IVIG infusion and 24 hr after; ECG q-shift; pediatric cardiology consultation
opts.rat: Surveillance for cardiac complications (arrhythmia, myocarditis, ischemia). KD can cause myocarditis with PR prolongation, T-wave changes, low voltage. Continuous monitoring during and after IVIG.

opts.text: If persistent fever >36 hr after IVIG completion: second-dose IVIG 2 g/kg OR IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse x 3 days OR infliximab (anti-TNFα); pediatric rheumatology/cardiology consultation
opts.rat: Escalation for IVIG-refractory KD (10–20% of cases). Higher aneurysm risk in refractory cases. Document fever curve; escalate within 36 hr if no defervescence after IVIG.

opts.text: Child Life consultation for age-appropriate explanation, distraction during IVIG infusion, and coping support
opts.rat: Pediatric standard of care. Age-appropriate communication ('your body is fighting something'); distraction (toys, games, parents reading); coping support for fear/pain. Parents rooming-in are central to comfort.

opts.text: Family education on warning signs to return for: new fever >38.5, chest pain, severe abdominal pain, syncope, unusual fatigue, severe irritability — ANY of these = return immediately
opts.rat: Discharge teaching. Coronary complications can occur in weeks-to-months after acute KD; parents must know what to watch for. Written instructions; verbal teach-back; PCP and cardiology follow-up confirmed.

opts.text: Strict isolation (contact + droplet + airborne) precautions to prevent transmission
opts.rat: KD is NOT infectious. Standard precautions only. Family fear of transmission is understandable — reassure clearly. The negative infection workup (strep, viral panel, blood cx, COVID PCR) supports this.

opts.text: Document IVIG date in EMR with 'NO LIVE VACCINES x 11 months' alert; notify PCP and school; plan re-vaccination after deferral period
opts.rat: Critical post-treatment documentation. Without the alert, MMR/varicella might be given inappropriately and rendered ineffective. PCP coordinates re-vaccination at the 11-month mark; school awareness for any vaccine-related school policy.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: What is the FIRST action sequence?
steps.inst: Rank the order in which the nurse should implement these actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Confirm weight 17.8 kg; calculate IVIG dose 35.6 g; pharmacy verifies; premedicate with acetaminophen 15 mg/kg + diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg PO 30 min before infusion; ensure PIV patency
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Weight-based dosing verification is the foundational pediatric safety step. Premedication reduces infusion reactions. PIV must be patent and well-secured for the 10–12 hr infusion.

opts.text: START IVIG 2 g/kg over 10–12 hr at low initial rate (0.5 mL/kg/hr first 30 min); first vitals at 15 min into infusion, then q15 min x 1 hr, then q30 min x 2 hr, then q1h; continuous pulse oximetry; cardiac monitor
opts.rat: #2 — Begin the core treatment with vigilant monitoring. Most infusion reactions occur in the first hour. Rate advances gradually if tolerated. Slow or pause if symptoms; can usually restart at lower rate.

opts.text: Begin HIGH-DOSE ASPIRIN 360 mg PO q6h; HOLD ibuprofen and other NSAIDs; acetaminophen scheduled for fever and discomfort; lubricant to lips; cool soft preferred foods; maintenance D5 1/2 NS at 56 mL/hr
opts.rat: #3 — Adjunctive treatment + comfort. ASA is the second component of the KD treatment bundle. Comfort measures reduce distress and support oral intake. Maintenance fluids during the acute phase.

opts.text: Family education during admission: what KD is, why ASA is being given to a child, IVIG monitoring, follow-up echo schedule at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks, vaccine deferral 11 months, warning signs to return for, Child Life consultation for the patient
opts.rat: #4 — Education while there is time and continuity with the unit team. Build understanding over the admission days; teach-back; written materials. Child Life for the child's coping.

opts.text: Track fever curve during and after IVIG; if persistent fever >36 hr after IVIG completion = IVIG REFRACTORY → consult rheumatology / cardiology / ID for second dose IVIG, IV methylprednisolone, or infliximab; document in EMR; coordinate discharge with cardiology follow-up scheduled, ASA transition plan, vaccine deferral documented
opts.rat: #5 — Sustained care planning. Escalation pathway if refractory; discharge planning for sustained outpatient management. Cardiology owns the longitudinal coronary surveillance; PCP coordinates general care + vaccine timing.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: 24 hr after IVIG completion: afebrile, alert, eating soft foods, less irritable, conjunctivitis resolving, lips healing; CRP 8.2 (down from 18.4), ESR 60 (down from 88); transition to low-dose ASA 60 mg PO daily planned
opts.rat: Excellent response to IVIG. Continue low-dose ASA for 6–8 weeks until labs normal and echo clear; longer if coronary abnormalities persist. Plan discharge with cardiology follow-up at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks. Family education on home regimen.

opts.text: Discharge day 3 (Day 9 of illness): afebrile x 48 hr, tolerating regular diet, ambulating normally, low-dose ASA daily, vaccine deferral documented in EMR, pediatric cardiology echo follow-up scheduled at 2 weeks; parents verbalize understanding of warning signs and return precautions
opts.rat: Successful trajectory. Discharge criteria met. Continued outpatient monitoring with serial echocardiograms. Parents armed with knowledge and follow-up plan. Schools and PCP notified.

opts.text: 2-week post-discharge follow-up: afebrile, eating normally, energy returning, fingertip desquamation spreading (expected), Beau's lines on nails developing (expected late finding), repeat echo shows LMCA z-score +1.6 (down from +2.4, now normal); CRP 1.2, ESR 22 (normal)
opts.rat: Excellent outcome. Coronary dilation has resolved. Continue low-dose ASA until 6–8 week echo confirms continued normalization; transition off ASA only after cardiology clearance. Normal activity. Continue regular pediatric care.

opts.text: 36 hr after IVIG completion: persistent fever 38.8°C, ongoing irritability, no improvement in oral or extremity findings — IVIG-REFRACTORY KD
opts.rat: Refractory KD — 10–20% of cases. Higher coronary aneurysm risk. Escalate to second-dose IVIG (2 g/kg), or IV methylprednisolone pulse (30 mg/kg x 3 days), or infliximab (anti-TNFα). Pediatric rheumatology/cardiology/ID consultation.

opts.text: 1 hr into IVIG infusion: develops chest tightness, dyspnea, flushing, BP 92/52 (mild drop), HR 138 — infusion reaction
opts.rat: Rate-related infusion reaction. SLOW or PAUSE the infusion; additional diphenhydramine PRN; reassess; can usually restart at lower rate after symptoms resolve. Severe reaction with hypotension/airway compromise = STOP infusion and manage as anaphylaxis (epinephrine, steroids, fluids).

opts.text: Week 4 post-discharge: 6-week echo shows new SMALL coronary aneurysm z-score +3.8; cardiology continues low-dose ASA; adds clopidogrel for dual antiplatelet; plan exercise stress testing later
opts.rat: Progression despite treatment. Dual antiplatelet for moderate-larger aneurysms; consider warfarin for giant aneurysms (z >10). Activity restrictions per cardiology (no contact sports). Long-term cardiology surveillance every 6–12 months; lifelong monitoring for some patients.

opts.text: Family asks the discharge nurse if they should give MMR booster (which is due next month) — nurse re-educates that live vaccines deferred for 11 months post-IVIG; documents teach-back; PCP plans rescheduled MMR
opts.rat: Expected teaching reinforcement. Documentation of vaccine deferral is critical. Without the alert, PCP might administer MMR and it would be ineffective. School should be informed of the temporary delay. Inactivated flu vaccine in season is recommended.

opts.text: Periungual desquamation extends from fingertips to toes over the next week (Day 14 of illness); skin coming off in sheets
opts.rat: Expected — desquamation is a LATE feature of KD (Week 2–3), benign, sometimes dramatic in appearance but not concerning. Reassure family; gentle skin care; no treatment needed. Often the most-asked-about finding by parents post-discharge.

opts.text: Mild bilateral knee arthralgia at week 3 of illness; no swelling or warmth; resolves with rest over 5 days
opts.rat: Expected — mild arthralgia/arthritis occurs in some KD patients during convalescent phase. Self-limited. Acetaminophen if needed for comfort (or transition from ASA if appropriate per cardiology). Distinguish from true arthritis (joint warmth, effusion, severe pain) — which would prompt rheumatology evaluation.

opts.text: Family report at 6-week visit: child sleeping well, eating normally, returned to preschool, energy at baseline, has not had any new fever; echo entirely normal — cardiology plans to D/C ASA
opts.rat: Best-case complete recovery. ASA discontinuation per cardiology clearance. Routine pediatric care resumed. Plan re-vaccination at 11-month mark per PCP. Document final outcome in EMR.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Eclampsia at 35 Weeks with Magnesium Sulfate Toxicity After Loading Dose
subtitle: Magnesium Is the Seizure Prophylaxis, Calcium Gluconate Is the Antidote — Reflexes, Respirations, and Urine Output Are the Three Things You Check at Every Pass

patient.name: T. Nguyen-Hartwell (G2P1 at 35+2 weeks)
patient.admitDate: Today, 0915 (L&D triage arrival via husband for severe headache + vision changes; witnessed eclamptic seizure at 0942)
patient.room: L&D Bed 3 → OR pending emergent cesarean for non-reassuring fetal heart tracing + maternal stabilization

vitals.time: 1030 (CURRENT — 30 min into magnesium maintenance after 4 g loading dose; new hyporeflexia, drowsy, RR 10)

labs.n: Serum magnesium level (stat — drawn 1025 after 30 min into maintenance infusion)
labs.r: THERAPEUTIC range for seizure prophylaxis in eclampsia/preeclampsia: 4–7 mEq/L (5–8 mg/dL); toxicity 7–10 mEq/L (loss of DTRs at ~10); 10–13 (respiratory depression); >13 cardiac arrest; nonpregnant normal 1.7–2.4

labs.n: Reflex assessment (the most important clinical assay)
labs.v: Patellar (knee jerk) reflex ABSENT bilaterally; biceps 1+; pre-magnesium reflexes were 3+ (mildly hyperreflexic from preeclampsia)
labs.r: DTR monitoring during magnesium infusion is the CLINICAL antidote-decision tool — loss of patellar reflex precedes respiratory depression by minutes-to-hours, signaling stop-the-mag time. Document q1h during infusion; reassess after any rate change

labs.v: Pre-mag RR 22; 15 min into loading dose RR 18; 30 min into maintenance RR 10 (current); clinically appears mildly drowsy + sleepy
labs.r: Respiratory rate is a key magnesium toxicity vital sign — target ≥12/min; <12 = toxicity warning; <8 = severe toxicity requiring respiratory support; mag depresses respiratory drive AND smooth muscle of respiratory accessory muscles

labs.v: Foley catheter placed at 0950; UOP 25 mL in 40 min (= ~38 mL/hr) — borderline; pre-mag UOP not measured (no catheter yet)
labs.r: MAGNESIUM is RENALLY EXCRETED; UOP <30 mL/hr = relative oliguria → mag accumulates → toxicity at the same infusion rate. UOP <100 mL in 4 hr = the typical cutoff for reducing or holding maintenance

labs.v: Tonic-clonic generalized seizure x 90 seconds at 0942 in L&D triage room; preceded by complaint of severe headache and seeing 'flashing spots'; no incontinence, brief tongue laceration, postictal x 8 min with confusion; one episode, no recurrence; on continuous fetal monitor throughout
labs.r: ECLAMPSIA = SEIZURE in pregnancy/postpartum without other identified cause, in setting of preeclampsia (HTN + proteinuria/end-organ); can occur antepartum (50%), intrapartum (20%), or postpartum (30%, with peak in first 48 hr but up to 6 weeks); seizure prophylaxis post-event is mandatory

labs.v: BP 178/118 (severe ≥160/110); proteinuria 4+ on dipstick (severe ≥5 g/24 hr quantitative); platelets 88 (low); AST 142 (elevated); LDH 380; creatinine 1.1; severe headache; visual changes (flashing spots = scotomata); brisk reflexes pre-mag (3+); no pulmonary edema currently; mild RUQ tenderness; estimated dry weight 3+ kg gain over baseline
labs.r: Severe preeclampsia features (ANY ONE of): BP ≥160/110, plt <100, AST/ALT >2x upper limit, Cr >1.1 or doubling, persistent severe headache or visual changes, pulmonary edema, severe RUQ pain. Eclampsia (seizure) overrides feature counting — proceed with full treatment regardless of count

labs.v: Loading dose 4 g IV over 20 min started 0950, completed 1010; maintenance 2 g/hr IV infusion started 1010 (currently running); total Mg given so far ~4.7 g (4 g load + 0.7 g of maintenance at 30 min mark)
labs.r: STANDARD eclampsia/severe preeclampsia regimen: LOAD 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, then MAINTENANCE 1–2 g/hr IV continuous; alternative IM regimen (5 g each buttock then 5 g IM q4h) used in low-resource settings; continue for 24 hr after delivery or 24 hr after last seizure (whichever later)

labs.v: Pre-seizure: Category I (reassuring) — baseline 145, moderate variability, accelerations present; during seizure: prolonged deceleration to 80 lasting 6 min (expected during maternal seizure from uteroplacental compromise); since seizure: tachycardia 175, MINIMAL variability, recurrent LATE DECELERATIONS — Category III (non-reassuring → emergent delivery indication)
labs.r: NICHD 3-tier FHR system: Cat I normal, Cat II indeterminate, Cat III abnormal (recurrent late decels with absent variability or sinusoidal — emergent delivery). The seizure caused acute uteroplacental compromise; recovery is expected but late decels post-event signal need for emergent delivery

labs.v: 35+2 weeks by certain LMP and confirmed by 1st trimester ultrasound; estimated fetal weight 2.4 kg by Leopold and recent growth ultrasound — appropriate for gestational age; head down; NICU notified for late preterm delivery (expect transient respiratory distress, possible RDS, thermoregulation, glucose monitoring)
labs.r: 35–36 weeks = LATE PRETERM (34–36+6); generally good outcomes but with elevated risk of respiratory issues, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, feeding difficulties, jaundice. Antenatal steroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM q24h x 2 doses) ideally completed >24 hr before delivery — NOT possible here given the emergent indication; neonatology aware

labs.v: G2P1: 1st pregnancy 3 yr ago — normal SVD at 39 weeks with mild gestational HTN (not preeclampsia); no chronic HTN; no prior preeclampsia; type 2 DM screened negative; BMI 32 (Class I obesity — risk factor); no prior surgeries; no family history of preeclampsia (per intake); irregular prenatal care this pregnancy — missed last 2 visits ('busy with work, didn't think it mattered')
labs.r: Risk factors for preeclampsia: nulliparity (vs multipara — she's multip but with prior gestational HTN), prior preeclampsia, chronic HTN, DM, obesity, advanced maternal age >35, family history, autoimmune (lupus, APLS), kidney disease, IVF/donor egg, multiple gestation. Inadequate prenatal care = missed BP trends

labs.v: CBC: WBC 14.2, Hgb 10.8, Plt 88 (low — preeclampsia/HELLP feature); BMP: Na 132, K 4.0, Cl 102, HCO3 22, BUN 14, Cr 1.1 (mildly elevated from pregnancy baseline ~0.7), glucose 92; LFTs: AST 142, ALT 96, total bili 0.8, LDH 380 (elevated; HELLP if ≥600); haptoglobin pending; coags: INR 1.0, fibrinogen 380 (normal); UA: 4+ protein, no nitrites/LE
labs.r: HELLP syndrome features partially present: hemolysis pending, ELEVATED LIVER ENZYMES present (mild), LOW PLATELETS present — partial HELLP variant. Could progress; monitor q4–6h; concerning for DIC if fibrinogen drops or INR rises

labs.v: Severe-range BP 178/118 → IV LABETALOL 20 mg IV push given at 0945; if BP not <160/110 in 10 min, repeat 40 mg; if not, repeat 80 mg; alternatives: hydralazine 5–10 mg IV slow push, nifedipine 10 mg PO; AVOID ACE inhibitors (teratogenic) and nitroprusside (cyanide toxicity in prolonged use)
labs.r: Target BP 140–155 / 90–105 (NOT 'normal' — over-correction reduces uteroplacental perfusion); labetalol contraindicated in asthma and bradycardia (this patient OK); hydralazine alternative for asthma; nifedipine alternative oral

labs.v: No pulmonary edema on lung auscultation (clear bilaterally); no abruptio placentae signs (no vaginal bleeding, no uterine tetany); no DIC clinically (no oozing from IV sites, fibrinogen 380); no focal neuro deficit post-seizure (rules out stroke); no history of seizure disorder
labs.r: Helps narrow differential of the seizure to eclampsia (most likely) rather than stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, epilepsy, hypoglycemia (glucose 92 — ruled out), illicit drug-induced

nursesNote: 1030 — 28 y/o G2P1 at 35+2 weeks presented to L&D triage at 0915 via husband for severe headache and 'flashing spots' in vision; BP on arrival 178/118 (severe range), 4+ proteinuria, platelets 88, AST 142, mild RUQ tenderness — SEVERE PREECLAMPSIA. At 0942 patient had a witnessed generalized TONIC-CLONIC SEIZURE lasting ~90 seconds in the triage room — ECLAMPSIA. Maintained airway during seizure with left-side positioning, suction at bedside, supplemental O2 by NRB; postictal 8 min with confusion then alert. During the seizure the continuous fetal monitor showed prolonged deceleration to 80 lasting 6 min (expected acute uteroplacental compromise during maternal seizure). Since seizure, FHR pattern has been NON-REASSURING (Category III): baseline tachycardia 175, MINIMAL variability, recurrent LATE decelerations — emergent cesarean section being prepared, anesthesia at bedside, OR being readied. MAGNESIUM SULFATE seizure prophylaxis initiated immediately after seizure stabilization: 4 g IV loading dose over 20 min (0950–1010), then 2 g/hr IV maintenance infusion started 1010 (currently running); also given LABETALOL 20 mg IV push at 0945 for the severe-range BP (BP improved to 162/104). At 1030 (30 min into maintenance infusion), bedside reassessment per protocol revealed concerning changes: PATELLAR REFLEX ABSENT bilaterally (was 3+ pre-magnesium); biceps 1+; RESPIRATORY RATE 10 (down from 18); patient drowsy; complaining of warmth and flushing (common at therapeutic levels but excessive here). Stat mag level drawn at 1025 returned 9.4 mEq/L — TOXIC RANGE. UOP 25 mL in 40 min via foley = ~38 mL/hr (borderline; magnesium is renally excreted, so reduced UOP → accumulation). IMMEDIATELY STOPPED THE MAGNESIUM INFUSION; CALCIUM GLUCONATE 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) IV slow push over 3 min started — the antidote for magnesium toxicity; reassessing reflexes, RR, mentation every 5 min initially. Notified attending OB physician (already at bedside for cesarean prep), anesthesia, NICU. The competing tensions: she needs seizure prophylaxis (mag) to prevent recurrent eclamptic seizure, AND she has mag toxicity (need to hold or reduce). Plan after calcium gluconate: monitor; once reflexes and RR recover, plan to RESTART maintenance magnesium at REDUCED RATE (1 g/hr) given her oliguria; continue close monitoring of reflexes, RR, UOP, level; remember magnesium continues postpartum (24 hr after delivery OR 24 hr after last seizure — whichever later). Continuous fetal monitoring; OR ready for emergent cesarean; foley to gravity (mag-mandated for accurate UOP monitoring); IV access x 2 (18g R AC, 20g L forearm); type & crossmatch 2 units PRBC and 2 FFP. Husband at bedside, very anxious but supportive; speaking with the chaplain. NICU on standby for late preterm delivery — antenatal betamethasone not feasible given emergent indication; neonate may need brief respiratory support, glucose monitoring, thermoregulation. Postpartum eclampsia risk remains for up to 6 weeks (peaks first 48 hr) — continue mag prophylaxis post-cesarean for 24 hr, then close BP monitoring, education on warning signs (severe headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, decreased urine output, swelling).
providerOrders: EMERGENT CESAREAN SECTION for Category III FHR (recurrent late decels with minimal variability post-eclamptic seizure) and severe preeclampsia/eclampsia in 35+2 wk gestation; anesthesia at bedside; OR ready; NICU notified

MAGNESIUM SULFATE seizure prophylaxis: LOAD 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min (DONE), MAINTENANCE 1–2 g/hr IV continuous; continue for 24 HR AFTER DELIVERY OR 24 HR AFTER LAST SEIZURE, whichever later; restart at REDUCED rate (1 g/hr) given current oliguria after mag toxicity resolves

MAGNESIUM TOXICITY (CURRENT EVENT — level 9.4, absent patellar reflex, RR 10): (1) STOP infusion immediately, (2) CALCIUM GLUCONATE 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV slow push over 3 min — the ANTIDOTE; antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction; effect within minutes

Magnesium MONITORING — q1h during infusion: (1) DEEP TENDON REFLEXES (patellar primary; biceps if epidural in place); (2) RESPIRATORY RATE (target ≥12/min; <12 = toxicity warning; <8 = stop and antidote); (3) URINE OUTPUT (target ≥30 mL/hr; <100 mL in 4 hr = reduce or hold maintenance); (4) Serum level q4–6h or with any clinical change
Magnesium therapeutic range 4–7 mEq/L; toxicity progression: 7–10 mEq/L loss of DTRs → 10–13 respiratory depression → >13 cardiac arrest; clinical findings track ahead of the lab value

ANTIHYPERTENSIVE for severe-range BP (≥160/110): LABETALOL 20 mg IV push (DONE); if BP not <160/110 in 10 min: repeat 40 mg, then 80 mg (max 220–300 mg total); ALTERNATIVES: HYDRALAZINE 5–10 mg IV slow push q15–20 min (preferred in asthma); NIFEDIPINE 10 mg PO short-acting (NOT sublingual which causes precipitous drops); target BP 140–155 / 90–105 (NOT 'normal' — over-correction reduces uteroplacental perfusion)
AVOID ACE inhibitors, ARBs (teratogenic — fetal renal toxicity, oligohydramnios, skull defects); AVOID nitroprusside (cyanide toxicity in prolonged use, fetal cyanide)
Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring; reassess FHR pattern q15 min during stabilization and during transport to OR
Continuous maternal cardiac monitoring; pulse oximetry; q15-min vitals during active treatment then q1h
Two large-bore IV accesses (≥18 g); type & crossmatch 2 units PRBC + 2 FFP; have on standby
Foley catheter to gravity (mag-mandated for accurate UOP monitoring during infusion); STRICT I&O hourly; UOP target ≥30 mL/hr
NPO for cesarean delivery; H2 blocker (famotidine 20 mg IV) for aspiration prophylaxis; sodium citrate 30 mL PO non-particulate antacid immediately pre-op
Position LEFT LATERAL TILT (10–15° wedge under right hip) to displace gravid uterus off IVC and aorta — improves cardiac output and uteroplacental perfusion

AIRWAY READY for seizure recurrence or worsening respiratory depression from mag — bag-mask, suction, oral airway, ET tube; anesthesia at bedside; consider IV access for emergent intubation drugs (succinylcholine for RSI — NOTE: succinylcholine MAY HAVE PROLONGED EFFECT IN MAGNESIUM TOXICITY due to NMJ interaction; cisatracurium or rocuronium may also be prolonged)

Seizure recurrence management: if seizure during mag infusion (breakthrough), give additional MAG SULFATE 2–4 g IV over 5–10 min; if persistent, escalate to LORAZEPAM 2–4 mg IV or LEVETIRACETAM 60 mg/kg IV; NEVER give phenytoin first-line in eclampsia (less effective than mag); manage airway, position left lateral, oxygen, document

Labs: STAT magnesium q4–6h or with clinical change; CBC, CMP, LFTs, coags, fibrinogen, LDH, haptoglobin, type & crossmatch q6h until stable (watch for HELLP/DIC progression); urine protein/creatinine ratio

NICU at delivery — late preterm 35+2 wk with non-reassuring FHR; expect transient respiratory issues; antenatal betamethasone NOT FEASIBLE given emergent indication; neonatal resuscitation team at delivery

Postpartum: CONTINUE magnesium for 24 hr after delivery (or 24 hr after last seizure, whichever later); BP monitoring q1h x 4 hr, q2h x 24 hr, q4h until discharge; warning signs education before discharge (severe headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, decreased UOP, severe swelling, chest pain, dyspnea); follow-up BP check at 3–7 days postpartum; 6-week postpartum visit
POSTPARTUM ECLAMPSIA RISK: up to 6 WEEKS postpartum, with PEAK in first 48 hr; education and warning-sign awareness; outpatient BP self-monitoring; PCP and OB f/u
Anti-D (RhoGAM) postpartum if mother Rh-negative (verify type)
VTE prophylaxis postpartum: pneumatic compression devices intraop and continued postop; LMWH (enoxaparin) once not actively bleeding (preeclampsia + cesarean + obesity = elevated VTE risk)
Family support: husband present; chaplain available; social work; lactation consult for postpartum (mother may face delayed milk-coming-in due to preterm + cesarean — encouragement and pump support)

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL findings that are clinically significant cues requiring immediate nursing attention.

opts.text: MAGNESIUM TOXICITY: serum level 9.4 mEq/L (therapeutic 4–7), ABSENT patellar reflex bilaterally, RR 10, drowsy, flushed — clinical + lab confirmation
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — drug toxicity in progress. STOP the infusion IMMEDIATELY; give CALCIUM GLUCONATE 1 g IV slow push (antidote). Reflex loss precedes respiratory depression — recognize early. Mag toxicity progression: loss of DTRs → respiratory depression → cardiac arrest at very high levels.

opts.text: Eclamptic seizure (witnessed tonic-clonic x 90 seconds) in a patient with severe preeclampsia (BP 178/118, 4+ proteinuria, platelets 88, AST 142, mild HELLP features)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — eclampsia defines need for magnesium seizure prophylaxis + delivery planning. Severe preeclampsia criteria already met pre-seizure; eclampsia (seizure) confirms the most severe form. Risk of recurrence without prophylaxis is high; mag must continue (at reduced rate after toxicity resolves).

opts.text: Non-reassuring FHR pattern (Category III): baseline tachycardia 175, minimal variability, recurrent late decelerations — post-seizure uteroplacental compromise
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — EMERGENT CESAREAN INDICATION. Category III FHR = abnormal = expedited/emergent delivery. Position mother left lateral tilt, O2 by NRB, IV fluid bolus, prepare OR, NICU notified.

opts.text: Severe-range BP 162/104 (down from 178/118 after labetalol) — still above the severe threshold of 160/110
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — additional antihypertensive needed. Target BP 140–155 / 90–105 (NOT 'normal'); over-correction reduces uteroplacental perfusion. Repeat labetalol 40 mg if BP remains ≥160/110 in 10 min; can escalate to 80 mg; or alternative hydralazine 5–10 mg IV slow.

opts.text: Oliguria UOP ~38 mL/hr — magnesium is renally excreted; reduced clearance = accumulation at the same infusion rate
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — explains the toxicity development. Magnesium clearance is renal; UOP <30 mL/hr or <100 mL in 4 hr should prompt reducing or holding maintenance. Patient was at borderline UOP, and her renal function compromised from preeclampsia (Cr 1.1) — predictable accumulation.

opts.text: Preeclampsia with HELLP features: platelets 88, AST 142 — partial HELLP
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — may progress; monitor q4–6h for full HELLP, DIC, hepatic dysfunction. Delivery is treatment for HELLP/preeclampsia; postpartum monitoring continues for at least 48 hr (HELLP can worsen postpartum).

opts.text: Late preterm 35+2 wk delivery imminent — NICU notified; antenatal betamethasone not feasible given emergent indication
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — neonatal considerations. Late preterm at risk of respiratory distress, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, feeding difficulty, jaundice. Neonatal resuscitation team at delivery. Mother–baby separation likely for NICU admission.

opts.text: Risk of postpartum eclampsia: up to 6 weeks postpartum, peaks first 48 hr — continued magnesium prophylaxis for 24 hr post-delivery
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — sustained care planning. Many providers and patients think 'baby out = problem solved' — wrong. Postpartum eclampsia is real and avoidable with continued mag and BP monitoring. Discharge education on warning signs is critical.

opts.text: Irregular prenatal care — missed last 2 visits; BP trend was rising (146/96 at last visit 4 days ago)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — modifiable risk factor for future pregnancy. Preeclampsia surveillance requires regular BP and urine monitoring; missed visits lose the trend. Patient education on importance of prenatal care; address barriers (work, transportation, childcare).

opts.text: Husband at bedside, supportive, very anxious
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — family support and communication. Anxious partner during obstetric emergency benefits from clear updates, chaplain support, and inclusion in decision-making when possible. Chaplain available; social work as needed.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA
opts.rat: Reassuring — no drug allergies. Document and proceed.

opts.text: Temperature 98.2°F
opts.rat: Reassuring — rules out infection / fever as confounding factor. Not the primary issue.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: What is happening pharmacologically and pathophysiologically?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate linkages between cues and underlying pharmacology / pathophysiology.

opts.text: ECLAMPSIA = seizure in a pregnant or postpartum patient (within 6 weeks) without other identified cause, in the setting of preeclampsia (HTN + proteinuria/end-organ); pathophysiology = endothelial dysfunction, cerebral vasospasm, hypertensive encephalopathy, possibly PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome)
opts.rat: CORRECT — definition and mechanism. Eclampsia can occur antepartum (50%), intrapartum (20%), postpartum (30%); postpartum eclampsia peaks first 48 hr but can occur up to 6 weeks. Delivery is the definitive treatment but does not eliminate immediate risk.

opts.text: MAGNESIUM SULFATE is the FIRST-LINE seizure prophylaxis AND treatment in eclampsia; mechanism likely via NMDA receptor antagonism, cerebral vasodilation, calcium channel modulation; superior to phenytoin and diazepam in obstetric trials (Magpie, Eclampsia Trial Collaborative); maternal AND fetal safety profile well-established
opts.rat: CORRECT — high-yield OB pharm. Standard dosing: LOAD 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, MAINTENANCE 1–2 g/hr IV continuous; continue 24 hr post-delivery or 24 hr after last seizure (whichever later). NEVER give phenytoin or benzo as first-line in eclampsia — less effective.

opts.text: MAGNESIUM TOXICITY progression: loss of deep tendon reflexes at ~7–10 mEq/L → respiratory depression at 10–13 → cardiac arrest at >13; CLINICAL findings track AHEAD of the lab value; monitor REFLEXES (patellar), RESPIRATIONS (rate), URINE OUTPUT (renal excretion) at every assessment pass
opts.rat: CORRECT — the three-check rule. Bedside clinical assessment is the most reliable real-time toxicity detection. Reflex loss precedes respiratory depression by minutes-to-hours. Document the trifecta q1h during infusion; reassess after any rate change or change in clinical status.

opts.text: CALCIUM GLUCONATE 1 g IV slow push over 3 min is the ANTIDOTE for magnesium toxicity — directly antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and cardiac membrane; effect within minutes; can be repeated if needed; have at bedside during any mag infusion
opts.rat: CORRECT — high-yield. Calcium gluconate (peripheral OK) over 3 min, NOT push too fast (cardiac risk). 1 g (10 mL of 10%) is standard initial; can repeat. Calcium chloride (3x more elemental Ca) only via central line (vesicant). The unique exception to 'don't give calcium for hyperK in dig toxicity' — here, calcium IS the answer.

opts.text: Magnesium is RENALLY EXCRETED; reduced UOP (<30 mL/hr or <100 mL in 4 hr) = accumulation at the same infusion rate; preeclampsia patients often have reduced renal function — monitor UOP closely and reduce mag rate if oliguric
opts.rat: CORRECT — explains the predictable toxicity pattern. Patient had borderline UOP 38 mL/hr with mildly elevated Cr 1.1 — accumulation was inevitable. After toxicity resolves, restart mag at reduced rate (1 g/hr instead of 2) given renal compromise.

opts.text: Eclampsia/severe preeclampsia BP target: 140–155 / 90–105 — NOT 'normal'; over-correction reduces uteroplacental perfusion. First-line IV: LABETALOL 20 mg → 40 → 80 (max 220–300); HYDRALAZINE 5–10 mg slow push (preferred in asthma); NIFEDIPINE 10 mg PO short-acting (NEVER sublingual)
opts.rat: CORRECT — BP target rationale. Severe HTN >160/110 = stroke risk in mother → treat; moderate HTN <160/110 acceptable. Labetalol contraindicated in asthma/bradycardia; hydralazine for asthma. NEVER short-acting nifedipine sublingually (precipitous drop, hypotension, fetal distress).

opts.text: ANTI-HYPERTENSIVES TO AVOID IN PREGNANCY: ACE inhibitors and ARBs (teratogenic — fetal renal toxicity, oligohydramnios, skull defects, IUGR); nitroprusside (cyanide toxicity in prolonged use, fetal cyanide); atenolol associated with growth restriction
opts.rat: CORRECT — drug safety in pregnancy. Methyldopa, labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine are mainstays. ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated 2nd-3rd trimester; some teratogenic effects in 1st trimester too. Document and educate.

opts.text: Definitive treatment for severe preeclampsia/eclampsia is DELIVERY; magnesium provides seizure prophylaxis bridging to delivery; antihypertensives manage BP; once delivered, the disease resolves over weeks (BP often elevated for 6 weeks postpartum; education on outpatient management)
opts.rat: CORRECT — only the placenta is the cure. Delivery timing balances maternal severity vs fetal maturity. Severe preeclampsia or eclampsia at ≥34 weeks → deliver. <34 weeks → individualize based on stability + betamethasone. At 35+2 weeks here, delivery is clearly indicated.

opts.text: Phenytoin (Dilantin) 20 mg/kg IV is the FIRST-LINE drug for eclampsia seizures
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium in eclampsia (multiple trials showed mag superior at reducing recurrent seizures). MAGNESIUM SULFATE is first-line. Phenytoin reserved for refractory cases or contraindications to mag. NCLEX trap if you generalize 'phenytoin for seizures.'

opts.text: Continue magnesium at the same rate (2 g/hr) despite the toxicity — the seizure prophylaxis benefit outweighs the risks
opts.rat: ⚠️ DANGEROUSLY WRONG. Toxicity at the current rate will progress to respiratory arrest. STOP, give calcium gluconate, then RESTART at REDUCED RATE (1 g/hr) once recovered. The competing tensions (seizure prevention vs toxicity) are managed by reducing rate, not continuing toxic levels.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Rank nursing concerns from highest to lowest priority
steps.inst: Rank these nursing concerns from #1 (HIGHEST priority) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Risk for Respiratory Arrest r/t magnesium toxicity (level 9.4, RR 10, absent reflexes) — imminent if not antidoted
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Mag toxicity progression to respiratory arrest is the imminent killer. STOP infusion + calcium gluconate IV is the immediate response. Airway equipment ready; anesthesia at bedside; reassess RR, reflexes, mentation in minutes.

opts.text: Risk for Fetal Compromise / Demise r/t Category III FHR pattern with recurrent late decels, post-seizure uteroplacental compromise
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. EMERGENT cesarean indicated. Position left lateral tilt, O2 by NRB, IV fluid bolus, OR ready, NICU notified. Fetal status dictates delivery urgency; maternal stabilization in parallel.

opts.text: Risk for Recurrent Eclamptic Seizure r/t severe preeclampsia, peripartum window; need for continued magnesium prophylaxis once toxicity resolves
opts.rat: #3 — HIGH. Mag remains the seizure prophylaxis; restart at reduced rate after toxicity recovers. Continue 24 hr post-delivery or 24 hr after last seizure. Maintain seizure precautions; airway readily accessible; benzodiazepines available for breakthrough.

opts.text: Severe Hypertension r/t severe preeclampsia BP 162/104 still above severe threshold — stroke risk
opts.rat: #4 — Significant. Treat to 140–155 / 90–105 (NOT 'normal'). Repeat labetalol 40 mg if BP ≥160/110 in 10 min; can escalate to 80 mg; or hydralazine alternative. Avoid over-correction (uteroplacental perfusion).

opts.text: Knowledge Deficit / Family Distress r/t complex emergent diagnosis, fear for mother and baby, planned cesarean and NICU admission
opts.rat: #5 — Important but lowest in immediate physiologic stack. Clear communication with husband; chaplain; social work; later education on postpartum eclampsia risk + warning signs + outpatient monitoring + future pregnancy considerations.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH intervention, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this client at this moment.

opts.text: STOP magnesium sulfate infusion immediately; CALCIUM GLUCONATE 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV slow push over 3 min — the antidote
opts.rat: Immediate reversal of magnesium toxicity. Antagonizes Mg at the neuromuscular junction and cardiac membrane. Effect within minutes. Can be repeated if needed. Have at bedside during any mag infusion.

opts.text: Continue magnesium at the same rate (2 g/hr) and add lorazepam 4 mg IV to prevent recurrent seizure
opts.rat: ⚠️ DANGEROUSLY WRONG. Continuing toxic levels leads to respiratory arrest. Stop, antidote, restart at REDUCED rate. Benzodiazepines additionally suppress respiratory drive in an already-mag-depressed patient — combined depression is dangerous.

opts.text: Once magnesium toxicity resolves (DTRs return, RR ≥12), RESTART maintenance at REDUCED rate 1 g/hr (not 2 g/hr) given oliguria
opts.rat: Resumption of seizure prophylaxis at adjusted rate. Renal function dictates rate. Continue 24 hr post-delivery or 24 hr after last seizure (whichever later). Reassess UOP and reflexes q1h.

opts.text: EMERGENT CESAREAN section for non-reassuring FHR + severe preeclampsia/eclampsia at 35+2 wk; anesthesia, OR, NICU coordinated
opts.rat: Definitive treatment for the eclampsia and the fetal compromise. Cesarean (rather than vaginal) given the Category III FHR and the maternal severity. Anesthesia choice typically regional if feasible; general if rapid airway needed or contraindication to neuraxial.

opts.text: LABETALOL 40 mg IV push if BP remains ≥160/110 after the 20 mg dose; alternative HYDRALAZINE 5–10 mg slow push if labetalol contraindicated; target 140–155 / 90–105
opts.rat: Sequential dose escalation for severe-range BP. Target maintains uteroplacental perfusion while preventing maternal stroke. Avoid over-correction. AVOID ACE inhibitors and nitroprusside in pregnancy.

opts.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg for rapid BP lowering
opts.rat: ⚠️ Sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous BP drops with severe maternal hypotension and fetal distress; NEVER use sublingually. Oral short-acting nifedipine 10 mg PO is an acceptable alternative when needed; IV labetalol or hydralazine preferred.

opts.text: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV loading dose as first-line for seizure prophylaxis
opts.rat: ⚠️ Less effective than magnesium for eclampsia seizure prevention (Magpie and Eclampsia Trial). Mag is first-line. Phenytoin reserved for refractory cases or mag contraindications.

opts.text: Left lateral tilt positioning (10–15° wedge under right hip) to displace gravid uterus off IVC and aorta; supplemental O2 by NRB
opts.rat: Improves cardiac output and uteroplacental perfusion. Acute intervention for non-reassuring FHR. Continue during transport to OR. Supplemental O2 supports both maternal and fetal oxygenation.

opts.text: Foley catheter to gravity for accurate UOP monitoring during magnesium infusion (target ≥30 mL/hr)
opts.rat: Mag-mandated monitoring — UOP is one of the three checks (reflexes, RR, UOP). Allows real-time detection of oliguria → mag accumulation. Continues postpartum during the 24-hr mag continuation.

opts.text: Two large-bore IVs; type & crossmatch 2 units PRBC + 2 FFP; have on standby; airway equipment + anesthesia at bedside
opts.rat: Pre-operative readiness for emergent cesarean. PRBC for surgical losses; FFP if HELLP/DIC progresses. Airway equipment for potential respiratory failure from mag toxicity OR for emergent intubation for cesarean.

opts.text: NICU notification for late preterm 35+2 wk delivery with non-reassuring FHR; antenatal betamethasone (cannot be administered given the emergent indication)
opts.rat: Neonatal team at delivery. Late preterm risks: respiratory distress, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, feeding difficulty, jaundice. Betamethasone would benefit if there were 24+ hr; emergent delivery precludes.

opts.text: Postpartum continuation of magnesium for 24 hr after delivery (or 24 hr after last seizure, whichever later); BP monitoring q1h x 4 hr then q2h x 24 hr; education on postpartum eclampsia warning signs
opts.rat: Postpartum eclampsia risk extends to 6 weeks with peak 48 hr. Continued mag and BP monitoring. Discharge education: severe headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, decreased UOP, severe swelling, chest pain, dyspnea — return for ANY.

opts.text: Anti-D (RhoGAM) postpartum if mother is Rh-negative; VTE prophylaxis with pneumatic compression and LMWH once not actively bleeding
opts.rat: Standard postpartum cesarean care. Verify Rh status; RhoGAM within 72 hr if Rh- mother with potentially Rh+ baby. VTE prophylaxis essential — preeclampsia + cesarean + obesity = elevated VTE risk.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: What is the FIRST action sequence?
steps.inst: Rank the order in which the nurse should implement these actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: STOP magnesium infusion immediately; CALCIUM GLUCONATE 1 g IV slow push over 3 min; airway equipment + anesthesia at bedside; reassess RR, reflexes, mentation q5 min
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. The mag toxicity is the imminent killer. Stop the cause; antidote the effect; have airway support ready. Calcium gluconate effect within minutes. Document time, dose, response.

opts.text: Left lateral tilt position; supplemental O2 by NRB; IV fluid bolus 500 mL NS; reassess FHR pattern; expedite OR transport for emergent cesarean
opts.rat: #2 — Fetal status interventions in parallel. Left lateral tilt + O2 + fluid bolus are the bedside interventions to improve uteroplacental perfusion while OR is being readied. FHR may improve; if not, expedite cesarean.

opts.text: Repeat LABETALOL 40 mg IV push for the BP 162/104 (still ≥160/110); reassess BP in 10 min; alternative HYDRALAZINE 5–10 mg if needed; target 140–155 / 90–105
opts.rat: #3 — BP control while readying for delivery. Target not 'normal' but below severe threshold. Document; reassess; can escalate to 80 mg labetalol if needed.

opts.text: Once magnesium toxicity resolves (DTRs return, RR ≥12, more alert): RESTART maintenance magnesium at REDUCED rate 1 g/hr given oliguria; continue close mag monitoring (reflexes, RR, UOP, level q4–6h)
opts.rat: #4 — Resumption of seizure prophylaxis at adjusted rate. Continue 24 hr post-delivery or 24 hr after last seizure (whichever later). Reduced rate accounts for the oliguria contributing to the toxicity event.

opts.text: Coordinate OR + anesthesia + NICU + neonatology for cesarean delivery; communicate with husband; chaplain; postpartum plan with continued mag, BP monitoring, education on postpartum eclampsia warning signs
opts.rat: #5 — Sustained care + family + delivery coordination. Postpartum: continue mag, BP monitoring q1h x 4 hr then q2h x 24 hr, q4h until discharge. Discharge education on warning signs and outpatient follow-up at 3–7 days postpartum.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: 10 min after calcium gluconate + mag infusion stopped: patellar reflex 2+ bilaterally; biceps 2+; RR 16; alert and oriented x3; flushing resolving; reassess level pending
opts.rat: Antidote effective. Magnesium toxicity reversed at the receptor level. Mag level will trend down over hours. Plan to restart mag at REDUCED rate 1 g/hr once stable; continue cesarean preparation; reassess UOP and renal function.

opts.text: Post-cesarean (90 min after toxicity event): live infant female 2.3 kg, Apgar 7/8 (mild respiratory distress, transferred to NICU on HFNC), mother stable with BP 142/88 on labetalol IV, mag at 1 g/hr running with reflexes 2+ RR 18 UOP 50 mL/hr
opts.rat: Successful delivery and stabilization. Mother on the postpartum eclampsia/preeclampsia path. Baby in NICU for late preterm care. Continue mag x 24 hr post-delivery; BP monitoring; communicate with NICU; lactation support for pumping if not directly nursing.

opts.text: Discharge day 4: BP 134/82 on PO labetalol (transitioned from IV); off magnesium; CBC, LFTs, Cr trending toward normal; baby still in NICU on minimal support; postpartum eclampsia education completed with husband; outpatient BP follow-up at 5 days; 2-week and 6-week postpartum visits scheduled
opts.rat: Comprehensive recovery. Continued outpatient management. Education on warning signs: severe headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, decreased UOP, severe swelling, chest pain, dyspnea — return for ANY. Lactation support continued; mental health screening for postpartum mood; follow-up echo if cardiac concerns.

opts.text: 5 min after calcium gluconate: reflexes still absent, RR 8, decreasing mentation, SpO2 89% — calcium NOT yet effective or insufficient response
opts.rat: Inadequate response. Repeat calcium gluconate 1 g IV slow push; prepare for intubation; bag-mask ventilation if needed; anesthesia at bedside. Cardiac monitoring throughout. Continue mag held; cesarean expedited.

opts.text: Hour 6 postpartum: BP 188/120 (severe-range again); severe headache returning; visual changes; reflexes 4+ — postpartum eclampsia warning
opts.rat: Postpartum preeclampsia/eclampsia recurrence. Continue mag (now restart with another loading dose if needed); IV labetalol or hydralazine for BP; preparedness for postpartum seizure (60% of postpartum eclampsia occurs within first 24 hr). Continue mag x 24 hr from this point.

opts.text: Day 2 postpartum: HELLP labs worsen with platelets 42, AST 280, LDH 880, hemolysis on smear; coagulation derangement INR 1.6, fibrinogen 180 — full HELLP with possible DIC
opts.rat: Progression to full HELLP +/- DIC. Postpartum HELLP can worsen for 48–72 hr before improving. Supportive care: platelet transfusion if active bleeding or for procedure, FFP/cryo if fibrinogen <100, monitor for end-organ dysfunction (hepatic rupture rare but catastrophic). Hematology consult if needed.

opts.text: Postpartum eclampsia teaching: husband verbalizes warning signs to watch for at home (severe headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, decreased UOP, severe swelling); writes down outpatient follow-up appointments; comfortable using home BP cuff
opts.rat: Successful education outcome. Postpartum eclampsia risk up to 6 weeks — preparedness matters. Husband as informed family member improves home monitoring; home BP cuff for daily checks; clear written instructions; follow-up appointments scheduled (5 days, 2 weeks, 6 weeks).

opts.text: 6-week postpartum visit: BP 122/76 off all antihypertensives; baby thriving at home (discharged from NICU at 2 weeks); patient asks about future pregnancy risk
opts.rat: Full recovery. Counseling on future pregnancy: ~20% recurrence risk for preeclampsia (higher if severe/early-onset); recommended LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN 81 mg PO daily starting in 1st trimester for prophylaxis; calcium supplementation if intake low; preconception counseling; close prenatal care; refer for maternal-fetal medicine if planning another pregnancy.

opts.text: BP 142/86 on PO labetalol at 6 weeks postpartum; continuing antihypertensive; PCP follow-up established for ongoing HTN management
opts.rat: Persistent postpartum hypertension — common. Some women have residual HTN for weeks-to-months postpartum or develop chronic HTN unmasked by pregnancy. Continue antihypertensive; PCP for ongoing management; reassess at 12 weeks postpartum; cardiovascular risk factor reduction long-term.

opts.text: Baby remains in NICU at week 2 for late preterm feeding and thermoregulation; mother pumping with success; bonding strong; discharge planning underway
opts.rat: Expected NICU course for late preterm with non-reassuring FHR delivery. Feeding and thermoregulation are common late-preterm issues. Mother pumping maintains supply; skin-to-skin and feeding involvement encouraged; lactation consult; NICU social work for family support and discharge planning.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Serotonin Syndrome from Fluoxetine + Linezolid + Tramadol Triple-Hit
subtitle: Hunter Criteria, the Clonus is the Key Clinical Finding, Cyproheptadine Is the Antidote — and Why Fluoxetine Makes the Recovery Weeks Long

patient.name: S. Petrosian
patient.admitDate: Today, 1430 (ED via ambulance — roommate called 911 for confusion, sweating, shaking; she had been complaining of feeling 'really weird' since yesterday)
patient.room: ED Resus 3 → MICU pending bed (severe presentation)

vitals.time: PCP visit 5 days ago (when linezolid was prescribed)
1530 (CURRENT — after 1 L NS, cooling measures, lorazepam 2 mg IV, cyproheptadine being mixed)

labs.v: (1) FLUOXETINE (Prozac) 40 mg PO daily x 6 months for major depressive disorder — SSRI; (2) LINEZOLID 600 mg PO BID started 5 days ago by PCP for MRSA cellulitis — HAS MAOI ACTIVITY (the prescribing miss); (3) TRAMADOL 50 mg PO taken yesterday for cellulitis pain — SEROTONERGIC OPIOID (inhibits serotonin reuptake)
labs.r: ALL THREE are serotonergic. Combinations with MAOIs (including linezolid) are listed as contraindicated/dangerous; tramadol added to SSRI doubles serotonin syndrome risk. The PCP did not check interactions; many EHRs flag this combination but the alert was clicked through

labs.n: HUNTER CRITERIA for serotonin syndrome diagnosis (meets criteria)
labs.v: In setting of serotonergic agent use AND ONE of: (1) spontaneous CLONUS [PRESENT — spontaneous ankle clonus bilaterally], OR (2) inducible clonus + agitation OR diaphoresis [BOTH present], OR (3) ocular clonus + agitation OR diaphoresis [ocular clonus present], OR (4) tremor + hyperreflexia [PRESENT — fine tremor + brisk 4+ patellar reflexes], OR (5) hypertonia + temp >38°C + ocular/inducible clonus [PRESENT — lower extremity rigidity, temp 40.1°C, ocular clonus]
labs.r: Hunter Toxicity Criteria Decision Rules — 84% sensitivity, 97% specificity for serotonin syndrome (better than older Sternbach criteria); CLONUS is the key clinical finding that distinguishes from NMS (which has BRADYREFLEXIA + lead-pipe rigidity)

labs.v: T 40.1°C (104.2°F — severe hyperthermia); HR 138 (tachycardia); BP 168/104 (hypertension); RR 28 (tachypnea); SpO2 94% RA (mildly low); diaphoretic; mydriasis (dilated pupils) bilateral
labs.r: Autonomic hyperactivity triad: hyperthermia + tachycardia + hypertension. Hyperthermia >41.1°C (106°F) is LIFE-THREATENING (rhabdomyolysis, DIC, multi-organ failure); aggressive cooling required

labs.v: SPONTANEOUS ankle CLONUS bilaterally (more on right); inducible clonus at knees with passive flexion; OCULAR CLONUS (sustained horizontal nystagmus with eyes at extreme gaze); fine TREMOR of all four extremities; HYPERREFLEXIA 4+ in lower extremities, 3+ upper; rigidity LOWER extremities > UPPER (greater leg than arm — characteristic); no nuchal rigidity; no focal deficit
labs.r: Serotonin syndrome neuromuscular pattern: CLONUS + HYPERREFLEXIA + tremor + lower-extremity-predominant rigidity. Compare NMS: BRADYREFLEXIA + LEAD-PIPE rigidity (generalized, not lower-predominant). Compare anticholinergic: NO clonus, NO hyperreflexia (DRY skin/mucosa)

labs.v: Agitated, anxious, restless, distractible, mumbling, picking at clothes; oriented to self and 'in hospital'; not date; intermittently follows commands; hyperactive delirium pattern
labs.r: Mental status changes: agitation, anxiety, restlessness, hyperactive delirium; can progress to coma. Compare NMS: more obtunded/altered; compare anticholinergic: 'mad as a hatter' similar agitation but with dry-skin profile and mydriasis predominant

labs.v: WBC 14.2 (mild stress leukocytosis), Hgb 13.2, Plt 218; CK 1840 (elevated — early rhabdomyolysis from rigidity + hyperthermia); Cr 1.4 (mildly elevated from rhabdomyolysis + dehydration); HCO3 18, lactate 3.6 (metabolic acidosis from hypermetabolic state and muscle activity); INR 1.1; LFTs mildly elevated (AST 88, ALT 64)
labs.r: Findings of hypermetabolic state: rhabdomyolysis (CK ↑), metabolic acidosis (HCO3 ↓ lactate ↑), early AKI; severe cases progress to DIC, multi-organ failure. Trend q4h

labs.v: Rules OUT: NMS (would have lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, gradual onset over days; this is acute onset hours after the triggering medication), anticholinergic toxidrome (would have DRY skin and mucosa; this patient is DIAPHORETIC), malignant hyperthermia (would be perioperative with succinylcholine or halogenated anesthetic), thyroid storm (TSH/T4 pending), sepsis (no infection source despite cellulitis — being treated; lactate not severely elevated), meningitis (no nuchal rigidity, no headache history)
labs.r: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS is the most-tested distinction: ONSET (hours vs days), REFLEXES (hyper vs hypo/normal), RIGIDITY (lower > upper vs generalized lead-pipe), TRIGGER (serotonergic vs dopamine-antagonist), TREATMENT (cyproheptadine vs bromocriptine/dantrolene)

labs.v: UDS: positive for opiates (consistent with tramadol); negative for cocaine, amphetamines, PCP, MDMA, methamphetamine, benzodiazepines (ED gave lorazepam after collection); ETOH 0; APAP 0; salicylate 0
labs.r: Rules out concurrent intoxication (cocaine, MDMA, amphetamines — these are also serotonergic and would worsen the picture); rules out tylenol/aspirin overdose as cause of confusion + tachycardia + fever

labs.v: Fluoxetine: stable on 40 mg daily x 6 months for MDD (responded well, no recent dose change). Linezolid: prescribed by PCP 5 days ago for MRSA skin infection of L lower leg (cellulitis, area improving); PCP did NOT check interactions; EHR drug interaction alert was clicked through. Tramadol: taken yesterday by patient for cellulitis pain — she had leftover tramadol from a 2024 dental procedure
labs.r: Linezolid is technically an antibiotic but has MAOI activity (inhibits monoamine oxidase) — labeled as an MAOI for serotonin syndrome risk; combination with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, meperidine, ondansetron (high-dose IV), triptans is hazardous. Patient self-medication with leftover prescriptions added the third hit

labs.v: Major depressive disorder dx age 24, well-controlled on fluoxetine 40 mg daily; previous trials of sertraline (sexual side effects), escitalopram (insomnia); migraine 2–3x/year (treated with rizatriptan PRN — also serotonergic, but not used in past month); no chronic medical conditions
labs.r: MDD patients are commonly on chronic SSRI/SNRI — any provider adding a new medication must check serotonin syndrome risk. Common offenders to be alert for: tramadol, meperidine, linezolid, methylene blue, MAOIs, triptans, ondansetron (high-dose IV), dextromethorphan, MDMA, herbals (St. John's wort, ginseng, ginkgo)

labs.v: Fluoxetine half-life 1–6 DAYS; ACTIVE METABOLITE norfluoxetine half-life 4–16 DAYS; clinically: even after stopping fluoxetine, serotonergic effect can persist 2–5 WEEKS
labs.r: CRITICAL TEACHING: stopping the fluoxetine does NOT immediately resolve the risk. Patient must avoid all serotonergic agents for at least 5 weeks after discontinuation. Other SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram) have shorter half-lives ~1 day; fluoxetine is the outlier

labs.n: Cellulitis status (the original reason for linezolid)
labs.v: L lower leg cellulitis improving on linezolid (erythema reduced from 12 cm to 4 cm); culture grew MRSA (susceptibility: linezolid S, vancomycin S, doxycycline S, TMP-SMX S, clindamycin S); 5 days into a planned 10-day course
labs.r: Linezolid MUST BE DISCONTINUED given serotonin syndrome. Alternative MRSA-active oral antibiotics: DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg PO BID, TMP-SMX DS BID, CLINDAMYCIN 450 mg PO QID, or IV VANCOMYCIN — pick based on susceptibilities and renal function; all are non-serotonergic. ID consultation if complex

labs.v: No nuchal rigidity (rules out meningitis); no focal neuro deficit (rules out stroke); no recent illicit drug use per roommate (UDS confirms); no recent travel; no insect bites; no shellfish or new food exposure (rules out scombroid)
labs.r: Differential narrowed to serotonin syndrome based on clinical findings + medication history + ruling out alternatives

nursesNote: 1530 — 28 y/o female with MDD on chronic fluoxetine 40 mg PO daily x 6 months brought to ED by ambulance at 1430 after roommate called 911 for acute onset confusion, profuse diaphoresis, tremor, and 'shaking all over' since yesterday. Roommate states patient was prescribed LINEZOLID 600 mg PO BID 5 days ago by PCP for MRSA skin infection on L lower leg, and yesterday patient self-medicated with TRAMADOL 50 mg from a leftover 2024 prescription for cellulitis pain. Symptoms developed within 24 hr of the tramadol dose, and accumulated over the 5 days of linezolid. On arrival: T 104.2°F (40.1°C), HR 138, BP 168/104, RR 28, SpO2 94% RA; agitated, anxious, restless, mumbling; SPONTANEOUS ANKLE CLONUS BILATERALLY (greater on R), inducible clonus at knees, OCULAR CLONUS (sustained horizontal nystagmus at extreme gaze), fine tremor of all extremities, HYPERREFLEXIA 4+ LE / 3+ UE, lower-extremity-predominant rigidity (characteristic finding), diaphoretic, mydriasis bilateral. Meets HUNTER CRITERIA for serotonin syndrome (multiple ways): spontaneous clonus + tremor + hyperreflexia + hypertonia + temp >38°C + ocular/inducible clonus — all present. Differential ruled out: NMS would have BRADYREFLEXIA + lead-pipe rigidity (generalized, not LE-predominant) + gradual onset over days; this is acute onset with hyperreflexia + LE-predominant. Anticholinergic toxidrome would have DRY skin and mucosa; this patient is DIAPHORETIC. Malignant hyperthermia is perioperative anesthetic-triggered. Thyroid storm pending TSH but clinical context fits triple-serotonergic drug stack. Sepsis ruled out (cellulitis already treated, no high lactate). Labs concerning: CK 1840 (early rhabdomyolysis from rigidity + hyperthermia), Cr 1.4 (mild AKI), HCO3 18, lactate 3.6 (hypermetabolic acidosis). Treatment initiated: (1) STOPPED ALL THREE serotonergic agents — discontinued fluoxetine, discontinued linezolid (will switch MRSA coverage to DOXYCYCLINE per susceptibilities), no further tramadol; (2) AGGRESSIVE COOLING — ice packs to axilla/groin/neck, cool IV fluids 1 L NS bolus given, cooling blanket placed, target temp ≤38°C, monitor q15 min; (3) LORAZEPAM 2 mg IV given for agitation + autonomic instability (benzodiazepines first-line for agitation in serotonin syndrome — they reduce muscle activity that generates heat); (4) CYPROHEPTADINE 12 mg PO via NG (the antidote — antihistamine with 5-HT2A antagonism that reverses serotonin syndrome), then 2 mg q2h until symptoms resolve, with max 32 mg/day; (5) Aggressive IV hydration with NS at 200 mL/hr for rhabdomyolysis prevention (goal UOP >1 mL/kg/hr to prevent myoglobinuric AKI); (6) STRICT AVOIDANCE of ANTIPYRETICS for fever (the hyperthermia is from muscle activity, not hypothalamic set-point — acetaminophen/NSAIDs DO NOT WORK for this hyperthermia; reduce muscle activity with benzo + cyproheptadine + cooling). AVOID succinylcholine if intubation needed (hyperkalemia risk in rhabdomyolysis); use non-depolarizing agents (rocuronium, cisatracurium). AVOID physical restraints — they worsen the muscle activity that drives hyperthermia. For severe progressive cases: intubation + paralysis (non-depolarizing) + ICU. Continuous cardiac monitoring; SpO2; q15-min vitals during active treatment; foley to gravity for UOP measurement and rhabdo monitoring; arterial line being considered for closer hemodynamic monitoring. MICU bed coordinated. The CRITICAL DISCHARGE TEACHING POINT — FLUOXETINE has a 1–6 day half-life AND an ACTIVE METABOLITE (norfluoxetine) with half-life 4–16 days; even after discontinuation, serotonergic risk persists for 2–5 WEEKS. Patient must AVOID all serotonergic agents (tramadol, meperidine, linezolid, MAOIs, triptans, MDMA, methylene blue, St. John's wort, dextromethorphan high-dose) for at least 5 weeks after fluoxetine stops. Psychiatry consult for management of underlying depression during fluoxetine washout (consider bupropion, mirtazapine — non-serotonergic options; or supportive management until safe to restart serotonergic agent). Roommate at bedside, very supportive, very afraid; clear communication and chaplain available. Notified PCP about the linezolid–fluoxetine interaction event for their own learning; pharmacy and safety officer aware; this would be a teachable case for system improvement.
providerOrders: ADMIT to MICU given severe presentation (T 40.1°C, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis); continuous cardiac monitoring; pulse oximetry; arterial line being placed for beat-to-beat BP and ABG access

STOP ALL SEROTONERGIC AGENTS: D/C fluoxetine (educate that washout takes weeks given active metabolite), D/C linezolid (switch to alternative MRSA antibiotic), no further tramadol; avoid adding any new serotonergic agent (ondansetron HIGH-DOSE IV >4 mg should be avoided; low-dose oral OK; metoclopramide if antiemetic needed)

CYPROHEPTADINE (Periactin) — the ANTIDOTE; 12 mg PO/NG initial dose, then 2 mg PO/NG q2h until symptoms resolve, max 32 mg/day; for severe cases can give 12 mg q2h until clinical improvement; serotonin antagonist (5-HT2A) + antihistamine; sedation is a side effect; available PO only (no IV form)

Benzodiazepine for agitation + autonomic stability: LORAZEPAM 1–2 mg IV q4–6h PRN; titrate to RASS −1 to 0 (calm, easy to arouse); avoid over-sedation but adequate sedation reduces muscle activity that drives hyperthermia; midazolam infusion if continuous needed

AGGRESSIVE COOLING for hyperthermia >38.5°C: ice packs axilla/groin/neck, cool IV fluids, cooling blanket, exposed skin, fan to facilitate evaporative cooling; TARGET ≤38°C; reassess q15 min; cooling for ANY temp >40°C is emergent (life-threatening at >41.1°C / 106°F)

⚠️ AVOID ANTIPYRETICS (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) — the hyperthermia is from MUSCLE ACTIVITY not hypothalamic set-point reset; antipyretics do NOT WORK for serotonin syndrome hyperthermia; treat the muscle activity with benzo + cyproheptadine + cooling

⚠️ AVOID physical restraints — they worsen the muscle activity that drives hyperthermia; verbal de-escalation + benzodiazepine; safety equipment (1:1 observation, bed alarm, padded side rails) instead of restraints

Aggressive IV hydration with NS 0.9% at 200 mL/hr initially; target UOP >1 mL/kg/hr (= >75 mL/hr for 75 kg patient) to prevent myoglobinuric AKI from rhabdomyolysis; titrate down once CK trending and UOP adequate; alkalinization with bicarbonate (urine pH >6.5) if severe rhabdo (CK >5000 or rising)
Foley catheter to gravity for accurate UOP monitoring; observe urine color (tea/cola = myoglobinuria); strict I&O hourly
Trend labs q4h: BMP, CK, lactate, ABG, CBC; coags (DIC risk in severe hyperthermia); LFTs; TSH/Free T4 to rule out thyroid storm

Treat MRSA cellulitis with alternative non-serotonergic antibiotic per susceptibilities: DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg PO BID, or TMP-SMX DS BID, or CLINDAMYCIN 450 mg PO QID, or IV VANCOMYCIN if severe (renal-dosed); complete a 10-day total course (counting the 5 days of linezolid already given — likely 5 more days of alternative)

If intubation needed for severe progression: AVOID SUCCINYLCHOLINE (hyperK risk in rhabdomyolysis); use non-depolarizing paralytic (ROCURONIUM 1.2 mg/kg, or CISATRACURIUM); pre-oxygenation; ketamine alternative for induction; mechanical ventilation per ARDSnet if respiratory failure

Hemodynamic support: NS bolus for hypotension; if persistent hypotension despite fluid, DIRECT-ACTING vasopressor (PHENYLEPHRINE) preferred over indirect-acting (dopamine, ephedrine — release more serotonin); norepinephrine acceptable
Continuous EEG if mental status not improving with treatment (rule out non-convulsive status epilepticus from extreme hyperthermia)
Psychiatry consult: management of underlying MDD during fluoxetine washout (5 weeks); consider non-serotonergic agents (bupropion, mirtazapine); supportive psychotherapy; safety planning
Pharmacy consult: comprehensive medication interaction review; document the linezolid–fluoxetine event for the patient's EHR allergy/interaction list; flag for any future provider
ID consult: MRSA antibiotic transition; ensure adequate coverage; monitor cellulitis course
