labs.n: NEONATAL OUTCOMES + brachial plexus injury surveillance + birth trauma
labs.v: NEONATAL OUTCOMES after shoulder dystocia: (1) BRACHIAL PLEXUS INJURY (BPI) — most common neonatal complication; ~1-30% of shoulder dystocia (varies); occurs primarily from EXCESSIVE TRACTION on fetal head during dystocia maneuvers; types: ERB-DUCHENNE PALSY (C5-C6 most common 90% — arm extended + adducted + internally rotated + 'waiter's tip' position; loss of biceps + deltoid + rotator cuff function); KLUMPKE PALSY (C8-T1 — claw hand + Horner syndrome possible; rare); TOTAL BRACHIAL PLEXUS INJURY (C5-T1 — entire arm flaccid + severe); MAJORITY (~70-90%) resolve spontaneously within 6-12 months with physical therapy; PERSISTENT (~5-10%) require surgical intervention (nerve grafting + transfer + tendon transfer + reconstruction) by pediatric orthopedic + plastic surgeon at 3-6 months + intensive PT/OT lifelong; (2) CLAVICLE FRACTURE — often intentional in shoulder relief (controlled by physician); spontaneous fractures occur in shoulder dystocia + macrosomia; usually heals well + position arm in sling; pain management + monitor; (3) HUMERAL FRACTURE — less common; treat with positioning + cast if needed; (4) HYPOXIC-ISCHEMIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (HIE) — from delayed delivery + cord compression + fetal hypoxia; assess Apgar + arterial cord pH (acidosis pH <7.0 + base deficit ≥12 = severe HIE risk + therapeutic hypothermia consideration); neonatal team monitoring + escalation; (5) FETAL DEATH — rare but possible with severe + prolonged dystocia; (6) OTHER birth trauma — cephalohematoma + caput succedaneum + facial nerve injury. ASSESSMENT for brachial plexus injury at delivery + nursery: arm position + symmetry + range of motion + reflexes (moro + grip + asymmetric tonic neck + sucking); pediatric ortho consult if concerns; PT/OT evaluation early. THIS PATIENT newborn: APGAR 6/9 (recovered well); weight 4350 g; right arm extended + diminished tone + limited movement + flexed elbow on right + early signs of ERB PALSY C5-C6 (anterior shoulder traction from dystocia); moro reflex weakened on right; no obvious clavicle fracture on palpation; pediatric ortho consult activated; PT/OT consultation; immobilize arm in elbow flexion across chest (no traction or pulling); positioning to support natural posture; expected partial spontaneous recovery + ongoing surveillance.
labs.r: NEONATAL OUTCOMES after shoulder dystocia primarily brachial plexus injury (Erb palsy C5-C6 most common; majority resolve; some require surgery); clavicle/humeral fracture; HIE rare with prolonged dystocia; assessment + pediatric ortho consult + PT/OT + immobilization + monitoring + family education. RN role: assessment + family education + multidisciplinary referral.

labs.n: MATERNAL COMPLICATIONS + postpartum hemorrhage risk + lacerations
labs.v: MATERNAL COMPLICATIONS after shoulder dystocia: (1) POSTPARTUM HEMORRHAGE (PPH) — ELEVATED RISK from prolonged labor + manipulation + macrosomia (over-distended uterus → atony) + manual maneuvers (uterine atony + lacerations); 4 Ts of PPH = TONE (uterine atony — most common cause; treat with uterotonics + massage + bimanual compression + tamponade balloon + IR + hysterectomy); TRAUMA (lacerations + uterine inversion + uterine rupture); TISSUE (retained products of conception); THROMBIN (coagulopathy + DIC); UTEROTONICS = oxytocin first-line + methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM (CONTRAINDICATED in HTN/preeclampsia) + carboprost 250 mcg IM q15 min × 8 (CONTRAINDICATED in asthma) + misoprostol 600-1000 mcg PR/PO/buccal; ESCALATION = uterine massage + bimanual compression + tamponade balloon (Bakri) + IR embolization + hysterectomy ladder; MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL if shock; (2) PERINEAL/VAGINAL LACERATIONS — 3rd/4th degree more common from manipulation + macrosomia; sutured by OB; pain management + ice + sitz baths + monitoring; (3) SYMPHYSEAL SEPARATION — uncommon; treated conservatively or surgically depending on severity + symptoms; (4) FEMORAL NEUROPATHY from McRoberts maneuver hyperflexion — uncommon; usually resolves; (5) BLADDER INJURY — uncommon; assess voiding + UA + ultrasound if concerns; (6) PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAUMA — birth experience + emergent intervention + concern for baby + may require counseling + support + EAP for staff + family. INFANT OF DIABETIC MOTHER (IDM) maternal considerations: continued insulin management postpartum (typically rapid decrease in insulin requirements; some women have transient GDM only + postpartum diabetes screen at 6-12 weeks + lifelong screening); breastfeeding strongly encouraged (improves maternal glucose + neonatal outcomes); contraception planning + future pregnancy planning + preconception counseling for next pregnancy (better GDM management + earlier OGTT + insulin pump consideration). FAMILY-CENTERED CARE + emotional support + chaplain + social worker + birth experience processing + bonding + breastfeeding + family integration. THIS PATIENT postpartum: 2nd degree perineal laceration + extensive vaginal mucosal laceration repaired; EBL ~600 mL (above 500 threshold for vaginal PPH; manageable); uterotonics responsive; uterine tone improving with massage + oxytocin; type & crossmatch pending; 2nd IV access in place; vital signs stable; emotional + family support throughout; spouse at bedside; postpartum vigilance × 24 hr + breastfeeding initiation.
labs.r: MATERNAL COMPLICATIONS after shoulder dystocia primarily PPH risk + lacerations + symphyseal separation + femoral neuropathy + psychological trauma; active management of 3rd stage + uterotonics + monitoring + laceration repair + emotional support. RN role: PPH surveillance + medication administration + family + psychological support.

labs.n: IDM NEONATAL HYPOGLYCEMIA + comprehensive newborn care
labs.v: INFANT OF DIABETIC MOTHER (IDM) RISKS + management: (1) NEONATAL HYPOGLYCEMIA — most concerning + immediate; pathophysiology = maternal hyperglycemia → fetal hyperinsulinemia (fetal pancreas hyperplasia to compensate) → at delivery + umbilical cord clamping the placental glucose source removed but fetal/newborn insulin levels remain elevated → REACTIVE HYPOGLYCEMIA; THRESHOLD varies by institutional protocol — typically <40 mg/dL in IDM at risk; SCREENING per protocol = glucose finger stick at 30 min + 1 hr + 2 hr + then q1h × 4-6 hr + q3h × 24 hr; SYMPTOMATIC vs asymptomatic — symptomatic (lethargy + jitteriness + apnea + seizure + poor feeding + cyanosis + temperature instability) warrants immediate treatment + IV dextrose; ASYMPTOMATIC hypoglycemia may be addressed with EARLY BREASTFEEDING + skin-to-skin + supplemental formula if breastfeeding unsuccessful + REPEAT screening; PERSISTENT or symptomatic = IV DEXTROSE 10% (D10) 2 mL/kg bolus then continuous infusion 60-80 mL/kg/day; THIS PATIENT newborn glucose 32 at 30 min = treat with breastfeeding/formula + repeat; (2) MACROSOMIA + birth trauma — addressed; assess for additional injuries; (3) RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME (RDS) — delayed surfactant production from fetal hyperinsulinemia; may need supplemental O2 + CPAP + surfactant in late preterm IDM; (4) POLYCYTHEMIA — hyperglycemia → increased EPO + erythropoiesis → polycythemia; may cause hyperviscosity + jaundice + thrombosis; partial exchange transfusion if severe; (5) HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA — RBC breakdown + bruising from birth trauma + immature hepatic conjugation; phototherapy + monitoring + serial bilirubin levels; (6) HYPOCALCEMIA — maternal hyperglycemia suppresses fetal parathyroid → relative hypocalcemia at birth; treat with calcium gluconate; (7) HYPOMAGNESEMIA — similar mechanism; (8) CARDIOMYOPATHY — transient septal hypertrophy (hyperinsulinemia stimulates myocardial cells); usually resolves over months without treatment; echocardiography if signs; (9) CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE + NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS — increased risk in T1DM-treated (3-5× general population); less in GDM if well-controlled (~1.5×); evaluation; (10) CAUDAL REGRESSION SYNDROME — rare but unique to IDM. NRP (Neonatal Resuscitation Program) framework: (1) WARM + DRY + STIMULATE; (2) ASSESS HR + RESPIRATIONS; (3) PROVIDE PPV (positive-pressure ventilation) if needed (T-piece + room air initially per NRP 2020); (4) CHEST COMPRESSIONS if HR <60 with PPV; (5) EPINEPHRINE 0.1-0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000 IV if HR <60 after PPV + compressions; (6) AIRWAY — intubation + suction; (7) RESPIRATIONS + ventilation; (8) ASSESSMENT + cardiopulmonary stability; algorithm by 1 min + 5 min + 10 min APGAR; team competency essential.
labs.r: IDM NEONATAL COMPLICATIONS = hypoglycemia (most immediate) + macrosomia + RDS + polycythemia + hyperbilirubinemia + hypocalcemia + hypomagnesemia + cardiomyopathy + congenital + neural tube. Standard monitoring + treatment per protocol. NRP framework for resuscitation. RN role: assessment + monitoring + treatment + family education + multidisciplinary.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters at shoulder dystocia recognition?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings that are obstetric emergency + significant cues requiring nursing attention.

opts.text: SHOULDER DYSTOCIA EMERGENCY recognized — TURTLE SIGN (fetal head retracts against perineum + external rotation fails to occur normally) + anterior shoulder NOT delivering with normal gentle downward traction; OB attending Dr. Lopez immediately recognizes + calls 'shoulder dystocia, get help, start timer' at 1545:15 within 15 sec of head delivery
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — recognition of shoulder dystocia. RAPID recognition is essential — each second of delay increases hypoxia + brachial plexus injury risk. RN role: recognize + activate team + scribe.

opts.text: TEAM ACTIVATION within 30 seconds via overhead page + phone + bed alarm; ROLE ASSIGNMENTS in 30 seconds via closed-loop communication: TEAM LEADER (OB attending) + SCRIBE (charge RN documenting precise times) + McROBERTS (2 nurses each at one leg) + SUPRAPUBIC PRESSURE (OB resident) + INTERNAL MANEUVERS (OB attending) + NEONATAL RESUSCITATION TEAM (RN + RT + NNP at warmer) + FAMILY LIAISON (charge RN)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — team activation + role assignment within 60 sec via closed-loop communication. Time-sensitive emergency. RN role: facilitate + execute role + scribe + escalate.

opts.text: HELPERR MNEMONIC maneuvers executed in sequence per ACOG/AAP: (H) HELP team activated; (L) LEGS = McROBERTS (sharp flexion of maternal hips); (P) PRESSURE = SUPRAPUBIC (NOT fundal — contraindicated); (E) ENTER = internal maneuvers (Rubin); (R) REMOVE posterior arm = sweep across chest + deliver; combined McRoberts + suprapubic + Rubin + posterior arm RESOLVED shoulder dystocia at 1547:15 within ~2 min head-to-body interval
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — HELPERR mnemonic systematic maneuver sequence. Standard ACOG/AAP recommendation. Foundation for shoulder dystocia management. RN role: assist + execute + scribe + escalate.

opts.text: AVOID FUNDAL PRESSURE (CONTRAINDICATED — worsens by impacting shoulder against bone + can cause uterine rupture); AVOID EXCESSIVE TRACTION on fetal head (causes brachial plexus injury — Erb palsy C5-C6 most common); APPROPRIATE force only + standard maneuvers
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — contraindications. Fundal pressure WORSENS + can cause uterine rupture. Excessive traction causes brachial plexus injury. Standard practice. RN role: prevent contraindicated actions.

opts.text: NEONATAL OUTCOMES + brachial plexus injury surveillance: newborn weight 4350 g LGA + APGAR 6/9 (recovered well); right arm extended + diminished tone + limited movement + flexed elbow on right = ERB PALSY C5-C6 likely from anterior shoulder traction; pediatric ortho consult + PT/OT early intervention; immobilize arm in flexion across chest (NO pulling or traction); expected partial spontaneous recovery 70-90% by 6-12 months; surgical intervention at 3-6 months if persistent
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — neonatal brachial plexus injury surveillance + management. Most common neonatal complication of shoulder dystocia. RN role: assessment + family education + pediatric ortho + PT/OT + ongoing care.

opts.text: MATERNAL POSTPARTUM MANAGEMENT: oxytocin 10 IM + 30 in 1L LR IV + fundal massage; methylergonovine NOT given (HTN history); carboprost available; misoprostol available; bimanual compression + tamponade balloon + IR + hysterectomy ladder if persistent; EBL 600 mL (above PPH threshold but manageable); 2nd degree perineal + extensive vaginal mucosal lacerations repaired; vital signs stable; postpartum vigilance × 24 hr
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — maternal postpartum management + PPH risk after shoulder dystocia. Active management 3rd stage + uterotonics + monitoring + escalation ladder + laceration repair. RN role: vigilant monitoring + medication + escalation.

opts.text: IDM NEONATAL MANAGEMENT — newborn glucose 32 at 30 min = NEONATAL HYPOGLYCEMIA (<40 in IDM at risk); early breastfeeding + skin-to-skin + supplemental formula + repeat glucose in 30 min + IV dextrose if symptomatic/persistent; q30 min × 2 then q1h × 4-6 hr screening per IDM protocol; RDS + polycythemia + hyperbilirubinemia + hypocalcemia + hypomagnesemia + cardiomyopathy + congenital screening; thermoregulation
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — IDM neonatal management with hypoglycemia central concern. Standard IDM protocol. RN role: assessment + monitoring + intervention + multidisciplinary + family education.

opts.text: LEADERSHIP + DELEGATION in obstetric emergency: TEAM ACTIVATION within 30 sec + ROLE ASSIGNMENTS in 30-60 sec via closed-loop communication + scribe + multidisciplinary; CHAIN OF COMMAND (primary RN → charge RN → CNS → CNO → Medical Director); RN scope = positioning + suprapubic pressure + medication + neonatal resuscitation + family communication + documentation; LPN/CNA scope = supportive role + supply transport; POST-EVENT DEBRIEFING within 30 min + formal review at 24-48 hr + just culture + EAP + peer support + second victim phenomenon

opts.text: FAMILY + multidisciplinary support: spouse at bedside + extended family in waiting room + chaplain (family Catholic — coordinated with hospital chaplain) + social worker + pediatric ortho + neonatology + lactation; transparent + compassionate post-event family meeting; emotional support throughout + cultural sensitivity
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — family-centered + multidisciplinary + emotional support. Foundation for trust + healing. RN role: facilitate + advocate + emotional support.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — document and proceed
opts.rat: Allergy documentation. No contraindications. Not priority cue at this moment but important for safety.

opts.text: APPLY FUNDAL PRESSURE during shoulder dystocia maneuvers to help deliver the shoulder + push the baby down + assist the OB maneuvers
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + CONTRAINDICATED. FUNDAL PRESSURE during shoulder dystocia is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — WORSENS by impacting the shoulder against the symphysis pubis (the bony obstruction) + INCREASES risk of UTERINE RUPTURE + does NOT help shoulder delivery. Standard practice: AVOID fundal pressure. CORRECT: SUPRAPUBIC PRESSURE (above symphysis) directed downward + inward to displace the anterior shoulder.

opts.text: Apply STRONG TRACTION on the fetal head to deliver the shoulder — exit the head through the perineum with force to relieve the impaction + free the shoulder
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + CAUSES INJURY. EXCESSIVE TRACTION on fetal head is the PRIMARY CAUSE of BRACHIAL PLEXUS INJURY (Erb palsy C5-C6) in shoulder dystocia. Standard practice: AVOID excessive traction + use GENTLE downward traction only + RELY on maneuvers (McRoberts + suprapubic + internal + posterior arm) to resolve dystocia. Avoiding excessive traction = central principle.

title: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in 47-Year-Old Man with Severe Alcohol Use Disorder (12+ Beers/Day × 10 Years) Admitted After Motor Vehicle Accident: CIWA-Ar Symptom-Triggered Benzodiazepine Protocol, Thiamine Administration BEFORE Glucose to Prevent Wernicke Encephalopathy, Delirium Tremens Prevention + Seizure Prophylaxis, and Multidisciplinary Substance Use Disorder Treatment with MAT Referral
subtitle: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME (AWS) develops in chronic heavy drinkers within 6-48 hr of last drink + can progress to LIFE-THREATENING delirium tremens (DTs) without appropriate treatment; STAGES + TIMELINE: (1) STAGE 1 MILD (6-12 hr post last drink) = anxiety + tremor + insomnia + GI upset + mild autonomic (HR + BP); (2) STAGE 2 MODERATE (12-48 hr) = worsening tremor + diaphoresis + N/V + HTN + tachycardia + auditory/tactile/visual hallucinations (without confusion = ALCOHOLIC HALLUCINOSIS); (3) STAGE 3 SEIZURES (12-48 hr typically) = generalized tonic-clonic seizures (single or multiple); (4) STAGE 4 DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs) (48-96 hr peak; can occur up to 7-10 days) = SEVERE autonomic instability + altered mental status + agitation + hallucinations + fever + seizures + 5-15% MORTALITY if untreated + 1-5% with treatment; RISK FACTORS for severe withdrawal/DTs = chronic heavy use + age >40 + comorbidities + prior history of DTs (single most predictive) + prior seizures + medical illness + concurrent infection + abnormal liver/electrolytes + thrombocytopenia + dehydration + heavy use within past 30 days; CIWA-Ar SCALE (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol — Revised) 10-item scale 0-67 measuring withdrawal severity for SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED therapy: nausea + tremor + autonomic + anxiety + agitation + tactile + auditory + visual hallucinations + headache + orientation; SCORES: <10 mild + 10-15 moderate + >15 moderate-severe + >20 severe + DT risk; ASSESS q1h initially when treatment started + q2-4h based on stability; SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED BENZODIAZEPINE protocol with CIWA-Ar threshold (e.g., LORAZEPAM 2-4 mg IV q1h PRN for CIWA ≥10) — more effective + lower total dose + shorter LOS than fixed-schedule; alternative FIXED-SCHEDULE for high-risk patients or institutions lacking CIWA monitoring capability; BENZODIAZEPINES = first-line + GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulators replace alcohol's effect + prevent seizures + reduce DT severity; choice = LORAZEPAM (Ativan; preferred in elderly + liver disease — no active metabolites + short-intermediate half-life), DIAZEPAM (Valium; long-acting metabolites + smooth withdrawal but accumulate in liver disease + elderly), CHLORDIAZEPOXIDE (Librium; long-acting + sometimes preferred for milder withdrawal); ROUTES = IV for unstable + ICU patients + PO for stable; FRONT-LOAD dosing for severe withdrawal/imminent DTs; PROPHYLACTIC PHENOBARBITAL or KETAMINE for refractory DTs (PICU-level + intubation often required); AVOID prolonged benzodiazepine use beyond acute withdrawal (dependence + accumulation); THIAMINE 100 mg IV BEFORE GLUCOSE administration is CRITICAL — IV glucose can precipitate WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY (acute thiamine deficiency triad = ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + confusion) + KORSAKOFF AMNESTIC SYNDROME (irreversible memory + confabulation if untreated) in thiamine-deficient chronic drinkers; THIAMINE 100 mg IV daily × 5 days then PO 100 mg daily long-term; FOLATE 1 mg + multivitamin + magnesium 2-4 g IV if low + electrolyte management; nutrition + hydration; HEALTHY DECISIONS = honest non-judgmental engagement + motivational interviewing + RISK STRATIFICATION + safe environment + 1:1 sitter for severe + family + chaplain + social worker; multidisciplinary including ADDICTION MEDICINE consultation + MEDICATION-ASSISTED TREATMENT (MAT) referral for outpatient (NALTREXONE oral or IM depot 380 mg q month; ACAMPROSATE 666 mg TID PO; DISULFIRAM 250 mg daily PO — produces aversion reaction with alcohol; GABAPENTIN off-label 300-900 mg TID; topiramate); 12-step program + AA + community support + relapse prevention + Naltrexone + Vivitrol injection + outpatient counseling + therapy + sober living + harm reduction approach when needed

labs.n: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL STAGES + CIWA-Ar SCALE + symptom-triggered protocol
labs.v: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME (AWS) STAGES + TIMELINE per ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) + clinical practice guidelines: (1) STAGE 1 MILD (6-12 hr post last drink) = anxiety + tremor + insomnia + GI upset (nausea + decreased appetite) + mild autonomic (HR + BP elevation); typically resolves with appropriate treatment + does not progress in 80% of patients; (2) STAGE 2 MODERATE (12-48 hr) = worsening tremor + diaphoresis + N/V + HTN + tachycardia + AUDITORY/TACTILE/VISUAL HALLUCINATIONS without confusion = ALCOHOLIC HALLUCINOSIS (vs DTs which has CONFUSION); some patients progress to DTs; (3) STAGE 3 SEIZURES (12-48 hr typically; can occur up to 6 days) = GENERALIZED TONIC-CLONIC SEIZURES (single or multiple); ~10% of untreated severe withdrawal patients experience seizures; risk factors = prior alcohol seizures, prior DTs, abnormal magnesium, abnormal calcium, chronic heavy use, age >40; (4) STAGE 4 DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs) (48-96 hr peak; can occur up to 7-10 days) = SEVERE autonomic instability (HR + BP + fever) + altered mental status + agitation + hallucinations + tremor + 5-15% MORTALITY IF UNTREATED + 1-5% MORTALITY WITH APPROPRIATE TREATMENT; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY = chronic alcohol → GABA receptor downregulation + glutamate (NMDA) receptor upregulation → acute alcohol cessation → relative GABA deficiency + glutamate excess = CNS hyperexcitability + autonomic instability + seizures + DTs. RISK FACTORS for SEVERE withdrawal/DTs: (1) PRIOR DTs OR alcohol-related seizures (SINGLE MOST PREDICTIVE — 50% recurrence); (2) chronic heavy use (years + amount); (3) age >40; (4) comorbidities (medical illness + infection + electrolyte abnormalities + hepatic disease + thrombocytopenia + dehydration); (5) heavy use within past 30 days (vs gradual cutdown); (6) concurrent benzodiazepine or opioid withdrawal. CIWA-Ar SCALE (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol — Revised) — STANDARD ASSESSMENT TOOL for withdrawal severity + symptom-triggered therapy; 10 ITEMS each scored 0-7 (orientation 0-4): (1) NAUSEA + VOMITING; (2) TREMOR (observation arms outstretched); (3) AUTONOMIC (paroxysmal sweats); (4) ANXIETY; (5) AGITATION; (6) TACTILE DISTURBANCES (pruritus + paresthesias + tactile hallucinations); (7) AUDITORY DISTURBANCES (hyperacusis + auditory hallucinations); (8) VISUAL DISTURBANCES (sensitivity + visual hallucinations); (9) HEADACHE + FULLNESS in head; (10) ORIENTATION + CLOUDING OF SENSORIUM (0 = oriented x3; up to 4 = disoriented to time + place + person + situation); TOTAL SCORE 0-67; CUTOFFS: <10 mild + 10-15 moderate + >15 moderate-severe + >20 severe + DT risk. ASSESSMENT FREQUENCY: q1h initially when treatment started; q2-4h when stable + improving; q1h again if worsening + after intervention. SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED BENZODIAZEPINE PROTOCOL (preferred over fixed-schedule for monitoring capability + ICU setting) = use CIWA-Ar threshold to administer benzodiazepine doses; EXAMPLE: CIWA ≥10 = LORAZEPAM 2 mg IV q1h PRN; CIWA ≥15 = lorazepam 4 mg IV q1h PRN; CIWA ≥20 = lorazepam 4 mg IV q30 min PRN + ICU consultation; CIWA ≥25 = continuous infusion or fixed-schedule + intubation if needed; reassess CIWA-Ar 30-60 min after each dose; advantages = lower total benzodiazepine dose + shorter ICU stay + lower respiratory depression; LIMITATIONS = requires trained staff + frequent assessment + may underdose if CIWA misapplied; FIXED-SCHEDULE BENZODIAZEPINE PROTOCOL = alternative for high-risk patients (prior DTs + severe withdrawal anticipated) or facilities without CIWA capability — example LORAZEPAM 2 mg IV q4h × 24 hr then taper; advantages = simpler + may prevent under-dosing in busy units; LIMITATIONS = higher cumulative dose + longer LOS in some studies; CHOICE varies by institution + patient factors.
labs.r: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL STAGES + CIWA-Ar SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED PROTOCOL = standard ASAM + clinical practice. RECOGNIZE risk factors + stage + assess CIWA-Ar + administer appropriate benzodiazepine. RN role: assessment + medication administration + monitoring + escalation.

labs.v: BENZODIAZEPINES = FIRST-LINE for alcohol withdrawal — GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators replace alcohol's effect on GABA + prevent seizures + reduce DT severity + mortality benefit. CHOICE of benzodiazepine: (1) LORAZEPAM (Ativan) — PREFERRED in ELDERLY + LIVER DISEASE + ICU + nursing home; SHORTER intermediate half-life (10-20 hr) + glucuronide conjugation (NO active metabolites) + safer in liver impairment + less accumulation; IV onset 5-15 min + PO onset 30-60 min + IM onset 15-30 min; dose 2-4 mg IV q1-4h PRN per CIWA-Ar or scheduled; max often 24-48 mg/day; can give IM if no IV access; (2) DIAZEPAM (Valium) — LONG-ACTING + active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam + nordiazepam + 30-200 hr) → SMOOTH WITHDRAWAL TAPER (self-tapering pharmacologically) but ACCUMULATION in liver disease + elderly + prolonged sedation + respiratory depression risk; dose 5-10 mg IV q1-4h PRN; max often 100-200 mg/day; PO option; preferred for younger + healthier patients without liver disease; (3) CHLORDIAZEPOXIDE (Librium) — LONG-ACTING + active metabolites + smooth taper; PO only (not IV); preferred for OUTPATIENT withdrawal management + milder withdrawal; dose 50-100 mg q4-6h × 24 hr then taper; (4) MIDAZOLAM — IV only + SHORT-ACTING + rapid onset; preferred for INTUBATION + ICU + procedural sedation; CONTINUOUS INFUSION for severe withdrawal not responsive to bolus; (5) OXAZEPAM — shorter-acting + no active metabolites; PO only; useful in elderly + liver disease; less common in US. ROUTES = IV for unstable + ICU + severe withdrawal; PO for stable + mild-moderate; IM acceptable but slower onset + variable absorption. FRONT-LOADING for severe withdrawal/imminent DTs = larger initial dose to rapidly achieve therapeutic level + prevent progression; EXAMPLE: diazepam 10-20 mg IV q10-15 min until CIWA-Ar <10 or sedation; then maintenance doses. CONTINUOUS INFUSION for refractory severe withdrawal/DTs = midazolam 1-10 mg/hr titrated; lorazepam 1-3 mg/hr titrated; PROPOFOL or DEXMEDETOMIDINE adjunct in refractory cases (PICU/ICU level). PHENOBARBITAL (long-acting barbiturate) — alternative or adjunct to benzodiazepines for severe + refractory withdrawal; smoother taper + reliable + less respiratory depression than diazepam; dose 200-300 mg IV/IM load + 30-60 mg q4h PO taper; CAUTION respiratory depression + need close monitoring. KETAMINE — NMDA antagonist + adjunct for refractory severe withdrawal/DTs in ICU; 0.5-1 mg/kg IV bolus then 0.1-0.5 mg/kg/hr infusion; rapid effect + opioid-sparing + dissociative + monitoring. AVOID OUTPATIENT BENZODIAZEPINE prescription beyond acute withdrawal taper (dependence + ongoing use); transition to non-benzodiazepine maintenance options (gabapentin for ongoing anxiety + sleep + sometimes; SSRI/SNRI for depression/anxiety; Naltrexone for AUD; outpatient counseling). MONITORING: respiratory rate + sedation level + cardiac monitor + pulse ox; flumazenil reversal RESERVED for life-threatening respiratory depression (CAUTION — can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patient). DOSE CALCULATIONS for THIS PATIENT (47 y/o + chronic heavy use + prior DTs + high risk + recent seizure): aggressive front-loading with lorazepam 4-8 mg IV q15-60 min titrated to CIWA-Ar <10 + sedation; ICU level + continuous monitoring + close observation + ready to escalate to phenobarbital + ketamine + intubation if refractory.
labs.r: BENZODIAZEPINES first-line for alcohol withdrawal; CHOICE = lorazepam preferred in elderly/liver disease (no active metabolites); diazepam smooth taper but accumulation risk; chlordiazepoxide for outpatient mild; midazolam for ICU + continuous infusion; phenobarbital + ketamine for refractory; AVOID outpatient long-term. RN role: dose titration + monitoring + escalation.

labs.n: THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE — Wernicke encephalopathy prevention
labs.v: WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY = ACUTE NEUROLOGIC EMERGENCY from THIAMINE (vitamin B1) DEFICIENCY in chronic alcohol users + malnutrition + hyperemesis + bariatric surgery + chronic GI disease + chronic kidney disease + chemotherapy + dialysis + magnesium deficiency. CLASSIC TRIAD (rare to see all three; many patients atypical presentation): (1) OPHTHALMOPLEGIA (nystagmus + lateral rectus palsy + ophthalmoparesis); (2) ATAXIA (broad-based stance + truncal ataxia + limb ataxia); (3) ENCEPHALOPATHY (confusion + altered mental status + apathy + memory disturbance). UNTREATED progresses to KORSAKOFF AMNESTIC SYNDROME (irreversible memory loss + confabulation + cognitive impairment) — 'WERNICKE-KORSAKOFF SYNDROME'; mortality 17-20% if untreated; significant morbidity in survivors. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY = thiamine is essential cofactor for KEY GLUCOSE METABOLISM ENZYMES (pyruvate dehydrogenase + α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase + transketolase); thiamine deficiency → impaired glucose metabolism + neuronal injury especially in mammillary bodies + thalamus + brainstem. CRITICAL PRINCIPLE = ADMINISTER THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE in chronic alcohol users + suspected thiamine deficiency; IV GLUCOSE administration without thiamine can PRECIPITATE WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY by acutely depleting marginal thiamine stores (glucose metabolism requires thiamine; sudden glucose load depletes thiamine reserve in deficient patient → acute deficiency → Wernicke). DOSING: THIAMINE 100 mg IV (or IM if no IV access) BEFORE any IV glucose/dextrose administration in chronic heavy drinkers + malnourished patients; THIAMINE 100 mg IV daily × 5 days for acute withdrawal + nutritional support; THIAMINE 100 mg PO daily long-term outpatient. SOME PROTOCOLS recommend HIGHER DOSE = 500 mg IV TID × 2-3 days then 250 mg IV daily × 5 days for established Wernicke; high-dose IV thiamine for acute encephalopathy + chronic + severe deficiency. THIAMINE administration: IV PUSH SLOW over 5-10 min OR DILUTE in 50 mL NS or D5W run over 30 min; well-tolerated; ANAPHYLAXIS rare (more common with IM); RARELY contraindicated. CONCURRENT supplementation: FOLATE 1 mg PO/IV daily (folate deficiency common); MULTIVITAMIN daily; MAGNESIUM 2-4 g IV (magnesium deficiency common + worsens seizure threshold + thiamine metabolism); VITAMIN B12 1000 mcg daily; nutrition + protein + caloric support. THIS PATIENT: chronic heavy alcohol use 10 years + likely malnourished + acute illness + needs IV access for hydration + medications + treatment for withdrawal → THIAMINE 100 mg IV given BEFORE any glucose-containing fluid (D5W or D5NS); patient also received magnesium 2 g IV + folate 1 mg PO + multivitamin + B12 1000 mcg IM; concerns about Wernicke encephalopathy + Korsakoff syndrome addressed; outpatient continuation of thiamine + multivitamin + nutrition counseling + abstinence + ongoing supervision.
labs.r: THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE is CRITICAL principle in chronic alcohol users + malnutrition to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Thiamine 100 mg IV daily × 5 days + multivitamin + folate + magnesium + B12 + nutrition. RN role: medication administration + monitoring + family education.

labs.v: DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs) = MOST SEVERE FORM of alcohol withdrawal; SEVERE autonomic instability + altered mental status + agitation + hallucinations + 5-15% MORTALITY IF UNTREATED + 1-5% MORTALITY WITH APPROPRIATE TREATMENT (early aggressive benzodiazepines + supportive care). TIMING: typically 48-96 hr post last drink (peak 72-96 hr); can occur up to 7-10 days; RARELY before 24 hr; less common with continuous monitoring + early benzo treatment. RECOGNITION: CIWA-Ar typically >20 + agitation + confusion + global disorientation (versus alcoholic hallucinosis where orientation preserved with hallucinations); SEVERE autonomic instability (HR >120 + SBP >160 + RR >24 + fever >38°C); HALLUCINATIONS (visual + tactile + auditory; classic 'lilliputian' formed visual hallucinations); GLOBAL DISORIENTATION + confusion + perception impairment; TREMOR severe; DIAPHORESIS profuse; AGITATION + restlessness; SEIZURES (50% of DT patients have prior seizures); DEHYDRATION + electrolyte derangement; sometimes psychosis + paranoia; LIFE-THREATENING. RISK STRATIFICATION + PREDICTION: PAWSS (Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale) ≥4 predicts DTs/severe withdrawal; previously discussed risk factors. PREVENTION: (1) EARLY recognition of withdrawal risk + CIWA-Ar assessment + symptom-triggered or scheduled benzodiazepine protocol; (2) AGGRESSIVE benzodiazepine therapy for moderate-severe withdrawal; (3) CORRECT electrolyte abnormalities + magnesium + phosphate + dehydration; (4) THIAMINE before glucose + nutritional support; (5) CARDIAC MONITORING + continuous monitoring + close observation; (6) MULTIDISCIPLINARY consultation including addiction medicine; (7) 1:1 SITTER for severe withdrawal + agitation + safety; (8) ICU TRANSFER for severe withdrawal/imminent DTs (continuous monitoring + escalation of benzodiazepines + supportive care). TREATMENT of established DTs: (1) ICU LEVEL of CARE with continuous monitoring + close observation + 1:1 sitter + safe environment + restraint AVOIDANCE if possible (worsens agitation + can cause harm); (2) AGGRESSIVE BENZODIAZEPINE THERAPY — large doses needed (often 100-300+ mg lorazepam-equivalent in 24 hr) titrated to CIWA-Ar <10 + appropriate sedation; continuous infusion may be needed (midazolam 1-10 mg/hr titrated); (3) PHENOBARBITAL (300-600 mg IV/IM load + maintenance) as alternative or adjunct; (4) KETAMINE (NMDA antagonist) infusion 0.1-0.5 mg/kg/hr as refractory adjunct; (5) PROPOFOL or DEXMEDETOMIDINE infusion in ICU for refractory; (6) INTUBATION if respiratory failure or excessive sedation; (7) SUPPORTIVE CARE — IV fluids + electrolyte replacement + nutrition + cardiac monitoring + vital signs q1h + neuro checks; (8) treat concurrent issues (infection + electrolyte + dehydration + nutrition + medical illness); (9) AVOID benzodiazepine reversal with flumazenil (can precipitate seizures + worse withdrawal); (10) MULTIDISCIPLINARY + addiction medicine + psychiatry + family + chaplain + social work + emotional support throughout + post-event debriefing for staff; (11) MOST cases recover with supportive care + 1-5 days of DT phase + resolution; SOME progress + require longer treatment + multidisciplinary management; (12) DEATH from DTs = arrhythmia + cardiovascular collapse + respiratory failure + seizure + hyperthermia + electrolyte derangement + aspiration + comorbid illness.
labs.r: DTs = severe alcohol withdrawal with significant mortality even with treatment; PREVENTION through early recognition + benzodiazepine therapy + nutrition + multidisciplinary; TREATMENT = ICU + aggressive benzodiazepine + phenobarbital/ketamine adjunct + supportive care; AVOID flumazenil. RN role: recognition + escalation + medication + monitoring + family + multidisciplinary.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters at this alcohol withdrawal admission?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings that are clinically + alcohol withdrawal significant cues requiring nursing attention.

opts.text: ALCOHOL USE DISORDER SEVERE × 10 years (12+ beers/day baseline + occasional liquor; CAGE 4/4 positive; AUDIT 25; 2 prior inpatient detox + 1 prior DTs with seizures + ICU 3 yr ago); LAST DRINK 6 AM today (~9.5 hr before admission) = entering STAGE 1 withdrawal; multiple risk factors for severe withdrawal/DTs (prior DTs MOST PREDICTIVE + chronic heavy use + age >40 + recent heavy use + medical stress from MVA)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — severe AUD + multiple risk factors for severe withdrawal/DTs. Foundation for assessment + planning + risk stratification. RN role: history + risk factor identification + anticipation.

opts.text: CIWA-Ar SCALE assessment q1h initially + symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocol; initial CIWA-Ar = 12 (MODERATE — triggers benzo therapy); escalating to 21 (SEVERE; DT risk) by 14 hr post last drink → withdrawal seizure × 1 at 18 hr post last drink → aggressive ICU management with continuous monitoring + 1:1 sitter + escalated benzo protocol
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — CIWA-Ar assessment + symptom-triggered protocol + escalation. Standard ASAM practice. RN role: assessment + medication administration + monitoring + escalation.

opts.text: BENZODIAZEPINES FIRST-LINE — LORAZEPAM (Ativan) preferred in this patient (no active metabolites + safer in liver + ICU); 2-4 mg IV q1h PRN per CIWA-Ar; escalation to 4 mg IV q30 min for CIWA ≥20; continuous infusion (midazolam 1-10 mg/hr) or PHENOBARBITAL or KETAMINE for refractory severe DTs; AVOID flumazenil (can precipitate seizures); AVOID outpatient long-term benzodiazepine prescription
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — benzodiazepine pharmacology + protocol. Standard practice. RN role: medication administration + monitoring + escalation + family education.

opts.text: THIAMINE 100 mg IV given BEFORE any GLUCOSE administration — CRITICAL principle to prevent WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY (ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + encephalopathy triad) + KORSAKOFF AMNESTIC SYNDROME (irreversible memory loss + confabulation) in chronic alcohol users with marginal thiamine stores; thiamine essential cofactor for glucose metabolism; sudden glucose load depletes thiamine reserve + precipitates Wernicke; 100 mg IV daily × 5 days then PO 100 mg daily long-term + folate + multivitamin + magnesium + B12
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — Wernicke-Korsakoff prevention. THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE is critical principle in chronic alcohol users. Standard practice. RN role: medication administration + family education + nutrition.

opts.text: WITHDRAWAL SEIZURE at 18 hr post last drink (~ Stage 3 timing 12-48 hr); generalized tonic-clonic × 90 sec; LORAZEPAM 4 mg IV given during/after seizure; seizure precautions + bed rail padded + suction + airway; ICU transfer activated for continuous monitoring + 1:1 sitter + escalated benzo protocol; risk for further seizures + progression to DTs
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — withdrawal seizure recognition + immediate response + ICU transfer + escalation. Standard ASAM practice. RN role: recognition + safety + medication + escalation + family communication.

opts.text: DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs) RISK + prevention + recognition — typically 48-96 hr post last drink (peak 72-96 hr); SEVERE autonomic instability + altered mental status + agitation + hallucinations + 5-15% mortality if untreated + 1-5% with treatment; prevention via early benzodiazepine + supportive care + multidisciplinary + ICU level care; AVOID restraints (worsens agitation + can cause harm); AGGRESSIVE benzodiazepine therapy (often 100-300+ mg lorazepam equivalent in 24 hr)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — DT recognition + prevention + treatment. Severe AWS complication. RN role: recognition + escalation + medication + safety + multidisciplinary.

opts.text: MULTIDISCIPLINARY CARE + MAT outpatient: addiction medicine + addiction counselor + social worker + chaplain + nutritionist + family therapist + PCP + hepatology (HCV management); NALTREXONE IM DEPOT (Vivitrol) 380 mg q month preferred for this patient; AA + 12-step + community + sober living; family therapy + couples; financial + employment; HCV direct-acting antiviral treatment + cure
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — comprehensive multidisciplinary care + MAT + lifelong AUD management. Standard practice. RN role: coordination + education + advocacy + family + community + insurance.

opts.text: FAMILY-CENTERED + multidisciplinary support: wife (RN at outside hospital + supportive but exhausted) + 2 teen daughters + brother flying in + chaplain + social worker; transparent + compassionate communication + emotional support + family therapy + couples therapy + cultural sensitivity (family Catholic + chaplain coordinated); patient receptive + motivated + grateful + recognizing wake-up call
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — family-centered + emotional support + multidisciplinary engagement. Foundation for sustained recovery. RN role: facilitate + advocate + emotional support.

opts.text: Allergies: PCN (mild rash 15 yr ago) — document and proceed
opts.rat: Allergy documentation. No medication contraindications in current regimen. Document and proceed. Not the priority cue but important for safety.

opts.text: Administer SODIUM BICARBONATE 1 mEq/kg IV bolus to alkalinize blood + treat lactic acidosis + improve withdrawal symptoms
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG approach. NO INDICATION for bicarbonate in standard alcohol withdrawal. Bicarbonate would be considered ONLY for severe metabolic acidosis with hemodynamic compromise or pH <6.9. Standard treatment = benzodiazepines + thiamine + electrolyte replacement + hydration + supportive care. Bicarbonate not indicated.

opts.text: Administer GLUCOSE 50% IV bolus immediately to provide energy + correct hypoglycemia + improve mental status; alcohol withdrawal patients are typically dehydrated + need rapid energy
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + DANGEROUS approach. GLUCOSE WITHOUT THIAMINE FIRST can precipitate WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY in chronic alcohol users with marginal thiamine. CRITICAL PRINCIPLE = THIAMINE 100 mg IV BEFORE any glucose-containing fluid; thiamine is essential cofactor for glucose metabolism + sudden glucose load depletes thiamine reserve. Standard: thiamine first + then glucose if needed for hypoglycemia (verify hypoglycemia present + use D50 if needed; typically not needed in this patient who is alert + oriented + appropriate).

opts.text: Apply 4-point physical restraints immediately to prevent patient from harming self or others during alcohol withdrawal; restraints will keep patient safe + control agitation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG approach. RESTRAINTS during alcohol withdrawal WORSEN agitation + can cause physical harm + violate dignity + may not be necessary if appropriate medication + 1:1 sitter + safe environment. STANDARD = 1:1 sitter for severe withdrawal/agitation + safe environment + bed rail padded + remove dangerous items + appropriate benzodiazepine therapy to control symptoms + multidisciplinary support. Restraints reserved for truly emergent situations with extensive documentation + alternatives tried + time-limited per institutional + state regulations.

opts.text: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL STAGES + TIMELINE per ASAM: STAGE 1 mild (6-12 hr post last drink — anxiety + tremor + insomnia + autonomic); STAGE 2 moderate (12-48 hr — worsening + hallucinations without confusion = alcoholic hallucinosis); STAGE 3 seizures (12-48 hr — generalized tonic-clonic); STAGE 4 DTs (48-96 hr peak — severe autonomic + altered mental status + agitation + hallucinations + confusion + 5-15% mortality if untreated)
opts.rat: CORRECT — alcohol withdrawal stages + timeline framework. Standard knowledge. Foundation for recognition + management + anticipation.

opts.text: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY = chronic alcohol → GABA-A receptor DOWNREGULATION + GLUTAMATE (NMDA) receptor UPREGULATION → acute alcohol cessation → relative GABA deficiency + glutamate excess = CNS HYPEREXCITABILITY + autonomic instability + seizures + DTs; BENZODIAZEPINES first-line because positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors REPLACE alcohol's effect + suppress hyperexcitability + prevent seizures + reduce DT severity + mortality benefit
opts.rat: CORRECT — pathophysiology + treatment rationale framework. Standard knowledge. Foundation for understanding + treatment.

opts.text: RISK FACTORS for SEVERE WITHDRAWAL/DTs: prior DTs OR alcohol-related seizures (SINGLE MOST PREDICTIVE — 50% recurrence); chronic heavy use (years + amount); age >40; comorbidities (medical illness + infection + electrolyte + hepatic disease + thrombocytopenia + dehydration); heavy use within past 30 days; concurrent benzodiazepine or opioid withdrawal; CIWA-Ar SCALE 10-item 0-67 measuring severity for symptom-triggered therapy
opts.rat: CORRECT — risk factors + CIWA-Ar framework. Standard practice. Foundation for risk stratification + monitoring.

opts.text: BENZODIAZEPINES first-line for alcohol withdrawal: LORAZEPAM preferred in elderly + liver disease + ICU (no active metabolites + safer); DIAZEPAM long-acting + active metabolites + smooth taper but accumulation in liver disease; CHLORDIAZEPOXIDE PO outpatient; MIDAZOLAM IV continuous infusion ICU; symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar threshold) preferred over fixed-schedule when monitoring capable + reduces total dose + LOS; FIXED-schedule alternative for high-risk patients or institutions lacking CIWA capability
opts.rat: CORRECT — benzodiazepine choice + dosing + protocol framework. Standard ASAM practice. Foundation for medication selection + administration.

opts.text: THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE is CRITICAL principle in chronic alcohol users + malnutrition + suspected thiamine deficiency to PREVENT WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY (acute thiamine deficiency triad = ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + encephalopathy) + KORSAKOFF AMNESTIC SYNDROME (irreversible memory loss + confabulation if untreated); thiamine 100 mg IV daily × 5 days + folate 1 mg + multivitamin + magnesium + B12 + nutrition support; high-dose 500 mg IV TID × 2-3 days for established Wernicke
opts.rat: CORRECT — Wernicke-Korsakoff prevention framework. Standard practice. RN role: medication administration + family education.

opts.text: DT TREATMENT in ICU = aggressive benzodiazepine therapy (large doses; often 100-300+ mg lorazepam equivalent in 24 hr) + phenobarbital (200-300 mg load) + ketamine infusion + propofol + dexmedetomidine + intubation if needed + 1:1 sitter + safe environment + AVOID restraints if possible + supportive care + multidisciplinary; mortality 1-5% with appropriate treatment + 5-15% if untreated

title: Severe Acute Gallstone Pancreatitis in 52-Year-Old Man with Ranson Score 4 + Atlanta Severe Classification: Aggressive Lactated Ringer's Fluid Resuscitation, Opioid Pain Management (No NSAIDs), Early Enteral Nutrition via NJ Tube, Emergent ERCP with Sphincterotomy for Biliary Obstruction, Interval Cholecystectomy, and Multi-System Complication Surveillance
subtitle: ACUTE PANCREATITIS = inflammation of pancreas with diverse etiologies (top causes: GALLSTONES 40% + ALCOHOL 30% + idiopathic + post-ERCP + hypertriglyceridemia >1000 + hypercalcemia + drugs + autoimmune + trauma + infections + neoplasms); DIAGNOSIS requires 2 of 3 ATLANTA 2012 CRITERIA: (1) ABDOMINAL PAIN consistent with pancreatitis (epigastric + radiating to back + worse supine + better leaning forward + N/V + abdominal distension); (2) LIPASE OR AMYLASE >3× upper limit of normal (lipase more specific + sensitive than amylase + remains elevated longer); (3) IMAGING findings of acute pancreatitis (CT abdomen with IV contrast typically 72 hr after onset to assess severity + complications; US for gallstone evaluation). SEVERITY per Atlanta 2012 = MILD (no organ failure + no local + systemic complications); MODERATELY SEVERE (transient organ failure <48 hr or local/systemic complications); SEVERE (PERSISTENT organ failure >48 hr in 1 or more systems — cardiovascular SBP <90 + respiratory PaO2/FiO2 <300 + renal Cr >1.9 — using modified Marshall scoring); RANSON CRITERIA (severity prediction at admission + 48 hr): AT ADMISSION = age >55 + WBC >16,000 + glucose >200 + AST >250 + LDH >350 (gallstone slightly different); AT 48 HR = HCT drop >10 + BUN rise >5 + calcium <8 + PaO2 <60 + base deficit >4 + fluid sequestration >6L; SCORE 0-2 = mild (<1% mortality); 3-4 = MODERATE (15% mortality — this patient); 5-6 = severe (40% mortality); 7+ = very severe (~100% mortality). APACHE II + BISAP also commonly used. AGGRESSIVE EARLY FLUID RESUSCITATION = LACTATED RINGER'S (LR) preferred over NS (LR less hyperchloremic acidosis + may reduce SIRS); 5-10 mL/kg/hr (250-500 mL/hr in 70 kg adult) × 24-48 hr OR until hemodynamic improvement + UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr + BUN downtrending; AVOID excessive fluid (associated with worse outcomes — ARDS + abdominal compartment syndrome + intra-abdominal HTN); MONITOR for fluid overload + serial assessment + reassess q2-4h; bolus only for shock. PAIN MANAGEMENT = OPIOIDS first-line (morphine + hydromorphone + fentanyl) — historical concern about morphine causing sphincter of Oddi spasm worsening pancreatitis NOT supported by current evidence; MEPERIDINE avoided historically + now also acceptable but has CNS toxic metabolite normeperidine especially in renal impairment + elderly; AVOID NSAIDs in pancreatitis (renal injury risk + GI bleeding + may worsen pancreatic inflammation); acetaminophen + IV opioids + PCA + multimodal; PCA pump common. EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION = preferred over parenteral (TPN) per current evidence — reduces infection + LOS + mortality + supports gut integrity; NPO traditionally but EARLY (within 24-72 hr) ENTERAL feeding via nasojejunal (NJ) tube past ligament of Treitz to bypass pancreatic stimulation OR NG feeding (recent evidence comparable per studies) with low residue + lower fat + standard formulas; TPN only if enteral not tolerated; ORAL diet advance when pain controlled + tolerating + decreasing inflammatory markers. ANTIBIOTICS NOT ROUTINELY indicated for acute pancreatitis (does not improve outcomes + selects for resistance); RESERVED FOR infected necrosis (clinical deterioration + organ failure + persistent fever + gas in pancreas on CT + positive cultures) or extra-pancreatic infections (cholangitis + pneumonia); broad-spectrum + ID consultation. ERCP for GALLSTONE PANCREATITIS with cholangitis or persistent obstruction = within 24-72 hr; URGENT (24 hr) if cholangitis; sphincterotomy + stone extraction; reduces complications + may shorten course. CHOLECYSTECTOMY for gallstone pancreatitis = same-admission (preferably) for mild cases; interval cholecystectomy after recovery for severe cases (typically 4-6 weeks); reduces recurrence. COMPLICATIONS surveillance = LOCAL (peripancreatic fluid collections + pseudocyst + walled-off necrosis + infected necrosis + hemorrhage + portal vein thrombosis + ascites) + SYSTEMIC (ARDS + AKI + cardiovascular shock + sepsis + DIC + hyperglycemia + hypocalcemia from saponification + ileus + abdominal compartment syndrome). MULTIDISCIPLINARY = gastroenterology + general surgery + critical care + pain medicine + nutrition + interventional radiology if indicated

labs.v: 52 y/o male F. Castro presents to ED at 0830 today with 1 day of progressive severe epigastric pain radiating to back + N/V × 8 episodes + inability to keep down fluids + worsening since dinner last night (large fatty meal + 3 beers — both gallstone + alcohol pancreatitis triggers). PMH: cholelithiasis × 5 years (gallstones on US 5 yr ago when investigated for episodic biliary colic; declined elective cholecystectomy at that time due to mild symptoms); HTN (lisinopril 10 mg daily — controlled); type 2 diabetes (metformin 1000 mg BID — HbA1c 7.8); hyperlipidemia (atorvastatin 40 mg daily); obesity (BMI 32); episodic biliary colic with meals × several years intermittent; remote moderate alcohol use (2-3 beers most weekends; not chronic heavy use; recent fatty meal + beer last night may have been trigger). SOCIAL: married 23 yr to wife (50, accountant); 3 adult children (2 sons + daughter; all nearby); works as engineer; insurance excellent; lives in suburban home; supportive family; cultural background Mexican-American + bilingual home + family identifies as Catholic. PRESENTING ILLNESS: dinner last night = large fatty Mexican meal + 3 beers + onset of postprandial RUQ + epigastric pain (similar to biliary colic episodes in past); pain worsened overnight + radiating to back + becoming SEVERE 9/10 + non-relieved by position + nausea + repeated vomiting + dehydration + pallor + diaphoresis; arrived ED 0830. CLINICAL ASSESSMENT: appearing acutely uncomfortable + lying still + minimizing movement + leaning slightly forward + severe epigastric pain radiating to back; mild jaundice + scleral icterus (biliary obstruction); diaphoresis + tachycardia + tachypnea + dehydration; abdomen distended + tender + guarding voluntary + decreased bowel sounds + no rebound + no peritoneal signs (no perforation); no Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising — late finding); no Grey-Turner's sign (flank bruising — late finding); GCS 15 + alert + oriented; weight 96 kg (BMI 32 obese). LABS revealed acute pancreatitis with biliary obstruction: LIPASE 1200 (>3× ULN — diagnostic for pancreatitis per Atlanta 2012); AMYLASE 850 (elevated; less specific); AST 285 + ALT 220 (>3× normal — suggests biliary obstruction in gallstone pancreatitis); total bilirubin 4.8 + direct 3.2 + alkaline phosphatase 320 + GGT 280 (cholestatic pattern — biliary obstruction); lactate 3.8 (elevated — perfusion); WBC 18,500 (leukocytosis SIRS); CRP 220 (inflammatory); BUN 28 + Cr 1.3 (mild AKI from dehydration); glucose 195 (mild hyperglycemia); calcium 7.6 (LOW — saponification with fatty acids common in severe pancreatitis); magnesium 1.4 + phosphate 2.4 (low); triglycerides 180 (normal — rules out hyperTG pancreatitis); coags normal + fibrinogen 480 (acute phase). CT ABDOMEN with IV contrast at 1030: acute pancreatitis with mild peripancreatic edema + no necrosis identified at this early time point (CT severity better at 72 hr after onset); GALLSTONES in gallbladder; common bile duct (CBD) dilated to 12 mm (normal <8 mm) + IMPACTED STONE at ampulla of Vater = GALLSTONE PANCREATITIS with biliary obstruction. ATLANTA 2012 CRITERIA met: pain + lipase >3× ULN + imaging findings = diagnosis confirmed. SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: RANSON CRITERIA at admission = 4 (WBC >16,000 + AST >250 + LDH >350 pending; predicts moderate-severe ~15% mortality); ATLANTA classification pending 48 hr — patient already has organ dysfunction (mild AKI Cr 1.3 + early ARDS pattern PaO2 76 on 2L NC + lactate 3.8) → progressing to SEVERE pancreatitis (organ failure persisting >48 hr); APACHE II + BISAP also commonly used. labs.r: ACUTE PANCREATITIS diagnosis requires 2 of 3 Atlanta criteria (pain + lipase/amylase >3× ULN + imaging); SEVERITY assessment via Ranson + Atlanta + APACHE II + BISAP. This patient = severe acute gallstone pancreatitis with biliary obstruction + early organ dysfunction requiring MICU + aggressive resuscitation + ERCP + supportive care + complications surveillance.

labs.v: AGGRESSIVE EARLY FLUID RESUSCITATION = cornerstone of acute pancreatitis management; goal = restore tissue perfusion + prevent organ failure + complications; LACTATED RINGER'S (LR) preferred over normal saline (NS) — multiple RCTs show LR associated with less hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis + may reduce SIRS + improve outcomes; INITIAL DOSING = 5-10 mL/kg/hr × 24-48 hr based on hemodynamic + clinical response (96 kg × 5 = 480 mL/hr; can be 480-960 mL/hr initially); REASSESS Q2-4H — target UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr (in 96 kg = >48 mL/hr); BUN downtrending (initial 28 → goal <20); HCT downtrending (from concentrated state at admission); hemodynamic improvement (HR + BP); lactate normalization; resolution of acidosis. AVOID EXCESSIVE FLUID OVERLOAD (associated with worse outcomes — ARDS + abdominal compartment syndrome + intra-abdominal hypertension + cardiovascular complications) — recent evidence (WATERFALL trial 2022) suggests MODERATE aggressive fluid (1.5 mL/kg/hr × 1 hr then 1.5 mL/kg/hr maintenance) may be as effective as more aggressive (250-500 mL/hr) with less fluid overload; INDIVIDUALIZED based on patient + severity + response. THIS PATIENT received LR at 500 mL/hr (5.2 mL/kg/hr) initial × 24 hr then 250 mL/hr × 12 hr then 150 mL/hr maintenance based on response. MONITORING: continuous cardiac monitoring + arterial line for BP + central venous pressure (if utility) + Foley for hourly UOP + I/O hourly + daily weights + serial labs (BMP + LFTs + lipase + CRP + lactate q4-12h initially → q12h → daily); abdominal exam + bowel sounds + signs of ileus or abdominal compartment syndrome (abdomen distended + tense + decreased UOP + organ failure); pulmonary assessment + risk of ARDS; CARDIAC + RESPIRATORY + RENAL + HEPATIC + NEUROLOGIC organ surveillance. ELECTROLYTE replacement: hypocalcemia common (saponification — replace calcium gluconate 1 g IV slowly with cardiac monitoring); hypomagnesemia (replace IV); hypophosphatemia (replace; common in refeeding); hypokalemia + sodium balance per BMP. GLUCOSE management — hyperglycemia common in pancreatitis (insulin sliding scale + target 140-180 in ICU; AVOID hypoglycemia in critically ill); insulin gtt if needed. NUTRITION (covered separately) — early enteral preferred over TPN.
labs.r: AGGRESSIVE EARLY FLUID RESUSCITATION with Lactated Ringer's is cornerstone of acute pancreatitis management — restores perfusion + prevents organ failure + reduces complications. Monitor closely + avoid excessive overload (ARDS + compartment syndrome). Reassess q2-4h based on UOP + BUN + clinical response. Replace electrolytes (calcium + magnesium + phosphate). RN role: fluid administration + monitoring + electrolyte replacement + escalation.

labs.n: PAIN MANAGEMENT — opioids first-line + avoid NSAIDs
labs.v: PAIN MANAGEMENT in acute pancreatitis: PAIN is severe + often refractory + requires aggressive management; OPIOIDS first-line — MORPHINE + HYDROMORPHONE + FENTANYL acceptable; HISTORICAL concern about MORPHINE causing SPHINCTER OF ODDI SPASM worsening pancreatitis NOT supported by current evidence (most studies show no clinically significant difference + opioids do not worsen pancreatitis); MEPERIDINE (Demerol) was historically preferred for this reason but is no longer first-line + has TOXIC METABOLITE NORMEPERIDINE accumulating with renal impairment + elderly + chronic use → seizures + neurotoxicity; ROUTES = IV preferred (rapid onset + titratable); PCA pump common for patient-controlled administration; ORAL transition as tolerated. DOSING: HYDROMORPHONE 0.5-1 mg IV q3-4h PRN + PCA 0.2 mg/dose with 10 min lock-out + max 1.2 mg/hr; MORPHINE 4-10 mg IV q4h PRN + PCA equivalent; FENTANYL 25-50 mcg IV q1h PRN (less histamine + better in renal impairment); SCHEDULED ACETAMINOPHEN 1000 mg IV/PO q6h (opioid-sparing + antipyretic + non-NSAID); ANTI-EMETIC ondansetron 4-8 mg IV q6-8h PRN + alternative scopolamine + prochlorperazine + dimenhydrinate. AVOID NSAIDs (ibuprofen + naproxen + ketorolac + indomethacin) in acute pancreatitis: (1) RENAL injury risk in volume-depleted patient + AKI common in pancreatitis; (2) GI BLEEDING + ulcers (already inflamed GI tract); (3) MAY WORSEN pancreatic inflammation in some studies + theoretical inhibition of beneficial inflammatory response; (4) bleeding risk in patient who may need ERCP + cholecystectomy; (5) interfere with assessment (anti-inflammatory + antipyretic masks signs). NON-PHARMACOLOGIC pain management: positioning (knees to chest or sitting forward — relieves pressure on pancreas), warm compress to abdomen, distraction + relaxation + breathing techniques, music + family presence + chaplain spiritual support, minimize movement, NPO initially (avoid stimulation), nasogastric decompression if vomiting persistent (not routine but may help). MULTIMODAL pain management = opioid PCA + scheduled acetaminophen + anti-emetic + non-pharmacologic + transition to oral opioids (oxycodone 5-10 mg PO q4-6h PRN) as tolerating. CHRONIC PAIN issues in pancreatitis: chronic pancreatitis can develop after recurrent acute episodes + may require chronic pain management; avoid escalation + risk of opioid use disorder; multimodal approach + pancreatic enzyme replacement + alcohol/triglyceride/gallstone management + interventional procedures (celiac plexus block + pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy PERT) + chronic pain specialist + outpatient management.
labs.r: PAIN MANAGEMENT in acute pancreatitis = OPIOIDS first-line (hydromorphone + morphine + fentanyl; meperidine no longer preferred + has toxic metabolite); PCA pump + scheduled acetaminophen + anti-emetic + multimodal; AVOID NSAIDs (renal + GI + may worsen pancreatic inflammation + bleeding risk for ERCP/surgery). RN role: pain assessment + medication administration + monitoring + escalation + non-pharmacologic + family education.

labs.n: EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION + NPO + nutrition support
labs.v: EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION in acute pancreatitis = paradigm shift over past 15 years; HISTORICAL approach was NPO + TPN (parenteral) for prolonged periods to 'rest the pancreas'; CURRENT EVIDENCE strongly supports EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION (within 24-72 hours of admission for mild-moderate cases; within 72 hours for severe cases when stable) — reduces infections (especially bacterial translocation from gut), shortens LOS, reduces mortality, supports gut integrity, reduces TPN-associated complications (bacterial translocation + line infections + cholestasis + hyperglycemia). NPO initially typically for first 24-48 hr while resuscitating + assessing severity + managing pain + nausea; ORAL diet advance when tolerating (clear liquids → soft diet → regular as pain controlled + tolerating). FOR PATIENTS NOT TOLERATING ORAL (severe + N/V persistent + pain refractory + concerns about gastric stimulation) = NASOENTERAL FEEDING preferred via: (1) NASOJEJUNAL (NJ) TUBE past ligament of Treitz — historically thought to bypass pancreatic stimulation + reduce pancreatic enzyme release; placed by GI/IR or endoscopy; (2) NASOGASTRIC (NG) feeding — recent meta-analyses (multiple RCTs) show COMPARABLE EFFICACY to NJ feeding; easier placement + may be preferred; (3) FORMULATIONS = semi-elemental (low-residue + lower fat + pre-digested protein + medium-chain triglycerides) preferred for pancreatic patients; standard polymeric formulas acceptable as well; (4) ADVANCEMENT = start 10-25 mL/hr + advance per protocol + goal 1-1.5 kcal/mL of formula at appropriate volume to meet caloric needs; (5) protein 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day in severe + ICU patients; (6) avoid bolus feeding (continuous + may need cyclic). TPN ROLE = reserved for patients NOT TOLERATING ENTERAL nutrition (refractory ileus + obstruction + severe abdominal compartment syndrome) — typically after 5-7 days of failed enteral; multiple complications (line infections + bacterial translocation + hyperglycemia + cholestasis + LFTs). REFEEDING SYNDROME considerations — chronic alcohol use + malnutrition + chronic pancreatitis can have refeeding syndrome with rapid nutrition (hypophosphatemia + hypokalemia + hypomagnesemia + thiamine deficiency); START LOW + GO SLOW + monitor electrolytes + replace BEFORE feeding + thiamine BEFORE carbs. THIS PATIENT plan: NPO Day 1 with aggressive fluid resuscitation + pain management; NJ tube placement at end of Day 2 ERCP + semi-elemental formula at 25 mL/hr starting Day 3 + advancing per protocol; transition to oral diet (clear liquids → soft → regular) as tolerating + pain controlled + LFTs improving; nutrition consult ongoing; pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) not needed for acute uncomplicated case but considered if chronic pancreatitis develops.
labs.r: EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION (within 24-72 hr) preferred over TPN in acute pancreatitis per current evidence — reduces infections + LOS + mortality + supports gut integrity; NJ vs NG tube comparable per recent evidence; semi-elemental formula; advance per protocol; AVOID prolonged NPO + TPN unless enteral truly not tolerated. RN role: NJ tube placement assistance + formula administration + monitoring + advancement + electrolyte monitoring + family education.

labs.v: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) for GALLSTONE PANCREATITIS with cholangitis or biliary obstruction: TIMING = URGENT (within 24 hr) if CHOLANGITIS (fever + jaundice + RUQ pain = Charcot's triad; or shock + altered mental status added = Reynolds' pentad — emergent + life-threatening); ELECTIVE-URGENT (within 72 hr) for persistent biliary obstruction without cholangitis; relative urgency for documented obstructing stones with worsening pancreatitis. PROCEDURE = endoscopic sphincterotomy + stone extraction + biliary stenting if residual edema + stricture; clearing common bile duct (CBD); diagnostic + therapeutic; usually performed by GI or HPB surgeon with interventional capability. RISKS of ERCP: (1) POST-ERCP PANCREATITIS (5-10% incidence) — most common complication; risk factors = young + female + history of pancreatitis + difficult cannulation + sphincterotomy of pancreatic duct + manipulation; prevention with PROPHYLACTIC RECTAL INDOMETHACIN 100 mg immediately after procedure (NSAID protective effect on post-ERCP pancreatitis); aggressive hydration; pancreatic duct stent for high-risk patients; recognize + manage if occurs; (2) BLEEDING from sphincterotomy site; (3) PERFORATION (rare; 0.5-1%); (4) infection (cholangitis + cholecystitis worsening); (5) anesthesia risks (procedural sedation + airway). PRE-ERCP — antibiotics if suspected cholangitis (ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin-tazobactam); coagulation status normal; consent + family + multidisciplinary; INR <1.5 + platelets >50k; address fluid + electrolytes + pain. POST-ERCP — monitoring for complications + serial lipase + recurrent pain + cardiopulmonary monitoring × 24-48 hr in high-risk patients; continue antibiotics if cholangitis; advance diet as tolerating + pain controlled. CHOLECYSTECTOMY for gallstone pancreatitis: (1) MILD CASES = same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy (preferably during initial hospitalization after pancreatitis improving + tolerating PO + within 1-2 weeks); reduces recurrence + readmissions; some institutions do within 48-72 hr if mild; (2) SEVERE CASES = INTERVAL CHOLECYSTECTOMY after recovery (typically 4-6 weeks; allow complete resolution of pancreatitis + complications); maintain ERCP + sphincterotomy in interim for biliary protection; (3) CHRONIC GALLBLADDER ISSUES post-cholecystectomy = post-cholecystectomy syndrome rare but can occur; (4) ALTERNATIVE for high-surgical-risk patients = ERCP + sphincterotomy alone (without cholecystectomy) for biliary access + prevention; (5) CHOLECYSTECTOMY recurrence prevention essential — without it, recurrent gallstone pancreatitis rate ~20-50% within months. THIS PATIENT plan: ERCP within 24-72 hr (Day 2) with sphincterotomy + stone extraction + biliary stent if needed; INTERVAL CHOLECYSTECTOMY at 4-6 weeks after recovery from severe pancreatitis (vs same-admission for mild cases); general surgery aware + outpatient follow-up + scheduling.
labs.r: ERCP for gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis (within 24 hr) or biliary obstruction (within 24-72 hr) — sphincterotomy + stone extraction + stent; complications = post-ERCP pancreatitis (5-10%; prevent with rectal indomethacin) + bleeding + perforation + infection. CHOLECYSTECTOMY = same-admission for mild + interval (4-6 wk) for severe to prevent recurrence. RN role: pre/post-procedure care + monitoring + family education + scheduling.

labs.v: ACUTE PANCREATITIS COMPLICATIONS surveillance + management: (1) LOCAL — PERIPANCREATIC FLUID COLLECTIONS (occur within first 4 weeks; usually resorb spontaneously); PSEUDOCYST (fluid collection persisting >4 weeks; encapsulated; may require drainage if symptomatic + endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage); WALLED-OFF NECROSIS (later; necrotic material + fluid in encapsulated cavity); INFECTED NECROSIS (clinical deterioration + organ failure + persistent fever + gas in pancreas on CT + positive cultures; antibiotic therapy + percutaneous drainage + endoscopic step-up approach + minimally invasive necrosectomy; surgery if refractory); HEMORRHAGE from pancreatic vasculature erosion (IR embolization + surgery); PORTAL VEIN THROMBOSIS + SPLENIC VEIN THROMBOSIS (anticoagulation if no contraindication); ASCITES + pleural effusions; (2) SYSTEMIC — ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome — bilateral pulmonary edema noncardiogenic from inflammatory + fluid; supplemental O2 → HFNC → NIPPV → mechanical ventilation; lung-protective ventilation Vt 6 mL/kg IBW + PEEP); ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (Cr rising + UOP dropping; from hypovolemia + cytokine + abdominal compartment; aggressive fluid initial then careful + CRRT if severe); CARDIOVASCULAR SHOCK (distributive + hypovolemic + cardiogenic mixed; norepinephrine first-line + supportive); SEPSIS from infected necrosis + bacterial translocation + cholangitis (low threshold to treat broad-spectrum antibiotics + ID consult); DIC (rare); HYPERGLYCEMIA (inflammation + stress + DM + insulin sliding scale + close monitoring); HYPOCALCEMIA (saponification — fatty acid soap formation with calcium — replace empirically + monitor + cardiac monitoring; severe hypoCa can cause arrhythmia + tetany + Chvostek + Trousseau); HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA + HYPOMAGNESEMIA + HYPOKALEMIA; ILEUS + DELAYED GASTRIC EMPTYING + abdominal distension; INTRA-ABDOMINAL HYPERTENSION + ABDOMINAL COMPARTMENT SYNDROME (intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg + organ failure — decompressive laparotomy if severe + refractory); thromboembolism + DVT/PE (prophylaxis with mechanical SCDs + heparin SC); pneumonia + line infections + UTI nosocomial; encephalopathy (uremia + hepatic if cholestasis severe + inflammation); pruritus from cholestasis; SECONDARY ORGAN FAILURE — multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS); chronic complications = chronic pancreatitis + diabetes + exocrine insufficiency + chronic pain + recurrent episodes + nutritional deficiencies. MULTIDISCIPLINARY for complications = MICU + GI + surgery + IR + pulmonology + nephrology + ID + nutrition + pain medicine + palliative care if severe + multidisciplinary rounds. PROGNOSIS = mortality 15% in severe per Ranson + Atlanta + APACHE II; higher if infected necrosis + multi-organ failure + persistent organ failure; LONG-TERM = full recovery typical for mild + moderate; chronic complications possible for severe + recurrent.
labs.r: ACUTE PANCREATITIS COMPLICATIONS = local (fluid collections + pseudocyst + walled-off necrosis + infected necrosis + hemorrhage + thrombosis + ascites) + systemic (ARDS + AKI + shock + sepsis + DIC + electrolyte + abdominal compartment + organ failure). Multidisciplinary surveillance + management. RN role: monitoring + escalation + multidisciplinary + family education.

labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES: NO acute respiratory failure currently (oxygenating on 2L NC + improving; will monitor for ARDS); NO need for vasopressors currently (hemodynamic improving with fluid resuscitation alone); NO acute MI or arrhythmia (cardiac monitor normal + ECG no acute changes); NO acute stroke; NO peritoneal signs or perforation; NO acute encephalopathy beyond mild from pain + medications; NO active bleeding (coags normal + Hgb stable); NO acute hypocalcemia tetany (calcium 7.6 mild low + corrected + cardiac monitor); NO acute pancreatic necrosis on initial CT (will reassess at 72 hr); NO active cholangitis (Charcot's triad not met currently — has jaundice + RUQ pain but no fever pattern + cultures pending); NO acute infected necrosis (early in course; will surveillance); NO acute DIC (coags + platelets stable); NO refractory severe hypocalcemia (replacing with calcium gluconate); NO acute mental health crisis; family supportive + appropriate; insurance + multidisciplinary team available + experienced. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: PROMPT recognition by ED + appropriate diagnosis + classification + risk stratification (Ranson + Atlanta); AGGRESSIVE early fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's + close monitoring; MULTIDISCIPLINARY team engaged (MICU + GI + general surgery + ID + nutrition + pain medicine); ICU LEVEL care with arterial line + central line + continuous monitoring + frequent reassessment; ERCP planned within 24-72 hr (appropriate timing for gallstone pancreatitis with biliary obstruction); EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION planned post-ERCP via NJ tube (per current evidence); APPROPRIATE pain management with opioid PCA + scheduled acetaminophen + AVOIDING NSAIDs; ELECTROLYTE replacement + hydration + nutrition support; FAMILY supportive + extended family available + insurance excellent + multidisciplinary outpatient care accessible + interval cholecystectomy planned for recurrence prevention; PATIENT alert + cooperative + receptive + ENGAGED with care + family translation supported (bilingual home); CULTURAL + SPIRITUAL support (Catholic + chaplain available); modifiable risk factors addressable (diet + alcohol + obesity + diabetes management); chronic disease management opportunity. STANDARD expected positive trajectory with comprehensive intervention.
labs.r: Despite serious initial presentation + severe acute pancreatitis with biliary obstruction + organ dysfunction, multiple PROTECTIVE FACTORS support good outcome: prompt recognition + aggressive resuscitation + multidisciplinary team + ICU care + ERCP + early enteral nutrition + family + insurance + cultural sensitivity. Standard expected positive trajectory with comprehensive intervention + interval cholecystectomy preventing recurrence.

opts.text: Allergies: sulfa (rash 10 yr ago — document); NKDA other medications

opts.text: Administer IBUPROFEN 800 mg PO q6h for pain control + reducing inflammation in this patient with severe acute pancreatitis
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG approach + DANGEROUS in acute pancreatitis. NSAIDs (ibuprofen + naproxen + ketorolac + indomethacin) CONTRAINDICATED in acute pancreatitis: (1) renal injury risk in volume-depleted patient + AKI common in pancreatitis; (2) GI BLEEDING + ulcers; (3) may worsen pancreatic inflammation; (4) bleeding risk for ERCP + cholecystectomy.
