labs.n: PRESENTATION + recognizing non-accidental trauma red flags
labs.v: 7-month-old male, 'Baby R.,' brought to the pediatric ED by a parent for 'fussiness and not acting right,' with a stated history that the infant 'ROLLED OFF THE COUCH.' On assessment he is LETHARGIC with episodes of VOMITING and a FULL/BULGING anterior FONTANELLE (concerning for increased intracranial pressure), and the exam reveals BRUISING in multiple locations including the TORSO and an EAR (relatively protected sites where accidental bruising is unusual) and an apparent patterned mark. Critically, the HISTORY is INCONSISTENT with the injuries and with the infant's DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE — at ~7 months the mechanism described is implausible for the severity/type of injury, and significant bruising in a young, minimally-mobile infant is itself a red flag ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise'). This constellation raises STRONG SUSPICION for CHILD PHYSICAL ABUSE / NON-ACCIDENTAL TRAUMA (NAT), including possible ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA. RED FLAGS to recognize generally: a vague/inconsistent/changing history; a mechanism implausible or inconsistent with the injury; injury inconsistent with developmental stage; delayed care-seeking; injuries in protected areas (torso/ears/neck/buttocks/frenulum) or in multiple stages of healing; patterned injuries (loop/cord, hand, bite, immersion burns); and specific fractures (metaphyseal corner, posterior rib, different ages, fractures in non-ambulatory infants). PMH/SOCIAL: per limited history; the nurse gathers information non-judgmentally and documents objectively. The nurse's priorities, in order: (1) ensure the child's immediate MEDICAL needs (ABCs, neuro) and SAFETY; (2) recognize the red flags; (3) support the medical WORKUP; (4) fulfill the MANDATED-REPORTER duty (report reasonable suspicion); (5) DOCUMENT objectively; (6) approach the caregiver NON-CONFRONTATIONALLY; and (7) coordinate the multidisciplinary CHILD-PROTECTION response. Recognizing abuse is a critical, life-saving nursing competency — missed abuse can be fatal (a sentinel injury overlooked can precede a lethal one).
labs.r: Child physical abuse/NAT red flags: history vague/inconsistent/changing or IMPLAUSIBLE for the injury, injury INCONSISTENT WITH DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE (e.g., significant injury/bruising in a non-mobile infant), delayed care, bruises in protected areas/multiple ages, patterned injuries, specific fractures, and abusive head trauma (subdural + retinal hemorrhages + encephalopathy, often no external signs). RN role: recognize red flags + ensure medical care/safety + report + document + non-confrontational care.

labs.n: Injury patterns, abusive head trauma, and the workup (with mimics)
labs.v: SPECIFIC INJURY PATTERNS that heighten concern for abuse: BRUISING in MULTIPLE STAGES of healing (different colors) and in unusual/protected locations — TORSO, EARS, NECK, buttocks, genitalia, and a torn frenulum; PATTERNED marks reflecting an implement or hand — LOOP/CORD marks, hand/slap marks, BITE marks, cigarette burns; and BURNS suggesting inflicted immersion — a sharp 'waterline' demarcation, a stocking-glove (immersion) distribution, or sparing of flexion creases (where the child pulled away). FRACTURES that are highly specific for abuse: classic METAPHYSEAL lesions ('bucket-handle'/corner fractures), POSTERIOR RIB fractures, fractures of DIFFERENT AGES (indicating repeated injury), and ANY fracture (especially long-bone) in a NON-AMBULATORY infant. ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA (AHT; formerly 'shaken baby syndrome') is a leading cause of abuse fatality and is often missed because external signs may be ABSENT: it classically combines SUBDURAL HEMORRHAGE, RETINAL HEMORRHAGES, and ENCEPHALOPATHY, presenting nonspecifically as LETHARGY, irritability, poor feeding, VOMITING, a FULL/BULGING FONTANELLE, increased head circumference, SEIZURES, or APNEA (as in this infant). WORKUP (medical team): a SKELETAL SURVEY (standardized radiographic series) to detect occult/healing fractures (recommended for children <2 years with suspected abuse; sometimes repeated in ~2 weeks); HEAD CT/MRI; a DILATED OPHTHALMOLOGIC exam for RETINAL HEMORRHAGES; LABS to assess for bleeding/CLOTTING disorders and BONE disease (CBC, coagulation studies, and others) to EXCLUDE MEDICAL MIMICS — e.g., a coagulopathy/bleeding disorder (can cause easy bruising), OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA or metabolic bone disease (can cause fractures), birthmarks/Mongolian spots (mistaken for bruises), and cultural practices (e.g., cupping/coining) — because the goal is ACCURATE assessment (neither missing abuse nor falsely accusing); and PHOTODOCUMENTATION of visible injuries. Importantly, evaluating for mimics does NOT delay reporting a reasonable suspicion — suspicion is reported while the workup proceeds. THIS INFANT'S findings (subdural + retinal hemorrhages + a healing posterior rib fracture, with an inconsistent history) are highly concerning for abusive head trauma/NAT. The nurse assists with/coordinates the workup, ensures injuries are photographed and documented, and recognizes the significance of these findings.
labs.r: Concerning injuries: bruises in multiple ages/protected areas (torso/ears/neck/frenulum); patterned marks (loop/hand/bite, immersion burns with sharp lines/sparing creases); fractures highly specific for abuse (metaphyseal/corner, posterior rib, different ages, any in a non-ambulatory infant); ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA = subdural + retinal hemorrhages + encephalopathy, often no external signs (lethargy/vomiting/bulging fontanelle/seizures/apnea). Workup: skeletal survey + head imaging + ophtho exam + labs to exclude mimics (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta) + photos. RN role: recognize + support workup + photodocument.

labs.v: Nurses are LEGALLY MANDATED REPORTERS of suspected child abuse and neglect — this is the pivotal ethical/legal nursing responsibility in this case. KEY PRINCIPLES: (1) REPORT REASONABLE SUSPICION, NOT PROOF — the legal threshold is a reasonable suspicion or 'reason to believe' that abuse/neglect has occurred; the nurse does NOT need to be CERTAIN, and does NOT need to (and should NOT try to) INVESTIGATE, gather forensic evidence, or 'prove' the abuse — investigation is the role of CHILD PROTECTIVE SERVICES (CPS) and law enforcement. (2) The duty is INDIVIDUAL and NON-DELEGABLE — a mandated reporter who personally has the suspicion is obligated to ensure a report is made and CANNOT simply assume that the physician, charge nurse, or someone else will do it (in many jurisdictions each mandated reporter is individually responsible); follow facility policy (which often involves notifying the provider/social work AND ensuring the report to CPS is filed), but the suspicion must be reported. (3) Reporting does NOT require PARENTAL CONSENT and OVERRIDES confidentiality/HIPAA — protecting the child takes precedence, and disclosure to CPS/authorities is legally permitted/required. (4) GOOD-FAITH reporting is PROTECTED from civil/criminal liability (immunity) even if abuse is ultimately not substantiated, whereas FAILURE TO REPORT a reasonable suspicion can result in legal penalties and professional discipline (and, worse, a child returned to danger). (5) Report TIMELY (immediately/within the legally specified window) to the designated agency (CPS hotline and/or law enforcement, per state law), and document the report. The nurse does NOT confront or accuse the caregiver as a prerequisite to reporting, does NOT need to tell the caregiver who reported, and does NOT delay reporting to 'be sure' or to await all test results. THIS NURSE recognized the reasonable suspicion (inconsistent history + concerning injuries + AHT findings) and ENSURED a report was made to CPS (and law enforcement per jurisdiction) without proof, without parental consent, and without assuming someone else would do it — fulfilling the mandated-reporter duty.
labs.r: Mandated reporter: REPORT reasonable SUSPICION (not proof) of child abuse/neglect to CPS (± law enforcement); do NOT investigate/prove it yourself (that's CPS's role). Duty is INDIVIDUAL + NON-DELEGABLE (don't assume someone else reports). No parental consent needed; OVERRIDES confidentiality. Good-faith reporting is immune from liability; failure to report = legal/professional penalties. Report TIMELY + document. RN role: ensure the report is made on reasonable suspicion.

labs.n: Child safety, non-confrontational approach, and objective documentation
labs.v: CHILD SAFETY + immediate MEDICAL care come first: stabilize and treat the child's injuries (ABCs, neuro monitoring for AHT/increased ICP), and ensure the child is NOT discharged into a potentially unsafe situation while the evaluation proceeds — this may mean ADMISSION and/or a protective hold with CPS/law-enforcement involvement; the nurse advocates for the child's safety throughout. NON-CONFRONTATIONAL, NON-JUDGMENTAL APPROACH WITH THE CAREGIVER: the nurse must NOT confront, accuse, interrogate, or express anger or suspicion toward the caregiver, and must NOT try to 'play detective' to elicit a confession — doing so is NOT the nurse's role and is counterproductive and potentially dangerous (it can escalate the situation, damage the ability to help the child, or prompt the caregiver to flee with the child); instead, obtain the history using OPEN, NON-LEADING questions, remain calm and professional, keep the focus on the child's care, and recognize that abuse occurs across ALL socioeconomic, racial, and cultural groups (guard against both under- and over-suspicion based on bias). OBJECTIVE, FACTUAL DOCUMENTATION is essential because the record may become LEGAL EVIDENCE: describe each injury PRECISELY — exact LOCATION, SIZE (measured), SHAPE/PATTERN, and COLOR — using BODY DIAGRAMS and PHOTOGRAPHS per facility policy; record the caregiver's statements (and any developmentally-appropriate statements from the child) VERBATIM in QUOTATION MARKS; document the timeline, the child's behavior/affect, and exactly WHO was notified and WHEN; and AVOID conclusory, judgmental, or accusatory language — do NOT write opinions like 'the parent abused the child'; instead document the objective findings, the quotes, and the fact that a report was made for SUSPECTED abuse. MULTIDISCIPLINARY: engage the CHILD-PROTECTION team / child-abuse pediatrician, SOCIAL WORK, CPS, and law enforcement/forensic evaluation as indicated; provide trauma-informed, developmentally appropriate support to the child; and support siblings who may also be at risk (CPS assesses the household). The nurse's calm, child-focused, objective stance both protects the child and preserves the integrity of the process. THIS NURSE prioritized the infant's medical stabilization and safety, remained non-confrontational with the caregiver, documented objectively with precise injury descriptions and verbatim quotes, and coordinated the child-protection team.
labs.r: Safety + medical care FIRST — treat injuries + do NOT discharge into an unsafe situation (admit/protective hold + CPS). Approach the caregiver NON-confrontationally/NON-judgmentally (don't accuse/interrogate/play detective — it's unsafe + not the nurse's role; abuse crosses all groups). DOCUMENT objectively (precise injury location/size/pattern/color + body diagram/photos + caregiver/child quotes verbatim + who/when notified; NO conclusory/accusatory language). Engage child-protection team/social work/CPS/forensics; assess siblings. RN role: child safety + non-confrontation + objective documentation + coordination.

labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT need PROOF to report — a reasonable SUSPICION suffices; did NOT try to INVESTIGATE/prove the abuse or extract a confession (that is CPS/law enforcement's role); did NOT ASSUME the physician or someone else would report (the duty is individual/non-delegable) and ensured the report was made; did NOT require PARENTAL CONSENT to report and recognized that reporting OVERRIDES confidentiality; did NOT delay reporting pending all test results or certainty; did NOT CONFRONT/accuse/interrogate the caregiver or show anger; did NOT discharge the child into a potentially unsafe situation; did NOT document conclusory/judgmental opinions; and did NOT let bias (about the family's demographics) cause under- or over-suspicion. The team also evaluated for MEDICAL MIMICS (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta, cultural practices/Mongolian spots) so as not to falsely accuse — while still reporting the reasonable suspicion. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: prompt RECOGNITION of the red flags (inconsistent history + injuries inconsistent with developmental stage + abusive-head-trauma findings); immediate medical stabilization + child SAFETY (no unsafe discharge); timely MANDATED REPORT to CPS; thorough, OBJECTIVE documentation (precise descriptions, photos, verbatim quotes, notification timeline) that supports the child's protection; a calm, non-confrontational caregiver approach that kept the situation safe; and a coordinated MULTIDISCIPLINARY child-protection response (child-abuse pediatrician, social work, CPS, law enforcement) including assessment of siblings. CONTEXT/CONTRAST: this is PHYSICAL abuse; child NEGLECT (failure to meet a child's basic needs) is ALSO reportable; and for MEDICAL neglect / parental refusal of clearly LIFE-SAVING treatment for a child, the state can intervene via COURT ORDER under the best-interest/parens patriae standard (parallel to overriding parental refusal — see [[case-080]]; and contrast with a competent ADULT's own refusal in [[case-122]]). EXPECTED outcome: the child receives needed medical care, is protected from further harm (safe disposition determined by CPS/the team), and the nurse fulfills the legal/ethical mandated-reporter and advocacy duties. NURSING ROLE: recognize NAT; stabilize + protect the child; report reasonable suspicion (without proof/consent, non-delegable, overriding confidentiality); document objectively; approach the caregiver non-judgmentally without confrontation; and coordinate the multidisciplinary child-protection response — the child's safety is the paramount concern.
labs.r: Negatives confirm correct practice: report SUSPICION not proof; don't investigate/confront/accuse or delegate the report away or wait for certainty/consent; don't discharge into danger; document objectively (no conclusory language); evaluate mimics but still report; avoid bias. Protective: recognition + stabilization/safety + timely mandated report + objective documentation + non-confrontational approach + multidisciplinary child protection (+ sibling assessment). Context: neglect also reportable; medical neglect → court order ([[case-080]]); contrast competent-adult refusal ([[case-122]]). RN role: recognize + protect + report + document + coordinate.

nursesNote: Pediatric ED — 7-month-old male 'Baby R.' brought by a parent for 'fussiness/not acting right'; reported history 'rolled off the couch.' EXAM: LETHARGIC + vomiting + FULL/BULGING anterior fontanelle (concern for increased ICP / abusive head trauma); BRUISING on the TORSO + an EAR (protected sites) + an apparent patterned mark; HISTORY INCONSISTENT with the injuries + with the infant's developmental stage (significant injury/bruising in a minimally-mobile 7-month-old — 'don't cruise rarely bruise') = RED FLAGS for NON-ACCIDENTAL TRAUMA. VS HR 150, RR 40, SpO2 97%, T 37.0 (infant). PRIORITIES: (1) MEDICAL stabilization + SAFETY first — ABCs + neuro monitoring; ensure the child is NOT discharged into a potentially unsafe situation pending evaluation; IV access + labs. (2) Recognized red flags. (3) Supported WORKUP — medical team ordered SKELETAL SURVEY (occult/healing fractures), HEAD CT/MRI, dilated OPHTHALMOLOGY exam (retinal hemorrhages), labs for bleeding/clotting + bone disease to EXCLUDE MIMICS (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta), injuries PHOTOGRAPHED + documented on a body diagram; findings = subdural hemorrhage + retinal hemorrhages + healing posterior rib fracture → highly concerning for abusive head trauma/NAT. (4) MANDATED REPORTER duty FULFILLED — reported REASONABLE SUSPICION to CPS (+ law enforcement per jurisdiction) WITHOUT needing proof, WITHOUT parental consent (overrides confidentiality), WITHOUT assuming someone else would report (individual/non-delegable duty), WITHOUT delaying for certainty/all results; report documented. (5) OBJECTIVE DOCUMENTATION — precise injury descriptions (location/size/shape-pattern/color) + body diagram/photos + caregiver and child statements VERBATIM in quotes + who/when notified; NO accusatory/conclusory language ('did not write opinions'). (6) NON-CONFRONTATIONAL caregiver approach — calm/professional, open non-leading questions; did NOT accuse/interrogate/play detective or show anger (unsafe + not the nurse's role; abuse crosses all demographics — avoid bias). (7) MULTIDISCIPLINARY — child-protection team/child-abuse pediatrician + social work + CPS + law enforcement coordinating safety evaluation/placement; trauma-informed support for the child; siblings/household assessed by CPS. DISPOSITION: admitted for injury treatment + neuro monitoring; CPS/team determine a SAFE disposition (child NOT released to an unsafe environment); follow-up arranged. CONTEXT: neglect is also reportable; medical neglect/refusal of life-saving treatment for a child → court order (best-interest/parens patriae, parallel [[case-080]]); contrast a competent ADULT's own refusal ([[case-122]]). Child safety paramount.
providerOrders: TRIAGE/ADMIT: pediatric ED → admission; 7-month-old with injuries concerning for non-accidental trauma (possible abusive head trauma)
DIAGNOSIS: suspected child physical abuse / non-accidental trauma; possible abusive head trauma; ensure medical care + child safety + mandated report
CODE STATUS: full code; child protection supersedes confidentiality where abuse is suspected
IMMEDIATE MEDICAL CARE + SAFETY:
Stabilize ABCs; neuro assessment/monitoring (lethargy, vomiting, bulging fontanelle → increased ICP/AHT); treat injuries; IV access; monitor
Ensure the child's SAFETY — do NOT discharge into a potentially unsafe situation pending evaluation (admit and/or protective hold with CPS/law-enforcement involvement)
WORKUP (per medical team):
Skeletal survey (occult/healing fractures; <2 years suspected abuse; consider repeat in ~2 weeks)
Head imaging (CT/MRI); dilated ophthalmology exam for retinal hemorrhages
Labs to evaluate for bleeding/clotting disorders and bone disease (exclude mimics: coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta, metabolic) — but do NOT delay reporting for results
Photograph injuries; document on a body diagram per policy
MANDATED REPORTING (nursing/legal duty):
Report a REASONABLE SUSPICION (not proof) of child abuse/neglect to Child Protective Services (and law enforcement per jurisdiction) — timely, per policy/law

Do NOT investigate/gather evidence/prove abuse yourself (CPS/law enforcement role); do NOT assume someone else will report (individual, non-delegable duty); parental consent NOT required; reporting overrides confidentiality
Document the report (agency, time, person notified)
CAREGIVER APPROACH:

Remain calm, professional, non-judgmental, and NON-CONFRONTATIONAL; obtain history with open, non-leading questions; do NOT accuse, interrogate, or 'play detective'/seek a confession; avoid bias (abuse occurs across all groups)
OBJECTIVE DOCUMENTATION (may become legal evidence):

Describe injuries precisely (location, size, shape/pattern, color) with body diagrams + photographs; record caregiver and child statements VERBATIM in quotation marks; document timeline + who/when notified
Avoid conclusory/judgmental/accusatory language; document objective findings + quotes + that a report was made for suspected abuse

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What raises concern for non-accidental trauma?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically and legally significant.

opts.text: A history inconsistent with the injuries and inconsistent with the infant's developmental stage (a minimally-mobile 7-month-old 'rolling off the couch' with significant injury) — a cardinal red flag for abuse
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — history inconsistent with injury/development is a hallmark of NAT. RN role: recognize the red flag.

opts.text: Bruising in protected/unusual areas (torso, ear) and patterned marks — concerning for inflicted injury
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — protected-site/patterned bruising suggests abuse. RN role: recognize concerning injury patterns.

opts.text: Lethargy, vomiting, and a full/bulging fontanelle — concerning for increased ICP / abusive head trauma (which often has no external signs)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — these signal possible abusive head trauma, a leading abuse fatality. RN role: recognize + ensure neuro assessment.

opts.text: Ensure the child's immediate medical care (ABCs/neuro) AND safety — the child must not be discharged into a potentially unsafe situation pending evaluation
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — medical care + child safety are paramount. RN role: stabilize + protect.

opts.text: The nurse is a mandated reporter and must report a reasonable suspicion (not proof) of abuse to CPS
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the central legal/ethical duty. RN role: report reasonable suspicion.

opts.text: Document objectively (precise injury descriptions, body diagram/photos, verbatim quotes, notification timeline) without conclusory/accusatory language
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — objective documentation may become legal evidence. RN role: factual, precise documentation.

opts.text: Approach the caregiver non-judgmentally and non-confrontationally; engage the multidisciplinary child-protection team
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — non-confrontation + multidisciplinary coordination protect the child + process. RN role: non-confrontational, coordinated care.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — document and proceed
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Wait until the abuse is definitively proven and all imaging/labs return before reporting, so as not to falsely accuse the family
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Mandated reporters report a reasonable SUSPICION, not proof — waiting for certainty/results delays protection and may leave the child in danger. Report the suspicion now; CPS investigates.

opts.text: Confront the parent directly, accuse them of hurting the child, and interrogate them until they admit what happened
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + unsafe. Confronting/accusing/interrogating is not the nurse's role, can escalate the situation or prompt flight with the child, and can compromise the investigation. Remain non-confrontational; report to CPS, who investigates.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Injury inconsistent with the stated mechanism or the child's developmental stage, injuries in protected areas/multiple healing stages, patterned marks, and specific fractures (metaphyseal, posterior rib, different ages) raise concern for abuse
opts.rat: CORRECT — the red-flag framework. Foundation for recognition.

opts.text: Abusive head trauma classically combines subdural hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhages, and encephalopathy and may present without external injury (lethargy, vomiting, bulging fontanelle, seizures, apnea)
opts.rat: CORRECT — AHT principle. Foundation for recognizing a leading abuse fatality.

opts.text: Nurses are mandated reporters who must report a reasonable suspicion (not proof) to CPS; the duty is individual/non-delegable, requires no parental consent, and overrides confidentiality
opts.rat: CORRECT — the mandated-reporter principle. Foundation for the legal/ethical duty.

opts.text: Good-faith reporting is protected from liability; the nurse does not investigate or prove abuse (CPS/law enforcement do)
opts.rat: CORRECT — immunity + role-clarity principle. Foundation for reporting without fear or over-reach.

opts.text: The child's safety and medical care come first; the child should not be discharged into a potentially unsafe situation; documentation must be objective and may become legal evidence
opts.rat: CORRECT — safety + objective-documentation principle. Foundation for protection.

opts.text: Evaluating for medical mimics (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta, cultural practices) is appropriate, but it does not delay reporting a reasonable suspicion
opts.rat: CORRECT — assess mimics without delaying the report. Foundation for accurate yet timely action.

opts.text: A nurse should only report abuse if they are certain it occurred and have gathered evidence to prove it
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The threshold is reasonable SUSPICION, not certainty/proof; the nurse does not gather evidence/investigate (CPS does). Requiring proof would dangerously delay protection.

opts.text: Because the family is well-dressed and affluent (or, conversely, poor), abuse is unlikely (or likely), so suspicion can be adjusted by demographics
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Abuse occurs across ALL socioeconomic, racial, and cultural groups; basing suspicion on demographics is biased and leads to both missed abuse and false accusation. Assess objectively.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Immediate medical stabilization + child SAFETY — treat injuries/ABCs/neuro and ensure the child is not discharged into a potentially unsafe situation
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. The child's life/medical needs + physical safety come first. RN role: stabilize + protect.

opts.text: Fulfill the mandated-reporter duty — report the reasonable suspicion to CPS (without proof/consent; do not delegate it away)
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Timely reporting triggers protection/investigation. RN role: report reasonable suspicion.

opts.text: Support the medical workup (skeletal survey, head imaging, ophthalmology, labs/mimics) and photodocument injuries
opts.rat: #3 — HIGH. The workup defines injuries + excludes mimics + supports protection. RN role: support workup + photodocument.

opts.text: Document objectively (precise descriptions, body diagram/photos, verbatim quotes, notification timeline) without conclusory language
opts.rat: #4 — Significant. Objective documentation may become legal evidence + supports the child. RN role: factual documentation.

opts.text: Approach the caregiver non-confrontationally and coordinate the multidisciplinary child-protection team; support the child + assess siblings
opts.rat: #5 — Important + ongoing. Non-confrontation + coordination protect the child + process. RN role: non-confrontational, coordinated care.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Stabilize the infant medically (ABCs, neuro for possible abusive head trauma) and ensure the child is not discharged into a potentially unsafe situation
opts.rat: Medical care + child safety first. RN role: stabilize + protect.

opts.text: Report the reasonable suspicion of abuse to CPS (and law enforcement per jurisdiction) promptly, without needing proof or parental consent
opts.rat: Core mandated-reporter duty. RN role: report reasonable suspicion timely.

opts.text: Support the workup (skeletal survey, head imaging, dilated eye exam, labs to exclude mimics) and photograph/document injuries on a body diagram
opts.rat: Defines injuries, excludes mimics, supports protection. RN role: support workup + photodocument.

opts.text: Document objectively with precise injury descriptions and verbatim caregiver/child quotes, plus who/when notified, avoiding conclusory language
opts.rat: Objective documentation (may be legal evidence). RN role: factual documentation.

opts.text: Remain calm and non-confrontational with the caregiver, obtain history with open non-leading questions, and engage the multidisciplinary child-protection team
opts.rat: Non-confrontational, coordinated, child-focused approach. RN role: non-confrontation + coordination.

opts.text: Recognize that abuse occurs across all demographics and assess objectively without bias; evaluate for medical mimics while still reporting the suspicion
opts.rat: Bias-free assessment + mimic evaluation without delaying the report. RN role: objective, unbiased assessment.

opts.text: Wait to report until all imaging/labs return and the abuse is definitively proven, to avoid falsely accusing the family
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — report reasonable SUSPICION, not proof; waiting delays protection. CPS investigates; the nurse reports the suspicion now.

opts.text: Confront and accuse the parent and interrogate them to obtain a confession before deciding whether to report
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG/unsafe — confronting/interrogating is not the nurse's role, can escalate/prompt flight, and compromises the investigation. Report to CPS without confrontation.

opts.text: Assume the physician or social worker will file the report, so the nurse does not need to do anything further
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the mandated-reporter duty is individual and non-delegable; the nurse must ensure a report is made, not assume someone else will.

opts.text: Discharge the infant home with the caregiver while the workup is pending to avoid upsetting the family
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG/DANGEROUS — the child must not be discharged into a potentially unsafe situation pending evaluation; ensure safety (admit/protective hold + CPS).

opts.text: Document the conclusion 'the mother physically abused this child' as the diagnosis in the chart
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — avoid conclusory/accusatory language; document objective findings + verbatim quotes + that a report was made for SUSPECTED abuse (the determination is CPS/legal).

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Address the infant's immediate medical needs (ABCs, neuro) and ensure physical safety (no unsafe discharge)
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Stabilize + protect the child. RN role: medical care + safety.

opts.text: Recognize the red flags and support the workup (skeletal survey, head imaging, eye exam, labs); photograph/document injuries
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Define injuries + exclude mimics + photodocument. RN role: support workup + documentation.

opts.text: Fulfill the mandated-reporter duty — report the reasonable suspicion to CPS (and law enforcement per jurisdiction), ensuring the report is made
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Trigger protection/investigation by reporting. RN role: report reasonable suspicion.

opts.text: Document objectively (precise descriptions, verbatim quotes, notification timeline) and engage the multidisciplinary child-protection team/social work
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Objective documentation + multidisciplinary coordination. RN role: documentation + coordination.

opts.text: Maintain a non-confrontational caregiver approach, support the child, ensure siblings are assessed, and coordinate a safe disposition with CPS
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing. Non-confrontation + child/sibling support + safe disposition. RN role: non-confrontational, coordinated, protective care.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action taken, classify as Appropriate or Inappropriate.

opts.text: The nurse stabilized the infant, ensured he was not discharged into a potentially unsafe situation, and supported the workup (skeletal survey, head imaging, eye exam, labs to exclude mimics)
opts.rat: Medical care + child safety + appropriate workup. Model handling.

opts.text: The nurse reported the reasonable suspicion to CPS promptly, without proof or parental consent, and ensured the report was made rather than assuming someone else would
opts.rat: Correct fulfillment of the individual, non-delegable mandated-reporter duty on reasonable suspicion. Model handling.

opts.text: Injuries were photographed and documented precisely with verbatim caregiver/child quotes and the notification timeline, avoiding conclusory language
opts.rat: Objective, legally sound documentation. Model handling.

opts.text: The nurse remained calm and non-confrontational, used open questions, and engaged the child-protection team/social work
opts.rat: Non-confrontational, coordinated, child-focused care. Model handling.

opts.text: The nurse decided to wait to report until all test results returned and the abuse was proven, to avoid a false accusation
opts.rat: ⚠️ Mandated reporters report reasonable SUSPICION, not proof; waiting delays protection. Incorrect.

opts.text: The nurse confronted and accused the parent and interrogated them to get a confession
opts.rat: ⚠️ Confronting/interrogating is unsafe, not the nurse's role, and can compromise the child's safety and the investigation. Incorrect.

opts.text: Assuming the physician would handle it, the nurse made no report and took no further action
opts.rat: ⚠️ The mandated-reporter duty is individual and non-delegable; failing to ensure a report is a legal/ethical breach. Incorrect.

opts.text: The nurse documented 'the parent abused this child' as a conclusion in the medical record
opts.rat: ⚠️ Avoid conclusory/accusatory language; document objective findings + quotes + that a report was made for SUSPECTED abuse. Incorrect.

opts.text: The infant was admitted for treatment and neuro monitoring, and CPS/the child-protection team determined a safe disposition (not released to an unsafe environment), with siblings assessed
opts.rat: Safe disposition + ongoing care + sibling assessment. Model handling protecting the child + household.

opts.text: Because the family appeared affluent and 'nice,' the nurse dismissed the concern and discharged the infant without reporting
opts.rat: ⚠️ Bias by demographics + dismissing red flags + failing to report + unsafe discharge — multiple serious errors that endanger the child. Incorrect.

title: Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal (Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome) in a 2-Day-Old Newborn Exposed to Maternal Opioid-Use-Disorder Treatment: Recognizing Withdrawal Signs, Assessing with Finnegan / Eat-Sleep-Console, NON-PHARMACOLOGIC Comfort Care FIRST (Rooming-In, Skin-to-Skin, Swaddling, Low Stimulation, Frequent Small Feeds, Breastfeeding When Appropriate), Pharmacologic Morphine for Severe Symptoms, and Non-Judgmental Maternal Support with a Plan of Safe Care
subtitle: NEONATAL ABSTINENCE SYNDROME (NAS) / NEONATAL OPIOID WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME (NOWS) is the constellation of withdrawal signs in a newborn who was exposed in utero to substances (most often OPIOIDS — including a mother appropriately treated with medication for opioid use disorder/MOUD such as methadone or buprenorphine, as well as illicit opioids). ONSET TIMING depends on the substance's half-life: SHORT-acting opioids (e.g., heroin) → signs within ~24-72 hours; LONG-acting opioids (METHADONE, buprenorphine) → signs may be DELAYED up to ~5-7 days (important for discharge timing/observation). SIGNS span systems: CNS (central) — IRRITABILITY, a HIGH-PITCHED CRY, TREMORS, HYPERTONIA/increased muscle tone, hyperactive/exaggerated Moro reflex, difficulty being consoled, disturbed/short SLEEP, and (severe) SEIZURES; GASTROINTESTINAL — POOR/UNCOORDINATED FEEDING, frantic/excessive sucking, regurgitation/vomiting, LOOSE/watery STOOLS, dehydration, and poor weight gain; AUTONOMIC/metabolic/respiratory — SWEATING, temperature instability/fever, frequent YAWNING and SNEEZING, nasal stuffiness, tachypnea, mottling, and skin EXCORIATION (from rubbing/movement). ASSESSMENT/SCORING: the FINNEGAN Neonatal Abstinence Scoring Tool quantifies the severity of signs at intervals to guide care/treatment; the newer, function-based EAT, SLEEP, CONSOLE (ESC) approach asks whether the infant can EAT adequately (e.g., feed well/take an age-appropriate volume), SLEEP undisturbed for ≥1 hour, and be CONSOLED within ~10 minutes — ESC PRIORITIZES non-pharmacologic care and the infant's function and has been shown to reduce unnecessary medication and length of stay. NON-PHARMACOLOGIC CARE IS FIRST-LINE and the mainstay (the heart of nursing for NAS): (1) ROOMING-IN — keep the mother and infant TOGETHER (mother as the primary caregiver) rather than routinely separating to the NICU, which reduces withdrawal severity, medication need, and length of stay and supports bonding; (2) SKIN-TO-SKIN (kangaroo) contact; (3) SWADDLING (snug) and gentle, slow handling; (4) a LOW-STIMULATION ENVIRONMENT — DIM lights, QUIET, minimal/clustered handling, avoid sudden movements/noise, protect sleep; (5) SOOTHING measures — holding, rocking, a pacifier (non-nutritive sucking), responding promptly to cues; (6) FEEDING — small, FREQUENT feeds (these infants have high caloric needs and uncoordinated/frantic feeding), with higher-calorie feeds if weight gain is poor; (7) BREASTFEEDING is ENCOURAGED when NOT contraindicated — it is recommended for mothers who are stable on MOUD (methadone/buprenorphine) and not using illicit drugs, are HIV-negative, and have no other contraindication; breastfeeding reduces NAS severity, supports bonding, and only small amounts of MOUD pass into milk (do NOT abruptly stop breastfeeding, which could precipitate worsening). PHARMACOLOGIC TREATMENT is added when non-pharmacologic measures are insufficient and the infant has SEVERE/persistent symptoms (e.g., high scores, inability to eat/sleep/console, poor weight gain, dehydration, or seizures): an OPIOID is first-line — oral MORPHINE (or methadone; buprenorphine is also used) titrated to control symptoms and then WEANED gradually; ADJUNCTS such as CLONIDINE (or phenobarbital, especially for non-opioid/polysubstance or as an adjunct) may be added; the goal is to control symptoms enough that the infant can EAT, SLEEP, and be CONSOLED and gain weight, then wean. SUPPORTIVE CARE: meticulous SKIN/DIAPER care for loose stools/excoriation (frequent changes, barrier cream), monitor WEIGHT/hydration/intake-and-output and temperature, safe positioning, and seizure precautions if severe. MATERNAL + FAMILY-CENTERED, NON-JUDGMENTAL care: treat the mother with respect and WITHOUT stigma (maternal OUD is a medical disease, and MOUD is appropriate, recommended treatment — NOT a reason to blame or separate); INVOLVE the mother in caregiving and soothing (empowering, bonding, and therapeutic for the infant), support her MOUD/treatment and (when appropriate) breastfeeding, and keep mother and baby together when safe. PLAN OF SAFE CARE: under federal law (CAPTA/CARA), a substance-exposed infant prompts a NOTIFICATION to the child-welfare/development-of-services system and the creation of a PLAN OF SAFE CARE addressing the health/substance-treatment needs of the infant AND mother/caregiver — this is intended as a SUPPORTIVE, service-connecting process (linking to treatment, home visiting, early intervention), NOT inherently a punitive abuse finding (distinguish from a child-abuse report); engage SOCIAL WORK. DISCHARGE/FOLLOW-UP: SAFE-SLEEP education, feeding support, maternal treatment continuity, early-intervention/developmental follow-up (NAS infants are at risk for feeding and developmental issues), and connection to community resources. NURSING ROLE: recognize NAS signs and assess with Finnegan/ESC; deliver and prioritize NON-PHARMACOLOGIC comfort care (rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, low stimulation, frequent feeds, breastfeeding when appropriate); administer/monitor pharmacologic therapy for severe symptoms; provide supportive skin/feeding/hydration care; support the mother-infant dyad non-judgmentally and involve her in care; and coordinate the Plan of Safe Care, social work, and follow-up

labs.v: Baby T. is a 2-day-old term newborn whose mother is in treatment for OPIOID USE DISORDER, stable on BUPRENORPHINE (medication for OUD/MOUD) during pregnancy — appropriate, recommended treatment. The infant is developing NEONATAL ABSTINENCE SYNDROME (NAS) / NEONATAL OPIOID WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME (NOWS): IRRITABILITY, a HIGH-PITCHED CRY, TREMORS, increased muscle tone with an exaggerated Moro, frequent YAWNING/SNEEZING and nasal stuffiness, POOR/UNCOORDINATED feeding with frantic sucking, LOOSE stools, mild temperature instability, and difficulty being consoled. ONSET TIMING is clinically important and depends on the substance half-life: SHORT-acting opioids (heroin) cause signs within ~24-72 hours, while LONG-ACTING opioids (METHADONE, BUPRENORPHINE) can cause DELAYED onset/peak up to ~5-7 days — so infants of mothers on MOUD require an adequate OBSERVATION period before discharge (signs may appear/peak after the typical 48-hour newborn stay). NAS signs span CNS (irritability/high-pitched cry/tremors/hypertonia/poor sleep/seizures), GI (poor feeding/vomiting/loose stools/poor weight gain/dehydration), and autonomic/metabolic/respiratory (sweating/temperature instability/yawning/sneezing/tachypnea/skin excoriation). SOCIAL/CONTEXT: mother engaged in addiction treatment + prenatal care; supportive; the care team approaches her NON-JUDGMENTALLY (maternal OUD is a medical disease; MOUD is correct treatment — NOT grounds for blame or routine separation). The nurse's priorities: recognize and assess the withdrawal (Finnegan/Eat-Sleep-Console), deliver NON-PHARMACOLOGIC comfort care FIRST (the mainstay), reserve pharmacologic treatment for severe/uncontrolled symptoms, support feeding/weight/skin, keep and support the mother-infant DYAD, and coordinate a Plan of Safe Care + follow-up.
labs.r: NAS/NOWS = in-utero (usually opioid) exposure withdrawal: CNS (irritability/high-pitched cry/tremors/hypertonia/seizures), GI (poor feeding/loose stools/poor weight gain), autonomic (sweating/yawning/sneezing/temperature instability). Onset: short-acting opioids 24-72h; LONG-acting (methadone/buprenorphine) delayed up to 5-7 days → observe before discharge. Mother on MOUD = appropriate (non-judgmental). RN role: recognize + assess + non-pharm care first + support the dyad.

labs.v: STANDARDIZED ASSESSMENT guides care and the decision to treat. The FINNEGAN NEONATAL ABSTINENCE SCORING TOOL (or modified versions) assigns points to a list of withdrawal signs across CNS, GI, and autonomic/metabolic/respiratory domains, scored at regular intervals (often every 3-4 hours, after feeds); higher/persistently elevated scores indicate more severe withdrawal and historically triggered escalating pharmacologic treatment. The NEWER, function-based EAT, SLEEP, CONSOLE (ESC) approach reframes assessment around the infant's FUNCTION and the adequacy of non-pharmacologic care, asking three questions: can the infant EAT adequately (feed well / take an age-appropriate volume, ~≥1 oz or breastfeed effectively), SLEEP undisturbed for ≥1 HOUR, and be CONSOLED within ~10 MINUTES (with non-pharmacologic measures and caregiver support)? ESC EMPHASIZES maximizing NON-PHARMACOLOGIC care and parental presence, and using medication only when the infant cannot eat/sleep/console despite optimized comfort measures; ESC has been associated with LESS pharmacologic treatment and SHORTER length of stay than scoring-driven approaches. Either way, ASSESSMENT is paired with monitoring of WEIGHT (and feeding adequacy), INTAKE/OUTPUT and hydration (loose stools), and SKIN integrity (excoriation), and is performed in a way that does not over-stimulate the infant (assess with minimal disturbance, ideally during routine cares). The nurse uses the chosen tool consistently, ensures non-pharmacologic care is OPTIMIZED before attributing inability to console to a need for medication, and communicates findings to the team to guide treatment/weaning decisions. THIS INFANT is assessed with Finnegan/ESC, with the team prioritizing whether optimized comfort care allows her to eat, sleep, and console before considering pharmacologic therapy.
labs.r: Assess NAS with the FINNEGAN scoring tool (points for CNS/GI/autonomic signs, scored q3-4h) and/or the function-based EAT-SLEEP-CONSOLE (ESC) approach (can the infant EAT well, SLEEP ≥1h, be CONSOLED within ~10 min with non-pharm care?) — ESC maximizes non-pharm care + parental presence and reduces medication/LOS. Pair with weight/feeding/hydration/skin monitoring; assess with minimal stimulation. RN role: consistent scoring + optimize non-pharm care before medicating.

labs.v: NON-PHARMACOLOGIC CARE is FIRST-LINE and the foundation of NAS management — it reduces withdrawal severity, the need for medication, and length of stay, and it is the heart of nursing care: (1) ROOMING-IN — keep the MOTHER and INFANT TOGETHER with the mother as the primary caregiver (rather than routine separation to the NICU); rooming-in is consistently associated with LOWER NAS severity, LESS medication, shorter stays, and better bonding. (2) SKIN-TO-SKIN (kangaroo) contact — calming and regulating. (3) SWADDLING — snug swaddling (with safe technique) contains the infant and reduces tremor-related distress. (4) LOW-STIMULATION ENVIRONMENT — DIM the lights, keep it QUIET, minimize and CLUSTER handling/care, avoid sudden noise/movement, and PROTECT SLEEP (these infants are easily overstimulated, which worsens withdrawal). (5) SOOTHING — gentle holding/rocking, a PACIFIER for non-nutritive sucking, vertical rocking/swaying, and responding PROMPTLY to early cues before escalation. (6) FEEDING — offer SMALL, FREQUENT feeds (these infants have increased caloric needs and may feed frantically or ineffectively); use higher-calorie feeds if weight gain is inadequate; pace feeds and burp frequently (vomiting/loose stools are common). (7) BREASTFEEDING is ENCOURAGED when NOT contraindicated — it is RECOMMENDED for mothers who are STABLE on MOUD (methadone/buprenorphine), are NOT using illicit drugs, are HIV-NEGATIVE, and have no other contraindication; breastfeeding REDUCES NAS severity (small amounts of MOUD in milk provide a gentle taper), supports bonding, and should NOT be abruptly stopped (abrupt weaning can worsen withdrawal); support the mother with lactation help. Throughout, INVOLVE the mother as the primary comfort provider (empowering and therapeutic). These measures are continued EVEN IF pharmacologic treatment becomes necessary. THIS INFANT was cared for with rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, a low-stimulation environment, frequent small feeds, and breastfeeding (mother eligible), and consoled more easily, fed better, and slept longer as a result.
labs.r: NON-PHARMACOLOGIC care is first-line + the mainstay: ROOMING-IN (keep mother + baby together — reduces severity/medication/LOS), SKIN-TO-SKIN, SWADDLING, LOW-STIMULATION environment (dim/quiet/cluster care/protect sleep), soothing (rocking/pacifier/prompt response), small FREQUENT feeds (higher-calorie if needed), and BREASTFEEDING when not contraindicated (mother stable on MOUD, no illicit drugs, HIV-negative — reduces NAS; don't abruptly stop). Involve the mother. RN role: optimize non-pharmacologic comfort + feeding.

labs.v: PHARMACOLOGIC TREATMENT is ADDED when NON-pharmacologic measures (optimized) are INSUFFICIENT and the infant has SEVERE or persistent withdrawal — indicated by an inability to EAT/SLEEP/CONSOLE despite comfort care (ESC), high/persistent FINNEGAN scores, poor weight gain or DEHYDRATION from feeding difficulty/loose stools, or SEIZURES. FIRST-LINE pharmacologic therapy for opioid withdrawal is an OPIOID — oral MORPHINE (most common) or METHADONE (longer-acting); buprenorphine is also used in some centers — titrated UP to control symptoms (so the infant can eat, sleep, and console and gain weight), maintained, and then WEANED gradually as the infant stabilizes. ADJUNCTIVE agents include CLONIDINE (an alpha-2 agonist) and PHENOBARBITAL (often reserved for non-opioid/polysubstance exposure or as an adjunct when an opioid alone is insufficient). KEY PRINCIPLE: non-pharmacologic care is NOT stopped when medication is started — it continues alongside, and the medication is titrated to the lowest effective dose and weaned. SUPPORTIVE CARE throughout: (a) SKIN/DIAPER care — frequent diaper changes and a barrier cream for the loose, frequent stools that cause perianal EXCORIATION, and protect skin from rubbing/tremor-related abrasion; (b) NUTRITION/HYDRATION — monitor WEIGHT daily, intake/output, and hydration (high caloric needs + GI losses), supplement calories as needed; (c) TEMPERATURE regulation; (d) SAFE POSITIONING and, if severe, SEIZURE PRECAUTIONS; (e) gentle, clustered care to avoid overstimulation. The treatment GOAL is symptom control sufficient for the infant to feed, sleep, console, and grow — then taper. THIS INFANT received non-pharmacologic care first; if her symptoms had remained severe/uncontrolled, oral morphine would be titrated (with continued comfort care) and later weaned, with meticulous skin and feeding/weight support throughout.
labs.r: Pharmacologic treatment is ADDED (not first) for SEVERE/uncontrolled withdrawal (can't eat/sleep/console, high scores, poor weight gain/dehydration, seizures): first-line OPIOID — oral MORPHINE (or methadone), titrated then WEANED; adjuncts clonidine/phenobarbital. CONTINUE non-pharmacologic care alongside. Supportive: skin/diaper care for excoriation, monitor weight/hydration/I&O, temperature, seizure precautions if severe. RN role: administer/titrate/wean meds + continue comfort + supportive care.

labs.n: Maternal/dyad support + Plan of Safe Care; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: MATERNAL + FAMILY-CENTERED, NON-JUDGMENTAL CARE is essential and therapeutic: maternal OUD is a chronic MEDICAL disease and MOUD (methadone/buprenorphine) in pregnancy is APPROPRIATE, recommended treatment that protects mother and fetus — the mother is NOT to be blamed, shamed, or routinely separated from her infant. INVOLVE the mother as the PRIMARY caregiver and comfort provider (rooming-in, skin-to-skin, soothing, feeding) — this reduces NAS severity AND strengthens BONDING and maternal confidence; support her ongoing MOUD/treatment and (when appropriate) BREASTFEEDING; provide stigma-free education and emotional support. PLAN OF SAFE CARE: under federal law (CAPTA, amended by CARA — the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act), a substance-exposed infant prompts a NOTIFICATION to the child-welfare/service system and the development of a PLAN OF SAFE CARE that addresses the health and substance-use-treatment needs of BOTH the infant and the mother/caregiver and family — this is intended as a SUPPORTIVE, SERVICE-CONNECTING process (linking to maternal treatment, home visiting, early intervention, and supports), NOT inherently a punitive child-abuse finding (it should be DISTINGUISHED from a report of suspected abuse/neglect, though a separate concern would still be reported); engage SOCIAL WORK. DISCHARGE/FOLLOW-UP: provide SAFE-SLEEP education (back to sleep, firm flat surface, no soft bedding — especially important as families manage a fussy infant), feeding support, ensure maternal treatment continuity, and arrange EARLY-INTERVENTION/developmental and pediatric FOLLOW-UP (NAS infants are at risk for feeding difficulties and developmental concerns) plus community resources. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the infant was NOT routinely separated from the mother / sent to the NICU when rooming-in was appropriate (rooming-in is preferred); non-pharmacologic comfort care was prioritized FIRST (not jumping straight to medication); the mother was NOT shamed/blamed or told to stop her MOUD; breastfeeding was NOT inappropriately withheld (she met criteria) NOR abruptly stopped (which worsens withdrawal); the environment was NOT bright/loud/overstimulating; and the Plan of Safe Care was framed as SUPPORTIVE service-linkage (not conflated with a punitive abuse report). PROTECTIVE FACTORS: maternal engagement in MOUD + prenatal care; a supportive, involved mother kept with her infant (rooming-in/skin-to-skin/breastfeeding); optimized non-pharmacologic care reducing severity/medication/LOS; appropriate observation for delayed onset (buprenorphine); meticulous feeding/skin/weight support; non-judgmental, stigma-free care strengthening the dyad; a Plan of Safe Care connecting mother + infant to services; and developmental follow-up. EXPECTED outcome: withdrawal is controlled (the infant eats, sleeps, consoles, and gains weight), pharmacologic therapy (if needed) is weaned, the dyad bonds, and both are connected to ongoing treatment/support. NURSING ROLE: recognize + assess NAS (Finnegan/ESC); deliver non-pharmacologic comfort care first (rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, low stimulation, frequent feeds, breastfeeding when appropriate); administer/monitor/wean pharmacologic therapy for severe symptoms while continuing comfort care; provide supportive skin/feeding/hydration care; support and involve the mother non-judgmentally; and coordinate the Plan of Safe Care, social work, safe-sleep teaching, and follow-up.
labs.r: Maternal/dyad care is non-judgmental: OUD is a disease + MOUD is correct treatment; keep mother + baby together, involve her as primary caregiver, support MOUD + breastfeeding. PLAN OF SAFE CARE (CAPTA/CARA) = SUPPORTIVE service-linkage for infant + mother (NOT inherently a punitive abuse report); social work. Discharge: safe sleep, feeding support, maternal-treatment continuity, early-intervention/developmental + pediatric follow-up. Negatives confirm correct practice (rooming-in not separation, non-pharm first, no shaming/MOUD-stopping, breastfeeding not withheld/abruptly stopped, low stimulation). RN role: dyad support + service coordination.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this newborn with withdrawal?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Signs of neonatal opioid withdrawal — irritability, high-pitched cry, tremors, hypertonia, frequent yawning/sneezing, poor uncoordinated feeding, and loose stools — in an opioid-exposed newborn
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — recognizing the NAS/NOWS picture drives assessment + care. RN role: recognize withdrawal signs.

opts.text: Onset depends on the substance: long-acting opioids (methadone/buprenorphine) can cause delayed onset/peak up to ~5-7 days, so adequate observation before discharge is needed
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — delayed onset with long-acting opioids affects observation/discharge timing. RN role: observe adequately before discharge.

opts.text: Assess with a standardized tool (Finnegan and/or Eat-Sleep-Console), monitoring whether the infant can eat, sleep ≥1 hour, and be consoled — with minimal stimulation during assessment
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — standardized, function-based assessment guides care/treatment. RN role: consistent scoring + minimal-stimulation assessment.

opts.text: Non-pharmacologic comfort care is first-line — rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, low stimulation, soothing, and frequent small feeds
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — non-pharmacologic care is the mainstay and reduces severity/medication/LOS. RN role: prioritize comfort care.

opts.text: Breastfeeding is encouraged when not contraindicated (mother stable on MOUD, not using illicit drugs, HIV-negative) and should not be abruptly stopped
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — breastfeeding reduces NAS severity + supports bonding when appropriate. RN role: support eligible breastfeeding; don't abruptly stop.

opts.text: Reserve pharmacologic treatment (oral morphine first-line, titrated then weaned) for severe symptoms not controlled by optimized comfort care; continue comfort care alongside
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — medication is added (not first) for severe/uncontrolled withdrawal. RN role: pharmacologic treatment for severe symptoms + continue non-pharm care.

opts.text: Support the mother non-judgmentally, keep the dyad together, and coordinate a Plan of Safe Care (supportive service linkage) + skin/feeding/hydration support
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — non-judgmental dyad support + Plan of Safe Care + supportive care. RN role: dyad support + service coordination.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — document and proceed
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine for the newborn. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Routinely separate the infant to the NICU, place under bright lights for observation, and start morphine immediately as the first intervention
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Rooming-in (keeping the dyad together) is preferred and reduces severity/medication/LOS; bright lights/overstimulation worsen withdrawal; and pharmacologic treatment is reserved for severe symptoms after optimizing non-pharmacologic comfort care first.

opts.text: Tell the mother she caused this and instruct her to stop her buprenorphine and stop breastfeeding immediately
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + harmful. Maternal OUD is a medical disease and MOUD is appropriate treatment; shaming her is counterproductive; stopping her MOUD is dangerous; and abruptly stopping appropriate breastfeeding can worsen the infant's withdrawal. Provide non-judgmental support.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: NAS/NOWS reflects in-utero (usually opioid) exposure; onset is earlier with short-acting opioids (24-72h) and delayed (up to ~5-7 days) with long-acting opioids (methadone/buprenorphine)
opts.rat: CORRECT — etiology + onset timing. Foundation for recognition + observation.

opts.text: Assessment uses Finnegan scoring and/or the function-based Eat-Sleep-Console approach, which maximizes non-pharmacologic care and reduces medication/length of stay
opts.rat: CORRECT — assessment frameworks. Foundation for guiding care.

opts.text: Non-pharmacologic care (rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, low stimulation, soothing, frequent feeds) is first-line and reduces severity, medication need, and length of stay
opts.rat: CORRECT — non-pharmacologic mainstay principle. Foundation for management.

opts.text: Breastfeeding is encouraged for mothers stable on MOUD without contraindications and reduces NAS severity; it should not be abruptly discontinued
opts.rat: CORRECT — breastfeeding principle. Foundation for feeding decisions.

opts.text: Pharmacologic treatment (first-line oral morphine, titrated then weaned; adjuncts clonidine/phenobarbital) is added for severe/uncontrolled symptoms while continuing comfort care
opts.rat: CORRECT — pharmacologic principle. Foundation for escalation when needed.

opts.text: Maternal OUD is a medical disease and MOUD is appropriate treatment; care is non-judgmental, keeps the dyad together, and uses a Plan of Safe Care for supportive service linkage (not inherently punitive)
opts.rat: CORRECT — non-judgmental dyad + Plan of Safe Care principle. Foundation for family-centered care.

opts.text: Overstimulation (bright lights, loud noise, frequent handling) soothes the withdrawing infant and should be maximized
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Overstimulation WORSENS withdrawal; a LOW-stimulation environment (dim, quiet, minimal/clustered handling, protected sleep) is therapeutic.

opts.text: Pharmacologic treatment should be the immediate first-line intervention for every opioid-exposed newborn regardless of symptom severity
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Non-pharmacologic comfort care is first-line; medication is reserved for severe/uncontrolled symptoms (can't eat/sleep/console, high scores, poor weight gain, seizures) after optimizing comfort care.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Optimize non-pharmacologic comfort care (rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, low stimulation, soothing) and assess withdrawal with Finnegan/ESC
opts.rat: #1 — Foundational/first-line. Optimized comfort care + assessment guide everything and often control symptoms. RN role: non-pharmacologic care + assessment.

opts.text: Support feeding/nutrition/hydration — small frequent feeds, breastfeeding when appropriate, monitor weight/I&O (high caloric needs + loose stools)
opts.rat: #2 — High. Feeding adequacy + hydration are central to NAS function/recovery. RN role: feeding + hydration support.

opts.text: Administer/titrate/wean pharmacologic treatment (oral morphine) for severe symptoms not controlled by comfort care, continuing non-pharmacologic care
opts.rat: #3 — When indicated. Medication controls severe symptoms; comfort care continues. RN role: pharmacologic management for severe symptoms.

opts.text: Provide supportive skin/diaper care for excoriation and monitor temperature/seizure risk
opts.rat: #4 — Significant. Skin protection + monitoring prevent complications. RN role: supportive care.

opts.text: Support the mother non-judgmentally, keep the dyad together, and coordinate the Plan of Safe Care + follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Important + ongoing. Dyad support + service coordination sustain outcomes. RN role: maternal support + Plan of Safe Care + follow-up.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this newborn with NAS.

opts.text: Room the infant in with the mother, provide skin-to-skin, swaddle snugly, and keep the environment dim and quiet with minimal/clustered handling
opts.rat: Core non-pharmacologic, first-line care. RN role: rooming-in + comfort + low stimulation.

opts.text: Assess withdrawal with Finnegan/Eat-Sleep-Console and monitor weight, intake/output, hydration, and skin integrity
opts.rat: Standardized assessment + supportive monitoring. RN role: scoring + monitoring.

opts.text: Offer small, frequent feeds and encourage breastfeeding (mother stable on buprenorphine, HIV-negative, not using illicit drugs)
opts.rat: Appropriate feeding + eligible breastfeeding (reduces NAS). RN role: feeding/breastfeeding support.

opts.text: Reserve oral morphine (titrated then weaned) for severe symptoms not controlled by optimized comfort care, continuing non-pharmacologic care alongside
opts.rat: Correct pharmacologic escalation for severe symptoms. RN role: medicate for severe symptoms + continue comfort.

opts.text: Provide barrier cream and frequent diaper changes for loose-stool excoriation; monitor temperature and weight
opts.rat: Supportive skin/nutrition care. RN role: skin protection + monitoring.

opts.text: Support the mother non-judgmentally, involve her in soothing/feeding, continue her MOUD, and develop a Plan of Safe Care with social work
opts.rat: Non-judgmental dyad support + service coordination. RN role: maternal support + Plan of Safe Care.

opts.text: Routinely separate the infant to the NICU and limit maternal contact to reduce stimulation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — rooming-in (keeping the dyad together with the mother as caregiver) reduces severity/medication/LOS; routine separation is counterproductive.

opts.text: Start oral morphine immediately as the first intervention for every opioid-exposed newborn
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — non-pharmacologic care is first-line; medication is reserved for severe/uncontrolled symptoms after optimizing comfort care.

opts.text: Place the infant under bright lights with frequent handling and noise for close observation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — overstimulation worsens withdrawal; provide a low-stimulation (dim, quiet, minimal-handling) environment.

opts.text: Instruct the mother to stop her buprenorphine and abruptly stop breastfeeding, and tell her she caused the baby's condition
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG/harmful — stopping appropriate MOUD is dangerous, abruptly stopping eligible breastfeeding worsens withdrawal, and shaming is counterproductive. Provide non-judgmental support.

opts.text: Treat the Plan of Safe Care as a punitive child-abuse report and threaten the mother with losing custody to motivate her
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the Plan of Safe Care is a SUPPORTIVE, service-connecting process (CAPTA/CARA), not inherently a punitive abuse report; threatening/coercing the mother is inappropriate and harmful.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Optimize non-pharmacologic comfort care (rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddle, dim/quiet environment, soothe) and assess withdrawal with Finnegan/ESC
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. First-line comfort care + assessment often control symptoms and guide care. RN role: comfort care + assessment.

opts.text: Support feeding (small frequent feeds, breastfeeding if appropriate) and monitor weight/intake/output/hydration
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Feeding/hydration are central to function and recovery. RN role: feeding + hydration.

opts.text: If symptoms remain severe/uncontrolled, administer and titrate pharmacologic treatment (oral morphine) while continuing comfort care
opts.rat: #3 — Third, when indicated. Medication controls severe symptoms with continued comfort care. RN role: pharmacologic management.

opts.text: Provide supportive skin/diaper care for excoriation and monitor temperature/seizure risk
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Supportive care prevents complications. RN role: skin/temperature/seizure monitoring.

opts.text: Support the mother non-judgmentally, coordinate the Plan of Safe Care + social work, provide safe-sleep teaching, and arrange follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing/discharge. Dyad support + service coordination + follow-up sustain outcomes. RN role: maternal support + Plan of Safe Care + follow-up.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: With rooming-in, skin-to-skin, swaddling, a low-stimulation environment, soothing, and frequent feeds, the infant consoles more easily, feeds better, and sleeps longer between cares
opts.rat: Optimized non-pharmacologic comfort care improving function (eat/sleep/console). Expected, desired response.

opts.text: Breastfeeding (mother eligible on buprenorphine) is supported and not abruptly stopped; the infant's withdrawal severity and feeding improve
opts.rat: Appropriate breastfeeding reduces NAS severity + supports bonding. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Despite optimized comfort care the infant cannot eat/sleep/console with high scores and poor weight gain, so oral morphine is started and titrated while comfort care continues, and symptoms come under control
opts.rat: Appropriate escalation to pharmacologic treatment for severe symptoms (with continued comfort care) controlling withdrawal. Correct, improving handling.

opts.text: The infant feeds well, gains weight, consoles, and sleeps; pharmacologic therapy (if used) is weaned, and the dyad is connected to services and developmental follow-up at discharge
opts.rat: Recovery + safe, supported discharge with follow-up. Ideal outcome.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the infant was routinely separated to the NICU under bright lights with frequent handling and no maternal involvement; withdrawal worsened and medication need/length of stay increased
opts.rat: ⚠️ Separation + overstimulation worsen withdrawal and increase medication/LOS. Demonstrates why rooming-in + low stimulation + maternal involvement are first-line.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — morphine was started immediately as the first intervention without optimizing comfort care, and the infant received unnecessary medication and a prolonged stay
opts.rat: ⚠️ Jumping to medication first (skipping non-pharmacologic care) leads to unnecessary medication/longer stays. Demonstrates non-pharmacologic-first management.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the mother was told to stop her buprenorphine and abruptly stop breastfeeding and was shamed; she disengaged from care and the infant's withdrawal worsened
opts.rat: ⚠️ Stopping appropriate MOUD/abruptly stopping eligible breastfeeding + shaming worsens outcomes and disengages the mother. Demonstrates the need for non-judgmental dyad support.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the long-acting-opioid-exposed infant was discharged at 48 hours before adequate observation; withdrawal peaked at home day 5 with poor feeding and dehydration
opts.rat: ⚠️ Premature discharge missed the delayed peak of long-acting-opioid withdrawal. Demonstrates the need for adequate observation before discharge.

opts.text: Early on, before comfort measures take full effect, the infant's withdrawal signs are present and essentially unchanged while the nurse optimizes the environment and feeding
opts.rat: Before non-pharmacologic measures take full effect, an unchanged baseline is expected; continue optimizing comfort care and reassess function (eat/sleep/console).

opts.text: At follow-up the infant is thriving and gaining weight, the mother remains in treatment and bonded, and both are connected to early-intervention and community services
opts.rat: Sustained recovery + dyad bonding + service linkage. Standard ideal longer-term outcome.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Basic Care and Comfort, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in a 34-Year-Old Combat Veteran Presenting to Outpatient Mental Health: Recognizing the Four DSM-5 Symptom Clusters, Screening for Suicide/Substance-Use Comorbidity, Delivering TRAUMA-INFORMED Care, Teaching GROUNDING/Coping for Flashbacks and Hyperarousal, and Connecting to First-Line Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy and SSRI/Prazosin (NOT Long-Term Benzodiazepines)
subtitle: POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER (PTSD) develops after EXPOSURE to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence — by directly experiencing it, witnessing it, learning it happened to a close family member/friend, or repeated/extreme exposure to aversive details (e.g., first responders, combat). DSM-5 describes FOUR SYMPTOM CLUSTERS: (1) INTRUSION — recurrent involuntary distressing MEMORIES, NIGHTMARES, FLASHBACKS (dissociative reliving as if the event is happening again), and intense psychological/physiological distress to internal or external CUES/TRIGGERS that resemble the trauma; (2) AVOIDANCE — persistent effort to avoid trauma-related thoughts/feelings AND external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, situations); (3) NEGATIVE ALTERATIONS in COGNITION and MOOD — inability to recall key features of the event, persistent negative beliefs about oneself/others/the world, distorted blame or GUILT, persistent negative emotional state (fear, horror, anger, shame), markedly diminished interest (anhedonia), feeling DETACHED/ESTRANGED from others, and an inability to experience positive emotions; (4) ALTERATIONS in AROUSAL and REACTIVITY — irritability/angry outbursts, reckless or self-destructive behavior, HYPERVIGILANCE, an exaggerated STARTLE response, problems with CONCENTRATION, and SLEEP disturbance. By definition the symptoms last MORE THAN 1 MONTH and cause significant DISTRESS or functional IMPAIRMENT (work, relationships); when the same picture lasts LESS than 1 month after the trauma it is ACUTE STRESS DISORDER. A dissociative subtype (depersonalization/derealization) may occur. ASSESSMENT + SAFETY: PTSD carries HIGH COMORBIDITY with DEPRESSION, SUBSTANCE/ALCOHOL USE DISORDER (often self-medication), and SUICIDE — so the nurse SCREENS for suicidal/self-harm ideation, substance use, and CURRENT SAFETY (e.g., ongoing abuse/intimate-partner violence) FIRST, and may use validated tools (e.g., the PCL-5). TRAUMA-INFORMED CARE is the framework for ALL interactions (SAMHSA principles: SAFETY; TRUSTWORTHINESS/transparency; PEER support; COLLABORATION/mutuality; EMPOWERMENT, VOICE and CHOICE; and cultural/historical/gender sensitivity) — it shifts the question from 'what is WRONG with you?' to 'what HAPPENED to you?', actively AVOIDS RE-TRAUMATIZATION, gives the client CONTROL and CHOICE, provides PREDICTABILITY (explain before doing, respect personal space, avoid surprising or cornering), and minimizes coercive/forced interventions. THERAPEUTIC COMMUNICATION: build TRUST with a calm, nonjudgmental, accepting presence; VALIDATE feelings; let the client set the PACE and do NOT force them to recount the traumatic event in detail before they are ready (a forced, premature trauma narrative can re-traumatize); do NOT MINIMIZE ('at least you survived,' 'just move on') or claim to know exactly how they feel. For FLASHBACKS, dissociation, or acute anxiety, teach and use GROUNDING techniques — the 5-4-3-2-1 sensory method, paced/diaphragmatic breathing, and ORIENTING to the present ('you are safe, you are here, it is [today], the event is over') — to reconnect the client to the here-and-now. TREATMENT: FIRST-LINE is trauma-focused PSYCHOTHERAPY — Trauma-Focused CBT, Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). First-line PHARMACOLOGY is an SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine — FDA-approved) or SNRI (venlafaxine); PRAZOSIN (an alpha-1 antagonist) is used for trauma-related NIGHTMARES and sleep disturbance. BENZODIAZEPINES are generally AVOIDED — they do NOT treat the core disorder, carry dependence/misuse risk (especially with comorbid substance use disorder), can impair the processing/extinction central to recovery, and may WORSEN outcomes; alcohol/illicit substances should be reduced (they worsen symptoms and sleep). HEALTH PROMOTION/RECOVERY: provide PSYCHOEDUCATION that normalizes symptoms as an understandable RESPONSE to trauma (reducing shame/self-blame and supporting engagement), encourage SLEEP hygiene, regular EXERCISE, SOCIAL/PEER support (e.g., veterans' groups), stress-management/relaxation skills, limiting alcohol/caffeine, and gradual return to function; screen at-risk populations (veterans, abuse/assault survivors, first responders) and connect to RESOURCES and follow-up. NURSING ROLE: recognize the four symptom clusters; screen for safety/suicide/substance comorbidity FIRST; deliver trauma-informed, nonjudgmental care that gives control/choice and avoids re-traumatization; teach grounding/coping for flashbacks and hyperarousal and stabilize sleep; facilitate evidence-based treatment (trauma-focused psychotherapy +/- SSRI/SNRI, prazosin for nightmares — NOT long-term benzodiazepines); and provide psychoeducation, peer support, and recovery-oriented follow-up.

patient.admitDate: A 34-year-old combat veteran (separated from service ~14 months ago) presents to the outpatient mental-health/primary-care clinic at his partner's urging. Symptoms have lasted more than a month and are impairing his work and relationships. He is being assessed for PTSD with attention to SAFETY (suicide/self-harm and alcohol use), with trauma-informed care, grounding/coping teaching, and connection to trauma-focused therapy and appropriate medication.
