labs.n: PRESENTATION + recognizing PTSD (DSM-5 four symptom clusters + timeframe)
labs.v: Marcus R. is a 34-year-old combat VETERAN presenting with several months of recurrent NIGHTMARES and intrusive memories, FLASHBACKS triggered by loud noises and crowds, marked AVOIDANCE (won't drive highways, avoids news/crowds/reminders), HYPERVIGILANCE with an exaggerated STARTLE response, irritability, poor concentration, severe SLEEP disturbance, detachment from his family, and persistent GUILT — present for MORE THAN 1 MONTH with clear functional impairment. This fits POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER (PTSD): a disorder that develops after EXPOSURE to actual/threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence (experienced, witnessed, learned of in a close other, or via repeated/extreme exposure to aversive details). DSM-5 organizes symptoms into FOUR CLUSTERS: (1) INTRUSION — distressing memories, nightmares, flashbacks (dissociative reliving), and intense distress/physiologic reactivity to trauma CUES; (2) AVOIDANCE — of trauma-related thoughts/feelings and external reminders; (3) NEGATIVE alterations in COGNITION/MOOD — distorted blame/guilt, persistent negative beliefs, anhedonia, detachment/estrangement, inability to feel positive emotions; (4) AROUSAL/REACTIVITY — irritability/anger, recklessness, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, concentration and sleep problems. The >1-MONTH timeframe distinguishes PTSD from ACUTE STRESS DISORDER (same picture but lasting <1 month after the trauma). The nurse's priorities: recognize the clusters, screen for SAFETY first, deliver trauma-informed care, teach grounding/coping, and connect him to evidence-based treatment.
labs.r: PTSD = post-trauma disorder with FOUR DSM-5 clusters — INTRUSION (memories/nightmares/FLASHBACKS/cue reactivity), AVOIDANCE (of reminders), NEGATIVE COGNITION/MOOD (guilt, negative beliefs, detachment, anhedonia), and AROUSAL (HYPERVIGILANCE, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep/concentration problems), lasting >1 MONTH with impairment (<1 month = acute stress disorder). RN role: recognize the clusters.

labs.n: Assessment + SAFETY first (suicide / substance comorbidity / current safety)
labs.v: SAFETY is assessed FIRST because PTSD carries HIGH COMORBIDITY: major DEPRESSION, SUBSTANCE and ALCOHOL USE DISORDER (frequently as self-medication for intrusion/sleep symptoms), and an elevated risk of SUICIDE and self-harm. The nurse SCREENS for SUICIDAL/self-harm IDEATION, intent, and plan; for ALCOHOL/substance use; and for CURRENT SAFETY — including access to lethal means (e.g., FIREARMS, especially relevant for veterans) and any ongoing danger such as intimate-partner violence. Validated tools support assessment (e.g., the PCL-5 for PTSD symptom severity, depression and substance screens, and a structured suicide-risk assessment). A positive suicide screen drives immediate safety planning, means-restriction counseling, and an appropriate level of care. The HISTORY is gathered in a trauma-informed way — letting the client share at HIS pace, NOT forcing a detailed trauma narrative before he is ready (which can re-traumatize), and focusing on current symptoms, function, triggers, sleep, substance use, supports, and safety. THIS VETERAN is screened for suicide and alcohol use and for firearm access and current safety, with results guiding the plan, before deeper trauma-processing work begins.
labs.r: SAFETY FIRST — PTSD has HIGH comorbidity with depression, substance/ALCOHOL use disorder (self-medication), and SUICIDE/self-harm. Screen for suicidal ideation/plan, substance use, and current safety (lethal means/firearms, intimate-partner violence); use validated tools (PCL-5, suicide-risk assessment). Gather history at the client's pace without forcing a premature trauma narrative. RN role: screen safety + comorbidity before trauma-processing work.

labs.v: TRAUMA-INFORMED CARE (TIC) is the framework for EVERY interaction. The SAMHSA principles are SAFETY (physical + emotional); TRUSTWORTHINESS and transparency; PEER support; COLLABORATION and mutuality (sharing power); EMPOWERMENT, VOICE, and CHOICE; and attention to CULTURAL, historical, and gender issues. Practically, TIC shifts the frame from 'what is WRONG with you?' to 'what HAPPENED to you?', actively works to AVOID RE-TRAUMATIZATION, and gives the client CONTROL: explain procedures BEFORE doing them, offer CHOICES, provide PREDICTABILITY, respect personal SPACE, avoid SURPRISING or CORNERING the client, keep an accessible exit, and minimize coercive/forced interventions. THERAPEUTIC COMMUNICATION: establish TRUST with a calm, nonjudgmental, accepting presence; use active listening and VALIDATE his experience and feelings; let HIM set the PACE; do NOT pressure him to recount the trauma in detail before he is ready; and AVOID minimizing statements ('at least you made it,' 'just move on') or false reassurance ('I know exactly how you feel'). For a FLASHBACK, dissociation, or acute anxiety, use GROUNDING to reconnect him to the present: speak calmly and ORIENT him ('you are SAFE, you are HERE in the clinic, it is [today], that event is in the PAST'), use the 5-4-3-2-1 SENSORY method (name 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you can touch, 2 you smell, 1 you taste), and coach PACED/diaphragmatic BREATHING — NOT confrontation, restraint, or 'snapping him out of it.' Teach him to recognize early cues and self-apply grounding and breathing between visits. THIS VETERAN had a flashback in clinic that resolved with calm orientation, 5-4-3-2-1 grounding, and paced breathing.
labs.r: TRAUMA-INFORMED CARE (SAMHSA: safety, trust/transparency, peer support, collaboration, empowerment/CHOICE, cultural sensitivity) frames every interaction — ask 'what HAPPENED to you?', avoid RE-TRAUMATIZATION, give control/choice, explain before doing, respect space, don't surprise/corner. Communication: nonjudgmental, validate, let him set the pace, don't force the trauma narrative, don't minimize. FLASHBACK → GROUNDING (orient to present, 5-4-3-2-1, paced breathing), not confrontation/restraint. RN role: trauma-informed relationship + grounding.

labs.n: Treatment — trauma-focused psychotherapy (first-line) + pharmacology + AVOID benzodiazepines
labs.v: EVIDENCE-BASED TREATMENT: FIRST-LINE is trauma-focused PSYCHOTHERAPY — Trauma-Focused CBT, PROLONGED EXPOSURE (PE), COGNITIVE PROCESSING THERAPY (CPT), and EYE MOVEMENT DESENSITIZATION AND REPROCESSING (EMDR); these have the strongest evidence and address the core disorder. PHARMACOLOGY (often combined with therapy): FIRST-LINE medications are SSRIs — SERTRALINE and PAROXETINE are FDA-approved for PTSD — or an SNRI such as VENLAFAXINE; these take several weeks for full effect, so set expectations and reinforce adherence. PRAZOSIN (an alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist) specifically targets trauma-related NIGHTMARES and sleep disturbance (monitor for orthostatic hypotension/dizziness, especially with the first dose). BENZODIAZEPINES are GENERALLY AVOIDED in PTSD: they do NOT treat the core disorder, carry significant DEPENDENCE/misuse risk (a major concern given the high rate of comorbid substance use disorder), can interfere with the emotional processing/extinction that recovery depends on, and are associated with WORSE outcomes; they are not a substitute for therapy. The nurse also counsels REDUCING ALCOHOL and illicit substances, which worsen symptoms, sleep, and risk. Care is COLLABORATIVE — the client is given information and CHOICE about therapy and medication options, consistent with trauma-informed, empowerment-based care. THIS VETERAN was referred for trauma-focused therapy (e.g., CPT) and started on sertraline with prazosin for nightmares, with benzodiazepines explicitly avoided.
labs.r: Treatment: FIRST-LINE = trauma-focused PSYCHOTHERAPY (TF-CBT, Prolonged Exposure, CPT, EMDR). First-line MEDS = SSRI (sertraline/paroxetine — FDA-approved) or SNRI (venlafaxine); takes weeks → reinforce adherence. PRAZOSIN for trauma NIGHTMARES/sleep (watch orthostasis). AVOID benzodiazepines — don't treat core PTSD, dependence/misuse risk (esp. with comorbid SUD), may worsen outcomes; reduce alcohol/substances. Collaborative, choice-based. RN role: facilitate therapy + appropriate meds, avoid benzos.

labs.n: Health promotion / recovery; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: HEALTH PROMOTION + RECOVERY are central to nursing care: provide PSYCHOEDUCATION that NORMALIZES symptoms as an understandable RESPONSE to trauma (not weakness or a character flaw) — this reduces SHAME and self-blame and improves treatment ENGAGEMENT; teach SLEEP hygiene; encourage regular EXERCISE/physical activity; promote SOCIAL connection and PEER support (e.g., veterans' support groups, which leverage shared experience); teach relaxation/stress-management and the grounding/breathing skills for ongoing use; counsel LIMITING ALCOHOL and CAFFEINE (which worsen sleep/arousal); and support a gradual RETURN to valued activities, work, and relationships. SCREEN at-risk populations routinely — veterans, survivors of abuse/assault/intimate-partner violence, first responders, and people after serious accidents/disasters — and CONNECT clients to RESOURCES (mental-health treatment, peer support, veterans' services, crisis lines) with structured FOLLOW-UP. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT force a detailed trauma narrative at first contact (which can re-traumatize); did NOT minimize/dismiss his symptoms or tell him to 'just move on'; did NOT start or rely on long-term benzodiazepines as primary treatment; did NOT encourage alcohol to cope; and did NOT surprise/corner him or remove his sense of control. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: a supportive partner who encouraged help-seeking; engagement in care; access to evidence-based treatment (trauma-focused therapy + appropriate medication); peer/veterans' support; reduced alcohol use; effective coping/grounding skills; safety planning and means-restriction; and recovery-oriented, trauma-informed, nonjudgmental care. EXPECTED outcome: with a trusting therapeutic relationship, safety, grounding/coping skills, trauma-focused therapy, and appropriate medication, symptoms decrease, sleep and function improve, and the client reconnects with his life and supports. NURSING ROLE: recognize PTSD; screen safety/comorbidity first; deliver trauma-informed care; teach grounding/coping and stabilize sleep; connect to evidence-based treatment; and provide psychoeducation, peer support, and recovery-oriented follow-up.
labs.r: HEALTH PROMOTION/RECOVERY: PSYCHOEDUCATION normalizing symptoms (reduces shame, boosts engagement), sleep hygiene, exercise, SOCIAL/PEER support (veterans' groups), relaxation/grounding skills, limit alcohol/caffeine, gradual return to function; SCREEN at-risk groups + connect to resources/follow-up. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no forced trauma narrative, no minimizing, no long-term benzos, no alcohol coping, no surprising/cornering. Protective: support, engagement, evidence-based treatment, peer support, coping skills, safety planning. RN role: psychoeducation + recovery support + follow-up.

nursesNote: Outpatient mental-health clinic — Marcus R., 34, combat VETERAN (separated ~14 months ago), here at partner's urging. Several months of recurrent NIGHTMARES + intrusive memories, FLASHBACKS triggered by loud noises/crowds, marked AVOIDANCE (no highway driving, avoids news/crowds), HYPERVIGILANCE + exaggerated startle, irritability, poor concentration, severe INSOMNIA, detachment from family, persistent GUILT — >1 MONTH with impaired work/relationships → PTSD (>1 month vs <1 month = acute stress disorder). FOUR DSM-5 clusters present: intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal/reactivity. SAFETY SCREENED FIRST (high comorbidity): suicidal/self-harm ideation/plan, ALCOHOL/substance use (self-medication), lethal-means access (FIREARMS) + current safety/IPV; validated tools (PCL-5, suicide-risk assessment) guide the plan. History gathered at HIS pace — did NOT force a detailed trauma narrative (re-traumatizing). TRAUMA-INFORMED CARE throughout (safety, trust, peer support, collaboration, empowerment/CHOICE, cultural sensitivity): 'what HAPPENED to you?' not 'what's wrong?'; explain before doing; offer choices; respect space; accessible exit; don't surprise/corner; minimize coercion. Communication: calm, nonjudgmental, validating; no minimizing ('just move on') or false reassurance. FLASHBACK in clinic (loud hallway noise → diaphoretic, tremulous, tachycardic/hypertensive, momentarily dissociated) RESOLVED with GROUNDING: calm orientation ('you are safe, here, it is [today], the event is over'), 5-4-3-2-1 sensory method, paced/diaphragmatic breathing — NOT confrontation/restraint; taught him to self-apply between visits. TREATMENT (collaborative, choice-based): referral to trauma-focused PSYCHOTHERAPY (CPT/PE/EMDR — first-line); first-line SSRI (SERTRALINE; or paroxetine/venlafaxine — weeks to effect, reinforce adherence); PRAZOSIN for trauma NIGHTMARES/sleep (watch orthostasis); AVOID long-term BENZODIAZEPINES (don't treat core PTSD, dependence/misuse risk esp. with comorbid SUD, may worsen outcomes); counsel reducing ALCOHOL/caffeine. HEALTH PROMOTION/RECOVERY: psychoeducation normalizing symptoms (reduce shame, improve engagement), sleep hygiene, exercise, SOCIAL/PEER support (veterans' group), relaxation/grounding skills, gradual return to function; routine screening of at-risk groups (veterans, abuse/assault survivors, first responders); connect to resources + structured follow-up; safety planning + means-restriction. PROTECTIVE: supportive partner, engagement in care, evidence-based treatment, peer support, reduced alcohol, coping skills. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no forced trauma narrative, no minimizing, no long-term benzos, no alcohol-coping advice, no surprising/cornering. Trauma-informed, nonjudgmental, recovery-oriented care.
providerOrders: SETTING: outpatient mental-health/primary-care clinic; quiet, low-stimulation room with accessible exit and non-cornering seating
DIAGNOSIS: post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) — combat-related; assess for comorbid depression and alcohol/substance use disorder
CODE STATUS / GOAL: establish safety, build a trauma-informed therapeutic relationship, teach grounding/coping, and connect to evidence-based treatment + recovery resources
SAFETY (FIRST):
Screen for suicidal/self-harm ideation, intent, and plan; complete a structured suicide-risk assessment; safety-plan as indicated
Screen alcohol/substance use; assess lethal-means access (firearms) and counsel means-restriction; assess current safety (e.g., intimate-partner violence)
Use validated tools as appropriate (e.g., PCL-5 for PTSD symptom severity; depression and substance screens)
TRAUMA-INFORMED CARE (all interactions):
Provide physical + emotional safety; explain before any procedure; offer choices; respect personal space; keep an accessible exit; avoid surprising or cornering
Calm, nonjudgmental, validating communication; let the client set the pace; do NOT force a detailed trauma narrative before he is ready; avoid minimizing statements
GROUNDING / FLASHBACK MANAGEMENT:
For flashback/dissociation/acute anxiety: speak calmly and orient to the present (safe, here, today, the event is over); use the 5-4-3-2-1 sensory method and paced/diaphragmatic breathing
Teach the client to recognize early cues and self-apply grounding and breathing between visits; avoid confrontation or restraint
TREATMENT (collaborative, choice-based):
Refer for trauma-focused psychotherapy — Cognitive Processing Therapy, Prolonged Exposure, Trauma-Focused CBT, or EMDR (first-line)
First-line medication: SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine); set expectation of several weeks to full effect; reinforce adherence and follow-up
Prazosin for trauma-related nightmares/sleep disturbance (monitor for orthostatic hypotension/dizziness, especially first dose)
AVOID long-term/scheduled benzodiazepines; counsel reduction of alcohol and caffeine
HEALTH PROMOTION / RECOVERY:
Psychoeducation normalizing symptoms as a treatable response to trauma (reduce shame/self-blame, support engagement); sleep hygiene; regular exercise; relaxation/stress management
Connect to peer/veterans' support, mental-health and veterans' resources, and crisis lines; support gradual return to valued activities/work/relationships
FOLLOW-UP:
Structured mental-health follow-up; coordinate with psychiatry/prescriber, therapist, peer-support specialist, and social work; reassess symptoms, function, safety, and medication response

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this veteran presenting with possible PTSD?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Intrusion symptoms — recurrent nightmares, intrusive memories, and flashbacks (dissociative reliving) with intense distress to trauma-related cues (loud noises, crowds)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — intrusion is a core DSM-5 PTSD cluster. RN role: recognize intrusion symptoms.

opts.text: Avoidance — he refuses to drive highways and avoids news, crowds, and reminders of the event
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — avoidance is a core DSM-5 PTSD cluster. RN role: recognize avoidance.

opts.text: Negative alterations in cognition/mood AND arousal — persistent guilt, detachment from family, irritability, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, poor concentration, and severe insomnia, lasting >1 month with impairment
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — negative cognition/mood + arousal clusters, >1 month with impairment, complete the PTSD picture (vs <1 month = acute stress disorder). RN role: recognize all four clusters + timeframe.

opts.text: SAFETY — screen for suicidal/self-harm ideation, alcohol/substance use, and lethal-means access (firearms) and current safety, given PTSD's high comorbidity
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — safety/suicide/substance comorbidity must be screened FIRST. RN role: screen safety first.

opts.text: A trauma-informed approach is needed — give control and choice, explain before doing, avoid surprising/cornering, and be nonjudgmental
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — trauma-informed care frames all interactions and avoids re-traumatization. RN role: deliver trauma-informed care.

opts.text: He needs grounding/coping skills for flashbacks and hyperarousal (orient to present, 5-4-3-2-1, paced breathing) and connection to evidence-based treatment
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — grounding + linkage to trauma-focused therapy/medication are central nursing actions. RN role: teach grounding + connect to treatment.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — document and proceed
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine before any medication. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Pressure him to recount every detail of the traumatic event in the first session 'to get it all out,' even as he becomes distressed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Forcing a detailed trauma narrative before the client is ready can RE-TRAUMATIZE him; let him set the pace and build safety/trust first.

opts.text: Since he 'survived and looks fine,' reassure him the symptoms aren't real and tell him to just move on
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Minimizing/dismissing symptoms is invalidating and erodes trust; PTSD is real and treatable. Validate and provide trauma-informed support.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: PTSD develops after exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence and features four DSM-5 clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal/reactivity) lasting >1 month
opts.rat: CORRECT — etiology + the four clusters + timeframe. Foundation for recognition.

opts.text: Flashbacks, dissociation, and nightmares are intrusion symptoms; grounding (orient to the present, 5-4-3-2-1, paced breathing) helps reconnect the client to the here-and-now
opts.rat: CORRECT — intrusion phenomena + grounding response. Foundation for managing flashbacks.

opts.text: PTSD has high comorbidity with depression, substance/alcohol use disorder, and suicide — so safety and comorbidity screening come first
opts.rat: CORRECT — comorbidity/safety principle. Foundation for safety-first care.

opts.text: First-line treatment is trauma-focused psychotherapy (TF-CBT, Prolonged Exposure, CPT, EMDR); first-line medications are SSRIs/SNRIs, with prazosin for nightmares
opts.rat: CORRECT — evidence-based treatment. Foundation for connecting to care.

opts.text: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in PTSD — they don't treat the core disorder, carry dependence/misuse risk (especially with comorbid substance use), and may worsen outcomes
opts.rat: CORRECT — benzodiazepine caution. Foundation for safe pharmacologic choices.

opts.text: Trauma-informed care (SAMHSA: safety, trust, peer support, collaboration, empowerment/choice, cultural sensitivity) avoids re-traumatization and gives the client control and predictability
opts.rat: CORRECT — trauma-informed-care principle. Foundation for every interaction.

opts.text: Avoidance and hypervigilance are simply character weakness that resolve with willpower, so no treatment is needed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + stigmatizing. PTSD is a treatable disorder, not weakness; symptoms respond to trauma-focused therapy and appropriate medication.

opts.text: Long-term benzodiazepines are the preferred first-line treatment for PTSD and should be started immediately
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Benzodiazepines are generally AVOIDED in PTSD; first-line is trauma-focused psychotherapy +/- an SSRI/SNRI (prazosin for nightmares).

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Establish safety — screen for and address suicidal/self-harm risk, substance use, lethal-means access, and current danger
opts.rat: #1 — Safety is always first; PTSD's high suicide/substance comorbidity makes risk assessment the priority. RN role: safety first.

opts.text: Build a trauma-informed, nonjudgmental therapeutic relationship — provide safety, trust, control, choice, and predictability
opts.rat: #2 — High. A trusting, trauma-informed relationship enables all further assessment and care and avoids re-traumatization. RN role: therapeutic relationship.

opts.text: Teach grounding/coping skills for flashbacks and hyperarousal and help stabilize sleep
opts.rat: #3 — Stabilizing. Grounding and sleep give the client immediate, usable tools to manage symptoms. RN role: coping skills + sleep.

opts.text: Connect him to evidence-based treatment — trauma-focused psychotherapy and appropriate medication (SSRI/SNRI; prazosin for nightmares)
opts.rat: #4 — Definitive treatment. Linkage to therapy/medication drives recovery once safety and rapport are established. RN role: connect to treatment.

opts.text: Provide health promotion/recovery support — psychoeducation, peer/veterans' support, exercise, limiting alcohol, and follow-up/resources
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing recovery. Psychoeducation, peer support, and lifestyle/follow-up sustain long-term outcomes. RN role: recovery support.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this veteran with PTSD.

opts.text: Screen for suicidal/self-harm ideation, substance/alcohol use, and lethal-means access (firearms), and assess current safety, before deeper trauma work
opts.rat: Safety-first screening for a high-comorbidity disorder. RN role: assess safety/suicide/substance use first.

opts.text: Use a trauma-informed approach — explain before doing, offer choices, respect personal space, keep an accessible exit, and remain calm and nonjudgmental while letting him set the pace
opts.rat: Core trauma-informed care that avoids re-traumatization. RN role: trauma-informed interaction.

opts.text: Teach grounding (orient to the present, 5-4-3-2-1 sensory method, paced breathing) for flashbacks, and validate that his symptoms are an understandable response to trauma
opts.rat: Grounding + validation manage intrusion/arousal and reduce shame. RN role: teach coping + validate.

opts.text: Refer for trauma-focused psychotherapy (CPT/PE/EMDR) and collaborate on first-line medication (SSRI/SNRI), with prazosin for nightmares
opts.rat: Evidence-based, first-line treatment. RN role: connect to therapy + appropriate medication.

opts.text: Provide psychoeducation, connect him to a veterans' peer-support group, and counsel sleep hygiene, exercise, and limiting alcohol/caffeine, with structured follow-up
opts.rat: Health promotion/recovery support sustains outcomes. RN role: psychoeducation + peer support + lifestyle + follow-up.

opts.text: Force him to recount the full trauma narrative in detail at the first contact regardless of his distress
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — a forced, premature trauma narrative can re-traumatize; let him set the pace after safety and trust are established.

opts.text: Start scheduled long-term benzodiazepines as the primary, first-line treatment for his PTSD
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — benzodiazepines don't treat core PTSD, risk dependence/misuse (especially with comorbid substance use), and may worsen outcomes; use trauma-focused therapy +/- SSRI/SNRI.

opts.text: Minimize and dismiss his symptoms ('you're fine, just move on') and discourage him from talking about what happened
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — minimizing is invalidating, erodes trust, and discourages care; validate and provide trauma-informed support.

opts.text: Approach him from behind without warning, corner him in a small room with no clear exit, and deliberately startle him to 'test' his reaction
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — surprising/cornering and provoking startle are re-traumatizing and unsafe; provide predictability, space, and an accessible exit.

opts.text: Advise him to manage his symptoms and insomnia by drinking alcohol to relax and fall asleep
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — alcohol worsens PTSD symptoms, sleep, and risk and fuels comorbid substance use; counsel reduction and teach healthy coping.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess and ensure safety first — screen for suicidal/self-harm ideation, substance use, lethal-means access, and current danger, and safety-plan as needed
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Safety/suicide-risk assessment precedes all other care in a high-comorbidity disorder. RN role: safety first.

opts.text: Establish a trauma-informed therapeutic relationship — calm, nonjudgmental, giving control/choice, explaining before doing, and letting him set the pace
opts.rat: #2 — Second. A trusting, trauma-informed relationship enables assessment and treatment and avoids re-traumatization. RN role: therapeutic relationship.

opts.text: Teach and practice grounding/coping for flashbacks and hyperarousal (orient to present, 5-4-3-2-1, paced breathing) and address sleep
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Grounding and sleep stabilization give immediate, usable tools. RN role: coping skills + sleep.

opts.text: Facilitate referral to trauma-focused psychotherapy and collaborate on medication (SSRI/SNRI; prazosin for nightmares), avoiding long-term benzodiazepines
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Linkage to definitive, evidence-based treatment drives recovery. RN role: connect to therapy + appropriate medication.

opts.text: Provide psychoeducation, connect to peer/veterans' support and resources, reinforce healthy coping, and arrange structured follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing/recovery. Psychoeducation, peer support, and follow-up sustain long-term recovery. RN role: recovery support + follow-up.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: After learning the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding method and paced breathing, he aborts a flashback in clinic, reorients to the present, and his heart rate and blood pressure settle
opts.rat: Grounding successfully manages a flashback and hyperarousal. Expected, desired response.

opts.text: Started on sertraline with prazosin for nightmares; over several weeks his sleep improves and intrusive symptoms and nightmares lessen
opts.rat: Appropriate first-line SSRI + prazosin for nightmares taking effect over weeks. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: He engages in trauma-focused therapy (CPT) and a veterans' peer-support group; avoidance decreases and function at work and home improves
opts.rat: Engagement in first-line trauma-focused therapy + peer support driving recovery. Improving.

opts.text: Psychoeducation reframes his symptoms as a treatable response to trauma; his self-blame and shame decrease and he stays engaged in care
opts.rat: Psychoeducation reduces shame and supports engagement. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — a clinician forced a detailed trauma retelling at the first visit; he became acutely distressed, dissociated, and dropped out of care
opts.rat: ⚠️ A forced, premature trauma narrative re-traumatized him and disrupted care. Demonstrates letting the client set the pace after safety/trust.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — he was started on long-term scheduled benzodiazepines; he developed dependence and worse sleep and began combining them with alcohol
opts.rat: ⚠️ Long-term benzodiazepines fostered dependence and combined dangerously with alcohol. Demonstrates why benzodiazepines are avoided in PTSD.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — his symptoms were dismissed as weakness and left untreated; he escalated alcohol use and developed suicidal ideation
opts.rat: ⚠️ Dismissing/minimizing and failing to treat led to escalating substance use and suicide risk. Demonstrates the need for validation, treatment, and safety monitoring.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — staff repeatedly surprised and cornered him and dismissed his need for predictability; his hypervigilance and mistrust worsened and he stopped attending
opts.rat: ⚠️ Non-trauma-informed handling (surprising/cornering, removing control) re-traumatized him and broke the therapeutic relationship. Demonstrates trauma-informed care.

opts.text: Early in care, before therapy and medication take effect, his symptoms are present and essentially unchanged while rapport, safety, and coping skills are being built
opts.rat: Before trauma-focused therapy and medication take effect, an unchanged baseline is expected; continue building safety, rapport, and coping and reassess.

opts.text: At follow-up he reports restored sleep, sustained therapy engagement, reduced symptoms, lower alcohol use, and reconnection with his family and supports
opts.rat: Sustained recovery with treatment engagement, symptom reduction, and reconnection. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: Mechanical Small Bowel Obstruction in a 64-Year-Old with Prior Abdominal Surgery (Adhesions): Recognizing the Classic Picture, Correcting Fluid/Electrolyte Loss, NPO + NASOGASTRIC DECOMPRESSION, Vigilant Monitoring for STRANGULATION/Perforation, and Coordinating Conservative-vs-Surgical Management
subtitle: A SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION (SBO) is a MECHANICAL blockage of the forward flow of intestinal contents. The MOST COMMON cause is post-surgical ADHESIONS (scar bands from prior abdominal/pelvic surgery); other causes include incarcerated HERNIAS, TUMORS, VOLVULUS, intussusception, strictures (e.g., Crohn disease), and gallstone ileus. This is distinct from a PARALYTIC ILEUS — a functional (non-mechanical) failure of peristalsis from recent surgery, opioids, electrolyte derangements (hypokalemia), peritonitis, or immobility — which presents with a silent, distended abdomen and absent bowel sounds rather than the mechanical pattern below. CLASSIC PRESENTATION of mechanical SBO: CRAMPY, COLICKY, intermittent abdominal PAIN; abdominal DISTENSION; VOMITING (early and profuse, often bilious, with a PROXIMAL obstruction; later, more distended and FECULENT/feculent-smelling with a DISTAL obstruction); and OBSTIPATION (inability to pass stool OR flatus, especially with a complete obstruction). BOWEL SOUNDS are classically HIGH-PITCHED, TINKLING, and hyperactive (borborygmi, rushes) EARLY/above the obstruction, then become HYPOACTIVE/ABSENT as the bowel fatigues or ischemia develops. FLUID & ELECTROLYTE consequences are central: vomiting plus 'THIRD-SPACING' of fluid into the obstructed, edematous bowel lumen/wall cause HYPOVOLEMIA (tachycardia, hypotension, low urine output, elevated BUN), and loss of gastric/intestinal contents produces HYPOKALEMIA and (with proximal/gastric loss) a metabolic ALKALOSIS — these derangements are an immediate physiologic threat. The CRITICAL distinction is SIMPLE vs STRANGULATED/closed-loop obstruction: a STRANGULATED obstruction has COMPROMISED BLOOD SUPPLY to the bowel, leading to ISCHEMIA → NECROSIS → PERFORATION → peritonitis and sepsis, and is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. RED FLAGS for strangulation/ischemia/perforation: pain that becomes SEVERE and CONSTANT (rather than colicky), FEVER, TACHYCARDIA, hypotension, PERITONEAL SIGNS (rigidity, guarding, rebound tenderness), a rising LACTATE and WBC, and metabolic acidosis. DIAGNOSIS: abdominal imaging — upright/flat abdominal X-RAY shows dilated bowel loops with AIR-FLUID LEVELS and a 'string-of-pearls' sign, while FREE AIR under the diaphragm indicates PERFORATION; CT scan localizes the obstruction, identifies the cause and the transition point, and detects ischemia/closed-loop obstruction. MANAGEMENT: initial care is supportive and the SAME first steps for nearly every SBO — make the patient NPO; insert a NASOGASTRIC (NG) TUBE to LOW INTERMITTENT SUCTION to DECOMPRESS the stomach/proximal bowel (relieves distension and vomiting, rests the bowel, and reduces aspiration risk); give IV ISOTONIC FLUID resuscitation and CORRECT ELECTROLYTES (replace potassium, address alkalosis); maintain STRICT INTAKE & OUTPUT (including NG output) and monitor labs and perfusion; provide analgesia and antiemetics; and perform SERIAL abdominal assessments and vital signs to detect deterioration. DEFINITIVE management depends on the type: a PARTIAL or adhesive obstruction often RESOLVES with this CONSERVATIVE management (bowel rest + decompression + resuscitation) over hours to days; a COMPLETE, CLOSED-LOOP, or STRANGULATED obstruction (or one that fails to resolve or shows signs of ischemia) requires SURGERY (lysis of adhesions, hernia repair, resection of necrotic bowel). KEY 'DO-NOTs': do NOT give oral feeding or bulk-forming fiber/oral laxatives to 'push it through' (worsens distension/vomiting/aspiration), and do NOT give ANTIMOTILITY agents (e.g., loperamide) for the vomiting (they worsen the obstruction and risk perforation/toxic dilation). NURSING ROLE: recognize the SBO picture and its cause; restore and protect fluid/electrolyte balance and perfusion; establish NPO + NG decompression with aspiration precautions; vigilantly MONITOR for strangulation/perforation and escalate emergently; control pain/nausea; and coordinate diagnostics, surgical consultation, and possible operative care while teaching the patient throughout.

patient.name: Harold P.
patient.code: Full code; goal = stabilize fluid/electrolyte status, decompress the bowel (NPO + NG suction), monitor for strangulation/perforation, and coordinate conservative-vs-surgical management of a mechanical small bowel obstruction
patient.admitDate: A 64-year-old man with a history of an open appendectomy and a prior partial colectomy presents to the ED with 2 days of worsening CRAMPY, colicky abdominal pain, marked abdominal DISTENSION, repeated BILIOUS VOMITING, and an inability to pass stool or flatus (OBSTIPATION). His abdomen is distended and tympanitic with high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds; he is mildly tachycardic and hypotensive with dry mucous membranes (hypovolemia). Imaging shows dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels consistent with a mechanical SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION, most likely from adhesions. He is being managed with NPO, NG decompression, IV fluid/electrolyte resuscitation, and close monitoring for strangulation while surgery is consulted.
patient.room: Surgical med-surg unit; NPO with NG tube to low intermittent suction; IV fluids/electrolyte replacement; strict intake & output; surgical service consulted; monitoring for signs of strangulation/perforation and response to conservative management

labs.n: PRESENTATION + recognizing mechanical SBO (causes + classic picture)
labs.v: Harold P. is a 64-year-old man with PRIOR abdominal surgery (open appendectomy, partial colectomy) presenting with 2 days of CRAMPY, COLICKY, intermittent abdominal PAIN, marked DISTENSION, repeated BILIOUS VOMITING, and OBSTIPATION (no stool or flatus). His abdomen is distended and tympanitic with HIGH-PITCHED, TINKLING bowel sounds, and he is mildly tachycardic/hypotensive with dry mucous membranes — a classic MECHANICAL SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION. The MOST COMMON cause is post-surgical ADHESIONS (very likely here given his surgical history); other causes include incarcerated HERNIAS, TUMORS, VOLVULUS, intussusception, strictures (Crohn), and gallstone ileus. The CLASSIC tetrad is colicky pain + distension + vomiting + obstipation; PROXIMAL obstructions vomit EARLY and profusely (often bilious), while DISTAL obstructions vomit LATER with more distension and FECULENT emesis. Bowel sounds are hyperactive/tinkling EARLY (above the blockage) and become HYPOACTIVE/ABSENT later as the bowel fatigues or ischemia develops. Recognizing this picture — and the patient's adhesion risk — drives the nurse's priorities: stabilize fluids/electrolytes, decompress (NPO + NG), monitor for strangulation, and coordinate management.
labs.r: Mechanical SBO = blockage of intestinal flow; ADHESIONS (prior surgery) are #1 cause (also hernia/tumor/volvulus). Classic: CRAMPY colicky pain + DISTENSION + VOMITING (proximal = early/bilious; distal = late/feculent) + OBSTIPATION (no stool/flatus). Bowel sounds high-pitched/TINKLING early → hypoactive/absent late. RN role: recognize the SBO picture + likely cause.

labs.n: Pathophysiology + types (mechanical vs ileus; partial vs complete; simple vs STRANGULATED) + fluid/electrolyte loss
labs.v: MECHANICAL obstruction (a physical blockage — adhesions, hernia, tumor) must be distinguished from PARALYTIC ILEUS, a FUNCTIONAL failure of peristalsis (post-op, opioids, HYPOKALEMIA, peritonitis, immobility) that produces a silent, distended abdomen with ABSENT bowel sounds and no mechanical lesion. Obstructions are further classified as PARTIAL (some flow continues — often resolves conservatively) vs COMPLETE (no passage of stool/flatus), and — most importantly — SIMPLE vs STRANGULATED/CLOSED-LOOP. A STRANGULATED obstruction has COMPROMISED BLOOD SUPPLY: the bowel becomes ISCHEMIC, then NECROTIC, then PERFORATES, causing peritonitis and sepsis — a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. FLUID & ELECTROLYTE derangement is a central, immediate threat: VOMITING and THIRD-SPACING (fluid sequestered into the distended, edematous bowel lumen and wall) cause HYPOVOLEMIA (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, elevated BUN/creatinine ratio, hemoconcentration); loss of potassium-rich gastric/intestinal fluid causes HYPOKALEMIA (which itself can worsen ileus and cause arrhythmias), and loss of gastric acid (proximal/NG losses) causes a metabolic ALKALOSIS, whereas advanced ischemia/sepsis causes a metabolic ACIDOSIS with rising lactate. The nurse anticipates and corrects these derangements while watching for the shift from a simple to a strangulated obstruction.
labs.r: MECHANICAL (physical block) vs PARALYTIC ILEUS (functional — no peristalsis, absent sounds, from post-op/opioids/HYPOKALEMIA/peritonitis). PARTIAL (may resolve) vs COMPLETE; SIMPLE vs STRANGULATED/closed-loop (compromised blood supply → ischemia→necrosis→PERFORATION = surgical emergency). Fluid/lyte: vomiting + THIRD-SPACING → HYPOVOLEMIA + HYPOKALEMIA + metabolic ALKALOSIS (acidosis/↑lactate if ischemic). RN role: anticipate + correct derangements; watch for strangulation.

labs.n: Diagnostics + MONITORING for strangulation/perforation (the surgical-emergency triggers)
labs.v: DIAGNOSIS rests on imaging and serial assessment. An upright/flat abdominal X-RAY shows dilated small-bowel loops with AIR-FLUID LEVELS and a 'STRING-OF-PEARLS' sign, paucity of colonic gas in complete obstruction, and — critically — FREE AIR under the diaphragm if PERFORATION has occurred. A CT scan localizes the obstruction and its TRANSITION POINT, identifies the cause (adhesion, hernia, mass), and detects signs of ISCHEMIA or a CLOSED-LOOP obstruction (bowel-wall thickening, pneumatosis, reduced enhancement). LABS support monitoring: a rising WBC, a rising LACTATE, and a metabolic ACIDOSIS suggest ISCHEMIA/strangulation; electrolytes and renal indices track the fluid deficit. The MOST IMPORTANT ongoing nursing job is to MONITOR for the conversion of a simple obstruction into a STRANGULATED one or a PERFORATION — performing SERIAL abdominal exams and vital signs and watching for these RED FLAGS: pain that becomes SEVERE and CONSTANT rather than intermittent/colicky; FEVER; TACHYCARDIA and hypotension; PERITONEAL SIGNS (rigidity, involuntary guarding, REBOUND tenderness, a board-like abdomen); markedly decreased/absent bowel sounds with worsening distension; and rising lactate/WBC. ANY of these mandates IMMEDIATE escalation to the surgeon — strangulation/perforation is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY where delay costs bowel and life.
labs.r: Imaging: abdominal X-RAY = dilated loops + AIR-FLUID LEVELS + string-of-pearls; FREE AIR = perforation; CT localizes + shows ischemia/closed-loop. Labs: rising WBC/LACTATE + metabolic ACIDOSIS = ischemia. MONITOR for STRANGULATION/perforation: SEVERE CONSTANT pain, fever, tachycardia/hypotension, PERITONEAL signs (rigidity/rebound/guarding), worsening distension → IMMEDIATE surgical escalation. RN role: serial exams/vitals + recognize + escalate the surgical emergency.

labs.n: Management — conservative (NPO/NG/IV) vs surgical; NG care; what to AVOID
labs.v: INITIAL management is supportive and is the SAME first set of steps for nearly every SBO — 'drip and suck' plus resuscitation: (1) NPO (nothing by mouth) to rest the bowel; (2) insert a NASOGASTRIC (NG) TUBE to LOW INTERMITTENT SUCTION to DECOMPRESS the stomach and proximal bowel — this relieves DISTENSION and VOMITING, rests the bowel, and reduces ASPIRATION risk (verify placement, keep patent, irrigate per policy, measure output and replace volume, and provide oral/nares care and aspiration precautions with the head of bed elevated); (3) IV ISOTONIC FLUID resuscitation with CORRECTION of electrolytes — especially POTASSIUM replacement and addressing the alkalosis — guided by STRICT intake/output (urine + NG + emesis) and labs; (4) ANALGESIA and ANTIEMETICS for comfort; (5) SERIAL monitoring. DEFINITIVE management depends on type: a PARTIAL or adhesive obstruction frequently RESOLVES with this conservative care over hours to days (return of flatus/stool, decreasing NG output, softening abdomen); a COMPLETE, CLOSED-LOOP, or STRANGULATED obstruction — or one that fails to resolve or shows ISCHEMIA — requires SURGERY (adhesiolysis, hernia repair, resection of nonviable bowel). The nurse prepares the patient for possible OR (consent, pre-op labs/teaching, NPO already in place). KEY 'DO-NOTs': do NOT give ORAL FEEDING or BULK-FORMING FIBER/oral LAXATIVES to try to 'push the obstruction through' (this worsens distension, vomiting, and aspiration risk); and do NOT give ANTIMOTILITY agents such as LOPERAMIDE to stop the vomiting (slowing the gut worsens an obstruction and risks perforation/toxic dilation).
labs.r: INITIAL (same for most SBO) = 'drip and suck' + resuscitate: NPO; NG tube to LOW INTERMITTENT SUCTION (decompress → relieve distension/vomiting + reduce aspiration; verify placement, measure/replace output, aspiration precautions); IV isotonic FLUIDS + correct electrolytes (replace K, treat alkalosis) with strict I&O; analgesia/antiemetics; serial monitoring. PARTIAL/adhesive often RESOLVES conservatively; COMPLETE/closed-loop/STRANGULATED → SURGERY (adhesiolysis/resection) — prep for OR. AVOID oral feeding/bulk laxatives + AVOID antimotility (loperamide). RN role: decompress + resuscitate + prep for surgery if needed.

labs.n: Nursing care + recovery + discharge teaching; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: ONGOING NURSING CARE: maintain NG patency and accurate measurement/replacement of output; protect the airway (semi-Fowler's, aspiration precautions, oral/nares care); titrate IV fluids/electrolytes to I&O, labs, and hemodynamics; assess pain and the ABDOMEN serially (distension, tenderness, bowel sounds, return of flatus) and watch for the strangulation red flags; provide analgesia/antiemetics; VTE prophylaxis and early mobilization as able; mouth care for the NPO patient; and emotional support and explanation throughout. RECOVERY: improvement is signaled by decreasing NG output, a softening/less-distended abdomen, RETURN OF FLATUS then stool, and normalized electrolytes — the NG tube is then clamped/removed and diet is advanced cautiously (clear liquids → as tolerated) per surgery, watching for recurrence. If surgery was required, post-op care follows (incision/ostomy if created, ileus prevention, ambulation, pain control). DISCHARGE TEACHING: most adhesive obstructions are managed successfully, but adhesions create a lifelong RECURRENCE risk — teach the patient to RETURN for recurrent crampy pain, distension, vomiting, or inability to pass stool/flatus, and to seek emergency care for severe constant pain or fever. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the patient was NOT given oral feeding or bulk laxatives to 'push it through'; was NOT given antimotility agents (loperamide) for the vomiting; the NG tube was NOT clamped or the IV fluids stopped prematurely just because he 'felt better'; and new fever/tachycardia/rigid abdomen were NOT dismissed as constipation. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: early recognition and decompression; prompt fluid/electrolyte correction; vigilant monitoring for strangulation with timely surgical escalation; and a coordinated surgical/medical plan. EXPECTED outcome: a partial adhesive obstruction resolves with conservative management (or is corrected surgically), bowel function returns, fluid/electrolyte balance is restored, and the patient is educated on recurrence. NURSING ROLE: recognize SBO and its cause; stabilize and protect fluids/electrolytes/airway; decompress (NPO + NG suction); monitor for and escalate strangulation/perforation; control pain/nausea; and coordinate diagnostics, surgery, and patient teaching.
labs.r: ONGOING: NG patency + measure/replace output; aspiration precautions/semi-Fowler's/oral care; titrate fluids/electrolytes to I&O+labs; SERIAL abdominal exams + watch strangulation red flags; analgesia/antiemetics; VTE prophylaxis. RECOVERY = ↓NG output + softening abdomen + RETURN OF FLATUS/stool + normalized lytes → clamp/remove NG + advance diet cautiously. TEACH adhesion-recurrence warning signs. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no oral feeding/bulk laxatives, no antimotility, no premature NG clamp/fluid stop, don't dismiss strangulation signs. RN role: decompress + resuscitate + monitor/escalate + coordinate + teach.

nursesNote: Surgical med-surg unit — Harold P., 64, with PRIOR abdominal surgery (open appendectomy + partial colectomy). 2 days of CRAMPY colicky abdominal pain, marked DISTENSION, repeated BILIOUS VOMITING, OBSTIPATION (no stool/flatus). Abdomen distended/tympanitic with HIGH-PITCHED/TINKLING bowel sounds; mildly tachycardic/hypotensive, dry mucous membranes (hypovolemia). Imaging: dilated small-bowel loops + AIR-FLUID LEVELS → mechanical SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION, likely ADHESIONS (#1 cause; also hernia/tumor/volvulus). Type matters: mechanical vs paralytic ileus (functional — absent sounds, post-op/opioids/HYPOKALEMIA/peritonitis); partial (may resolve) vs complete; SIMPLE vs STRANGULATED/closed-loop (compromised blood supply → ischemia→necrosis→PERFORATION = surgical emergency). Fluid/lyte: vomiting + THIRD-SPACING → hypovolemia + HYPOKALEMIA (K 3.1) + metabolic ALKALOSIS (HCO3 30/pH 7.49) + prerenal azotemia + low UOP. MANAGEMENT ('drip and suck' + resuscitate): NPO; NG tube to LOW INTERMITTENT SUCTION (decompress → relieve distension/vomiting + reduce aspiration; verify placement, keep patent, MEASURE + REPLACE output, oral/nares care); IV isotonic FLUIDS + POTASSIUM replacement + treat alkalosis, titrated to STRICT I&O (urine+NG+emesis) + labs; semi-Fowler's + aspiration precautions; analgesia + antiemetics; VTE prophylaxis. MONITOR for STRANGULATION/perforation (serial abdominal exams + vitals): RED FLAGS = SEVERE CONSTANT pain (not colicky), FEVER, tachycardia, hypotension, PERITONEAL signs (rigidity/rebound/guarding), worsening distension, rising LACTATE/WBC, metabolic acidosis → IMMEDIATE surgical escalation (free air on X-ray = perforation). DEFINITIVE: partial/adhesive often RESOLVES conservatively (↓NG output, softening abdomen, RETURN OF FLATUS/stool, normalized lytes → clamp/remove NG + advance diet cautiously); COMPLETE/closed-loop/STRANGULATED or failure-to-resolve → SURGERY (adhesiolysis/hernia repair/resection) — prep for OR (consent, pre-op). AVOID: oral feeding or bulk-forming fiber/oral laxatives to 'push it through' (worsens distension/vomiting/aspiration); ANTIMOTILITY agents (loperamide) for vomiting (worsen obstruction, risk perforation/toxic dilation). DISCHARGE TEACHING: adhesions = lifelong recurrence risk → return for recurrent distension/vomiting/obstipation/severe pain or fever. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT feed orally/give bulk laxatives, did NOT give antimotility, did NOT clamp NG/stop fluids prematurely on 'feels better,' did NOT dismiss strangulation signs as constipation. Coordinated surgical/medical plan; patient updated throughout.
providerOrders: ADMIT: surgical med-surg unit; mechanical small bowel obstruction (likely adhesive); surgery consulted
DIAGNOSIS: small bowel obstruction — monitor for progression to strangulation/perforation
CODE STATUS: full code
DIET/GI: NPO; nasogastric tube to LOW INTERMITTENT suction; verify placement, keep patent (irrigate per policy), measure output each shift and replace volume per orders
FLUIDS/ELECTROLYTES:
IV isotonic crystalloid resuscitation; replace potassium per protocol; correct metabolic alkalosis
Strict intake & output (urine, NG, emesis); daily weights; titrate fluids to I&O, labs, and hemodynamics
MONITORING:
Serial abdominal assessments (distension, tenderness, bowel sounds, passage of flatus/stool) and vital signs

Notify surgeon IMMEDIATELY for strangulation/perforation signs: severe constant pain, fever, tachycardia/hypotension, peritoneal signs (rigidity/rebound/guarding), rising lactate/WBC, or free air on imaging
DIAGNOSTICS:
Abdominal X-ray (upright/flat) and CT abdomen/pelvis as ordered; CBC, CMP, lactate, type & screen
COMFORT/SAFETY:
Analgesia and antiemetics per orders; semi-Fowler's position with aspiration precautions; frequent oral and nares care
VTE prophylaxis; early mobilization as tolerated
AVOID:
No oral feeding or bulk-forming fiber/oral laxatives to 'push through' the obstruction
No antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide) for the vomiting
SURGERY:

Prepare for possible operative management (lysis of adhesions/hernia repair/resection) if complete, closed-loop, strangulated, or failing conservative management — consent, pre-op labs, NPO maintained
DISCHARGE TEACHING (when resolved):
Adhesion-related recurrence risk; return for recurrent crampy pain, distension, vomiting, or inability to pass stool/flatus; emergency care for severe constant pain or fever; surgical follow-up

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this patient with a likely bowel obstruction?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Crampy, colicky abdominal pain with distension, bilious vomiting, and obstipation (no stool or flatus) — the classic mechanical SBO picture
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the classic SBO tetrad. RN role: recognize mechanical obstruction.

opts.text: Bowel sounds high-pitched and tinkling early (above the obstruction), becoming hypoactive/absent later
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the characteristic bowel-sound evolution of mechanical obstruction. RN role: assess and interpret bowel sounds.

opts.text: History of prior abdominal surgery — adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — surgical history points to the likely adhesive cause. RN role: identify the probable etiology.

opts.text: Hypovolemia and electrolyte loss — tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, low urine output, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis from vomiting and third-spacing
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — fluid/electrolyte derangement is the immediate physiologic threat. RN role: recognize and correct hypovolemia/electrolytes.

opts.text: Watch for STRANGULATION — severe constant (not colicky) pain, fever, tachycardia, a rigid/rebound abdomen, and rising lactate/WBC indicate ischemia/perforation and a surgical emergency
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — recognizing the simple-to-strangulated conversion is critical and time-sensitive. RN role: monitor for and escalate strangulation.

opts.text: NPO with NG tube decompression to low intermittent suction, plus IV fluids — and imaging to confirm the obstruction (dilated loops/air-fluid levels; free air = perforation)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — decompression/resuscitation and confirmatory imaging are the foundational steps. RN role: decompress, resuscitate, and obtain diagnostics.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — document and proceed
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine before medications/surgery. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Give the patient a full oral meal and bulk-forming fiber/oral laxatives to 'push the blockage through'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The patient must be NPO; oral feeding and bulking/laxatives worsen distension, vomiting, and aspiration risk and do not relieve a mechanical obstruction.

opts.text: Administer loperamide (an antimotility agent) to stop the vomiting and 'rest the bowel'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Antimotility agents slow the gut, worsen an obstruction, and risk perforation/toxic dilation; they are contraindicated. Decompress with an NG tube instead.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: A mechanical SBO is a physical blockage of intestinal flow; adhesions from prior surgery are the most common cause, followed by hernias, tumors, and volvulus
opts.rat: CORRECT — definition + etiology. Foundation for recognition.

opts.text: A mechanical obstruction (hyperactive/tinkling then absent sounds, distension) differs from a paralytic ileus — a functional loss of peristalsis (post-op, opioids, hypokalemia, peritonitis) with a silent, distended abdomen and no mechanical lesion
opts.rat: CORRECT — mechanical vs functional distinction. Foundation for correct management.

opts.text: Vomiting and third-spacing cause hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, so fluid/electrolyte correction is an early priority
opts.rat: CORRECT — fluid/electrolyte consequences. Foundation for resuscitation.

opts.text: A strangulated or closed-loop obstruction has compromised blood supply leading to ischemia, necrosis, and perforation — a surgical emergency
opts.rat: CORRECT — the critical strangulation concept. Foundation for monitoring/escalation.

opts.text: Partial/adhesive obstructions often resolve with conservative management (NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids), while complete, closed-loop, or strangulated obstructions require surgery
opts.rat: CORRECT — conservative-vs-surgical principle. Foundation for the plan of care.

opts.text: NG tube decompression to low intermittent suction relieves distension and vomiting, rests the bowel, and reduces aspiration risk
opts.rat: CORRECT — rationale for NG decompression. Foundation for the key intervention.

opts.text: The priority treatment for every bowel obstruction is immediate oral feeding to stimulate motility
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The patient is kept NPO; oral feeding worsens distension/vomiting/aspiration and does not relieve a mechanical obstruction.

opts.text: A strangulated obstruction is a minor issue that can safely be observed for several days without surgery
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Strangulation is a surgical emergency — delay leads to necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, and sepsis; it requires prompt operative intervention.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Establish NPO and NG tube decompression to low intermittent suction with aspiration precautions (relieve distension/vomiting, protect the airway, rest the bowel)
opts.rat: #1 — Foundational + protects the airway from vomiting/aspiration while decompressing. RN role: NPO + NG decompression.

opts.text: Restore fluid/electrolyte balance and perfusion — IV isotonic fluids, potassium replacement, correct alkalosis, strict I&O
opts.rat: #2 — High. Hypovolemia and hypokalemia are immediate physiologic threats. RN role: fluid/electrolyte resuscitation.

opts.text: Monitor vigilantly for strangulation/perforation — serial abdominal exams, vitals, lactate/WBC — and escalate emergently
opts.rat: #3 — Critical and ongoing. Detecting the simple-to-strangulated conversion drives emergency surgery. RN role: monitor + escalate.

opts.text: Control pain and nausea and maintain comfort/positioning
opts.rat: #4 — Significant. Analgesia/antiemetics improve comfort once stabilization and monitoring are underway. RN role: pain/nausea management.

opts.text: Coordinate diagnostics and surgical consultation and prepare for possible operative management
opts.rat: #5 — Important + ongoing. Imaging, surgical consult, and OR prep define definitive care. RN role: coordinate diagnostics + surgery.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this patient with an SBO.

opts.text: Keep the patient NPO and insert an NG tube to low intermittent suction; verify placement, keep it patent, and measure/record output
opts.rat: Core decompression and bowel rest. RN role: NPO + NG suction.

opts.text: Start IV isotonic fluids, replace potassium per orders, correct the alkalosis, and monitor electrolytes with strict intake & output
opts.rat: Corrects the immediate hypovolemia/electrolyte threat. RN role: fluid/electrolyte resuscitation + I&O.

opts.text: Position in semi-Fowler's, maintain aspiration precautions, and provide frequent oral/nares care
opts.rat: Protects the airway in a vomiting/NG patient and maintains comfort. RN role: aspiration precautions + comfort.

opts.text: Perform serial abdominal assessments and monitor vitals/lactate/WBC; escalate emergently if severe constant pain, fever, or peritoneal signs develop
opts.rat: Detects and escalates strangulation/perforation. RN role: serial monitoring + escalation.

opts.text: Obtain ordered imaging (abdominal X-ray/CT) and labs and consult surgery; prepare for possible operative management
opts.rat: Confirms diagnosis/type and arranges definitive care. RN role: diagnostics + surgical coordination.

opts.text: Provide ordered analgesia and antiemetics and reassess the response
opts.rat: Appropriate comfort management with reassessment. RN role: pain/nausea control.

opts.text: Offer a full oral diet and bulk-forming fiber/oral laxatives to push the obstruction through
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the patient must be NPO; oral feeding/bulking worsens distension, vomiting, and aspiration risk and does not relieve a mechanical obstruction.

opts.text: Give loperamide (an antimotility agent) to stop the vomiting
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — antimotility agents worsen an obstruction and risk perforation/toxic dilation; decompress with the NG tube instead.

opts.text: Clamp the NG tube and discontinue IV fluids because the patient 'feels better' after initial decompression
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — premature clamping/stopping fluids before resolution risks recurrent distension/vomiting and rebound hypovolemia; continue per the plan and surgery's guidance.

opts.text: Encourage ambulation with a heating pad and dismiss new fever, tachycardia, and a rigid abdomen as ordinary constipation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — those are strangulation/perforation red flags requiring immediate surgical escalation, not reassurance; missing them risks necrosis and sepsis.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Establish NPO, insert the NG tube to low intermittent suction, and position with aspiration precautions
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Decompression relieves distension/vomiting and protects the airway while resting the bowel. RN role: NPO + NG decompression.

opts.text: Start IV fluid resuscitation and replace electrolytes (potassium) per orders; monitor strict intake & output
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Correcting hypovolemia and hypokalemia addresses the immediate physiologic threat. RN role: fluid/electrolyte resuscitation.

opts.text: Obtain ordered imaging and labs and notify/consult surgery to confirm the type and plan
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Diagnostics and surgical input establish whether conservative or operative management is needed. RN role: diagnostics + consult.

opts.text: Continuously monitor for strangulation/perforation (serial abdominal exams, vitals, lactate/WBC) and escalate emergently if it develops
opts.rat: #4 — Ongoing/critical. Vigilant surveillance catches the surgical emergency early. RN role: monitor + escalate.

opts.text: Provide analgesia/antiemetics, comfort, and prepare the patient for possible surgery (consent, pre-op teaching), reassessing the response
opts.rat: #5 — Comfort + readiness. Pain/nausea control and OR preparation round out care once stabilization and monitoring are in place. RN role: comfort + surgical prep.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: After NG decompression and IV fluids, distension and vomiting decrease, NG output declines, and flatus then stool return
opts.rat: Decompression + bowel rest resolving the obstruction. Expected, desired response.

opts.text: Electrolytes and urine output normalize with isotonic fluids and potassium replacement, and the partial adhesive obstruction resolves with conservative management
opts.rat: Successful fluid/electrolyte correction + conservative resolution. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: After surgical lysis of a complete/strangulated obstruction, the patient recovers, bowel function returns, and diet is advanced gradually
opts.rat: Appropriate operative management of a surgical obstruction with recovery. Improving.

opts.text: The NG tube is patent and draining, the abdomen is softening and less tender, and pain is decreasing — conservative management is working
opts.rat: Objective signs that bowel rest/decompression are succeeding. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — staff gave a full oral diet and bulk laxatives; vomiting worsened, the patient aspirated, and distension increased
opts.rat: ⚠️ Oral feeding/bulking a mechanical obstruction worsens distension/vomiting and caused aspiration. Demonstrates why the patient stays NPO with NG decompression.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — loperamide was given to stop the vomiting; the obstruction worsened with increasing distension and pain
opts.rat: ⚠️ Antimotility agents worsen an obstruction and risk perforation. Demonstrates why they are contraindicated.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — new fever, tachycardia, severe constant pain, a rigid/rebound abdomen, and rising lactate/WBC were dismissed as constipation; the bowel strangulated and perforated
opts.rat: ⚠️ Missed strangulation/perforation — the dismissed red flags are a surgical emergency. Demonstrates the need for serial monitoring and immediate escalation.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the NG tube was clamped and IV fluids stopped early because he 'felt better'; distension and vomiting recurred and he became hypovolemic again
opts.rat: ⚠️ Premature discontinuation before true resolution caused rebound obstruction/hypovolemia. Demonstrates continuing decompression/resuscitation until resolved per surgery.

opts.text: Early in management, before decompression and fluids take full effect, distension and pain are present and essentially unchanged while the nurse continues NG suction and resuscitation
opts.rat: Before bowel rest/resuscitation take effect, an unchanged baseline is expected; continue decompression, fluids, and serial monitoring and reassess.

opts.text: At follow-up the patient tolerates a regular diet, has normal bowel function, and verbalizes the warning signs of recurrence and adhesion-related risk
opts.rat: Sustained recovery with effective discharge teaching. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (Code Blue) in a Monitored 58-Year-Old: High-Quality CPR, Rhythm-Based ACLS (Defibrillate SHOCKABLE VF/Pulseless VT — NOT Asystole/PEA), Epinephrine + Antiarrhythmic Timing, the H's and T's, and HIGH-PERFORMANCE CODE-TEAM LEADERSHIP with Role Assignment and CLOSED-LOOP Communication
subtitle: An IN-HOSPITAL CARDIAC ARREST ('CODE BLUE') is the abrupt loss of effective cardiac function — the patient is UNRESPONSIVE, NOT breathing (or only gasping/agonal), and PULSELESS. RECOGNITION + BLS FIRST: confirm unresponsiveness, CALL FOR HELP / activate the code and call for the crash cart + DEFIBRILLATOR, and check breathing and a central (carotid) pulse SIMULTANEOUSLY for NO MORE THAN 10 SECONDS; if no definite pulse, begin HIGH-QUALITY CHEST COMPRESSIONS immediately. HIGH-QUALITY CPR is the foundation of survival: a RATE of 100-120/min, a DEPTH of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not more than ~2.4 inches (6 cm) in adults, ALLOW FULL CHEST RECOIL between compressions, MINIMIZE INTERRUPTIONS (keep any pause under 10 seconds), ROTATE COMPRESSORS every 2 minutes (or sooner if fatigued) to maintain quality, use a firm surface/backboard, and AVOID EXCESSIVE VENTILATION; the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed, after which compressions are continuous with one breath every 6 seconds (~10/min). Apply defibrillator pads as soon as the device arrives and analyze the rhythm. ACLS is RHYTHM-BASED: SHOCKABLE rhythms — VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION (VF) and PULSELESS VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA (pVT) — are treated with IMMEDIATE DEFIBRILLATION (early defibrillation is the single most important determinant of survival in these rhythms), after which CPR is resumed IMMEDIATELY for 2 minutes before the next rhythm/pulse check; NON-SHOCKABLE rhythms — ASYSTOLE and PULSELESS ELECTRICAL ACTIVITY (PEA) — are NOT defibrillated and are treated with high-quality CPR, epinephrine, and correction of the underlying cause (a classic, dangerous error is attempting to 'shock asystole'). MEDICATIONS: EPINEPHRINE 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes (given as soon as possible in non-shockable arrest; after the second shock in shockable arrest); an ANTIARRHYTHMIC — AMIODARONE 300 mg (then 150 mg) or LIDOCAINE — is added for VF/pVT that is REFRACTORY to defibrillation. Obtain IV or IO access, consider an advanced airway, and attach WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY (a sudden rise in ETCO2 suggests Return Of Spontaneous Circulation/ROSC; a persistently low ETCO2 <10 mmHg suggests poor compression quality). Pulse/rhythm checks occur about every 2 minutes, coinciding with the compressor switch, with interruptions minimized. The team must continually search for and treat REVERSIBLE CAUSES — the 'H's and T's': HYPOVOLEMIA, HYPOXIA, HYDROGEN ION (acidosis), HYPO-/HYPERKALEMIA, HYPOTHERMIA; TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX, cardiac TAMPONADE, TOXINS, and THROMBOSIS (pulmonary or coronary). CODE STATUS is verified — full ACLS is not provided to a patient with a valid DNR order. The chief NURSING-LEADERSHIP focus: a resuscitation runs best as a HIGH-PERFORMANCE TEAM with a clearly defined TEAM LEADER who maintains the overview, assigns ROLES, monitors CPR quality and the algorithm, makes decisions, and does NOT get tunnel-visioned doing a single task; defined ROLES include the compressor(s) (rotating every 2 minutes), airway/ventilation (BVM/respiratory therapy), the defibrillator operator, the IV/IO + medication nurse, the recorder/timekeeper, a runner, and a family liaison. Communication uses CLOSED-LOOP technique: the leader gives a CLEAR order to a SPECIFIC person ('Sara, give 1 mg epinephrine IV now'), the receiver REPEATS it back ('Giving 1 mg epinephrine IV now'), and CONFIRMS completion ('Epinephrine 1 mg IV given'); team members share information, speak up (constructive intervention), and the leader summarizes/reevaluates. The FIRST nurse at the bedside LEADS until the code team/provider arrives — starting CPR, calling the code, getting the defibrillator, and delegating. DELEGATION BY SCOPE: unlicensed assistive personnel can perform compressions and retrieve equipment and act as runners, while the RN performs assessment, defibrillation, and medication administration. On ROSC, the team transitions to POST-CARDIAC-ARREST CARE (optimize oxygenation/ventilation avoiding hyperoxia and hypocapnia, support blood pressure, obtain a 12-lead ECG and pursue PCI for STEMI, initiate targeted temperature management if comatose, and identify/treat the cause) and conducts a DEBRIEF. NURSING ROLE: recognize arrest and start high-quality CPR; defibrillate shockable rhythms early; deliver ACLS medications on schedule while minimizing interruptions; lead or function within a high-performance team using role assignment and closed-loop communication; identify and treat reversible causes; verify code status; and transition to post-arrest care.

patient.name: Frank D.
patient.code: FULL CODE (verified — no DNR); goal = high-quality CPR, early defibrillation of the shockable rhythm, rhythm-based ACLS, treat reversible causes, and run a coordinated high-performance code team to achieve and sustain ROSC
patient.admitDate: A 58-year-old man admitted to the cardiac step-down/telemetry unit with an acute coronary syndrome (rule-out MI) is being monitored when he suddenly clutches his chest, slumps, and becomes unresponsive. The bedside nurse finds him not breathing (only occasional agonal gasps) and pulseless within 10 seconds; the telemetry monitor shows VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION. A CODE BLUE is called, high-quality CPR is begun, and the crash cart/defibrillator is brought to the bedside. The resuscitation requires high-quality CPR, early defibrillation of the shockable rhythm, ACLS medications, a search for reversible causes (H's and T's), and coordinated high-performance team leadership with role assignment and closed-loop communication.
patient.room: Cardiac step-down/telemetry unit; witnessed, monitored arrest; crash cart + defibrillator at bedside; code team responding (code-team leader/provider, compressors, airway/RT, medication nurse, recorder, runner); transition to ICU and post-cardiac-arrest care after ROSC
