labs.n: PRESENTATION + arrest recognition + high-quality CPR (BLS foundation)
labs.v: Frank D., a 58-year-old on telemetry for an acute coronary syndrome, suddenly becomes UNRESPONSIVE with agonal gasping; the bedside nurse confirms no breathing and NO PULSE within a ≤10-second check while the monitor shows VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION — an IN-HOSPITAL CARDIAC ARREST. The immediate sequence: ACTIVATE the code (call for help / code blue) and call for the crash cart and DEFIBRILLATOR, and START HIGH-QUALITY CHEST COMPRESSIONS without delay. HIGH-QUALITY CPR is the foundation of survival and the nurse's first hands-on priority: compress at a RATE of 100-120/min, to a DEPTH of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not more than ~2.4 inches (6 cm), ALLOW FULL RECOIL between compressions, MINIMIZE INTERRUPTIONS (any pause <10 seconds), ROTATE COMPRESSORS every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue and preserve quality, place the patient on a firm surface/backboard, and AVOID EXCESSIVE VENTILATION. Ventilate 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed, then give continuous compressions with one breath every 6 seconds (~10/min). Apply defibrillator pads as soon as the device arrives and analyze the rhythm. A witnessed, MONITORED arrest with prompt CPR and EARLY DEFIBRILLATION carries the best chance of survival, so seconds matter and the response must be organized.
labs.r: Cardiac arrest = unresponsive + not breathing (or agonal) + pulseless (check ≤10 s). Sequence: call code + get defibrillator + START high-quality CPR. HIGH-QUALITY CPR: rate 100-120/min, depth ≥2 in (≤2.4 in), FULL recoil, interruptions <10 s, ROTATE compressors q2min, firm surface, avoid over-ventilation; 30:2 until advanced airway then 1 breath q6s. Apply pads + analyze rhythm. RN role: recognize arrest + start high-quality CPR immediately.

labs.n: Rhythm-based ACLS — SHOCKABLE (VF/pVT) vs NON-SHOCKABLE (asystole/PEA) + medications
labs.v: ACLS is RHYTHM-BASED. SHOCKABLE rhythms are VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION (VF) and PULSELESS VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA (pVT): treat with IMMEDIATE DEFIBRILLATION — early defibrillation is the SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT determinant of survival in these rhythms — then RESUME CPR IMMEDIATELY for 2 minutes (do not pause to recheck the pulse right after a shock) before the next rhythm/pulse check, keeping the peri-shock pause minimal. NON-SHOCKABLE rhythms are ASYSTOLE and PULSELESS ELECTRICAL ACTIVITY (PEA): these are NOT defibrillated (a dangerous, classic error is to 'shock asystole') — treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine, and correction of the underlying cause. MEDICATIONS: EPINEPHRINE 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes — given AS SOON AS POSSIBLE in a non-shockable arrest, and after the SECOND shock in a shockable arrest; an ANTIARRHYTHMIC is added for VF/pVT that is REFRACTORY to defibrillation — AMIODARONE 300 mg IV/IO (with a repeat 150 mg) or LIDOCAINE. Defibrillation 'clears' the team (no one touching the patient/bed) before the shock for safety. The cycle repeats: 2 minutes of CPR → rhythm/pulse check (at the compressor switch) → shock if shockable / no shock if non-shockable → medications on schedule → reassess, all while minimizing interruptions.
labs.r: SHOCKABLE = VF + pulseless VT → DEFIBRILLATE immediately (early defib = key to survival), resume CPR x2 min, then recheck. NON-SHOCKABLE = asystole + PEA → do NOT shock; CPR + epinephrine + fix the cause. EPINEPHRINE 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min (ASAP in non-shockable; after 2nd shock in shockable). AMIODARONE 300 then 150 mg (or lidocaine) for REFRACTORY VF/pVT. 'Clear' before shocking. RN role: identify shockable vs non-shockable + treat correctly.

labs.n: Reversible causes (H's and T's) + access, airway, and capnography
labs.v: Throughout the code the team must continually search for and TREAT REVERSIBLE CAUSES — the 'H's and T's' — because a code will not resolve until the underlying cause is corrected: HYPOVOLEMIA (give fluids/blood), HYPOXIA (oxygenate/ventilate/secure the airway), HYDROGEN ION/acidosis, HYPOKALEMIA or HYPERKALEMIA (e.g., calcium, insulin/dextrose, bicarbonate for hyperkalemia; replace for hypokalemia), HYPOTHERMIA (rewarm); TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX (needle/finger decompression), cardiac TAMPONADE (pericardiocentesis), TOXINS (antidotes — e.g., naloxone, bicarbonate for sodium-channel-blocker toxicity), and THROMBOSIS — pulmonary (massive PE) or coronary (acute MI). SUPPORT measures: obtain IV or IO access (IO if IV access is not rapidly achievable), consider an advanced airway (without prolonged interruption of compressions), and attach WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY — a SUDDEN RISE in ETCO2 suggests ROSC, while a persistently LOW ETCO2 (<10 mmHg) signals INADEQUATE compression quality (push harder/faster, switch compressors). Point-of-care labs (potassium, glucose, ABG) and bedside ultrasound help identify causes. The team leader keeps the H's and T's on the verbal checklist and assigns someone to address likely causes (here, coronary thrombosis/acute MI is the probable trigger).
labs.r: Always hunt + treat REVERSIBLE CAUSES (H's & T's): Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion/acidosis, Hypo-/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (PE/MI). Support: IV/IO access, advanced airway (no long CPR pause), waveform CAPNOGRAPHY (sudden ETCO2 rise = ROSC; <10 = poor compressions). POC labs/ultrasound find causes. RN role: identify + help correct the cause while sustaining CPR.

labs.n: HIGH-PERFORMANCE CODE-TEAM LEADERSHIP — roles, closed-loop communication, delegation
labs.v: A resuscitation succeeds or fails on TEAM PERFORMANCE. There must be ONE clearly defined TEAM LEADER who maintains the OVERVIEW — directing the algorithm, ASSIGNING ROLES, monitoring CPR quality (rate/depth/recoil/interruptions), making decisions, and keeping the big picture — and who does NOT become 'tunnel-visioned' performing a single hands-on task. Defined ROLES distribute the work: COMPRESSOR(S) rotating every 2 minutes; AIRWAY/VENTILATION (BVM, respiratory therapy); the DEFIBRILLATOR operator; the IV/IO + MEDICATION nurse; the RECORDER/TIMEKEEPER (documents times of compressions, shocks, medications, and rhythm and prompts the 2-minute cycle and epinephrine intervals); a RUNNER (for supplies/labs/blood); and a FAMILY LIAISON (supporting family, who may be offered the option of presence with support). COMMUNICATION uses CLOSED-LOOP technique to prevent errors: the leader gives a CLEAR, DIRECTED order to a SPECIFIC person ('Sara, give 1 mg epinephrine IV now'), the receiver REPEATS it back ('Giving 1 mg epinephrine IV now'), and CONFIRMS completion ('Epinephrine 1 mg IV given, time 14:06'); team members share information openly, use CONSTRUCTIVE INTERVENTION (speak up if something is wrong or missed), and the leader periodically SUMMARIZES and REEVALUATES. The FIRST nurse at the bedside LEADS until the code team/provider arrives — calling the code, starting CPR, getting the defibrillator, and delegating. DELEGATION BY SCOPE: UNLICENSED ASSISTIVE PERSONNEL can perform CHEST COMPRESSIONS, retrieve the crash cart/equipment, and act as a runner; the RN performs ASSESSMENT, DEFIBRILLATION, and MEDICATION administration and other licensed tasks. After the event, a DEBRIEF reviews what went well and what to improve.
labs.r: High-performance team: ONE clear LEADER keeps the overview, assigns ROLES, monitors quality, decides — does NOT tunnel-vision on a task. Roles: compressors (rotate q2min), airway/RT, defib operator, med nurse, RECORDER/timer, runner, family liaison. CLOSED-LOOP communication: directed order to a named person → repeat-back → confirmation. First nurse LEADS until code team arrives. DELEGATE by scope: UAP = compressions/equipment/runner; RN = assessment/defib/meds. Debrief after. RN role: lead or function in a coordinated team.

labs.n: ROSC + post-cardiac-arrest care; code status; Pertinent NEGATIVES + debrief
labs.v: RETURN OF SPONTANEOUS CIRCULATION (ROSC) is recognized by a palpable pulse with an organized rhythm and often a SUDDEN RISE in ETCO2. Care then shifts to POST-CARDIAC-ARREST management (the start of which links to dedicated post-arrest TTM care): OPTIMIZE OXYGENATION/VENTILATION — titrate FiO2 to avoid HYPEROXIA (target SpO2 ~92-98%) and ventilation to avoid HYPOCAPNIA (avoid over-ventilation); SUPPORT BLOOD PRESSURE (fluids/vasopressors for post-arrest hypotension, target adequate MAP); obtain a 12-LEAD ECG and pursue emergent CORONARY ANGIOGRAPHY/PCI if STEMI or suspected coronary cause; initiate TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT if the patient remains comatose; identify and treat the precipitating cause; and transfer to ICU with a clear HANDOFF. CODE STATUS: full ACLS is provided only to a FULL CODE — a valid DNR order must be honored, so the team verifies code status. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the team did NOT delay compressions/defibrillation to obtain access or document first; did NOT 'shock' asystole/PEA; did NOT pause compressions for prolonged periods or hyperventilate the patient; did NOT run a leaderless, uncoordinated code with un-acknowledged orders; and did NOT continue full ACLS against a valid DNR. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: a witnessed, MONITORED arrest with immediate high-quality CPR and EARLY defibrillation of a shockable rhythm; a coordinated high-performance team with closed-loop communication; prompt epinephrine/antiarrhythmic and correction of the cause; and organized post-arrest care — all maximize survival with good neurologic outcome. A DEBRIEF after the code supports the team and improves future performance. NURSING ROLE: recognize arrest and start high-quality CPR; defibrillate shockable rhythms early; deliver ACLS medications and treat reversible causes; lead or function within a high-performance team using role assignment and closed-loop communication; verify code status; and transition to post-cardiac-arrest care.
labs.r: ROSC = pulse + organized rhythm (sudden ETCO2 rise). Post-arrest care: titrate O2 (avoid HYPEROXIA, SpO2 ~92-98%) + avoid hypocapnia; support BP; 12-lead + PCI for STEMI; TTM if comatose; treat cause; ICU handoff. Verify CODE STATUS (honor DNR). NEGATIVES (correct practice): no delaying CPR/defib, no shocking asystole/PEA, no long CPR pauses/hyperventilation, no leaderless code, no ACLS against valid DNR. RN role: ROSC recognition + post-arrest care + team leadership.

nursesNote: Cardiac step-down/telemetry — Frank D., 58, admitted for ACS (rule-out MI). WITNESSED, MONITORED arrest: sudden unresponsiveness + agonal gasps, NO pulse on ≤10-second check, monitor = VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION. CODE BLUE called; crash cart/defibrillator to bedside; FULL CODE verified (no DNR). BLS: started HIGH-QUALITY CPR immediately — rate 100-120/min, depth ≥2 in (≤2.4 in), FULL recoil, interruptions <10 s, ROTATE compressors q2min, firm surface, avoid hyperventilation; 30:2 until advanced airway then 1 breath q6s; pads applied + rhythm analyzed; waveform CAPNOGRAPHY (ETCO2 gauges quality — <10 = push harder/switch; sudden rise = ROSC). RHYTHM-BASED ACLS: SHOCKABLE (VF/pVT) → DEFIBRILLATE immediately ('clear' team) → resume CPR x2 min before recheck (minimize peri-shock pause); NON-SHOCKABLE (asystole/PEA) → do NOT shock, CPR + epi + fix cause. MEDS: EPINEPHRINE 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min (after 2nd shock in shockable); AMIODARONE 300 then 150 mg (or lidocaine) for REFRACTORY VF/pVT. IV/IO access; advanced airway without long CPR pause. REVERSIBLE CAUSES (H's & T's): Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, H+/acidosis, Hypo-/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (PE/MI — likely coronary here) — POC K+/glucose/ABG + ultrasound. TEAM LEADERSHIP (high-performance): ONE clear LEADER keeps overview + assigns ROLES + monitors quality + decides (no tunnel-vision); roles = compressors (rotate), airway/RT, defib operator, MED nurse, RECORDER/timer (logs compressions/shocks/meds/rhythm + prompts cycles + epi intervals), runner, family liaison. CLOSED-LOOP communication: directed order to a NAMED person → repeat-back → confirmation. First nurse LEADS until code team arrives. DELEGATE by scope: UAP = compressions/equipment/runner; RN = assessment/defib/meds. ROSC = pulse + organized rhythm (ETCO2 rise) → POST-ARREST care: titrate O2 (avoid HYPEROXIA, SpO2 ~92-98%) + avoid hypocapnia; support BP (post-arrest hypotension 94/58 → fluids/pressors); 12-lead + emergent PCI for STEMI; TTM if comatose; treat cause; ICU handoff. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT delay CPR/defib for access/documentation, did NOT shock asystole/PEA, did NOT pause compressions excessively or hyperventilate, did NOT run a leaderless code, did NOT override a valid DNR. DEBRIEF held after the event.
providerOrders: EMERGENCY: in-hospital cardiac arrest (code blue) — witnessed, monitored; initial rhythm ventricular fibrillation; FULL CODE (no DNR)

BLS: start high-quality CPR immediately — rate 100-120/min, depth ≥2 in (≤2.4 in), full recoil, interruptions <10 s, rotate compressors every 2 minutes, firm surface; 30:2 until advanced airway, then continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds; avoid hyperventilation

DEFIBRILLATION: apply pads and analyze rhythm; defibrillate shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT) immediately and resume CPR for 2 minutes before the next rhythm/pulse check; 'clear' the team before each shock; do NOT defibrillate asystole/PEA
MEDICATIONS:
Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes (as soon as possible in non-shockable arrest; after the second shock in shockable arrest)
Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO (repeat 150 mg) — or lidocaine — for VF/pulseless VT refractory to defibrillation

ACCESS/MONITORING: establish IV or IO access; consider advanced airway without prolonged interruption of compressions; attach waveform capnography (sudden ETCO2 rise = ROSC; ETCO2 <10 mmHg = improve compression quality)

REVERSIBLE CAUSES: identify and treat the H's and T's (hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion/acidosis, hypo-/hyperkalemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis — pulmonary/coronary); point-of-care potassium/glucose/ABG; consider bedside ultrasound

TEAM/LEADERSHIP: designate a team leader who assigns roles (compressors, airway/RT, defibrillator, medication nurse, recorder/timekeeper, runner, family liaison) and uses closed-loop communication (directed order → repeat-back → confirmation); delegate within scope (UAP: compressions/equipment/runner; RN: assessment/defibrillation/medications)
CODE STATUS: verify full code; honor any valid DNR/POLST order

POST-ROSC: titrate oxygen to SpO2 ~92-98% (avoid hyperoxia) and avoid hypocapnia; support blood pressure (fluids/vasopressors); obtain 12-lead ECG and pursue emergent coronary angiography/PCI for STEMI; initiate targeted temperature management if comatose; identify/treat the cause; transfer to ICU with structured handoff
AFTER EVENT: conduct a team debrief; complete the code documentation

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters at the moment of this witnessed arrest?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Unresponsive, not breathing (only agonal gasps), and pulseless within a ≤10-second check → cardiac arrest; call a code blue and get the crash cart/defibrillator
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — rapid arrest recognition and activation drive everything that follows. RN role: recognize arrest + call for help.

opts.text: The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation — a SHOCKABLE rhythm requiring early defibrillation
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — VF is shockable; early defibrillation is the key survival determinant. RN role: identify the shockable rhythm.

opts.text: Start high-quality CPR immediately — rate 100-120/min, depth ≥2 in, full recoil, minimal interruptions, on a firm surface
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — high-quality CPR is the foundation of survival. RN role: begin high-quality compressions without delay.

opts.text: A clear team leader and assigned roles (compressions, airway, defibrillator, medications, recorder) with closed-loop communication are needed
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a coordinated high-performance team is essential to an effective code. RN role: establish leadership and roles.

opts.text: Establish IV/IO access, prepare epinephrine and an antiarrhythmic, and attach waveform capnography
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — access, medications, and capnography support the algorithm and gauge CPR quality. RN role: access + medications + monitoring.

opts.text: Search for and treat reversible causes — the H's and T's — and verify the patient is a full code (no DNR)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — reversible causes must be corrected, and code status governs whether ACLS proceeds. RN role: address causes + confirm code status.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — note for medication administration
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; relevant before code medications. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Delay chest compressions and defibrillation to first obtain IV access, draw labs, and complete a full assessment
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Compressions and early defibrillation are the time-critical priorities; access/labs/documentation must not delay them.

opts.text: Have everyone focus on compressions while no one takes a leadership/overview role or assigns tasks
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. A leaderless, unassigned code is chaotic and error-prone; one leader must maintain the overview and assign roles.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: VF and pulseless VT are shockable — immediate defibrillation is the key determinant of survival, and CPR is resumed for 2 minutes right after each shock
opts.rat: CORRECT — shockable-rhythm management. Foundation for ACLS.

opts.text: Asystole and PEA are non-shockable — do NOT defibrillate; treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine, and correction of the cause
opts.rat: CORRECT — non-shockable-rhythm management (and the 'don't shock asystole' rule). Foundation for ACLS.

opts.text: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO is given every 3-5 minutes, and an antiarrhythmic (amiodarone or lidocaine) is added for refractory VF/pVT
opts.rat: CORRECT — medication principles. Foundation for drug therapy in the code.

opts.text: High-quality CPR means a rate of 100-120/min, depth ≥2 in (≤2.4 in), full recoil, interruptions under 10 seconds, compressor rotation every 2 minutes, and avoiding excessive ventilation
opts.rat: CORRECT — high-quality CPR metrics. Foundation for effective resuscitation.

opts.text: A high-performance team uses a defined leader, clear role assignment, and closed-loop communication (directed order → repeat-back → confirmation)
opts.rat: CORRECT — team-dynamics principle. Foundation for safe, coordinated codes.

opts.text: Reversible causes are the H's and T's (hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion/acidosis, hypo-/hyperkalemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis)
opts.rat: CORRECT — the reversible-cause checklist. Foundation for treating the underlying problem.

opts.text: Asystole should be treated with immediate defibrillation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Asystole is NON-shockable; defibrillation has no role — treat with CPR, epinephrine, and correcting the cause.

opts.text: Chest compressions should be paused frequently and for as long as needed for procedures such as IV placement and intubation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Interruptions must be minimized (<10 s); procedures are done with minimal/no interruption of compressions to preserve perfusion.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Rank the immediate priorities for this VF arrest
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Start high-quality chest compressions immediately (while calling the code and getting the defibrillator)
opts.rat: #1 — Compressions begin at once and sustain perfusion until defibrillation. RN role: immediate high-quality CPR.

opts.text: Defibrillate the shockable VF rhythm as soon as the defibrillator is available, then immediately resume CPR
opts.rat: #2 — Early defibrillation is the key survival determinant for VF/pVT. RN role: defibrillate the shockable rhythm.

opts.text: Assign a team leader and roles and use closed-loop communication to organize the resuscitation
opts.rat: #3 — A coordinated team sustains quality and prevents errors throughout. RN role: leadership + role assignment.

opts.text: Establish IV/IO access and give epinephrine every 3-5 minutes (and an antiarrhythmic for refractory VF)
opts.rat: #4 — Medications support the algorithm once CPR/defibrillation and the team are underway. RN role: access + medications.

opts.text: Identify and treat reversible causes (H's and T's) and prepare for post-ROSC care
opts.rat: #5 — Correcting the cause and planning post-arrest care sustain the resuscitation and recovery. RN role: treat causes + transition to post-arrest care.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED during this code.

opts.text: Deliver high-quality compressions (100-120/min, ≥2 in, full recoil), rotating compressors every 2 minutes
opts.rat: Core high-quality CPR. RN role: effective compressions with rotation.

opts.text: Defibrillate the VF/pulseless VT, then immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check
opts.rat: Correct management of a shockable rhythm with minimal peri-shock pause. RN role: defibrillate + resume CPR.

opts.text: Establish IV/IO access and give epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes; give amiodarone for refractory VF
opts.rat: Correct ACLS medication therapy. RN role: access + scheduled medications.

opts.text: Assign a clear team leader and roles and use closed-loop communication for every order
opts.rat: High-performance team structure that prevents errors. RN role: leadership + closed-loop communication.

opts.text: Search for and treat reversible causes (H's and T's) and attach capnography to gauge CPR quality and detect ROSC
opts.rat: Treating the cause and monitoring quality/ROSC. RN role: address causes + capnography.

opts.text: Delegate within scope — UAP perform compressions and retrieve equipment while the RN gives medications and defibrillates
opts.rat: Appropriate delegation by scope during a code. RN role: delegate compressions/equipment, retain licensed tasks.

opts.text: Defibrillate the rhythm even when it is asystole or PEA
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — asystole/PEA are non-shockable; defibrillation has no role and wastes time. Treat with CPR, epinephrine, and correcting the cause.

opts.text: Pause compressions for prolonged periods for IV placement, intubation, and documentation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — long interruptions reduce perfusion and survival; minimize pauses (<10 s) and perform procedures around continuous compressions.

opts.text: Have the team leader personally do compressions, manage the airway, and push medications alone without delegating
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the leader must keep the overview and delegate; getting tunnel-visioned on tasks degrades the whole resuscitation.

opts.text: Hyperventilate the patient with rapid, high-volume breaths throughout the code
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return/coronary perfusion, and worsens outcomes; ventilate at the recommended rate.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Confirm unresponsiveness/pulselessness (≤10 s), call the code blue, and start high-quality CPR; call for the crash cart/defibrillator
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Recognition, activation, and immediate compressions start the chain of survival. RN role: recognize + call + start CPR.

opts.text: Attach the defibrillator, analyze the rhythm, and defibrillate the VF immediately; resume CPR right away
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Early defibrillation of the shockable rhythm is the key survival intervention. RN role: defibrillate + resume CPR.

opts.text: Assign the team leader and roles and establish closed-loop communication
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Organizing a high-performance team sustains quality and coordination for the rest of the code. RN role: leadership + roles.

opts.text: Establish IV/IO access and give epinephrine (and amiodarone for refractory VF) on schedule, minimizing CPR interruptions
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Scheduled medications support the algorithm while compressions continue. RN role: access + medications.

opts.text: Identify and treat reversible causes (H's and T's); on ROSC, begin post-cardiac-arrest care and hand off to ICU
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing/after ROSC. Correcting the cause and transitioning to post-arrest care complete the resuscitation. RN role: treat causes + post-arrest care.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action during the code, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The team kept compression interruptions under 10 seconds and rotated compressors every 2 minutes to maintain quality
opts.rat: High-quality CPR with minimal interruptions and compressor rotation maximizes perfusion. Correct practice.

opts.text: VF was defibrillated promptly, and CPR was resumed immediately after the shock without a prolonged pulse check
opts.rat: Early defibrillation with immediate resumption of CPR minimizes the peri-shock pause. Correct practice.

opts.text: The leader used closed-loop communication: 'Sara, give 1 mg epinephrine IV now' → 'Giving 1 mg epinephrine IV now' → 'Epinephrine given'
opts.rat: Directed order, repeat-back, and confirmation prevent medication/communication errors. Correct practice.

opts.text: Epinephrine was given every 3-5 minutes and amiodarone was added for refractory VF, with capnography monitored throughout
opts.rat: Correct medication timing for shockable arrest plus quality/ROSC monitoring. Correct practice.

opts.text: On ROSC, the team titrated oxygen (avoiding hyperoxia), supported blood pressure, obtained a 12-lead ECG, and initiated post-arrest care/TTM with handoff
opts.rat: Organized post-cardiac-arrest care optimizes neurologic and survival outcomes. Correct practice.

opts.text: When a rhythm check showed asystole, the team delivered a defibrillation shock
opts.rat: ⚠️ Asystole is NON-shockable; defibrillation has no role and interrupts CPR. Treat with CPR, epinephrine, and correcting the cause.

opts.text: Compressions were repeatedly paused for long stretches for IV access and documentation
opts.rat: ⚠️ Prolonged interruptions reduce perfusion and survival; minimize pauses and work around continuous compressions.

opts.text: No one took a leadership/overview role; orders were shouted to no one in particular and were never confirmed
opts.rat: ⚠️ A leaderless code with un-acknowledged orders causes errors and duplication; one leader must direct and use closed-loop communication.

opts.text: The patient was hyperventilated with rapid, forceful breaths for the duration of the code
opts.rat: ⚠️ Excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return/coronary perfusion, worsening outcomes. Ventilate at the recommended rate.

opts.text: The team ran full ACLS without ever checking code status, despite a valid DNR order documented on the chart
opts.rat: ⚠️ A valid DNR must be honored; performing resuscitation against it violates the patient's documented wishes. Always verify code status.

title: Informed Consent for an 80-Year-Old with Advanced Dementia and a Hip Fracture Who LACKS Decisional Capacity and Has NO Advance Directive or Named Health-Care Proxy: Capacity vs Competence, the Elements of Valid Consent and the NURSE'S Witness (NOT Obtain) Role, the Statutory SURROGATE Hierarchy, Substituted Judgment vs Best Interest, Emergency (Implied) Consent, and Ethics/Guardianship as a Last Resort
subtitle: When an older adult needs a treatment decision but may not be able to make it, the nurse must understand DECISIONAL CAPACITY and INFORMED CONSENT. CAPACITY is a CLINICAL, DECISION-SPECIFIC, and PRESUMED determination — can the person UNDERSTAND the relevant information, APPRECIATE how it applies to them, REASON about the options, and COMMUNICATE a stable CHOICE? It can fluctuate and is specific to the decision at hand. COMPETENCE, by contrast, is a GLOBAL LEGAL status determined by a COURT (the clinical team assesses capacity; only a court declares incompetence). Before concluding a patient has DURABLE incapacity, the nurse SCREENS FOR and OPTIMIZES REVERSIBLE contributors — DELIRIUM (use CAM), infection (e.g., UTI), PAIN, sedating MEDICATIONS, metabolic/electrolyte derangements, hypoxia, and sensory deficits (hearing aids/glasses) — and reassesses, because an unwise choice, old age, a dementia label, or simple disagreement do NOT by themselves equal incapacity. ELEMENTS of VALID INFORMED CONSENT: (1) the decision-maker has CAPACITY and the AUTHORITY to decide; (2) the decision is VOLUNTARY (free of coercion); (3) adequate DISCLOSURE — the diagnosis, the NATURE and PURPOSE of the proposed procedure, the material RISKS and BENEFITS, the ALTERNATIVES (including the option of NO treatment) and their consequences; (4) the decision-maker UNDERSTANDS; and (5) CONSENT is given. The PROVIDER who will perform the procedure is responsible for the DISCLOSURE and for OBTAINING informed consent; the NURSE'S role is to WITNESS the signature, confirm the consent appears VOLUNTARY and that the signer appears to UNDERSTAND, reinforce/clarify teaching, ADVOCATE, and NOTIFY the provider if the patient/surrogate has questions or does not understand — the nurse does NOT provide the disclosure for or obtain consent on behalf of the provider, and never signs FOR the patient. WHEN THE PATIENT LACKS CAPACITY: first look for an ADVANCE DIRECTIVE (living will) or a designated HEALTH-CARE PROXY / durable power of attorney for health care; a directive completed while the patient HAD capacity is binding. If there is NO advance directive and NO named proxy (as here), a SURROGATE is identified per the STATE SURROGATE-CONSENT STATUTE HIERARCHY — a typical order is: a court-appointed GUARDIAN (if one exists) → SPOUSE → ADULT CHILDREN (often by majority) → PARENTS → ADULT SIBLINGS → other relatives or a close friend who knows the patient's values. The surrogate decides using the SUBSTITUTED-JUDGMENT standard (what the PATIENT would have wanted, based on previously expressed values, beliefs, and statements) and, only when those wishes are unknown, the BEST-INTEREST standard (the option that best promotes the patient's welfare). EMERGENCY (IMPLIED) CONSENT: in an IMMEDIATE life- or limb-threatening EMERGENCY when no surrogate is reachable, treatment needed to prevent death or serious harm may proceed under implied consent (a reasonable person would consent) — but this does NOT apply to a non-emergent decision when a surrogate IS available (as with this semi-urgent hip repair). WHEN SURROGATES CONFLICT, no surrogate exists (the 'unrepresented/unbefriended' patient), or the decision is ethically complex → obtain an ETHICS CONSULT, and pursue COURT-APPOINTED GUARDIANSHIP (guardian of the PERSON for health decisions; a conservator/guardian of the ESTATE for finances) only as a LAST RESORT and least-restrictive option. Throughout, the patient is INVOLVED to the extent possible (simple explanations, ASSENT, daily preferences) and her DIGNITY and rights are protected; CODE STATUS is established with the surrogate. NURSING ROLE: assess capacity and optimize reversible causes; identify the correct decision-maker (advance directive/proxy, then the surrogate hierarchy); ensure the PROVIDER obtains valid informed consent while the nurse witnesses, verifies understanding, and advocates; support substituted judgment then best interest; involve the patient and protect dignity; and escalate to ethics/guardianship only when truly needed.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + capacity vs competence + assessing capacity/reversible causes
labs.v: Eleanor V., an 80-year-old with ADVANCED dementia, is admitted with a displaced femoral-neck HIP FRACTURE for which orthopedics recommends surgical fixation — important and semi-urgent, but NOT an immediate life-threatening emergency. The first question is whether she can make this decision herself. DECISIONAL CAPACITY is a CLINICAL, DECISION-SPECIFIC, and PRESUMED determination assessed by the team: can she UNDERSTAND the relevant information, APPRECIATE how it applies to her, REASON among the options, and COMMUNICATE a stable CHOICE? Here she cannot state where she is or grasp the proposed surgery or its risks, so she LACKS capacity for this decision. This differs from COMPETENCE, a GLOBAL LEGAL status that only a COURT can determine. Critically, before concluding she has DURABLE incapacity, the nurse SCREENS FOR and OPTIMIZES REVERSIBLE contributors: DELIRIUM (CAM), infection (her mild fever prompts a UTI evaluation), PAIN, sedating MEDICATIONS, metabolic/electrolyte issues, hypoxia, and missing sensory aids (hearing aids/glasses) — and then reassesses. An unwise choice, advanced age, a dementia label, or mere disagreement do NOT by themselves equal incapacity; but in advanced dementia, after optimizing reversible factors, durable incapacity for a complex surgical decision is expected. Establishing the capacity determination correctly is the foundation for everything that follows.
labs.r: CAPACITY = clinical, decision-SPECIFIC, presumed (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate a choice); fluctuates. COMPETENCE = global LEGAL status decided by a COURT. Before declaring durable incapacity, screen/optimize REVERSIBLE causes (delirium/CAM, infection/UTI, pain, sedating meds, metabolic, sensory aids) + reassess. Unwise choice/old age/dementia label/disagreement ≠ incapacity. RN role: assess capacity + rule out reversible contributors.

labs.n: Elements of valid informed consent + the NURSE'S role (witness, NOT obtain)
labs.v: VALID INFORMED CONSENT has defined ELEMENTS: (1) the decision-maker has CAPACITY and the legal AUTHORITY to decide; (2) the decision is VOLUNTARY — free of coercion or undue pressure; (3) adequate DISCLOSURE — the diagnosis, the NATURE and PURPOSE of the proposed procedure, the material RISKS and BENEFITS, and the ALTERNATIVES (including the option of NO treatment) with their consequences; (4) the decision-maker UNDERSTANDS the information; and (5) CONSENT is given (or refused). RESPONSIBILITY: the PROVIDER who will perform the procedure (here the surgeon) is legally responsible for the DISCLOSURE and for OBTAINING informed consent. The NURSE'S ROLE is distinct and important but limited: WITNESS the signature; confirm the consent appears VOLUNTARY and that the signer appears to UNDERSTAND; reinforce and clarify teaching within the nurse's scope; serve as the patient's ADVOCATE; and NOTIFY the provider if the patient/surrogate has unanswered questions, seems not to understand, or wishes to change/withdraw the decision (consent can be withdrawn at any time). The nurse does NOT deliver the procedure-specific disclosure for the provider, does NOT obtain consent on the provider's behalf, and NEVER signs the form FOR the patient or surrogate. If the signer does not understand, the nurse stops the process and calls the provider back — a signature without understanding is not valid consent.
labs.r: Valid informed consent = capable/authorized decision-maker + VOLUNTARY + DISCLOSURE (diagnosis, procedure nature/purpose, risks/benefits, ALTERNATIVES incl. no treatment) + UNDERSTANDING + consent. The PROVIDER obtains consent (disclosure is their duty). NURSE = WITNESS signature + confirm voluntary/understanding + reinforce + advocate + notify provider of questions/withdrawal. Nurse NEVER provides the disclosure for the provider or signs FOR the patient. RN role: witness + verify + advocate, not obtain.

labs.n: No advance directive/proxy → surrogate hierarchy + substituted judgment vs best interest + emergency consent
labs.v: Because Eleanor lacks capacity, the team looks for an ADVANCE DIRECTIVE (living will) or a designated HEALTH-CARE PROXY / durable power of attorney for health care — a directive made while she HAD capacity would be binding. There is NONE on file. With no advance directive and no named proxy, a SURROGATE is identified per the STATE SURROGATE-CONSENT STATUTE HIERARCHY; a typical order is: a court-appointed GUARDIAN (if any) → SPOUSE → ADULT CHILDREN (often by majority agreement) → PARENTS → ADULT SIBLINGS → another relative or close friend who knows her values. Eleanor is widowed, so her two ADULT CHILDREN are the surrogates and are engaged together. The surrogate must decide by the SUBSTITUTED-JUDGMENT standard — choosing what ELEANOR would have wanted based on her previously expressed values, beliefs, religious/cultural views, and prior statements — and only when her wishes are truly unknown does the surrogate use the BEST-INTEREST standard (the option that best promotes her welfare, weighing benefits, burdens, and quality of life). The EMERGENCY (IMPLIED) CONSENT exception allows treatment to proceed WITHOUT formal consent ONLY in an IMMEDIATE life- or limb-threatening emergency when no surrogate is reachable, because a reasonable person would consent to life-saving care — but this hip repair is semi-urgent and a surrogate IS available, so emergency consent does NOT apply and proper surrogate consent is required before surgery.
labs.r: No capacity → check advance directive/health-care proxy (binding if made with capacity). NONE → SURROGATE per statutory HIERARCHY: guardian → spouse → adult children → parents → siblings → close other. Surrogate uses SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what the PATIENT would want) → BEST INTEREST only if wishes unknown. EMERGENCY (IMPLIED) consent ONLY for immediate life-/limb-threatening emergency with no surrogate reachable — NOT for a non-emergent decision when a surrogate is available. RN role: find the right decision-maker + support substituted judgment.

labs.n: Conflict / no surrogate → ethics + guardianship (last resort); patient involvement + dignity
labs.v: Surrogate decision-making is not always straightforward. If the adult children DISAGREE with each other, if NO surrogate exists or can be found (the 'UNREPRESENTED' or 'unbefriended' patient), or if the decision is ETHICALLY COMPLEX (e.g., high-risk surgery vs comfort care, conflicting values), the team obtains an ETHICS CONSULT to facilitate a values-based, structured discussion rather than forcing a decision or letting one family member dominate. COURT-APPOINTED GUARDIANSHIP/CONSERVATORSHIP is pursued only as a LAST RESORT and least-restrictive option when there is no appropriate surrogate or unresolvable conflict — a GUARDIAN OF THE PERSON makes health-care and personal decisions, while a CONSERVATOR/GUARDIAN OF THE ESTATE manages finances; guardianship is a significant restriction of autonomy and should not be the first move. Throughout, the patient is INVOLVED to the extent possible: give simple, honest explanations at her level, seek her ASSENT and honor her expressed daily preferences (comfort, food, music, presence of loved ones), and protect her DIGNITY and remaining rights — advanced dementia does NOT erase her personhood. CODE STATUS and goals of care are established with the surrogate using substituted judgment. The bedside nurse advocates for Eleanor, keeps her comfortable (pain control, delirium prevention), documents the capacity assessment, the identified decision-maker, the consent, and code status, and ensures the process is transparent and patient-centered.
labs.r: Surrogate conflict / no surrogate (unrepresented) / ethically complex → ETHICS CONSULT; court GUARDIANSHIP only as LAST RESORT/least-restrictive (guardian of PERSON = health/personal; conservator/guardian of ESTATE = finances). Always INVOLVE the patient to the extent possible (simple explanation, assent, daily preferences, dignity — dementia ≠ loss of personhood). Establish code status via substituted judgment. RN role: advocate, involve, escalate appropriately, document.

labs.n: Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors + nursing summary
labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the team did NOT conclude durable incapacity without first screening/optimizing reversible contributors (delirium, UTI, pain, sedating meds) and reassessing; the nurse did NOT sign the consent FOR the patient and did NOT provide the procedure-specific disclosure for or obtain consent on behalf of the surgeon; the team did NOT proceed with the NON-emergent surgery without consent simply because the patient 'can't decide,' and did NOT misapply the emergency/implied-consent exception when a surrogate was available; staff did NOT coerce or pressure the surrogate to sign quickly to keep the OR schedule; the surrogate was guided to use SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what Eleanor would want) rather than the surrogate's own preference; and the patient was NOT excluded or stripped of dignity/rights because she has dementia. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: a careful capacity assessment with reversible-cause optimization; correct identification of the decision-maker via the statutory hierarchy; valid provider-obtained informed consent witnessed and verified by the nurse; decisions grounded in the patient's known values; patient involvement and dignity preserved; availability of an ethics consult for conflict; and thorough documentation. EXPECTED outcome: a valid, ethically and legally sound decision is reached, the appropriate surgery proceeds with proper consent (or is declined per the patient's values), the patient is kept comfortable and involved, and family is aligned with what Eleanor would have wanted. NURSING ROLE: assess capacity and optimize reversible causes; identify the correct decision-maker (advance directive/proxy, then the surrogate hierarchy); ensure the PROVIDER obtains valid informed consent while the nurse witnesses, verifies understanding, and advocates; support substituted judgment then best interest; involve the patient and protect dignity; establish code status; escalate to ethics/guardianship only when truly needed; and document the process.
labs.r: NEGATIVES (correct practice): didn't skip reversible-cause workup, nurse didn't sign FOR patient or obtain the disclosure, didn't operate without consent on a non-emergency, didn't misuse emergency consent, didn't coerce the surrogate, didn't substitute the surrogate's own wishes, didn't exclude/demean the patient. PROTECTIVE: capacity assessment + reversible optimization, correct surrogate per hierarchy, provider-obtained/nurse-witnessed consent, substituted judgment, patient involvement/dignity, ethics consult availability, documentation. RN role: assess capacity + right decision-maker + witness/verify consent + advocate + involve + document.

providerOrders: ADMIT: orthopedic/surgical unit; 80-year-old with advanced dementia and a displaced femoral-neck hip fracture; orthopedic surgery (fixation/hemiarthroplasty) recommended — semi-urgent, not an immediate life-threatening emergency
DECISIONAL CAPACITY:
Assess capacity for this decision (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate a choice); document findings
Screen for and optimize reversible contributors: CAM for delirium, evaluate for UTI/infection, control pain, review sedating medications, ensure hearing aids/glasses; reassess capacity
DECISION-MAKER:
Search the record for an advance directive (living will) or designated health-care proxy/durable power of attorney for health care
If none, identify the surrogate per the state statutory hierarchy (guardian → spouse → adult children → parents → siblings → close other); engage both adult children
INFORMED CONSENT:
Surgeon to disclose diagnosis, procedure nature/purpose, material risks/benefits, and alternatives (including no surgery) and obtain consent from the surrogate
RN to witness the signature, confirm it is voluntary and that the surrogate appears to understand, reinforce teaching, and notify the surgeon of any questions or withdrawal
DECISION STANDARD:
Guide the surrogate to use substituted judgment (what the patient would have wanted) and, if her wishes are unknown, the best-interest standard
Establish code status/goals of care with the surrogate
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE:
Involve the patient to the extent possible (simple explanations, assent, honor daily preferences), protect dignity and rights; provide pain control and delirium-prevention measures
ESCALATION:
Obtain an ethics consult if surrogates disagree, no surrogate is available, or the decision is ethically complex; pursue court-appointed guardianship only as a last resort
DOCUMENTATION: capacity assessment, identified decision-maker, informed-consent process, code status, and patient involvement

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this consent decision?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: The patient lacks decisional capacity for this surgical decision — she cannot understand, appreciate, reason about, or communicate a stable choice due to advanced dementia
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — establishing the capacity determination is the foundation of the consent process. RN role: assess decision-specific capacity.

opts.text: Screen for and optimize reversible contributors to impaired cognition (delirium/CAM, possible UTI, pain, sedating meds, sensory aids) and reassess before concluding durable incapacity
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — reversible causes must be excluded/optimized; capacity is presumed and decision-specific. RN role: rule out reversible contributors.

opts.text: There is no advance directive and no named health-care proxy → a surrogate must be identified per the state statutory hierarchy
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the correct decision-maker must be identified when capacity is lacking. RN role: identify the surrogate.

opts.text: The hip repair is semi-urgent but not an immediate life-threatening emergency, and a surrogate is available → proper surrogate informed consent is required (not emergency/implied consent)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — emergency consent does not apply when the situation is non-emergent and a surrogate exists. RN role: require proper consent.

opts.text: The surgeon must obtain informed consent (disclosure); the nurse's role is to witness the signature, confirm voluntariness/understanding, advocate, and notify the provider of questions
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the provider obtains consent; the nurse witnesses and verifies. RN role: witness/verify, not obtain.

opts.text: Guide the decision by substituted judgment (Eleanor's known values) and involve the patient to the extent possible, protecting her dignity
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — substituted judgment and patient involvement/dignity govern the decision. RN role: support the patient's voice and values.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — document for the perioperative record
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine before surgery. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Because the patient 'can't decide,' the nurse should sign the consent form on her behalf and obtain the consent herself
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The nurse never signs for the patient and does not obtain the provider's informed consent; an authorized surrogate decides, the surgeon discloses/obtains consent, and the nurse witnesses.

opts.text: Proceed straight to surgery under emergency/implied consent even though it is not an immediate life-threatening emergency and a surrogate is available
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Emergency/implied consent applies only to immediate life-/limb-threatening emergencies with no surrogate reachable; here proper surrogate consent must be obtained first.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: What consent and capacity principles apply?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Capacity is a clinical, decision-specific, presumed determination (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate a choice), while competence is a global legal status decided by a court
opts.rat: CORRECT — the capacity-vs-competence distinction. Foundation for the determination.

opts.text: Valid informed consent requires an authorized decision-maker with capacity, voluntariness, disclosure (diagnosis, procedure, risks/benefits, alternatives including no treatment), understanding, and consent
opts.rat: CORRECT — the elements of valid informed consent. Foundation for a lawful decision.

opts.text: The provider performing the procedure obtains informed consent; the nurse witnesses the signature, verifies understanding, advocates, and notifies the provider of concerns
opts.rat: CORRECT — division of responsibility for consent. Foundation for the nurse's role.

opts.text: With no advance directive or proxy, a surrogate is identified per the statutory hierarchy (guardian → spouse → adult children → parents → siblings) and decides by substituted judgment, then best interest
opts.rat: CORRECT — surrogate identification and decision standards. Foundation for who decides and how.

opts.text: Emergency (implied) consent permits treatment only in an immediate life-/limb-threatening emergency when no surrogate is reachable
opts.rat: CORRECT — the scope of the emergency-consent exception. Foundation for when it applies.

opts.text: Surrogate conflict, no available surrogate, or ethically complex decisions warrant an ethics consult, with court guardianship only as a last resort
opts.rat: CORRECT — escalation pathway. Foundation for resolving difficult cases.

opts.text: A nurse may legally provide the procedure-specific disclosure and obtain informed consent for the surgeon's operation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Disclosure and obtaining consent are the provider's legal responsibility; the nurse witnesses, verifies, and advocates but does not obtain the consent.

opts.text: An advanced-dementia diagnosis alone means the patient has no rights and need not be involved or informed in any way
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Dementia does not erase personhood or rights; the patient is involved to the extent possible (simple explanation, assent, preferences) and her dignity is protected.

title: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI) in a 72-Year-Old Post-Op Patient with a Lingering Indwelling Catheter: Recognizing Symptomatic CAUTI (Including New Confusion) vs ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA, the CAUTI PREVENTION BUNDLE and Early Catheter Removal, Proper Specimen Collection, Treatment, and Preventing Progression to Urosepsis
subtitle: A CATHETER-ASSOCIATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION (CAUTI) is a urinary tract infection occurring in a patient with an indwelling urinary (Foley) catheter or one recently removed; it is the MOST COMMON healthcare-associated infection. The RISK rises with EACH DAY the catheter remains in place, because the catheter provides a direct route for organisms and supports BIOFILM formation on its surface, leading first to bacteriuria and then to infection. RECOGNITION: in a catheterized patient the classic UTI symptoms of dysuria, frequency, and urgency are often ABSENT (the catheter bypasses the urethra), so the nurse watches for NEW FEVER, SUPRAPUBIC tenderness/pain, COSTOVERTEBRAL-ANGLE (flank) tenderness, NEW-ONSET or WORSENING CONFUSION/DELIRIUM (in OLDER ADULTS this may be the ONLY sign), rigors, hematuria, and laboratory leukocytosis; urinalysis may show pyuria, bacteriuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and nitrites. A CRITICAL distinction is SYMPTOMATIC CAUTI versus ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA (ASB) — a POSITIVE urine culture WITHOUT signs/symptoms of infection. ASB is generally NOT TREATED with antibiotics (key exceptions: pregnancy and before certain urologic procedures), because treating it drives ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE and C. difficile risk without benefit; likewise, CLOUDY or FOUL-SMELLING urine ALONE, without symptoms, is NOT a reason to culture or treat. SPECIMEN: obtain the urine culture ASEPTICALLY from the catheter SAMPLING PORT (after cleansing it) — NOT from the drainage bag; if the catheter has been in place a long time (e.g., >2 weeks) and infection is suspected, replace it and collect from the fresh catheter. The CAUTI PREVENTION BUNDLE is the heart of nursing care: (1) AVOID unnecessary catheters — insert ONLY for an APPROPRIATE INDICATION (acute urinary retention or obstruction; need for accurate output in the critically ill; selected perioperative use; healing of open sacral/perineal wounds in incontinent patients; prolonged immobilization; comfort at end of life) and NOT for convenience, routine incontinence, or simply to obtain urine from a cooperative patient; (2) ASEPTIC/STERILE insertion by trained personnel (sterile gloves, drape, antiseptic, single-use lubricant); (3) maintain a CLOSED drainage system (do not disconnect; if the system is breached, replace it aseptically); (4) SECURE the catheter to prevent movement/urethral traction and keep urine flowing freely (no kinks/dependent loops); (5) keep the drainage BAG BELOW THE LEVEL OF THE BLADDER at ALL times (including transport/ambulation) and off the floor, and empty it regularly into a clean, separate container; (6) MEATAL/PERINEAL HYGIENE with soap and water (routine antiseptic ointments are not recommended); (7) HAND HYGIENE before and after any catheter manipulation and gloves for handling; (8) perform a DAILY REVIEW of CONTINUED NECESSITY and REMOVE the catheter as EARLY as possible — early removal is the SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE intervention, supported by nurse-driven removal protocols and reminders; (9) do NOT perform routine bladder irrigation, routine catheter changes, or give prophylactic antibiotics to prevent CAUTI; and (10) use ALTERNATIVES when possible (intermittent straight catheterization, EXTERNAL/condom catheters, a bladder scanner for retention, scheduled voiding/toileting). TREATMENT of a SYMPTOMATIC CAUTI: obtain the culture, REMOVE the catheter if it is no longer indicated, or REPLACE it (to eliminate biofilm) if it must remain, then give APPROPRIATE antibiotics (empiric, then narrowed per culture and sensitivities) with hydration; practice ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP (treat only true symptomatic infection and tailor therapy). The nurse MONITORS for progression to UROSEPSIS — fever, tachycardia, HYPOTENSION, rising lactate/WBC, and altered mentation — which is a sepsis emergency requiring rapid cultures, antibiotics, and fluids. NURSING ROLE: prevent CAUTI through the bundle and early removal; distinguish symptomatic CAUTI from asymptomatic bacteriuria; collect the specimen correctly; treat symptomatic infection and remove/replace the catheter; monitor for and prevent urosepsis; advocate for daily necessity review; and educate the patient and team.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + recognizing CAUTI (the most common HAI; signs; confusion in the older adult)
labs.v: Walter K. is post-operative day 4 after an open sigmoid colectomy, with an indwelling urinary (Foley) catheter placed in the OR that REMAINS in place even though he is now stable, ambulating, and no longer needs strict output monitoring. He develops a NEW fever (38.5°C), SUPRAPUBIC discomfort, CLOUDY/malodorous urine, and NEW-ONSET CONFUSION. This suggests a CATHETER-ASSOCIATED UTI (CAUTI) — a UTI in a patient with an indwelling catheter (or recently removed), and the MOST COMMON healthcare-associated infection. The catheter provides a direct route for organisms and supports BIOFILM formation, and the RISK rises with EACH catheter-day. In a catheterized patient, the classic dysuria/frequency/urgency are often ABSENT (the catheter bypasses the urethra), so recognition relies on NEW FEVER, SUPRAPUBIC pain, COSTOVERTEBRAL-ANGLE (flank) tenderness, NEW or WORSENING CONFUSION/DELIRIUM — which in OLDER ADULTS may be the ONLY sign — rigors, hematuria, and leukocytosis. The nurse's priorities: recognize symptomatic CAUTI (and distinguish it from asymptomatic bacteriuria), collect a proper specimen, address the lingering catheter, support treatment, and watch for urosepsis.
labs.r: CAUTI = UTI with an indwelling (or recently removed) catheter — the MOST COMMON HAI; risk rises with EACH catheter-day (biofilm). Classic dysuria/frequency often ABSENT in catheterized patients → watch for NEW fever, suprapubic/CVA (flank) tenderness, NEW CONFUSION (may be the ONLY sign in elders), hematuria, leukocytosis. RN role: recognize symptomatic CAUTI in a catheterized patient.

labs.n: Symptomatic CAUTI vs ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA + proper specimen collection
labs.v: A pivotal distinction is SYMPTOMATIC CAUTI versus ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA (ASB). ASB is a POSITIVE urine culture WITHOUT signs or symptoms of infection; it is COMMON in catheterized patients and is generally NOT TREATED with antibiotics — the important EXCEPTIONS are PREGNANCY and BEFORE certain urologic procedures. Treating ASB provides NO benefit and drives ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE and C. difficile infection; therefore CLOUDY or FOUL-SMELLING urine ALONE, without symptoms, is NOT a reason to send a culture or start antibiotics (a key antibiotic-stewardship point and a common test trap). A symptomatic CAUTI, by contrast, has the systemic/local SIGNS above plus laboratory evidence. SPECIMEN COLLECTION matters: obtain the urine culture ASEPTICALLY from the catheter's SAMPLING PORT after cleansing it — NEVER from the DRAINAGE BAG (where organisms multiply and contaminate the sample) and never by disconnecting the closed system. If the catheter has been in place a long time (e.g., >2 weeks) and infection is suspected, the catheter should be REPLACED and the specimen collected from the FRESH catheter so the culture reflects bladder urine rather than catheter biofilm. Urinalysis findings (pyuria, bacteriuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites) support but do not alone diagnose infection without symptoms.
labs.r: ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA (positive culture, NO symptoms) → do NOT treat (exceptions: pregnancy + before urologic procedures); treating it = resistance + C. diff with no benefit. Cloudy/foul urine ALONE ≠ CAUTI. Symptomatic CAUTI = symptoms + lab evidence. Specimen: aseptic from the SAMPLING PORT (NOT the bag); if catheter old (>2 wk), replace then collect. RN role: distinguish symptomatic CAUTI from ASB + collect the specimen correctly.

labs.n: CAUTI PREVENTION BUNDLE + early catheter removal (the core of nursing care)
labs.v: Most CAUTIs are PREVENTABLE, and the bundle is core nursing care: (1) AVOID unnecessary catheters — place ONLY for an APPROPRIATE INDICATION (acute urinary RETENTION or obstruction; accurate output in the CRITICALLY ill; selected PERIOPERATIVE use; open SACRAL/PERINEAL wounds in incontinent patients; prolonged immobilization; end-of-life COMFORT) and NOT for convenience, routine incontinence, or simply to obtain a specimen from a cooperative patient. (2) ASEPTIC/sterile INSERTION by trained staff (sterile gloves, drape, antiseptic, single-use lubricant). (3) Maintain a CLOSED drainage system — do not disconnect; replace aseptically if breached. (4) SECURE the catheter to prevent traction/movement and keep urine flowing freely (no kinks/dependent loops). (5) Keep the drainage BAG BELOW the level of the BLADDER at ALL times — including during transport and ambulation — and OFF the floor, emptying it regularly into a clean, separate container (avoid touching the spout to the container). (6) MEATAL/PERINEAL HYGIENE with soap and water (routine antiseptic ointments are not recommended). (7) HAND HYGIENE before and after any catheter manipulation; gloves for handling. (8) Perform a DAILY REVIEW of continued NECESSITY and REMOVE the catheter as EARLY as possible — EARLY REMOVAL is the SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE intervention (nurse-driven removal protocols and reminders help). (9) Do NOT perform routine bladder irrigation or routine catheter changes, and do NOT give prophylactic antibiotics. (10) Use ALTERNATIVES — intermittent straight catheterization, EXTERNAL/condom catheters, a BLADDER SCANNER for suspected retention, and scheduled toileting. For Walter, the catheter has lingered without a current indication, so the nurse advocates for prompt removal.
labs.r: CAUTI PREVENTION BUNDLE: insert ONLY for appropriate indications (retention/obstruction, critical-illness output, selected perioperative, sacral wounds + incontinence, immobilization, comfort) — NOT convenience/incontinence; ASEPTIC insertion; CLOSED system; SECURE + free flow; BAG BELOW BLADDER + off floor; perineal care; HAND HYGIENE; DAILY necessity review + EARLY REMOVAL (most effective); NO routine irrigation/changes/prophylactic abx; use ALTERNATIVES (intermittent/external cath, bladder scanner). RN role: prevent CAUTI + advocate early removal.

labs.n: Treatment of symptomatic CAUTI + progression to urosepsis + stewardship
labs.v: When a SYMPTOMATIC CAUTI is diagnosed: obtain the urine culture; then REMOVE the catheter if it is no longer indicated, or REPLACE it (to eliminate the infected BIOFILM) if it must remain; and start APPROPRIATE antibiotics — empiric coverage initially, then NARROWED per culture and sensitivities — with hydration. ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP is essential: treat only a TRUE symptomatic infection (not ASB), choose the right drug/dose/duration, and de-escalate per results to limit resistance and C. difficile. The nurse MONITORS for progression to UROSEPSIS — the spread of infection to the bloodstream causing sepsis — signaled by rising fever (or hypothermia), TACHYCARDIA, HYPOTENSION, tachypnea, worsening CONFUSION, decreased urine output, and a rising LACTATE/WBC. Urosepsis is a SEPSIS EMERGENCY requiring rapid blood and urine CULTURES, BROAD-SPECTRUM antibiotics within the first hour, IV FLUID resuscitation, and close hemodynamic monitoring (escalating to vasopressors/ICU if shock develops). Removing or replacing the SOURCE (the colonized catheter) is part of source control. For Walter, the team obtains the culture, removes the lingering catheter, starts antibiotics and fluids, and watches closely for any sign of urosepsis.
labs.r: Symptomatic CAUTI treatment: culture → REMOVE catheter (if not indicated) or REPLACE it (clear biofilm) → APPROPRIATE antibiotics (empiric then narrowed) + hydration; STEWARDSHIP (treat only true infection, de-escalate). MONITOR for UROSEPSIS (fever, tachycardia, HYPOTENSION, worsening confusion, rising lactate/WBC) → sepsis emergency: rapid cultures + broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1h + IV fluids + source control (remove/replace catheter). RN role: treat the infection + prevent/recognize urosepsis.

labs.n: Nursing role + education; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: ONGOING NURSING CARE + EDUCATION: maintain the prevention bundle for every catheterized patient; assess catheter NECESSITY daily and advocate for the earliest safe REMOVAL; perform proper perineal care and hand hygiene; keep the closed system intact with the bag dependent; monitor intake/output, temperature, and mental status; collect specimens correctly; administer culture-directed antibiotics and ensure adequate hydration; and watch for urosepsis. EDUCATE the patient/family on the reason for (and prompt removal of) the catheter, perineal hygiene, keeping the bag below the bladder, hand hygiene, and reporting fever, suprapubic/flank pain, or confusion. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the team did NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria or culture/treat based on cloudy/foul urine ALONE; did NOT collect the specimen from the drainage bag; did NOT leave the catheter in for convenience or perform routine irrigation/changes/prophylactic antibiotics; did NOT raise the drainage bag above the bladder; and did NOT delay recognizing and treating the symptomatic infection or its progression to urosepsis. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: prompt recognition of symptomatic CAUTI; correct specimen collection; early catheter removal/replacement and source control; culture-directed, stewardship-minded antibiotics; diligent prevention bundle; and patient education. EXPECTED outcome: the symptomatic CAUTI resolves on appropriate therapy, the catheter is removed, urosepsis is prevented (or rapidly treated), and prevention practices reduce future infections. NURSING ROLE: prevent CAUTI through the bundle and early removal; distinguish symptomatic CAUTI from asymptomatic bacteriuria; collect the specimen correctly; treat symptomatic infection and remove/replace the catheter; monitor for and prevent urosepsis; and educate.
labs.r: ONGOING: maintain prevention bundle, DAILY necessity review + early removal, perineal care/hand hygiene, closed dependent system, monitor I&O/temp/mentation, culture-directed antibiotics + hydration, watch urosepsis; EDUCATE (catheter purpose/removal, hygiene, bag below bladder, report fever/flank pain/confusion). NEGATIVES (correct practice): no treating ASB/cloudy urine alone, no specimen from the bag, no convenience catheter/routine irrigation/prophylactic abx, no raising the bag, no delayed treatment. RN role: prevent + recognize + treat + educate.

opts.text: Consider alternatives to indwelling catheterization (intermittent straight catheter, external/condom catheter, bladder scanner for retention)
opts.rat: Reduces catheter use and CAUTI risk. RN role: use alternatives when possible.

opts.text: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with antibiotics whenever a culture is positive
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — asymptomatic bacteriuria is generally not treated (exceptions: pregnancy, pre-urologic procedures); treating it drives resistance/C. diff.

opts.text: Diagnose and treat a CAUTI based on cloudy/foul-smelling urine alone, without symptoms
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — appearance/odor alone does not indicate infection; this leads to overtreatment. Require symptoms plus lab evidence.

opts.text: Perform routine bladder irrigation, routine catheter changes, and give prophylactic antibiotics to prevent CAUTI
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — none of these prevent CAUTI; prevention relies on the bundle and early removal.

opts.text: Keep the catheter in for convenience and raise the drainage bag above the bladder when moving the patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — convenience is not an indication, and raising the bag above the bladder causes reflux of contaminated urine, increasing infection risk.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess the patient (vitals, mental status, abdomen/flank), recognize the symptomatic CAUTI and possible urosepsis, and notify the provider
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Recognition and assessment for sepsis drive urgency and the plan. RN role: assess + recognize + escalate.

opts.text: Obtain the urine culture aseptically from the sampling port (and blood cultures/labs if septic) before antibiotics
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Cultures before antibiotics ensure accurate, targeted therapy. RN role: collect specimens.

opts.text: Remove or replace the indwelling catheter per orders (source control)
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Addressing the colonized catheter is essential to resolution. RN role: remove/replace the catheter.

opts.text: Administer appropriate antibiotics and IV fluids per orders and monitor the response
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Treats the infection and supports perfusion. RN role: antibiotics + fluids + monitoring.

opts.text: Reinforce the prevention bundle, advocate daily catheter-necessity review and early removal, educate, and document
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing. Prevention, advocacy, education, and documentation sustain the outcome. RN role: prevention + education.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: After catheter removal, cultures, culture-directed antibiotics, and hydration, the fever resolves, mental status clears, and the urine clears
opts.rat: Source control plus appropriate therapy resolving the infection. Expected, desired response.

opts.text: The catheter was removed once it no longer met an indication, and the patient voided normally without recurrent infection
opts.rat: Early removal eliminates the source and risk. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: With the prevention bundle (closed system, bag below the bladder, perineal care, hand hygiene, daily necessity review), no new CAUTI develops
opts.rat: Effective prevention practice. Improving/safe trajectory.

opts.text: Antibiotics were narrowed to the cultured organism's sensitivities, and the symptomatic infection resolved
opts.rat: Culture-directed stewardship with resolution. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — asymptomatic bacteriuria was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics; the patient then developed C. difficile and a resistant organism
opts.rat: ⚠️ Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria caused harm (C. diff, resistance). Demonstrates why ASB is not treated.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the catheter was kept for convenience with the bag resting on the floor and the closed system repeatedly opened; bacteriuria and then a symptomatic CAUTI developed
opts.rat: ⚠️ Bundle breaches (unnecessary catheter, contaminated bag, open system) caused infection. Demonstrates why the bundle and early removal matter.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the symptomatic CAUTI was not treated and the catheter was not addressed; the patient progressed to urosepsis with hypotension
opts.rat: ⚠️ Untreated infection without source control progressed to urosepsis. Demonstrates the need for timely treatment and monitoring.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the drainage bag was raised above the bladder during transport, causing reflux of contaminated urine and increasing infection risk
opts.rat: ⚠️ Raising the bag above the bladder causes reflux. Demonstrates keeping the bag dependent at all times.

opts.text: Early after starting treatment, before antibiotics take effect, the fever and confusion are still present and essentially unchanged while cultures are pending
opts.rat: Before antibiotics take effect, an unchanged baseline is expected; continue treatment, hydration, and monitoring and reassess.

opts.text: At follow-up the patient is afebrile, catheter-free, voiding normally, and able to describe prevention measures
opts.rat: Sustained recovery with effective education. Ideal longer-term outcome.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Safety and Infection Control, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Malignant Hyperthermia During General Anesthesia in a 19-Year-Old Undergoing Surgery: Recognizing the EARLIEST Sign (an Unexplained Rising End-Tidal CO2) and Masseter/Muscle Rigidity, STOPPING the Triggering Agents, Activating the MH Protocol, Giving DANTROLENE, Cooling, and Coordinating the Emergency Team Response
subtitle: MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA (MH) is a rare, life-threatening, INHERITED (autosomal dominant, usually a RYR1/ryanodine-receptor mutation) HYPERMETABOLIC crisis of skeletal muscle triggered by exposure to specific anesthetic agents: the VOLATILE INHALED ANESTHETICS (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane) and the depolarizing neuromuscular blocker SUCCINYLCHOLINE. In susceptible patients these agents cause UNCONTROLLED CALCIUM RELEASE from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, producing sustained muscle contraction and a runaway hypermetabolic state. It usually appears INTRAOPERATIVELY but can occur in the early post-anesthesia (PACU) period. RISK/SCREENING: a personal or FAMILY HISTORY of MH, of problems/death under anesthesia, or of muscle disorders is the key red flag — screen preoperatively and alert the anesthesia team. RECOGNITION (the nurse must know the order of signs): the EARLIEST and most SENSITIVE sign is an unexplained, RAPIDLY RISING END-TIDAL CO2 (EtCO2) that does NOT respond to increased ventilation (hypermetabolism generates excess CO2); TACHYCARDIA is often the first vital-sign change, with tachypnea and unstable/elevated blood pressure; MASSETER (jaw) MUSCLE RIGIDITY — especially right after succinylcholine — and then generalized muscle rigidity are highly suggestive; a mixed RESPIRATORY and METABOLIC ACIDOSIS and hypoxemia develop; HYPERKALEMIA from muscle breakdown causes dysrhythmias; and RHABDOMYOLYSIS produces a markedly elevated CK and MYOGLOBINURIA (dark/cola-colored urine) with risk of acute kidney injury. CRITICALLY, HYPERTHERMIA is a LATE sign (the temperature can then rise extremely fast, more than 1-2°C every 5 minutes, to very high levels) — the team must NOT wait for a fever to act; the rising EtCO2, tachycardia, and rigidity prompt immediate action. EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT (activate the MH protocol — a coordinated team response): (1) IMMEDIATELY STOP the triggering agents — discontinue the volatile anesthetic and succinylcholine; CALL FOR HELP and ACTIVATE the MH PROTOCOL, get the MH CART, designate roles, and call the MH hotline (MHAUS) as needed; conclude/abort surgery as soon as feasible. (2) Deliver 100% OXYGEN at HIGH FLOW and HYPERVENTILATE to wash out CO2 (increase fresh-gas flow; do not delay treatment to change the anesthesia machine). (3) Give DANTROLENE SODIUM — the specific antidote, a skeletal-muscle relaxant that blocks sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release — IV as soon as possible: ~2.5 mg/kg rapid IV, repeated every ~5 minutes (titrated up to ~10 mg/kg or more) until the signs (EtCO2, rigidity, tachycardia, temperature) subside; the older formulation (20 mg/vial reconstituted with 60 mL sterile water) is LABOR-INTENSIVE and requires MULTIPLE staff to mix many vials quickly (the newer concentrated formulation reconstitutes faster), so the team is mobilized to prepare it. (4) COOLING measures for hyperthermia — cold IV fluids, surface ice packs to the groin/axillae/neck, cooling blankets, and cold lavage as indicated — STOPPING active cooling around 38°C to avoid overshoot hypothermia. (5) Treat HYPERKALEMIA (calcium, insulin with dextrose, bicarbonate; albuterol) and DYSRHYTHMIAS with standard antiarrhythmics — but AVOID CALCIUM-CHANNEL BLOCKERS, which combined with dantrolene can cause hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse. (6) Treat acidosis (sodium bicarbonate) and protect the KIDNEYS from myoglobin with fluids to maintain urine output (± diuretics/mannitol). (7) MONITOR continuously — EtCO2, CORE temperature, ECG, ABGs, potassium, CK, coagulation (DIC risk), and urine output/color. (8) After the crisis, transfer to ICU for ≥24-48 hours of monitoring because RECRUDESCENCE can occur; continue dantrolene per protocol. PREVENTION/TEACHING: for MH-susceptible patients use NON-TRIGGERING ('clean') anesthesia (total IV anesthesia with propofol, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, regional/local techniques) and have dantrolene immediately available; provide patient/family EDUCATION — inform all future anesthesia providers, wear a medical-alert identification, pursue FAMILY screening (autosomal dominant; muscle contracture/genetic testing), and use MHAUS resources. NURSING ROLE: identify risk preoperatively; recognize the earliest signs (rising EtCO2, tachycardia, rigidity) without waiting for fever; immediately help STOP triggers and ACTIVATE the MH protocol; mobilize and coordinate the team to prepare and give DANTROLENE; deliver cooling and treat hyperkalemia/acidosis/rhabdomyolysis; monitor for complications and recrudescence; and educate the patient and family.

patient.admitDate: A previously healthy 19-year-old man is undergoing general anesthesia for elective orthopedic surgery (open reduction/internal fixation of a fractured ankle). Anesthesia was induced with a volatile inhaled agent and succinylcholine. Roughly 30 minutes into the case, the anesthesia provider notes an unexplained, RAPIDLY RISING end-tidal CO2 that does not respond to increased ventilation, along with sinus tachycardia and masseter/generalized muscle rigidity; the core temperature begins to climb. This is a MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA crisis. The perioperative team must immediately stop the triggers, activate the MH protocol, give dantrolene, cool the patient, treat hyperkalemia/acidosis, and coordinate a rapid, role-based emergency response.
