labs.n: PRESENTATION + recognizing MH (trigger exposure, EARLIEST signs, hyperthermia is LATE)
labs.v: Tyler M., a healthy 19-year-old, is under general anesthesia (a VOLATILE agent plus SUCCINYLCHOLINE) for ankle ORIF when, ~30 minutes in, the anesthesia provider notes an unexplained, RAPIDLY RISING END-TIDAL CO2 unresponsive to increased ventilation, sinus TACHYCARDIA, and MASSETER then generalized muscle RIGIDITY, with the core temperature beginning to climb. This is MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA (MH) — an inherited hypermetabolic crisis of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine. The NURSE must know the ORDER of signs: the EARLIEST/most sensitive is the rising EtCO2 (hypermetabolism floods the body with CO2); tachycardia is often the first vital-sign change; masseter/generalized rigidity is highly suggestive; and HYPERTHERMIA is a LATE sign that can then rise extremely fast. The team must NOT wait for a fever — the rising EtCO2, tachycardia, and rigidity demand immediate action. RISK: a personal or FAMILY history of MH, anesthesia problems/death, or muscle disorders is the key preoperative red flag. Early recognition and an immediate, coordinated response are what save the patient.
labs.r: MH = inherited hypermetabolic crisis triggered by VOLATILE anesthetics + SUCCINYLCHOLINE. EARLIEST/most sensitive sign = unexplained RISING EtCO2 unresponsive to ventilation; tachycardia often first vital change; MASSETER→generalized RIGIDITY; HYPERTHERMIA is LATE (don't wait for fever). Red flag = personal/FAMILY history of MH/anesthesia problems/muscle disorders → screen pre-op. RN role: recognize the earliest signs and act immediately.

labs.v: MH is usually caused by an AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT mutation (most often in the RYR1 gene encoding the ryanodine receptor) that, on exposure to a trigger, causes UNCONTROLLED CALCIUM RELEASE from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. The result is sustained muscle contraction and a HYPERMETABOLIC state: massive oxygen consumption and CO2 production, heat generation, acidosis, and muscle breakdown. TRIGGERS are the VOLATILE INHALED ANESTHETICS (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane) and the depolarizing neuromuscular blocker SUCCINYLCHOLINE; non-triggering agents (propofol, etomidate, ketamine, opioids, nitrous oxide, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, and local/regional anesthetics) are safe. SCREENING is preventive: ask every surgical patient about a personal or FAMILY history of MH, of adverse/unexplained reactions or death under anesthesia, and of muscle disorders; susceptibility can be confirmed by the caffeine-halothane contracture test or genetic testing. An MH-susceptible patient should receive a NON-TRIGGERING ('clean') anesthetic (total IV anesthesia, regional techniques) with dantrolene immediately available and a prepared, vapor-free machine. Because MH is autosomal dominant, identifying it in one patient has implications for biological relatives.
labs.r: MH = autosomal dominant (RYR1) defect → uncontrolled sarcoplasmic-reticulum CALCIUM release → sustained contraction + hypermetabolism. TRIGGERS = volatile anesthetics (sevo/iso/des/halothane) + SUCCINYLCHOLINE. SAFE = propofol/etomidate/ketamine/opioids/nitrous/non-depolarizing NMBs/regional. SCREEN personal/family history of MH/anesthesia problems/muscle disease (contracture/genetic testing). Susceptible → NON-triggering anesthesia + dantrolene available. RN role: screen risk + ensure trigger avoidance.

labs.n: EMERGENCY TREATMENT — stop triggers, dantrolene, oxygen, MH protocol (coordinated team response)
labs.v: MH is an EMERGENCY managed by ACTIVATING the MH PROTOCOL — a coordinated, role-based team response: (1) IMMEDIATELY STOP the triggering agents (discontinue the volatile anesthetic and succinylcholine); CALL FOR HELP, activate the protocol, bring the MH CART, assign roles, and call the MH hotline (MHAUS) as needed; conclude or abort surgery as soon as feasible. (2) Provide 100% OXYGEN at HIGH FLOW and HYPERVENTILATE to wash out CO2 (increase fresh-gas flow; do not delay treatment to swap the machine). (3) Give DANTROLENE SODIUM — the specific ANTIDOTE that blocks sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release — IV ASAP at ~2.5 mg/kg rapidly, REPEATED every ~5 minutes (titrated up to ~10 mg/kg or more) until EtCO2, rigidity, tachycardia, and temperature subside. RECONSTITUTING dantrolene is LABOR-INTENSIVE (the older 20 mg vials each need 60 mL of sterile water and many vials are required), so MULTIPLE staff are mobilized to mix and administer it quickly (the newer concentrated formulation is faster); this team mobilization, role assignment, and closed-loop communication are central nursing-management tasks during the crisis. The circulating nurse coordinates the MH cart, helps prepare dantrolene, documents the timeline, and communicates with pharmacy/ICU/blood bank. Speed matters: outcomes are far better when dantrolene and supportive care are delivered early.
labs.r: MH protocol (coordinated team): (1) STOP triggers (volatile + succinylcholine) + CALL FOR HELP + MH cart + MHAUS hotline + end surgery; (2) 100% O2 high-flow + HYPERVENTILATE (don't delay to change machine); (3) DANTROLENE 2.5 mg/kg rapid IV, repeat q5min up to ~10 mg/kg until signs subside — reconstitution is labor-intensive → MOBILIZE MULTIPLE staff. Circulating RN coordinates cart/dantrolene prep/documentation/communication. Early treatment = better outcomes. RN role: stop triggers + activate protocol + coordinate team + give dantrolene.

labs.n: Complications + supportive care (cooling, hyperkalemia, dysrhythmias, acidosis, rhabdo; recrudescence)
labs.v: Alongside dantrolene, the team treats the hypermetabolic complications: COOLING for hyperthermia — cold IV fluids, surface ICE PACKS to the groin/axillae/neck, cooling blankets, and cold lavage as indicated — STOPPING active cooling around 38°C to avoid overshoot hypothermia. HYPERKALEMIA (from muscle breakdown) is treated with CALCIUM (membrane stabilization), INSULIN plus DEXTROSE, sodium BICARBONATE, and albuterol, with cardiac monitoring. DYSRHYTHMIAS are treated with standard antiarrhythmics and ACLS as needed — but CALCIUM-CHANNEL BLOCKERS are AVOIDED because given with dantrolene they can cause severe hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse. Metabolic ACIDOSIS is treated with sodium bicarbonate guided by ABGs. RHABDOMYOLYSIS releases myoglobin (dark/cola-colored urine) that can cause acute kidney injury, so the team gives FLUIDS to maintain a good URINE OUTPUT (± mannitol/diuretics) to protect the kidneys, and monitors CK. Watch for DISSEMINATED INTRAVASCULAR COAGULATION (a grave late sign). MONITORING is continuous: EtCO2, CORE temperature, ECG, ABGs, potassium, CK, coagulation, and urine output/color. After the acute crisis, the patient is transferred to the ICU for at least 24-48 HOURS because RECRUDESCENCE (a recurrence of the crisis) can occur, with dantrolene continued per protocol.
labs.r: Supportive care: COOL (cold IV fluids/ice to groin-axillae-neck/blankets; STOP near 38°C). Treat HYPERKALEMIA (calcium, insulin+dextrose, bicarb, albuterol) + dysrhythmias — but AVOID CALCIUM-CHANNEL BLOCKERS with dantrolene (→ hyperkalemia/collapse). Treat acidosis (bicarb); protect kidneys from myoglobin (RHABDO) with fluids → urine output ± mannitol; watch DIC. Monitor EtCO2/core temp/ECG/ABG/K/CK/coags/urine. ICU ≥24-48h — RECRUDESCENCE risk; continue dantrolene. RN role: cooling + treat hyperkalemia/acidosis/rhabdo + monitor.

labs.n: Prevention/teaching + nursing role; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: PREVENTION + EDUCATION close the loop: for an MH-susceptible patient, use a NON-TRIGGERING ('clean') anesthetic — total IV anesthesia (propofol), non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, regional/local techniques — with a vapor-free machine and dantrolene immediately available. Teach the patient and family to INFORM ALL future anesthesia/surgery/dental providers, to wear a MEDICAL-ALERT identification, and (because MH is AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT) to pursue FAMILY screening and genetic/contracture testing; connect them to MHAUS resources. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the team did NOT wait for a fever before acting (hyperthermia is a late sign); did NOT continue the triggering agents or delay treatment to change the anesthesia machine; did NOT give a calcium-channel blocker with dantrolene; did NOT under-dose or delay dantrolene; and did NOT discharge the patient from the PACU/OR without ICU monitoring for recrudescence. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: preoperative risk screening; immediate recognition of the earliest signs (rising EtCO2, tachycardia, rigidity); rapid trigger discontinuation and MH-protocol activation; early, adequately dosed dantrolene delivered by a mobilized team; effective cooling and treatment of hyperkalemia/acidosis/rhabdomyolysis; and ICU monitoring with family/genetic counseling. EXPECTED outcome: with early recognition and aggressive, coordinated treatment, the crisis is reversed, complications are prevented or managed, and the patient and family are protected for the future. NURSING ROLE: screen risk preoperatively; recognize MH early without waiting for fever; help stop triggers and activate the MH protocol; mobilize/coordinate the team to prepare and give dantrolene; provide cooling and treat complications; monitor for recrudescence; and educate the patient and family.
labs.r: PREVENTION: MH-susceptible → NON-triggering anesthesia (TIVA/propofol, non-depolarizing NMBs, regional) + vapor-free machine + dantrolene available. EDUCATE: inform all future providers, medical-alert ID, FAMILY screening (autosomal dominant), MHAUS. NEGATIVES (correct practice): didn't wait for fever, didn't continue triggers/delay for machine swap, NO calcium-channel blocker with dantrolene, didn't under-dose/delay dantrolene, didn't skip ICU monitoring. PROTECTIVE: pre-op screening, early recognition, fast trigger stop + protocol, early dantrolene, cooling/complication care, ICU + counseling. RN role: screen + recognize + treat + coordinate + educate.

HYPERTHERMIA is LATE — did NOT wait for fever; acted on rising EtCO2/tachycardia/rigidity. RED FLAG screen = personal/FAMILY history of MH/anesthesia problems/muscle disease. providerOrders: EMERGENCY: intraoperative malignant hyperthermia — activate the MH protocol; full code

STOP TRIGGERS: discontinue the volatile inhaled anesthetic and succinylcholine immediately; conclude/abort surgery as soon as feasible; call for help and bring the MH cart; call the MH hotline (MHAUS) as needed
OXYGENATION: 100% oxygen at high flow; hyperventilate to eliminate CO2 (increase fresh-gas flow; do not delay treatment to change the anesthesia machine)

DANTROLENE: dantrolene sodium 2.5 mg/kg rapid IV; repeat every 5 minutes (titrate up to ~10 mg/kg or more) until EtCO2, rigidity, tachycardia, and temperature subside; mobilize additional staff to reconstitute and administer
COOLING: cold IV fluids, surface ice packs (groin/axillae/neck), cooling blanket, and cold lavage as indicated; STOP active cooling near 38°C to avoid overshoot hypothermia

HYPERKALEMIA/DYSRHYTHMIAS: treat hyperkalemia (calcium, insulin with dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, albuterol); treat dysrhythmias with standard antiarrhythmics/ACLS — AVOID calcium-channel blockers (dangerous with dantrolene)
ACIDOSIS/RENAL: sodium bicarbonate per ABG; IV fluids to maintain urine output (± mannitol/diuretics) to protect kidneys from myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis)
MONITORING: continuous EtCO2, core temperature, ECG, and pulse oximetry; serial ABGs, potassium, CK, coagulation studies (DIC); strict intake/output and urine color
DISPOSITION: transfer to ICU after stabilization for at least 24-48 hours (recrudescence risk); continue dantrolene per protocol

PREVENTION/FUTURE CARE: document MH event; for any future anesthesia use non-triggering agents (total IV anesthesia, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, regional) with a vapor-free machine and dantrolene available

EDUCATION: instruct patient/family to inform all future anesthesia/surgical/dental providers, obtain medical-alert identification, and pursue family screening/genetic testing (autosomal dominant); refer to MHAUS resources

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters in this intraoperative emergency?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: An unexplained, rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 unresponsive to increased ventilation — the earliest, most sensitive sign of malignant hyperthermia
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — rising EtCO2 is the earliest MH sign and drives immediate action. RN role: recognize the earliest sign.

opts.text: Sinus tachycardia (often the first vital-sign change) with masseter and then generalized muscle rigidity, especially after succinylcholine
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — tachycardia and rigidity are key early/suggestive signs. RN role: recognize the MH pattern.

opts.text: Exposure to triggering agents — a volatile inhaled anesthetic and succinylcholine — in this case
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — trigger exposure is the precipitant; stopping it is the first treatment. RN role: identify and stop the triggers.

opts.text: Hyperthermia is a LATE sign — the team must act on the early signs and not wait for a fever
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — waiting for fever delays life-saving treatment. RN role: act before hyperthermia appears.

opts.text: Anticipated complications — mixed acidosis, hyperkalemia, dysrhythmias, and rhabdomyolysis (dark urine, elevated CK)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — these complications must be monitored and treated. RN role: anticipate and address complications.

opts.text: The need to immediately activate the MH protocol — call for help, get the MH cart, and mobilize the team to prepare dantrolene
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a coordinated, role-based protocol response is essential. RN role: activate the protocol + coordinate the team.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — documented for the perioperative record
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine. Not the central cue in this crisis.

opts.text: Because the temperature is still near-normal, continue the anesthetic and simply observe, treating only if a high fever develops
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Hyperthermia is a LATE sign; waiting for fever before stopping triggers and treating costs critical time and worsens outcomes.

opts.text: Treat the rising heart rate with a calcium-channel blocker while continuing the volatile anesthetic
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The triggers must be stopped, not continued; and calcium-channel blockers are contraindicated with dantrolene (risk of hyperkalemia/cardiovascular collapse).

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: MH is an inherited (autosomal dominant) hypermetabolic crisis of skeletal muscle from uncontrolled sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release, triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine
opts.rat: CORRECT — etiology and triggers. Foundation for recognition and prevention.

opts.text: The earliest, most sensitive sign is a rising end-tidal CO2; hyperthermia is a late sign
opts.rat: CORRECT — the order of signs. Foundation for early recognition.

opts.text: Dantrolene sodium is the specific antidote, given rapidly IV and repeated until signs subside
opts.rat: CORRECT — definitive pharmacologic treatment. Foundation for management.

opts.text: Management includes stopping triggers, 100% oxygen with hyperventilation, cooling, and treating hyperkalemia, acidosis, and rhabdomyolysis
opts.rat: CORRECT — the supportive components of the MH protocol. Foundation for comprehensive care.

opts.text: Calcium-channel blockers should be avoided with dantrolene because together they can cause hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse
opts.rat: CORRECT — a key drug-safety caution in MH. Foundation for safe treatment.

opts.text: MH-susceptible patients should receive non-triggering anesthesia, and a personal/family history is screened preoperatively
opts.rat: CORRECT — prevention and screening principle. Foundation for avoiding future crises.

opts.text: Hyperthermia is the earliest sign of MH, so treatment should be withheld until the temperature is clearly elevated
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Hyperthermia is LATE; the earliest sign is a rising EtCO2, and treatment must begin immediately on the early signs.

opts.text: The triggering volatile anesthetic should be continued during treatment to keep the patient anesthetized
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The triggering agents must be STOPPED immediately; anesthesia is maintained with non-triggering agents if needed.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Stop the triggering agents and activate the MH protocol (call for help, MH cart, mobilize the team)
opts.rat: #1 — Removing the trigger and activating the coordinated response is the first and most urgent step. RN role: stop triggers + activate protocol.

opts.text: Give 100% oxygen with hyperventilation and administer dantrolene rapidly, repeating until signs subside
opts.rat: #2 — Oxygenation and the antidote directly reverse the hypermetabolic crisis. RN role: oxygenate + dantrolene.

opts.text: Initiate cooling measures for hyperthermia (stopping near 38°C)
opts.rat: #3 — Active cooling counters the dangerous, rapidly rising temperature. RN role: cooling.

opts.text: Treat hyperkalemia, dysrhythmias, and acidosis, and protect the kidneys from myoglobinuria
opts.rat: #4 — Managing the metabolic complications prevents arrest and renal injury. RN role: treat complications.

opts.text: Transfer to ICU for monitoring of recrudescence and provide patient/family education and family screening
opts.rat: #5 — Post-crisis monitoring and education protect the patient and relatives going forward. RN role: ICU monitoring + education.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this MH crisis.

opts.text: Immediately stop the volatile anesthetic and succinylcholine, call for help, activate the MH protocol, and bring the MH cart
opts.rat: First and most urgent step — remove the trigger and mobilize the response. RN role: stop triggers + activate protocol.

opts.text: Provide 100% oxygen at high flow and hyperventilate to eliminate CO2
opts.rat: Counters hypoxemia and washes out the excess CO2 of hypermetabolism. RN role: oxygenate/hyperventilate.

opts.text: Administer dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg rapid IV and repeat every 5 minutes until signs subside, mobilizing staff to reconstitute it quickly
opts.rat: Definitive antidote; reconstitution is labor-intensive, so the team is mobilized. RN role: prepare/give dantrolene.

opts.text: Begin cooling (cold IV fluids, ice packs to groin/axillae/neck, cooling blanket), stopping near 38°C
opts.rat: Treats the dangerous hyperthermia while avoiding overshoot hypothermia. RN role: cooling.

opts.text: Treat hyperkalemia (calcium, insulin/dextrose, bicarbonate) and dysrhythmias, and give fluids to protect the kidneys from myoglobin
opts.rat: Manages the metabolic complications and prevents renal injury. RN role: treat complications.

opts.text: Transfer to ICU for at least 24-48 hours of monitoring for recrudescence and continue dantrolene per protocol
opts.rat: Recrudescence can occur; continued monitoring and dantrolene are required. RN role: ICU monitoring.

opts.text: Continue the volatile anesthetic and wait for a high fever before treating
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the trigger must be stopped immediately and treatment begun on the early signs; hyperthermia is a late sign.

opts.text: Give a calcium-channel blocker together with dantrolene to control the heart rate
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — calcium-channel blockers with dantrolene can cause hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse; they are contraindicated.

opts.text: Delay dantrolene to first change out the entire anesthesia machine
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — do not delay treatment; increase fresh-gas flow/high-flow oxygen and give dantrolene immediately rather than waiting to swap the machine.

opts.text: After the signs resolve, send the patient directly home from the PACU without further monitoring
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — recrudescence can occur; the patient requires ICU monitoring for ≥24-48 hours with continued dantrolene.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's/team's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Stop the triggering agents, call for help, and activate the MH protocol (bring the MH cart, assign roles)
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Removing the trigger and mobilizing the team is the immediate priority. RN role: stop triggers + activate protocol.

opts.text: Deliver 100% oxygen with hyperventilation and administer dantrolene rapidly, repeating until signs subside
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Oxygenation and the antidote reverse the crisis. RN role: oxygenate + dantrolene.

opts.text: Initiate active cooling for hyperthermia, stopping near 38°C
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Cooling counters the rapidly rising temperature. RN role: cooling.

opts.text: Treat hyperkalemia, dysrhythmias, and acidosis and maintain urine output to protect the kidneys
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Managing complications prevents arrest and renal failure. RN role: treat complications.

opts.text: Transfer to ICU for recrudescence monitoring; document the event and provide patient/family education and screening
opts.rat: #5 — After stabilization. Monitoring, documentation, and education protect the patient and family. RN role: ICU + education.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: After stopping triggers, hyperventilating, and giving dantrolene, the end-tidal CO2 falls, the rigidity relaxes, and the heart rate slows
opts.rat: The hallmark response to correct MH treatment. Expected, desired improvement.

opts.text: Active cooling brings the temperature down and is stopped near 38°C to avoid overshoot hypothermia
opts.rat: Effective, appropriately limited cooling. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Hyperkalemia is corrected and dysrhythmias resolve with treatment; urine output is maintained and stays clear, protecting the kidneys
opts.rat: Successful management of metabolic complications and renal protection. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: In the ICU the patient remains stable on continued dantrolene with no recurrence, and family screening/education is arranged
opts.rat: Stable recovery with recrudescence prevented and future protection. Ideal outcome.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the team waited for a fever before acting; the EtCO2 and temperature climbed further and the patient deteriorated
opts.rat: ⚠️ Waiting for the late sign delayed treatment and worsened the crisis. Demonstrates acting on the earliest signs.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the volatile anesthetic was continued and dantrolene was delayed to change the machine; rigidity, hyperthermia, and acidosis worsened
opts.rat: ⚠️ Continuing the trigger and delaying dantrolene worsened the crisis. Demonstrates stopping triggers and giving dantrolene without delay.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — a calcium-channel blocker was given with dantrolene; the patient developed severe hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse
opts.rat: ⚠️ The contraindicated combination caused life-threatening deterioration. Demonstrates avoiding calcium-channel blockers with dantrolene.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the patient was sent home from the PACU after the signs resolved; the crisis recrudesced hours later without monitoring
opts.rat: ⚠️ Skipping ICU monitoring missed recrudescence. Demonstrates the need for ≥24-48 hours of monitoring.

opts.text: Immediately after the first dantrolene dose, before it takes full effect, the EtCO2 and rigidity are still present and essentially unchanged
opts.rat: Before the antidote takes full effect, an unchanged baseline is expected; continue repeating dantrolene and supportive care and reassess.

opts.text: At discharge the patient verbalizes the need to inform future providers, wear a medical-alert ID, and have family screened for MH
opts.rat: Effective education protecting the patient and relatives. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: Safe Administration of HIGH-ALERT Intravenous Potassium Chloride for Symptomatic Hypokalemia in a 68-Year-Old on a Loop Diuretic and Digoxin: Recognizing Hypokalemia and Its ECG/Cardiac Effects, the Cardinal RULE That IV Potassium Is NEVER Pushed (Always Diluted and Pump-Controlled with Rate/Route Limits), Pre-Administration and Monitoring Safeguards, and Preventing Over-Correction
subtitle: POTASSIUM is the major intracellular cation and is tightly regulated because both LOW and HIGH levels are dangerous to the heart. HYPOKALEMIA (serum potassium below ~3.5 mEq/L) commonly results from LOOP or THIAZIDE DIURETICS, GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea, nasogastric suction), poor intake, intracellular SHIFTS (alkalosis, insulin, beta-agonists), hyperaldosteronism, and MAGNESIUM depletion (which makes hypokalemia REFRACTORY until magnesium is also replaced). EFFECTS: the most dangerous are CARDIAC — dysrhythmias and characteristic ECG changes (FLATTENED T waves, prominent U WAVES, ST-segment depression, and a prolonged QT) that can progress to life-threatening arrhythmias; hypokalemia also POTENTIATES DIGOXIN TOXICITY (a key danger in patients on both a diuretic and digoxin). Other features include muscle WEAKNESS, cramps, diminished reflexes, fatigue, decreased bowel motility/ileus, and polyuria. CORRECTION: when possible, the ORAL route is PREFERRED (safer); INTRAVENOUS replacement is reserved for SEVERE or SYMPTOMATIC hypokalemia or when oral is not tolerated — and IV potassium is a designated HIGH-ALERT MEDICATION (ISMP) whose misadministration can be FATAL. The CARDINAL SAFETY RULE: IV potassium is NEVER given by IV PUSH, bolus, or undiluted — a rapid potassium bolus causes fatal cardiac arrest/arrhythmia. It must ALWAYS be DILUTED and infused SLOWLY by an INFUSION PUMP. Concentrated potassium chloride vials are REMOVED from floor/unit stock (a national safety practice); commercially PREMIXED bags are used, and potassium is NOT added to a hanging/infusing IV bag (risk of an inadvertent bolus). RATE and ROUTE limits: through a PERIPHERAL line, the rate is typically limited to about 10 mEq/hr (with dilute concentrations, e.g., ~10 mEq/100 mL) because potassium is irritating to veins and causes pain/phlebitis; FASTER infusion (e.g., up to ~20 mEq/hr or more) requires a CENTRAL line WITH CONTINUOUS CARDIAC MONITORING in a monitored setting — never exceed the ordered rate, and always use a pump (never gravity/free-flow). PRE-ADMINISTRATION safeguards: verify the order and the serum potassium; ASSESS RENAL FUNCTION and URINE OUTPUT, because impaired kidneys/oliguria greatly raise the risk of dangerous HYPERKALEMIA ('do not give potassium without adequate renal function/urine output'); obtain a baseline ECG; check and replace MAGNESIUM if low; and perform an INDEPENDENT DOUBLE-CHECK of this high-alert drug (right drug, concentration, rate, pump settings) with barcode scanning and the rights of medication administration. DURING/AFTER administration: place high-rate infusions on a CARDIAC MONITOR; frequently assess the IV SITE for pain, burning, phlebitis, or infiltration (potassium is a vesicant-like irritant — slow/stop and reassess for site reactions); recheck the serum potassium; and watch for signs of OVER-CORRECTION to HYPERKALEMIA (peaked T waves, widening QRS, bradycardia, muscle weakness). PATIENT TEACHING: dietary potassium sources (bananas, oranges/citrus, potatoes, tomatoes, spinach, beans, dried fruit), the importance of follow-up labs, and reporting weakness, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat; for patients on diuretics, discuss potassium-sparing options and monitoring. NURSING ROLE: recognize hypokalemia and its cardiac/ECG effects; correct it SAFELY (oral preferred; IV NEVER pushed — always diluted, pump-controlled, within rate/route limits, with cardiac monitoring for high rates); assess renal function/urine output and magnesium first; perform the high-alert double-check; monitor the ECG, the IV site, and repeat levels; prevent over-correction; and educate the patient.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + recognizing hypokalemia (causes + cardiac/ECG effects + digoxin link)
labs.v: Doris L., 68, with heart failure/hypertension on FUROSEMIDE (a loop diuretic) and DIGOXIN, presents with fatigue, generalized muscle WEAKNESS, leg cramps, and palpitations; her serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L (HYPOKALEMIA, normal ~3.5-5.0) and her ECG shows FLATTENED T waves with prominent U WAVES, ST depression, and occasional premature beats. HYPOKALEMIA commonly results from DIURETICS (loop/thiazide), GI losses (vomiting/diarrhea/NG suction), poor intake, intracellular shifts (alkalosis/insulin/beta-agonists), hyperaldosteronism, and MAGNESIUM depletion. Its most dangerous effects are CARDIAC — dysrhythmias and the classic ECG changes above that can progress to lethal arrhythmias — and it POTENTIATES DIGOXIN TOXICITY, a key hazard for Doris who takes both a diuretic and digoxin. Other features: muscle weakness/cramps, decreased reflexes, fatigue, reduced bowel motility/ileus, and polyuria. Because she is symptomatic with a significantly low level, the provider orders IV potassium replacement (and a magnesium check). The nurse's central task is to recognize the hypokalemia and its cardiac risk and then administer the high-alert IV potassium SAFELY.
labs.r: HYPOKALEMIA (K <3.5) — causes: DIURETICS, GI losses, poor intake, intracellular shifts, hyperaldosteronism, low Mg. Effects: CARDIAC (FLAT T waves, U WAVES, ST depression, arrhythmias) — most dangerous; POTENTIATES DIGOXIN TOXICITY; muscle weakness/cramps, ↓reflexes, ileus, polyuria. Symptomatic/severe → IV replacement. RN role: recognize hypokalemia + its cardiac/ECG effects + digoxin risk.

labs.n: KCl is HIGH-ALERT — oral preferred; NEVER IV push; dilute + pump + rate/route limits + cardiac monitoring
labs.v: Intravenous potassium chloride is a designated HIGH-ALERT MEDICATION (ISMP) because misadministration can be FATAL. When feasible, the ORAL route is PREFERRED (safer and adequate for mild deficits); IV is reserved for SEVERE or SYMPTOMATIC hypokalemia or when oral is not tolerated. The CARDINAL RULE: IV potassium is NEVER given by IV PUSH, bolus, or undiluted — a rapid potassium bolus causes fatal cardiac arrest/arrhythmia. It is ALWAYS DILUTED and infused SLOWLY via an INFUSION PUMP (never by gravity/free-flow). Use commercially PREMIXED bags; do NOT add potassium to a hanging/infusing bag (risk of an inadvertent bolus), and concentrated KCl vials are removed from unit stock as a national safety measure. RATE/ROUTE limits protect the patient: via a PERIPHERAL line, typically limit to about 10 mEq/hr with a dilute concentration (e.g., ~10 mEq/100 mL) because potassium irritates veins and causes pain/phlebitis; FASTER infusion (e.g., up to ~20 mEq/hr or higher) requires a CENTRAL line WITH CONTINUOUS CARDIAC MONITORING in a monitored/ICU setting. Never exceed the ordered rate to 'catch up.' For Doris, a premixed, diluted bag is infused by pump at a peripheral-appropriate rate with telemetry monitoring.
labs.r: IV KCl = HIGH-ALERT; ORAL preferred when feasible; IV for severe/symptomatic. CARDINAL RULE: NEVER IV push/bolus/undiluted (fatal) — ALWAYS DILUTE + INFUSION PUMP. Use PREMIXED bags; don't add to a hanging bag; concentrated KCl off floor stock. PERIPHERAL ~10 mEq/hr (dilute, vein irritation); FASTER (~20 mEq/hr+) only CENTRAL line + CONTINUOUS cardiac monitoring. Never exceed ordered rate. RN role: administer IV KCl safely (never push, dilute, pump, rate/route limits).

labs.v: Before giving IV potassium, the nurse performs critical SAFEGUARDS: VERIFY the order and the current serum POTASSIUM level; ASSESS RENAL FUNCTION and URINE OUTPUT — adequate kidney function and urine output are essential because impaired kidneys/oliguria sharply increase the risk of dangerous HYPERKALEMIA (the classic teaching: do NOT administer potassium without confirming adequate renal function/urine output); obtain a BASELINE ECG given the cardiac risk; check and REPLACE MAGNESIUM if low, because hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia REFRACTORY to potassium replacement; and confirm IV access is patent and appropriate for the planned rate (central line for high rates). Because KCl is HIGH-ALERT, perform an INDEPENDENT DOUBLE-CHECK with a second nurse (verifying the right drug, the concentration/total dose, the rate, and the pump programming), use BARCODE scanning, and apply the rights of medication administration (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation). The nurse also confirms the infusion is a premixed, diluted bag on a pump — not a concentrate to be pushed or added to a running line. These steps prevent the catastrophic errors historically associated with potassium.
labs.r: PRE-ADMIN safeguards: verify order + serum K; ASSESS RENAL FUNCTION + URINE OUTPUT (oliguria/renal failure → hyperkalemia risk — don't give K without adequate output); baseline ECG; check/replace MAGNESIUM (low Mg → refractory hypokalemia); confirm appropriate IV access/route. HIGH-ALERT → INDEPENDENT DOUBLE-CHECK (drug/concentration/rate/pump) + barcode + the rights. Confirm premixed/diluted on a pump (not a push/added concentrate). RN role: complete safety checks before administering.

labs.v: DURING and AFTER the infusion, the nurse MONITORS closely: for higher rates, keep the patient on CONTINUOUS CARDIAC MONITORING and watch the ECG; frequently assess the IV SITE for PAIN, burning, redness, phlebitis, or infiltration, because potassium is a vein irritant — if the site reacts, SLOW or STOP the infusion and reassess (a central line is preferred for higher concentrations/rates); RECHECK the serum potassium after replacement to guide further dosing; and assess for resolution of symptoms and ECG changes. Critically, WATCH FOR OVER-CORRECTION to HYPERKALEMIA — peaked T waves, widening QRS, bradycardia, and muscle weakness — which can occur with too-rapid/excessive replacement or impaired renal excretion; if hyperkalemia develops, STOP the potassium and treat (calcium, insulin/dextrose, etc.). Also ensure MAGNESIUM is corrected, since hypokalemia will not resolve while magnesium is low. Do NOT give a 'bolus to catch up,' do NOT increase the rate beyond the order, and do NOT bypass the pump. For Doris, telemetry showed restoration of normal T waves and resolution of U waves as the potassium normalized, with no arrhythmia, digoxin toxicity, or site reaction.
labs.r: MONITOR: continuous cardiac monitoring (high rates) + ECG; frequent IV-SITE checks (pain/burning/phlebitis/infiltration → slow/stop, central preferred); RECHECK serum K; assess symptom/ECG resolution. PREVENT OVER-CORRECTION → HYPERKALEMIA (peaked T, wide QRS, bradycardia, weakness) from too-fast/excessive replacement or renal impairment → STOP + treat. Correct MAGNESIUM (refractory hypokalemia). No bolus 'to catch up,' no exceeding ordered rate, no bypassing the pump. RN role: monitor ECG/site/levels + prevent over-correction.

labs.n: Nursing role + patient teaching; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: PATIENT TEACHING: review dietary POTASSIUM sources (bananas, oranges/citrus, potatoes, tomatoes, spinach, beans, dried fruit, dairy) for at-risk patients, the importance of FOLLOW-UP LABS while on diuretics, and reporting WEAKNESS, PALPITATIONS, or an irregular heartbeat; for patients on loop/thiazide diuretics, discuss potassium monitoring and potassium-sparing strategies, and (given digoxin) the danger of hypokalemia-potentiated digoxin toxicity. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT give potassium by IV push/bolus or undiluted; did NOT add potassium to a hanging bag or bypass the infusion pump; did NOT exceed the ordered rate or run a high rate through a peripheral line without central access/monitoring; did NOT administer without confirming adequate renal function/urine output; did NOT skip the independent double-check; and did NOT ignore IV-site pain or signs of over-correction. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: recognition of hypokalemia and its cardiac risk; oral replacement when feasible; strict adherence to dilution/pump/rate/route rules; premixed bags with concentrated KCl off unit stock; pre-administration renal/urine and magnesium assessment; independent double-check and barcode scanning; cardiac and IV-site monitoring; recheck of levels; and prevention of over-correction. EXPECTED outcome: potassium is corrected safely to the normal range, the ECG and symptoms resolve, no arrhythmia or digoxin toxicity occurs, the IV site stays intact, and the patient understands prevention. NURSING ROLE: recognize hypokalemia and its effects; correct it SAFELY (oral preferred; IV never pushed — diluted, pump-controlled, within rate/route limits, with cardiac monitoring); assess renal function/urine output and magnesium first; perform the high-alert double-check; monitor ECG/site/levels; prevent over-correction; and educate.
labs.r: TEACH: dietary potassium (bananas/citrus/potatoes/tomatoes/spinach/beans), follow-up labs on diuretics, report weakness/palpitations/irregular HR; diuretic + digoxin risks. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no IV push/undiluted, no adding to a hanging bag/bypassing pump, no exceeding rate or high peripheral rate without central/monitoring, no giving without renal/urine check, no skipping double-check, didn't ignore site pain/over-correction. PROTECTIVE: recognition, oral when feasible, dilution/pump/rate rules, premixed bags, pre-assessment, double-check/barcode, ECG/site monitoring, recheck levels. RN role: recognize + administer safely + monitor + educate.

nursesNote: Telemetry/med-surg — Doris L., 68, HF/HTN on FUROSEMIDE + DIGOXIN. Fatigue, generalized muscle WEAKNESS, leg cramps, palpitations; ECG = FLATTENED T waves + prominent U WAVES + ST depression + occasional PVCs; serum K 2.8 (HYPOKALEMIA). HIGH RISK: hypokalemia POTENTIATES DIGOXIN TOXICITY. Hypokalemia causes: diuretics, GI losses, poor intake, intracellular shifts, low Mg; effects: cardiac (arrhythmias/ECG changes — most dangerous), weakness/cramps/↓reflexes, ileus, polyuria. Symptomatic + significantly low → IV potassium ordered (+ Mg check). IV KCl = HIGH-ALERT (ISMP) — ORAL preferred when feasible; IV for severe/symptomatic. CARDINAL RULE: NEVER IV push/bolus/undiluted (fatal arrest) — ALWAYS DILUTE + INFUSION PUMP; commercially PREMIXED bag; do NOT add to a hanging bag; concentrated KCl off unit stock. RATE/ROUTE: peripheral ~10 mEq/hr (dilute, vein irritation/phlebitis); faster (~20 mEq/hr+) ONLY central line + CONTINUOUS cardiac monitoring; never exceed ordered rate; never gravity/free-flow. PRE-ADMIN: verified order + K; confirmed adequate RENAL FUNCTION + URINE OUTPUT (oliguria/renal failure → hyperkalemia risk — 'no K without output'); baseline ECG; checked/replaced MAGNESIUM (low Mg → refractory hypokalemia); INDEPENDENT DOUBLE-CHECK of high-alert drug (drug/concentration/rate/pump) + barcode + rights. ADMINISTER: premixed diluted KCl via pump, peripheral rate-limited, telemetry on. MONITOR: continuous ECG; frequent IV-SITE checks (pain/burning/phlebitis/infiltration → slow/stop, central preferred); RECHECK serum K; watch OVER-CORRECTION → HYPERKALEMIA (peaked T, wide QRS, bradycardia, weakness → STOP + treat). TEACH: dietary potassium (bananas/citrus/potatoes/tomatoes/spinach/beans), follow-up labs on diuretics, report weakness/palpitations/irregular HR. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no IV push/undiluted, no adding to hanging bag/bypassing pump, no exceeding rate or high peripheral rate w/o central+monitoring, no giving without renal/urine check, no skipping double-check, didn't ignore site pain/over-correction. Outcome: K corrected to 4.0, ECG/symptoms resolved, no arrhythmia/digoxin toxicity, site intact.
providerOrders: ADMIT/CONTINUE: telemetry/med-surg with continuous cardiac monitoring; symptomatic hypokalemia (K 2.8) on furosemide + digoxin
DIAGNOSIS: hypokalemia — replace potassium safely; monitor for arrhythmia and digoxin toxicity
CODE STATUS: full code
LABS/DIAGNOSTICS: serum potassium and magnesium now and after replacement; basic metabolic panel/renal function; baseline and ongoing ECG; digoxin level if toxicity suspected
POTASSIUM REPLACEMENT (HIGH-ALERT):
Use oral potassium when feasible; IV potassium for severe/symptomatic hypokalemia
IV potassium chloride: commercially PREMIXED, diluted; infuse via infusion PUMP — NEVER IV push, bolus, undiluted, or by gravity; do NOT add potassium to a hanging IV bag
Peripheral line: limit to ~10 mEq/hr with dilute concentration; faster rates (e.g., up to ~20 mEq/hr) only via central line with continuous cardiac monitoring; do not exceed the ordered rate
Independent double-check of the high-alert medication (drug, concentration, rate, pump settings) with barcode scanning and the rights of medication administration
PRE-ADMINISTRATION SAFETY:
Confirm adequate renal function and urine output before administering potassium
Replace magnesium if low (hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia refractory)
MONITORING:
Continuous cardiac monitoring during higher-rate infusion; assess the IV site frequently for pain/burning/phlebitis/infiltration and slow/stop if a reaction occurs
Recheck serum potassium after replacement; watch for over-correction to hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, widening QRS, bradycardia, weakness) and stop/treat if it develops
EDUCATION: dietary potassium sources, the need for follow-up labs on diuretics, and reporting weakness, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat

opts.text: IV potassium is a high-alert medication that must never be pushed — it must be diluted and pump-controlled within rate/route limits

opts.text: Assess renal function and urine output and check magnesium before replacing potassium
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — renal/urine status and magnesium are essential pre-administration safeguards. RN role: pre-administration assessment.

opts.text: Plan continuous cardiac monitoring, IV-site monitoring, a recheck of potassium, and vigilance for over-correction
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — monitoring during/after protects against arrhythmia, site injury, and over-correction. RN role: monitor.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — documented before medication administration

opts.text: Because the level is dangerously low, give a rapid IV potassium push to correct it quickly

opts.text: Administer the potassium without checking renal function or urine output to avoid delay
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Adequate renal function/urine output must be confirmed first; giving potassium with impaired kidneys/oliguria risks dangerous hyperkalemia.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Hypokalemia commonly results from diuretics, GI losses, and magnesium depletion, and causes dangerous cardiac dysrhythmias and ECG changes (flat T waves, U waves)
opts.rat: CORRECT — causes and cardiac effects. Foundation for recognition.

opts.text: Hypokalemia potentiates digoxin toxicity, so a patient on a diuretic plus digoxin is at heightened risk
opts.rat: CORRECT — the digoxin interaction. Foundation for risk awareness.

opts.text: Oral potassium is preferred when feasible; IV potassium is a high-alert drug reserved for severe/symptomatic hypokalemia
opts.rat: CORRECT — route selection principle. Foundation for safe replacement.

opts.text: IV potassium is never pushed or given undiluted; it is always diluted and infused by pump, with peripheral rates limited (~10 mEq/hr) and faster rates only via a central line with cardiac monitoring
opts.rat: CORRECT — the cardinal administration rules. Foundation for preventing fatal errors.

opts.text: Renal function/urine output must be adequate before giving potassium, and magnesium must be corrected because low magnesium makes hypokalemia refractory
opts.rat: CORRECT — pre-administration safeguards. Foundation for safe, effective replacement.

opts.text: Over-correction can cause hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, widening QRS, bradycardia), so potassium is rechecked and the patient monitored
opts.rat: CORRECT — over-correction risk and monitoring. Foundation for ongoing safety.

opts.text: A rapid IV potassium bolus is an acceptable way to correct severe hypokalemia quickly
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. A potassium bolus/push is potentially fatal (cardiac arrest); potassium is always diluted and infused slowly by pump.

opts.text: Potassium can be safely added by the nurse to an already-hanging IV bag at the bedside
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Adding potassium to a hanging bag risks an inadvertent bolus and uneven concentration; use commercially premixed bags.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Recognize the symptomatic hypokalemia and its cardiac/ECG risk (and the digoxin-toxicity danger) and ensure cardiac monitoring
opts.rat: #1 — The cardiac threat (arrhythmia, digoxin toxicity) is the immediate danger to detect and monitor. RN role: recognize + monitor the heart.

opts.text: Complete pre-administration safety checks — verify the order/level, assess renal function/urine output, check magnesium, and obtain a baseline ECG
opts.rat: #2 — These safeguards must precede administration to prevent hyperkalemia and ensure effective replacement. RN role: pre-administration assessment.

opts.text: Administer the IV potassium SAFELY — premixed/diluted, by pump, within rate/route limits, never pushed — with an independent double-check
opts.rat: #3 — Safe administration of the high-alert drug prevents fatal errors. RN role: safe administration + double-check.

opts.text: Monitor during/after — ECG, IV site, and a recheck of potassium — and prevent over-correction
opts.rat: #4 — Ongoing monitoring catches arrhythmia, site reactions, and over-correction. RN role: monitor + prevent over-correction.

opts.text: Educate the patient on dietary potassium, follow-up labs, and reporting symptoms
opts.rat: #5 — Education sustains correction and prevents recurrence. RN role: patient teaching.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for safe potassium replacement.

opts.text: Verify the order and serum level, assess renal function and urine output, check magnesium, and obtain a baseline ECG before administering
opts.rat: Essential pre-administration safeguards. RN role: complete safety checks.

opts.text: Use a commercially premixed, diluted potassium bag and infuse it via an infusion pump
opts.rat: Safe formulation and controlled delivery. RN role: premixed + pump.

opts.text: Limit a peripheral infusion to about 10 mEq/hr; use a central line with continuous cardiac monitoring for faster rates
opts.rat: Correct rate/route limits protect veins and the heart. RN role: respect rate/route limits.

opts.text: Perform an independent double-check of the high-alert medication (drug, concentration, rate, pump) with barcode scanning
opts.rat: High-alert medication safeguard. RN role: independent double-check.

opts.text: Monitor the ECG, assess the IV site frequently (slow/stop for pain or phlebitis), recheck potassium, and watch for over-correction
opts.rat: Appropriate during/after monitoring. RN role: monitor + prevent over-correction.

opts.text: Use oral potassium instead when the deficit is mild and the patient can tolerate it
opts.rat: Oral is the preferred, safer route when feasible. RN role: choose the safest effective route.

opts.text: Give a rapid IV potassium push/bolus to correct the level quickly
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG and potentially fatal — IV potassium is never pushed; rapid bolus causes cardiac arrest. Always dilute and infuse by pump.

opts.text: Add concentrated potassium to the patient's already-hanging IV bag at the bedside
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — risks an inadvertent bolus/uneven concentration; concentrated KCl is off floor stock and premixed bags are used.

opts.text: Administer potassium without confirming adequate renal function or urine output
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — impaired kidneys/oliguria greatly raise the risk of dangerous hyperkalemia; confirm renal function/urine output first.

opts.text: Increase the infusion rate beyond the order or run a high rate through a peripheral line without monitoring to 'catch up'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — exceeding the rate or high peripheral rates without central access/monitoring risks arrhythmia and severe vein injury.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Recognize the symptomatic hypokalemia and cardiac risk, place the patient on a cardiac monitor, and obtain a baseline ECG
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Establishing the cardiac risk and monitoring frames safe replacement. RN role: recognize + monitor.

opts.text: Complete pre-administration checks — verify the order/level, confirm renal function/urine output, and check/replace magnesium
opts.rat: #2 — Second. These safeguards must precede giving potassium. RN role: pre-administration assessment.

opts.text: Perform the independent high-alert double-check, then administer the premixed/diluted potassium by pump within rate/route limits (never push)
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Safe administration with verification prevents fatal errors. RN role: double-check + safe administration.

opts.text: Monitor the ECG and IV site during the infusion and recheck the potassium afterward, watching for over-correction
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Ongoing monitoring detects arrhythmia, site reactions, and hyperkalemia. RN role: monitor + recheck.

opts.text: Educate the patient on dietary potassium, follow-up labs, and reporting symptoms; document
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Education and documentation sustain safe correction. RN role: teach + document.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The nurse confirmed adequate urine output and renal function and checked/replaced magnesium before giving potassium
opts.rat: Renal/urine confirmation and magnesium correction are essential pre-administration safeguards. Correct practice.

opts.text: A commercially premixed, diluted potassium bag was infused by pump at a peripheral-appropriate rate (~10 mEq/hr) with telemetry
opts.rat: Safe formulation, controlled delivery, and rate/route compliance. Correct practice.

opts.text: An independent double-check of the high-alert medication and barcode scanning were performed before administration
opts.rat: High-alert medication safeguards prevent errors. Correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse monitored the ECG and IV site, rechecked the potassium, and watched for over-correction to hyperkalemia
opts.rat: Appropriate during/after monitoring. Correct practice.

opts.text: When the IV site became painful and reddened, the nurse slowed/stopped the infusion and reassessed access
opts.rat: Potassium is a vein irritant; responding to site reaction protects the patient. Correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse gave a rapid IV potassium push to correct the dangerously low level quickly
opts.rat: ⚠️ Potentially fatal — IV potassium is never pushed; rapid bolus causes cardiac arrest. Improper practice.

opts.text: The nurse added concentrated potassium to the hanging IV bag at the bedside to save time
opts.rat: ⚠️ Risks an inadvertent bolus and uneven concentration; premixed bags must be used. Improper practice.

opts.text: The nurse increased the infusion well beyond the ordered rate through a peripheral line to 'catch up'
opts.rat: ⚠️ Exceeding the rate (and high peripheral rates without central access/monitoring) risks arrhythmia and vein injury. Improper practice.

opts.text: The nurse administered the potassium despite the patient being oliguric with rising creatinine, without notifying the provider
opts.rat: ⚠️ Impaired renal function/oliguria contraindicates routine potassium and risks lethal hyperkalemia; the provider must be notified. Improper practice.

opts.text: After correction, the nurse taught the patient about dietary potassium and the need for follow-up labs while on diuretics
opts.rat: Education sustains correction and prevents recurrence. Correct practice.

title: Fall Prevention in a High-Risk Hospitalized 78-Year-Old: Multifactorial Fall-Risk Assessment, the Universal-Plus-Targeted Prevention Bundle (Hourly Rounding/4 Ps, Scheduled Toileting, Bed-Exit Alarm, Med Review, Treating Orthostasis), Why Side Rails/Restraints Are NOT Fall Prevention, the POST-FALL Response, and Home-Safety Education
subtitle: FALLS are the leading cause of injury in older adults and a major preventable source of harm in the hospital (an in-hospital fall WITH INJURY is a serious, often-reportable event); consequences include HIP and other FRACTURES, HEAD INJURY (especially dangerous on ANTICOAGULANTS), loss of independence, fear of falling, and death. RISK FACTORS are INTRINSIC and EXTRINSIC. INTRINSIC: advanced age; a HISTORY OF FALLS (the single strongest predictor); gait/balance/mobility impairment and lower-extremity weakness; COGNITIVE impairment, dementia, or DELIRIUM; visual impairment; ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION; urinary urgency/frequency/nocturia or incontinence; foot problems; and chronic conditions (stroke, Parkinson disease, neuropathy). EXTRINSIC/SITUATIONAL: high-risk MEDICATIONS (benzodiazepines/sedative-hypnotics, opioids, antihypertensives/DIURETICS, hypoglycemics, anticholinergics, and POLYPHARMACY), environmental hazards (clutter, poor lighting, cords, throw rugs, wet floors), improper FOOTWEAR, the UNFAMILIAR hospital environment, tethers (IV lines, urinary catheters, telemetry), and RESTRAINTS. ASSESSMENT: screen EVERY patient with a VALIDATED fall-risk tool (e.g., the MORSE Fall Scale or Hendrich II) on admission, each shift, after a status change, and after any fall, and perform a MULTIFACTORIAL assessment (gait/balance such as the Timed Up and Go, ORTHOSTATIC vital signs, vision, medication review, cognition/delirium screen, continence, footwear, and the environment). PREVENTION uses a UNIVERSAL bundle for ALL patients PLUS TARGETED interventions for high-risk patients. UNIVERSAL: keep the CALL LIGHT and frequently used items within reach and answer calls PROMPTLY; bed in the LOW, LOCKED position; adequate LIGHTING/night-light; NON-SKID footwear; a clutter-free, dry, well-lit path; and orient the patient to the room. TARGETED (high-risk): flag the patient (wristband/sign); use a BED-/CHAIR-EXIT ALARM; perform PURPOSEFUL HOURLY ROUNDING addressing the 4 Ps (PAIN, POTTY/toileting, POSITION, POSSESSIONS); provide SCHEDULED/ASSISTED TOILETING and do NOT leave a high-risk patient alone on the toilet/commode (toileting-related falls are very common); ASSIST with ambulation and transfers using a GAIT BELT; ensure correct use of ASSISTIVE DEVICES (walker/cane) within reach; obtain a PT/OT consult; REVIEW and minimize fall-risk MEDICATIONS; treat ORTHOSTASIS (rise slowly, dangle before standing); manage delirium/pain; consider a SITTER or relocating the patient nearer the nurses' station; and use low beds/floor mats. IMPORTANTLY, SIDE RAILS and RESTRAINTS are NOT fall-prevention tools: raising ALL FOUR side rails is considered a RESTRAINT and patients climb over them (causing worse injury), and physical restraints do NOT reduce falls and increase injury, deconditioning, and death — the least-restrictive approach is used instead. POST-FALL RESPONSE: STAY WITH the patient and do NOT move them immediately; ASSESS for injury (level of consciousness, head injury — obtain neuro checks and imaging especially if anticoagulated or a head strike, pain, deformity/suspected fracture, range of motion, vital signs and orthostatics, skin); call for help; NOTIFY the provider; move the patient only after serious injury is excluded; REASSESS fall risk and UPDATE the care plan; complete an INCIDENT/OCCURRENCE REPORT (objective, factual; a quality-improvement and JUST-CULTURE tool, NOT a blame document, and NOT part of the medical record) and hold a POST-FALL HUDDLE to find the cause; and DOCUMENT objectively in the chart. EDUCATION (patient/family and discharge/HOME safety): remove throw rugs/clutter/cords, install GRAB BARS and a raised toilet seat, use non-slip mats and adequate lighting/night-lights, secure stair rails, wear proper footwear (not socks alone or loose slippers); encourage EXERCISE focused on STRENGTH and BALANCE (e.g., physical therapy, tai chi), a VISION check, a MEDICATION review, vitamin D if indicated, rising slowly to avoid orthostasis, correct assistive-device use, a personal emergency response system, and knowing how to call for help and when to seek care after a fall. NURSING ROLE: assess fall risk with a validated tool and multifactorial evaluation; implement the universal-plus-targeted prevention bundle; avoid side rails/restraints as 'fall prevention'; respond correctly to a fall (assess injury, neuro checks, notify, report, update the plan); and educate the patient and family for safety at home.

patient.admitDate: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the medical unit with community-acquired pneumonia and dehydration. She has a HISTORY of a fall 3 months ago, mild cognitive impairment, urinary urgency with nocturia, and an unsteady gait for which she uses a walker at home. Her medications include furosemide and a nightly benzodiazepine (lorazepam) for sleep, and her sitting-to-standing blood pressure shows orthostatic hypotension. On a validated fall-risk screen she scores HIGH RISK. In the unfamiliar hospital environment, tethered to IV fluids, she is at substantial risk of a fall with injury. The nurse must complete a multifactorial fall-risk assessment, implement the universal-plus-targeted prevention bundle, avoid inappropriate restraints/side rails, respond correctly if she falls, and teach her and her family about home safety.
