labs.n: PRESENTATION + why falls matter + risk factors (intrinsic + extrinsic/medications)
labs.v: Margaret S., 78, admitted with pneumonia and dehydration, carries MANY fall risk factors and screens HIGH RISK. FALLS are the leading cause of injury in older adults and a major preventable hospital harm — an in-hospital fall WITH INJURY is a serious, often-reportable event — with consequences including HIP and other FRACTURES, HEAD INJURY (especially dangerous on ANTICOAGULANTS, where a ground-level fall can cause an intracranial bleed), loss of independence, fear of falling, and death. RISK FACTORS divide into INTRINSIC — a HISTORY OF FALLS (strongest predictor, present here), advanced age, gait/balance impairment and weakness (she uses a walker), COGNITIVE impairment/delirium (she has mild cognitive impairment), visual impairment, ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION (documented), urinary urgency/nocturia/incontinence (present), foot problems, and chronic neurologic disease — and EXTRINSIC/SITUATIONAL — high-risk MEDICATIONS (her benzodiazepine and diuretic; also opioids, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, anticholinergics, polypharmacy), environmental hazards (clutter, poor lighting, cords, rugs, wet floors), improper FOOTWEAR, the UNFAMILIAR hospital environment, tethers (IV lines, catheters), and RESTRAINTS. Recognizing this constellation drives a targeted, multifactorial prevention plan.
labs.r: Falls = leading injury cause in elders + major preventable hospital harm (fall WITH injury = reportable). Consequences: hip/other fractures, HEAD bleed (esp. anticoagulated), lost independence, death. INTRINSIC risks: HISTORY OF FALLS (strongest), age, gait/balance/weakness, cognitive impairment/delirium, vision, ORTHOSTASIS, urinary urgency/nocturia. EXTRINSIC: high-risk MEDS (benzos/opioids/diuretics/antihypertensives/hypoglycemics/anticholinergics/polypharmacy), hazards, footwear, unfamiliar setting, tethers, restraints. RN role: recognize the multifactorial risk.

labs.v: Every patient is SCREENED with a VALIDATED fall-risk tool — the MORSE Fall Scale or the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model are common — on ADMISSION, each SHIFT, after any CHANGE in status (new sedative, post-op, new delirium), and after ANY fall. A high score triggers the high-risk prevention bundle. Beyond the score, the nurse performs a MULTIFACTORIAL assessment to target modifiable causes: GAIT and BALANCE (e.g., the Timed Up and Go test, ability to transfer/ambulate, use of an assistive device); ORTHOSTATIC vital signs (lying/sitting/standing — a drop with symptoms is a key reversible cause); VISION; a MEDICATION review for fall-risk drugs (sedatives/benzodiazepines, opioids, diuretics/antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, anticholinergics, polypharmacy — candidates for timing changes or deprescribing); COGNITION and a DELIRIUM screen (CAM); CONTINENCE and toileting needs (urgency/nocturia greatly raises risk); FOOTWEAR (non-skid vs socks/loose slippers); and the ENVIRONMENT (clutter, lighting, cords, bed height, tethers, call-light reach). For Margaret, the assessment flags her history of falls, orthostasis, the benzodiazepine and diuretic, urinary urgency, walker dependence, and the unfamiliar tethered environment as the targets for intervention.
labs.r: Screen with a VALIDATED tool (MORSE / Hendrich II) on admission, each shift, after status change, and after any fall. Add a MULTIFACTORIAL assessment: gait/balance (Timed Up and Go), ORTHOSTATIC vitals, vision, MEDICATION review (sedatives/diuretics/etc.), cognition/delirium (CAM), continence/toileting, footwear, environment. Target the modifiable causes. RN role: validated screen + multifactorial evaluation.

labs.n: PREVENTION BUNDLE — universal + targeted; why side rails/restraints are NOT fall prevention
labs.v: Prevention combines a UNIVERSAL bundle for ALL patients with TARGETED measures for high-risk patients. UNIVERSAL: keep the CALL LIGHT and needed items within REACH and answer calls PROMPTLY; bed in the LOW and LOCKED position; adequate LIGHTING/night-light; NON-SKID footwear; a dry, CLUTTER-FREE, well-lit path; and orient the patient to the room/routine. TARGETED for high risk: visibly FLAG the patient (wristband/door sign); use a BED-/CHAIR-EXIT ALARM; perform PURPOSEFUL HOURLY ROUNDING covering the 4 Ps — PAIN, POTTY (offer toileting), POSITION (comfort/repositioning), and POSSESSIONS (within reach); provide SCHEDULED, ASSISTED TOILETING and do NOT leave a high-risk patient alone on the toilet/commode (toileting falls are very common); ASSIST with ambulation/transfers using a GAIT BELT and ensure the ASSISTIVE DEVICE (walker/cane) is correct and within reach; obtain a PT/OT consult; REVIEW and minimize fall-risk MEDICATIONS (deprescribe the benzodiazepine, time the diuretic earlier); TREAT ORTHOSTASIS (rise slowly, dangle before standing, hydrate); manage delirium/pain; consider a SITTER or moving the patient nearer the nurses' station; and use LOW beds/floor mats. CRITICAL TEACHING POINT: SIDE RAILS and RESTRAINTS are NOT fall-prevention tools — raising ALL FOUR side rails is legally a RESTRAINT and patients try to CLIMB OVER them (causing worse injury), and physical restraints do NOT prevent falls while increasing injury, deconditioning, agitation, and death; the LEAST-RESTRICTIVE approach (the bundle above) is used instead. Half/two side rails as a mobility aid to assist repositioning are acceptable, but rails are never the fall-prevention strategy.
labs.r: UNIVERSAL bundle (all): call light + items in REACH + answer promptly, bed LOW/locked, lighting/night-light, NON-SKID footwear, clutter-free path, orient. TARGETED (high risk): flag, BED-EXIT ALARM, purposeful HOURLY ROUNDING (4 Ps: Pain/Potty/Position/Possessions), SCHEDULED assisted TOILETING (don't leave alone), assisted ambulation + gait belt, assistive device in reach, PT/OT, MED review/deprescribe, treat orthostasis, sitter/near station, low bed/mats. SIDE RAILS (4 up) + RESTRAINTS are NOT fall prevention (= restraint, climb-over injury, more harm) — least-restrictive instead. RN role: universal + targeted bundle, no restraints.

labs.n: POST-FALL response + incident reporting / just culture
labs.v: If a fall occurs, the response is structured: STAY WITH the patient and do NOT move them immediately; ASSESS for injury — level of consciousness, HEAD injury (obtain NEURO CHECKS and consider CT, ESPECIALLY if the patient is on an ANTICOAGULANT or struck the head), PAIN, deformity/suspected FRACTURE, range of motion, VITAL SIGNS and orthostatics, and skin/lacerations; CALL FOR HELP and do not lift alone; NOTIFY the provider; and move the patient only AFTER serious injury is excluded (using safe technique/lift equipment). Then REASSESS fall risk and UPDATE the care plan to address the cause (here: urgent toileting plus orthostasis plus a sedative). Complete an INCIDENT/OCCURRENCE REPORT — an OBJECTIVE, FACTUAL account used for QUALITY IMPROVEMENT and a JUST-CULTURE review (focused on system causes, NOT blaming the patient or staff); the incident report is NOT filed in the medical record and is NOT referenced in the chart (chart documentation is a separate, objective note of the assessment and care). A POST-FALL HUDDLE with the team identifies contributing factors and immediate fixes. Continuous monitoring follows, especially for delayed injury (e.g., a slow intracranial bleed in an anticoagulated patient — serial neuro checks). For Margaret, no serious injury is found, the plan is intensified (toileting schedule, sitter consideration, sedative deprescribing), and the event is reported and analyzed.
labs.r: POST-FALL: STAY with patient + do NOT move immediately; ASSESS injury (LOC, HEAD/neuro checks + CT esp. if anticoagulated/head strike, pain, deformity/fracture, ROM, vitals/orthostatics, skin); call for help; NOTIFY provider; move only after serious injury excluded. REASSESS risk + UPDATE plan. INCIDENT/OCCURRENCE report = objective, just-culture/QI tool, NOT in the chart, NOT blame; post-fall HUDDLE for cause; document objectively in chart; watch for delayed injury (serial neuro checks). RN role: assess + protect + notify + report + update plan.

labs.n: Education / home safety + nursing role; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: EDUCATION (patient/family + discharge/HOME safety) reduces recurrence: modify the HOME — remove THROW RUGS, clutter, and cords; install GRAB BARS and a raised toilet seat in the bathroom; use NON-SLIP mats and adequate LIGHTING/night-lights; secure STAIR RAILS; store items at reachable height; and wear proper FOOTWEAR (not socks alone or loose slippers). Encourage EXERCISE focused on STRENGTH and BALANCE (physical therapy, tai chi), a VISION check, a MEDICATION review to reduce fall-risk drugs, VITAMIN D if indicated, rising SLOWLY to avoid orthostasis, correct ASSISTIVE-DEVICE use, a PERSONAL EMERGENCY RESPONSE SYSTEM, and knowing how to call for help and when to seek care after a fall (head injury, inability to bear weight). PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the team did NOT rely on raising all four side rails or on physical restraints to 'prevent' falls; did NOT leave the high-risk patient alone on the toilet/commode; did NOT ignore orthostasis or the sedating medications; did NOT move her immediately after the fall before assessing for injury; and did NOT treat the incident report as a punitive/blame document or place it in the chart. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: validated screening with multifactorial assessment; the universal-plus-targeted bundle (hourly rounding/4 Ps, scheduled toileting, bed-exit alarm, assisted ambulation, medication review, orthostasis treatment); least-restrictive care without restraints; a correct post-fall response with reassessment and just-culture analysis; and thorough home-safety education with PT/OT and family engagement. EXPECTED outcome: fall risk is reduced, injury is prevented or promptly managed, the cause is addressed, and the patient is prepared for safe mobility at home. NURSING ROLE: assess fall risk (validated tool + multifactorial); implement the universal-plus-targeted prevention bundle; avoid side rails/restraints as fall prevention; respond correctly to a fall and report/analyze it; and educate the patient and family.
labs.r: EDUCATE/home safety: remove rugs/clutter/cords, GRAB BARS + raised toilet seat, non-slip mats, lighting/night-lights, stair rails, proper FOOTWEAR; strength/BALANCE exercise (PT/tai chi), vision check, MEDICATION review, vitamin D, rise slowly, assistive-device use, PERS, when to seek care. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no 4-side-rails/restraints as prevention, didn't leave alone on toilet, didn't ignore orthostasis/sedatives, didn't move before injury assessment, didn't treat incident report as blame/put in chart. PROTECTIVE: validated screen + bundle + least-restrictive + correct post-fall + home teaching/PT/family. RN role: assess + prevent + respond + educate.

nursesNote: Medical unit — Margaret S., 78, admitted with pneumonia + dehydration; HIGH FALL RISK. Risk factors: HISTORY of a fall 3 mo ago (strongest predictor), mild cognitive impairment, unsteady gait/walker, urinary URGENCY + nocturia, ORTHOSTATIC hypotension (138/82 sit → 116/70 stand), meds = FUROSEMIDE + nightly LORAZEPAM (benzodiazepine), unfamiliar tethered (IV) environment. ASSESSMENT: validated tool (MORSE/Hendrich II) on admission/each shift/status change/after any fall + MULTIFACTORIAL eval — gait/balance (TUG), orthostatic vitals, vision, MEDICATION review, cognition/delirium (CAM), continence/toileting, footwear, environment. PREVENTION = UNIVERSAL (call light + items in REACH + answer promptly, bed LOW/locked, lighting/night-light, NON-SKID footwear, clutter-free path, orient) + TARGETED (flag high-risk, BED-EXIT ALARM, purposeful HOURLY ROUNDING/4 Ps = Pain/Potty/Position/Possessions, SCHEDULED assisted TOILETING — don't leave alone on toilet/commode, assisted ambulation + GAIT BELT, walker in reach, PT/OT, MED review/deprescribe benzo + time diuretic, TREAT ORTHOSTASIS [rise slowly/dangle/hydrate], sitter/near nurses' station, low bed/mats). SIDE RAILS (all 4 up = RESTRAINT, climb-over injury) + RESTRAINTS are NOT fall prevention (more harm; least-restrictive instead — links restraint case 110). POST-FALL (found on floor reaching for bathroom): STAY with her + do NOT move immediately; ASSESS injury (LOC, HEAD/neuro checks ± CT esp. if anticoagulated/head strike, pain, deformity/fracture, ROM, vitals/orthostatics, skin); call for help; NOTIFY provider; move only after serious injury excluded. REASSESS risk + UPDATE plan (intensify toileting, consider sitter, review sedative). INCIDENT/OCCURRENCE report = objective/factual, JUST-CULTURE + QI tool, NOT in chart, NOT blame; post-fall HUDDLE for cause (urgent toileting + orthostasis + sedative); document objectively; watch delayed injury (serial neuro checks). EDUCATE/home safety: remove rugs/clutter/cords, GRAB BARS + raised toilet seat, non-slip mats, lighting/night-lights, stair rails, proper FOOTWEAR; strength/BALANCE exercise (PT/tai chi), vision check, med review, vitamin D, rise slowly, assistive-device use, PERS. NEGATIVES (correct practice): no 4-rails/restraints as prevention, didn't leave alone on toilet, didn't ignore orthostasis/sedatives, didn't move before injury assessment, didn't treat report as blame/put in chart. Outcome: no serious injury; risk reduced; safe ambulation with walker; family engaged.
providerOrders: ADMIT: medical unit; community-acquired pneumonia + dehydration; HIGH fall risk

FALL RISK: screen with a validated tool (Morse/Hendrich II) on admission, each shift, after status change, and after any fall; multifactorial assessment (gait/balance, orthostatic vitals, vision, medications, cognition/delirium, continence, footwear, environment)
CODE STATUS: full code
UNIVERSAL FALL PRECAUTIONS:
Call light and needed items within reach; answer calls promptly; bed low and locked; adequate lighting/night-light; non-skid footwear; clutter-free, dry, well-lit path; orient to room
HIGH-RISK TARGETED INTERVENTIONS:
Flag high risk (wristband/sign); bed-/chair-exit alarm; purposeful hourly rounding (4 Ps: pain, potty/toileting, position, possessions)
Scheduled, assisted toileting; do NOT leave the patient alone on the toilet/commode; assist ambulation/transfers with a gait belt; assistive device (walker) within reach

PT/OT consult; pharmacy medication review to minimize fall-risk drugs (deprescribe benzodiazepine; adjust diuretic timing); treat orthostasis (rise slowly, dangle, hydrate); manage delirium/pain; consider sitter or relocation near the nurses' station; low bed/floor mats
Do NOT use four side rails up or physical restraints as fall prevention (least-restrictive approach)
POST-FALL PROTOCOL:

Stay with the patient; do not move until assessed; evaluate for injury (LOC, head/neuro checks and imaging if head strike or anticoagulated, pain, fracture, ROM, vitals/orthostatics, skin); notify provider; move only after serious injury excluded

Reassess fall risk and update the plan; complete an incident/occurrence report (objective, just-culture, not in the chart); post-fall huddle; document objectively; serial neuro checks if head injury suspected

EDUCATION/DISCHARGE: home-safety modifications (remove rugs/clutter/cords, grab bars, raised toilet seat, lighting, stair rails, footwear), strength/balance exercise (PT/tai chi), vision and medication review, vitamin D if indicated, assistive-device use, personal emergency response system, and how/when to seek help after a fall

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this high-fall-risk patient?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: A history of a recent fall plus unsteady gait/walker use, mild cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/nocturia — strong intrinsic fall risk factors
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — these intrinsic factors (especially a prior fall) make her high-risk. RN role: recognize intrinsic risk.

opts.text: Orthostatic hypotension and fall-risk medications (a benzodiazepine and a diuretic) that can be modified
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — orthostasis and sedating/diuretic drugs are modifiable, high-yield contributors. RN role: identify modifiable causes.

opts.text: Screen with a validated fall-risk tool and perform a multifactorial assessment (gait/balance, orthostatic vitals, vision, meds, cognition, continence, footwear, environment)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — validated screening plus multifactorial assessment targets the plan. RN role: assess fall risk.

opts.text: Implement the universal-plus-targeted prevention bundle (call light in reach, low bed, bed-exit alarm, hourly rounding/4 Ps, scheduled toileting, assisted ambulation)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the bundle is the core of prevention. RN role: implement universal + targeted measures.

opts.text: The unfamiliar, tethered hospital environment (IV lines) and improper footwear add extrinsic/situational risk
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — situational/environmental factors are modifiable and important. RN role: address the environment.

opts.text: Know the correct post-fall response and that side rails/restraints are NOT fall prevention
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — restraints/4-rails cause harm, and a correct post-fall response is essential. RN role: least-restrictive care + correct post-fall response.

opts.text: Allergies: NKDA — documented for the record
opts.rat: Allergy documentation; routine. Not the central cue.

opts.text: Raise all four side rails and apply a vest restraint to keep her in bed and prevent falls
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Four side rails up is a restraint (patients climb over → worse injury), and restraints do not prevent falls and increase harm; use the least-restrictive bundle.

opts.text: Leave the high-risk patient alone on the toilet to give her privacy
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Toileting-related falls are very common; a high-risk patient should be assisted and not left alone on the toilet/commode.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: A history of falls is the single strongest predictor of future falls, and risk is both intrinsic and extrinsic/situational
opts.rat: CORRECT — risk-factor framework. Foundation for assessment.

opts.text: Fall risk is screened with a validated tool on admission, each shift, after a status change, and after any fall, with a multifactorial assessment to target causes
opts.rat: CORRECT — assessment principle. Foundation for a targeted plan.

opts.text: Prevention combines universal precautions for all with targeted interventions for high-risk patients (alarms, hourly rounding, scheduled toileting, assisted ambulation, medication review)
opts.rat: CORRECT — universal-plus-targeted bundle. Foundation for prevention.

opts.text: Orthostatic hypotension and sedating/diuretic medications are modifiable contributors that should be treated or reviewed
opts.rat: CORRECT — modifiable-cause principle. Foundation for targeted intervention.

opts.text: Side rails (all four up) and physical restraints are not fall-prevention tools and can increase injury; the least-restrictive approach is used
opts.rat: CORRECT — the restraint/side-rail principle. Foundation for safe, least-restrictive care.

opts.text: After a fall, the patient is assessed for injury before being moved, the provider is notified, and an objective incident report is completed for quality improvement
opts.rat: CORRECT — post-fall response principle. Foundation for correct handling.

opts.text: Applying physical restraints is the most effective evidence-based way to prevent falls
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Restraints do NOT prevent falls and increase injury, deconditioning, and death; least-restrictive interventions are used.

opts.text: An incident report should be placed in the medical record and used to discipline the staff involved
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The incident report is a separate quality-improvement/just-culture document, not part of the chart, and is not a blame/discipline tool.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Screen fall risk with a validated tool and complete a multifactorial assessment to identify modifiable causes
opts.rat: #1 — Assessment identifies who is at risk and why, driving the whole plan. RN role: validated screen + multifactorial assessment.

opts.text: Implement the universal-plus-targeted prevention bundle (call light, low bed, alarm, hourly rounding, scheduled toileting, assisted ambulation)
opts.rat: #2 — The bundle is the core preventive intervention once risk is identified. RN role: implement the bundle.

opts.text: Treat modifiable contributors — orthostasis, fall-risk medications, toileting needs — and consult PT/OT
opts.rat: #3 — Addressing the specific causes reduces risk further. RN role: treat modifiable factors.

opts.text: Respond correctly to any fall (assess for injury before moving, neuro checks, notify, report) and avoid restraints/side rails as prevention
opts.rat: #4 — Correct post-fall response and least-restrictive care prevent additional harm. RN role: safe response + least-restrictive care.

opts.text: Educate the patient and family on home safety and arrange follow-up/PT for safe mobility after discharge
opts.rat: #5 — Education and follow-up sustain prevention beyond the hospital. RN role: home-safety teaching.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this high-fall-risk patient.

opts.text: Keep the call light and needed items within reach, the bed low and locked, the path clear, and provide non-skid footwear
opts.rat: Universal fall precautions for all patients. RN role: universal bundle.

opts.text: Use a bed-exit alarm, perform purposeful hourly rounding (4 Ps), and provide scheduled, assisted toileting
opts.rat: Targeted high-risk interventions that prevent unassisted attempts. RN role: targeted bundle.

opts.text: Review and minimize fall-risk medications (deprescribe the benzodiazepine, adjust diuretic timing) and treat orthostasis (rise slowly, hydrate)
opts.rat: Addresses modifiable pharmacologic and physiologic causes. RN role: treat modifiable factors.

opts.text: Assist ambulation/transfers with a gait belt, ensure correct walker use, and obtain a PT/OT consult
opts.rat: Mobility support reduces falls while preserving function. RN role: assisted mobility + PT/OT.

opts.text: Provide home-safety education (remove rugs, grab bars, lighting, footwear) and strength/balance exercise referral for discharge
opts.rat: Education and rehabilitation sustain prevention after discharge. RN role: home-safety teaching.

opts.text: If a fall occurs, stay with the patient, assess for injury before moving, perform neuro checks if indicated, and notify the provider
opts.rat: Correct post-fall response that prevents additional harm. RN role: safe post-fall response.

opts.text: Raise all four side rails and apply a vest restraint to keep the patient in bed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — four rails up is a restraint (climb-over injury) and restraints do not prevent falls and increase harm; use least-restrictive measures.

opts.text: Leave the high-risk patient alone on the commode to finish toileting
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — toileting falls are common; stay with/assist the high-risk patient rather than leaving them alone.

opts.text: After a fall, immediately lift the patient back to bed before assessing for injury
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — assess for injury (including head/spine/fracture) before moving; moving first can worsen an injury.

opts.text: File the incident report in the patient's chart and use it to identify who is to blame
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the incident report is a separate just-culture/QI document, not part of the chart, and is not used to assign blame.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Screen fall risk with a validated tool and complete a multifactorial assessment
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Identifying risk and its causes drives the plan. RN role: assess fall risk.

opts.text: Implement universal precautions plus targeted high-risk measures (alarm, hourly rounding, scheduled toileting, assisted ambulation, call light in reach)
opts.rat: #2 — Second. The bundle puts prevention into action. RN role: implement the bundle.

opts.text: Treat modifiable contributors — review/adjust fall-risk medications, treat orthostasis, consult PT/OT
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Targeting specific causes further reduces risk. RN role: treat modifiable factors.

opts.text: If a fall occurs, stay with the patient, assess for injury before moving, perform neuro checks if indicated, notify the provider, and complete an incident report/huddle
opts.rat: #4 — When a fall happens. A correct, structured response limits harm and improves the system. RN role: post-fall response + report.

opts.text: Reassess and update the plan and provide home-safety education for safe mobility at discharge
opts.rat: #5 — Ongoing/discharge. Reassessment and education sustain prevention. RN role: update plan + educate.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The nurse screened fall risk with a validated tool, kept the bed low with the call light in reach, and used a bed-exit alarm with purposeful hourly rounding
opts.rat: Validated screening plus the universal/targeted bundle is correct fall-prevention practice. Correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse provided scheduled, assisted toileting and did not leave the high-risk patient alone on the commode
opts.rat: Toileting falls are common; assisted, scheduled toileting is correct. Correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse reviewed fall-risk medications for deprescribing, treated orthostasis, and consulted PT/OT
opts.rat: Addressing modifiable causes reduces risk. Correct practice.

opts.text: After the fall, the nurse stayed with the patient, assessed for injury and performed neuro checks before moving her, and notified the provider
opts.rat: A correct, structured post-fall response prevents additional harm. Correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse completed an objective incident report for quality improvement and held a post-fall huddle to find the cause
opts.rat: Just-culture, QI-focused reporting and analysis improve safety. Correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse raised all four side rails and applied a vest restraint to prevent the patient from getting up
opts.rat: ⚠️ Four rails up is a restraint (climb-over injury) and restraints do not prevent falls and increase harm. Improper practice.

opts.text: The nurse left the high-risk patient alone on the toilet to answer another call light
opts.rat: ⚠️ Leaving a high-risk patient alone on the toilet risks a common, preventable fall. Improper practice.

opts.text: After the fall, the nurse immediately lifted the patient back into bed before assessing for injury
opts.rat: ⚠️ Moving before assessing for head/spine/fracture injury can worsen harm. Improper practice.

opts.text: The nurse documented the incident report in the medical record and named the staff at fault
opts.rat: ⚠️ The incident report is a separate just-culture/QI document, not part of the chart, and is not a blame tool. Improper practice.

opts.text: Before discharge, the nurse taught the patient and family about removing rugs, installing grab bars, proper footwear, and balance exercise
opts.rat: Home-safety education sustains prevention after discharge. Correct practice.

title: Pediatric Asthma CONTROL and Self-Management Education in a 9-Year-Old with Poorly Controlled Persistent Asthma: Assessing Control, the CONTROLLER (Daily Inhaled Corticosteroid) vs RELIEVER (PRN Albuterol) Distinction, Correct Inhaler-and-Spacer Technique (and Rinsing After ICS), Peak-Flow Zones and a Written ASTHMA ACTION PLAN, Trigger Reduction, and When to Seek Care
subtitle: ASTHMA is a chronic INFLAMMATORY airway disease in which airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, edema, and mucus produce recurrent WHEEZE, COUGH (often worse at NIGHT/early morning), chest tightness, and dyspnea, provoked by TRIGGERS (viral URIs — the most common pediatric trigger; allergens such as dust mites, pets, pollen, mold; TOBACCO/secondhand SMOKE; exercise; cold air; strong odors; GERD; and stress). This case is about CHRONIC CONTROL and SELF-MANAGEMENT (distinct from the acute, life-threatening status asthmaticus emergency). The GOAL of management is ASTHMA CONTROL: minimal/no daytime symptoms, NO nighttime awakenings, reliever use no more than ~2 days/week, NO activity limitation (a child with controlled asthma should play and exercise normally), normal lung function, and prevention of exacerbations. ASSESSING CONTROL drives therapy: a child is NOT well controlled if there are daytime symptoms or reliever (SABA) use MORE than ~2 days/week, ANY frequent nighttime awakenings, activity limitation, reduced peak flow/spirometry, or recurrent exacerbations/ED visits — findings that warrant STEPPING UP therapy and reviewing technique/adherence/triggers FIRST. The CENTRAL teaching distinction is CONTROLLER vs RELIEVER: the CONTROLLER (long-term, anti-inflammatory) medication — an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID (ICS, e.g., fluticasone, budesonide) — is taken EVERY DAY, even when the child feels well, to reduce airway inflammation and prevent attacks; it does NOT relieve an acute attack and takes weeks for full effect. Step-up options add a long-acting beta-agonist (ICS-LABA), a leukotriene modifier (montelukast), or higher-dose ICS. The RELIEVER/RESCUE medication — a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA, ALBUTEROL) — is used PRN for acute symptoms and before exercise and works within minutes. OVERUSE of the reliever (e.g., needing it more than twice a week, or going through canisters quickly) signals POOR CONTROL and undertreated inflammation — not a reason to simply use more albuterol. COMMON, DANGEROUS ERRORS to correct: relying ONLY on the reliever while SKIPPING the daily controller; trying to use the CONTROLLER to stop an acute attack (it won't work fast); and not understanding which inhaler is which. INHALER + SPACER technique is high-yield nursing teaching: use a SPACER (valved holding chamber) with a metered-dose inhaler to improve lung delivery and reduce oropharyngeal deposition (add a MASK for younger children) — shake, attach the spacer, exhale, seal the lips, actuate ONE puff, take a slow deep breath (or several tidal breaths with a mask), HOLD the breath ~10 seconds, and wait ~30-60 seconds between puffs; after using an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID, RINSE the mouth and SPIT (and clean the spacer) to prevent oral CANDIDIASIS (thrush) and hoarseness; track doses with the dose counter and prime/clean the device. PEAK-FLOW MONITORING and a WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN guide self-management: establish the child's PERSONAL BEST, then use ZONES — GREEN (≥80% of personal best = good control, continue the controller), YELLOW (50-79% = caution, take the reliever and step up per the plan, watch closely), and RED (<50% = medical alert, take the reliever and seek emergency care) — and give the family and SCHOOL a written green/yellow/red action plan. TRIGGER REDUCTION and PREVENTION: maintain a SMOKE-FREE environment (eliminating secondhand smoke is the strongest modifiable factor), reduce dust-mite/allergen/pet exposure, treat allergic rhinitis/GERD, PRE-TREAT exercise-induced symptoms with a reliever rather than avoiding activity, get the annual INFLUENZA vaccine (and stay current on immunizations), and recognize and avoid the child's specific triggers. WHEN TO SEEK CARE / ADHERENCE / SCHOOL: teach the family to recognize WORSENING (increasing reliever use, night symptoms, yellow/red peak flow, fast or hard breathing, retractions, inability to speak in full sentences) and to follow the action plan/seek emergency care; support daily controller ADHERENCE with routines; ensure SCHOOL access to the reliever and a copy of the action plan; and arrange follow-up. NURSING ROLE: assess asthma control; teach the controller-vs-reliever distinction and correct inhaler/spacer technique (with mouth-rinsing after ICS); establish peak-flow zones and a written action plan; promote trigger reduction, immunization, and normal activity; teach recognition of worsening and when to seek care; and support adherence, school management, and follow-up.

labs.v: Mateo R., 9, with persistent asthma, is seen for follow-up after an ED visit for an exacerbation. ASTHMA is a chronic INFLAMMATORY airway disease causing recurrent wheeze, cough (worse at night/early morning), chest tightness, and dyspnea, triggered by viral URIs (the most common pediatric trigger), allergens (dust mites, pets, pollen, mold), TOBACCO/secondhand SMOKE, exercise, cold air, odors, GERD, and stress. The GOAL is ASTHMA CONTROL: minimal/no daytime symptoms, NO nighttime awakenings, reliever use ≤2 days/week, NO activity limitation (the child should exercise/play normally), normal lung function, and prevention of exacerbations. ASSESSING CONTROL guides therapy: Mateo is NOT well controlled — daytime symptoms most days, nighttime awakenings several times/week, albuterol use ~5 days/week, activity limitation (sitting out of sports), and a recent ED visit. NOT-well-controlled asthma warrants STEPPING UP therapy AND first reviewing INHALER TECHNIQUE, ADHERENCE, and TRIGGER exposure (frequently the real problem). The nurse's central role here is to assess control accurately and then deliver comprehensive self-management education to move him toward control.
labs.r: Asthma = chronic INFLAMMATORY airway disease (wheeze/cough worse at night, chest tightness, dyspnea); triggers = viral URI (most common in kids), allergens, SMOKE, exercise, cold, GERD. GOAL = CONTROL: minimal symptoms, NO night awakenings, reliever ≤2 days/wk, NO activity limit, normal lung function, no exacerbations. NOT controlled if symptoms/SABA >2 days/wk, night symptoms, activity limit, low peak flow, ED visits → STEP UP + review technique/adherence/triggers. RN role: assess control.

labs.n: CONTROLLER (daily ICS) vs RELIEVER (PRN albuterol) — the central distinction
labs.v: The most important teaching point is the difference between the two kinds of asthma medicine. The CONTROLLER (long-term-control, anti-inflammatory) medication — an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID (ICS, e.g., fluticasone, budesonide) — is taken EVERY DAY, even when the child feels completely well, to reduce the underlying airway INFLAMMATION and PREVENT attacks; it works over days to weeks and does NOT relieve an acute attack. When control is inadequate, therapy is STEPPED UP (add a long-acting beta-agonist as an ICS-LABA combination, add a leukotriene modifier such as montelukast, or increase the ICS dose) — and stepped down once stable. The RELIEVER/RESCUE medication — a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA, ALBUTEROL) — is used as needed for acute symptoms and BEFORE EXERCISE, and works within minutes by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. CRUCIALLY, frequent reliever use (more than ~2 days/week, or going through albuterol canisters quickly) is a RED FLAG for POOR CONTROL and undertreated inflammation — the correct response is to optimize the controller, technique, and triggers, NOT simply to use more albuterol. COMMON ERRORS the nurse corrects: using ONLY the reliever and SKIPPING the daily controller (Mateo's pattern); trying to use the controller to abort an acute attack (it is too slow); and confusing which inhaler is which. Clear labeling ('every-day medicine' vs 'rescue medicine') and teach-back help the child and family use them correctly.
labs.r: CONTROLLER = INHALED CORTICOSTEROID, taken DAILY even when well, anti-inflammatory, PREVENTS attacks, NOT for acute relief (step up: ICS-LABA, montelukast, higher ICS). RELIEVER = SABA (ALBUTEROL), PRN for acute symptoms + before exercise, works in minutes. Frequent reliever use (>2 days/wk) = POOR CONTROL → optimize controller/technique/triggers, NOT just more albuterol. ERRORS: reliever-only/skipping controller; using controller for acute attack; confusing the two. RN role: teach controller-vs-reliever.

labs.n: Inhaler + spacer technique + rinsing after ICS
labs.v: Correct device technique is essential — many 'uncontrolled' children simply use their inhaler incorrectly. Use a SPACER (valved holding chamber) with a metered-dose inhaler: it improves medication delivery to the lungs and reduces deposition in the mouth/throat; younger children add a MASK. STEPS: remove the cap and SHAKE the inhaler; attach it to the spacer; have the child EXHALE fully; seal the lips around the spacer mouthpiece; actuate ONE puff into the spacer; take a SLOW, DEEP breath in (or, with a mask, breathe normally for several breaths); HOLD the breath for ~10 seconds; and WAIT about 30-60 seconds before a second puff (repeat the steps for each puff). After using an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID, the child should RINSE the mouth with water and SPIT it out (and the spacer should be cleaned periodically) to PREVENT oral CANDIDIASIS (thrush) and hoarseness — a key, frequently-missed step. Teach families to track doses with the device's DOSE COUNTER (so the inhaler is not used past empty), to PRIME and CLEAN the device per instructions, and to store it properly. The nurse uses demonstration and TEACH-BACK (have the child show the technique) and reassesses at each visit, because technique drifts. Mateo was using no spacer, poor coordination, and not rinsing — all corrected with teaching.
labs.r: Use a SPACER with the MDI (mask for young kids) — improves lung delivery, reduces oral deposition. Technique: shake → attach spacer → exhale → seal lips → ONE puff → slow deep breath → HOLD ~10 sec → wait 30-60 sec between puffs. After ICS: RINSE mouth + SPIT (prevent thrush/hoarseness); clean spacer. Track doses (counter), prime/clean. Use demonstration + TEACH-BACK + reassess (technique drifts). RN role: teach + verify inhaler/spacer technique.

labs.n: Peak-flow zones + written ASTHMA ACTION PLAN + when to seek care
labs.v: Self-management is structured by PEAK-FLOW monitoring and a WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN. A peak-flow meter measures how fast the child can exhale; first establish the child's PERSONAL BEST (highest of readings when well), then interpret using ZONES based on percent of personal best: GREEN ZONE (≥80% = good control — continue the daily controller and usual activities); YELLOW ZONE (50-79% = CAUTION — an exacerbation may be starting; take the reliever and follow the step-up instructions on the plan, and monitor closely); and RED ZONE (<50% = MEDICAL ALERT — take the reliever and SEEK EMERGENCY CARE). The provider creates an individualized WRITTEN ACTION PLAN in green/yellow/red format specifying the daily controller, the reliever dose, what to do in each zone, and when to call or go to the ED, and copies are given to the FAMILY and the SCHOOL. Teach the family to recognize WORSENING regardless of the meter: increasing reliever use, nighttime symptoms, fast or labored breathing, retractions or nasal flaring, difficulty speaking in full sentences, or a poor response to the reliever — these mean follow the yellow/red plan and seek care. The action plan turns symptoms and numbers into clear, pre-decided actions, reducing delays and ED visits.
labs.r: PEAK FLOW: establish PERSONAL BEST, then zones — GREEN ≥80% (good, continue controller), YELLOW 50-79% (caution, reliever + step up per plan), RED <50% (emergency, reliever + seek care). Provider writes an individualized green/yellow/red WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN → copies to FAMILY + SCHOOL. Seek care for: rising reliever use, night symptoms, fast/labored breathing, retractions, can't speak full sentences, poor reliever response. RN role: peak-flow zones + action plan + recognize worsening.

labs.n: Trigger reduction + prevention + adherence/school; Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: TRIGGER REDUCTION and PREVENTION reduce exacerbations: keep a SMOKE-FREE home and car (eliminating SECONDHAND SMOKE is the single strongest modifiable factor — counsel/refer for tobacco cessation), reduce DUST-MITE exposure (allergen-proof mattress/pillow covers, wash bedding in hot water, reduce stuffed toys/carpet), manage PET allergens (keep the cat out of the bedroom or rehome if severe), treat ALLERGIC RHINITIS and GERD, and identify/avoid the child's specific triggers. Encourage NORMAL ACTIVITY: a child with controlled asthma should play and exercise — for exercise-induced symptoms, PRE-TREAT with the reliever ~15 minutes before activity and warm up, rather than avoiding sports. PREVENTIVE care: the annual INFLUENZA vaccine and keeping immunizations current. ADHERENCE and SCHOOL: support a daily controller ROUTINE (link to brushing teeth, reminders/charts), ensure the SCHOOL has the reliever available and a copy of the action plan, and arrange FOLLOW-UP to reassess control and step therapy up or down. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT tell the family to just use more albuterol for frequent symptoms (a sign to optimize the controller/technique/triggers); did NOT advise stopping the daily controller when feeling well; did NOT recommend avoiding all exercise; did NOT skip the spacer or the post-ICS mouth rinse; and did NOT overlook the secondhand smoke. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: accurate control assessment; correct controller-vs-reliever use; proper inhaler/spacer technique with mouth-rinsing; peak-flow zones and a written action plan shared with school; trigger reduction (especially smoke-free) and immunization; normal activity with exercise pre-treatment; and adherence support with follow-up. EXPECTED outcome: symptoms and reliever use decrease, nighttime awakenings stop, activity is normal, peak flow stays green, and exacerbations/ED visits fall. NURSING ROLE: assess control; teach controller-vs-reliever and inhaler/spacer technique (rinse after ICS); establish peak-flow zones and a written action plan; promote trigger reduction, immunization, and normal activity; teach recognition of worsening/when to seek care; and support adherence, school management, and follow-up.
labs.r: TRIGGER reduction: SMOKE-FREE (strongest modifiable — cessation referral), dust-mite/pet-allergen measures, treat rhinitis/GERD, avoid personal triggers. NORMAL activity — PRE-TREAT exercise with reliever (don't avoid sports). Annual FLU vaccine + immunizations. ADHERENCE routine + SCHOOL has reliever + action-plan copy + follow-up. NEGATIVES (correct practice): didn't say 'just use more albuterol,' didn't stop controller when well, didn't avoid exercise, didn't skip spacer/post-ICS rinse, didn't ignore secondhand smoke. PROTECTIVE: control assessment, correct med use/technique, action plan, trigger reduction, immunization, adherence/follow-up. RN role: prevention + adherence + school + follow-up.

nursesNote: Pediatric clinic — Mateo R., 9, persistent asthma, follow-up after an ED exacerbation last month. NOT well controlled: daytime symptoms most days, nighttime awakenings several times/wk, albuterol ~5 days/wk, sits out of sports (activity limitation). Asthma = chronic INFLAMMATORY airway disease (wheeze/cough worse at night/AM, chest tightness, dyspnea); triggers = viral URI (#1 in kids), allergens (dust mites/cat), SECONDHAND SMOKE (home), exercise, cold, GERD. GOAL = CONTROL (minimal symptoms, no night awakenings, reliever ≤2 days/wk, NO activity limit, normal lung function, no exacerbations). Not controlled → STEP UP + review technique/adherence/triggers FIRST. CENTRAL TEACHING — CONTROLLER vs RELIEVER: CONTROLLER = daily INHALED CORTICOSTEROID (fluticasone/budesonide), taken EVERY DAY even when well (anti-inflammatory, PREVENTS attacks, NOT fast relief; step up = ICS-LABA/montelukast/higher ICS); RELIEVER = SABA ALBUTEROL PRN for acute symptoms + before exercise (works in minutes). Frequent reliever use (>2 days/wk) = POOR CONTROL → optimize controller/technique/triggers, NOT just more albuterol. Mateo's errors: uses albuterol for everything + takes ICS only 'when he feels bad' (must be DAILY); MDI without spacer + poor coordination + no post-ICS rinse. INHALER/SPACER teaching: use a SPACER (mask for young kids); shake → attach → exhale → seal lips → ONE puff → slow deep breath → HOLD ~10 sec → wait 30-60 sec between puffs; after ICS RINSE mouth + SPIT (prevent thrush/hoarseness); clean spacer, track doses, prime; demonstration + TEACH-BACK + reassess. PEAK FLOW: personal best → GREEN ≥80% (continue controller), YELLOW 50-79% (reliever + step up per plan), RED <50% (reliever + EMERGENCY care). WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN (green/yellow/red) → copies to FAMILY + SCHOOL. Seek care: rising reliever use, night symptoms, fast/labored breathing, retractions/flaring, can't speak full sentences, poor reliever response. TRIGGER reduction: SMOKE-FREE home/car (strongest modifiable → cessation referral), dust-mite covers/wash bedding hot/reduce carpet+stuffed toys, cat out of bedroom, treat allergic rhinitis/GERD. NORMAL activity — PRE-TREAT exercise with reliever (keep playing). Annual FLU vaccine + immunizations. ADHERENCE routine + SCHOOL reliever access + action-plan copy + follow-up. NEGATIVES (correct practice): didn't say 'just use more albuterol,' didn't stop controller when well, didn't advise avoiding exercise, didn't skip spacer/post-ICS rinse, didn't ignore secondhand smoke. Outcome at follow-up: minimal symptoms, no night awakenings, rare reliever use, back to sports, peak flow green — controlled.
providerOrders: VISIT: pediatric clinic follow-up; persistent asthma, not well controlled (recent ED exacerbation)
ASSESSMENT: assess asthma control (daytime symptoms, nighttime awakenings, reliever frequency, activity limitation, exacerbations); spirometry/peak flow; review technique, adherence, and triggers

CONTROLLER: daily inhaled corticosteroid (e.g., fluticasone) — take EVERY day even when well; step up therapy (ICS-LABA, leukotriene modifier, or higher-dose ICS) for inadequate control; step down once stable

RELIEVER: short-acting beta-agonist (albuterol) as needed for acute symptoms and 15 minutes before exercise; frequent use (>2 days/week) indicates poor control and should prompt controller/technique/trigger review

DEVICE TEACHING: use a spacer (with mask for younger children) with the MDI; teach shake/exhale/one puff/slow deep breath/10-second hold/wait between puffs; RINSE mouth and spit after the inhaled corticosteroid; verify with teach-back at each visit; track doses with the counter

PEAK FLOW + ACTION PLAN: establish personal best; provide an individualized written asthma action plan (green ≥80% continue controller; yellow 50-79% reliever + step up; red <50% reliever + emergency care); give copies to the family and school
TRIGGER REDUCTION: smoke-free home/car (counsel/refer for tobacco cessation); dust-mite and pet-allergen measures; treat allergic rhinitis/GERD; identify/avoid the child's triggers
PREVENTION/ACTIVITY: encourage normal activity with pre-exercise reliever; annual influenza vaccine and current immunizations

EDUCATION: recognize worsening (increasing reliever use, night symptoms, fast/labored breathing, retractions, inability to speak in full sentences) and follow the action plan/seek care; support daily controller adherence; coordinate school management
FOLLOW-UP: reassess control and adjust therapy (step up/down); reinforce technique and adherence

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this child's asthma control?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Daytime symptoms most days, nighttime awakenings several times a week, albuterol use ~5 days/week, and activity limitation — signs of poorly controlled asthma
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — these define inadequate control and the need to step up and re-educate. RN role: assess control.

opts.text: He takes the daily inhaled-corticosteroid controller only 'when he feels bad' and uses the albuterol reliever for everything
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a central, correctable misunderstanding of controller vs reliever. RN role: teach the medication distinction.

opts.text: His inhaler technique is poor — no spacer, poor coordination, and no mouth-rinsing after the steroid inhaler
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — poor technique is a common cause of 'uncontrolled' asthma and thrush risk. RN role: assess/teach technique.

opts.text: Frequent reliever use is a red flag for poor control, not a reason to simply use more albuterol
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — over-reliance on the reliever signals undertreated inflammation. RN role: recognize the red flag + optimize the controller.

opts.text: Modifiable triggers — secondhand smoke in the home and a cat — and the need for a peak-flow plan and trigger reduction
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — trigger reduction (especially smoke-free) is high-impact prevention. RN role: address triggers.

opts.text: The need for a written asthma action plan, normal activity with exercise pre-treatment, the flu vaccine, and school coordination
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — an action plan, activity, immunization, and school access support control. RN role: action plan + prevention + school.

opts.text: Allergies: environmental (dust mites, cat dander) documented
opts.rat: Relevant to trigger reduction; documented. Supports the plan rather than being the central cue.

opts.text: Advise the family to just increase albuterol use and stop the daily controller whenever he feels well
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Frequent reliever use signals poor control; the daily controller must continue even when well to prevent inflammation — stopping it worsens control.

opts.text: Tell him to avoid all sports and exercise permanently because he has asthma
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. A child with controlled asthma should play and exercise; pre-treat exercise-induced symptoms with the reliever rather than avoiding activity.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease, and the goal is control — minimal symptoms, no nighttime awakenings, reliever use ≤2 days/week, and normal activity
opts.rat: CORRECT — disease nature and the control goal. Foundation for assessment.

opts.text: The controller (daily inhaled corticosteroid) is taken every day to prevent inflammation and does not relieve an acute attack
opts.rat: CORRECT — controller principle. Foundation for correct daily use.

opts.text: The reliever (albuterol) is for acute symptoms and before exercise; frequent use signals poor control
opts.rat: CORRECT — reliever principle and the overuse red flag. Foundation for recognizing inadequate control.

opts.text: A spacer improves delivery, and the mouth should be rinsed after an inhaled corticosteroid to prevent thrush
opts.rat: CORRECT — device technique and post-ICS rinsing. Foundation for effective, safe use.

opts.text: Peak-flow zones (green ≥80%, yellow 50-79%, red <50%) and a written action plan guide self-management
opts.rat: CORRECT — peak-flow/action-plan principle. Foundation for structured self-management.

opts.text: Reducing triggers (especially eliminating secondhand smoke), getting the flu vaccine, and pre-treating exercise support control and normal activity
opts.rat: CORRECT — trigger reduction and prevention. Foundation for fewer exacerbations.

opts.text: The inhaled corticosteroid should be used as a quick-relief medicine during an acute asthma attack
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The inhaled corticosteroid is a daily controller that works over time; it does not provide quick relief — the SABA reliever is used for acute symptoms.

opts.text: Needing the reliever many times a week is fine as long as it keeps working, and the controller can be skipped
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Frequent reliever need indicates poor control/undertreated inflammation; the controller must be continued and therapy/technique/triggers optimized.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Assess asthma control and review inhaler technique, adherence, and trigger exposure
opts.rat: #1 — Accurate control assessment (and finding technique/adherence/trigger gaps) drives the whole plan. RN role: assess control + identify gaps.

opts.text: Teach the controller-vs-reliever distinction — daily inhaled corticosteroid to prevent, albuterol PRN to relieve
opts.rat: #2 — Correcting this central misunderstanding is the highest-impact education. RN role: teach medication roles.

opts.text: Teach and verify correct inhaler/spacer technique, including rinsing the mouth after the steroid inhaler
opts.rat: #3 — Proper technique makes the medications actually work and prevents thrush. RN role: device teaching + teach-back.

opts.text: Establish peak-flow zones and provide a written asthma action plan (with a school copy)
opts.rat: #4 — Structured self-management turns symptoms/numbers into pre-decided actions. RN role: action plan.

opts.text: Promote trigger reduction (smoke-free), immunization, normal activity with exercise pre-treatment, and follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Prevention and follow-up sustain control over time. RN role: trigger reduction + prevention + follow-up.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this child's asthma care.

opts.text: Teach that the daily inhaled corticosteroid is taken every day, even when well, to prevent inflammation
opts.rat: Correct controller use is the foundation of control. RN role: teach daily controller.

opts.text: Teach that albuterol is the reliever for acute symptoms and before exercise, and that frequent use means control should be optimized
opts.rat: Correct reliever use and the overuse red flag. RN role: teach reliever role.

opts.text: Provide a spacer and teach correct technique, including rinsing the mouth after the steroid inhaler
opts.rat: Improves delivery and prevents thrush. RN role: device technique + post-ICS rinse.

opts.text: Establish a personal-best peak flow and provide a green/yellow/red written action plan, with a copy for the school
opts.rat: Structured self-management with school access. RN role: peak flow + action plan.

opts.text: Counsel a smoke-free home, dust-mite/pet measures, the annual flu vaccine, and pre-treating exercise so he can keep playing sports
opts.rat: Trigger reduction, prevention, and normal activity. RN role: trigger reduction + prevention.

opts.text: Use demonstration and teach-back and arrange follow-up to reassess control and technique
opts.rat: Verifies learning and sustains control. RN role: teach-back + follow-up.

opts.text: Advise stopping the daily controller whenever he feels well and just using more albuterol for symptoms
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — stopping the controller worsens control, and frequent reliever use signals undertreatment; the controller continues and therapy is optimized.

opts.text: Tell him to use the inhaled corticosteroid as his quick-relief medicine during an attack
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the inhaled corticosteroid is a slow-acting daily controller, not a rescue medicine; the SABA reliever is used for acute symptoms.

opts.text: Recommend he avoid all sports and physical activity because of his asthma
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — controlled asthma allows normal activity; pre-treat exercise with the reliever rather than avoiding it.

opts.text: Tell the family that secondhand smoke in the home is unrelated to his asthma
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — secondhand smoke is a major modifiable trigger; a smoke-free environment is one of the most important interventions.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess asthma control and review current technique, adherence, and triggers
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Understanding control and the gaps directs all teaching. RN role: assess + identify gaps.

opts.text: Teach the controller-vs-reliever distinction and confirm the daily controller routine
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Correcting the central misunderstanding has the greatest impact. RN role: teach medication roles.

opts.text: Teach and verify inhaler/spacer technique (with mouth-rinsing after the steroid) using teach-back
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Proper technique makes the medications effective and prevents thrush. RN role: device teaching.

opts.text: Establish peak-flow zones and provide a written action plan with a school copy
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Structured self-management guides home/school response. RN role: action plan.

opts.text: Counsel trigger reduction, immunization, and normal activity, and arrange follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Prevention and follow-up sustain control. RN role: prevention + follow-up.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: After daily controller use, correct spacer technique, and trigger reduction, his daytime symptoms and nighttime awakenings decrease and reliever use drops to rare
opts.rat: The hallmark of regained control with correct self-management. Expected, desired improvement.

opts.text: He returns to playing soccer, pre-treating with his reliever before exercise, with peak flow in the green zone
opts.rat: Normal activity and green-zone peak flow reflect good control. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: The family makes the home smoke-free and uses dust-mite covers, and his exacerbations and ED visits decrease
opts.rat: Trigger reduction lowering exacerbations. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: He demonstrates correct inhaler/spacer technique and rinses after the steroid inhaler, with no thrush
opts.rat: Effective technique and thrush prevention. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the family stops the daily controller when he feels well and relies on frequent albuterol; symptoms, night awakenings, and exacerbations increase
opts.rat: ⚠️ Skipping the controller and over-relying on the reliever worsens control. Demonstrates why the daily controller continues.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — he continues to use the inhaler without a spacer and never rinses after the steroid; he gets poor delivery and develops oral thrush
opts.rat: ⚠️ Poor technique reduces effectiveness and causes thrush. Demonstrates the importance of spacer use and post-ICS rinsing.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — secondhand smoke continues at home and the cat sleeps in his room; he has frequent nighttime symptoms and yellow-zone peak flows
opts.rat: ⚠️ Ongoing trigger exposure perpetuates poor control. Demonstrates the impact of trigger reduction (especially smoke-free).

opts.text: Alternative scenario — told to avoid all exercise, he becomes deconditioned and anxious while his asthma remains poorly controlled
opts.rat: ⚠️ Avoiding activity is incorrect and harmful; controlled asthma should allow exercise with pre-treatment. Demonstrates promoting normal activity.

opts.text: Right after the visit, before the controller takes full effect, his symptoms and peak flow are essentially unchanged while he begins daily use
opts.rat: The controller works over days to weeks; an unchanged short-term baseline is expected while adherence builds. Continue and reassess at follow-up.

opts.text: At follow-up he is well controlled, demonstrates his action plan, and the school has a copy and his reliever on hand
opts.rat: Sustained control with effective self-management and school coordination. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: Uterine Rupture During a Trial of Labor After Cesarean (TOLAC/VBAC) in a 32-Year-Old G3P2 on Oxytocin Augmentation: Recognizing Sudden Severe Abdominal Pain + Abrupt Fetal Bradycardia + Loss of Fetal Station as an Obstetric Catastrophe, Stopping Oxytocin and Resuscitating the Mother, and LEADING the Emergency Team to an Immediate Laparotomy/Cesarean
subtitle: UTERINE RUPTURE = a complete, full-thickness disruption of the uterine wall (often through the serosa) during pregnancy or labor, through which the fetus, placenta, and/or umbilical cord may extrude into the peritoneal cavity — abruptly cutting off fetal oxygenation and producing rapid intra-abdominal MATERNAL HEMORRHAGE. It is one of the most catastrophic obstetric emergencies, threatening BOTH the mother (hemorrhagic shock, DIC, death) and the fetus (acute hypoxia, neurologic injury, death), and outcomes are decided in minutes by RECOGNITION and a fast, coordinated team response. It must be distinguished from a UTERINE SCAR DEHISCENCE — an incomplete separation of a prior scar with the visceral peritoneum still intact, usually asymptomatic and often found incidentally — whereas a COMPLETE rupture is symptomatic and life-threatening. RISK FACTORS center on a WEAKENED or OVERSTRESSED uterus: a PRIOR CESAREAN or uterine scar is the leading risk (a classical/vertical incision carries the highest risk; a prior low-transverse incision is lower but NOT zero — the setting of a TRIAL OF LABOR AFTER CESAREAN, TOLAC/VBAC), other uterine surgery (e.g., myomectomy), EXCESSIVE OXYTOCIN or uterine TACHYSYSTOLE/hyperstimulation, induction of a scarred uterus with PROSTAGLANDINS, grand multiparity, a short interpregnancy interval, obstructed labor/cephalopelvic disproportion, fetal macrosomia, malpresentation, external cephalic version, and abdominal TRAUMA. RECOGNITION (high-yield cues): the MOST COMMON and often EARLIEST sign is an ABRUPT, ABNORMAL FETAL HEART RATE pattern — a sudden PROLONGED FETAL BRADYCARDIA or new recurrent late/variable decelerations, or loss of the FHR; classic maternal signs include SUDDEN, SEVERE, CONSTANT abdominal/uterine PAIN (sometimes described as a 'tearing' or 'ripping' sensation, occasionally a 'pop' that may transiently feel like relief), LOSS OF FETAL STATION (the presenting part recedes/rises and is no longer palpable at the previously documented station as the fetus extrudes upward), CESSATION or sudden change in the uterine contraction pattern / loss of uterine tone, PALPABLE FETAL PARTS through the maternal abdomen, a change in abdominal contour, and signs of MATERNAL HEMORRHAGE/HYPOVOLEMIC SHOCK (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, restlessness, air hunger) — note that vaginal bleeding may be present, scant, or CONCEALED because much of the bleeding is intra-abdominal. IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT — the goals are to STOP the precipitant, RESUSCITATE the mother, and EXPEDITE DELIVERY (the only definitive treatment): (1) RECOGNIZE the catastrophe and CALL FOR HELP / activate the obstetric emergency (rapid-response) team instantly — mobilize the obstetrician/surgeon, anesthesia, the neonatal/NICU team, the OR, the BLOOD BANK, and the charge nurse — do not manage it alone or leave the patient; (2) STOP the OXYTOCIN immediately (it intensifies the contractions and worsens the rupture/bleeding); (3) RESUSCITATE the mother for hemorrhagic shock: high-flow OXYGEN, TWO large-bore IVs, rapid IV crystalloid, send labs (CBC, coagulation studies/fibrinogen, type & crossmatch), and ACTIVATE THE MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL — anticipate transfusion of packed red cells and clotting products and watch for DIC; (4) maintain CONTINUOUS fetal heart rate monitoring and optimize maternal perfusion while preparing for surgery (definitive relief is delivery, not intrauterine resuscitation alone); (5) EXPEDITE TRANSFER TO THE OR for an IMMEDIATE (STAT) LAPAROTOMY → emergency CESAREAN delivery and HEMORRHAGE CONTROL (the surgeon performs uterine REPAIR if feasible or a HYSTERECTOMY if bleeding is uncontrolled), minimizing the decision-to-incision interval; (6) have the NEONATAL team present and ready for RESUSCITATION (NRP) because the fetus is likely hypoxic/acidotic; insert a Foley, and DOCUMENT the timeline. LEADERSHIP / DELEGATION / TEAMWORK are decisive and are the focus of this case: the nurse must instantly RECOGNIZE the emergency, CALL IT OUT and activate the team, ASSIGN CLEAR ROLES with CLOSED-LOOP COMMUNICATION (one person stops the oxytocin and runs fluids/resuscitation and stays with the patient; others notify/mobilize the surgeon + anesthesia + neonatal team + OR + blood bank, obtain/expedite consent and surgical prep, draw labs and start blood, monitor maternal and fetal status, support the terrified family, and document times), hand off with SBAR, and DELEGATE BY SCOPE (unlicensed/support staff fetch equipment, transport, set up the OR, and run blood; licensed staff perform assessment, medication administration, and FHR interpretation). PREVENTION/AWARENESS: select TOLAC candidates carefully (favor prior low-transverse incisions, avoid in classical/high-vertical scars), use oxytocin judiciously and AVOID tachysystole, avoid prostaglandin cervical ripening of a scarred uterus, monitor the laboring VBAC patient closely with continuous FHR, and maintain heightened vigilance for the cues above. NURSING ROLE: recognize uterine rupture the instant the fetal heart rate drops and the mother reports sudden severe pain, STOP the oxytocin, lead and delegate the coordinated emergency response, resuscitate the mother for hemorrhagic shock (with the massive transfusion protocol), and expedite a STAT laparotomy/cesarean with the neonatal team ready — all while supporting the frightened mother and family.

patient.admitDate: Admitted in active labor at term (G3P2) attempting a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC/VBAC) after one prior LOW-TRANSVERSE cesarean; oxytocin augmentation in progress. At approximately 7 cm dilated she SUDDENLY developed severe, constant abdominal pain with a 'tearing' sensation, an ABRUPT PROLONGED FETAL BRADYCARDIA (FHR ~70), LOSS OF FETAL STATION (the presenting part receded), cessation of the contraction pattern, palpable fetal parts through the abdomen, and rising maternal tachycardia/hypotension — UTERINE RUPTURE, an obstetric catastrophe. The nurse must recognize it instantly, stop the oxytocin, lead the coordinated emergency response, resuscitate the mother, and expedite a STAT laparotomy/cesarean.
