nursesNote: Med-surg — 72 y/o man, ~3 weeks post ischemic stroke with severe oropharyngeal DYSPHAGIA (failed swallow eval, high aspiration risk); new PEG placed for long-term enteral nutrition, X-ray-confirmed before first use. Enteral preferred because the gut works. ROUTE by duration (NG <4-6 wks; PEG long-term). PLACEMENT checks: external markings/length (migration), gastric pH (≤5), site/bumper — AUSCULTATION is UNRELIABLE, not used. ASPIRATION PREVENTION (key risk): HOB ≥30-45° during feeds + 30-60 min after; confirm placement before intermittent feeds/meds; watch for cough/choking/distress/desat/crackles/fever → STOP/slow + keep HOB up + reassess. TOLERANCE: soft non-distended abdomen, BS present, no nausea; residual per policy within limits and RETURNED (not discarded); slow/hold for distension/vomiting/diarrhea/high residual. PATENCY: flush ~30 mL WATER before/after feeds + before/after AND between meds + q4-6h continuous (water, not juice/soda). MEDS: liquids preferred; crush only crushable immediate-release; NEVER crush enteric-coated/extended-release; give separately + flush between; don't add to formula; hold feeds around phenytoin per policy. FORMULA: clean technique, hang-time limits, closed system, refrigerate opened, don't 'top off.' HYDRATION: scheduled FREE-WATER flushes (formula insufficient) + monitor I&O/lytes. COMPLICATIONS watched: aspiration pneumonia, diarrhea (rate/osmolality/sorbitol meds/contamination/C. diff), constipation, dehydration, REFEEDING (phos 2.4 low, K 3.6, Mg — start low/advance slow/replete), hyperglycemia (glucose 142), clog/dislodgement, peristomal skin/buried bumper; prealbumin 12 (baseline undernutrition). DISLODGED fresh PEG (<~4 wks) → notify provider, DON'T blindly reinsert. Oral care given despite NPO; psychosocial support for loss of eating; SLP (swallow re-eval) + dietitian involved. During one bolus a brief cough → slowed feed, HOB up, lungs clear, SpO2 recovered. TEACHING (teach-back with daughter): HOB elevation, placement/patency checks + flushing, feeding/med technique, free-water schedule, skin care, and warning signs (cough/choking, respiratory distress, fever, abdominal pain/distension, persistent diarrhea/no output, tube dislodgement, dehydration). NEGATIVES (correct practice): not fed flat, not auscultation-only, no crushing ER/adding meds to formula, no juice flushes, free water given, no blind reinsertion. Outcome: tolerating goal feeds, nutrition/hydration improving, skin intact, no aspiration, family demonstrates safe technique.
providerOrders: DIET/NUTRITION: enteral nutrition via PEG; dietitian to set formula, goal rate/volume, and free-water flush schedule; advance per tolerance; NPO by mouth (severe dysphagia)

PLACEMENT VERIFICATION: radiographic confirmation obtained before first use; nurse to verify external tube length/markings, gastric pH, and exit-site/bumper each shift and before intermittent feeds/medications; do NOT use auscultation to confirm placement

ASPIRATION PRECAUTIONS: keep head of bed elevated at least 30-45 degrees during feeding and for 30-60 minutes after (continuously for continuous feeds); monitor for coughing/respiratory distress/desaturation/crackles/fever; stop/slow the feed and keep the head of bed elevated if intolerance or aspiration is suspected

TOLERANCE MONITORING: assess abdomen, nausea/vomiting, bowel function, and gastric residual per facility policy; return aspirated residuals; hold and notify the provider for high residuals or signs of intolerance

TUBE PATENCY: flush with ~30 mL water before and after each feeding and each medication, between medications, and every 4-6 hours during continuous feeds; water only (not juice/soda); manage clogs with warm water per policy

MEDICATIONS via tube: use liquid formulations when available; crush only crushable immediate-release tablets; do NOT crush enteric-coated or extended/sustained-release products; give each medication separately and flush between; do not add medications to the formula; hold feeds before/after phenytoin per pharmacy guidance
HYDRATION: scheduled free-water flushes for hydration; strict intake/output; monitor electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, and glucose
REFEEDING PRECAUTIONS: advance feeds gradually in this undernourished patient; monitor and replete phosphate, potassium, and magnesium

PEG SITE CARE: assess and protect peristomal skin; verify external bumper position; report leakage, redness, breakdown, or a buried bumper; for a dislodged tube (fresh tract), notify the provider immediately and do NOT blindly reinsert
COMFORT/PSYCHOSOCIAL: provide oral care despite NPO; support coping with the loss of oral intake; speech-language pathology for ongoing swallow re-evaluation; dietitian follow-up

EDUCATION/DISCHARGE: teach the patient and family (teach-back) head-of-bed elevation, placement/patency checks and flushing, feeding and medication technique, the free-water schedule, skin care, and warning signs to report; case management to arrange home enteral therapy and follow-up

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for safe enteral feeding in this patient?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Severe dysphagia with a failed swallow evaluation makes him high-risk for aspiration — head-of-bed elevation and tolerance monitoring are essential
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — aspiration is the key risk of tube feeding, especially with dysphagia. RN role: aspiration prevention.

opts.text: Tube placement must be verified — X-ray confirmed the new PEG before first use, and ongoing checks use external markings and gastric pH (not auscultation)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — correct placement verification prevents instilling feed/medication into a misplaced tube. RN role: verify placement correctly.

opts.text: Tolerance signs — abdominal distension, nausea/vomiting, bowel function, and residuals per policy — guide whether to continue, slow, or hold feeds
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — monitoring tolerance prevents distension/aspiration and detects intolerance. RN role: assess tolerance.

opts.text: The tube must be flushed with water to stay patent, and medications must be given correctly (liquids; never crushing extended-release/enteric-coated)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — flushing prevents clogs and correct medication technique prevents toxicity/clogging. RN role: patency + safe med admin.

opts.text: Enteral formula provides insufficient free water — scheduled free-water flushes and intake/output monitoring are needed for hydration
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — dehydration is a common, preventable complication. RN role: ensure free-water hydration.

opts.text: He is undernourished (low prealbumin/phosphate) — advance feeds gradually and monitor for refeeding syndrome; watch glucose and the peristomal skin
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — refeeding risk, glycemic monitoring, and skin integrity all matter. RN role: refeeding precautions + skin/glucose surveillance.

opts.text: Lay the patient flat during feeding to make administration easier
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + DANGEROUS. Feeding flat sharply increases aspiration risk; keep the head of bed elevated at least 30-45° during and after feeding.

opts.text: Confirm tube placement simply by injecting air and auscultating a 'whoosh' over the stomach before each feeding
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Auscultation is unreliable and is not an acceptable method to confirm placement; use external markings/length, gastric pH, and X-ray for new tubes.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Enteral feeding is preferred when the GI tract works; route depends on duration (NG short-term, PEG long-term)
opts.rat: CORRECT — the indication and route principle. Foundation for the plan.

opts.text: X-ray is the gold standard to confirm a newly placed tube before first use; ongoing verification uses external markings and gastric pH, not auscultation
opts.rat: CORRECT — placement verification. Foundation for safe instillation.

opts.text: Keeping the head of bed elevated at least 30-45° during and after feeding is a primary aspiration-prevention measure
opts.rat: CORRECT — head-of-bed elevation. Foundation for aspiration prevention.

opts.text: Flushing with water keeps the tube patent; medications are given as liquids when possible, separately, with flushes between — never crushing extended-release/enteric-coated forms
opts.rat: CORRECT — patency and medication principles. Foundation for safe administration.

opts.text: Free-water flushes are needed for hydration, and a malnourished patient must be advanced slowly with monitoring for refeeding syndrome
opts.rat: CORRECT — hydration and refeeding principles. Foundation for fluid/electrolyte safety.

opts.text: When gastric residual is checked per policy, the aspirated contents are returned (not discarded) to avoid fluid/electrolyte loss
opts.rat: CORRECT — residual handling. Foundation for tolerance monitoring without causing losses.

opts.text: Medications can simply be added to the feeding formula bag to save time
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Medications are never added to the formula (incompatibilities, clogging, inaccurate dosing); give them separately and flush between.

opts.text: If the tube clogs, flushing with cranberry juice or soda is the best way to dissolve the clog
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Juice/soda can worsen clogging; use warm water with gentle pressure per policy, and flush routinely with water to prevent clogs.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Confirm correct tube placement and elevate the head of bed to at least 30-45° before instilling any feeding or medication
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Verifying placement and elevating the head of bed prevent misplaced instillation and aspiration — the most dangerous risks. RN role: placement + positioning first.

opts.text: Assess feeding tolerance (abdomen, nausea, residual per policy) and slow/hold for intolerance
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Tolerance assessment prevents distension/aspiration and catches problems early. RN role: monitor tolerance.

opts.text: Administer the feeding and medications correctly (right rate; liquids/flushes; never crushing extended-release/enteric-coated)
opts.rat: #3 — Delivers nutrition and medications safely once placement/positioning/tolerance are addressed. RN role: correct administration.

opts.text: Maintain hydration with free-water flushes and keep the tube patent and the peristomal skin intact
opts.rat: #4 — Sustains hydration, tube function, and skin integrity. RN role: hydration + patency + skin care.

opts.text: Provide oral care and psychosocial support and teach the patient/family for safe self-management
opts.rat: #5 — Comfort, dignity, and education sustain safe long-term care. RN role: comfort + teaching.

opts.rat: Successful teach-back supports safe home self-management. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the patient is fed lying flat without placement confirmation; he coughs, desaturates, and develops crackles and a fever (aspiration pneumonia)
opts.rat: ⚠️ Feeding flat without verification caused aspiration. Demonstrates why head-of-bed elevation and placement checks are essential.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — an extended-release tablet is crushed into the formula and flushes are skipped; the tube clogs and he develops medication toxicity
opts.rat: ⚠️ Crushing extended-release forms and skipping flushes caused clogging and toxicity. Demonstrates correct medication technique and flushing.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — no free-water flushes are given and intake/output is not tracked; he becomes dehydrated with rising sodium and BUN
opts.rat: ⚠️ Inadequate free water caused dehydration. Demonstrates the need for scheduled free-water flushes and monitoring.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — a freshly dislodged PEG is blindly reinserted and feeding resumed; formula enters a false tract into the peritoneum
opts.rat: ⚠️ Blind reinsertion of a fresh PEG created a false passage. Demonstrates notifying the provider and not reinserting/feeding until confirmed.

opts.text: Early in therapy, before full nutritional repletion, his weight is stable while he tolerates feeds and advances toward goal
opts.rat: Nutritional repletion takes time; a stable short-term weight while tolerating and advancing feeds is expected. Continue and reassess.

opts.text: At follow-up he is at goal feeds with adequate hydration and intact skin, and speech therapy continues to reassess for any safe future oral intake
opts.rat: Sustained safe enteral nutrition with ongoing swallow reassessment. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: Safe Nursing Care of the Mechanically Ventilated Patient in the ICU (64-Year-Old, Day 2 of Intubation for Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure): The VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA (VAP) PREVENTION BUNDLE, Troubleshooting HIGH-Pressure vs LOW-Pressure Ventilator Alarms, Responding to Desaturation by Manually Ventilating with a BVM (DOPE), Endotracheal Tube/Cuff Care and Appropriate Suctioning, and Communication/Comfort for the Intubated Patient
subtitle: Caring for a mechanically ventilated patient is a core ICU nursing responsibility centered on AIRWAY SAFETY, PREVENTING ventilator-associated harm, and RESPONDING correctly to alarms. This case deliberately focuses on the day-to-day SAFE CARE and INFECTION PREVENTION of the ventilated patient (distinct from ARDS-specific lung-protective ventilation/prone positioning and from the sedation/awakening-and-breathing-trial focus of ICU liberation). VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA (VAP) — pneumonia developing > 48 hours after intubation — is a serious, largely PREVENTABLE hospital-acquired infection; the nurse-driven VAP PREVENTION BUNDLE reduces it: ELEVATE THE HEAD OF BED to 30-45° (unless contraindicated) to reduce aspiration; DAILY SEDATION INTERRUPTION and assessment of READINESS TO EXTUBATE (paired spontaneous awakening + breathing trials — less sedation means fewer ventilator days and less VAP); ORAL CARE with CHLORHEXIDINE and regular oral hygiene; SUBGLOTTIC SECRETION drainage when the tube has a suction port; PEPTIC-ULCER (stress-ulcer) PROPHYLAXIS and DVT (VTE) PROPHYLAXIS; meticulous HAND HYGIENE; and avoiding unnecessary ventilator-circuit changes and breaks in the circuit. VENTILATOR ALARMS must NEVER be ignored or simply silenced/reset without assessing the patient — 'assess the patient, not just the machine.' A HIGH-PRESSURE (high peak-pressure) alarm means INCREASED AIRWAY RESISTANCE or DECREASED LUNG COMPLIANCE: common, often reversible causes are SECRETIONS (needs suctioning), the patient BITING the tube (needs a bite block) or coughing, a KINKED/obstructed tube, water in the circuit tubing, BRONCHOSPASM, anxiety/asynchrony, and more dangerous causes such as a PNEUMOTHORAX, mucus plug, or worsening compliance (pulmonary edema/ARDS) — the nurse assesses (auscultate, look at the tube/circuit, check the patient) and corrects the cause. A LOW-PRESSURE or LOW EXHALED-TIDAL-VOLUME alarm means a LEAK or DISCONNECTION with loss of circuit pressure: a CIRCUIT DISCONNECTION (most common — reconnect it), a CUFF LEAK/under-inflated cuff, or TUBE DISPLACEMENT/dislodgement — the priority is to restore a closed, functioning system. CRUCIAL SAFETY RULE: if the patient is DESATURATING or unstable and the problem cannot be quickly identified and corrected, DISCONNECT from the ventilator and MANUALLY VENTILATE with a BAG-VALVE-MASK and 100% OXYGEN while calling for respiratory therapy/help — never delay oxygenation troubleshooting a machine. The DOPE mnemonic guides the acute deterioration of an intubated patient: Displacement (tube out of the trachea/dislodged/mainstem), Obstruction (secretions/kink/biting), Pneumothorax, and Equipment failure (disconnection/vent/O2 source) — confirm the tube and ventilate by hand. ENDOTRACHEAL TUBE / AIRWAY CARE: SECURE the tube and document/verify its depth (cm at the lip) and bilateral breath sounds + waveform CAPNOGRAPHY to confirm placement; maintain CUFF PRESSURE about 20-30 cmH2O (enough to prevent aspiration/leak, not so high as to cause tracheal ischemia); and SUCTION ONLY WHEN INDICATED (visible secretions, high-pressure alarm, coughing, desaturation, audible secretions) — NOT on a fixed routine schedule — using HYPEROXYGENATION before/after, sterile technique, limited duration (≤ 10-15 seconds per pass), while monitoring for HYPOXEMIA, BRADYCARDIA/arrhythmia, and mucosal trauma; do NOT routinely instill normal saline before suctioning. COMMUNICATION/COMFORT/SAFETY: the intubated patient cannot speak — provide a communication board/writing/yes-no questions, explain all care, treat PAIN and target LIGHT (not deep) sedation, give EYE care and oral care, prevent self-extubation with appropriate (least-restrictive) measures, support the family, and prevent immobility complications. COMPLICATIONS to prevent/monitor: VAP, self/accidental EXTUBATION, tube displacement/mainstem intubation, barotrauma/pneumothorax, oxygen toxicity, GI stress ulcers, VTE, delirium, and ICU-acquired weakness. NURSING ROLE: keep the airway secure and the tube confirmed and patent; respond to every alarm by assessing the patient and manually ventilating if needed; troubleshoot high- vs low-pressure alarms; suction appropriately; deliver the full VAP-prevention bundle; provide communication, comfort, and protection from complications; and continually assess readiness to wean and extubate.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + safe care of the mechanically ventilated patient
labs.v: 64 y/o man R. Castellano, ICU day 2 of intubation and mechanical ventilation for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (severe pneumonia/sepsis), now hemodynamically stabilizing on lung-protective settings (FiO2 40%, PEEP 5), lightly sedated and intermittently awake. Safe care of the ventilated patient rests on three pillars: AIRWAY SECURITY (tube secured, depth documented, placement confirmed by bilateral breath sounds + waveform capnography, cuff pressure maintained), PREVENTING ventilator-associated harm (especially VAP, but also self-extubation, barotrauma, GI ulcers, VTE, delirium, weakness), and RESPONDING to ventilator ALARMS by assessing the patient — not merely silencing the machine. A bag-valve-mask and suction are kept ready at the bedside for emergencies. This case centers on the everyday safe care and infection prevention of the ventilated patient — distinct from ARDS-specific lung-protective/prone management and from the sedation/awakening-trial focus of ICU liberation. The nurse's focus: keep the airway safe, deliver the VAP-prevention bundle, troubleshoot alarms (manually ventilating if needed), suction appropriately, provide communication/comfort, and assess readiness to wean.
labs.r: Safe vent care = AIRWAY SECURITY (secure tube, document depth, confirm placement via breath sounds + capnography, cuff ~20-30 cmH2O) + PREVENT ventilator-associated harm (VAP, self-extubation, barotrauma, ulcers, VTE, delirium, weakness) + ALARM response (assess the patient, BVM ready). Distinct from ARDS lung-protective/prone and ICU-liberation sedation focus. RN role: airway + VAP prevention + alarms + suction + comfort + weaning readiness.

labs.v: VAP — pneumonia developing > 48 hours after intubation — is a serious but largely PREVENTABLE hospital-acquired infection (aspiration of contaminated secretions around the tube). The nurse-driven VAP PREVENTION BUNDLE: (1) ELEVATE THE HEAD OF BED to 30-45° unless contraindicated (reduces aspiration); (2) DAILY SEDATION INTERRUPTION and assessment of READINESS TO EXTUBATE — paired spontaneous awakening + breathing trials (less sedation → fewer ventilator days → less VAP); (3) ORAL CARE with CHLORHEXIDINE plus regular oral hygiene (reduces oropharyngeal colonization); (4) SUBGLOTTIC SECRETION drainage when the endotracheal tube has a suction port; (5) PEPTIC-ULCER (stress-ulcer) PROPHYLAXIS; (6) DVT/VTE PROPHYLAXIS; (7) meticulous HAND HYGIENE and avoiding unnecessary ventilator-circuit breaks/changes. Additional measures include maintaining adequate cuff pressure to limit micro-aspiration and keeping the circuit free of pooled condensate. Signs of VAP to monitor: new fever, leukocytosis, increased/purulent secretions, a new infiltrate on chest X-ray, and worsening oxygenation/rising ventilator requirements → obtain cultures (endotracheal aspirate) and treat per HAP/VAP guidelines. The bundle is a shared, audited responsibility; consistent adherence is what lowers VAP rates.
labs.r: VAP = pneumonia > 48h after intubation; largely PREVENTABLE. BUNDLE: HOB 30-45°; daily sedation interruption + extubation-readiness (SAT/SBT); oral care + CHLORHEXIDINE; subglottic suction; stress-ulcer (PUD) prophylaxis; DVT prophylaxis; hand hygiene + avoid unnecessary circuit breaks; maintain cuff pressure + drain condensate. Monitor for VAP: new fever/leukocytosis/purulent secretions/new infiltrate/worsening oxygenation → culture + treat. RN role: deliver/audit the VAP bundle.

labs.n: Ventilator ALARM troubleshooting + airway emergency (DOPE) + suctioning/ETT care
labs.v: Ventilator alarms are NEVER ignored or blindly silenced/reset — assess the PATIENT, not just the machine. HIGH-PRESSURE (high peak-pressure) alarm = INCREASED RESISTANCE or DECREASED COMPLIANCE: SECRETIONS (suction), BITING the tube (bite block) or coughing, a KINKED/obstructed tube, WATER in the circuit, BRONCHOSPASM, ventilator asynchrony/anxiety, or dangerous causes like a PNEUMOTHORAX, mucus plug, or worsening edema/ARDS — assess (auscultate, inspect tube/circuit, look at the patient) and correct the cause. LOW-PRESSURE / LOW EXHALED-TIDAL-VOLUME alarm = a LEAK or DISCONNECTION: a CIRCUIT DISCONNECTION (most common — reconnect), a CUFF LEAK/under-inflation, or TUBE DISPLACEMENT — restore a closed, working system. SAFETY RULE: if the patient is DESATURATING/unstable and the cause is not quickly correctable, DISCONNECT and MANUALLY VENTILATE with a BAG-VALVE-MASK + 100% O2 and call respiratory therapy/help — oxygenation comes before troubleshooting a machine. The DOPE mnemonic frames acute deterioration of an intubated patient: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure — confirm the tube and hand-ventilate. SUCTIONING is done ONLY when indicated (visible/audible secretions, high-pressure alarm, coughing, desaturation) — NOT on a fixed routine schedule — with HYPEROXYGENATION before/after, STERILE technique, limited duration (≤ 10-15 seconds per pass), monitoring for HYPOXEMIA, BRADYCARDIA/arrhythmia, and mucosal trauma; do NOT routinely instill normal saline into the tube. ETT/CUFF: secure the tube, document depth (cm at the lip), confirm placement (breath sounds + capnography), and maintain cuff pressure ~20-30 cmH2O.
labs.r: Assess the PATIENT, not just the machine. HIGH-pressure alarm = ↑resistance/↓compliance (secretions→suction, biting→bite block, kink, water in tubing, bronchospasm, PNEUMOTHORAX). LOW-pressure/low-volume alarm = LEAK/DISCONNECTION (reconnect circuit, cuff leak, tube displacement). DESATURATING + not quickly fixable → DISCONNECT + BVM + 100% O2 + call RT (DOPE: Displacement/Obstruction/Pneumothorax/Equipment). SUCTION only when indicated (not routine): hyperoxygenate, sterile, ≤10-15 sec, watch hypoxia/bradycardia; NO routine saline instillation. Cuff ~20-30 cmH2O; confirm tube depth/placement. RN role: troubleshoot alarms + protect oxygenation + airway care.

labs.n: Communication/comfort + complications + Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: COMMUNICATION/COMFORT/SAFETY: the intubated patient cannot speak — provide a COMMUNICATION board, writing, or yes/no questions; explain all care; treat PAIN and target LIGHT (not deep) sedation with daily assessment; provide EYE care (lubrication/lids) and oral care; prevent SELF-EXTUBATION using the least-restrictive effective measures; support the family; and prevent immobility complications with positioning, skin care, and early mobility/PT-OT. COMPLICATIONS to prevent/monitor: VAP; self/accidental EXTUBATION and tube displacement/MAINSTEM intubation (sudden distress, asymmetric breath sounds, falling SpO2 → confirm placement, manually ventilate); BAROTRAUMA/pneumothorax (sudden high-pressure alarm + decreased unilateral breath sounds + hypotension → emergency); OXYGEN toxicity (wean FiO2 to the lowest effective); GI stress ULCERS and VTE (prophylaxis); DELIRIUM (minimize sedation, reorient); and ICU-ACQUIRED WEAKNESS (early mobility). PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT silence/reset alarms without assessing the patient; did NOT leave a desaturating patient on a malfunctioning circuit to keep troubleshooting (used the BVM); did NOT suction routinely on a schedule or instill saline before suctioning; did NOT keep the patient flat or deeply/continuously oversedated; and did NOT over-inflate or ignore the cuff. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: airway secured and confirmed; bag-valve-mask + suction at the bedside; prompt patient-focused alarm response with manual ventilation when needed; the full VAP-prevention bundle; appropriate suctioning and cuff/tube care; light sedation with daily awakening/breathing trials; communication/comfort/eye-oral care; and complication prevention. EXPECTED outcome: the airway stays secure, alarms are correctly managed, VAP and other ventilator-associated harms are prevented, and the patient progresses toward weaning and extubation.
labs.r: Comfort/communication: communication board/writing/yes-no, explain care, treat pain + LIGHT sedation, eye + oral care, prevent self-extubation (least restrictive), early mobility/family. Complications: VAP, self/accidental extubation + mainstem, barotrauma/pneumothorax, O2 toxicity, ulcers/VTE, delirium, ICU weakness. Negatives confirm correct practice (didn't silence alarms blindly, didn't leave a desaturating patient on a bad circuit, no routine suction/saline instillation, not flat/oversedated, cuff managed). Protective: secured airway + BVM ready + patient-focused alarm response + VAP bundle + correct suction/cuff care + light sedation/SAT-SBT + comfort. RN role: comfort + complication prevention + liberation.

providerOrders: RESPIRATORY: mechanical ventilation for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure; lung-protective settings; respiratory therapy to manage the ventilator with the team; wean FiO2/PEEP to lowest effective; daily spontaneous awakening + breathing trial when safe

AIRWAY: secure endotracheal tube and document depth (cm at lip); confirm placement with bilateral breath sounds and waveform capnography; maintain cuff pressure ~20-30 cmH2O; keep bag-valve-mask and suction at the bedside at all times

VAP PREVENTION BUNDLE: head of bed 30-45° unless contraindicated; daily sedation interruption + extubation-readiness assessment; oral care with chlorhexidine and regular oral hygiene; subglottic secretion drainage if available; stress-ulcer prophylaxis; DVT/VTE prophylaxis; strict hand hygiene; avoid unnecessary circuit changes/breaks

ALARMS/SAFETY: respond to every alarm by assessing the patient; for a high-pressure alarm evaluate for secretions/biting/kink/water in tubing/bronchospasm/pneumothorax and correct; for a low-pressure/low-volume alarm evaluate for disconnection/cuff leak/tube displacement and restore the circuit; if the patient is desaturating/unstable and not quickly corrected, disconnect and manually ventilate with a BVM and 100% oxygen and call respiratory therapy (DOPE)

SUCTIONING: suction only when indicated (not on a fixed routine); hyperoxygenate before and after; sterile technique; limit each pass to ≤10-15 seconds; monitor SpO2 and heart rate; do NOT routinely instill normal saline
SEDATION/ANALGESIA: treat pain; target light sedation with a validated scale; daily sedation interruption

MONITORING: continuous pulse oximetry, waveform capnography, and cardiac monitoring; ABGs as indicated; monitor for VAP (fever, leukocytosis, purulent secretions, new infiltrate, worsening oxygenation) — obtain endotracheal aspirate culture and treat per HAP/VAP guidelines if suspected
COMFORT/COMMUNICATION: provide a communication board/writing/yes-no questions; explain all care; eye care; prevent self-extubation using least-restrictive measures; involve and update the family

MOBILITY/COMPLICATIONS: reposition and provide skin care; early mobility/PT-OT as tolerated; monitor for barotrauma/pneumothorax, accidental extubation/mainstem intubation, delirium, and ICU-acquired weakness

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters in caring for this ventilated patient?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: He is intubated and mechanically ventilated — airway security, VAP prevention, and correct alarm response are central nursing responsibilities
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the framework for safe care of any ventilated patient. RN role: airway + prevention + alarms.

opts.text: The VAP-prevention bundle (HOB ≥30°, oral chlorhexidine, daily sedation interruption/readiness, subglottic suction, DVT + stress-ulcer prophylaxis, hand hygiene) reduces ventilator-associated pneumonia
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — VAP is preventable with the bundle. RN role: deliver the VAP bundle.

opts.text: A HIGH-pressure alarm signals increased airway resistance or decreased compliance (secretions, biting, kink, bronchospasm, or pneumothorax) — assess and correct the cause
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — high-pressure alarms point to reversible (and some dangerous) causes. RN role: assess + correct.

opts.text: A LOW-pressure / low-exhaled-volume alarm signals a leak or disconnection (circuit disconnect, cuff leak, tube displacement) — restore a closed system
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — low-pressure alarms mean lost pressure that must be restored. RN role: find and fix the leak/disconnection.

opts.text: If he desaturates and the cause cannot be quickly corrected, disconnect from the ventilator and manually ventilate with a BVM and 100% O2 while calling for help (DOPE)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — oxygenation comes before troubleshooting a machine. RN role: manual ventilation when unstable.

opts.text: Endotracheal tube/cuff care, suctioning only when indicated (hyperoxygenate, sterile, ≤10-15 sec), and communication/comfort are essential
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — airway care, appropriate suctioning, and comfort are core to safe ventilator care. RN role: airway care + comfort.

opts.text: Silence and reset the ventilator alarms without assessing the patient, since alarms are usually false
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + DANGEROUS. Alarms must trigger a patient assessment; silencing them blindly can miss a disconnection, obstruction, or pneumothorax.

opts.text: Keep the patient flat and deep-suction routinely every hour on a fixed schedule whether or not secretions are present
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Flat positioning raises aspiration/VAP risk, and routine scheduled suctioning causes hypoxemia and mucosal trauma — suction only when indicated and keep the head of bed elevated.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: VAP is a preventable hospital-acquired infection; head-of-bed elevation, oral care, and minimizing sedation are key bundle elements that lower it
opts.rat: CORRECT — the VAP/bundle principle. Foundation for prevention.

opts.text: High-pressure alarms reflect increased resistance or decreased compliance; common reversible causes include secretions, a kinked tube, biting, and bronchospasm
opts.rat: CORRECT — high-pressure alarm causes. Foundation for troubleshooting.

opts.text: Low-pressure / low-volume alarms reflect a leak or disconnection; the priority is restoring a closed, functioning circuit
opts.rat: CORRECT — low-pressure alarm meaning. Foundation for the correct fix.

opts.text: When the patient is unstable and the problem isn't quickly fixable, manual ventilation with a BVM + 100% O2 protects the patient (DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment)
opts.rat: CORRECT — the emergency safety rule and DOPE framework. Foundation for protecting oxygenation.

opts.text: Suctioning is done only when indicated, with hyperoxygenation and limited duration, because it can cause hypoxemia, bradycardia, and mucosal trauma
opts.rat: CORRECT — appropriate suctioning principle. Foundation for safe airway clearance.

opts.text: Cuff pressure is maintained around 20-30 cmH2O and tube position/depth confirmed to prevent aspiration, leaks, and tracheal injury
opts.rat: CORRECT — cuff/tube principle. Foundation for airway integrity.

opts.text: Routine deep suctioning on a schedule and instilling normal saline before each suction pass improve outcomes
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Routine suctioning and saline instillation are not recommended — they cause hypoxemia/trauma and can push secretions/contaminants downward; suction only when indicated.

opts.text: Ventilator alarms should be permanently silenced or disabled so they do not disturb the patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Alarms are critical safety signals and must remain active; they are assessed and addressed, never disabled.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Rank the priorities when an alarm sounds with desaturation
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Assess the patient (airway/breathing/oxygenation) when the alarm sounds; if not quickly correctable and he is desaturating, manually ventilate with a BVM + 100% O2 and call for help
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Protecting oxygenation and assessing the patient come first — never troubleshoot a machine while the patient deteriorates. RN role: assess + manually ventilate if needed.

opts.text: Identify and correct the specific alarm cause (high-pressure: suction/unkink/bite block/treat bronchospasm; low-pressure: reconnect/fix leak/cuff)
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Once oxygenation is secured, fixing the cause restores effective ventilation. RN role: targeted troubleshooting.

opts.text: Maintain airway safety — secure the tube, confirm placement/depth and cuff pressure, and suction appropriately
opts.rat: #3 — Ensures the airway remains correct and patent. RN role: airway/tube/cuff care.

opts.text: Deliver the VAP-prevention bundle (HOB ≥30°, oral chlorhexidine, sedation/readiness assessment, prophylaxis, hand hygiene)
opts.rat: #4 — Prevents the most important ventilator-associated infection over the stay. RN role: VAP bundle.

opts.text: Provide communication, comfort, and eye/oral care, and assess readiness to wean/extubate
opts.rat: #5 — Comfort, dignity, and liberation readiness round out safe care. RN role: comfort + weaning assessment.

opts.text: Assess the patient when an alarm sounds and manually ventilate with a BVM + 100% O2 if the cause is not quickly correctable

opts.text: For a high-pressure alarm, suction secretions, relieve a kinked tube or biting (bite block), and treat bronchospasm

opts.text: For a low-pressure/low-volume alarm, check for and correct a disconnection, cuff leak, or tube displacement

opts.rat: Reduces aspiration and ventilator-associated pneumonia. RN role: VAP bundle.

opts.text: Repeatedly silence and reset alarms without assessing the patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — alarms must prompt a patient assessment; blind silencing can miss a disconnection, obstruction, or pneumothorax.

opts.text: Instill normal saline into the tube and deep-suction routinely every hour regardless of need
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — routine suctioning and saline instillation cause hypoxemia/trauma and may worsen infection; suction only when indicated.

opts.text: Keep the patient flat and continuously deeply sedated to keep him quiet
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — flat positioning increases VAP risk and deep continuous sedation prolongs ventilation and increases delirium; keep HOB elevated and target light sedation.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: Action sequence when the alarm sounds
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Respond to the alarm by assessing the patient (airway/breathing/SpO2); if he is desaturating/unstable and not quickly fixable, disconnect and manually ventilate with a BVM + 100% O2 and call respiratory therapy
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Assess and protect oxygenation before anything else. RN role: assess + manual ventilation.

opts.text: Identify and correct the specific alarm cause (high- vs low-pressure)
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Fix the underlying problem to restore effective ventilation. RN role: targeted troubleshooting.

opts.text: Secure the airway and suction appropriately (hyperoxygenate, sterile, brief), and confirm cuff pressure/tube position
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Keep the airway correct and patent. RN role: airway/tube/cuff care.

opts.text: Re-establish the VAP-prevention bundle and prophylaxis, and document the event and response
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Sustain infection prevention and the record. RN role: VAP bundle + documentation.

opts.text: Provide communication and comfort, support the family, and assess readiness to wean
opts.rat: #5 — Closing/ongoing. Comfort and liberation readiness complete safe care. RN role: comfort + weaning assessment.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: On the high-pressure alarm the nurse assessed the patient, found and suctioned secretions, and the peak pressure normalized with SpO2 recovering
opts.rat: Correct patient-focused troubleshooting resolved a reversible cause. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: On the low-pressure alarm with desaturation, the nurse manually ventilated with a BVM + 100% O2, found and corrected a circuit disconnection, and oxygenation recovered
opts.rat: Protecting oxygenation first and restoring the circuit is the model response. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: The full VAP bundle is maintained; he stays afebrile with a normal white count and no new infiltrate (no VAP) while FiO2/PEEP are weaned
opts.rat: Bundle adherence preventing VAP with improving oxygenation. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: He passes the awakening/breathing-trial readiness screen and tolerates a spontaneous breathing trial, progressing toward extubation
opts.rat: Liberation readiness reflects effective, complication-free ventilator care. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the nurse silenced and reset the alarms without assessing the patient; an unrecognized circuit disconnection led to severe desaturation
opts.rat: ⚠️ Blindly silencing alarms missed a disconnection and caused harm. Demonstrates why every alarm prompts a patient assessment.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — routine hourly deep suctioning with saline instillation was performed regardless of need; he became hypoxemic with mucosal trauma and a new infection
opts.rat: ⚠️ Routine suctioning and saline instillation caused hypoxemia, trauma, and infection. Demonstrates suctioning only when indicated without saline.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the patient was kept flat and continuously deeply sedated; he developed ventilator-associated pneumonia and prolonged ventilation with delirium
opts.rat: ⚠️ Flat positioning and deep continuous sedation increased VAP, ventilator days, and delirium. Demonstrates HOB elevation and light sedation/daily interruption.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — a sudden high-pressure alarm with unilateral absent breath sounds and hypotension was treated by silencing the alarm; an untreated tension pneumothorax progressed
opts.rat: ⚠️ A dangerous cause (pneumothorax) was missed by not assessing. Demonstrates that high-pressure alarms can signal emergencies requiring assessment and escalation.

opts.text: Early in the shift, hemodynamically stable on unchanged settings with the bundle maintained, he does not yet meet weaning criteria
opts.rat: A stable baseline before meeting weaning criteria is expected; continue the bundle and reassess readiness. Unchanged is appropriate here.

opts.text: At reassessment the airway remains secure and confirmed, alarms are correctly managed, and no ventilator-associated events have occurred
opts.rat: Sustained safe ventilator care with no associated harm. Ideal trajectory toward liberation.

title: Proactive Outpatient Advance Care Planning at a Medicare Annual Wellness Visit for a CAPABLE 75-Year-Old Man with Chronic Heart Failure, CKD Stage 3, and Early Mild Cognitive Impairment (No Advance Directive on File): Distinguishing the LIVING WILL from the DURABLE POWER OF ATTORNEY FOR HEALTHCARE, Adding a POLST/MOLST as a Portable Clinician's Order, Confirming Decision-Making Capacity, Eliciting Values and Goals of Care, Selecting and EDUCATING a Surrogate, Clarifying What a DNR/DNAR Order Does and Does NOT Mean, and Ensuring Cross-Setting Portability — All Without Coercion
subtitle: ADVANCE CARE PLANNING (ACP) is the process by which a person clarifies and communicates their values, goals, and treatment preferences for FUTURE medical care in case they lose decision-making capacity — and identifies a SURROGATE who can speak for them. Done PROACTIVELY in the outpatient setting with a CAPABLE patient (and not waiting for a crisis or surrogate conflict), ACP preserves autonomy, reduces decisional burden on family, aligns care with values, and decreases unwanted aggressive treatment at the end of life. This case is the proactive outpatient/wellness-visit ACP conversation — distinct from acute family conflict over honoring an existing directive (case-092), surrogate decision-making when the patient already LACKS capacity (case-132), and capacity assessment for a current decision/'dignity of risk' (case-116). TWO BROAD CATEGORIES of document apply. (A) ADVANCE DIRECTIVES — completed by any adult with capacity, for FUTURE possible incapacity: a LIVING WILL (instructional directive) states what treatments the patient WOULD WANT or REFUSE under specific future conditions (e.g., mechanical ventilation, artificial nutrition/hydration, dialysis, antibiotics in terminal illness); a DURABLE POWER OF ATTORNEY FOR HEALTHCARE (DPOA-HC / healthcare proxy / agent) names a SURROGATE authorized to make decisions if the patient cannot — high yield: a DPOA-HC alone is often more useful than a living will because no document can anticipate every clinical scenario, and a well-informed surrogate can. (B) POLST / MOLST (Physician/Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is NOT an advance directive — it is a portable, signed CLINICIAN'S ORDER for CURRENT treatment preferences in seriously ill or frail patients; it covers CPR (Attempt vs Do Not Attempt), level of intervention (Full / Selective / Comfort-focused), and medically administered nutrition; it TRAVELS across settings (home, EMS, ED, hospital, SNF), is followed by emergency responders, and SUPPLEMENTS (does NOT replace) an advance directive. Documents are STATE-SPECIFIC (witnesses, notary, forms): execute per state law and review when moving states. CONFIRM CAPACITY first (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate a stable choice) — capacity is DECISION-SPECIFIC and presumed; mild cognitive impairment ALONE, an unwise choice, age, or disagreement do NOT equal incapacity (link to [[case-116]]). ELICIT VALUES and goals (open questions: 'what makes life meaningful?' 'what worries you most?' 'what trade-offs would you accept?'), explore cultural, religious, and personal context, and use plain language at the patient's health-literacy level. EDUCATE about code status: a DNR/DNAR/AND order limits ONLY cardiopulmonary resuscitation in cardiac arrest — it does NOT mean 'no care' (other treatments continue per the plan), does NOT require unit transfer, and does NOT preclude hospice/aggressive comfort care. SURROGATE SELECTION + EDUCATION: choose someone who knows the patient's values, is willing and able to advocate, can manage stress, and is reachable; the patient should EDUCATE the surrogate about his values so the surrogate can apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT later. Document and ensure CROSS-SETTING PORTABILITY: file in the chart/EHR, give copies to the patient/family/healthcare agent, send copies to PCP and specialists and the local hospital, and consider a wallet card; a properly signed POLST belongs visibly in the home for EMS. Frame ACP as an ongoing PROCESS, not a one-time form: revisit at the next Annual Wellness Visit and around the 'five Ds' — Decade (new), Death (in family), Divorce, Diagnosis (new), Decline — and when goals change. Respect AUTONOMY including the right to DEFER or DECLINE ACP — never coerce; never sign documents the patient does not understand. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: making decisions for him 'because he's old and sick'; treating mild cognitive impairment as automatic incapacity and bypassing him; pressuring a specific code status; telling him a DNR means no care/transfer; completing documents but never sharing them across settings (the most common operational failure); confusing POLST with an advance directive or expecting a living will to anticipate every scenario. NURSING ROLE: confirm capacity, elicit values, educate the patient/family in plain language about advance directives + POLST/MOLST + code status, support surrogate selection and surrogate education, coordinate proper document execution per state law, ensure cross-setting portability, document objectively, and treat ACP as an ongoing values-based conversation.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + the proactive outpatient ACP framework
labs.v: 75 y/o man K. Pelletier (CHF NYHA II / EF 38%, CKD stage 3a, HTN, mild cognitive impairment with PRESERVED capacity) at his Medicare Annual Wellness Visit, with NO advance directive, no DPOA-HC, and no POLST — and a stated wish to 'get my paperwork in order.' Proactive outpatient ACP done now, while he can speak for himself, preserves autonomy, reduces surrogate distress, and aligns future care with his values. It is distinct from acute conflict over an EXISTING directive ([[case-092]]), surrogate decision-making for an INCAPACITATED patient with no proxy ([[case-132]]), and capacity assessment for a CURRENT decision/dignity of risk ([[case-116]]). The nurse's flow: confirm capacity → elicit values/goals → educate about the document types and code status in plain language → support surrogate selection + EDUCATION → coordinate document execution per state law → ensure cross-setting PORTABILITY → frame ACP as an ongoing process. Throughout: respect autonomy (including the right to defer/decline) and document objectively.
labs.r: Proactive outpatient ACP for a CAPABLE older adult with serious illness preserves autonomy, reduces surrogate burden, and aligns care with values. Flow: confirm capacity → elicit values → educate (AD types + POLST + code status) → surrogate selection + EDUCATION → execute per state law → portability → ongoing process. Respect autonomy (incl. right to defer/decline); document. RN role: facilitate without coercion.

labs.n: Types of ADVANCE DIRECTIVES + POLST/MOLST distinction + DNR/DNAR clarifications
labs.v: TWO categories of document apply. (A) ADVANCE DIRECTIVES (any capable adult, for FUTURE possible incapacity): the LIVING WILL is an INSTRUCTIONAL directive stating what treatments the patient would WANT or REFUSE in specific future conditions (e.g., mechanical ventilation, artificial nutrition/hydration, dialysis, antibiotics in terminal illness, CPR); the DURABLE POWER OF ATTORNEY FOR HEALTHCARE (DPOA-HC / healthcare proxy / agent) DESIGNATES a SURROGATE to decide if the patient loses capacity — high yield: the DPOA-HC alone is often more useful than a living will because no document anticipates every scenario but an educated surrogate can apply substituted judgment. (B) POLST / MOLST is NOT an advance directive — it is a portable, signed CLINICIAN'S ORDER for CURRENT preferences in seriously ill/frail patients, covering CPR (Attempt vs Do Not Attempt), level of intervention (Full / Selective / Comfort-focused), and medically administered nutrition; it TRAVELS across settings (home, EMS, ED, hospital, SNF), is followed by emergency responders, and SUPPLEMENTS (does NOT replace) the advance directive. CODE STATUS: a DNR/DNAR/AND order limits ONLY CARDIOPULMONARY RESUSCITATION in cardiac arrest — it does NOT mean 'no care' (other treatments continue per plan), it does NOT require a different unit, and it does NOT preclude hospice/aggressive comfort care. Documents are STATE-SPECIFIC (forms, witnesses, notary): execute per state law; review when moving states. Teach in plain language at the patient's health-literacy level.
labs.r: ADVANCE DIRECTIVES: LIVING WILL = treatment preferences for FUTURE conditions; DPOA-HC = NAMES a surrogate (often more useful — no form anticipates everything). POLST/MOLST = portable CLINICIAN'S ORDER for CURRENT preferences in seriously ill/frail pts (CPR/level/nutrition); travels across settings; SUPPLEMENTS — does NOT replace — the AD. DNR/DNAR/AND limits ONLY CPR — not 'no care,' no unit transfer, compatible w/ comfort care. STATE-SPECIFIC documents — execute per state law. RN role: teach the distinctions in plain language.

labs.n: Capacity, surrogate selection + EDUCATION, values, cultural sensitivity
labs.v: CAPACITY (decision-specific, presumed): the four-element test — understand information, appreciate how it applies to him, reason through options, and communicate a stable choice; mild cognitive impairment ALONE, an unwise choice, age, or disagreement do NOT equal incapacity ([[case-116]]). Screen/optimize reversible factors (delirium, depression, pain, sensory aids) before declaring durable incapacity. SURROGATE SELECTION: a DPOA-HC should be someone who knows the patient's values, is WILLING and ABLE to advocate, can manage stress, and is reachable — not necessarily the eldest child or default spouse; he may name an alternate. The patient must EDUCATE the surrogate about his values and likely preferences so the surrogate can apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what the patient would want) — not their own preferences — when the time comes. Include the family in the conversation when the patient consents. VALUES elicitation uses OPEN questions ('what makes life meaningful?', 'what worries you most about getting sicker?', 'what trade-offs would you accept?', 'have you watched a loved one go through serious illness?') and avoids leading or scaring. CULTURAL/RELIGIOUS sensitivity: ACP norms vary; some traditions emphasize family-centered or collective decision-making; clarify the patient's preferred role and involve chaplaincy/cultural broker as desired — but always preserve his autonomy. The nurse FACILITATES the conversation, never coerces, and supports the patient's right to DEFER or DECLINE ACP.
labs.r: CAPACITY = decision-specific, presumed: understand/appreciate/reason/communicate stable choice (MCI/age/unwise choice/disagreement ≠ incapacity); optimize reversible factors. SURROGATE = knows values, willing/able to advocate, reachable; EDUCATE the surrogate about values to apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT later. Elicit values w/ OPEN questions. Cultural/religious sensitivity (collective decision-making OK if patient chooses); chaplain/broker on request. Facilitate without coercion; respect the right to defer/decline. RN role: facilitate, never coerce.

labs.n: Document execution + cross-setting portability + follow-up + Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: EXECUTION: follow state-specific requirements (witnesses, notary, forms); the LIVING WILL and DPOA-HC are signed by the patient (and witnesses/notary); a POLST is signed by a clinician (and many states also require patient/surrogate signature). PORTABILITY (the most common operational failure point): file in the chart and EHR; give COPIES to the patient, the wife/DPOA-HC, and the alternate (daughter); share with the PCP, cardiology, and the local hospital ED; provide a wallet card; place the POLST in a visible location at home for EMS. Verify documents are actually accessible — a perfect document that lives only in a clinic chart fails when the patient arrives in an ED elsewhere. FOLLOW-UP: ACP is an ongoing PROCESS. Revisit at every AWV and around the 'five Ds' — Decade (new), Death (of someone close), Divorce, new Diagnosis, Decline — and any time goals change; remind him he can change his mind at any time. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT make decisions for him 'because he is older and has multiple conditions'; did NOT treat mild cognitive impairment as automatic incapacity and bypass him; did NOT pressure him toward a particular code status or have him sign documents he did not understand; did NOT tell him a DNR means 'no care' or that he would be moved to a different ward; and did NOT complete documents without ensuring portability and access across settings. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: proactive timing while capacity is intact; capacity confirmed; values-based, plain-language conversation; correct teaching of advance directives vs POLST and accurate DNR clarification; surrogate selected and EDUCATED about values; family included with consent and cultural sensitivity; documents executed per state law and made portable; ongoing-process framing; objective documentation. EXPECTED outcome: his autonomy is preserved, his wishes are clear and accessible, his surrogate is prepared to advocate for him, and the care team can honor his goals across settings.
labs.r: EXECUTION per state law (witnesses/notary); LIVING WILL/DPOA-HC = patient-signed; POLST = clinician-signed. PORTABILITY = the common failure: chart/EHR + copies to patient/wife/agent/daughter + share w/ PCP/cardiology/local hospital + wallet card + POLST visible at home. FOLLOW-UP = ongoing process: every AWV + 'five Ds' (Decade/Death/Divorce/Diagnosis/Decline); he can change his mind. Negatives confirm correct practice (didn't decide for him, didn't treat MCI as incapacity, didn't coerce/pressure, didn't say DNR = no care, didn't skip portability). Protective: proactive timing + capacity + plain-language values conversation + correct AD/POLST teaching + educated surrogate + cultural sensitivity + portable documents + ongoing process + documentation. RN role: facilitate + execute + portability.

nursesNote: Outpatient clinic — Medicare AWV. 75 y/o man, CHF NYHA II (LVEF 38%), CKD 3a (eGFR 48), HTN, mild cognitive impairment with PRESERVED CAPACITY on prior formal eval. NO advance directive, no DPOA-HC, no POLST on file. He requests proactive ACP. Wife at bedside, adult daughter on speakerphone. ACP flow: (1) CAPACITY confirmed (understands/appreciates/reasons/communicates stable choice; MCI alone ≠ incapacity); reversible factors screened. (2) VALUES elicited with OPEN questions — independence, time with family, quality over length, fears prolonged ICU/mechanical ventilation. (3) EDUCATED in plain language on the two categories: ADVANCE DIRECTIVES — LIVING WILL (future treatment preferences) + DURABLE POA-HC (NAMES a surrogate; often the most useful piece since no form anticipates every scenario); POLST/MOLST — portable CLINICIAN'S ORDER for CURRENT preferences in seriously ill/frail patients (CPR/level/nutrition) that TRAVELS across settings and SUPPLEMENTS (does NOT replace) the AD; DNR/DNAR/AND limits ONLY CPR — NOT 'no care,' no unit transfer, compatible w/ comfort/hospice care. State-specific documents acknowledged. (4) SURROGATE selected — wife as primary DPOA-HC + daughter as alternate — and EDUCATED about his values so they can apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT later (not their own preferences). Family included with his consent; cultural/religious context explored; chaplain offered. No coercion; his right to defer/decline respected. (5) EXECUTION per state law (witnesses/notary as required); PCP signed a POLST consistent with his stated wishes (SELECTIVE INTERVENTION + Do Not Attempt CPR). (6) PORTABILITY — copies filed in chart/EHR, given to patient/wife/daughter, shared with cardiology + local hospital + ED; wallet card carried; POLST visible at home for EMS. (7) Framed as an ongoing PROCESS — revisit at next AWV + around the 'five Ds' (Decade/Death/Divorce/Diagnosis/Decline) or any change; he can change his mind anytime. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT decide for him, did NOT treat MCI as automatic incapacity, did NOT pressure a code status or have him sign what he didn't understand, did NOT say DNR = no care, did NOT skip portability. Documentation objective and contemporaneous; team aligned; wife/daughter prepared.
providerOrders: VISIT: Medicare Annual Wellness Visit with Advance Care Planning (ACP) element; outpatient primary care

CAPACITY: confirm decision-making capacity (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate stable choice); screen/optimize reversible factors (delirium, depression, pain, sensory aids); MCI alone does not equal incapacity

ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: facilitate a values-based ACP conversation in plain language; respect autonomy including the right to defer or decline; do not coerce or sign documents the patient does not understand

EDUCATION: teach the distinction between advance directives (living will + durable POA-HC) and POLST/MOLST as a portable clinician's order; clarify what a DNR/DNAR/AND order does and does not mean (only limits CPR; not 'no care'; not unit transfer; compatible with hospice/comfort care)

SURROGATE: support selection of a primary DPOA-HC and an alternate; educate the surrogate(s) about the patient's values so they can apply substituted judgment; involve family with the patient's consent
DOCUMENTS: complete and execute advance directive (living will + DPOA-HC) per state law (witnesses/notary as required); PCP to sign a POLST consistent with the patient's stated preferences

PORTABILITY: file copies in the chart and EHR; provide copies to the patient, primary surrogate (wife), and alternate (daughter); share with cardiology, the local hospital ED, and other specialists; provide a wallet card; place the POLST in a visible location at home for EMS
CULTURAL/SPIRITUAL: explore cultural and religious preferences; offer chaplaincy and cultural broker as desired; preserve the patient's autonomy throughout

FOLLOW-UP: frame ACP as an ongoing process — revisit at each Annual Wellness Visit and around the 'five Ds' (Decade, Death, Divorce, Diagnosis, Decline) or any change in goals; remind the patient he can change his mind at any time

DOCUMENTATION: objective, contemporaneous record of capacity, values elicited, education delivered, surrogate selection and education, documents executed, where copies were sent, and the patient's expressed wishes (in his own words)

opts.text: A capable older adult with serious chronic illness and NO advance directive on file — proactive ACP is indicated while he can speak for himself
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the timing (capable, before a crisis) is what makes ACP most useful. RN role: facilitate proactively.

opts.text: Two categories of document apply: ADVANCE DIRECTIVES (living will + durable POA-HC) for future incapacity, and POLST/MOLST as a portable clinician's order for current preferences in seriously ill/frail patients

opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — capacity is decision-specific and presumed; MCI/age/unwise choice ≠ incapacity. RN role: confirm capacity.

opts.text: The surrogate (DPOA-HC) must be educated about the patient's values so they can apply substituted judgment later
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a named surrogate is only useful if they actually know the patient's values. RN role: support surrogate education.

opts.text: A DNR/DNAR/AND order limits ONLY CPR — it does NOT mean 'no care,' does NOT require a unit transfer, and is compatible with comfort/hospice care

opts.text: Capacity is decision-specific and presumed; mild cognitive impairment, age, an unwise choice, or disagreement do not by themselves equal incapacity

opts.text: Confirm capacity, elicit values/goals with open questions, and use plain-language teaching at his health-literacy level
opts.rat: Capacity and values anchor the entire conversation; plain language supports informed choice. RN role: capacity + values + plain language.

opts.text: Explain living will, durable POA-HC, and POLST/MOLST distinctions and clarify what a DNR/DNAR order does and does not mean
opts.rat: Accurate education enables informed decisions. RN role: teach the distinctions.

opts.text: Support selection of a primary and alternate surrogate and educate them about his values so they can apply substituted judgment
opts.rat: An informed surrogate is essential to substituted judgment. RN role: surrogate selection + education.

opts.text: Complete and execute the advance directive per state law; have the PCP sign a POLST consistent with his stated preferences
opts.rat: Valid documents reflecting his wishes are the operational output. RN role: coordinate execution.

opts.text: Ensure cross-setting portability — chart/EHR + copies to patient/family + share with PCP/specialists/local hospital + visible POLST at home
opts.rat: Documents must reach the point of care; portability is the most common operational failure. RN role: ensure access.

opts.text: Respect his autonomy — including the right to defer or decline ACP — and frame ACP as an ongoing process to revisit
opts.rat: Autonomy includes the right to decline; ACP is a process, not a one-time form. RN role: respect + revisit.

opts.text: Explore cultural and religious considerations and offer chaplaincy/cultural broker, while preserving his autonomy
opts.rat: Cultural sensitivity makes ACP authentic to the patient. RN role: include cultural/spiritual context.

opts.text: Decide the code status and treatment plan for him because he is older and has multiple conditions
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — deciding for a capable patient ignores autonomy. ACP is patient-centered.

opts.text: Pressure him to choose DNR and have him sign documents he does not understand
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — coercion and uninformed signing invalidate the process. Educate, do not pressure.

opts.text: Tell him a DNR means no care will be provided and he will be moved to a separate ward
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — a DNR limits only CPR; other care continues per plan, with no required unit transfer.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Confirm capacity and elicit values and goals using open questions in plain language
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Anchors the conversation in the patient's own values. RN role: capacity + values.

opts.text: Teach the distinction between living will, durable POA-HC, and POLST/MOLST, and clarify what a DNR/DNAR order does and does not mean
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Informed understanding precedes informed choices. RN role: education.

opts.text: Facilitate surrogate selection and education; include family with his consent and explore cultural/religious context
opts.rat: #3 — Third. A named, informed surrogate is central to substituted judgment. RN role: surrogate selection + education.

opts.text: Complete and execute documents per state law and ensure cross-setting portability and access
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Turns the conversation into operational, accessible care plans. RN role: execute + make portable.

opts.text: Document objectively and contemporaneously and frame ACP as an ongoing process to revisit
opts.rat: #5 — Closing/ongoing. Sustains alignment with values over time. RN role: document + revisit.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action/outcome, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The nurse confirmed capacity, elicited values in plain language, taught the document distinctions accurately, and supported surrogate selection and education
opts.rat: Patient-centered, values-based ACP is the standard. Supports autonomy.

opts.text: The advance directive (living will + DPOA-HC) was executed per state law and the PCP signed a POLST consistent with his stated wishes
opts.rat: Valid documents that match his words. Operationalizes his wishes.

opts.text: Copies were filed in the chart/EHR, given to the patient and surrogates, and shared with cardiology and the local hospital ED — and the POLST is visible at home for EMS
opts.rat: Portability is the key operational success. Documents that follow him.

opts.text: ACP was framed as an ongoing process with planned reassessment at the next AWV and around the 'five Ds' — and he understands he can change his mind anytime
opts.rat: Sustained, values-aligned care over time. Correct framing.

opts.text: Alternative — the team decided his code status without his input because he is older and has multiple conditions
opts.rat: ⚠️ Ignores his preserved capacity and autonomy. Demonstrates the central error to avoid.

opts.text: Alternative — the nurse pressured him to choose DNR and had him sign documents he did not understand
opts.rat: ⚠️ Coercion and uninformed signing invalidate consent. Educate, do not pressure.

opts.text: Alternative — he was told a DNR means 'no care' and that he would be moved to a separate ward
opts.rat: ⚠️ A DNR limits only CPR; other care continues per plan, with no required unit transfer.

opts.text: Alternative — documents were completed but filed only in the clinic chart with no copies shared; in a later ED visit the team did not know his wishes
opts.rat: ⚠️ Portability failure is the most common operational error in ACP. Always share across settings.

opts.text: Alternative — staff treated mild cognitive impairment as automatic incapacity and bypassed him to ask the wife to decide
opts.rat: ⚠️ MCI alone does not equal incapacity; capacity is decision-specific and presumed.

opts.text: He left empowered, with accessible documents, an educated surrogate, and the understanding that he can update his wishes anytime
opts.rat: The ideal outcome of proactive outpatient ACP. Autonomy preserved; wishes accessible.

title: Discharge Teaching for a 68-Year-Old Woman with NEWLY DIAGNOSED Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation Started on the DIRECT ORAL ANTICOAGULANT (DOAC) APIXABAN 5 mg PO BID for Stroke Prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc 4 = High Stroke Risk): WHY Lifelong Anticoagulation, Exact Dose/Timing and the DOAC-Specific MISSED-DOSE Rule, the Key Distinctions from WARFARIN (NO Routine INR, NO Vitamin K Dietary Restriction), Drug/Food Interactions (NSAID AVOIDANCE; CYP3A4 + P-gp Inhibitors/Inducers), Bleeding Precautions and the SIGNS of Bleeding to Report, Perioperative Holds, Reversal Availability (Andexanet Alfa), Medical-Alert ID, and ADHERENCE/Follow-Up
subtitle: DIRECT ORAL ANTICOAGULANTS (DOACs) — apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran — have largely replaced warfarin for stroke prevention in NONVALVULAR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION (NVAF) and for treatment of venous thromboembolism. They have predictable pharmacokinetics, do NOT require routine coagulation (INR/PT) monitoring, and have FEW food interactions — a major shift from warfarin. NURSING TEACHING is the heart of safe DOAC use, because ADHERENCE and BLEEDING SAFETY are entirely patient-driven. INDICATION here: a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 4 (age 65-74 = 1, female sex = 1, hypertension = 1, diabetes = 1) places her at HIGH annual stroke risk; anticoagulation is indicated for stroke prevention and is LIFELONG unless AFib is permanently eliminated. APIXABAN is a direct factor Xa inhibitor; the standard NVAF dose is 5 mg PO BID; DOSE REDUCTION to 2.5 mg BID applies if she meets 2 of 3: age >= 80, weight <= 60 kg, serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (she meets none and stays on 5 mg BID). DOSING/TIMING: BID, about 12 hours apart, with or without food, with water. MISSED DOSE (high yield and DOAC-specific): if remembered on the SAME day, take it as soon as remembered and continue the schedule; if she misses it and it is already CLOSE to the next dose (the next day for a BID schedule), SKIP the missed dose and resume — NEVER DOUBLE UP. MONITORING is KEY DIFFERENCE FROM WARFARIN: NO routine INR/PT — predictable PK means no titration; instead obtain periodic CBC and renal/hepatic function (apixaban dosing follows renal function; significant changes in renal function may shift dose). INTERACTIONS: AVOID NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) and aspirin/other antiplatelets unless directed — additive GI/intracranial bleeding risk; use ACETAMINOPHEN for pain. STRONG dual CYP3A4 + P-glycoprotein INHIBITORS (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, clarithromycin) RAISE apixaban levels and bleeding risk and require dose adjustment or avoidance. STRONG dual CYP3A4 + P-gp INDUCERS (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, ST JOHN'S WORT) LOWER apixaban levels and reduce stroke protection — avoid. Avoid combining with other anticoagulants. DIET: there is NO vitamin K restriction with DOACs (unlike warfarin) — she may eat normal amounts of leafy greens (broccoli, spinach, kale); a frequent over-teaching error is applying warfarin dietary rules to DOACs. ALCOHOL: moderation, since heavy use raises bleeding risk. BLEEDING PRECAUTIONS: soft toothbrush, electric razor, avoid contact sports, watch for falls; carry a MEDICAL-ALERT ID and a wallet card stating she takes apixaban. SIGNS OF BLEEDING to report immediately — overt: nosebleed that will not stop, blood in urine (pink/red), black-tarry or bloody stool, vomiting blood or 'coffee grounds,' heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, unusual bruising; OCCULT/SERIOUS: severe headache, sudden severe abdominal or back pain, sudden weakness/numbness, change in vision, dizziness, fainting (possible intracranial or retroperitoneal hemorrhage). PERIOPERATIVE: do NOT stop without her provider's direction; planned procedures require provider-coordinated holds based on procedure bleeding risk and her renal function (typically 24-48 hours for moderate risk; longer for higher risk or impaired renal function); inform ALL providers (dentists, surgeons, ED, gastroenterology) that she takes apixaban. REVERSAL/EMERGENCIES: andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban/rivaroxaban) in life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding; 4F-PCC may be used when andexanet alfa is unavailable; if she has a fall with head strike, severe bleeding, or signs of intracranial bleed, she should go to the ED immediately and state she takes apixaban. ADHERENCE is the single most important predictor of effectiveness — missed doses lose stroke protection within HOURS due to short half-life; encourage a pill organizer/phone reminder, keep refills stocked, and explore cost/insurance/assistance programs (DOACs are expensive — non-adherence due to cost is common and dangerous). PREGNANCY: not recommended; counsel women of childbearing potential. CARDIOVERSION nuance: if AFib has been present >48 hours (or unknown duration), 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation is required BEFORE elective cardioversion (or TEE to exclude left-atrial thrombus). FOLLOW-UP: lifelong anticoagulation while AFib persists; reassess CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED periodically; periodic CBC/renal/hepatic labs; do NOT self-discontinue. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: applying warfarin's vitamin-K dietary rules to a DOAC; taking ibuprofen/aspirin for routine pain; doubling up after a missed dose; stopping the drug whenever she 'feels fine' (AFib is often asymptomatic, but stroke risk persists); not informing dentists/surgeons; not carrying medical-alert ID. NURSING ROLE: teach the WHY (NVAF + CHA2DS2-VASc → lifelong stroke prevention), the exact regimen and DOAC-specific missed-dose rule, the WARFARIN-vs-DOAC distinctions (no routine INR, no vitamin K restriction), interactions (NSAID avoidance, CYP3A4 + P-gp inhibitors/inducers), bleeding precautions and the signs to report, perioperative coordination and reversal awareness, and a robust adherence plan — verified by TEACH-BACK with the patient and family.

labs.v: 68 y/o woman E. Wagner with newly diagnosed NONVALVULAR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION (clinic ECG), HTN, T2DM, osteoarthritis (routine ibuprofen — to STOP). CHA2DS2-VASc = 4 (age 65-74 = 1, female sex = 1, HTN = 1, DM = 1) = HIGH annual stroke risk → anticoagulation indicated for stroke prevention; HAS-BLED reviewed and modifiable risk factors addressed. Provider chose APIXABAN — a direct factor Xa inhibitor — over warfarin for predictable PK, no routine INR monitoring, fewer food interactions, and a favorable safety profile in many patients. Dose: APIXABAN 5 mg PO BID; she does NOT meet dose-reduction criteria (would require 2 of: age >= 80, weight <= 60 kg, SCr >= 1.5 — she is 68, 72 kg, SCr 0.9). labs.r: NVAF + CHA2DS2-VASc 4 = HIGH stroke risk → lifelong anticoagulation. APIXABAN (direct factor Xa inhibitor) 5 mg PO BID standard NVAF dose; dose-reduce to 2.5 BID ONLY if 2 of (age >=80, wt <=60 kg, SCr >=1.5) — she meets none.
