labs.n: PRESENTATION + indications for ECT + capacity confirmation + informed consent
labs.v: 45 y/o woman M. Pavlik with SEVERE treatment-resistant major depressive disorder (melancholic features, marked psychomotor retardation, persistent active suicidal ideation with a plan, food/fluid refusal with ~14 lb weight loss) after adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, and augmentation (mirtazapine then aripiprazole). ECT is indicated for treatment-resistant depression, especially with suicidality, food/fluid refusal, catatonia, or psychotic features; for severe mania; for NMS; and for selected treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Response in severe depression is ~70-80%; safety is comparable to general anesthesia for minor procedures. There are NO ABSOLUTE contraindications — RELATIVE precautions include recent MI/unstable cardiac disease, severe HTN, recent stroke or raised ICP, severe pulmonary disease, severe osteoporosis, pheochromocytoma, and retinal detachment. CAPACITY in severe depression is the high-yield ethical point: depression alone does NOT negate decisional capacity (links [[case-116]]/[[case-132]]/[[case-142]]). Psychiatry confirms capacity by the 4-element test (understands/appreciates/reasons/communicates a stable choice); active suicidality does not preclude capacity for ECT consent. The psychiatrist obtains consent; the NURSE WITNESSES the signature and confirms understanding and voluntariness, addresses remaining questions, and screens for coercion. If capacity were absent, surrogate consent applies per substituted judgment (links [[case-132]]); emergency ECT is reserved for immediate life-threat (refractory catatonia, refusal of all food/fluids causing imminent harm). Husband is involved and supportive; family/cultural context explored.
labs.r: ECT indications: treatment-resistant depression (#1), severe depression w/ suicidality / food refusal / catatonia / psychotic features, severe mania, NMS, selected schizophrenia. Response ~70-80% in severe depression; safety like minor general anesthesia. NO ABSOLUTE contraindications; RELATIVE: recent MI/unstable cardiac, severe HTN, recent stroke/↑ICP, severe pulm, severe osteoporosis, pheo, retinal detachment. CAPACITY in severe depression is PRESUMED + decision-specific (4 elements); active suicidality ≠ incapacity. Psychiatrist obtains consent; NURSE WITNESSES + confirms understanding/voluntariness + addresses questions + screens for coercion. RN role: capacity + consent + family.

labs.n: PRE-procedure preparation + medication decisions (HOLD lithium / benzos / anticonvulsants; NO routine anxiolytic)
labs.v: Pre-procedure preparation is procedural-safety work coordinated by the RN. Verify IDENTITY and procedure with two identifiers and the consent; review medical clearance — H&P, ECG (cardiac risk), basic labs, and a DENTAL evaluation (loose teeth/removable appliances). NPO AFTER MIDNIGHT for general anesthesia (~6-8 hours; sips of water for essential meds per protocol). Have the patient REMOVE dentures, jewelry, hairpins, and contact lenses; ensure HAIR is clean (no oils/sprays that block electrode contact); empty the bladder; ensure a patent IV; baseline vital signs; explain the day in plain language to the patient and family. MEDICATION DECISIONS are high-yield. HOLD LITHIUM around ECT (it potentiates the seizure, prolongs post-ECT delirium, and adds neurotoxicity risk; coordinate stop-and-resume with the prescriber). HOLD BENZODIAZEPINES and HOLD ANTICONVULSANTS for the period defined by the protocol (they RAISE the seizure threshold and blunt the ECT seizure); a flumazenil reversal is considered only in special cases. ANTIDEPRESSANTS and most ANTIPSYCHOTICS are usually continued (specific exceptions per protocol — e.g., bupropion can lower seizure threshold and is sometimes held). Routine pre-op ANXIOLYTIC is NOT given because it would suppress the seizure; address anxiety with therapeutic communication, the family at bedside, and a clear walk-through of the day. Confirm a final time-out with the team before transport to the ECT suite.
labs.r: Pre-procedure: two identifiers + consent + clearance (H&P/ECG/labs/DENTAL); NPO after midnight; REMOVE dentures/jewelry/hairpins/contacts; clean hair (no oils/sprays); empty bladder; patent IV; baseline vitals; plain-language explanation. MEDS: HOLD LITHIUM (prolonged seizure/delirium/neurotoxicity), HOLD BENZOS + ANTICONVULSANTS (raise threshold → blunt seizure); antidepressants + most antipsychotics usually continued (bupropion sometimes held). NO routine pre-op ANXIOLYTIC (suppresses seizure); manage anxiety with TC + family + walk-through. RN role: prep + meds + time-out.

labs.n: INTRA-procedure team + POST-procedure recovery + side effects + family education
labs.v: INTRA-PROCEDURE in the ECT suite uses pre-OXYGENATION; brief general anesthesia (commonly METHOHEXITAL — propofol can blunt seizure quality; etomidate is an option); SUCCINYLCHOLINE for short-acting muscle relaxation; ATROPINE or glycopyrrolate to blunt vagal bradycardia and reduce secretions; a BITE BLOCK to protect the teeth and tongue; continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP monitoring; the brief generalized SEIZURE is verified on EEG (typical target ~25-60 seconds for an adequate treatment). A 'cuff' tourniquet on one limb before succinylcholine isolates the motor seizure for observation. The cardiovascular pattern is typically an initial PARASYMPATHETIC dip (transient bradycardia/hypotension) followed by a SYMPATHETIC surge (tachycardia/hypertension), managed by anesthesia. RIGHT-UNILATERAL placement is often chosen for cognitive preservation; BILATERAL placement may be used when faster efficacy is needed. POST-PROCEDURE — transfer to recovery in the SIDE-LYING position (sedated airway is at risk of aspiration), oxygen as needed, continuous oximetry and q5-15 min vitals until awake, GENTLE re-orientation with simple words and a calm voice (expect TRANSIENT confusion ~30-60 minutes and short-term memory effects); treat HEADACHE/MUSCLE ACHES with acetaminophen and NAUSEA with antiemetics per orders; assess fall risk and ambulate only with assistance; resume diet and routine medications when alert and able to swallow safely. SIDE EFFECTS to expect across the course: headache, muscle aches, nausea, transient confusion, and short-term MEMORY effects (RETROGRADE for events around the procedure and ANTEROGRADE for new learning during the course) that usually improve within weeks; persistent memory complaints can occur and are discussed openly. COURSE: typically 6-12 sessions, 3x/week (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri) with meaningful mood improvement often after 3-4 sessions; maintenance ECT (less frequent) may follow to prevent relapse. FAMILY education partners with the patient throughout and DISPELS STIGMA: modern ECT is performed under general anesthesia with minimal motor convulsion, is one of the most evidence-supported treatments in psychiatry, and has no demonstrated structural brain injury on imaging — it is NOT the 'shock therapy' of old films.
labs.r: INTRA: pre-O2; METHOHEXITAL (propofol blunts seizures; etomidate option) + SUCCINYLCHOLINE + ATROPINE/glycopyrrolate; BITE BLOCK; continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP; seizure ~25-60s on EEG; cuff tourniquet isolates motor seizure. CV pattern: PARASYMPATHETIC dip (brady/hypoT) → SYMPATHETIC surge (tachy/HTN) — managed by anesthesia. RIGHT-UNILATERAL preserves cognition; BILATERAL faster efficacy. POST: SIDE-LYING (aspiration), O2 + q5-15 min vitals + oximetry, GENTLE re-orientation (transient confusion 30-60 min + short-term memory effects); acetaminophen for HA/myalgia, antiemetics for nausea; assisted ambulation (fall risk); resume diet/meds when alert + swallow intact. COURSE: 6-12 sessions 3x/wk; improvement after 3-4; maintenance ECT possible. EDUCATE: side effects + memory + stigma (modern ECT ≠ old 'shock therapy'; evidence-supported). RN role: intra-team + recovery + side effects + family.

labs.n: Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors + course documentation + transition
labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT assume severe depression equals incapacity and bypass the patient (psychiatry confirmed capacity; the patient signed consent with full understanding); did NOT skip the dental evaluation or fail to remove dentures/jewelry/hairpins (airway and dental injury risk); did NOT give a routine pre-op ANXIOLYTIC or continue LITHIUM/BENZODIAZEPINES/ANTICONVULSANTS through the morning of ECT against protocol (they would suppress or distort the seizure or add neurotoxicity); did NOT position the still-sedated patient supine in recovery (aspiration risk — sidelying instead); did NOT over-explain or quiz during early post-ictal confusion (gentle reorientation only); did NOT describe ECT to the patient/family as 'shock therapy' or 'frying the brain' (modern ECT is performed under general anesthesia and is one of the most evidence-supported treatments in psychiatry — stigma is actively addressed). PROTECTIVE FACTORS: documented capacity assessment and witnessed consent; comprehensive preprocedure preparation (clearance + NPO + dental + appliances removed + correct medication holds + baseline vitals); coordinated intra-procedure care (psychiatry + anesthesia + ECT RN with bite block + monitoring + EEG-verified adequate seizure + cardiovascular management); safe recovery (sidelying + airway + vitals + gentle reorientation + comfort + fall prevention); consistent EDUCATION across the course (side effects + memory + course schedule + stigma); family partnership; objective DOCUMENTATION at every step (consent, capacity, vitals, anesthesia, seizure duration, recovery, response, side effects); and a clear TRANSITION PLAN to maintenance therapy + outpatient psychiatry + psychotherapy + safety planning. EXPECTED outcome: a safe ECT course with meaningful mood improvement after sessions 3-4 and remission by course completion; transient confusion and short-term memory effects that resolve over weeks; sustained recovery with maintenance pharmacotherapy and/or maintenance ECT and active relapse-prevention follow-up.
labs.r: Negatives confirm correct practice (didn't equate severe depression w/ incapacity, didn't skip dental/remove appliances, didn't give routine anxiolytic or fail to hold lithium/benzos/anticonvulsants, didn't position supine in recovery, didn't over-quiz post-ictal, didn't label modern ECT 'shock therapy'). Protective: documented capacity + witnessed consent + comprehensive prep + coordinated intra-procedure care + safe sidelying recovery w/ gentle reorientation + consistent education across course + family partnership + objective documentation + clear transition (maintenance pharm + outpatient psych/therapy + safety planning + maintenance ECT consideration). RN role: coordinate the course safely and humanely.

nursesNote: Inpatient psychiatry, day 4 — 45 y/o woman w/ SEVERE treatment-resistant MDD (melancholic features, marked psychomotor retardation, persistent active SI w/ plan, food/fluid refusal, ~14 lb weight loss) after failed adequate trials (sertraline → venlafaxine + mirtazapine then aripiprazole augmentation). ECT recommended as the appropriate next step given severity + refractoriness + suicidality + food refusal. Psychiatry CAPACITY assessment today: intact (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate stable choice — severe depression alone does NOT negate capacity); active SI does NOT preclude capacity. Informed consent for an acute ECT course (6-12 sessions, 3x/wk) signed with husband present; RN WITNESSED + confirmed understanding/voluntariness + addressed questions + screened for coercion. PRE-PROCEDURE (morning of first treatment): two-identifier ID + consent verified; medical clearance ECG/labs reviewed; DENTAL exam — no loose teeth; dentures + jewelry + hairpins REMOVED; hair clean (no sprays/oils); bladder emptied; patent IV; baseline vitals normal; LITHIUM and BENZOS + ANTICONVULSANTS HELD per protocol (raise threshold/blunt seizure or add neurotoxicity); antidepressants continued; NO routine pre-op anxiolytic (would suppress seizure); time-out completed; husband at bedside. INTRA-PROCEDURE in ECT suite — psychiatrist + anesthesiologist + ECT RN: pre-O2 → methohexital induction + SUCCINYLCHOLINE muscle relaxation + ATROPINE for vagal blockade; BITE BLOCK placed; continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP; right-unilateral electrode placement chosen for cognitive preservation; brief generalized SEIZURE ~38 sec on EEG (adequate); typical parasympathetic dip → sympathetic surge managed by anesthesia. POST-PROCEDURE: transferred to recovery SIDE-LYING (aspiration risk); continuous oximetry + q5-15 min vitals + supplemental O2 prn; gentle re-orientation w/ simple words + calm voice (transient confusion ~30-60 min, short-term memory effects expected); HA treated w/ acetaminophen + nausea w/ ondansetron per order; assisted ambulation only (fall risk); resumed diet + meds once alert + swallowing intact. COURSE — Mon/Wed/Fri x 6-12 sessions: meaningful mood improvement after sessions 3-4 (better eye contact + more spontaneous speech + appetite returning + no current SI), transient short-term memory effects discussed openly w/ pt + husband; lithium + benzos remain held; antidepressants continued. TRANSITION: maintenance antidepressant + outpatient psychiatry + psychotherapy + safety planning + possible MAINTENANCE ECT (less frequent) for relapse prevention; family educated on warning signs; follow-up scheduled. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT assume severe depression = incapacity, did NOT skip dental/remove-appliances, did NOT give routine pre-op anxiolytic or continue lithium/benzos/anticonvulsants against protocol, did NOT position supine in recovery, did NOT over-quiz during post-ictal confusion, did NOT label modern ECT 'shock therapy' (stigma actively addressed). Documentation complete at every step (consent + capacity + vitals + anesthesia + seizure duration + recovery + response + side effects).
providerOrders: DIAGNOSIS: severe treatment-resistant major depressive disorder with melancholic features, active suicidal ideation, and food/fluid refusal; capacity confirmed by psychiatry; informed consent witnessed by the RN

TREATMENT: acute electroconvulsive therapy course — 6-12 sessions, 3x/week (Mon/Wed/Fri) per psychiatry; right-unilateral electrode placement initially for cognitive preservation; reassess response and side effects after each session

MEDICATION HOLDS around ECT: HOLD lithium per protocol (prolonged seizure/delirium/neurotoxicity); HOLD benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants per protocol (raise seizure threshold and blunt the seizure); continue antidepressants and most antipsychotics per protocol; do NOT give a routine pre-op anxiolytic on the morning of ECT

PRE-PROCEDURE PREPARATION: verify identity and procedure with two identifiers; confirm consent and capacity documentation; complete medical clearance (H&P, ECG, labs) and dental evaluation; remove dentures, jewelry, hairpins, and contact lenses; clean hair (no oils or sprays); empty bladder; patent IV; baseline vital signs; NPO after midnight; final team time-out

INTRA-PROCEDURE TEAM (ECT suite): pre-oxygenation; methohexital induction (or alternative per anesthesia); SUCCINYLCHOLINE for muscle relaxation; ATROPINE or glycopyrrolate for vagal blockade and secretions; BITE BLOCK in place; continuous ECG, EEG, SpO2, and BP monitoring; verify an adequate brief generalized seizure on EEG (typically ~25-60 seconds); a 'cuff' tourniquet on one limb to isolate motor seizure for observation; anesthesia manages the parasympathetic dip then sympathetic surge

POST-PROCEDURE RECOVERY: transfer to PACU/recovery in the SIDE-LYING position (aspiration risk); supplemental O2 as needed; continuous oximetry and frequent vital signs (q5-15 minutes until awake); gentle re-orientation with simple words and a calm voice; treat headache and muscle aches with acetaminophen and nausea with ondansetron per order; assess fall risk and ambulate with assistance only; resume diet and routine medications when alert and able to swallow safely

MONITORING ACROSS THE COURSE: response (mood, suicidal ideation, sleep, appetite, function), side effects (headache, myalgia, nausea, transient confusion, short-term memory effects — retrograde and anterograde), and any prolonged seizure (>2 minutes) or post-ECT delirium

EDUCATION (patient + family): expected course (6-12 sessions; improvement often after 3-4), common side effects, memory effects (typically transient; discuss openly), what ECT looks like under modern anesthesia (DISPEL STIGMA — not the 'shock therapy' of old films), and how to support the patient between sessions

TRANSITION/RELAPSE PREVENTION: maintenance antidepressant per psychiatry; consider maintenance ECT (less frequent) if relapse-risk warrants; outpatient psychiatry and psychotherapy follow-up; safety planning; involve family

DOCUMENTATION: capacity assessment, witnessed informed consent, pre-procedure verification + holds, intra-procedure participants and seizure duration, post-procedure vitals/recovery/side effects, response across the course, and the transition plan

opts.text: Severe, treatment-resistant major depression with active suicidality and food/fluid refusal — ECT is indicated as the appropriate next step
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — this is exactly the high-yield NCLEX indication set for ECT. RN role: recognize indication.

opts.text: Severe depression does NOT automatically negate decisional capacity; psychiatry confirmed intact capacity by the 4-element test and the RN WITNESSES the informed consent
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the capacity-in-depression rule and the nurse's witness role. RN role: capacity + consent.

opts.text: Pre-procedure preparation must include medical clearance, dental evaluation, removal of dentures/jewelry/hairpins, NPO after midnight, an empty bladder, and a clean scalp (no oils/sprays)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — procedural-safety steps that prevent aspiration, dental injury, and electrode-contact failure. RN role: prep checklist.

opts.text: Medication decisions are protocol-driven: HOLD lithium, HOLD benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants, continue most antidepressants/antipsychotics, and do NOT give a routine pre-op anxiolytic
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — high-yield medication holds that determine seizure quality and safety. RN role: coordinate holds.

opts.text: In the ECT suite the team uses pre-oxygenation, methohexital, succinylcholine, atropine/glycopyrrolate, a bite block, and continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP monitoring with verification of an adequate brief generalized seizure on EEG
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the standard intra-procedure team and monitoring. RN role: collaborate intra-procedure.

opts.text: Post-procedure recovery is in the SIDE-LYING position with gentle re-orientation; transient confusion and short-term memory effects (retrograde + anterograde) are expected and improve over weeks
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — recovery position + expected side effects. RN role: safe recovery + reorientation.

opts.text: Assume severe depression equals incapacity and have the husband sign the consent for her without her involvement
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Depression alone does NOT negate capacity; capacity is decision-specific and presumed, and the patient must consent if capable.

opts.text: Give a routine pre-procedure anxiolytic on the morning of ECT to help her relax and continue her lithium and clonazepam through the morning dose
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Anxiolytics raise the seizure threshold and suppress the ECT seizure; lithium and benzodiazepines/anticonvulsants are held per protocol around ECT.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: ECT is indicated for treatment-resistant depression and for severe depression with suicidality, food/fluid refusal, catatonia, or psychotic features; for severe mania; for NMS; and for selected treatment-resistant schizophrenia
opts.rat: CORRECT — indication set. Foundation for choosing ECT.

opts.text: There are NO absolute contraindications to ECT; relative precautions include recent MI/unstable cardiac disease, severe HTN, recent stroke or raised ICP, severe pulmonary disease, severe osteoporosis, pheochromocytoma, and retinal detachment
opts.rat: CORRECT — contraindications principle. Foundation for risk stratification.

opts.text: Capacity in severe depression is presumed and decision-specific; active suicidality does not by itself preclude capacity for ECT consent
opts.rat: CORRECT — capacity principle. Foundation for honoring autonomy.

opts.text: Lithium and benzodiazepines/anticonvulsants are held per protocol around ECT; routine pre-op anxiolytics are NOT given because they suppress the seizure
opts.rat: CORRECT — medication principle. Foundation for seizure quality and safety.

opts.text: Intra-procedure team includes psychiatrist + anesthesiologist + ECT RN with pre-oxygenation, methohexital, succinylcholine, atropine/glycopyrrolate, bite block, and continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP monitoring with seizure verification on EEG
opts.rat: CORRECT — intra-procedure principle. Foundation for safe technique.

opts.text: Post-procedure recovery uses the side-lying position with gentle re-orientation; common side effects include headache, myalgia, nausea, and transient confusion/short-term memory effects that usually improve within weeks
opts.rat: CORRECT — recovery and side-effect principles. Foundation for safe care.

opts.text: Modern ECT causes lasting structural brain damage and is essentially the same as the 'shock therapy' shown in old films
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Modern ECT is performed under general anesthesia with minimal motor convulsion; imaging shows no demonstrated structural injury; outcomes data are strongly in favor of efficacy and safety.

opts.text: The patient should be placed supine immediately after ECT to make airway management easier in recovery
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The side-lying position protects the still-sedated airway from aspiration; supine increases aspiration risk.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Confirm decisional capacity and witness informed consent (involve the family with the patient's consent)
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Capacity and consent are the ethical and legal foundation of the entire course. RN role: capacity + consent.

opts.text: Complete pre-procedure preparation — medical clearance, dental check, NPO, removal of dentures/jewelry/hairpins, clean scalp, baseline vitals, patent IV — and confirm medication holds (lithium, benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants) with NO routine pre-op anxiolytic
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Correct prep prevents aspiration/dental injury and ensures an adequate seizure. RN role: prep + holds.

opts.text: Collaborate with the intra-procedure team — pre-oxygenation, methohexital, succinylcholine, atropine, bite block, ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP — and verify an adequate seizure
opts.rat: #3 — Safe technique in the suite. RN role: collaborate intra-procedure.

opts.text: Deliver safe post-procedure recovery in the side-lying position with airway, vitals, gentle re-orientation, comfort, and fall prevention
opts.rat: #4 — Protects the airway and supports the disoriented patient. RN role: recovery.

opts.text: Provide consistent education across the course (side effects, memory, schedule, stigma), partner with family, plan the transition (maintenance therapy + outpatient follow-up + safety plan), and document objectively
opts.rat: #5 — Sustains gains and prevents relapse. RN role: course education + transition + documentation.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this ECT course.

opts.text: Have psychiatry confirm capacity with the 4-element test; the RN witnesses informed consent and confirms understanding/voluntariness
opts.rat: Honors autonomy and meets the legal-ethical foundation. RN role: capacity + consent witness.

opts.text: NPO after midnight, dental evaluation, remove dentures/jewelry/hairpins/contacts, clean scalp (no oils/sprays), empty bladder, patent IV, baseline vitals, and a team time-out
opts.rat: Core procedural-safety steps. RN role: prep.

opts.text: HOLD lithium and HOLD benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants around ECT per protocol; continue antidepressants and most antipsychotics; do NOT give a routine pre-op anxiolytic
opts.rat: Determines safe seizure quality. RN role: med holds.

opts.text: Use pre-oxygenation, methohexital, succinylcholine, atropine/glycopyrrolate, a bite block, and continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP monitoring with EEG-verified seizure
opts.rat: Standard intra-procedure care. RN role: intra-procedure team.

opts.text: Position the patient SIDE-LYING in recovery with continuous oximetry and frequent vitals; gentle re-orientation; treat headache/myalgia/nausea per order; assisted ambulation only
opts.rat: Protects airway and supports the disoriented patient. RN role: recovery.

opts.text: Educate patient and family across the course (side effects, memory, schedule), dispel stigma about ECT, partner with the family, and plan transition (maintenance + outpatient + safety planning)
opts.rat: Sustains the course and prevents relapse. RN role: education + transition.

opts.text: Assume severe depression equals incapacity and have the husband sign consent for her without her involvement
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — depression alone does not negate capacity; the patient must consent if capable.

opts.text: Give a routine pre-op anxiolytic and continue her lithium and clonazepam through the morning of ECT
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — anxiolytics suppress the seizure; lithium and benzodiazepines/anticonvulsants are held per protocol.

opts.text: Place the patient supine immediately after ECT and quiz her on dates and details to test her memory while she is still confused
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — supine risks aspiration; quizzing during post-ictal confusion is unkind and unhelpful. Use side-lying and gentle re-orientation.

opts.text: Describe modern ECT to the patient and family as 'shock therapy' or 'frying the brain'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — stigmatizing language is harmful; describe modern ECT accurately and dispel stigma.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Confirm capacity and witness informed consent, involve the husband with the patient's consent, and answer questions
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. The ethical and legal foundation comes first. RN role: capacity + consent.

opts.text: Complete pre-procedure preparation (medical clearance + dental + NPO + remove appliances + clean scalp + baseline vitals + patent IV) and confirm medication holds; do NOT give a routine pre-op anxiolytic
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Correct preparation enables a safe, adequate treatment. RN role: prep + holds.

opts.text: Collaborate with the intra-procedure team — pre-oxygenation, methohexital, succinylcholine, atropine, bite block, continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP — and verify an adequate seizure
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Safe technique in the suite. RN role: intra-procedure team.

opts.text: Deliver post-procedure recovery in the side-lying position with airway, vitals, gentle re-orientation, comfort, and fall prevention
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Protects airway and supports the disoriented patient. RN role: recovery.

opts.text: Provide consistent education across the course, partner with family, dispel stigma, and plan the transition (maintenance therapy + outpatient + safety planning) with documentation throughout
opts.rat: #5 — Closing/ongoing. Sustains gains and prevents relapse. RN role: education + transition + documentation.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action/outcome, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: Psychiatry confirmed decisional capacity; the RN witnessed informed consent and addressed questions; the husband was included with the patient's permission
opts.rat: Honors autonomy and meets the ethical-legal foundation. Model practice.

opts.text: Pre-procedure preparation was complete (medical clearance + dental + NPO + appliances removed + clean scalp + baseline vitals + patent IV) with the correct medication holds (lithium + benzodiazepines + anticonvulsants) and NO routine pre-op anxiolytic
opts.rat: Procedural-safety bundle done correctly. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Intra-procedure: pre-oxygenation, methohexital + succinylcholine + atropine, bite block, continuous ECG/EEG/SpO2/BP, EEG-verified brief generalized seizure ~38 seconds, parasympathetic dip then sympathetic surge managed by anesthesia
opts.rat: Safe, monitored, EEG-verified adequate treatment. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Post-procedure: side-lying recovery, frequent vitals and oximetry, gentle re-orientation, acetaminophen for headache and ondansetron for nausea, assisted ambulation; education across the course dispelled stigma and prepared the family
opts.rat: Protects airway, supports disorientation, and sustains the course. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: By session 4, mood improves, eye contact and speech increase, appetite returns, and active suicidal ideation resolves; the course is completed with remission and a transition plan
opts.rat: Expected response to an evidence-supported treatment, followed by relapse-prevention planning. Ideal outcome.

opts.text: Alternative — the team assumed severe depression equals incapacity and had the husband sign consent for her without her involvement
opts.rat: ⚠️ Depression alone does not negate capacity; bypassing a capable patient violates autonomy.

opts.text: Alternative — lithium and clonazepam were continued through the morning, and a routine pre-op lorazepam was given; the seizure was suboptimal and the treatment was ineffective
opts.rat: ⚠️ Anxiolytics and benzodiazepines/anticonvulsants/lithium suppress or distort the seizure. Demonstrates the medication-hold rule.

opts.text: Alternative — the patient was placed supine in recovery while still sedated; she aspirated and required suctioning
opts.rat: ⚠️ Side-lying protects the still-sedated airway. Demonstrates the recovery-position rule.

opts.text: Alternative — the nurse described ECT to the patient and family as 'shock therapy' that 'fries your brain'; the patient withdrew consent in distress
opts.rat: ⚠️ Stigmatizing language is harmful and inaccurate. Describe modern ECT correctly and dispel stigma.

opts.text: Alternative — dentures were left in place; the patient sustained dental injury during the treatment
opts.rat: ⚠️ Dentures must be removed before ECT; loose teeth identified. Demonstrates the pre-procedure dental/appliances rule.

title: WOUND DEHISCENCE with EVISCERATION on Postoperative Day 5 in a 68-Year-Old Man After Exploratory Laparotomy and Sigmoid Colectomy for Complicated Diverticulitis (Risk Factors: Type 2 Diabetes with A1c 8.4, Obesity BMI 34, Former Heavy Smoking, Postoperative Ileus with Persistent Coughing, Clean-Contaminated Wound) — The Classic 'Popping' Sensation During a Forceful Cough with Visible BOWEL LOOPS Through the Incision: Recognizing the Emergency, IMMEDIATE NURSING RESPONSE (STAY With Patient, LOW-Fowler's With KNEES FLEXED, Cover with STERILE NORMAL-SALINE-MOISTENED Gauze, DO NOT Push Viscera Back, KEEP MOIST, NPO), STAT Surgeon Notification + IV Access + Isotonic Fluid + Labs + Type & Screen + Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics, Coordinated Emergent Return to OR for Fascial Repair, and Postoperative Care + Recurrence-Prevention Teaching (Abdominal Binder, SPLINTING, Stool Softeners, Glycemic and Nutritional Optimization)
subtitle: WOUND DEHISCENCE is partial or complete SEPARATION of the layers of a surgical wound (skin and/or fascia/muscle); EVISCERATION is PROTRUSION OF VISCERA (typically intestine) through the wound — a true SURGICAL EMERGENCY. The CLASSIC patient story is a 'POPPING' or 'GIVING WAY' sensation during a forceful cough, sneeze, retch, or strain on POSTOPERATIVE DAY 5-12 (the window after sutures are tested by mobilization and before full tensile strength is restored — earlier suggests technical failure; later suggests infection/poor healing), with sudden warm wet drainage at the incision, often serosanguineous or 'salmon-colored,' followed by visible separation of the wound edges and, in evisceration, EXPOSED BOWEL LOOPS. RISK FACTORS cluster around impaired healing or increased intra-abdominal pressure: ADVANCED AGE; MALNUTRITION (low albumin/prealbumin, vitamin C and zinc deficiency); DIABETES with poor glycemic control (microangiopathy, neutrophil dysfunction); OBESITY (poor wound perfusion, mechanical stress); IMMUNOSUPPRESSION (chronic corticosteroids, chemotherapy, transplant medications); SMOKING (vasoconstriction, hypoxia); SURGICAL SITE INFECTION (the single most modifiable post-op factor); INCREASED INTRA-ABDOMINAL PRESSURE (coughing, sneezing, vomiting, straining at stool, ileus, ascites, abdominal distention); HEMATOMA/seroma; emergency surgery or contamination; repeated incisions through the same site; and technical factors. IMMEDIATE NURSING ACTIONS — high-yield NCLEX — are choreographed and must NOT be delayed by 'going to get supplies' or 'pushing it back in': (1) STAY WITH THE PATIENT and CALL FOR HELP — do not leave the bedside, do not try to manage alone; (2) POSITION the patient in LOW-FOWLER'S (about 15-20 degrees of head elevation) with KNEES FLEXED on a pillow — this RELAXES the abdominal wall and REDUCES intra-abdominal pressure on the defect; AVOID high-Fowler's, sitting upright, or flat with legs extended (all increase tension on the wound); (3) COVER the exposed viscera with STERILE GAUZE MOISTENED with sterile NORMAL SALINE and KEEP IT MOIST throughout — re-moisten with sterile saline as needed; (4) DO NOT push the viscera back into the abdomen (causes contamination, peritonitis, mesenteric injury, and ischemia), DO NOT use DRY gauze (the bowel will dry/necrose), DO NOT use cold dressings or apply povidone-iodine/hydrogen peroxide/tap water to the bowel; (5) NPO immediately (anticipating the OR); (6) NOTIFY THE SURGEON STAT — and the rapid-response/OR team per facility policy; (7) ESTABLISH/secure two large-bore IVs and run isotonic fluid (typically NS or LR) per orders; (8) SEND labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type and screen) and INITIATE broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per the surgeon (contamination/infection risk); (9) MONITOR vital signs frequently and watch for SHOCK (tachycardia, hypotension), peritonitis (rigidity, rebound, guarding), and worsening; (10) PREPARE FOR THE OR — confirm consent for the emergency repair, hold transport, alert anesthesia, and document the time of the event, the precipitating event (cough/strain), the wound findings, interventions, vital signs, and response. Pain control is given per surgeon order — never delay the surgical call to medicate for pain. DEFINITIVE management is EMERGENT RETURN TO THE OR for surgical repair: re-approximation of the fascia (often through-and-through sutures or retention sutures), peritoneal washout, hemostasis, and, depending on tissue quality and defect size, possible mesh placement; broad-spectrum antibiotics continue; post-operatively the patient often returns with NG decompression, an abdominal binder, and a slowed mobilization plan, with close watch for re-dehiscence, surgical site infection, and ileus. PREVENTION focuses on the modifiable: pre-operative optimization (nutrition, glycemia, smoking cessation), abdominal binders for high-risk patients, SPLINTING the incision with a pillow during cough/sneeze/vomit/bowel movement, treating ileus and managing post-op nausea (antiemetics), STOOL SOFTENERS to prevent straining, careful incentive spirometry technique (deep breathing without bracing the wound), early but graded mobilization, and recognizing/treating surgical site infection promptly. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: pushing viscera back into the abdomen; using DRY gauze, ice, tap water, povidone-iodine, or hydrogen peroxide on the bowel; positioning the patient high-Fowler's or sitting upright or flat with legs extended; leaving the patient alone to fetch supplies; giving oral fluids or food; delaying the surgeon call to perform a full charting or to medicate first; and forgetting to document the precipitating event and timeline. NURSING ROLE: recognize the classic 'popping/sudden drainage' presentation; stay with the patient and call for help; position low-Fowler's with knees flexed; cover the exposed viscera with sterile saline-moistened gauze and keep it moist; NPO; notify the surgeon STAT; establish IV access and labs/antibiotics; monitor for shock; prepare for the OR; and after repair coordinate prevention-focused post-operative care and teaching.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + dehiscence vs evisceration + risk factors + classic POD 5-12 timing
labs.v: 68 y/o man J. Larsen, POD 5 from exploratory laparotomy + sigmoid colectomy for complicated diverticulitis (clean-contaminated). RISK FACTORS for poor wound healing: T2DM with A1c 8.4 (perioperative hyperglycemia), obesity (BMI 34), former heavy smoker, borderline nutrition (low prealbumin/albumin), post-op ileus with persistent cough (raises intra-abdominal pressure). During a forceful coughing fit at 1015 he reported a sudden POPPING sensation at the midline incision with warm wet 'salmon-colored' drainage; on assessment the incision had SEPARATED and BOWEL loops were protruding through the fascial defect = WOUND DEHISCENCE WITH EVISCERATION. DEHISCENCE = partial/complete separation of wound layers (skin and/or fascia/muscle); EVISCERATION = protrusion of viscera through the wound — more emergent than dehiscence alone. CLASSIC TIMING is postoperative day 5-12 (sutures stressed by mobilization, full tensile strength not yet reached); earlier suggests technical failure, later suggests infection/poor healing. The nursing task: an immediate, choreographed response and coordination of the emergent OR return — with recurrence-prevention teaching afterward.
labs.r: Dehiscence = wound-layer separation; EVISCERATION = viscera through the wound (more emergent). Classic 'popping' on cough/strain on POD 5-12 + 'salmon-colored' drainage. Risks: age, DM (poor A1c), obesity, malnutrition (low albumin/prealbumin), smoking, immunosuppression, SSI, ↑intra-abdominal pressure (cough/strain/ileus/ascites/distension), repeat incisions, emergency/contaminated cases. RN role: recognize the popping + drainage cue + visualize evisceration.

labs.n: IMMEDIATE nursing response (position + sterile saline-moist gauze + NPO + surgeon STAT)
labs.v: The immediate response is choreographed and must NOT be delayed. (1) STAY WITH the patient and CALL FOR HELP — do not leave the bedside to fetch supplies and do not try to manage alone. (2) POSITION the patient LOW-FOWLER'S (about 15-20 degrees) with KNEES FLEXED on a pillow — this RELAXES the abdominal wall and REDUCES intra-abdominal pressure on the defect; AVOID high-Fowler's, sitting upright, or flat with legs extended (all increase tension and worsen evisceration). (3) COVER the exposed viscera with STERILE GAUZE MOISTENED with sterile NORMAL SALINE and KEEP IT MOIST throughout (re-moisten with sterile saline as needed). (4) DO NOT push the viscera back into the abdomen (causes contamination, peritonitis, mesenteric injury, ischemia); DO NOT use DRY gauze (bowel will dry/necrose); DO NOT apply cold dressings, povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, or tap water to the bowel. (5) NPO immediately (anticipating OR). (6) NOTIFY THE SURGEON STAT and activate rapid-response/OR per facility policy. (7) Establish two LARGE-BORE IVs; run isotonic fluid (NS or LR) per orders; send labs (CBC, BMP, coags, type and screen); give a BROAD-SPECTRUM IV ANTIBIOTIC per surgeon order (contamination/infection risk). (8) Frequent vital signs — watch for SHOCK (tachycardia, hypotension), PERITONITIS (rigidity, rebound, guarding), and worsening status. (9) PREPARE for the OR — confirm INFORMED CONSENT for the emergency repair, alert anesthesia, arrange transport. (10) DOCUMENT the time of the event, the precipitating event (cough/strain), wound findings, every intervention, vital signs, and patient response. Pain control is given per surgeon order — never delay the surgical call to medicate first.
labs.r: (1) STAY + call for help; (2) LOW-FOWLER'S ~15-20° + KNEES FLEXED (relaxes abdominal wall) — NOT high-Fowler's/upright/flat-with-legs-extended; (3) STERILE NORMAL-SALINE-MOISTENED gauze over viscera, KEEP MOIST; (4) DON'T push viscera back, NO dry gauze/cold/povidone-iodine/peroxide/tap water; (5) NPO; (6) SURGEON STAT + OR team; (7) 2 large-bore IVs + isotonic fluid + labs (CBC/BMP/coags/T&S) + broad-spectrum IV abx per order; (8) frequent vitals — watch shock/peritonitis; (9) prep OR (consent + anesthesia + transport); (10) document. Never delay the surgical call for charting/pain meds first. RN role: choreographed response.

labs.n: Definitive surgical management + post-op care + complication surveillance
labs.v: Definitive treatment is EMERGENT RETURN TO THE OR for repair: re-approximation of the fascia with retention or through-and-through sutures, peritoneal washout, hemostasis; mesh placement is considered for larger defects but often deferred in a clean-contaminated field. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics continue per surgeon. Post-operatively the patient typically returns with an NG tube for decompression (if ileus persists), an ABDOMINAL BINDER for support, and a SLOWED graded mobilization plan. Continue glycemic control (target the perioperative range per protocol), optimize NUTRITION (protein + vitamin C + zinc; dietitian consult), provide stool softeners to prevent straining, teach and have the patient PRACTICE SPLINTING the incision with a pillow during cough/sneeze/bowel movement, treat post-op pain effectively, and use incentive spirometry with gentle technique (deep breathing without bracing too tightly). COMPLICATION surveillance: re-dehiscence (especially if persistent cough, ileus, or infection is not addressed), surgical site infection (fever, increasing pain, erythema, purulent drainage), peritonitis (rigid abdomen, rebound, hypotension/tachycardia, lactate), ileus or bowel obstruction (links case-130), VTE (post-op high risk — prophylaxis per protocol), and pulmonary complications. Engage family and address anxiety; describe the next steps in plain language.
labs.r: Emergent OR = fascial re-approximation (retention/through-and-through sutures) + peritoneal washout + hemostasis ± mesh (often deferred in contaminated field). Continue broad-spectrum abx. Post-op: NG decompression if ileus, ABDOMINAL BINDER, GLYCEMIC control, NUTRITION (protein/vit C/zinc, dietitian), STOOL softeners, SPLINTING with cough/sneeze/BM, gentle IS, effective pain control. Surveillance: re-dehiscence, SSI, peritonitis, ileus/SBO ([[case-130]]), VTE, pulmonary. RN role: post-op care + complication surveillance.

labs.n: Prevention + discharge teaching + Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: PREVENTION: pre-operative optimization (nutrition, glycemic control, smoking cessation) when elective; ABDOMINAL BINDER for high-risk patients; SPLINTING the incision with a pillow during cough/sneeze/vomit/BM; treat ileus and post-op nausea (antiemetics); stool softeners to prevent straining; gentle incentive-spirometry technique; early but graded mobility; recognize and treat surgical site infection early. DISCHARGE TEACHING after repair: NO lifting greater than about 10 pounds for 6-8 weeks (or per surgeon); SPLINT the incision with cough/sneeze/bowel movements; wear the ABDOMINAL BINDER per surgeon orders for activity; take STOOL softeners and stay hydrated to avoid straining; recognize signs of RECURRENCE (popping/sudden drainage/wound separation) and INFECTION (fever, increasing pain, erythema, purulent drainage); maintain glycemic and nutritional plans; do NOT submerge the incision in baths or pools until cleared; report all warning signs to the provider; keep all follow-up appointments. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct emergency practice): the nurse did NOT push the viscera back into the abdomen; did NOT use a dry, cold, or chemical-soaked dressing (povidone-iodine/hydrogen peroxide/tap water); did NOT position the patient high-Fowler's or sitting upright or flat with legs extended; did NOT leave the patient alone to fetch supplies; did NOT give oral fluids or food; did NOT delay the surgical call to chart fully or medicate for pain first; and did NOT forget to document the precipitating cough and the timeline. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: instant recognition of the classic popping/sudden drainage cue; presence at the bedside; correct positioning (low-Fowler's with knees flexed); sterile saline-moistened gauze KEPT MOIST; NPO; STAT surgeon notification; large-bore IV access + isotonic resuscitation + labs/type and screen + broad-spectrum antibiotics; coordinated emergent OR; effective post-op care (binder, splinting, glycemia, nutrition, stool softeners); discharge teaching with teach-back; objective documentation. EXPECTED outcome (as here): the patient is stabilized, repaired safely, recovers without recurrence or major infection, and goes home with a robust prevention plan.
labs.r: PREVENTION: pre-op optimization + binder + SPLINTING with cough/sneeze/BM + treat ileus/nausea + stool softeners + gentle IS + early graded mobility + early SSI care. DISCHARGE: no lifting >10 lb x 6-8 wk, SPLINT, BINDER, stool softeners + hydration, recognize recurrence/SSI, glycemic + nutrition plans, no submerging incision, follow-up. Negatives confirm correct practice (didn't push viscera back, no dry/cold/chemical dressings, not high-Fowler's/sitting/flat-with-legs-extended, didn't leave patient, no oral intake, didn't delay surgeon call). Protective: recognition + bedside presence + correct positioning + sterile saline-moist gauze KEPT MOIST + NPO + surgeon STAT + IV/labs/abx + coordinated OR + post-op binder/splinting/glycemia/nutrition + teach-back + documentation.

12 mg/dL (low — better short-term nutrition marker; supports nutrition optimization plan)
12.4 x10^9/L (mildly elevated — possible contributing surgical site infection vs stress response)
188 mg/dL (perioperative hyperglycemia — impairs wound healing; tighten glycemic control)
11.0 g/dL (mildly low — baseline and trend after the event; type and screen in case transfusion needed)

nursesNote: Med-surg, 1015 — 68 y/o man POD 5 ex-lap + sigmoid colectomy for complicated diverticulitis (clean-contaminated). Risk profile: T2DM A1c 8.4, BMI 34, former 40-pk-yr smoker, borderline nutrition (albumin 2.8, prealbumin 12), post-op ileus + persistent cough. During forceful cough → sudden POPPING at midline incision + warm wet 'salmon-colored' drainage soaking dressing → on assessment incision SEPARATED with loops of BOWEL protruding through the fascial defect = WOUND DEHISCENCE WITH EVISCERATION (classic POD 5-12 presentation). RN choreographed response: (1) STAYED at bedside + called for help; (2) positioned LOW-FOWLER'S ~20° w/ KNEES FLEXED on pillow (relaxes abdominal wall — NOT high-Fowler's/sitting/flat-w/legs-extended); (3) covered exposed viscera with STERILE NORMAL-SALINE-MOISTENED gauze + KEPT MOIST (re-moistened w/ sterile saline as needed); (4) did NOT push viscera back, no dry/cold gauze, no povidone-iodine/peroxide/tap water; (5) NPO; (6) SURGEON paged STAT + OR/anesthesia/rapid-response activated; (7) 2 large-bore IVs + isotonic fluid + labs sent (CBC/BMP/coags/T&S — H/H 11.0, WBC 12.4, glucose 188) + broad-spectrum IV antibiotic per surgeon order (contamination risk); (8) frequent vitals (mild tachycardia → stabilizing); watch shock/peritonitis; (9) informed CONSENT for emergency repair signed, transport to OR arranged; (10) documented time + precipitating cough + wound findings + interventions + vitals + response. Pain mgmt per surgeon order (NOT delayed to medicate before calling). EMERGENT OR: fascial re-approximation w/ retention/through-and-through sutures + peritoneal washout + hemostasis; mesh deferred (contaminated field); NG decompression placed; abdominal BINDER applied; broad-spectrum IV abx continued. POST-OP: nutrition consult (protein + vit C + zinc), glycemic control tightened, SPLINTING with cough/sneeze/BM taught + practiced, abdominal binder for activity, stool softeners + hydration to avoid straining, graded mobilization, gentle IS, VTE prophylaxis, surveillance for re-dehiscence/SSI/peritonitis/ileus. DISCHARGE TEACHING (teach-back): no lifting >10 lb x 6-8 wk, SPLINT + BINDER + stool softeners + recognize warning signs of recurrence/SSI (popping/sudden drainage; fever/increasing pain/erythema/purulence) → call surgeon; glycemic + nutrition plans; no submerging incision in baths/pools until cleared; follow-up scheduled. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT push viscera back, did NOT use dry/cold/povidone/peroxide/tap-water dressings, did NOT position high-Fowler's/sitting/flat-with-legs-extended, did NOT leave the patient to get supplies, did NOT give PO intake, did NOT delay surgeon call for full charting or pain meds first. Family updated.
providerOrders: EMERGENCY: wound dehiscence with EVISCERATION on POD 5 after exploratory laparotomy with sigmoid colectomy — emergent return to OR for fascial repair

BEDSIDE NURSING ACTIONS (immediate): stay with the patient; position low-Fowler's (about 15-20 degrees) with knees flexed; cover exposed viscera with sterile gauze moistened with sterile normal saline and keep it moist (re-moisten as needed); do NOT push viscera back into the abdomen; do not use dry, cold, or antiseptic-soaked dressings (no povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, or tap water on bowel); NPO immediately; obtain frequent vital signs; do not leave the bedside
NOTIFICATION: STAT page surgeon; activate rapid response/OR team per facility; alert anesthesia; notify family

ACCESS/FLUIDS/LABS: two large-bore peripheral IVs; isotonic crystalloid resuscitation per surgeon order; STAT CBC, BMP, coagulation studies, type and screen; lactate as indicated; ABG if shock features
ANTIBIOTICS: broad-spectrum IV antibiotic per surgeon order for the contamination/infection risk
PAIN: analgesia per surgeon order — do not delay the surgical call to medicate first; document
OR PREPARATION: confirm informed consent for emergency wound exploration and repair; verify NPO, baseline labs, and identifying details; arrange transport to OR

POSTOPERATIVE: NG decompression as ordered; abdominal binder; advance diet slowly per surgeon (clear liquids → as tolerated); continue IV antibiotics; glycemic control (insulin sliding scale + basal optimization for A1c 8.4); nutrition consult (protein, vitamin C, zinc); stool softeners; graded mobilization; gentle incentive spirometry technique with splinting; VTE prophylaxis per protocol; surveillance for re-dehiscence, SSI, peritonitis, ileus, and pulmonary complications

PREVENTION/EDUCATION (teach-back at discharge): no lifting greater than about 10 pounds for 6-8 weeks; SPLINT the incision with a pillow during cough/sneeze/bowel movement; wear the abdominal binder during activity per surgeon orders; take stool softeners and stay hydrated to avoid straining; recognize warning signs (popping/sudden drainage/wound separation, fever, increasing pain, erythema, purulent drainage) and contact the surgeon; do not submerge the incision in baths or pools until cleared; keep all follow-up appointments
DOCUMENTATION: time of event, precipitating event (cough/strain), wound findings, every intervention with time, vital signs and responses, notifications, OR transfer, and post-op care

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters at this wound emergency?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: A sudden 'POPPING' sensation during a forceful cough in a POD 5 abdominal-laparotomy patient with sudden warm wet 'salmon-colored' drainage is the CLASSIC presentation of wound dehiscence
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — classic story; recognize and act. RN role: instant recognition.

opts.text: Visible loops of BOWEL protruding through the fascial defect = EVISCERATION, a surgical emergency more urgent than dehiscence alone
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — confirms the emergency and the OR pathway. RN role: visualize + act.

opts.text: Risk factors present: advanced age, T2DM with A1c 8.4, obesity (BMI 34), former heavy smoker, low albumin/prealbumin, ileus with persistent cough (increases intra-abdominal pressure)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — risk-factor cluster explains why this happened now. RN role: recognize the risk profile.

opts.text: Immediate nursing actions: STAY with the patient and call for help; LOW-FOWLER'S with KNEES FLEXED; cover viscera with STERILE NORMAL-SALINE-MOISTENED gauze and KEEP MOIST; NPO
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the choreographed bedside response. RN role: stay + position + sterile saline-moist gauze + NPO.

opts.text: Notify the SURGEON STAT; establish two large-bore IVs; send CBC/BMP/coags/type and screen; give broad-spectrum IV antibiotic per surgeon order; monitor vital signs for shock and peritonitis
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — escalation, resuscitation, and surveillance. RN role: notify + IV + labs + abx + monitor.

opts.text: Prepare for emergent OR — confirm informed consent, alert anesthesia, arrange transport; document time of event, precipitating cough, interventions, vitals, response
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — pathway to definitive repair + the record. RN role: OR prep + documentation.

opts.text: Push the bowel loops back into the abdomen and tape the wound closed before calling the surgeon
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + DANGEROUS. Pushing viscera back contaminates and injures the bowel and delays surgical care.

opts.text: Place the patient flat with legs extended and apply a DRY sterile gauze to the bowel while you go find the supplies
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Flat-with-legs-extended raises intra-abdominal tension; dry gauze dries/necroses the bowel; never leave the patient. Low-Fowler's with knees flexed + sterile saline-moistened gauze + stay with the patient.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Dehiscence = partial or complete separation of wound layers; evisceration = protrusion of viscera through the wound — evisceration is the more emergent of the two
opts.rat: CORRECT — the definitions. Foundation for triage and language.

opts.text: Common risk factors include advanced age, malnutrition, diabetes/poor glycemic control, obesity, smoking, immunosuppression, surgical site infection, and increased intra-abdominal pressure (cough/strain/ileus/ascites/distension)
opts.rat: CORRECT — risk-factor principle. Foundation for prevention.

opts.text: The classic timing is postoperative day 5-12; earlier suggests technical failure and later suggests infection or poor healing
opts.rat: CORRECT — timing principle. Foundation for clinical suspicion.

opts.text: The immediate bedside response is to stay with the patient, position low-Fowler's with knees flexed, cover viscera with sterile saline-moistened gauze kept moist, keep the patient NPO, and call the surgeon STAT
opts.rat: CORRECT — the response bundle. Foundation for safe action.

opts.text: Definitive treatment is emergent return to the OR for fascial repair with washout, hemostasis, and possible mesh (often deferred in contaminated fields); broad-spectrum IV antibiotics continue
opts.rat: CORRECT — surgical principle. Foundation for the pathway.

opts.text: Prevention focuses on glycemic and nutrition optimization, abdominal binders for high-risk patients, splinting with cough/sneeze/BM, stool softeners, treating ileus, gentle IS, and early but graded mobility
opts.rat: CORRECT — prevention principle. Foundation for recurrence-prevention teaching.

opts.text: Pushing the viscera back into the abdomen at the bedside is appropriate to prevent infection and avoid the OR
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Never push viscera back — causes contamination, mesenteric injury, peritonitis. The OR is required.

opts.text: The patient should be ambulated immediately at the bedside to 'shake the bowel back' and prevent further evisceration
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Ambulation increases intra-abdominal pressure and worsens evisceration. Low-Fowler's with knees flexed; NPO; OR.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Stay with the patient; position LOW-FOWLER'S with KNEES FLEXED; cover exposed viscera with STERILE NORMAL-SALINE-MOISTENED gauze and KEEP MOIST; do NOT push viscera back
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. The bedside response protects the viscera and the patient and is what only the nurse can do right now. RN role: stay + position + sterile saline-moist gauze.

opts.text: Call the SURGEON STAT and activate rapid response/OR team; keep the patient NPO; establish IV access and obtain vital signs
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Escalation and access are needed in parallel. RN role: notify + NPO + IV.

opts.text: Initiate isotonic IV fluid; send labs (CBC, BMP, coags, type and screen); give broad-spectrum IV antibiotic per surgeon order; monitor for shock and peritonitis
opts.rat: #3 — Stabilizes and prepares for the OR while watching for deterioration. RN role: resuscitation + labs + antibiotic + monitoring.

opts.text: Prepare for emergent OR — confirm informed consent, alert anesthesia, arrange transport
opts.rat: #4 — Moves the patient to definitive repair. RN role: OR prep.

opts.text: Document the event and coordinate post-op care + recurrence-prevention teaching (binder, splinting, glycemia, nutrition, stool softeners, signs of recurrence/SSI)
opts.rat: #5 — Closes the loop and prevents recurrence. RN role: documentation + post-op + prevention.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this evisceration.

opts.text: Stay with the patient and call for help; position low-Fowler's (about 15-20 degrees) with knees flexed on a pillow
opts.rat: Reduces abdominal-wall tension and protects the patient. RN role: stay + position.

opts.text: Cover the exposed viscera with sterile gauze moistened with sterile normal saline and keep it moist (re-moisten with sterile saline as needed)
opts.rat: Protects the viscera from drying/necrosis and contamination. RN role: sterile saline-moistened gauze, kept moist.

opts.text: NPO immediately; call the surgeon STAT and activate rapid response/OR; alert anesthesia
opts.rat: Anticipates OR and mobilizes the team. RN role: NPO + notification + activation.

opts.text: Establish two large-bore IVs; run isotonic crystalloid per orders; send CBC/BMP/coags/type and screen; give broad-spectrum IV antibiotic per surgeon order
opts.rat: Supports resuscitation, OR readiness, and infection prevention. RN role: IV + labs + abx.

opts.text: Confirm informed consent for emergency repair; obtain frequent vital signs; arrange OR transport; document the event and timeline
opts.rat: Completes the pathway to definitive treatment with the record. RN role: OR prep + monitoring + documentation.

opts.text: Plan post-op care (NG decompression if ileus, abdominal binder, glycemic and nutritional optimization, stool softeners, splinting, gentle IS, VTE prophylaxis, complication surveillance) and recurrence-prevention discharge teaching
opts.rat: Sustains recovery and prevents recurrence. RN role: post-op + prevention + teaching.

opts.text: Push the bowel back into the abdomen and tape the wound closed before calling the surgeon
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — contaminates and injures the bowel and delays surgical care.

opts.text: Apply DRY gauze to the bowel and leave the bedside to find supplies
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — dry gauze dries/necroses the bowel and the patient should not be left alone.

opts.text: Place the patient in HIGH-Fowler's or upright sitting to make the wound easier to dress
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — increases intra-abdominal tension and worsens evisceration; use low-Fowler's with knees flexed.

opts.text: Give the patient oral fluids 'because he is thirsty' and pour povidone-iodine or hydrogen peroxide over the bowel to 'sterilize' it
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — NPO for the OR; antiseptics on bowel cause chemical injury. Use sterile normal saline only.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Stay with the patient and call for help; position low-Fowler's with knees flexed; cover viscera with sterile saline-moistened gauze and keep it moist; do NOT push viscera back
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. The bedside response that only the nurse can do right now. RN role: stay + position + sterile saline-moist gauze.

opts.text: Call the surgeon STAT and activate rapid response/OR; keep the patient NPO; establish IV access; obtain vital signs
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Escalation, NPO, and access in parallel. RN role: notify + NPO + IV.

opts.text: Initiate isotonic IV fluid; send labs (CBC, BMP, coags, type and screen); give broad-spectrum IV antibiotic per surgeon order; monitor for shock and peritonitis
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Resuscitation, OR readiness, and surveillance. RN role: fluids + labs + abx + monitor.

opts.text: Prepare for emergent OR — confirm informed consent, alert anesthesia, arrange transport
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Pathway to definitive repair. RN role: OR prep.

opts.text: Document the event objectively; coordinate post-op care (NG decompression, abdominal binder, glycemic and nutritional optimization, splinting, stool softeners) and discharge teaching
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Documentation + post-op + prevention complete the response. RN role: document + post-op + teaching.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: The nurse stayed with the patient, positioned low-Fowler's with knees flexed, covered viscera with sterile saline-moistened gauze kept moist, called the surgeon STAT, established IV access, and kept NPO — vitals stabilize while awaiting OR transport
opts.rat: Correct choreographed response that protects viscera and patient. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Emergent OR completed fascial re-approximation with peritoneal washout; IV antibiotics continued; the patient returned with an NG tube and abdominal binder, stable
opts.rat: Definitive repair with appropriate post-op support. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Post-op care included glycemic and nutritional optimization, stool softeners, splinting practice with cough/sneeze/BM, abdominal binder for activity, and graded mobilization without recurrence
opts.rat: Sustained recovery with recurrence prevention. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Discharge teaching was teach-back verified — no lifting greater than 10 pounds for 6-8 weeks, splinting, binder use, stool softeners, and warning signs of recurrence/SSI
opts.rat: Family + patient prepared for safe home recovery. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the nurse pushed the bowel back into the abdomen and taped the wound closed before calling; the patient developed peritonitis and sepsis
opts.rat: ⚠️ Pushing viscera back contaminates and injures the bowel. Demonstrates the absolute rule against this.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — a DRY gauze was placed over the bowel and not moistened; bowel sections dried and required resection in the OR
opts.rat: ⚠️ Dry gauze caused necrosis. Demonstrates the sterile-saline-moist-gauze-kept-moist rule.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the patient was placed flat with legs extended and then briefly left alone to fetch supplies; bowel further protruded and he had a vasovagal collapse
opts.rat: ⚠️ Flat-with-legs-extended raised tension; leaving the patient violated the bedside-presence rule. Demonstrates low-Fowler's with knees flexed and staying with the patient.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the nurse delayed the surgeon call to medicate for pain first and to complete a long charting note; OR transfer was significantly delayed
opts.rat: ⚠️ The surgical call comes first. Demonstrates the priority of escalation; pain medication and charting come after the call.

opts.text: In the minutes after the bedside response, with sterile moist gauze in place, low-Fowler's with knees flexed, NPO, IV in, and the OR being mobilized — vital signs and visceral position are stable while awaiting transport
opts.rat: An expected stable trajectory while waiting for the OR; continue current management and reassess frequently. Unchanged is appropriate here.

opts.text: A year later, with splinting, binder use during heavy activity, ongoing glycemic and nutrition plans, smoking remaining quit, and follow-up complete — the patient has not had a recurrence
opts.rat: Sustained prevention worked. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: WITHDRAWAL of LIFE-SUSTAINING TREATMENT and COMPASSIONATE TERMINAL EXTUBATION in the ICU for a 78-Year-Old Man on Day 8 of Refractory Septic Shock with Multi-Organ Failure (Mechanical Ventilation + Vasopressors + CRRT) After an Interdisciplinary Family Meeting Confirms Continued Aggressive Care Is No Longer Aligned with His Documented Values: SURROGATE SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT by His Wife (DPOA-HC) Per His Advance Directive, the DOUBLE-EFFECT Principle (Aggressive Opioid + Benzodiazepine + Antimuscarinic Comfort Titration Is NOT Euthanasia), a Structured Compassionate Withdrawal Protocol (Pre-Medicate → Discontinue Vasopressors and Devices → REMOVE the Ventilator → Continue Comfort Titration) with FAMILY PRESENCE, and Bereavement + Team Support
subtitle: WITHDRAWAL of life-sustaining treatment is a routine but profoundly important ICU practice when continued aggressive care no longer aligns with the patient's values or goals — distinct from EUTHANASIA. The patient is dying of his illness; the team is removing interventions that are no longer beneficial and providing intensive COMFORT care. This case is about the ETHICAL and PROCEDURAL framework: confirming the decision (goals-of-care reassessment with the surrogate, anchored in the patient's advance directive and known values), executing a COMPASSIONATE WITHDRAWAL protocol (pre-medicating with opioid + benzodiazepine ± antimuscarinic, discontinuing non-comfort interventions, REMOVING the ventilator, and titrating to comfort throughout), and supporting the family and team. It is distinct from non-ICU hospice (case-082), non-ICU acute goals-of-care conflict (case-092), brain death and organ donation (case-107 — the patient is already dead by neurologic criteria), and outpatient proactive advance care planning (case-142). DECISION-MAKING anchors in the patient's PRIOR EXPRESSED VALUES: an executed ADVANCE DIRECTIVE plus a DPOA-HC who applies SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what the PATIENT would want, not what the surrogate would prefer). When prior wishes are unknown, the standard is BEST INTEREST. Treating teams may declare an intervention non-beneficial when the clinical evidence shows it cannot achieve the patient's stated goals; conflict is managed by clarifying goals, time-limited trials, ethics consultation, and (rarely) institutional dispute-resolution policies. WITHDRAWAL is permissible at the patient's or surrogate's informed request — competent adults may refuse any treatment (links case-122) and surrogates may refuse on the basis of the patient's known wishes (links case-132). The DOUBLE-EFFECT PRINCIPLE governs aggressive symptom management at the end of life: an act that has a foreseeable but unintended harmful effect (e.g., respiratory depression from opioids) is ethically permissible when (1) the act itself is morally neutral or good, (2) the intent is the good effect (comfort), (3) the good effect is not achieved through the bad effect, and (4) there is proportionate reason. Opioids and benzodiazepines used to relieve dyspnea, pain, and anxiety at the end of life are NOT euthanasia — euthanasia is the intentional act of causing death, which is not what is being done here. SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT is the active work: OPIOID (morphine or fentanyl) titrated to relieve dyspnea and pain; BENZODIAZEPINE (midazolam, lorazepam) for anxiety/agitation; ANTIMUSCARINIC (glycopyrrolate or scopolamine) for terminal SECRETIONS (the 'death rattle') while educating the family that the rattle is not distressing to the patient; antiemetics if needed; minimize alarms and unnecessary stimuli. The COMPASSIONATE WITHDRAWAL PROTOCOL: (1) confirm decision and document orders (comfort-focused: DNAR; discontinue ventilator, vasopressors, dialysis, blood draws, monitoring devices not needed for comfort; suspend artificial nutrition/hydration per the patient's wishes), (2) prepare the room (lights soft, alarms off where safe, minimize equipment, position the patient comfortably, allow family at the bedside, chaplaincy as requested), (3) PRE-MEDICATE adequately (a generous opioid + benzodiazepine bolus before any maneuver to reduce dyspnea and air hunger), (4) DISCONTINUE the vasopressors and other non-comfort interventions (typically at the same time as withdrawal — they are not slowly titrated down because the goal is comfort, not survival), (5) REMOVE the ventilator (extubation if not contraindicated by airway/secretion concerns; otherwise convert to flow-by oxygen for visible comfort while withdrawing pressure support) and (6) CONTINUE titration to comfort — assessing dyspnea (use of accessory muscles, grimacing, restlessness), pain, secretions, agitation, and family-perceived distress; reassess and re-medicate as often as needed. TIME-TO-DEATH varies (minutes to hours to occasionally days) and is shaped by the underlying physiology — share this honestly with the family. FAMILY presence is supported: explain what to expect (irregular and slowing breathing, possible agonal respirations, color changes, secretions, transient eye opening, sometimes a brief 'rally'), invite them to speak, touch, play music, and be present in their way; offer chaplaincy and bereavement resources. After death: pronounce per policy; allow family time at the bedside; offer mortuary/funeral information; complete documentation; conduct a TEAM DEBRIEF — moral distress in ICU teams during withdrawal is real and supporting each other is part of the work. KEY DISTINCTIONS: WITHDRAWAL/WITHHOLDING are ethically equivalent (you may withhold an intervention you could also stop). PHYSICIAN-ASSISTED DEATH/MEDICAL AID IN DYING is jurisdiction-specific and is NOT what is happening here. DNAR addresses only CPR; comfort care continues across other interventions. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: equating compassionate symptom titration with euthanasia; under-medicating because of fear of 'hastening' death; abruptly extubating without adequate pre-medication; failing to discontinue non-comfort interventions (continuing labs, pressors, dialysis after the goal has changed); over-disclosing or imposing values; describing comfort medications as 'a lethal injection'; failing to support the family or team. NURSING ROLE: anchor decisions in the patient's documented values via the surrogate; coordinate the interdisciplinary plan (ICU, palliative care, chaplaincy, social work, ethics if needed); pre-medicate, reassess, and titrate aggressively to COMFORT under the double-effect principle (this is not euthanasia); execute the structured withdrawal protocol; support family presence with honest, gentle anticipatory guidance; document objectively; lead the team debrief afterward.
