labs.v: 78 y/o man, ICU day 8 for refractory septic shock with multi-organ failure (mechanical ventilation + dual vasopressors at maximum + CRRT for AKI/hyperK + encephalopathy + transaminitis); aggressive interventions are no longer achieving the patient's stated goals. An EXECUTED ADVANCE DIRECTIVE specifies 'no prolonged life support if no meaningful recovery,' and his WIFE is the documented DPOA-HC. After an interdisciplinary family meeting (intensivist + palliative care + nurse + chaplain), the wife applies SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what HE would want, anchored in the directive and his values) and decides to TRANSITION to COMFORT CARE with WITHDRAWAL of life-sustaining treatment. This is ETHICALLY DISTINCT from euthanasia: the patient is dying of his illness, and the team is REMOVING non-beneficial interventions and providing intensive COMFORT care — NOT intentionally causing death. WITHHOLDING and WITHDRAWING are ethically equivalent (an intervention that could be withheld may also be withdrawn). When prior wishes are unknown, the standard is BEST INTEREST. DNAR addresses only CPR; comfort care continues across other interventions. Conflict is addressed by clarifying goals, time-limited trials, ethics consultation, and (rarely) institutional dispute-resolution policies. This case is distinct from non-ICU hospice ([[case-082]]), non-ICU acute goals-of-care family conflict ([[case-092]]), brain death and organ donation ([[case-107]] — already dead by neurologic criteria), and outpatient proactive ACP ([[case-142]]).
labs.r: Anchor in the patient's PRIOR VALUES: executed AD + DPOA-HC applying SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what HE would want); BEST INTEREST when wishes unknown. WITHHOLDING/WITHDRAWING are ethically equivalent. WITHDRAWAL of non-beneficial therapy + intensive COMFORT = NOT EUTHANASIA (he is dying of his illness; team removes non-beneficial interventions and provides comfort — not intentionally causing death). DNAR = only CPR. Conflict → clarify goals + time-limited trials + ethics + institutional policy. RN role: anchor decisions in values; coordinate the team.

labs.n: DOUBLE-EFFECT principle + symptom management at end of life
labs.v: The DOUBLE-EFFECT principle governs aggressive symptom management at the end of life: an act with a foreseeable but UNINTENDED harmful effect (e.g., respiratory depression from opioids) is ETHICALLY PERMISSIBLE when (1) the act is morally neutral or good, (2) the INTENT is the good effect (comfort), (3) the good effect is NOT achieved through the bad effect, and (4) there is PROPORTIONATE reason. Opioids and benzodiazepines used to relieve dyspnea, pain, and anxiety at the end of life are NOT euthanasia. Under-medicating because of fear of 'hastening' death is a common, harmful error. SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT for compassionate withdrawal: OPIOID (morphine or fentanyl) titrated to relieve DYSPNEA and PAIN (assess by face, accessory-muscle use, grimacing, restlessness — not by an arbitrary respiratory rate cutoff); BENZODIAZEPINE (midazolam, lorazepam) for ANXIETY/AGITATION (especially before withdrawal of vent support); ANTIMUSCARINIC (glycopyrrolate IV or scopolamine patch) for terminal SECRETIONS (the 'death rattle' — educate the family it does NOT distress the patient); antiemetics if needed; antipyretic and skin/mouth care for comfort; minimize alarms and unnecessary stimuli. Re-bolus and titrate AS OFTEN AS NEEDED — there is no 'maximum dose' when the goal is comfort and the patient is dying. Document the doses and indications objectively.
labs.r: DOUBLE-EFFECT: act morally neutral/good + INTENT = comfort + good effect NOT achieved through bad effect + proportionate reason. Opioids + benzodiazepines for EOL symptoms = NOT euthanasia. Under-medicating from fear of 'hastening' death is harmful. SYMPTOMS: OPIOID (morphine/fentanyl) for dyspnea/pain; BENZO (midazolam/lorazepam) for anxiety/agitation; ANTIMUSCARINIC (glycopyrrolate/scopolamine) for secretions ('death rattle' — educate family it doesn't distress pt); antiemetics + skin/mouth care; minimize alarms. Titrate to comfort; no max dose at EOL. RN role: aggressive comfort under double-effect.

labs.n: Structured compassionate withdrawal protocol + family presence + after-death care
labs.v: The COMPASSIONATE WITHDRAWAL PROTOCOL is choreographed: (1) confirm the decision and document COMFORT-FOCUSED orders — DNAR; discontinue ventilator/vasopressors/dialysis/blood draws/non-comfort devices; suspend artificial nutrition/hydration per the patient's wishes; transition all monitoring to comfort assessment; (2) PREPARE the room — soft lights, alarms minimized/silenced where safe, unnecessary equipment removed, patient positioned comfortably, family at the bedside, chaplaincy as requested; (3) PRE-MEDICATE adequately with an opioid + benzodiazepine BOLUS BEFORE any maneuver (the most under-done step in many withdrawals); (4) DISCONTINUE vasopressors and remaining non-comfort interventions (typically at the SAME TIME as withdrawal — they are not slowly titrated down because the goal is comfort, not survival); (5) REMOVE the ventilator (extubation when feasible; otherwise convert to flow-by O2 for visible comfort while withdrawing pressure support); (6) CONTINUE titration to comfort — reassess every few minutes and re-bolus opioid/benzodiazepine for dyspnea/grimacing/restlessness, glycopyrrolate for secretions, and reposition/mouth care/skin care; (7) FAMILY presence is supported throughout — explain what to expect (irregular and slowing breathing, possible agonal respirations, color changes, secretions, transient eye opening, occasional brief 'rally'); invite them to speak, touch, play music, and be present in their way; (8) AFTER DEATH — pronounce per policy; allow private time at the bedside; mortuary/funeral information; bereavement coordinator engaged; document objectively (decision-making, medications/doses/times, procedure timeline, family interactions); (9) TEAM DEBRIEF — moral distress in ICU teams during withdrawal is real and supporting each other is part of the work; chaplaincy/peer support offered. TIME-TO-DEATH is variable (minutes to hours, occasionally days) and is shaped by the underlying physiology — share this HONESTLY with the family.
labs.r: PROTOCOL: (1) confirm + document comfort orders (DNAR + d/c vent/pressors/dialysis/non-comfort + suspend ANH per wishes); (2) prepare room (soft lights, alarms min, equipment cleared, family + chaplain); (3) PRE-MEDICATE adequately (opioid + benzo BOLUS before any maneuver — most under-done step); (4) DISCONTINUE pressors + non-comfort (NOT slowly titrated — goal is comfort); (5) REMOVE ventilator (extubation when feasible, otherwise flow-by O2); (6) CONTINUE comfort titration q few min — opioid/benzo for dyspnea/grimace/restless, glyco for secretions, reposition/mouth/skin care; (7) FAMILY presence + honest expectations (irregular breathing, agonal, color, 'rally'); (8) AFTER DEATH — pronounce + private time + mortuary/bereavement + objective doc; (9) TEAM DEBRIEF. Time to death variable (min-hours-days); honest sharing.

labs.n: Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors + bereavement + team support
labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the team did NOT equate compassionate symptom titration with euthanasia; did NOT under-medicate from fear of 'hastening' death; did NOT abruptly extubate without adequate pre-medication; did NOT slowly titrate down vasopressors as if survival were the goal; did NOT continue CRRT/labs/non-comfort interventions after the goals had changed; did NOT describe comfort medications to the family as 'a lethal injection'; did NOT impose the team's values on the surrogate; did NOT proceed without documenting the surrogate's substituted-judgment rationale; did NOT skip the family preparation about what to expect; and did NOT neglect family bereavement or team debrief. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: an executed advance directive + a DPOA-HC applying substituted judgment; a formal interdisciplinary family meeting documented objectively; comfort-focused orders (DNAR + discontinuation of non-comfort interventions); adequate PRE-MEDICATION (opioid + benzodiazepine bolus) BEFORE any maneuver; structured withdrawal sequence (discontinue vasopressors and remaining non-comfort interventions → remove ventilator → continue titration); aggressive symptom assessment and titration (opioid for dyspnea/pain, benzodiazepine for anxiety, antimuscarinic for secretions, mouth/skin care); family presence with honest, gentle anticipatory guidance; chaplaincy and bereavement support; after-death care with private time and mortuary/funeral resources; and a team DEBRIEF acknowledging moral distress. EXPECTED outcome: the patient dies comfortably with his family present, his values honored, and his team supported.
labs.r: Negatives confirm correct practice (didn't equate comfort titration w/ euthanasia, didn't under-medicate, didn't extubate w/o pre-med, didn't slow-titrate pressors as if survival were goal, didn't continue non-comfort interventions, didn't say 'lethal injection,' didn't impose values, didn't proceed without surrogate rationale documented, didn't skip family prep, didn't skip bereavement/debrief). Protective: AD + DPOA-HC + substituted judgment + documented family meeting + comfort orders + pre-med opioid+benzo + structured protocol + aggressive symptom mgmt + family presence w/ honest anticipatory guidance + chaplaincy + bereavement + after-death private time + team DEBRIEF.

labs.v: 8.6 mmol/L (severe tissue hypoperfusion; refractory shock; not retreated after goals changed)
0.6 mcg/kg/min (max) plus vasopressin 0.04 units/min — MAP not maintained despite maximal therapy
labs.r: Variable; this is at the upper limit of usual ICU titration

labs.n: Pre-medication: morphine + midazolam bolus before ventilator removal
labs.v: Morphine 4-6 mg IV + midazolam 1-2 mg IV given as a comfort bolus before withdrawal; titrate every few minutes to relaxed face/no accessory-muscle use/calm — there is no 'maximum dose' when the goal is comfort and the patient is dying (double-effect principle)
labs.r: Doses are titrated to comfort, not to a target number

labs.v: Glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg IV given for 'death rattle' secretions; family taught that secretions do NOT distress the patient

Orders updated: DNAR; d/c ventilator/vasopressors/CRRT/labs/non-comfort devices; suspend artificial nutrition/hydration per the directive; comfort-focused medications. Private time at bedside; mortuary/funeral information offered; bereavement coordinator engaged. Objective DOCUMENTATION (substituted-judgment rationale + family-meeting summary + every medication w/ dose/time/indication + procedure timeline + family interactions). TEAM DEBRIEF held — moral distress acknowledged + chaplaincy/peer support offered. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT equate comfort titration w/ euthanasia, did NOT under-medicate from fear of 'hastening' death, did NOT abruptly extubate w/o pre-med, did NOT slow-titrate pressors as if survival were the goal, did NOT continue CRRT/labs/non-comfort interventions, did NOT label comfort meds 'a lethal injection,' did NOT impose values on the surrogate, did NOT skip family anticipatory guidance, did NOT skip bereavement/debrief.
providerOrders: GOALS OF CARE: transition to COMFORT CARE per the surrogate's substituted-judgment decision anchored in the patient's executed advance directive; document the family meeting and rationale
CODE STATUS: DNAR

DISCONTINUE: ventilator (extubation), vasopressors (norepinephrine + vasopressin), CRRT, routine blood draws and imaging, non-comfort monitors/devices; suspend artificial nutrition and hydration per the patient's wishes; minimize alarms

SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT (DOUBLE-EFFECT principle — comfort, NOT euthanasia): morphine IV bolus and infusion for dyspnea and pain titrated to comfort; midazolam IV bolus and infusion for anxiety and agitation; glycopyrrolate IV (or scopolamine patch) for terminal secretions; antiemetic if needed; pre-medicate adequately BEFORE any maneuver (extubation, repositioning); reassess and re-titrate every few minutes to relaxed face/no accessory-muscle use/calm — there is no 'maximum dose' at end of life

ROOM/FAMILY: private room; soft lights; alarms minimized where safe; remove unnecessary equipment; allow family at the bedside; chaplaincy as requested; honest anticipatory guidance (variable time to death; irregular and slowing breathing; possible agonal respirations; color changes; secretions; possible brief 'rally')

WITHDRAWAL PROTOCOL: pre-medicate; discontinue vasopressors and remaining non-comfort interventions (not slow titration — the goal is comfort); remove the ventilator (extubation when feasible; otherwise flow-by oxygen for visible comfort while withdrawing pressure support); continue comfort titration
AFTER-DEATH CARE: pronounce per policy; private time at the bedside; mortuary and funeral information; bereavement coordinator; cultural and spiritual practices honored
DOCUMENTATION: substituted-judgment rationale and family-meeting summary; every medication with dose/time/indication; procedure timeline; family interactions; debrief
TEAM SUPPORT: team debrief; acknowledge moral distress; offer chaplaincy and peer support

DO NOT: equate comfort titration with euthanasia; under-medicate from fear of 'hastening' death; abruptly extubate without adequate pre-medication; slowly titrate vasopressors as if survival were the goal; continue non-comfort interventions after the goals have changed; describe comfort medications to the family as 'a lethal injection'; impose the team's values on the surrogate

opts.text: WITHDRAWING life-sustaining treatment is ETHICALLY EQUIVALENT to WITHHOLDING it; both are permissible when consistent with the patient's wishes — and DNAR addresses only CPR (comfort care continues across other interventions)

opts.text: Compassionate withdrawal with intensive symptom management is NOT euthanasia — under the DOUBLE-EFFECT principle, opioids and benzodiazepines used to relieve suffering are ethically permissible even if they may shorten life

steps.sub: What end-of-life ethics + practice principles apply?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Decisions are anchored in the patient's prior expressed values — through an advance directive plus a DPOA-HC applying SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what the patient would want, not what the surrogate would prefer)
opts.rat: CORRECT — the standard. Foundation for honoring autonomy.

opts.text: When prior wishes are unknown, the standard is BEST INTEREST; conflict is managed by clarifying goals, time-limited trials, ethics consultation, and institutional dispute-resolution policies
opts.rat: CORRECT — best-interest and conflict principles. Foundation for difficult cases.

opts.text: Withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment are ethically equivalent
opts.rat: CORRECT — equivalence principle. Foundation for permitting withdrawal.

opts.text: Under the DOUBLE-EFFECT principle, aggressive symptom management with opioids and benzodiazepines at end of life is permissible because the INTENT is relief of suffering — this is NOT euthanasia
opts.rat: CORRECT — double-effect principle. Foundation for aggressive comfort care.

opts.text: Compassionate withdrawal is procedural — pre-medicate adequately, discontinue non-comfort interventions, remove the ventilator (extubation when feasible), and continue titration to comfort; family presence is supported
opts.rat: CORRECT — the protocol principle. Foundation for safe execution.

opts.text: Time to death after withdrawal is variable (minutes to hours, occasionally days) and is shaped by the underlying physiology — share this honestly with the family
opts.rat: CORRECT — honest expectations principle. Foundation for family support.

opts.text: Vasopressors should be slowly titrated DOWN over many hours during compassionate withdrawal because the goal is to preserve survival as long as possible
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The goal at withdrawal is comfort, not survival — vasopressors and other non-comfort interventions are typically discontinued, not slowly titrated; comfort medications are titrated to comfort.

opts.text: DNAR (do-not-attempt-resuscitate) means the patient receives no medical care of any kind and must be transferred to a separate ward
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. DNAR addresses only CPR; other treatments — including aggressive comfort care — continue per plan; no unit transfer is required.

title: RAPID RESPONSE TEAM (RRT) Activation + Coordinated Bedside LEADERSHIP for an 82-Year-Old Frail Woman (Clinical Frailty Scale 6, Executed Advance Directive on File) on a Medical Floor Day 3 of Treatment for Community-Acquired Pneumonia, with a RISING NEWS/MEWS EARLY-WARNING TREND Over Hours (Tachypnea, Tachycardia, Falling SpO2, NEW CONFUSION, Soft BP) Signaling Septic Decompensation: Recognizing the TREND Before the Crash, Escalating Per Protocol Without Delay, ASSEMBLING and LEADING the RRT Bedside Until the Provider Arrives, SBAR Handoff with Closed-Loop Role Assignment, Reversing the Reversible (Oxygen, IV Fluids, Cultures + Antibiotic Re-Dose), Re-Engaging GOALS OF CARE with the Family in the Context of Frailty and Her Advance Directive (Time-Limited ICU Trial vs Continued Floor Care vs Comfort-Focused Plan), and Documenting the Episode + Team Debrief — A LEADERSHIP-FIRST Case Distinct from the Post-Operative RRT Scenarios (cases 079 and 091)
subtitle: Hospitals fail patients in two predictable ways: not noticing the EARLY-WARNING TREND, and noticing it but failing to ESCALATE. Both are leadership failures, and both are why the RAPID RESPONSE TEAM (RRT, sometimes called the Medical Emergency Team) exists: a structured way for any clinician at the bedside to summon a multi-disciplinary team when a patient is deteriorating but has not yet arrested — so the team can intervene before the code. The RRT is one of the most studied patient-safety interventions in hospital medicine; it depends on EARLY recognition, LOW-THRESHOLD activation, and EFFECTIVE coordinated leadership. EARLY WARNING SCORES (NEWS/NEWS-2, MEWS) sum points across respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, temperature, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, and level of consciousness; a RISING score over hours — not a single deranged number — is the most useful signal in an older adult. Activation criteria commonly include any of: RR ≥ 25 or ≤ 8, HR ≥ 130 or ≤ 40, SBP ≤ 90 (or a fall of ≥ 40 from baseline), SpO2 ≤ 90% on oxygen, NEW altered mental status, decreased urine output, repeated/persistent concern by the nurse or family ('staff or family worry' is itself a legitimate criterion), threatened airway, or seizure. In OLDER ADULTS the trend matters more than the headline number — they may be tachypneic with a SpO2 still > 90, or with only NEW confusion as the first marker of sepsis ('atypical' presentation). Once activated, the RRT typically includes a critical-care MD or rapid-response APP, an ICU/respiratory therapist, and the primary RN; the BEDSIDE RN LEADS until the team arrives and then continues to anchor the bedside (the bedside RN knows the patient best). LEADERSHIP at the bedside means CLOSED-LOOP COMMUNICATION (named recipient, directed task, repeat-back), a clear SBAR HANDOFF when the team arrives, role assignment as bodies appear (one person manages airway/oxygen, one places IV access and draws labs/cultures, one runs medications/fluids, one documents, one handles family/charge nurse, one stays in clinical command), and a debrief afterward. CLINICAL response treats the reversible — high-flow oxygen, two large-bore IVs, isotonic fluids per provider, blood cultures and lactate, repeat or expand antibiotics for likely septic decompensation, electrolytes/ABG, focused exam — and watches for shock, respiratory failure, and persistent altered mental status. GOALS OF CARE are RE-ENGAGED in real time, especially for frail older adults: the Clinical Frailty Scale 6 here (moderately frail — needs help with all outside activities and many inside ones) predicts higher ICU mortality, longer length of stay, and worse functional recovery; an EXECUTED ADVANCE DIRECTIVE on file specifies her preferences. The decision pathway is not just 'ICU vs floor' but includes a TIME-LIMITED TRIAL of aggressive therapy in the ICU (e.g., 48-72 hours with defined success criteria), continued aggressive treatment on the floor with comfort emphasis if the family declines ICU, or a COMFORT-FOCUSED transition (links case-149) if continued aggressive care is not consistent with her values. The family conversation uses ASK-TELL-ASK, the SERIOUS-ILLNESS conversation framework, and shared decision-making — never an ultimatum and never a single 'yes/no on the ventilator' question. NURSING ROLE: notice the rising NEWS/MEWS TREND in an older adult and escalate per protocol (don't wait for a single deranged number); activate the RRT promptly without apology; LEAD the bedside until the team arrives and anchor it after; communicate with SBAR + closed-loop; treat the reversible while the team assembles; re-engage goals of care with the family in the context of frailty + the advance directive (time-limited trial vs floor with comfort emphasis vs comfort-focused plan); and document + debrief.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + the early-warning TREND in an older adult (recognize before the crash)
labs.v: 82 y/o woman, day 3 of inpatient treatment for community-acquired pneumonia, with a RISING NEWS over the past 4-6 hours: tachypnea (RR 22 → 28), tachycardia (HR 102 → 118), falling oxygen saturation despite added oxygen (SpO2 94% on 2 L → 88% on 4 L), drifting blood pressure (128/72 → 102/64), and NEW CONFUSION (baseline alert). PMH: HFrEF (LVEF 35%), COPD on home O2, CKD3, advanced frailty (CFS 6 — moderately frail), executed advance directive on file. labs.r: The TREND on early warning scores (NEWS/MEWS) is the cue, not a single deranged number — especially in older adults (atypical presentations; NEW CONFUSION can be the first sepsis sign). Activation criteria include RR ≥25 or ≤8, HR ≥130 or ≤40, SBP ≤90 or drop ≥40 from baseline, SpO2 ≤90% on O2, NEW altered mental status, ↓UOP, threatened airway/seizure, AND staff or family WORRY (a legitimate trigger). RN role: recognize the trend, escalate without delay, activate RRT, do NOT manage alone.

labs.n: Rapid response team activation + structure + bedside leadership (closed-loop + SBAR)
labs.v: The RAPID RESPONSE TEAM (RRT / Medical Emergency Team) is a structured, low-threshold response for the deteriorating but not-yet-arrested patient. Typical composition: critical-care MD or rapid-response APP, ICU/RT, the primary nurse, pharmacy, and the charge RN; some teams include palliative care or chaplaincy on call. The BEDSIDE RN LEADS until the team arrives and continues to anchor the bedside (the bedside RN knows the patient best). LEADERSHIP at the bedside means CLOSED-LOOP COMMUNICATION (NAMED recipient, DIRECTED task, repeat-back, confirmation) and CLEAR ROLE ASSIGNMENT as people arrive (one manages airway/oxygen, one places IV access and draws labs/cultures, one runs medications/fluids, one documents, one handles family/charge nurse, one stays in clinical command). The HANDOFF to the responding team uses SBAR (Situation: what's happening now; Background: relevant history, medications, advance directive, baseline; Assessment: your clinical impression; Recommendation: what you're asking for) and is delivered concisely and without apology. The RN does NOT step away from the patient to manage the team alone; the RN also does NOT defer all decision-making to the responding clinician but continues to advocate as the bedside expert. DEBRIEF after the response — what went well, what to do differently, family + team support — and document the timeline objectively.
labs.r: RRT structure: critical-care MD or APP + ICU/RT + primary RN + pharmacy + charge RN (palliative/chaplaincy on call). The bedside RN LEADS until team arrives and anchors the bedside after. CLOSED-LOOP communication: named recipient + directed task + repeat-back + confirmation. ROLE assignment as people arrive (airway/O2, IV/labs, meds/fluids, documenter, family/charge, command). SBAR handoff to the responder (S-B-A-R); concise + no apology. Don't manage alone; don't defer all decision-making — advocate as bedside expert. DEBRIEF + objective documentation. RN role: lead + delegate + SBAR + debrief.

labs.n: Clinical response + goals-of-care reassessment with frailty + advance directive
labs.v: CLINICAL response treats the reversible while the team assembles: high-flow OXYGEN, TWO LARGE-BORE IVs and isotonic FLUIDS per provider (cautious in HFrEF — small boluses with frequent reassessment), BLOOD CULTURES + lactate + ABG + CBC/BMP/coagulation, broad-spectrum ANTIBIOTIC re-dose for likely septic decompensation, ECG, focused exam. Watch for SHOCK (rising lactate, persistent hypotension after fluids), RESPIRATORY FAILURE (rising work of breathing, falling SpO2 despite oxygen), and persistent ALTERED mental status. GOALS-OF-CARE re-engagement in real time is the high-yield leadership skill — especially in frail older adults: the CLINICAL FRAILTY SCALE 6 here (moderately frail — needs help with all outside activities and many inside ones) predicts higher ICU mortality, longer ICU length of stay, and worse functional recovery; the executed ADVANCE DIRECTIVE specifies her preference for comfort over prolonged ICU care if prognosis is poor. The decision pathway is NOT just 'ICU vs floor' — it includes a TIME-LIMITED TRIAL of aggressive therapy in the ICU (e.g., 48-72 hours with DEFINED success criteria — improving lactate, MAP > 65 off pressors within 24-48 hours, no progression to mechanical ventilation OR a clear reversibility), continued aggressive treatment on the floor with comfort emphasis if the family declines ICU, or a COMFORT-FOCUSED transition ([[case-149]]) if continued aggressive care is not consistent with her values. Communicate with the family using ASK-TELL-ASK, the SERIOUS-ILLNESS conversation framework, and shared decision-making — never a single 'yes/no on the ventilator' question and never an ultimatum. The bedside RN advocates for the patient's values throughout.
labs.r: Reversible treatment: high-flow O2 + 2 large-bore IVs + isotonic fluids per provider (cautious in HFrEF), cultures + lactate + ABG + labs, broad-spectrum abx re-dose, ECG, focused exam. Watch shock/respiratory failure/persistent AMS. GOALS-OF-CARE re-engagement in real time = the high-yield skill. CLINICAL FRAILTY SCALE 6 predicts higher ICU mortality/LOS + worse functional recovery; AD specifies comfort over prolonged ICU. Pathway = TIME-LIMITED TRIAL (defined success criteria) vs continued floor care w/ comfort emphasis vs COMFORT-FOCUSED ([[case-149]]). Communicate w/ ASK-TELL-ASK + serious-illness framework + shared decision-making — NOT a 'yes/no on the ventilator' ultimatum. RN advocates for patient values.

labs.n: Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors + debrief + documentation
labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct emergency practice): the RN did NOT wait for a single 'enough' value before escalating (recognized the TREND); did NOT try to manage alone or defer the call to the day-shift provider; did NOT skip SBAR or 'just do it yourself'; did NOT collapse the goals-of-care conversation into a single 'do you want the ventilator?' question; did NOT bypass the family or assume frailty alone made the decision; did NOT skip the RN-to-RN handoff or the medication reconciliation at ICU transfer; did NOT forget to document timeline + interventions + medications + family conversation + advance-directive review; and did NOT skip the team debrief. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: timely recognition of the rising NEWS trend; prompt RRT activation without delay; the bedside RN LEADING until the team arrived and anchoring the bedside after; closed-loop role assignment; clear SBAR handoff to the responding APP; reversible treatment (O2, fluids cautious in HFrEF, cultures, antibiotic re-dose); real-time goals-of-care re-engagement using the serious-illness framework with the family; an option-rich decision (time-limited ICU trial vs continued floor care with comfort emphasis vs comfort-focused plan); a structured RN-to-RN handoff at ICU transfer with medication reconciliation and AD/POLST transmission; objective documentation; and a team debrief afterward. EXPECTED outcome: the deterioration is recognized and treated early, the family is supported in a values-aligned decision, and either the patient improves on a time-limited ICU trial or transitions to a comfort-focused plan — but in either case her preferences guide the path.
labs.r: Negatives: didn't wait for a single 'enough' value, didn't manage alone, didn't skip SBAR, didn't collapse goals to 'ventilator yes/no,' didn't bypass family, didn't skip RN-to-RN handoff + med rec, didn't skip documentation/debrief. Protective: timely trend recognition + prompt RRT activation + RN leading + closed-loop roles + SBAR + reversible treatment + real-time goals-of-care reengagement w/ serious-illness framework + option-rich decision (time-limited ICU trial vs floor w/ comfort vs comfort-focused) + structured RN-to-RN handoff + med rec + AD/POLST + documentation + debrief. RN role: trend recognition + leadership + advocacy.

opts.text: Goals of care were re-engaged with the family using the serious-illness framework + ask-tell-ask + shared decision-making, anchored in the advance directive and Clinical Frailty Scale, and an option-rich pathway was offered (time-limited ICU trial / floor with comfort emphasis / comfort-focused)
opts.rat: Patient values drive the decision. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: A structured RN-to-RN handoff at ICU transfer included SBAR + two identifiers + medication reconciliation + lines/drains/devices + family contacts + AD/POLST transmission; the team debriefed afterward
opts.rat: Safe handoff and closed-loop response. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative — the RN waited for a single 'enough' value before activating the RRT and tried to manage the deterioration alone; the patient progressed to cardiac arrest before the team arrived
opts.rat: ⚠️ Waiting for a single deranged number and managing alone is the classic leadership failure that turns a deterioration into a code.

opts.text: Alternative — the goals-of-care conversation was collapsed into 'do you want her on a ventilator, yes or no?' and the daughter was pressured to answer immediately; the family was traumatized
opts.rat: ⚠️ A serious-illness conversation is about values + goals using ask-tell-ask + shared decision-making, not an ultimatum on a single intervention.

opts.text: Alternative — frailty (CFS 6) alone was treated as sufficient justification for a unilateral comfort-focused transition without re-engaging the family or reviewing the advance directive
opts.rat: ⚠️ Frailty informs the conversation; it does not replace the patient's values, the surrogate, or the advance directive.

opts.text: Alternative — the bedside RN stepped away as soon as the team arrived and deferred all decision-making without further bedside advocacy; documentation was incomplete and the patient's values were not represented
opts.rat: ⚠️ The bedside RN remains the patient's anchor and clinical expert; continued advocacy is part of the response.

opts.text: Alternative — handoff to the ICU was verbal only without SBAR, two identifiers, medication reconciliation, or advance-directive transmission; a critical medication was missed at ICU arrival
opts.rat: ⚠️ Verbal-only handoffs without structure are the most common transition failure. Use SBAR + identifiers + medication reconciliation + AD/POLST.

opts.text: On reassessment at 48 hours, the time-limited ICU trial showed clear improvement (lactate trending down, MAP > 65 off pressors, no progression to mechanical ventilation); plan continued with step-down + post-ICU care
opts.rat: Time-limited trial with defined success criteria followed and acted on. Ideal trajectory.

title: Comprehensive LEVOTHYROXINE Teaching for a Newly Diagnosed 52-Year-Old Woman with Primary Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's) — TSH 18 + Low Free T4 + Classic Symptoms (Fatigue, Cold Intolerance, Weight Gain, Constipation, Dry Skin, Hair Thinning, Depression): Why LIFELONG Replacement, the High-Yield TIMING Rule (Take ONCE DAILY in the MORNING on an EMPTY STOMACH with WATER, 30-60 Minutes BEFORE Food/Coffee/Other Medications), Drug-Food-Mineral Interactions That REDUCE Absorption (CALCIUM, IRON, ANTACIDS, PPIs, Soy, Coffee, High-Fiber — SEPARATE by ~4 Hours), Interactions That Affect Metabolism (Estrogen, Phenytoin/Carbamazepine/Rifampin, Warfarin Potentiation), TSH MONITORING (q6-8 Weeks Until Stable, Then q6-12 Months), Recognizing OVER- and UNDER-Replacement, BRAND CONSISTENCY, the Pregnancy Dose-Increase Rule (~30%), Missed-Dose Rule (Same Day Take; Next Day SKIP), and Cardiac Cautions in Older Patients with CAD
subtitle: Hypothyroidism is one of the most common chronic endocrine conditions and one of the most teachable. PRIMARY hypothyroidism — gland failure (most often AUTOIMMUNE Hashimoto's thyroiditis) — drops circulating T4/T3, removes the negative-feedback brake on the pituitary, and elevates TSH; classic symptoms include FATIGUE, COLD INTOLERANCE, WEIGHT GAIN, CONSTIPATION, dry skin, hair thinning, bradycardia, depression, menorrhagia, and a delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes. The diagnosis is made by an elevated TSH with low free T4 (primary), or — much less commonly — a low/normal TSH with low free T4 (secondary/pituitary). Treatment is LEVOTHYROXINE, a synthetic T4 (thyroxine) that the body deconverts to active T3 — taken as a SINGLE DAILY tablet, LIFELONG, with a NARROW therapeutic index. Adult dosing typically starts near 1.6 mcg/kg/day for healthy patients under 50-60 with no cardiac disease (a common conservative empiric start is 75-100 mcg daily; titrate up); for OLDER ADULTS (>60) or anyone with CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE/cardiac history, start LOW (12.5-25 mcg daily) and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating ANGINA, MI, or arrhythmias as metabolic demand rises. The HIGH-YIELD TIMING RULE is the single most important teaching point and is heavily tested: take it ONCE DAILY in the MORNING on an EMPTY STOMACH with a full glass of WATER, 30-60 MINUTES BEFORE breakfast, coffee, tea, juice, milk, or any other medication. Coffee and high-fiber meals dramatically reduce absorption — they are food, not water. Bedtime dosing 3-4 hours after the last meal is an acceptable alternative; consistency in timing is more important than the exact clock-time. DRUG/FOOD/MINERAL INTERACTIONS that REDUCE absorption — SEPARATE by AT LEAST 4 HOURS — include CALCIUM (carbonate or citrate, dairy supplements), IRON (ferrous sulfate/gluconate), MAGNESIUM and ALUMINUM antacids, SUCRALFATE, CHOLESTYRAMINE and other bile-acid sequestrants, PROTON PUMP INHIBITORS and H2 blockers (reduce stomach acid needed for absorption), SOY products, and high-fiber foods. INTERACTIONS that affect MAY require dose changes include: ESTROGENS (oral contraceptives, HRT) raise thyroid-binding globulin and often require a higher dose; PHENYTOIN, CARBAMAZEPINE, and RIFAMPIN induce metabolism and may require a higher dose; LEVOTHYROXINE may POTENTIATE WARFARIN (monitor INR more closely when starting/adjusting). MONITORING: check a TSH 6-8 weeks after starting or after any dose change; once stable, check TSH every 6-12 months. Target TSH ranges vary, but a common goal in primary hypothyroidism is approximately 0.5-2.5 mIU/L; secondary hypothyroidism is monitored using free T4 (TSH is unreliable). OVER-replacement (TSH suppressed; FT4 high) produces hyperthyroid symptoms — PALPITATIONS, ATRIAL FIBRILLATION, anxiety, insomnia, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, diarrhea — and chronic over-replacement raises ATRIAL FIBRILLATION and OSTEOPOROSIS risk. UNDER-replacement (TSH still high) shows persistent fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, and depression. BRAND CONSISTENCY matters because small inter-manufacturer differences in bioavailability can shift the TSH; do NOT switch brand or generic without notifying the provider and rechecking TSH. PREGNANCY is a special situation: requirements increase by approximately 20-30%, often by an additional 25-50 mcg daily, and the provider must be notified IMMEDIATELY upon a confirmed/planned pregnancy with a TSH check every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy. MISSED-DOSE rule: if remembered the same day, take it; if it is already close to the next dose, SKIP and resume the next day — never double up. LIFELONG adherence is the rule — do NOT stop when feeling better; the symptoms will recur and the cycle resets. Cardiac patients on dose escalation report any chest pain, palpitations, or new dyspnea immediately. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: taking the dose with coffee or breakfast; taking it at the same time as calcium, iron, or a multivitamin (or routine PPI/H2 blocker) without the 4-hour separation; doubling up after a missed dose; switching between brands without TSH recheck; stopping the medication when feeling better; failing to notify the provider of a planned/confirmed pregnancy; assuming TSH normalizes immediately (steady state takes weeks); and aggressive titration in older adults with CAD. NURSING ROLE: teach the WHY (lifelong replacement of a hormone), the precise timing rule, the interaction/separation rules, monitoring expectations, signs of over/under-replacement, brand consistency, the pregnancy rule, the missed-dose rule, cardiac cautions, and the adherence frame — verified by TEACH-BACK with the patient and family.

providerOrders: DIAGNOSIS: primary autoimmune hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's); TSH 18.4, free T4 0.6, anti-TPO positive
MEDICATION: levothyroxine 75 mcg PO daily; lifelong replacement; do not stop without provider direction

TIMING/ADMINISTRATION: take once daily in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, 30-60 minutes before breakfast/coffee/tea/juice/milk/any other medication; bedtime dosing 3-4 hours after the last meal is an acceptable alternative; consistency of timing matters more than exact clock-time

SEPARATE BY AT LEAST 4 HOURS: calcium, iron (including prenatal vitamins with iron), magnesium and aluminum antacids, sucralfate, cholestyramine and other bile-acid sequestrants, proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers, soy products, walnuts, and high-fiber foods

INTERACTIONS to monitor: estrogen/oral contraceptive/HRT may raise required dose; phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin may raise required dose; levothyroxine may potentiate warfarin — monitor INR more closely at initiation and dose changes
MONITORING: TSH 6-8 weeks after starting or any dose change; once stable, TSH every 6-12 months; common target on therapy approximately 0.5-2.5 mIU/L

OVER-REPLACEMENT WARNINGS: report palpitations, atrial fibrillation, anxiety/insomnia, heat intolerance, unintended weight loss, tremor, or diarrhea (suppressed TSH risks atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis over time)
UNDER-REPLACEMENT WARNINGS: report persistent fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, or depression (suggest TSH still high — dose increase likely needed)
BRAND CONSISTENCY: do not switch brand or generic without notifying the provider; if switched, recheck TSH 6-8 weeks after the change

PREGNANCY RULE: notify the provider immediately at planned or confirmed pregnancy — dose typically increases by approximately 20-30% and TSH is checked every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy
MISSED DOSE: if remembered the same day, take it; if close to the next dose, skip and resume the next day — do not double up
CARDIAC CAUTION: in older adults or anyone with CAD, start low and titrate slowly; report any new chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath during titration
EDUCATION/ADHERENCE: pill organizer + morning routine + reminder; lifelong therapy — do not stop when feeling better; follow-up appointments and labs as scheduled

opts.text: Brand consistency matters because of inter-manufacturer bioavailability differences; missed-dose rule = same day take, otherwise skip — never double; lifelong adherence
opts.rat: CORRECT — operational principles. Foundation for safe use.

opts.text: Levothyroxine should be taken with a hot cup of coffee to improve absorption, and TSH normalizes within 24-48 hours after starting therapy
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Coffee reduces absorption (food, not water); TSH steady state takes weeks — recheck at 6-8 weeks.

opts.text: Over-replacement is harmless and there is no need to monitor for atrial fibrillation or osteoporosis with long-term suppressed TSH
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Chronic over-replacement raises AFib and osteoporosis risk; monitor TSH and adjust.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Ensure she understands the WHY (lifelong replacement of a hormone) and is committed to ADHERENCE — do NOT stop when feeling better
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Without the WHY and adherence, nothing else holds. RN role: WHY + lifelong adherence.

opts.text: Teach the precise TIMING rule (once daily morning on empty stomach with water 30-60 min before food/coffee/other medications) and the 4-HOUR separation from calcium/iron/antacids/PPIs/sucralfate/cholestyramine/soy/high-fiber
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. The timing and separation rules are the most heavily tested teaching points. RN role: timing + separation.

opts.text: Review TSH MONITORING schedule (q6-8 wk after change/initiation, then q6-12 mo) and what to expect (steady state takes weeks)
opts.rat: #3 — Sets expectations and adherence to follow-up. RN role: monitoring.

opts.text: Teach recognition of OVER-replacement (palpitations/AFib, anxiety, heat intolerance, weight loss) and UNDER-replacement (continued hypothyroid symptoms), and the brand-consistency, pregnancy, and missed-dose rules
opts.rat: #4 — Safety net for the long road. RN role: signs + brand + pregnancy + missed dose.

opts.text: Cardiac caution (CAD/older adult — report chest pain/palpitations/dyspnea on titration) and confirm understanding with TEACH-BACK; involve family
opts.rat: #5 — Cardiac safety + verified understanding close the loop. RN role: cardiac caution + teach-back + family.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this levothyroxine teaching.

opts.text: Take 75 mcg PO once daily in the MORNING on an EMPTY STOMACH with WATER, 30-60 minutes before breakfast/coffee/tea/juice/milk/any other medication
opts.rat: The high-yield timing rule. RN role: precise administration.

opts.text: Separate by AT LEAST 4 HOURS from calcium, iron, antacids, sucralfate, cholestyramine, PPIs/H2 blockers, soy, and high-fiber foods
opts.rat: Prevents reduced absorption. RN role: interaction/separation.

opts.text: Notify the provider for any new medication, supplement, or herbal product (especially estrogen/OCPs/HRT, phenytoin/carbamazepine/rifampin, warfarin) and at planned/confirmed pregnancy (dose may increase 20-30%)
opts.rat: Captures metabolism/effect interactions and the pregnancy rule. RN role: interactions + pregnancy.

opts.text: Check TSH 6-8 weeks after starting or any dose change; once stable, every 6-12 months; keep brand consistency (do not switch without provider + TSH recheck)
opts.rat: Monitoring + brand consistency drive stability. RN role: TSH schedule + brand.

opts.text: Report over-replacement (palpitations, AFib, anxiety/insomnia, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, diarrhea) and under-replacement (continued fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, depression); cardiac patients report chest pain/palpitations/dyspnea on titration
opts.rat: Early detection of over/under-replacement and cardiac warning signs. RN role: signs to report.

opts.text: Apply the missed-dose rule (same day = take when remembered; close to next dose = skip; never double) and continue therapy LIFELONG even when feeling well
opts.rat: Prevents both under-dosing and over-dosing. RN role: missed dose + lifelong adherence.

opts.text: Take the dose with a cup of coffee and breakfast alongside her calcium supplement and oral contraceptive each morning
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — coffee/food/calcium dramatically reduce absorption; separate by ≥4 hours and take on an empty stomach with water.

opts.text: Double the dose the next day if she misses a dose; stop the medication when she starts feeling better
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — doubling causes over-replacement; stopping causes symptom recurrence.

opts.text: Switch between manufacturers/generics whenever the pharmacy has one in stock without notifying the provider
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — inter-manufacturer bioavailability differences can shift TSH; do not switch without provider and TSH recheck.

opts.text: Tell her TSH normalizes within 24-48 hours, so feeling better that quickly is expected and any persistent fatigue means the drug is not working
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — steady state takes weeks; recheck TSH at 6-8 weeks and adjust if needed.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Teach the WHY (lifelong T4 replacement) and frame adherence as non-negotiable — do not stop when feeling better
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Without the WHY, adherence will not hold. RN role: WHY + adherence.

opts.text: Teach the precise TIMING rule (morning, empty stomach, water only, 30-60 min before food/coffee/other meds; bedtime alternative; consistency matters)
opts.rat: #2 — Second. The timing rule is the highest-impact teaching point. RN role: timing.

opts.text: Teach the 4-HOUR SEPARATION from calcium/iron/antacids/sucralfate/cholestyramine/PPIs/H2 blockers/soy/high-fiber and the metabolism/effect interactions (estrogen, phenytoin/carbamazepine/rifampin, warfarin)
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Eliminates the highest-yield absorption and metabolism pitfalls. RN role: interactions.

opts.text: Teach TSH monitoring + over/under-replacement signs + brand consistency + pregnancy rule + missed-dose rule + cardiac caution
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. The safety net for the long road. RN role: monitoring + signs + special rules.

opts.text: Verify with TEACH-BACK, set up a pill organizer + morning routine + reminder, involve family, and schedule follow-up TSH
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Verification + routine + family + follow-up sustain the plan. RN role: teach-back + adherence support.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: She demonstrates a pill organizer + reminders and on teach-back correctly verbalizes the timing rule, the 4-hour separation, the monitoring schedule, the missed-dose rule, brand consistency, and the pregnancy notification rule
opts.rat: Verified understanding + adherence plan. The hallmark of safe levothyroxine self-management.

opts.text: At the 6-8-week follow-up her TSH has fallen from 18.4 to 4.2 and her energy, cold intolerance, bowel function, and mood are improving — continue current dose and recheck
opts.rat: Expected response to effective therapy with correct administration. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: She informs the provider of a planned pregnancy and her dose is increased ~25 mcg with TSH checks every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy
opts.rat: Correct application of the pregnancy rule. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Years later, she maintains brand consistency, takes the dose with water on an empty stomach 30-60 min before breakfast/coffee, separates calcium/iron by 4 hours, and her TSH stays in target
opts.rat: Sustained safe self-management. Ideal long-term outcome.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — she takes the dose with coffee and breakfast and at the same time as her calcium supplement; her TSH remains high and her symptoms continue
opts.rat: ⚠️ Coffee/food/calcium reduced absorption. Demonstrates the timing and 4-hour-separation rules.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — she doubles the dose after missing one and develops palpitations, anxiety, insomnia, and a new tremor; ECG shows new AFib
opts.rat: ⚠️ Doubling caused over-replacement and AFib. Demonstrates the missed-dose rule (same day take, otherwise skip — never double).

opts.text: Alternative scenario — she stops the medication when she feels better; symptoms return within months and her TSH rises again
opts.rat: ⚠️ Stopping causes recurrence. Demonstrates the lifelong-adherence rule.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the pharmacy switches her between brands repeatedly without provider notification; her TSH fluctuates in and out of target
opts.rat: ⚠️ Brand inconsistency shifts bioavailability. Demonstrates the brand-consistency rule + TSH recheck after any switch.

opts.text: In the first 1-2 weeks of therapy, before steady state, her TSH and symptoms are essentially unchanged while she takes the medication correctly
opts.rat: Expected — steady state takes weeks; continue and recheck TSH at 6-8 weeks. Unchanged is appropriate here.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — she is told the dose may be reduced to allow a long-term TSH below the lower limit 'to feel her best'; she develops new atrial fibrillation and reduced bone density on later screening
opts.rat: ⚠️ Chronic over-replacement raises AFib and osteoporosis risk. Demonstrates targeting an appropriate TSH range rather than suppressed levels.

title: OCCUPATIONAL BLOODBORNE PATHOGEN EXPOSURE — Percutaneous NEEDLESTICK Injury in a 32-Year-Old Medical-Surgical RN from a Hollow-Bore IV Catheter While Disposing of It from a KNOWN HIV-POSITIVE Source Patient (Detectable Viral Load) Plus Unknown HBV/HCV Status: The Choreographed Immediate Response (WASH with Soap + Water, Do NOT Use Bleach/Alcohol/Peroxide, REPORT to Supervisor + Occupational/Employee Health Without Delay), OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard Compliance (Exposure Log + Confidentiality), Rapid SOURCE-Patient + EXPOSED-WORKER Baseline Serologies (HIV, HBV-HBsAg, HCV-Antibody), Pathogen-Specific POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS — HIV PEP Within HOURS (Ideally <2 h, No Later Than 72 h) with a 3-Drug Regimen (TDF + FTC + an INTEGRASE Inhibitor like Raltegravir/Dolutegravir) for 28 Days, HBV HBIG + Vaccine per Vaccination Status, HCV NO PEP but Monitor (HCV RNA at 3 Weeks + Antibody Follow-Up), Post-Exposure Counseling (Safer Sex + No Donation × 6 Months + Pregnancy/Breastfeeding Considerations), Serial Follow-Up Testing (HIV at 6 Weeks, 3 Months, 6 Months — Earlier with 4th-Generation Assays), Emotional + Peer Support, and PREVENTION (Engineered Safety Devices + NEVER RECAP + Sharps Containers at Point of Use + Standard Precautions)
subtitle: Occupational bloodborne pathogen (BBP) exposure is a common but high-stakes event: tens of thousands of percutaneous injuries occur annually among US healthcare workers, and the response in the first MINUTES TO HOURS shapes the outcome. Three pathogens dominate the calculus — HIV, HEPATITIS B (HBV), and HEPATITIS C (HCV) — and each has a different baseline risk per percutaneous exposure from a known-infected source (approximately 0.3% for HIV from a known-positive source, 6-30% for HBV from an HBeAg-positive source in an unvaccinated worker, and ~1.8% for HCV), a different prophylaxis pathway, and a different monitoring plan. IMMEDIATE bedside care for the exposed worker is straightforward: WASH the puncture site immediately with SOAP and WATER (mucous-membrane exposures with saline or clean water; eye exposures flush with copious water at an eye-wash station for 15 minutes); allow gentle bleeding under running water — do NOT vigorously squeeze the wound (no efficacy benefit and may cause additional tissue trauma); and do NOT apply BLEACH, ALCOHOL, HYDROGEN PEROXIDE, or other caustic agents (no benefit and tissue damage). REPORT the injury IMMEDIATELY to the charge nurse/supervisor and Occupational/Employee Health (or the Emergency Department after hours) — time is the most important variable for HIV PEP. The OSHA BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS STANDARD (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires annual training, free HBV vaccination, engineered safety devices, sharps containers at the point of use, an EXPOSURE INCIDENT REPORT, and CONFIDENTIALITY around the exposed worker and the source. SOURCE-PATIENT TESTING is performed per state law (most states permit testing for an occupational BBP exposure with informed consent; some allow without consent for occupational exposure) — rapid HIV, HBsAg, and anti-HCV are obtained where possible; ideally rapid 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody assays. EXPOSED-WORKER BASELINE labs include rapid HIV, HBV (anti-HBs to confirm immune status if vaccinated, HBsAg to exclude prior infection), anti-HCV, plus a pregnancy test if applicable. HIV PEP is TIME-CRITICAL — start WITHIN HOURS (ideally < 2 h, NO LATER than 72 h, with steeply declining efficacy after 72 h). The current US standard regimen is TENOFOVIR DISOPROXIL FUMARATE (TDF) + EMTRICITABINE (FTC) as a single tablet PLUS an INTEGRASE-STRAND-TRANSFER INHIBITOR — RALTEGRAVIR or DOLUTEGRAVIR — for 28 DAYS (4 weeks); continue if the source HIV status is confirmed positive (or unknown after risk assessment), discontinue if the source is confirmed negative on adequate testing. Counsel about expected side effects (GI upset, fatigue, headache) and arrange follow-up. HBV management depends on the EXPOSED WORKER'S vaccination + immune status and the SOURCE'S HBsAg status: a vaccinated worker with a documented anti-HBs of at least 10 mIU/mL needs no action; a vaccinated non-responder OR a worker with unknown response needs HEPATITIS B IMMUNE GLOBULIN (HBIG) plus a vaccine booster (and a revaccination series for known non-responders); an unvaccinated worker needs HBIG plus initiation of the HBV vaccine series — HBIG is ideally given WITHIN 24 HOURS and efficacy declines over the first 7 days. HCV currently has NO post-exposure prophylaxis available; the worker is monitored with anti-HCV + HCV RNA at baseline, HCV RNA at 3 weeks, and anti-HCV at 4-6 months (some institutions use HCV RNA at additional intervals). If the worker seroconverts to HCV, the standard treatment is a direct-acting antiviral (DAA) course with cure rates over 95%. FOLLOW-UP testing for HIV is at 6 WEEKS, 3 MONTHS, and 6 MONTHS (the 6-month time point can sometimes be omitted with a 4th-generation assay if all earlier results are negative). POST-EXPOSURE COUNSELING for the worker until cleared: use barrier protection (CONDOMS) for sexual activity; do NOT donate blood, tissue, plasma, organs, or sperm; pregnancy/breastfeeding counseling and obstetric/maternal-fetal medicine input if pregnant; symptoms of acute seroconversion (fever, fatigue, rash, lymphadenopathy, mononucleosis-like illness) to report. PEER and emotional SUPPORT are part of the standard — exposed workers commonly experience anxiety, sleep disturbance, and shame about the event; chaplaincy and employee assistance programs are offered, and confidentiality is preserved. PREVENTION is the most important long-term lesson: safety-ENGINEERED sharps devices (retractable, blunting, needleless systems), SHARPS CONTAINERS AT THE POINT OF USE, the NEVER-RECAP rule (recapping is the most common cause of needlestick), the SCOOP technique only if recapping is unavoidable (one-handed), passing sharps via a neutral zone rather than hand-to-hand, gloves and other PPE under standard precautions, and reinforcing a culture of immediate reporting without blame. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: using bleach/alcohol/peroxide on the wound; vigorously squeezing the wound; delaying or not reporting the exposure; delaying source-patient or exposed-worker testing; delaying HIV PEP beyond hours; missing the HBIG window or HBV vaccine algorithm based on serostatus; recapping needles; failing to maintain confidentiality. NURSING ROLE: deliver immediate bedside care (wash with soap and water, no caustics, no aggressive squeezing); REPORT immediately to supervisor and Occupational Health without delay; complete the OSHA exposure incident report; coordinate rapid source-patient and exposed-worker baseline serologies; ensure HIV PEP is started within hours of exposure as appropriate; apply the HBV HBIG + vaccine algorithm correctly; monitor HCV; arrange serial follow-up testing and counseling; support the worker emotionally; and reinforce prevention (engineered devices + never recap + sharps containers at point of use + standard precautions).

HIV PEP STARTED within hours (TDF + FTC + integrase inhibitor [raltegravir or dolutegravir]) x 28 days; counseled on adherence + side effects (GI upset/fatigue/headache). HBV algorithm: if anti-HBs < 10 mIU/mL → HBIG within 24 h + revaccinate; if ≥ 10 → no action. HCV: NO PEP — baseline negative, plan HCV RNA at 3 wk + anti-HCV at 4-6 mo. COUNSELING: safer sex (condoms) + NO blood/tissue/organ/sperm donation × 6 mo + pregnancy/breastfeeding considerations + acute-seroconversion sx to report (fever/fatigue/rash/LAD/mono-like). Chaplaincy + EAP offered. SERIAL HIV testing scheduled at 6 wk + 3 mo + 6 mo (6 mo may be omitted w/ 4th-gen assay if earlier negative). PREVENTION reinforced at unit huddle (engineered safety devices + NEVER RECAP + sharps containers at point of use + activate safety mechanism + neutral-zone sharps passing + standard precautions + just-culture reporting). Confidentiality preserved throughout. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT apply bleach/alcohol/peroxide to wound, did NOT vigorously squeeze, did NOT delay report or OSHA log, did NOT wait beyond hours for HIV PEP decision, did NOT miss HBV algorithm step based on serostatus, did NOT continue working w/o coverage + support, did NOT recap the needle, did NOT compromise confidentiality.
providerOrders: OCCUPATIONAL BLOODBORNE PATHOGEN EXPOSURE: percutaneous needlestick from a hollow-bore IV catheter, source known HIV+ with detectable viral load; HBV/HCV source status pending

IMMEDIATE BEDSIDE: wash the puncture site with soap and water under running water; allow gentle bleeding; do NOT vigorously squeeze the wound; do NOT apply bleach/alcohol/hydrogen peroxide or other caustic agents; clean dressing

REPORTING: report immediately to charge nurse/supervisor and Occupational/Employee Health (or Emergency Department after hours); complete OSHA exposure incident report (date/time/route/source/device/circumstances) with confidentiality maintained for the exposed worker and source
SOURCE-PATIENT TESTING: obtain consent per state law; rapid HIV antigen/antibody, HBsAg, anti-HCV; document and communicate results per protocol
EXPOSED-WORKER BASELINE LABS: rapid 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody; anti-HBs (and HBsAg as indicated); anti-HCV; pregnancy test if applicable

HIV POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP): initiate within hours of exposure (ideally < 2 h, no later than 72 h); 3-drug regimen for 28 days — tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + emtricitabine plus an integrase-strand-transfer inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir); continue if source HIV-positive (or unknown after risk assessment), discontinue if source HIV-negative on adequate testing; counsel on adherence and side effects

HBV MANAGEMENT (by status): vaccinated worker with anti-HBs >= 10 mIU/mL — no action; vaccinated non-responder OR unknown response — HBIG + vaccine booster (consider second HBIG and revaccination per protocol if known non-responder); unvaccinated — HBIG + initiate vaccine series; HBIG ideally within 24 hours (efficacy declines over 7 days)
HCV MANAGEMENT: no PEP available; baseline anti-HCV (and HCV RNA as indicated); HCV RNA at 3 weeks; anti-HCV at 4-6 months; if seroconverts, refer for direct-acting antiviral therapy

COUNSELING: barrier protection (condoms) for sexual activity, no blood/tissue/plasma/organ/sperm donation, address pregnancy/breastfeeding considerations, report acute seroconversion symptoms (fever, fatigue, rash, lymphadenopathy, mononucleosis-like illness); chaplaincy and Employee Assistance Program

FOLLOW-UP TESTING: HIV at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (the 6-month time point may be omitted with a 4th-generation assay if earlier results are negative); HCV per schedule above; HBV per algorithm

PREVENTION/REINFORCEMENT: engineered safety devices; sharps containers at point of use; never recap (one-handed scoop only if unavoidable); neutral-zone sharps passing during procedures; activate safety mechanism after each use; PPE under standard precautions; just-culture reporting; annual OSHA training

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters in this occupational needlestick?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Percutaneous needlestick from a hollow-bore IV catheter just used on a KNOWN HIV+ source with a detectable viral load — high-risk exposure that requires the choreographed response in MINUTES TO HOURS
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — this is a high-risk exposure; time is the most important variable. RN role: recognize + respond.

opts.text: Immediate bedside care: WASH with SOAP and WATER under running water; allow gentle bleeding; do NOT vigorously squeeze; do NOT apply bleach/alcohol/hydrogen peroxide
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — correct first-aid; caustic agents cause tissue damage without benefit. RN role: bedside care.

opts.text: Report IMMEDIATELY to supervisor and Occupational/Employee Health (or ED after hours); complete the OSHA exposure incident report; preserve confidentiality for the exposed worker and source
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — reporting drives PEP timing and OSHA compliance. RN role: report + log + confidentiality.

opts.text: Obtain rapid SOURCE and EXPOSED-WORKER baseline serologies (HIV, HBV-HBsAg, HCV-Ab; anti-HBs to confirm immune status; pregnancy test if applicable)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — baseline testing guides PEP and follow-up. RN role: baseline labs.

opts.text: HIV PEP is TIME-CRITICAL — start within HOURS (ideally < 2 h, no later than 72 h); standard 3-drug regimen TDF + FTC + integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir) for 28 days
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — efficacy declines after 72 h; do not wait. RN role: HIV PEP within hours.

opts.text: HBV management is by EXPOSED-WORKER status (vaccinated responder = no action; non-responder or unknown = HBIG + booster; unvaccinated = HBIG + start series — HBIG within 24 h); HCV has NO PEP — monitor (anti-HCV + HCV RNA per schedule)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — pathogen-specific pathways. RN role: apply correct HBV algorithm + HCV monitoring.

opts.text: Apply BLEACH or HYDROGEN PEROXIDE to the wound and vigorously squeeze to 'force the blood out'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Caustics damage tissue and vigorous squeezing has no benefit. Wash with soap and water; allow gentle bleeding.

opts.text: Delay reporting and finish the shift first; consider HIV PEP only the next day if she still has symptoms
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG + DANGEROUS. Delayed reporting and delayed HIV PEP markedly reduce efficacy; report immediately and start PEP within hours.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Baseline risk per percutaneous exposure is approximately 0.3% for HIV from a known-positive source, 6-30% for HBV from an HBeAg-positive source in an unvaccinated worker, and approximately 1.8% for HCV
opts.rat: CORRECT — relative-risk principle. Foundation for prioritizing PEP urgency.

opts.text: Immediate bedside care is to wash with soap and water; mucous membranes with saline or clean water; eyes with copious water at an eye-wash station for ~15 minutes — never bleach, alcohol, or peroxide
opts.rat: CORRECT — first-aid principle. Foundation for safe initial care.

opts.text: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires annual training, free HBV vaccination, engineered safety devices, sharps containers at the point of use, an exposure incident report, and confidentiality
opts.rat: CORRECT — regulatory principle. Foundation for compliant response.

opts.text: HIV PEP is most effective when started WITHIN HOURS of exposure (ideally < 2 h) and is not recommended after 72 h; the US standard is TDF + FTC + an integrase inhibitor for 28 days
opts.rat: CORRECT — PEP principle. Foundation for time-critical action.

opts.text: HBV decisions depend on the exposed worker's vaccination/immune status and the source's HBsAg status; HBIG is most effective within 24 hours, with efficacy declining over the first 7 days
opts.rat: CORRECT — HBV principle. Foundation for the correct algorithm.

opts.text: HCV has no post-exposure prophylaxis; the worker is monitored with anti-HCV at baseline and 4-6 months and HCV RNA at 3 weeks; seroconversion is treated with direct-acting antivirals with cure rates over 95%
opts.rat: CORRECT — HCV principle. Foundation for correct monitoring.

opts.text: Applying bleach or hydrogen peroxide to the wound improves outcomes and reduces seroconversion
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. No benefit and tissue damage; wash with soap and water and allow gentle bleeding.

opts.text: Recapping needles two-handed after each use is the safest practice and is recommended by OSHA
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Recapping is the most common cause of needlestick; the rule is NEVER RECAP (one-handed scoop only if unavoidable).

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Immediate bedside care — wash with soap and water under running water; allow gentle bleeding; clean dressing; no caustics; arrange coverage for her patients
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. The first-aid response is the only thing only the worker can do right now. RN role: bedside care.

opts.text: Report immediately to supervisor and Occupational/Employee Health; complete the OSHA exposure incident report with confidentiality maintained
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Reporting drives PEP timing and OSHA compliance. RN role: report + log.

opts.text: Obtain rapid source-patient and exposed-worker baseline serologies (HIV, HBV anti-HBs/HBsAg, HCV); pregnancy test if applicable; start HIV PEP within hours as appropriate
opts.rat: #3 — HIGH. Time-critical baseline + PEP. RN role: baseline labs + HIV PEP.

opts.text: Apply the HBV HBIG + vaccine algorithm to status; arrange HCV baseline + monitoring; counsel on safer sex + no donation + pregnancy/breastfeeding + acute-seroconversion symptoms
opts.rat: #4 — Pathogen-specific management + counseling. RN role: HBV algorithm + HCV monitor + counseling.

opts.text: Arrange serial HIV follow-up testing (6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months) and HCV follow-up; provide emotional support (chaplaincy + EAP) and reinforce prevention (engineered devices + never recap + sharps containers at point of use + standard precautions)
opts.rat: #5 — Follow-up + support + prevention sustain the response. RN role: follow-up + support + prevention.

steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Immediate bedside care — wash with soap and water under running water; allow gentle bleeding; clean dressing; arrange coverage for her patients
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. The only thing only the worker can do right now. RN role: bedside care.

opts.text: Report immediately to supervisor and Occupational/Employee Health (or ED after hours); complete the OSHA exposure incident report with confidentiality maintained
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Drives PEP timing and OSHA compliance. RN role: report + log.

opts.rat: #3 — Third. Time-critical baseline + PEP. RN role: baseline + HIV PEP.

opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Pathogen-specific management + counseling + support. RN role: HBV + HCV + counseling.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action/outcome, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The RN washed the site with soap and water under running water, allowed gentle bleeding, applied a clean dressing, reported immediately, and the OSHA exposure incident report was completed with confidentiality maintained
opts.rat: Correct first-aid + prompt reporting + OSHA compliance. Model practice.

opts.text: Rapid baseline serologies were obtained and HIV PEP (TDF + FTC + integrase inhibitor) was started within hours of exposure
opts.rat: Time-critical action consistent with the standard. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: The HBV HBIG + vaccine algorithm was applied to her vaccination/immune status; HCV baseline and follow-up monitoring were arranged; counseling and EAP/chaplaincy support were provided
opts.rat: Pathogen-specific pathways + counseling + support. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Serial HIV follow-up at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months was arranged; the unit reinforced prevention (engineered devices, never-recap, sharps containers at point of use, standard precautions); confidentiality was preserved
opts.rat: Follow-up + prevention + confidentiality. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative — the nurse applied bleach to the wound and vigorously squeezed it to 'force out the blood'; tissue damage worsened and PEP timing was delayed
opts.rat: ⚠️ Caustics + aggressive squeezing have no benefit and harm tissue. Wash with soap and water and allow gentle bleeding.

opts.text: Alternative — the exposure was not reported until the next day and HIV PEP was started only at 48 hours; the efficacy window was missed
opts.rat: ⚠️ Delayed reporting and delayed HIV PEP markedly reduce efficacy and violate the standard.

opts.text: Alternative — the needle was recapped two-handed before discarding, and the exposed worker's name plus the source's HIV status were announced at unit huddle to 'inform everyone'
opts.rat: ⚠️ Recapping is the leading cause of needlesticks (never recap); confidentiality must be maintained for both the exposed worker and the source.

opts.text: Alternative — the HBV algorithm was skipped because the worker said 'I had the vaccine a long time ago,' without checking anti-HBs or considering HBIG/booster
opts.rat: ⚠️ The algorithm requires anti-HBs documentation (or assessment if undocumented); unknown response or non-responder triggers HBIG + booster.

opts.text: Alternative — no counseling on safer sex, donation deferral, pregnancy/breastfeeding considerations, or acute-seroconversion symptoms was given; the worker received no peer/EAP support
opts.rat: ⚠️ Counseling + support are part of the standard response; missing them risks transmission to others and harms the worker.

opts.text: At 6 months her HIV, HBV, and HCV testing remain negative; she returned to work using engineered safety devices, never recapping, and discarding sharps at the point of use
opts.rat: Sustained correct practice + completed follow-up. Ideal outcome.

title: Acute BRONCHIOLITIS (RSV-Positive) in a 5-Month-Old Former 35-Week Late-Preterm Infant Girl Presenting in Mid-Winter with 3 Days of URI Progressing to TACHYPNEA + RETRACTIONS + Crackles/Wheezing + DECREASED ORAL FEEDING (Risk Factors for Severe Disease: Young Infant, Late Preterm, Winter, Household Smoke Exposure): Mostly SUPPORTIVE Nursing Care ('LESS IS MORE') — Elevate the Head of Bed, NASAL SALINE + BULB SUCTION BEFORE FEEDS and PRN (the Most Evidence-Based Intervention), Small Frequent Feeds with NG/IV Hydration Only If Intake Inadequate, Oxygen for Persistent SpO2 < 90-92%, MINIMAL HANDLING with Cluster Care, CONTACT + DROPLET Isolation with Cohorting + Strict Hand Hygiene + Gown/Gloves/Mask, Watchful Monitoring for APNEA (Especially Young Infants), Increased Work of Breathing, and Dehydration — and Explicitly NO Routine BRONCHODILATORS, NO Routine SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS, NO Routine ANTIBIOTICS, NO Routine Chest X-Ray, NO Deep Suctioning: Family Teaching and Discharge Criteria, and PREVENTION (Hand Hygiene, Smoke-Free Home, PALIVIZUMAB/NIRSEVIMAB for High-Risk Infants, Maternal RSV Vaccination in Pregnancy)
subtitle: BRONCHIOLITIS is the most common lower-respiratory tract infection in infants and one of the most over-treated conditions in pediatrics — making it a paradigm NCLEX 'less is more' case. The illness is INFLAMMATION and OBSTRUCTION of the small bronchioles from a VIRAL infection (most often RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS — RSV — and also rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza) leading to upper-airway congestion followed in 1-3 days by lower-respiratory involvement (TACHYPNEA, WHEEZING, CRACKLES, RETRACTIONS, NASAL FLARING, grunting), DECREASED ORAL FEEDING, and — in the youngest infants (especially under 2-3 months) — APNEA. The illness peaks in late fall through early spring; almost all children are infected by age 2. RISK FACTORS for SEVERE bronchiolitis: AGE < 12 weeks (especially < 6 weeks — apnea risk), PREMATURITY (any, but particularly < 32 weeks), chronic lung disease of prematurity (BPD), congenital heart disease (especially hemodynamically significant), immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease, and exposure to TOBACCO SMOKE. DIAGNOSIS is CLINICAL; routine chest X-ray and routine viral testing are NOT recommended (rapid RSV testing is used selectively to guide isolation/cohorting and to inform palivizumab decisions when relevant — not to direct routine care); routine laboratory studies are NOT recommended. NURSING CARE is MOSTLY SUPPORTIVE — the AAP guideline frames this clearly: do what helps and stop doing what does not. PRIMARY interventions: (1) NASAL SUCTIONING with saline drops + bulb suction (or a NoseFrida-style aspirator) BEFORE FEEDS, BEFORE SLEEP, and as needed — this is the most evidence-based single intervention and improves feeding and comfort; (2) POSITIONING — elevate the head of bed; comfort positioning held by a parent when possible; (3) HYDRATION — small frequent oral feeds; if intake is inadequate, use nasogastric or IV fluids (no absolute respiratory-rate cutoff — base on work of breathing + safe swallow + dehydration); (4) OXYGEN if SpO2 is persistently below approximately 90-92% (institutional variation; avoid over-oxygenation and continuous monitoring of well-appearing infants for transient dips); (5) MINIMAL HANDLING and CLUSTER CARE (agitation worsens respiratory distress); (6) ISOLATION with CONTACT + DROPLET precautions (gown, gloves, mask, dedicated equipment) and COHORTING of RSV-positive patients; STRICT HAND HYGIENE is the single most important infection-prevention step; (7) WATCHFUL MONITORING for APNEA (especially in young infants), increasing work of breathing, falling SpO2 or rising O2 requirement, poor feeding, dehydration, and lethargy; and (8) escalation as needed — heated high-flow nasal cannula (HHFNC) → CPAP → endotracheal intubation. SECONDARY/'do not do' (high-yield NCLEX): do NOT use routine BRONCHODILATORS (albuterol/levalbuterol) — they do not improve outcomes (a trial is occasionally considered in a child with atopy or family history of asthma but is stopped if no benefit); do NOT use routine SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS; do NOT use routine ANTIBIOTICS (viral); do NOT use routine RACEMIC EPINEPHRINE in inpatients; do NOT obtain routine chest X-ray; do NOT use DEEP SUCTIONING (nasal/oral pharynx only — deep beyond the nasopharynx has no evidence and may worsen); do NOT use ribavirin routinely. ESCALATION TRIGGERS to alert the team: progressive retractions, grunting, nasal flaring; apnea; new or rising O2 requirement; falling SpO2 despite suctioning and positioning; poor feeding/dehydration; lethargy or altered mental status. DISCHARGE CRITERIA: stable SpO2 in room air, adequate oral feeding, hydration, family able to monitor and provide care at home, and reliable follow-up. FAMILY TEACHING: nasal saline + bulb suction technique (BEFORE FEEDS + BEFORE SLEEP + PRN); small frequent feeds with signs of dehydration to report (fewer wet diapers, sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, lethargy); signs of worsening (faster or harder breathing, retractions, decreased feeding, lethargy, cyanosis); strict hand hygiene; SMOKE-FREE home/car (a key modifiable factor); usual course 7-14 days with cough that can persist; when to seek care; safe-sleep reinforcement. PREVENTION: hand hygiene; avoid sick contacts; smoke-free environment; PALIVIZUMAB (Synagis) monthly during RSV season for selected high-risk infants (per AAP criteria — e.g., premature with chronic lung disease, hemodynamically significant CHD); NIRSEVIMAB (Beyfortus), a long-acting monoclonal antibody, is recommended for all infants entering or during their first RSV season (per current immunization guidance), and MATERNAL RSV VACCINATION during pregnancy provides infant protection. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: giving routine albuterol, systemic steroids, antibiotics, or racemic epinephrine; deep suctioning; obtaining unnecessary chest X-rays; over-monitoring well-appearing infants with continuous pulse oximetry; not suctioning the nose before feeds; under-recognizing apnea in the youngest infants; missing dehydration; missing the smoke-exposure history; and breaching contact + droplet precautions. NURSING ROLE: assess severity and risk; deliver supportive care anchored in nasal saline + bulb suction, small frequent feeds (with NG/IV if needed), positioning, and minimal handling; oxygenate per the threshold; maintain contact + droplet precautions and strict hand hygiene; watch closely for apnea, worsening work of breathing, and dehydration; escalate to HHFNC/CPAP/intubation when needed; teach the family (suctioning technique, signs to report, smoke-free home); and apply prevention strategies including palivizumab/nirsevimab and maternal RSV vaccination as appropriate.

labs.r: Bronchiolitis = viral inflammation/obstruction of small bronchioles (RSV most common; also rhinovirus/hMPV/parainfluenza). Peak severity 2-6 mo. CLINICAL diagnosis — routine CXR + routine labs + routine viral testing NOT recommended (rapid RSV used selectively for isolation/cohorting + palivizumab decisions). Risk for severe disease: age < 12 wk (especially < 6 wk apnea risk), preterm, CLD/BPD, hemodynamically significant CHD, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease, smoke exposure. RN role: assess severity + risk; deliver supportive care.
