labs.v: The AAP guideline frames care simply: do what helps and stop doing what does not. PRIMARY interventions: (1) NASAL SUCTIONING with saline drops + bulb suction (or NoseFrida-style aspirator) BEFORE FEEDS, BEFORE SLEEP, and as needed — this is the most evidence-based single intervention and improves feeding and comfort; deep suctioning beyond the nasopharynx is NOT recommended (no benefit, may worsen). (2) POSITIONING — elevate the head of bed; comfort positioning held by a parent when possible; calming environment to reduce agitation. (3) HYDRATION — offer small frequent oral feeds; if intake is inadequate or the work of breathing is unsafe for oral feeding, use NASOGASTRIC or IV fluids (there is no absolute respiratory-rate cutoff — base the decision on work of breathing, safe swallow, dehydration). (4) OXYGEN if SpO2 is persistently below approximately 90-92% (institutional variation; avoid over-oxygenation; do NOT pursue brief asymptomatic dips that resolve on their own). (5) MINIMAL HANDLING + CLUSTER CARE (agitation worsens respiratory distress). (6) ISOLATION with CONTACT + DROPLET precautions — gown, gloves, mask, dedicated equipment — and COHORTING of RSV-positive patients; STRICT HAND HYGIENE is the single most important infection-prevention step. (7) WATCHFUL MONITORING for APNEA (especially in young or preterm infants), increasing work of breathing, falling SpO2 or rising O2 requirement, poor feeding, dehydration, and lethargy. (8) Escalation as needed — heated high-flow nasal cannula (HHFNC) → CPAP → endotracheal intubation.
labs.r: DO: nasal saline + BULB SUCTION (most evidence-based) BEFORE FEEDS + BEFORE SLEEP + PRN (NO deep suction beyond nasopharynx); ELEVATE HOB + parent comfort positioning + calm environment; SMALL FREQUENT FEEDS, NG/IV if inadequate (no RR cutoff — assess WOB/swallow/hydration); OXYGEN if persistent SpO2 < ~90-92% (avoid over-O2); MINIMAL HANDLING + cluster care; CONTACT + DROPLET isolation + COHORT + strict hand hygiene + PPE; WATCH for apnea (young/preterm) + ↑WOB + ↓SpO2 + poor feeding + dehydration; ESCALATE HHFNC → CPAP → intubation. RN role: supportive care framework.

labs.n: SECONDARY — the 'do NOT do' list (high-yield NCLEX) + escalation + family teaching
labs.v: Do NOT use routine BRONCHODILATORS (albuterol/levalbuterol) — they do NOT improve outcomes; a single trial may be considered in a child with atopy or family history of asthma but is DISCONTINUED if no benefit. Do NOT use routine SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS. Do NOT use routine ANTIBIOTICS — bronchiolitis is VIRAL; reserve for clear bacterial superinfection. Do NOT use routine RACEMIC EPINEPHRINE in inpatients. Do NOT obtain a routine chest X-ray (only if a different diagnosis is suspected). Do NOT use DEEP suctioning beyond the nasopharynx (no evidence; may worsen). Do NOT use ribavirin routinely. ESCALATION TRIGGERS to alert the team: progressive retractions, grunting, nasal flaring; APNEA; new or rising O2 requirement; falling SpO2 despite suctioning and positioning; poor feeding/dehydration; lethargy or altered mental status. Pathway: HHFNC → CPAP → intubation. FAMILY TEACHING is central: nasal saline + bulb suction technique (BEFORE FEEDS + BEFORE SLEEP + PRN); small frequent feeds with signs of dehydration to report (fewer wet diapers, sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, lethargy); signs of WORSENING (faster or harder breathing, deeper retractions, decreased feeding, lethargy, color change/cyanosis); strict hand hygiene at home; SMOKE-FREE home and car (residual smoke from a 'smoking jacket' still exposes the infant — counsel on cessation resources); usual course 7-14 days with cough that can persist; when to seek care; safe-sleep reinforcement.
labs.r: DO NOT routinely: ALBUTEROL (no benefit), systemic STEROIDS, ANTIBIOTICS, racemic EPI inpatient, CXR, DEEP suctioning, ribavirin. ESCALATION triggers: progressive retractions/grunting/flaring, APNEA, new/rising O2 need, falling SpO2 despite suction/position, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy → HHFNC → CPAP → intubation. FAMILY TEACHING: bulb-suction technique BEFORE FEEDS + sleep, small frequent feeds, signs of dehydration + worsening, hand hygiene, SMOKE-FREE home/car (residual smoke from 'smoking jacket' still exposes), course 7-14 d, when to seek care, safe sleep.

labs.n: Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors + PREVENTION (smoke-free + palivizumab/nirsevimab + maternal RSV vaccine)
labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT give routine albuterol/levalbuterol, systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, or racemic epinephrine; did NOT obtain a routine chest X-ray; did NOT use deep suctioning beyond the nasopharynx; did NOT continuously pulse-oximeter monitor a well-appearing older infant for transient dips (institutional variation — but use clinically); did NOT skip nasal suctioning before feeds; did NOT under-recognize apnea risk in a young/preterm infant; did NOT miss the smoke-exposure history; did NOT breach contact + droplet precautions; and did NOT discharge before stable feeding, oxygenation, and family teach-back. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: timely supportive care anchored in nasal saline + bulb suction; correct positioning + cluster care + minimal handling; appropriate oxygen threshold; NG/IV hydration when oral intake was inadequate; contact + droplet isolation with strict hand hygiene and cohorting; vigilant apnea + work-of-breathing + dehydration monitoring; escalation pathway readiness (HHFNC → CPAP → intubation); robust family teaching (suctioning + feeds + warning signs + smoke-free home); prevention reinforcement. PREVENTION: hand hygiene; avoid sick contacts; smoke-free home/car (counsel cessation; addresses residual smoke from a 'smoking jacket'); PALIVIZUMAB (Synagis) monthly during RSV season for selected high-risk infants per AAP criteria (e.g., premature with chronic lung disease, hemodynamically significant CHD); NIRSEVIMAB (Beyfortus) — long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody — for all infants entering or during their first RSV season per current immunization guidance; MATERNAL RSV vaccine during pregnancy provides infant protection through transferred antibodies. EXPECTED outcome: gradual respiratory and feeding recovery over days; safe discharge with strong family preparation and a clear smoke-free + prevention plan.
labs.r: Negatives: no routine albuterol/steroids/abx/racemic epi/CXR/deep suction; no continuous-monitoring of well infants; no skipping nasal suction before feeds; no under-recognition of apnea in young/preterm; no missed smoke history; no precautions breach; no premature discharge. Protective: nasal saline + bulb suction + positioning + cluster care + appropriate O2 + NG/IV hydration prn + contact+droplet+cohort+hand hygiene + apnea/WOB/dehydration monitoring + escalation pathway + family teaching + smoke-free + prevention. PREVENTION: hand hygiene + avoid sick contacts + SMOKE-FREE + PALIVIZUMAB (per AAP) + NIRSEVIMAB (all infants entering/during 1st RSV season) + MATERNAL RSV VACCINE in pregnancy. RN role: supportive care + protection + prevention.

labs.v: Positive (used for isolation/cohorting and palivizumab eligibility; does NOT direct routine care)

labs.n: SpO2 at admission on room air
labs.v: 89% (below threshold; supplemental low-flow O2 initiated to maintain ≥ 90-92%; wean off as tolerated)

Capillary refill < 2 sec; mucous membranes moist; anterior fontanelle level — adequately hydrated at admission with mother reporting fewer wet diapers (~ 4-5/day) — supports adding NG feeds if oral intake remains ~ 50-60% of usual
labs.r: Cap refill < 2 sec; mucous membranes moist; flat fontanelle; ≥ 6 wet diapers/day at this age

labs.v: Not performed (not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis; would be obtained only if an alternative diagnosis were suspected — e.g., pneumonia, foreign body, congenital cardiac anatomy)

nursesNote: Peds inpatient — 5-mo-old former 35-wk late-preterm infant, mid-winter, 3 d URI → progressive tachypnea + RETRACTIONS + crackles/wheezing + decreased oral feeding (~50%) + brief apneic episode at home reported by mom; rapid RSV+. Admit SpO2 89% RA → 95% on 0.5 L NC. Brother (4y) w/ 'cold'; father smokes outside but residual smoke from 'smoking jacket' = ongoing exposure. PROTECTIVE precautions: CONTACT + DROPLET isolation; private room w/ RSV+ cohorting; gown + gloves + mask + dedicated equipment; STRICT hand hygiene (#1 IC step). PRIMARY supportive care: NASAL SALINE + BULB SUCTION BEFORE FEEDS + before sleep + PRN (most evidence-based intervention) — moderate clear secretions cleared; HOB elevated + comfort positioning in mother's arms; CLUSTER CARE/minimal handling; SMALL FREQUENT feeds; oxygen 0.5 L NC to maintain SpO2 ≥ 90-92% (avoid over-O2); continuous CR monitor + pulse ox given age + reported apnea. Oral intake stayed ~60% → NG feeds started for next 24-48 h to ensure hydration w/o aspiration (no absolute RR cutoff — based on WOB/swallow/dehydration assessment). 'DO NOT' (high-yield): NO routine albuterol/levalbuterol, NO systemic corticosteroids, NO antibiotics (viral), NO racemic epi inpatient, NO routine CXR, NO deep suctioning beyond nasopharynx, NO ribavirin. ESCALATION pathway prepared (progressive retractions/grunting/flaring, apnea, rising O2 need, falling SpO2 despite suction/position, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy → HHFNC → CPAP → intubation). FAMILY TEACHING (teach-back verified by mom): bulb-suction technique BEFORE feeds + sleep; small frequent feeds w/ dehydration signs (fewer wet diapers, sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, lethargy); worsening signs (faster/harder breathing, deeper retractions, decreased feeding, lethargy, color change → seek care); strict hand hygiene; SMOKE-FREE home/car w/ cessation resources (jacket residual smoke counts); usual course 7-14 d w/ cough lingering; safe sleep. Day 2: weaned off O2; feeding ~75%; no further apnea; respiratory effort improved. DISCHARGE: stable RA SpO2 + adequate feeding/hydration + family ready + reliable follow-up. PREVENTION: smoke-free reinforced; NIRSEVIMAB for all infants entering/during 1st RSV season per current immunization guidance discussed; PALIVIZUMAB eligibility per AAP/protocol; MATERNAL RSV vaccine during next pregnancy mentioned. NEGATIVES (correct practice): didn't give routine albuterol/steroids/abx/racemic epi/CXR/deep suction; didn't skip nasal suction before feeds; didn't under-recognize apnea risk in young/preterm; didn't miss smoke history; didn't breach contact + droplet precautions; didn't discharge before stable feeding + O2 + family teach-back.
providerOrders: ADMIT: pediatric inpatient unit for supportive care for RSV-positive acute bronchiolitis in a 5-month-old former 35-week late-preterm infant with one reported brief apneic episode at home

ISOLATION: contact + droplet precautions; private room (or cohort with other RSV-positive patients); gown, gloves, mask; dedicated equipment; strict hand hygiene as the single most important infection-prevention step
MONITORING: continuous cardiopulmonary + pulse oximetry given age and reported apnea; vital signs and work-of-breathing assessment per protocol; intake/output and daily weight

RESPIRATORY/AIRWAY: nasal saline drops + bulb suction (or NoseFrida-style aspirator) before feeds, before sleep, and as needed; do NOT use deep suctioning beyond the nasopharynx; elevate head of bed; comfort positioning held by parent; minimize handling/cluster care
OXYGEN: supplemental low-flow nasal cannula if SpO2 is persistently below approximately 90-92%; wean as tolerated; avoid over-oxygenation

HYDRATION/FEEDING: small frequent oral feeds as tolerated; nasogastric or IV fluids if oral intake is inadequate or work of breathing precludes safe feeding (do not require an absolute respiratory-rate cutoff — base on work of breathing, swallow safety, hydration)

DO NOT (routine): bronchodilators (albuterol/levalbuterol), systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, racemic epinephrine, chest X-ray, deep suctioning, ribavirin — reserve antibiotics for clear bacterial superinfection

ESCALATION: heated high-flow nasal cannula → CPAP → endotracheal intubation for progressive retractions/grunting/flaring, apnea, new/rising O2 requirement, falling SpO2 despite suction/position, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy

FAMILY TEACHING: nasal saline + bulb suction technique (before feeds and before sleep); small frequent feeds and signs of dehydration to report; warning signs of worsening (faster/harder breathing, retractions, decreased feeding, lethargy, cyanosis); strict hand hygiene; smoke-free home and car with cessation resources

PREVENTION: nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for all infants entering or during their first RSV season per current immunization guidance; palivizumab (Synagis) for selected high-risk infants per AAP/insurance protocol; maternal RSV vaccination during a future pregnancy to provide infant protection
DISCHARGE CRITERIA: stable SpO2 in room air, adequate oral feeding and hydration, family able to monitor and provide care at home with teach-back verification, reliable follow-up scheduled

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters about this RSV bronchiolitis admission?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Classic clinical bronchiolitis picture (URI → tachypnea + retractions + crackles/wheezing + decreased feeding) with rapid RSV positive in a former late-preterm 5-month-old infant — supportive care is the framework
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the diagnosis is clinical and care is supportive. RN role: recognize + frame supportive care.

opts.text: Risk factors for severe disease present (former late-preterm; brief apneic episode reported at home; household smoke exposure even though father smokes outside; winter season) warrant close monitoring and inpatient care
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — risk-factor cluster shapes intensity of monitoring. RN role: assess risk.

opts.text: PRIMARY supportive interventions: NASAL SALINE + BULB SUCTION before feeds and before sleep (the most evidence-based intervention), HOB elevation + comfort positioning, MINIMAL HANDLING/cluster care
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — these are the high-yield supportive interventions. RN role: deliver supportive care.

opts.text: HYDRATION via small frequent feeds with NG or IV if intake is inadequate; OXYGEN if SpO2 persistently below ~ 90-92%; CONTACT + DROPLET isolation with strict hand hygiene and cohorting
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — hydration, oxygenation, and infection control complete the supportive framework. RN role: feeds + O2 + isolation.

opts.text: Do NOT routinely give bronchodilators (albuterol), systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, racemic epinephrine, or obtain a routine chest X-ray; do NOT use deep suctioning beyond the nasopharynx
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the high-yield 'less is more' list. RN role: avoid non-beneficial interventions.

opts.text: Watch for APNEA (especially in young/preterm infants), increasing work of breathing, falling SpO2 or rising O2 need, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy — and escalate to HHFNC → CPAP → intubation as needed; teach the family and reinforce prevention (smoke-free + nirsevimab/palivizumab + maternal RSV vaccine)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — escalation triggers and teaching/prevention close the loop. RN role: monitor + escalate + teach + prevention.

opts.text: Start a routine course of nebulized albuterol and IV ceftriaxone for the wheezing infant
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Routine bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis (no outcome benefit); antibiotics are reserved for clear bacterial superinfection.

opts.text: Perform deep nasotracheal suctioning every 2 hours regardless of need to 'clear secretions' and skip nasal saline before feeds
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Deep suctioning beyond the nasopharynx has no evidence and may worsen; nasal saline + bulb suction before feeds is the most evidence-based intervention.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower-respiratory infection — most often RSV — diagnosed CLINICALLY; routine viral testing, routine CXR, and routine labs are NOT recommended
opts.rat: CORRECT — the diagnostic principle. Foundation for avoiding overtesting.

opts.text: Highest-risk infants for severe disease include those < 12 weeks (especially < 6 weeks for apnea), preterm, with chronic lung disease/BPD, hemodynamically significant CHD, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease, and tobacco-smoke exposure
opts.rat: CORRECT — the risk-factor principle. Foundation for stratifying monitoring.

opts.text: The PRIMARY supportive interventions are nasal saline + bulb suction before feeds and sleep, HOB elevation/comfort positioning, small frequent feeds with NG/IV if inadequate, oxygen for persistent SpO2 < ~ 90-92%, minimal handling, and contact + droplet isolation with hand hygiene
opts.rat: CORRECT — the supportive-care principle. Foundation for safe nursing care.

opts.text: Routine BRONCHODILATORS, systemic CORTICOSTEROIDS, ANTIBIOTICS, RACEMIC EPINEPHRINE, routine CXR, and deep suctioning are NOT recommended
opts.rat: CORRECT — the 'do not' principle. Foundation for avoiding non-beneficial care.

opts.text: Escalation triggers include progressive retractions/grunting/flaring, APNEA, new/rising O2 requirement, falling SpO2 despite suctioning/positioning, poor feeding/dehydration, and lethargy — pathway HHFNC → CPAP → intubation
opts.rat: CORRECT — escalation principle. Foundation for safe upgrading of care.

opts.text: Prevention includes hand hygiene, smoke-free home/car, palivizumab for selected high-risk infants per AAP, nirsevimab for all infants entering or during their first RSV season per current immunization guidance, and maternal RSV vaccination during pregnancy
opts.rat: CORRECT — prevention principle. Foundation for future protection.

opts.text: All wheezing infants with bronchiolitis should receive routine systemic corticosteroids to suppress airway inflammation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Routine systemic corticosteroids are not recommended; they do not improve outcomes in viral bronchiolitis.

opts.text: Smoke exposure is not a meaningful factor as long as the father smokes outdoors
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Third-hand smoke and residual smoke from clothing/'smoking jackets' still expose the infant; smoke-free homes/cars/vehicles are essential.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Maintain a patent airway and oxygenation — nasal saline + bulb suction before feeds and PRN, HOB elevation + comfort positioning, supplemental O2 for persistent SpO2 < ~ 90-92%, and minimal handling/cluster care
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Airway + oxygenation are the foundation of bronchiolitis care. RN role: airway/O2.

opts.text: Maintain hydration with small frequent feeds; NG or IV fluids if oral intake is inadequate or the work of breathing is unsafe for oral feeding
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Hydration sustains the infant and supports recovery. RN role: feeds + hydration.

opts.text: Apply contact + droplet isolation with strict hand hygiene, cohorting, and PPE; monitor for apnea, increased work of breathing, dehydration, lethargy; escalate to HHFNC → CPAP → intubation as needed
opts.rat: #3 — HIGH. Infection control + watchful monitoring + readiness to escalate. RN role: isolation + monitor + escalate.

opts.text: Avoid non-beneficial routine interventions — no routine albuterol, systemic steroids, antibiotics, racemic epinephrine, routine CXR, or deep suctioning
opts.rat: #4 — Prevents harm and aligns with the AAP guideline. RN role: avoid non-beneficial care.

opts.text: Teach the family (bulb suction before feeds and sleep; signs of dehydration and worsening; hand hygiene; smoke-free home/car); reinforce prevention (nirsevimab/palivizumab; maternal RSV vaccine); schedule follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Closing/ongoing. Teaching + prevention sustain the response. RN role: teach + prevention.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this bronchiolitis admission.

opts.text: Perform nasal saline drops + bulb suction before feeds, before sleep, and as needed; elevate the head of bed and use comfort positioning held by a parent; minimize handling/cluster care
opts.rat: Primary supportive interventions. RN role: airway + comfort.

opts.text: Offer small frequent oral feeds; start NG or IV fluids if intake is inadequate or the work of breathing makes oral feeding unsafe
opts.rat: Supports hydration without aspiration risk. RN role: feeds + hydration.

opts.text: Apply supplemental low-flow O2 to maintain SpO2 ≥ 90-92%; avoid over-oxygenation; wean as tolerated
opts.rat: Appropriate threshold-based oxygen use. RN role: oxygenation.

opts.text: Maintain contact + droplet isolation, cohort with other RSV+ patients, use PPE (gown, gloves, mask), and reinforce strict hand hygiene
opts.rat: Infection prevention. RN role: isolation + hand hygiene.

opts.text: Continuously monitor cardiopulmonary + SpO2 given age and reported apnea; watch for increased work of breathing, falling SpO2, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy; escalate to HHFNC → CPAP → intubation as needed
opts.rat: Watchful monitoring + escalation readiness. RN role: monitor + escalate.

opts.text: Teach the family bulb-suction technique, signs of dehydration and worsening, strict hand hygiene, and a smoke-free home/car (residual smoke from a 'smoking jacket' still exposes the infant); reinforce prevention (nirsevimab; maternal RSV vaccine; palivizumab for high-risk per AAP)
opts.rat: Family teaching + prevention. RN role: teach + prevention.

opts.text: Give a routine course of nebulized albuterol, systemic corticosteroids, and IV ceftriaxone for the wheezing infant
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — routine bronchodilators and systemic steroids are not recommended; antibiotics are reserved for clear bacterial superinfection.

opts.text: Perform routine deep nasotracheal suctioning every 2 hours regardless of need; skip nasal saline before feeds
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — deep suctioning has no evidence and may worsen; nasal saline + bulb suction before feeds is the most evidence-based intervention.

opts.text: Obtain a routine chest X-ray and rapid viral panel on every admitted bronchiolitis patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — routine CXR and routine viral testing are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis (rapid RSV may be used selectively for isolation/cohorting and palivizumab decisions).

opts.text: Reassure the family that smoking outside is sufficient — they do not need to make the home or car smoke-free
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — residual smoke from clothing exposes the infant; smoke-free home and car are required.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Perform nasal saline + bulb suction; elevate the HOB and use comfort positioning; supplemental O2 to maintain SpO2 ≥ ~ 90-92%; minimal handling/cluster care
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Airway + oxygenation are foundational. RN role: airway/O2.

opts.text: Offer small frequent feeds; start NG or IV fluids if intake is inadequate or work of breathing makes oral feeding unsafe
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Hydration sustains the infant. RN role: feeds + hydration.

opts.text: Apply contact + droplet isolation with cohorting, PPE, and strict hand hygiene; continuously monitor cardiopulmonary + SpO2 and watch for apnea/worsening; escalate to HHFNC → CPAP → intubation as needed
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Infection control + monitoring + escalation readiness. RN role: isolation + monitor + escalate.

opts.text: Avoid non-beneficial routine interventions — no routine albuterol, systemic steroids, antibiotics, racemic epinephrine, routine CXR, or deep suctioning
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Prevents harm and aligns with guideline. RN role: avoid non-beneficial care.

opts.text: Teach the family (bulb suction before feeds and sleep, signs of dehydration/worsening, hand hygiene, smoke-free home/car), reinforce prevention (nirsevimab/palivizumab/maternal RSV vaccine), schedule follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Teaching + prevention complete the response. RN role: teach + prevention.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each finding, classify the trajectory.

opts.text: After nasal saline + bulb suction, HOB elevation, comfort positioning, and supplemental O2, the infant's respiratory rate falls from 62 to ~48, retractions ease, SpO2 stays ≥ 95%, and feeding improves
opts.rat: Correct supportive response — airway clearance and oxygenation work. Improving trajectory.

opts.text: Oral intake stays ~ 60% of usual → NG feeds begun without aspiration; hydration is maintained without escalating respiratory support
opts.rat: Safe hydration with the right tool. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Day 2 — weaned to room air with stable SpO2, feeding ~ 75%, no further apnea, mother teaches back bulb-suction technique, signs to report, hand hygiene, and the smoke-free home plan
opts.rat: Sustained recovery + verified family understanding. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Discharge with stable SpO2 in room air, adequate feeding, family ready, and reliable follow-up; nirsevimab/palivizumab and maternal RSV vaccine discussed for prevention
opts.rat: Safe discharge with prevention reinforced. Ideal outcome.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — routine albuterol nebs, systemic corticosteroids, and antibiotics were given; no clinical improvement and the infant developed adverse effects
opts.rat: ⚠️ Non-recommended routine interventions added burden without benefit. Demonstrates the 'do not' list.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — deep nasotracheal suctioning every 2 hours was performed; the infant became agitated, work of breathing worsened, and SpO2 fell
opts.rat: ⚠️ Deep suctioning has no evidence and may worsen status. Demonstrates the limit of nasopharyngeal suction.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the family was told smoking outside is sufficient with no smoke-free home/car counseling; the infant's recovery was prolonged and exposure continued
opts.rat: ⚠️ Residual third-hand smoke from clothing exposes the infant; smoke-free home and car are required.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the infant continued to be agitated by frequent unnecessary checks and handling; SpO2 fluctuated and feeding fell despite supportive measures
opts.rat: ⚠️ Over-handling worsens respiratory effort in bronchiolitis. Demonstrates cluster care + minimal handling.

opts.text: In the first hours after supportive care begins, before measurable improvement, vital signs and work of breathing are essentially unchanged while the infant tolerates suction, positioning, and small feeds
opts.rat: An expected stable trajectory before improvement; continue supportive care and reassess. Unchanged is appropriate here.

opts.text: Long-term — the family maintains a smoke-free home/car, hand hygiene, and the older sibling stays distanced when ill; the infant receives nirsevimab/palivizumab per protocol and the next pregnancy includes maternal RSV vaccination
opts.rat: Sustained prevention reduces future risk for the infant and household. Ideal longer-term outcome.

title: NEWBORN RESUSCITATION (NRP) and TEAM LEADERSHIP in the Delivery Room for a Term Newborn Boy Born by EMERGENT CESAREAN for a Category III Fetal Heart Tracing (Recurrent Late Decelerations + Minimal Variability) Who Arrives APNEIC, FLOPPY, BLUE, and BRADYCARDIC (HR ~70) — Pre-Resuscitation HUDDLE and Equipment CHECK Before Delivery, CLOSED-LOOP ROLE ASSIGNMENT (Team Leader + Airway/RT + Compressor + Vascular-Access/Medications + Documenter + Family Liaison), the GOLDEN MINUTE Sequence of INITIAL STEPS (Warm + Dry + Position + Clear Airway PRN + Stimulate), Beginning POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION at 40-60/min with ROOM AIR for a Term Infant When HR < 100 or Apneic/Gasping, CORRECTING Inadequate PPV with MR SOPA (Mask + Reposition + Suction + Open Mouth + Pressure + Alternative Airway), Pulse Oximetry on the RIGHT WRIST (Preductal), Adding CHEST COMPRESSIONS at a 3:1 Ratio (Two-Thumb Encircling) When HR < 60 After 30 Seconds of Effective PPV, EPINEPHRINE 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO via Rapidly Placed Umbilical Vein Catheter When HR < 60 Despite Compressions, Therapeutic-Hypothermia Eligibility Screening, NICU Hand-Off Using SBAR, Family Communication, and a Team DEBRIEF
subtitle: Newborn resuscitation is a high-stakes, low-frequency event for which the QUALITY of TEAM PREPARATION and LEADERSHIP is the single biggest predictor of outcome. Approximately 10% of newborns need some help to begin breathing at birth and about 1% need extensive resuscitation; the FIRST MINUTE — the 'GOLDEN MINUTE' — sets the trajectory. The NEONATAL RESUSCITATION PROGRAM (NRP) provides a standardized algorithm that the team rehearses, anticipates, and executes together. PRE-RESUSCITATION preparation (before the baby is delivered) is itself a leadership act: the team performs a HUDDLE that identifies the at-risk delivery (here, an emergent cesarean for a Category III FHR tracing), assigns CLOSED-LOOP ROLES (team leader, airway/RT, chest-compression provider, vascular-access/medications, documenter/recorder, family liaison), verifies a PRE-WARMED radiant warmer + warm blankets + plastic wrap if preterm < 32 weeks + suction with bulb/catheter + appropriately sized bag-mask + appropriately sized endotracheal tubes (2.5/3.0/3.5) + functioning laryngoscope with blades + pulse oximeter + ECG + UVC tray + epinephrine + normal saline, and CONFIRMS gestational age, anticipated weight, and any maternal/fetal risk factors. AT BIRTH the team performs the rapid INITIAL ASSESSMENT — TERM gestation? GOOD TONE? BREATHING or CRYING? — all YES → routine care with mother (warm + dry + skin-to-skin + delayed cord clamping when appropriate). Any NO → bring to the radiant warmer for INITIAL STEPS (about 30 seconds): WARM, DRY (vigorous drying serves as the first stimulation and removes wet linens; for preterm < 32 weeks place into a plastic bag/wrap WITHOUT drying to maintain heat), POSITION the airway in the 'sniffing' position, CLEAR the airway only if obstructed (mouth before nose; bulb syringe or suction catheter), and STIMULATE (rubbing the back, flicking the soles); avoid hyperthermia. EVALUATE breathing and HEART RATE (auscultate at the precordium for 6 seconds and multiply by 10, or use ECG leads). HR ≥ 100 with effective breathing → continue routine. HR < 100 OR apneic/gasping → begin POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION (PPV) within the golden minute at a rate of 40-60 breaths/minute (chanted as 'Breathe . . . Two . . . Three . . .') with ROOM AIR (FiO2 21%) for term infants and FiO2 21-30% for preterm; place a pulse oximeter on the RIGHT WRIST (PREDUCTAL) and an ECG for accurate HR. The single most important sign of effective PPV is a RISING HEART RATE; CHEST RISE is reassuring but HR is the metric. If HR is not rising, perform the corrective steps in MR SOPA order: (M) Mask adjust to a good seal, (R) Reposition the airway, (S) Suction mouth/nose, (O) Open the mouth, (P) Pressure increase, (A) Alternative airway (intubate or place a laryngeal mask). If HR remains < 60 after 30 SECONDS of EFFECTIVE PPV, start CHEST COMPRESSIONS — preferred two-thumb-encircling-hands technique on the lower third of the sternum at a 3:1 ratio (3 compressions : 1 breath) for a total of 120 events per minute (90 compressions + 30 breaths), depth about one third of the AP chest diameter; intubate or place an alternative airway if not already done, and switch FiO2 to 100% once compressions begin. Reassess HR after 60 seconds of compressions + PPV. If HR remains < 60, give EPINEPHRINE 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL solution) — via an UMBILICAL VEIN CATHETER (UVC) for fastest access, or IO if UVC fails; the endotracheal route at 0.1 mg/kg may be used briefly while IV/IO is being established but is less reliable; repeat every 3-5 minutes as needed. Consider a volume bolus of normal saline 10 mL/kg IV/IO if hypovolemia is suspected (blood loss/abruption/cord accident). Continue resuscitation; if there is no detectable heart rate after 20 minutes of complete and effective resuscitation, withdrawing is reasonable in consultation with the team and family. THERMOREGULATION is preserved throughout — radiant warmer, pre-warmed blankets, plastic wrap for preterm < 32 weeks, avoid hyperthermia (which worsens HIE). Once stabilized, screen for therapeutic-hypothermia eligibility (≥ 36 weeks gestation, within 6 hours of birth, with evidence of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy) and arrange NICU admission. Communicate with the family as soon as possible — honest, brief updates from the leader or family-liaison nurse; bring the family to the bedside as feasible. After the event, a STRUCTURED DEBRIEF identifies what went well, what to do differently, and supports the team and the family. KEY LEADERSHIP behaviors: BRIEF the team before delivery; assign CLOSED-LOOP ROLES with named directed tasks and required readbacks; protect the AIRWAY first; the QUALITY of PPV is the most common difference between success and failure (MR SOPA); start COMPRESSIONS only when HR < 60 despite 30 seconds of EFFECTIVE PPV; use the UVC for fastest medication access; communicate using SBAR for the NICU hand-off; and protect thermoregulation throughout. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: starting compressions before the airway/PPV is effective (the cause of bradycardia in newborns is almost always hypoxia from inadequate ventilation); using a 30:2 ratio (that is for older infants/children/adults — newborn is 3:1); starting at 100% O2 in a term newborn (start at 21%, escalate as needed); skipping the right-wrist pulse oximeter (preductal); forgetting MR SOPA when PPV is ineffective; suctioning vigorously or deeply before stimulation; routinely intubating and suctioning meconium-stained non-vigorous newborns (no longer routine — only if needed for ventilation); allowing hyperthermia; over-explaining clinical details to the family at the bedside; and skipping the team debrief. NURSING ROLE in the bedside team: as team leader (when an RN is the designated leader for the initial response) — pre-deliver brief; assign closed-loop roles; lead the algorithm; protect thermoregulation; place pulse oximeter on the right wrist; ensure effective PPV with MR SOPA; coordinate compressions and meds with UVC access; communicate honestly with the family; hand off to the NICU using SBAR; lead the debrief. As a team member — execute the assigned role with closed-loop communication; speak up about safety concerns; advocate for the newborn and family.

labs.n: PRE-RESUSCITATION huddle + equipment check + closed-loop role assignment
labs.v: Pre-resuscitation preparation is itself a leadership act. The team HUDDLES BEFORE delivery to identify the at-risk situation (here, an emergent cesarean for a Category III FHR tracing with intrapartum maternal fever); ASSIGN CLOSED-LOOP ROLES (TEAM LEADER, AIRWAY/RT, CHEST-COMPRESSION provider, VASCULAR-ACCESS/MEDICATIONS, DOCUMENTER/RECORDER, FAMILY LIAISON); VERIFY equipment (pre-warmed radiant warmer + warm blankets + plastic wrap if preterm < 32 weeks + suction with bulb/catheter + appropriately sized BMV + ETT sizes 2.5/3.0/3.5 + functioning laryngoscope with blades + pulse oximeter + ECG + UVC tray + epinephrine + normal saline); and CONFIRM gestational age, anticipated weight, and maternal/fetal risk factors. CLOSED-LOOP communication uses named recipients, directed tasks, and repeat-back/confirmation. The team leader's job is to keep the OVERVIEW, prevent freelancing, protect the airway-first sequence, time the algorithm, and communicate with the family — not to perform every task.
labs.r: PRE-DELIVERY: huddle + identify at-risk delivery + assign CLOSED-LOOP roles (leader + airway/RT + compressor + access/meds + documenter + family liaison) + verify equipment (warmer/blankets/plastic wrap if preterm<32/suction/BMV/ETT 2.5-3.5/laryngoscope/pulse ox/ECG/UVC tray/epi/NS) + confirm GA/weight/risks. Closed-loop = named + directed + repeat-back + confirm. Team leader keeps overview, doesn't freelance. RN role: brief + delegate + lead.

labs.n: INITIAL ASSESSMENT + initial steps + PPV within the GOLDEN MINUTE + MR SOPA + right-wrist pulse ox
labs.v: AT BIRTH the rapid initial assessment is three questions: TERM gestation? GOOD TONE? BREATHING or CRYING? Any NO → bring to the radiant warmer. INITIAL STEPS (~30 seconds): WARM (radiant warmer; plastic wrap for preterm < 32 weeks without drying first); DRY vigorously (the first stimulation; removes wet linens); POSITION the airway in a sniffing position; CLEAR the airway only if obstructed (mouth before nose; bulb or suction catheter); STIMULATE (rub the back, flick the soles); avoid hyperthermia. EVALUATE breathing and HEART RATE (auscultate 6 seconds × 10 or use ECG leads). HR ≥ 100 + effective breathing → routine care; HR < 100 OR apnea/gasping → begin PPV within the GOLDEN MINUTE at 40-60 breaths/min ('Breathe . . . Two . . . Three . . .') with ROOM AIR (FiO2 21%) for term infants (FiO2 21-30% preterm). Place the PULSE OXIMETER on the RIGHT WRIST (PREDUCTAL) and use ECG for accurate HR. The single most important sign of effective PPV is a RISING HEART RATE; chest rise is reassuring but HR is the metric. If HR is not rising, perform CORRECTIVE STEPS in MR SOPA order: M (mask seal), R (reposition airway), S (suction mouth/nose), O (open mouth), P (pressure increase), A (alternative airway — intubate or place a laryngeal mask). Effective PPV alone reverses most newborn bradycardia.
labs.r: Birth questions: TERM? TONE? BREATHING/crying? Any NO → warmer for initial steps (WARM + DRY (first stim, remove wet linens; preterm <32 wk plastic wrap w/o drying) + POSITION sniffing + CLEAR airway only if obstructed (mouth before nose) + STIMULATE). Evaluate respiration + HR (6 sec auscultate ×10 or ECG). HR ≥100 + breathing → routine. HR <100 OR apnea/gasping → PPV within Golden Minute at 40-60/min with ROOM AIR (21%) for term (21-30% preterm). Pulse ox on RIGHT WRIST (preductal) + ECG. Best sign of effective PPV = RISING HR (not just chest rise). If HR not rising → MR SOPA: Mask seal / Reposition / Suction / Open mouth / Pressure ↑ / Alternative airway. RN role: PPV is the most important intervention.

labs.n: Chest compressions (3:1) + UVC + EPINEPHRINE + volume + thermoregulation + SBAR hand-off + debrief
labs.v: If the HR remains < 60 after 30 SECONDS of EFFECTIVE PPV, start CHEST COMPRESSIONS — preferred two-thumb-encircling-hands technique on the LOWER THIRD of the sternum at a 3:1 ratio (3 COMPRESSIONS : 1 BREATH) for a total of 120 events per minute (90 compressions + 30 breaths), depth about ONE THIRD of the AP chest diameter; intubate or place an alternative airway if not already done; switch to FiO2 100% once compressions begin. Reassess HR after 60 SECONDS of effective compressions + PPV. If HR remains < 60, give EPINEPHRINE 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL solution) via UMBILICAL VEIN CATHETER (UVC, the fastest access in the newborn), or via IO if UVC fails. The endotracheal route at 0.1 mg/kg may be used briefly while IV/IO is being established but is less reliable. REPEAT epinephrine every 3-5 minutes as needed. Consider a VOLUME bolus of NORMAL SALINE 10 mL/kg IV/IO if hypovolemia is suspected (blood loss/abruption/cord accident); blood may be used if available. If there is no detectable heart rate after 20 minutes of complete and effective resuscitation, withdrawing is reasonable in consultation with the team and family. THERMOREGULATION is preserved throughout (radiant warmer; pre-warmed blankets; plastic wrap for preterm < 32 weeks; avoid hyperthermia, which worsens HIE). Once stabilized, screen for THERAPEUTIC HYPOTHERMIA eligibility (≥ 36 weeks gestation, within 6 HOURS of birth, with evidence of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy on standardized exam ± blood gas). Hand off to the NICU using SBAR (Situation/Background/Assessment/Recommendation). COMMUNICATE with the family as soon as possible — honest, brief updates from the leader or family-liaison nurse; bring the family to the bedside as feasible. After the event, lead a STRUCTURED DEBRIEF.
labs.r: Compressions if HR <60 after 30 sec of EFFECTIVE PPV: TWO-THUMB ENCIRCLING preferred, lower third sternum, ~1/3 AP depth, 3:1 ratio = 90 comp + 30 breaths/min = 120 events/min; intubate or place alt airway; FiO2 100% with compressions. Reassess HR after 60 sec compressions + PPV. If HR <60 → EPINEPHRINE 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL) via UVC (fastest newborn access) or IO; ET 0.1 mg/kg less reliable bridge. Repeat q3-5 min. VOLUME NS 10 mL/kg if hypovolemia. After 20 min of complete effective resuscitation w/ no detectable HR, withdrawing is reasonable. Thermoregulation preserved (no hyperthermia). Therapeutic hypothermia screen if ≥36 wk + <6 h + HIE. SBAR NICU handoff. Family communication. Team DEBRIEF. RN role: lead the protocol + handoff + family + debrief.

labs.n: Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors + family communication + bereavement readiness
labs.v: PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct emergency practice): the team did NOT start chest compressions before PPV was effective (the cause of newborn bradycardia is almost always hypoxia from inadequate ventilation); did NOT use the older 30:2 ratio (that is for older infants/children/adults — newborn is 3:1); did NOT start at 100% O2 in a term newborn (start at 21%, escalate as needed); did NOT skip the right-wrist preductal pulse oximeter; did NOT forget MR SOPA when PPV was ineffective; did NOT routinely intubate and tracheally suction a non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn (no longer routine — only if needed for effective ventilation); did NOT allow hyperthermia; did NOT over-explain clinical details to the family at the bedside; and did NOT skip the team debrief or family follow-up. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: pre-resuscitation huddle + equipment verification + closed-loop role assignment; rapid initial assessment + initial steps; airway-first sequence with PPV within the golden minute at correct rate and FiO2 with right-wrist pulse ox + ECG; MR SOPA when ineffective; chest compressions 3:1 only when HR < 60 after effective PPV; UVC + epinephrine 0.02 mg/kg as needed; volume if hypovolemia suspected; thermoregulation preserved; therapeutic-hypothermia eligibility screening when applicable; SBAR NICU hand-off; honest family communication with bereavement/chaplaincy readiness; team debrief. EXPECTED outcome (as here): with effective PPV, brief compressions, and one dose of epinephrine via UVC, the newborn achieves ROSC with spontaneous respirations, transfers safely to NICU, and the family is supported throughout.
labs.r: Negatives: did NOT start compressions before effective PPV, did NOT use 30:2 ratio (newborn = 3:1), did NOT start 100% O2 in term (start 21%), did NOT skip right-wrist preductal pulse ox, did NOT forget MR SOPA, did NOT routinely intubate-suction non-vigorous meconium newborn, did NOT allow hyperthermia, did NOT over-explain at bedside, did NOT skip debrief/family follow-up. Protective: huddle + equipment + closed-loop roles + initial steps + PPV within Golden Minute at correct rate/FiO2 + right-wrist pulse ox + ECG + MR SOPA + compressions 3:1 only when HR <60 after effective PPV + UVC + epi + volume if hypovolemic + thermoregulation + hypothermia eligibility screen + SBAR NICU handoff + honest family + bereavement readiness + team debrief.

opts.text: Rapid initial assessment (term? tone? breathing/crying?) — if any NO, bring to the radiant warmer for initial steps (~30 sec: warm + dry + position + clear airway only if obstructed + stimulate)

opts.text: For HR < 100 or apnea/gasping, begin PPV within the Golden Minute at 40-60/min with ROOM AIR (21%) for term infants; right-wrist preductal pulse ox + ECG; the best sign of effective PPV is a RISING HR

opts.text: If HR is not rising, perform MR SOPA in order — Mask seal, Reposition airway, Suction mouth/nose, Open mouth, Pressure ↑, Alternative airway

opts.text: If HR remains < 60 after 30 sec of EFFECTIVE PPV, begin chest compressions (two-thumb encircling, lower 1/3 sternum, ~1/3 AP depth) at a 3:1 ratio (90 compressions + 30 breaths = 120 events/min) with FiO2 100%

opts.text: Start chest compressions immediately at birth for any HR < 100, before PPV is effective
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Compressions start only if HR remains < 60 after 30 seconds of EFFECTIVE PPV; newborn bradycardia is almost always hypoxia from inadequate ventilation — fix ventilation first.

steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Approximately 10% of newborns need help to begin breathing and about 1% need extensive resuscitation; pre-delivery huddle + equipment check + closed-loop role assignment are core leadership steps
opts.rat: CORRECT — epidemiology + preparation principle. Foundation for readiness.

opts.text: Initial steps (warm + dry + position + clear airway PRN + stimulate) are completed in about 30 seconds; the best sign of effective PPV is a rising HR (chest rise reassures but HR is the metric)
opts.rat: CORRECT — initial-steps and effectiveness principle. Foundation for the algorithm.

opts.text: MR SOPA (Mask, Reposition, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure, Alternative airway) is the corrective sequence when PPV is ineffective
opts.rat: CORRECT — MR SOPA principle. Foundation for troubleshooting.

opts.text: Compressions begin if HR < 60 after 30 seconds of EFFECTIVE PPV; preferred technique is two-thumb encircling on the lower third of the sternum at a 3:1 ratio with FiO2 100%
opts.rat: CORRECT — compression principle. Foundation for correct technique and ratio.

opts.text: Epinephrine is 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL solution) via UVC (fastest newborn access); ET 0.1 mg/kg is a less-reliable bridge; repeat every 3-5 minutes; volume 10 mL/kg if hypovolemia is suspected

opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Routine ET intubation/suctioning of non-vigorous meconium-stained newborns is no longer recommended; intervene only as needed for effective ventilation.

opts.text: Allowing the newborn to become hyperthermic during resuscitation improves outcomes
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Hyperthermia worsens HIE outcomes; preserve thermoregulation and avoid overheating.

opts.text: Perform MR SOPA when PPV is ineffective (Mask seal, Reposition airway, Suction mouth/nose, Open mouth, Pressure ↑, Alternative airway)

opts.text: Start chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio with two-thumb encircling on the lower third of the sternum and FiO2 100% if HR remains < 60 after 30 sec of effective PPV; reassess after 60 sec
opts.rat: Correct compressions only after effective PPV. RN role: 3:1 compressions.

opts.text: Place an umbilical vein catheter and give epinephrine 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO if HR remains < 60 after compressions; consider volume 10 mL/kg if hypovolemia suspected; preserve thermoregulation; screen for therapeutic hypothermia; SBAR hand-off + family communication + debrief
opts.rat: Medications + post-resuscitation + family + debrief complete the response. RN role: UVC + epi + volume + thermoregulation + handoff.

opts.text: Start chest compressions immediately at birth for any HR < 100 before PPV is effective
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — compressions begin only if HR < 60 after 30 sec of EFFECTIVE PPV. Newborn bradycardia is almost always hypoxia — fix ventilation first.

opts.text: Use a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio with 100% O2 from the start for a term newborn
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — newborn ratio is 3:1; start FiO2 21% in a term infant and escalate to 100% when compressions begin.

opts.text: Routinely intubate and tracheally suction a non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn at birth
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — no longer routine; intervene only as needed for effective ventilation.

opts.text: Allow the newborn to become hyperthermic during resuscitation to 'support metabolism'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — hyperthermia worsens HIE outcomes; preserve thermoregulation and avoid overheating.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Pre-delivery huddle + closed-loop role assignment + equipment verification
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Preparation determines speed and quality at the event. RN role: brief + delegate + verify.

opts.text: Initial assessment + initial steps within ~30 sec; begin PPV within the Golden Minute at 40-60/min with room air (term) for HR < 100 or apnea/gasping; right-wrist preductal pulse ox + ECG
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Airway + ventilation are the highest-impact bedside actions. RN role: PPV within the Golden Minute.

opts.text: MR SOPA when PPV is ineffective (intubate/LMA at A if needed)
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Troubleshoot ventilation before escalating. RN role: MR SOPA.

opts.text: Chest compressions at 3:1 (two-thumb encircling) with FiO2 100% if HR < 60 after 30 sec of effective PPV; reassess after 60 sec
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Correct compressions only after effective PPV. RN role: compressions.

opts.text: Place UVC and give epinephrine 0.02 mg/kg IV; consider volume; preserve thermoregulation; screen for therapeutic hypothermia; SBAR hand-off + family + debrief
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Medications + thermoregulation + handoff + family + debrief complete the response. RN role: meds + handoff + debrief.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action/outcome, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The team pre-briefed before delivery, assigned closed-loop roles, and verified equipment; the radiant warmer was pre-heated and warm blankets ready
opts.rat: Preparation done correctly. Model leadership.

opts.text: Initial steps were completed in about 30 seconds and PPV at 40-60/min with room air was started within the Golden Minute when the newborn remained apneic with HR ~70; pulse oximeter was placed on the right wrist and ECG attached
opts.rat: Correct PPV with the right monitor placement. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: When PPV was not effective, MR SOPA was performed in order; an alternative airway was placed when needed and PPV became effective; FiO2 escalated only when compressions began
opts.rat: Correct troubleshooting and oxygen escalation. Correct trajectory.

opts.text: Compressions at 3:1 with two-thumb encircling were started only after 30 sec of effective PPV with HR still < 60; UVC placed and epinephrine 0.02 mg/kg IV given when HR remained < 60 after 60 sec of compressions + PPV; ROSC achieved; thermoregulation preserved; SBAR hand-off to NICU; family communication + team debrief
opts.rat: Full sequence executed correctly. Ideal trajectory.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — chest compressions were started immediately at birth for HR ~70 before PPV was even effective; the newborn's hypoxia was not addressed and HR continued to fall
opts.rat: ⚠️ Newborn bradycardia is almost always hypoxia — fix ventilation first. Compressions start only if HR < 60 after 30 sec of effective PPV.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — a 30:2 ratio was used with 100% O2 from the start in a term newborn; the rhythm was uncoordinated and oxygen use was inappropriate for a term infant
opts.rat: ⚠️ Newborn ratio is 3:1; start FiO2 21% in a term infant and escalate when compressions begin.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn was routinely intubated and tracheally suctioned before any PPV; effective ventilation was delayed
opts.rat: ⚠️ Routine intubation/suctioning of non-vigorous meconium-stained newborns is no longer recommended; intervene only as needed for effective ventilation.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the team allowed hyperthermia during resuscitation; HIE outcome was worsened
opts.rat: ⚠️ Hyperthermia worsens HIE outcomes; preserve thermoregulation and avoid overheating.

opts.text: Alternative scenario — the family was given a lengthy technical explanation at the bedside during compressions and the hand-off to NICU skipped SBAR; communication failed
opts.rat: ⚠️ Honest brief updates by the leader or family liaison; SBAR hand-off prevents transition errors.

opts.text: After the event, the team held a structured debrief identifying what went well and what to improve; chaplaincy and peer support were offered; therapeutic-hypothermia eligibility was screened and the family was updated honestly
opts.rat: Closes the response for the team and the family. Ideal outcome.

title: Proactive Outpatient PSYCHIATRIC ADVANCE DIRECTIVE (PAD) for a STABLE, Capable 41-Year-Old Man with Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) Maintained on a Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotic and Lithium: Documenting Treatment Preferences for a FUTURE Crisis (Preferred and Refused Medications WITH the Reasons, Hospital and ECT Preferences, De-escalation/Seclusion/Restraint Preferences, Visitors, and Care of Dependents), Naming and EDUCATING a Health-Care Agent for Mental-Health Decisions, Confirming PRESENT Capacity, Clarifying WHEN a PAD Activates and Its Legal LIMITS, and Ensuring Cross-Setting Portability — All Without Coercion
subtitle: A PSYCHIATRIC ADVANCE DIRECTIVE (PAD) is a legal document a person with a serious mental illness completes WHILE STABLE AND CAPABLE to record their treatment preferences and/or to name a health-care agent for use during a FUTURE mental-health crisis in which they may temporarily LOSE decision-making capacity. It is the mental-health parallel to a medical advance directive and, done PROACTIVELY in the outpatient setting during a stable phase (not in the middle of an acute episode), it preserves autonomy, reduces coercion, can shorten crises, and helps the crisis/inpatient team treat the patient the way the patient themselves chose when well. This case is the proactive outpatient PAD conversation with a CAPABLE patient — distinct from proactive MEDICAL advance care planning/POLST (case-142), involuntary civil commitment + duty to warn (case-139), and informed consent for ECT (case-147), though a PAD can be combined with a medical advance directive. TWO COMPONENTS apply, mirroring a medical AD. (A) An INSTRUCTIONAL directive states the patient's psychiatric treatment PREFERENCES: medications that have WORKED and those to REFUSE or AVOID and WHY (e.g., 'I had an acute dystonic reaction to IM haloperidol — avoid it; I respond well to my long-acting injectable and to oral olanzapine'), preferred hospital/facility, preferences about ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY, de-escalation strategies that calm them and preferences about SECLUSION/RESTRAINT, who may and may NOT visit or be notified, and practical instructions for care of dependents/pets/bills/housing during hospitalization, plus their personal EARLY WARNING SIGNS of relapse. (B) A HEALTH-CARE POWER OF ATTORNEY for mental health NAMES an AGENT/PROXY to make psychiatric decisions when the patient cannot — high yield, because no document anticipates every scenario and a well-EDUCATED agent can apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT. CONFIRM PRESENT CAPACITY first: capacity is decision-specific and PRESUMED; a chronic diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder, prior hospitalizations, taking psychiatric medication, an unwise choice, or simple disagreement do NOT by themselves equal incapacity (link to [[case-116]] and [[case-142]]). The PAD must be authored during a period of capacity — NOT during acute psychosis or mania. ACTIVATION: a PAD becomes OPERATIVE only when the patient is determined to LACK capacity (by a clinician/process per state law), and it is SUSPENDED again once capacity returns — the capable patient otherwise speaks for themselves. LEGAL LIMITS (teach honestly): a PAD generally CANNOT compel treatment that is not clinically indicated or available, cannot force the system to hospitalize the patient, and cannot override emergency treatment needed to prevent serious imminent harm or a valid court commitment order; a clinician MAY decline to follow a specific PAD instruction that is not clinically appropriate or feasible but must DOCUMENT the clinical reason. Many states allow ADVANCE CONSENT to treatment over a future incapacitated objection (a key value of PADs — it lets the well self authorize the unwell self's care), and REVOCATION rules are STATE-SPECIFIC: many states allow revocation ONLY while the patient has capacity (so a crisis-time refusal does not automatically void the PAD), while others allow revocation at any time — teach the patient their state's rule. Documents are STATE-SPECIFIC (witnesses/notary/forms). PORTABILITY is the most common operational failure: a perfect PAD that the crisis team cannot find does nothing — file it in the chart/EHR and any state PAD/crisis registry, give copies to the agent and outpatient psychiatrist, share it with the preferred hospital ED and the local crisis team, and provide the patient a wallet card. Frame the PAD as an ONGOING PROCESS to revisit when treatment response, supports, or wishes change. Respect AUTONOMY including the right to DEFER or DECLINE; never coerce and never have the patient sign what they do not understand. PERTINENT MISTAKES TO AVOID: treating the schizoaffective diagnosis as automatic incapacity and bypassing him; trying to author the PAD during an acute episode; pressuring specific choices or having him sign what he doesn't understand; promising the PAD can FORCE the team to hospitalize him or can ALWAYS override a safety-driven emergency/valid commitment; completing the document but never making it portable; and, later, ignoring a valid, applicable PAD during a crisis. NURSING ROLE: facilitate the conversation while the patient is stable, confirm present capacity, elicit treatment history and preferences in plain language, support agent selection and EDUCATION, teach activation/limits/revocation accurately, coordinate execution per state law, ensure cross-setting portability, honor a valid applicable PAD during a future crisis, and document objectively.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + the proactive outpatient PSYCHIATRIC ADVANCE DIRECTIVE (PAD) framework
labs.v: 41 y/o man D. Okafor with schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type), STABLE x ~14 months on a paliperidone palmitate monthly LAI + lithium, euthymic and capable, at a routine community-mental-health visit, who wants to create a PSYCHIATRIC ADVANCE DIRECTIVE 'while I'm doing well.' A PAD lets a competent person with serious mental illness record psychiatric treatment preferences and/or name a mental-health agent for use during a FUTURE crisis in which capacity may be lost. Done PROACTIVELY in the stable phase (not during an acute episode), it preserves autonomy, reduces coercion, can shorten crises, and lets the crisis/inpatient team honor the choices the patient made when well. It is distinct from medical advance care planning/POLST ([[case-142]]), involuntary commitment + duty to warn ([[case-139]]), and ECT consent ([[case-147]]) — though a PAD may be combined with a medical AD. The nurse's flow: confirm present capacity -> elicit treatment history and preferences in plain language -> teach the components, activation, limits, and revocation -> support agent selection + EDUCATION -> coordinate execution per state law -> ensure cross-setting portability -> frame as an ongoing process. Throughout: respect autonomy (including the right to defer/decline) and document objectively.
labs.r: PAD = a competent person with serious mental illness records psychiatric treatment preferences + names a mental-health agent for a FUTURE incapacitated crisis. Authored WHILE STABLE/capable. Flow: confirm capacity -> elicit history/preferences -> teach components/activation/limits/revocation -> agent selection + EDUCATION -> execute per state law -> portability -> ongoing process. Respect autonomy (incl. right to defer/decline); document. RN role: facilitate without coercion.

labs.n: What a PAD IS — the two components + ACTIVATION (when it takes effect)
labs.v: TWO components, mirroring a medical AD. (A) INSTRUCTIONAL directive — the patient's psychiatric treatment PREFERENCES: medications that have WORKED and those to REFUSE/AVOID and WHY (here: prefers his LAI and oral olanzapine; AVOID IM haloperidol after an acute dystonic reaction), preferred HOSPITAL/facility, preference about ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY, de-escalation strategies that calm him and preferences about SECLUSION/RESTRAINT, WHO may visit or be notified (and who may not), and practical instructions for care of dependents/pets/bills/housing during hospitalization, plus his personal EARLY WARNING SIGNS of relapse. (B) HEALTH-CARE POWER OF ATTORNEY for mental health — NAMES an AGENT/PROXY to make psychiatric decisions when he cannot; high-yield because no document anticipates every scenario, and a well-EDUCATED agent can apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what HE would want). ACTIVATION: a PAD is authored while the person HAS capacity but becomes OPERATIVE only when the patient is later determined to LACK capacity (by a clinician/process per state law); it is SUSPENDED once capacity returns — at all other times the capable patient speaks for themselves. The PAD must NOT be authored during acute psychosis or mania.
labs.r: TWO components: (A) INSTRUCTIONAL preferences = preferred/refused meds WITH reasons, hospital choice, ECT preference, de-escalation + seclusion/restraint preferences, visitors/notification, dependent/pet/bill care, early warning signs; (B) AGENT (mental-health POA) who applies SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT. ACTIVATION: authored while CAPABLE; operative ONLY when capacity is later lost; SUSPENDED when capacity returns. Never author during acute psychosis/mania. RN role: elicit preferences + support agent designation.

labs.n: Capacity to execute + LEGAL LIMITS of a PAD + state-specific REVOCATION
labs.v: CAPACITY (decision-specific, presumed): the four-element test — understand the information, appreciate how it applies to him, reason through options, and communicate a stable choice; a chronic schizoaffective diagnosis, prior hospitalizations, taking psychiatric medication, an unwise choice, or disagreement do NOT by themselves equal incapacity ([[case-116]], [[case-142]]). The PAD must be created during a period of capacity. LEGAL LIMITS (teach honestly, do not over-promise): a PAD generally CANNOT compel treatment that is not clinically indicated or available; CANNOT force the system to hospitalize him; and CANNOT override emergency treatment necessary to prevent serious imminent harm, or a valid court civil-commitment order. A clinician MAY decline to follow a specific PAD instruction that is not clinically appropriate/feasible, but must DOCUMENT the clinical reason. ADVANCE CONSENT: many states let a PAD give consent to treatment over a future INCAPACITATED objection — a central value of a PAD, letting the well self authorize the unwell self's care. REVOCATION is STATE-SPECIFIC: many states allow revocation ONLY while the patient has capacity (so a crisis-time refusal does not automatically void the PAD); others allow revocation at any time — teach him HIS state's rule. Documents are state-specific (witnesses/notary/forms): execute per state law and review when moving states.
labs.r: CAPACITY = decision-specific, presumed: understand/appreciate/reason/communicate a stable choice (schizoaffective dx / prior hospitalizations / taking meds / unwise choice / disagreement != incapacity); author while capable. LIMITS: a PAD can't compel non-indicated/unavailable care, can't force hospitalization, can't override a safety emergency or valid commitment; clinician may decline an instruction WITH documented reason. Many states allow ADVANCE CONSENT over future objection. REVOCATION is state-specific (often only while capable). RN role: teach limits/revocation honestly.

labs.n: Execution + cross-setting PORTABILITY + ongoing process + Pertinent NEGATIVES + protective factors
labs.v: EXECUTION: follow state-specific requirements (witnesses, notary, forms); the patient signs while capable. PORTABILITY (the most common operational failure point): a perfect PAD the crisis team cannot find does nothing — file it in the chart/EHR and any state PAD/crisis registry; give COPIES to the patient and to the agent (his sister); share with the outpatient psychiatrist, the PREFERRED HOSPITAL ED, and the local mobile crisis team; provide a wallet card noting he has a PAD and where it is. FOLLOW-UP: a PAD is an ongoing PROCESS — revisit when treatment response, supports, or wishes change, and remind him he can update it any time while capable. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT treat his schizoaffective diagnosis as automatic incapacity and bypass him; did NOT try to author the PAD during an acute episode; did NOT pressure specific choices or have him sign what he did not understand; did NOT promise the PAD could FORCE hospitalization or ALWAYS override a safety emergency/valid commitment; and did NOT complete the document without making it portable. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: proactive timing during a stable, capable phase; capacity confirmed; values/treatment-history conversation in plain language; accurate teaching of components, activation, limits, and revocation; an agent selected and EDUCATED about his values; documents executed per state law and made portable across settings; ongoing-process framing; objective documentation. EXPECTED outcome: his autonomy is preserved, his crisis preferences are clear and accessible, his agent is prepared to advocate, and — as occurred at his next relapse — the team honored the PAD (used his LAI/oral olanzapine, AVOIDED haloperidol, engaged his agent), shortening and de-escalating the crisis.
labs.r: EXECUTION per state law (witnesses/notary); patient signs while capable. PORTABILITY = the common failure: chart/EHR + state PAD/crisis registry + copies to patient/agent + share w/ outpatient psychiatrist + preferred hospital ED + mobile crisis team + wallet card. FOLLOW-UP = ongoing process; update anytime while capable. Negatives confirm correct practice (didn't equate dx w/ incapacity, didn't author during an episode, didn't coerce/over-promise force-hospitalization, didn't skip portability). Protective: proactive stable-phase timing + capacity + plain-language preferences + educated agent + portable documents + ongoing process. RN role: execute + portability + honor in crisis.

nursesNote: Outpatient community-mental-health clinic — routine maintenance visit. 41 y/o man, schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type), STABLE x ~14 months on paliperidone palmitate monthly LAI + lithium (level 0.8 mEq/L; TSH/renal normal; tox negative). Alert, calm, euthymic, linear thought, NO psychosis/mania/SI/HI. He requests creation of a PSYCHIATRIC ADVANCE DIRECTIVE 'while I'm doing well.' Sister (proposed agent) on speakerphone. PAD flow: (1) CAPACITY confirmed (understands/appreciates/reasons/communicates a stable choice; chronic schizoaffective dx + prior hospitalizations + taking meds do NOT equal incapacity); must be authored while capable, not during an episode. (2) TREATMENT HISTORY + PREFERENCES elicited in plain language — prefers his LAI and oral olanzapine; AVOID IM haloperidol (prior acute dystonic reaction/oculogyric crisis); preferred hospital recorded; ECT preference recorded; de-escalation = quiet low-stimulation room + explain the plan, prefers to avoid seclusion; visitors/notification list; instructions for care of his dog + rent during any hospitalization; personal early warning signs. (3) EDUCATED on the two components (instructional preferences + named mental-health AGENT) and on ACTIVATION (operative only when capacity is later lost; suspended when capacity returns), with HONEST teaching of LIMITS (a PAD cannot force hospitalization, cannot override a safety emergency or valid commitment, and a clinician may decline a non-indicated instruction with documented reason) and state-specific REVOCATION (often only while capable). (4) AGENT — sister named and EDUCATED about his values so she can apply SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT. No coercion; right to defer/decline respected. (5) EXECUTION per state law (witnesses/notary as required); patient signed while capable. (6) PORTABILITY — copies in chart/EHR + state PAD/crisis registry, given to patient + sister/agent, shared with outpatient psychiatrist + preferred hospital ED + mobile crisis team; wallet card carried. (7) Framed as an ongoing PROCESS to revisit; he can update anytime while capable. NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT treat the diagnosis as automatic incapacity, did NOT author during an acute episode, did NOT pressure choices or have him sign what he didn't understand, did NOT promise the PAD could force hospitalization or override a safety emergency, did NOT skip portability. Documentation objective and contemporaneous; team aligned; agent prepared.
providerOrders: VISIT: routine outpatient maintenance visit, community mental-health clinic; element = proactive creation of a psychiatric advance directive (PAD) with a stable, capable patient

CAPACITY: confirm present decision-making capacity (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate a stable choice); document that a chronic schizoaffective diagnosis, prior hospitalizations, or taking psychiatric medication do NOT by themselves equal incapacity; author the PAD only while capacity is intact

FACILITATION: support a values-based, plain-language PAD conversation; respect autonomy including the right to defer or decline; do not coerce or have the patient sign documents he does not understand

PREFERENCES: elicit and document treatment history and preferences — preferred and refused medications WITH reasons (prefers LAI + oral olanzapine; AVOID IM haloperidol after acute dystonic reaction), preferred hospital, ECT preference, de-escalation strategies + seclusion/restraint preferences, visitors/notification list, care of dependents/pet/bills/housing, and personal early warning signs

EDUCATION: teach the two PAD components (instructional preferences + named mental-health agent), ACTIVATION (operative only when capacity is later lost; suspended when capacity returns), and an HONEST account of LIMITS (cannot compel non-indicated/unavailable care, cannot force hospitalization, cannot override a safety emergency or valid civil-commitment order; clinician may decline a non-indicated instruction with documented reason) and state-specific REVOCATION rules

AGENT: support selection of a mental-health health-care agent (and alternate as desired) and EDUCATE the agent about the patient's values so they can apply substituted judgment; involve the agent/family with the patient's consent
DOCUMENT: complete and execute the PAD per state-specific law (witnesses/notary as required); coordinate legal-aid/social-work assistance as needed

PORTABILITY: file copies in the chart/EHR and any state PAD/crisis registry; provide copies to the patient and the agent; share with the outpatient psychiatrist, the preferred hospital ED, and the local mobile crisis team; provide a wallet card indicating a PAD exists and where to find it
FOLLOW-UP: frame the PAD as an ongoing process — revisit when treatment response, supports, or wishes change; remind the patient he can update it any time while capable

DOCUMENTATION: objective, contemporaneous record of capacity, treatment history and preferences elicited (in the patient's own words), education delivered, agent selection and education, document execution, and where copies were sent
