title: ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP and the Nurse's Role on Hospital Day 5 in a 64-Year-Old Man with Community-Acquired Pneumonia Who Is Clinically IMPROVING on Empiric Broad-Spectrum IV Vancomycin + Piperacillin-Tazobactam: DE-ESCALATING to a Narrow-Spectrum Agent Once a Penicillin-SUSCEPTIBLE Organism Is Identified, CLARIFYING a Low-Risk 'Penicillin Allergy' Label, IV-to-PO Conversion, Setting a DEFINED Duration/Stop Date, Therapeutic Drug Monitoring, and Preventing Resistance + C. difficile — Because LONGER and BROADER Is NOT Safer
subtitle: Antibiotic (antimicrobial) STEWARDSHIP is the coordinated effort to use antimicrobials only when needed and to optimize the DRUG, DOSE, ROUTE, and DURATION — getting the patient the RIGHT therapy while minimizing resistance, Clostridioides difficile infection, drug toxicity, and cost. The nurse is a FRONTLINE steward, and the CDC frames the daily questions as the 'Four Moments of Antibiotic Decision-Making': (1) Does this patient have an infection that requires antibiotics? (2) Have appropriate CULTURES been obtained BEFORE starting, and what empiric therapy is indicated? (3) Can therapy be stopped, NARROWED (de-escalated), or switched from IV to ORAL? (4) What DURATION is needed? This case follows a 64-year-old man admitted 5 days ago for community-acquired pneumonia and started — appropriately — on EMPIRIC broad-spectrum IV vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam after blood and respiratory cultures were drawn. He is now clearly IMPROVING (afebrile > 48 hours, normalized white count, breathing comfortably, eating a regular diet), and the culture data have returned: respiratory culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae that is PENICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE and blood cultures show NO growth at 48 hours. This is the textbook moment to ACT: DE-ESCALATE the broad regimen to a NARROW-spectrum agent the organism is susceptible to (here a penicillin-class/beta-lactam), STOP the vancomycin (no resistant gram-positive organism was found), CONVERT IV-to-PO because he is hemodynamically stable, improving, and absorbing orally (which also lets the unnecessary IV line come out — reducing bloodstream-infection risk and length of stay), and CONFIRM a DEFINED total DURATION/stop date (many infections, including uncomplicated CAP, need SHORTER courses than tradition suggests). A pivotal barrier is his chart's 'PENICILLIN ALLERGY' label, which on history is only a vague CHILDHOOD RASH with no features of anaphylaxis (no hives/angioedema/throat tightness/hypotension, no recent reaction) — a LOW-RISK history. Such labels are frequently inaccurate, yet they push clinicians toward broader, more toxic, second-line agents like vancomycin and fluoroquinolones and are associated with worse outcomes. The steward's job is to take a DETAILED allergy history, RISK-STRATIFY, and — per institutional pathways — pursue DELABELING (clarification, and where appropriate, beta-lactam challenge/skin testing) so the patient can receive the most effective first-line therapy; true IgE-mediated anaphylaxis is a hard contraindication, but a remote benign rash usually is not. ADVERSE-EFFECT and RESISTANCE stewardship continues: monitor the VANCOMYCIN TROUGH and renal function while he remains on it (nephrotoxicity), watch for superinfection and especially C. DIFFICILE (antibiotic-associated diarrhea) — for which, if suspected, the nurse uses CONTACT precautions and SOAP-AND-WATER hand hygiene because alcohol-based rub does NOT kill spores ([[case-053]] covers C. diff in depth) — and avoids unnecessary antibiotics that select for resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE) and for asymptomatic bacteriuria (which is NOT treated). The nurse OPERATIONALIZES stewardship by reviewing culture/susceptibility results daily, prompting the team with an SBAR de-escalation recommendation, championing the IV-to-PO switch and line removal, confirming a stop date, administering doses on time at correct intervals, reconciling allergies accurately, and teaching the patient to COMPLETE the prescribed (appropriately short) course and to report rash or diarrhea — never to 'save' or share antibiotics. The overarching principle the case drives home: broader and longer antibiotic therapy is NOT inherently safer — it is often MORE harmful — and timely de-escalation is high-quality, safe care. This is DISTINCT from the deep-dive C. difficile infection-control case ([[case-053]]), the febrile-neutropenia empiric-antibiotic case, the active-TB RIPE/DOT case ([[case-102]]), and the sepsis bundle cases ([[case-091]]). Step-6 evaluates whether each finding/response reflects IMPROVEMENT, WORSENING, or is UNCHANGED.

patient.name: M. Tran
patient.allergies: Charted 'Penicillin — rash' (per patient: a vague rash as a child; no hives, swelling, breathing trouble, or recent exposure recalled)
patient.admitDate: 5 days ago — admitted for community-acquired pneumonia (right lower lobe) with fever, productive cough, and leukocytosis. Blood and respiratory cultures were drawn, then EMPIRIC broad-spectrum IV vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam was appropriately started. Course: defervesced by hospital day 3, now afebrile > 48 hours, WBC normalized, breathing comfortably on room air, eating a regular diet, and ambulating. Today the microbiology has returned: respiratory culture = Streptococcus pneumoniae, PENICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE; blood cultures = no growth at 48 hours. He remains on full broad-spectrum IV therapy with a peripheral IV and no documented stop date. Plan: antibiotic stewardship review — de-escalate, address the allergy label, convert IV-to-PO, set a duration.
patient.room: 6-East, Bed 2; medical floor; pharmacy and stewardship team available; wife at bedside

vitals.spo2: 97% on room air; afebrile 36.9°C (> 48 hours afebrile); comfortable, eating breakfast, ambulating in halls; lungs improving with decreased crackles

98% RA; respiratory culture finalized as Streptococcus pneumoniae, PENICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE; blood cultures no growth at 48 h; nurse reviews results and prepares an SBAR de-escalation recommendation for the team

98% RA; detailed allergy history obtained — vague childhood rash, NO anaphylaxis features, no recent exposure = LOW-RISK label; stewardship pathway pursued to clarify/delabel so an effective first-line beta-lactam can be used

98% RA; remains afebrile with normal WBC on oral therapy; no rash or diarrhea; no parenteral line in place; tolerating PO well; preparing for discharge to complete a short oral course

labs.n: PRESENTATION + what ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP is + the nurse's role (Four Moments)
labs.v: 64 y/o man, hospital day 5 for community-acquired pneumonia, clinically IMPROVING on EMPIRIC broad-spectrum IV vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam (appropriately started after cultures). ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP = using antimicrobials only when needed and optimizing DRUG/DOSE/ROUTE/DURATION to get the right therapy while minimizing resistance, C. difficile, toxicity, and cost. The nurse is a frontline steward; CDC's FOUR MOMENTS of antibiotic decision-making: (1) Does the patient need antibiotics at all? (2) Were appropriate CULTURES obtained BEFORE starting, and what empiric therapy is right? (3) Can therapy be STOPPED, NARROWED (de-escalated), or switched IV-to-PO? (4) What DURATION is needed? CORE PRINCIPLE: broader/longer is NOT safer — it is often more harmful. Distinct from the deep C. difficile case ([[case-053]]), febrile neutropenia, active TB/RIPE ([[case-102]]), and sepsis bundles ([[case-091]]).
labs.r: Stewardship = right DRUG/DOSE/ROUTE/DURATION; minimize resistance, C. diff, toxicity, cost. CDC Four Moments: (1) needs antibiotics? (2) cultures before starting + right empiric choice? (3) stop/narrow/IV-to-PO? (4) duration? Nurse = frontline steward. Principle: broader/longer is NOT safer. RN role: ask the four moments daily and act on culture data.

labs.n: CULTURES before antibiotics -> DE-ESCALATION + IV-to-PO + DURATION/stop date
labs.v: Cultures are drawn BEFORE the first antibiotic dose so the organism can be identified and therapy tailored. Empiric BROAD-spectrum therapy is correct at the start of a serious infection, but once the patient improves and a susceptible organism is known, DE-ESCALATE: narrow to the most targeted effective agent and STOP drugs aimed at organisms not found (here, STOP vancomycin since no resistant gram-positive organism grew; narrow to a penicillin-class agent for penicillin-susceptible S. pneumoniae). IV-to-PO CONVERSION is appropriate when the patient is hemodynamically stable, clinically improving, able to take/absorb oral meds, and a suitable oral option exists — it removes the need for an IV line (lowering bloodstream-infection risk), improves mobility, and shortens stay. Set a DEFINED total DURATION/STOP DATE: many infections (including uncomplicated CAP, often ~5 days when afebrile and stable) need SHORTER courses than tradition; an open-ended order invites excessive exposure. AVOID treating ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA or colonization, and avoid antibiotics for viral illness.
labs.r: Cultures BEFORE antibiotics. Empiric broad -> DE-ESCALATE once improving + susceptibility known (narrow + stop unneeded drugs; stop vanco if no resistant gram-positive). IV-to-PO when stable/improving/absorbing -> pull the line. Set a DEFINED duration/stop date (often shorter than tradition; uncomplicated CAP ~5 days). Don't treat asymptomatic bacteriuria/colonization or viral illness. RN role: prompt de-escalation, champion IV-to-PO + line removal, confirm a stop date.

labs.n: PENICILLIN ALLERGY clarification/delabeling + ADVERSE-EFFECT/C. difficile monitoring + TDM
labs.v: A charted 'PENICILLIN ALLERGY' that is only a vague CHILDHOOD RASH — no hives/angioedema/throat tightness/hypotension, no recent reaction — is a LOW-RISK history; ~90-95% of such labels are not true IgE-mediated allergy. These inaccurate labels push patients to broader, more toxic second-line drugs (vancomycin, fluoroquinolones, aztreonam) and are linked to worse outcomes, more C. difficile, and more resistance. The steward takes a DETAILED history, RISK-STRATIFIES, and pursues DELABELING per pathway (clarification +/- beta-lactam challenge/skin testing); true anaphylaxis is a hard contraindication, but a remote benign rash usually is not. ADVERSE-EFFECT/RESISTANCE monitoring: track the VANCOMYCIN TROUGH and renal function while on it (nephrotoxicity; AUC/trough-guided dosing); watch for superinfection and especially C. DIFFICILE diarrhea — if suspected, use CONTACT precautions and SOAP-AND-WATER hand hygiene (alcohol rub does NOT kill spores; full detail in [[case-053]]). Administer doses on time/at correct intervals to maintain efficacy and limit resistance.
labs.r: A vague childhood rash = LOW-RISK penicillin label (~90-95% aren't true allergy); inaccurate labels force broader/toxic drugs + worse outcomes -> take detailed history, risk-stratify, DELABEL per pathway (true anaphylaxis is a hard stop; remote benign rash usually not). Monitor VANCOMYCIN trough + renal (nephrotoxicity); watch for C. DIFFICILE diarrhea -> contact precautions + SOAP-AND-WATER (alcohol doesn't kill spores, [[case-053]]). RN role: accurate allergy reconciliation + TDM + timely dosing.

labs.n: Resistance, infection-prevention, the nurse operationalizing stewardship + PERTINENT NEGATIVES
labs.v: Unnecessary/overbroad/prolonged antibiotics select for RESISTANT organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL- and carbapenem-resistant gram-negatives/CRE) and drive C. difficile — a patient-safety and public-health harm. The nurse OPERATIONALIZES stewardship: review culture/susceptibility results daily and flag de-escalation opportunities; deliver an SBAR de-escalation recommendation to the prescriber; champion the IV-to-PO switch and removal of unnecessary lines; confirm a stop date and question open-ended orders; reconcile allergies accurately; give doses on time at the correct interval; practice hand hygiene and indicated precautions; and TEACH the patient to COMPLETE the prescribed (appropriately short) course, NOT to save/share leftover antibiotics, and to report rash or diarrhea. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT broaden therapy or add empiric antifungals 'to be safe' in an improving patient with a known susceptible pathogen; did NOT continue full broad-spectrum IV indefinitely without a stop date; did NOT keep the line in for convenience after the oral switch; did NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria; did NOT accept the unverified allergy label and withhold first-line therapy; and did NOT rely on alcohol rub for suspected C. difficile. PROTECTIVE FACTORS: cultures before antibiotics, prompt de-escalation, allergy clarification, IV-to-PO + line removal, defined duration, TDM, and patient teaching.
labs.r: Overbroad/prolonged antibiotics -> resistance (MRSA/VRE/ESBL/CRE) + C. diff. Nurse operationalizes stewardship: daily culture review + SBAR de-escalation, IV-to-PO + line removal, confirm stop date, accurate allergy rec, on-time dosing, precautions, teach complete-the-course/don't-save-or-share/report rash-or-diarrhea. NEGATIVES confirm correct practice (no broadening/antifungal, no open-ended IV, pull the line, don't treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, don't withhold first-line over a vague label, no alcohol rub for C. diff).

labs.v: Streptococcus pneumoniae, PENICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE (a narrow-spectrum, first-line target is now identified)
No growth at 48 hours (no bacteremia; no resistant gram-positive organism to justify continued vancomycin)
8.4 x10^9/L (NORMALIZED from 16.2 on admission — supports clinical resolution and de-escalation)
0.3 ng/mL, down from 2.4 on admission (declining; supports bacterial resolution and stopping/narrowing therapy)
15 mcg/mL (within target while still on it; monitor with renal function — discontinuation now planned with de-escalation)
1.0 mg/dL (normal; stable — monitor for vancomycin nephrotoxicity while on therapy)

nursesNote: 0800 — Hospital Day 5, CAP. 64 y/o man, afebrile > 48 h, WBC normalized (8.4 from 16.2), SpO2 98% RA, eating/ambulating, crackles improving — clinically resolving on empiric IV vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam (started day 1 AFTER blood + respiratory cultures). Micro back: respiratory culture = S. pneumoniae, PENICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE; blood cultures no growth at 48 h; procalcitonin down to 0.3. STEWARDSHIP review (CDC Four Moments): patient improving + susceptible organism known = time to DE-ESCALATE. Recommending via SBAR: STOP vancomycin (no resistant gram-positive grew) and narrow to a penicillin-class agent; CONVERT IV-to-PO (stable, improving, tolerating diet) and REMOVE the unnecessary peripheral IV; SET a defined total duration/stop date (uncomplicated CAP often ~5 days). Addressed the charted 'penicillin allergy': detailed history = vague childhood rash, NO anaphylaxis features, no recent exposure = LOW-RISK; pursuing clarification/delabeling per pathway so an effective first-line beta-lactam can be used. While vancomycin continues: trough 15 (target), creatinine 1.0 stable — monitoring nephrotoxicity. Monitoring for superinfection/C. difficile diarrhea — if it occurs, CONTACT precautions + SOAP-AND-WATER hand hygiene (alcohol rub does not kill spores). Did NOT broaden therapy/add antifungal, did NOT continue open-ended broad-spectrum IV, did NOT keep the line for convenience, did NOT treat any asymptomatic bacteriuria, did NOT withhold first-line therapy over the unverified label. Teaching: complete the prescribed short course, do not save/share antibiotics, report rash or diarrhea. Allergy record to be updated to reflect clarified history. Wife at bedside; pharmacy/stewardship team engaged.
providerOrders: STEWARDSHIP REVIEW: apply the CDC Four Moments daily; review culture/susceptibility results and assess for stop/narrow/IV-to-PO opportunities; nurse to deliver SBAR de-escalation recommendation
CULTURES: respiratory culture = S. pneumoniae PENICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE; blood cultures no growth at 48 h; do not draw or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria/colonization
DE-ESCALATE: discontinue vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam; narrow to a penicillin-class/beta-lactam agent appropriate for penicillin-susceptible pneumococcus once the allergy is clarified

ALLERGY CLARIFICATION: obtain detailed penicillin-allergy history and risk-stratify; pursue delabeling per institutional pathway (clarification +/- beta-lactam challenge/skin testing) for this low-risk childhood-rash label; update the allergy record
IV-to-PO CONVERSION: convert to oral therapy now that the patient is stable, improving, and tolerating diet; DISCONTINUE the peripheral IV when no longer needed
DURATION: set a DEFINED total antibiotic duration/stop date (uncomplicated CAP commonly ~5 days when afebrile/stable); avoid open-ended orders; reassess daily
THERAPEUTIC DRUG MONITORING: while on vancomycin, monitor trough/AUC and renal function (creatinine) for nephrotoxicity; administer all doses on time at correct intervals

MONITOR/PRECAUTIONS: assess for superinfection and C. difficile-associated diarrhea; if suspected, initiate CONTACT precautions and SOAP-AND-WATER hand hygiene (alcohol-based rub does not kill spores); monitor for drug rash/allergic reaction

PATIENT TEACHING: complete the full prescribed (short) course exactly as ordered; do NOT save or share leftover antibiotics; report any rash, hives, swelling, breathing difficulty, or diarrhea promptly
FOLLOW-UP: discharge on the defined oral course with clear instructions and follow-up; reinforce that resolving symptoms do not mean antibiotics should be stopped early unless directed

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters on this stewardship review?
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically significant cues.

opts.text: He is clinically improving — afebrile > 48 hours, normalized WBC, comfortable on room air, eating and ambulating — yet still on day 5 of broad-spectrum IV vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — clinical resolution on broad empiric therapy is the trigger to reassess for de-escalation, IV-to-PO, and a stop date.

opts.text: The respiratory culture grew penicillin-SUSCEPTIBLE S. pneumoniae and blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a narrow, first-line target is identified and there is no bacteremia or resistant organism justifying continued vancomycin.

opts.text: The chart lists a 'penicillin allergy' that, on history, is only a vague childhood rash with no anaphylaxis features
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a low-risk, likely inaccurate label that is steering therapy toward broader, more toxic drugs and warrants clarification/delabeling.

opts.text: There is no documented antibiotic stop date or total duration on the orders
opts.rat: RELEVANT — open-ended orders invite excessive exposure; a defined duration is a core stewardship safeguard.

opts.text: He is tolerating a regular diet and has a peripheral IV used solely for antibiotics
opts.rat: RELEVANT — a candidate for IV-to-PO conversion, after which the unnecessary line should be removed to reduce infection risk.

opts.text: The vancomycin trough is 15 mcg/mL with a stable creatinine of 1.0
opts.rat: RELEVANT — therapeutic level with normal renal function while on the drug; monitoring continues until vancomycin is discontinued with de-escalation.

opts.text: Because he is improving, the team should broaden coverage further and add an empiric antifungal to be safe
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Improvement with a known susceptible pathogen calls for narrowing, not broadening; needless antifungals add toxicity and resistance.

opts.text: The penicillin-allergy label means he can never receive any beta-lactam and must remain on vancomycin
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. A vague childhood rash is a low-risk history; most such labels are not true allergy and can be clarified/delabeled to allow first-line beta-lactams.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: Once the patient is improving and a susceptible organism is identified, empiric broad-spectrum therapy should be DE-ESCALATED to the narrowest effective agent and drugs targeting unfound organisms (vancomycin) stopped
opts.rat: CORRECT — the central de-escalation principle of stewardship.

opts.text: A vague childhood rash without anaphylaxis features is a LOW-RISK penicillin-allergy history that can usually be clarified/delabeled to permit first-line beta-lactam therapy
opts.rat: CORRECT — most penicillin-allergy labels are inaccurate; risk-stratification opens up better therapy.

opts.text: Continuing unnecessary broad-spectrum IV antibiotics increases resistance, C. difficile, line-associated infection, drug toxicity, and cost — longer/broader is not safer
opts.rat: CORRECT — the harms of overtreatment that stewardship exists to prevent.

opts.text: IV-to-PO conversion is appropriate because he is hemodynamically stable, improving, and absorbing orally — and it allows the unnecessary line to be removed
opts.rat: CORRECT — the criteria and benefits of switching to oral therapy.

opts.text: A defined duration/stop date is needed because many infections, including uncomplicated CAP, require shorter courses than tradition suggests
opts.rat: CORRECT — shorter evidence-based courses reduce harm without sacrificing cure.

opts.text: Negative blood cultures and a normal white count mean the safest action is simply to continue the full broad-spectrum regimen unchanged
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Those data support de-escalation/stopping unneeded agents — not indefinite continuation of broad therapy.

opts.text: Antibiotic stewardship is solely the pharmacist's and physician's job, with no meaningful nursing role
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Nurses are frontline stewards — reviewing cultures, prompting de-escalation, championing IV-to-PO, reconciling allergies, and teaching patients.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these stewardship actions from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Recommend DE-ESCALATION to a narrow-spectrum agent and stopping vancomycin now that a susceptible organism is identified and he is improving
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. De-escalation is the central, highest-impact stewardship action given the culture data and clinical improvement.

opts.text: Clarify/risk-stratify the penicillin allergy so an effective first-line beta-lactam is not wrongly withheld
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. The label is the main barrier to optimal narrow therapy; clarifying it enables the best drug choice.

opts.text: Convert IV-to-PO and remove the unnecessary peripheral line once de-escalated and tolerating oral therapy
opts.rat: #3 — Reduces line-associated risk and length of stay once the narrower oral option is in place.

opts.text: Confirm a defined total duration/stop date and continue monitoring the vancomycin trough/renal function until it is discontinued
opts.rat: #4 — Prevents excessive exposure and catches toxicity while the drug is still on board.

opts.text: Reinforce hand hygiene/infection prevention and teach the patient to complete the course and report rash or diarrhea
opts.rat: #5 — Important ongoing safety and teaching that supports, but follows, the core regimen decisions.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Communicate the susceptibility results via SBAR and recommend de-escalating to a narrow-spectrum agent while stopping vancomycin
opts.rat: Targets therapy to the identified susceptible organism and removes coverage for organisms not found.

opts.text: Obtain a detailed allergy history and, with the team, risk-stratify and clarify/delabel the low-risk penicillin allergy
opts.rat: Enables first-line beta-lactam therapy and prevents unnecessary use of broader, more toxic alternatives.

opts.text: Recommend IV-to-PO conversion now that he is improving and tolerating diet, and remove the unnecessary peripheral IV
opts.rat: Lowers bloodstream-infection risk, improves mobility, and shortens length of stay.

opts.text: Confirm a defined total duration/stop date and reassess the plan daily
opts.rat: Prevents excessively long courses; an explicit stop date is a core stewardship safeguard.

opts.text: While vancomycin continues, monitor the trough and renal function; if new diarrhea occurs, suspect C. difficile and use contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene
opts.rat: Catches nephrotoxicity and manages the most important antibiotic-associated superinfection correctly (spores are not killed by alcohol rub).

opts.text: Broaden the regimen and add an empiric antifungal 'to be safe' even though he is improving with a known susceptible pathogen
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — needless broadening adds toxicity, C. difficile, and resistance risk with no benefit.

opts.text: Continue full broad-spectrum IV therapy indefinitely with no stop date
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — open-ended broad therapy is the harm stewardship prevents; set a duration and de-escalate.

opts.text: Keep the peripheral IV in place for convenience after switching to oral antibiotics
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — an unnecessary line is an avoidable infection risk and should be removed.

opts.text: Accept the unverified penicillin-allergy label and keep him on vancomycin rather than clarifying it
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — failing to clarify a low-risk label perpetuates broader/toxic therapy and worse outcomes.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Review the culture/susceptibility results and communicate them to the provider with an SBAR de-escalation recommendation
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Acting on the new culture data drives every subsequent regimen decision.

opts.text: Obtain and document a detailed allergy history and collaborate to clarify/delabel the penicillin allergy
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Clarifying the label unlocks the most effective first-line narrow agent.

opts.text: Implement de-escalation and IV-to-PO conversion, then discontinue the unnecessary peripheral line
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Narrows therapy and removes line-associated risk once the oral option is set.

opts.text: Confirm the total duration/stop date and continue vancomycin trough/renal monitoring until it is stopped
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Locks in an appropriate course length and watches for toxicity while the drug remains on board.

opts.text: Teach the patient to complete the course and report rash/diarrhea, and reinforce hand hygiene/infection prevention
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Sustains safe use and early detection of adverse effects after the plan is set.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as the patient IMPROVING, WORSENING, or UNCHANGED.

opts.text: After de-escalation to oral amoxicillin he stays afebrile with a normal white count and continued clinical improvement
opts.rat: Targeted narrow therapy maintains cure — the goal of de-escalation.

opts.text: The peripheral IV was removed after the oral switch and there is no longer any parenteral-line infection risk
opts.rat: Eliminating an unnecessary line reduces bloodstream-infection risk — a concrete stewardship win.

opts.text: The allergy history is clarified as a low-risk childhood rash and he tolerates the beta-lactam without any reaction
opts.rat: Accurate delabeling enabled effective first-line therapy with no adverse reaction.

opts.text: Three days into therapy he develops frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and a low-grade fever
opts.rat: ⚠️ Suspect C. difficile-associated diarrhea — send stool testing, start contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene, and reassess antibiotics ([[case-053]]).

opts.text: His vancomycin trough rises to 28 mcg/mL and creatinine climbs from 1.0 to 1.8 mg/dL
opts.rat: ⚠️ Supratherapeutic vancomycin with nephrotoxicity — hold/adjust the dose and notify the team; reinforces the value of de-escalating off vancomycin.

opts.text: Shortly after a dose he develops hives, lip swelling, and throat tightness
opts.rat: ⚠️ Acute IgE-mediated allergic/anaphylactic reaction — stop the drug, assess airway/ABCs, give epinephrine per protocol, and update the allergy record as a true allergy.

opts.text: An incidental urine culture is positive but he has no urinary symptoms, and no antibiotic is added for it
opts.rat: Correct stewardship — asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated; his status is unchanged and appropriately managed.

opts.text: On the first day after de-escalation his temperature and white count remain normal and stable
opts.rat: Stable normal parameters confirm the narrowed regimen is maintaining control — expected and reassuring.

opts.text: He completes the defined short oral course and is discharged on no unnecessary ongoing antibiotics
opts.rat: Right drug, route, and duration with a clean stop — the ideal stewardship outcome.

title: A MEDICATION ERROR That Reached the Patient — Wrong-Patient Administration of Another Patient's Metoprolol + Apixaban After a Bypassed Barcode Scan on a Med-Surg Unit: Protecting the PATIENT FIRST, Honest FACTUAL Charting in the Medical Record vs the SEPARATE Confidential OCCURRENCE/Incident Report, Truthful ERROR DISCLOSURE to the Patient, and a JUST-CULTURE, System-Focused Response (Human Error vs At-Risk Behavior vs Reckless) with Root-Cause Analysis and Prevention (Rights of Administration, Two Identifiers, BCMA Without Workarounds, Independent Double-Checks, LASA/Tall-Man Lettering, the 'Do Not Use' Abbreviation List) — Because Punishing Individuals for SYSTEM Failures Drives Underreporting and Repeat Harm
subtitle: A MEDICATION ERROR is any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm; an error that REACHES the patient is an adverse drug event (whether or not harm results), distinct from a NEAR-MISS that is caught before reaching the patient and a SENTINEL EVENT that causes serious harm or death. This case follows R. Delgado, a 67-year-old man admitted for a COPD exacerbation, who at the 0800 medication pass mistakenly received his ROOMMATE'S scheduled medications — metoprolol 50 mg and apixaban 5 mg — NEITHER of which is ordered for him. The proximate cause is a classic WRONG-PATIENT process failure: the nurse pulled two patients' medications together and BYPASSED barcode-medication-administration (BCMA) scanning after the scanner battery died, verifying identity only by room/bed rather than by TWO patient identifiers. The single most important principle is that PATIENT SAFETY COMES FIRST: the nurse must immediately ASSESS the patient (vital signs, level of consciousness, and for the specific risks of the drugs given — BRADYCARDIA/HYPOTENSION from the beta-blocker and BLEEDING from the anticoagulant), ensure safety, NOTIFY the provider and charge nurse without delay, and carry out resulting orders (telemetry, holding scheduled antihypertensives, coagulation/CBC labs, and continued monitoring) BEFORE turning to paperwork. DOCUMENTATION has two strictly separate channels that nurses routinely confuse: (1) the MEDICAL RECORD, in which the nurse charts only the OBJECTIVE FACTS — the medications actually given, the time, the patient's assessment and response, the provider/charge-nurse notifications, and the interventions performed — WITHOUT subjective blame, conclusions of fault, or the words 'error/mistake,' and WITHOUT ever mentioning that an incident report was filed; and (2) the OCCURRENCE / INCIDENT / VARIANCE REPORT, a SEPARATE confidential internal quality-improvement document that is NOT part of the medical record, is not referenced in the chart, and exists to TREND and analyze events to improve systems — not to punish. ERROR DISCLOSURE to the patient (and family) is an ethical duty of VERACITY/TRUTH-TELLING and transparency — increasingly required by accreditation and policy: the disclosure is honest, timely, and compassionate, typically LED by the provider with the nurse participating, and explains what happened, the clinical implications, and what is being done, with empathy and (per institutional policy) an apology — hiding or minimizing the event is never acceptable. The organizational response should reflect JUST CULTURE, which distinguishes HUMAN ERROR (an unintended slip — console and support the person, fix the system), AT-RISK BEHAVIOR (a drift such as the barcode workaround that has become normalized — COACH and remove the incentive to cut corners), and RECKLESS BEHAVIOR (conscious disregard of substantial risk — appropriately disciplined). Most errors are SYSTEM failures (the Swiss-cheese model), so a blame-and-shame response only drives UNDERREPORTING and repeat harm; serious events trigger a ROOT-CAUSE ANALYSIS (RCA, retrospective) while proactive risk is reduced with FAILURE MODE AND EFFECTS ANALYSIS (FMEA). PREVENTION is built into the system: the rights of medication administration (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response), TWO patient identifiers (never the room number), reliable BCMA used AS DESIGNED with no workarounds, INDEPENDENT DOUBLE-CHECKS for high-alert drugs (anticoagulants are high-alert), smart infusion pumps, separation and TALL-MAN LETTERING of look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) drugs, avoidance of error-prone abbreviations (the 'Do Not Use' list: U/IU, QD/QOD, trailing zeros and naked decimal points, MS/MSO4/MgSO4), medication reconciliation at transitions, and minimizing interruptions during the med pass ('no-interruption zone'). This is DISTINCT from the high-alert IV potassium safe-administration case ([[case-135]]), the needlestick/occupational-exposure case ([[case-152]]), and the hospital-fire RACE/PASS case ([[case-144]]) — here the focus is the human/system response to an error that reached the patient. Step-6 evaluates whether each nursing action or organizational response is APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

patient.name: R. Delgado
patient.admitDate: 2 days ago — admitted for an acute COPD exacerbation; improving on scheduled bronchodilators, inhaled/systemic corticosteroids, and supplemental oxygen. His ordered medications do NOT include any beta-blocker or anticoagulant. He shares a semi-private room with another patient. At the 0800 medication pass the nurse — after the handheld barcode scanner's battery died — pulled medications for both roommates together and identified this patient by ROOM/BED rather than two identifiers, then administered the ROOMMATE'S metoprolol 50 mg PO and apixaban 5 mg PO to Mr. Delgado. The mistake was recognized minutes later at the second bedside when the scanner (now charged) flagged a mismatch.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + what a MEDICATION ERROR is + the FIRST principle (patient safety)
labs.v: 67 y/o man admitted for a COPD exacerbation who mistakenly received his ROOMMATE'S 0800 medications — metoprolol 50 mg + apixaban 5 mg — neither ordered for him, after the nurse pulled two patients' meds together and BYPASSED barcode scanning (dead scanner) and verified by room/bed instead of TWO identifiers. A MEDICATION ERROR = a preventable event that may lead to inappropriate use or patient harm; one that REACHES the patient is an adverse drug event (vs a NEAR-MISS caught before reaching the patient, vs a SENTINEL EVENT causing serious harm/death). THE FIRST PRINCIPLE: PATIENT SAFETY COMES FIRST — assess the patient immediately (vitals, LOC, and the specific drug risks: BRADYCARDIA/HYPOTENSION from the beta-blocker, BLEEDING from the anticoagulant), ensure safety, notify the provider + charge nurse, and carry out orders BEFORE any paperwork. Distinct from high-alert IV potassium ([[case-135]]), needlestick exposure ([[case-152]]), and hospital fire ([[case-144]]).
labs.r: Medication error reached the patient (wrong-patient adverse drug event) due to a barcode workaround + single identifier. FIRST = PATIENT SAFETY: assess (vitals/LOC + drug-specific risks — beta-blocker bradycardia/hypotension, anticoagulant bleeding), ensure safety, notify provider + charge nurse, carry out orders — THEN paperwork. Error types: near-miss (caught) vs adverse event (reached) vs sentinel (serious harm).

labs.n: DOCUMENTATION: the MEDICAL RECORD (facts only) vs the SEPARATE OCCURRENCE/INCIDENT report
labs.v: Two strictly SEPARATE channels nurses often confuse. (1) MEDICAL RECORD — chart the OBJECTIVE FACTS: the medications actually given, the dose/route/time, the patient's assessment and response, who was notified (provider, charge nurse) and when, and the interventions carried out. Do NOT chart subjective blame, opinions, or conclusions of fault; do NOT label it 'error/mistake' editorially; and NEVER document that an incident report was completed. (2) OCCURRENCE / INCIDENT / VARIANCE REPORT — a confidential INTERNAL quality-improvement document that is NOT part of the medical record, is NOT referenced in the chart, and is completed factually and objectively to TREND and analyze events and improve systems — not to assign punishment. Keeping the report out of the chart preserves its quality-improvement purpose and avoids creating a self-incriminating, discoverable narrative within the legal record.
labs.r: MEDICAL RECORD = objective facts only (drugs given, time, assessment/response, notifications, interventions); NO blame/opinion, NO 'incident report filed.' OCCURRENCE/INCIDENT report = SEPARATE confidential QI document, NOT in the chart, NOT referenced in the chart, factual/objective, used to trend + fix systems (not to punish).

labs.n: ERROR DISCLOSURE (veracity/truth-telling) + JUST CULTURE (human error vs at-risk vs reckless)
labs.v: DISCLOSURE to the patient/family is an ethical duty of VERACITY and transparency, increasingly required by accreditation/policy: honest, timely, and compassionate, typically LED BY THE PROVIDER with the nurse participating — explain WHAT happened, the clinical implications, and WHAT is being done, with empathy and (per policy) an apology. Hiding/minimizing the event is never acceptable. JUST CULTURE balances accountability with system thinking and distinguishes: HUMAN ERROR (an unintended slip/lapse — CONSOLE the person, fix the system); AT-RISK BEHAVIOR (a normalized drift like the barcode workaround — COACH and remove the incentive to cut corners); and RECKLESS BEHAVIOR (conscious disregard of a substantial, unjustifiable risk — appropriately DISCIPLINED). Most errors are SYSTEM failures (the Swiss-cheese model of aligned latent holes), so a blame-and-shame response drives UNDERREPORTING and repeat harm. Serious events trigger a ROOT-CAUSE ANALYSIS (RCA, retrospective); proactive risk reduction uses FAILURE MODE AND EFFECTS ANALYSIS (FMEA, prospective).
labs.r: DISCLOSE honestly/timely/compassionately (provider-led, nurse participates; what happened + implications + plan + empathy/apology) — never hide. JUST CULTURE: human error -> console + fix system; at-risk behavior (barcode workaround) -> COACH; reckless -> discipline. Errors are mostly SYSTEM failures (Swiss-cheese) -> blame culture causes underreporting. Serious event -> RCA (retrospective); proactive -> FMEA.

labs.n: PREVENTION (the rights, two identifiers, BCMA, double-checks, LASA/Tall-Man, 'Do Not Use') + PERTINENT NEGATIVES
labs.v: System-level prevention: the RIGHTS of medication administration (right PATIENT, DRUG, DOSE, ROUTE, TIME, plus documentation, reason, and response); TWO PATIENT IDENTIFIERS (name + DOB/MRN — NEVER the room/bed number); reliable BARCODE medication administration (BCMA) used AS DESIGNED with NO workarounds (charged backup scanners, never scanning a copied/duplicate wristband, never pulling two patients' meds together); INDEPENDENT DOUBLE-CHECKS for HIGH-ALERT drugs (anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, concentrated electrolytes); SMART infusion pumps with dose-error reduction; separation, distinct storage, and TALL-MAN LETTERING for look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) drugs; avoidance of error-prone abbreviations (the Joint Commission 'Do Not Use' list: U/IU, QD/QOD, trailing zero '1.0', naked decimal '.5', MS/MSO4/MgSO4); medication RECONCILIATION at every transition; and a 'NO-INTERRUPTION ZONE' to reduce distraction during the med pass. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): the nurse did NOT delay assessing the patient to fill out paperwork first; did NOT hide or fail to report the event; did NOT chart blame or note 'incident report filed' in the medical record; did NOT assume 'he looks fine' and skip notification/monitoring; and the organization did NOT simply punish the individual while leaving the barcode workaround unaddressed.
labs.r: PREVENT with the RIGHTS + TWO identifiers (never room number) + BCMA used as designed (no workarounds) + INDEPENDENT double-checks for high-alert drugs + smart pumps + LASA separation/Tall-Man lettering + 'Do Not Use' abbreviations + med reconciliation + no-interruption zone. NEGATIVES (correct): don't paperwork-before-patient, don't hide/underreport, don't chart blame or 'incident report filed,' don't skip notification because he 'looks fine,' don't punish the person while ignoring the system fix.

nursesNote: 0820 — Med-surg, COPD exacerbation. At the 0800 pass the scanner battery died; meds for both roommates were pulled together and this patient was identified by room/bed rather than two identifiers, and he received his ROOMMATE'S metoprolol 50 mg PO + apixaban 5 mg PO — neither ordered for him. Recognized minutes later when the charged scanner flagged a mismatch at the second bedside. PATIENT SAFETY FIRST: returned immediately and assessed him before any paperwork — alert/oriented, no dizziness, NO bleeding/bruising/melena; HR 58 and BP 110/64 (trending down after an unintended beta-blocker). Notified the provider and charge nurse at once; orders carried out: continuous telemetry, scheduled antihypertensives held, stat CBC + coagulation studies (Hgb 13.8, platelets 242, INR 1.1 — normal INR does NOT exclude DOAC effect; apixaban-specific anti-Xa detectable), creatinine 1.0. Monitoring closely for bradycardia/hypotension and bleeding. CHARTING the FACTS only — drugs actually given, dose/route/time, assessment/response, notifications, and interventions — with NO blame and NO mention of an incident report. Completing a SEPARATE confidential occurrence/variance report (objective facts) for quality review. Provider to lead honest DISCLOSURE to the patient with me present (what happened, implications, monitoring plan, empathy). This reflects a likely AT-RISK behavior (a barcode workaround) within a system gap (no charged backup scanner) — a JUST-CULTURE review and prevention (reliable BCMA, two identifiers, independent double-check for the high-alert anticoagulant) to follow, NOT blame-and-shame. Did NOT delay assessment for paperwork, did NOT hide/underreport, did NOT chart blame or 'report filed,' did NOT skip notification because he 'looked fine.' Daughter reachable by phone.
providerOrders: PATIENT SAFETY FIRST: assess immediately after the error — full vital signs, level of consciousness, and focused checks for bradycardia/hypotension (beta-blocker) and any bleeding (anticoagulant); ensure patient safety before completing documentation
NOTIFY: notify the provider and charge nurse of the wrong-patient medication error without delay; provide an SBAR report of the medications given, time, and current assessment

MONITOR: place on continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry); HOLD scheduled antihypertensive/rate-controlling medications; frequent vital signs; monitor for bleeding (bruising, GI/GU bleeding, neuro changes) given the erroneous anticoagulant dose

LABS: stat CBC and coagulation studies; note that PT/INR/aPTT do NOT reliably reflect a direct oral anticoagulant — use an apixaban-specific anti-Xa level if quantification is needed; monitor renal function (creatinine)

DOCUMENTATION — MEDICAL RECORD: chart objective FACTS only (medications actually administered, dose/route/time, patient assessment and response, notifications, interventions); do NOT record subjective blame or conclusions of fault and do NOT reference that an incident report was filed

OCCURRENCE/INCIDENT REPORT: complete a SEPARATE confidential occurrence/variance report with objective, factual information for quality-improvement review; this report is NOT part of the medical record and is not mentioned in the chart

DISCLOSURE: provider to lead a prompt, honest, compassionate disclosure to the patient (and family per his wishes) — what happened, clinical implications, and the monitoring plan, with empathy/apology per institutional policy; nurse participates and supports the patient

JUST-CULTURE REVIEW: report the event for a non-punitive, system-focused review; distinguish human error vs at-risk behavior (the barcode workaround) vs reckless behavior; initiate root-cause analysis for system contributors (scanner availability, two-identifier verification, high-alert double-check)

PREVENTION: reinforce the rights of medication administration and TWO patient identifiers (never room number); ensure reliable BCMA with a charged backup scanner and no workarounds; require an independent double-check for high-alert drugs (anticoagulants); review LASA storage/Tall-Man lettering and 'Do Not Use' abbreviations

REASSESS/FOLLOW-UP: continue monitoring until the beta-blocker/anticoagulant effects have resolved and labs are stable; resume the patient's correct ordered regimen; document resolution and the patient's understanding after disclosure

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters immediately after this error?
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically significant cues.

opts.text: The patient received another patient's metoprolol 50 mg and apixaban 5 mg — neither medication is ordered for him
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a wrong-patient medication error that reached the patient; the specific drugs determine the immediate physiologic risks to assess.

opts.text: Identity was verified by room/bed and the barcode scan was bypassed after the scanner battery died, with both roommates' medications pulled together
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the process/system failure (workaround + single identifier) that caused the error and must be addressed to prevent recurrence.

opts.text: After the unintended beta-blocker, his heart rate fell to 58 and blood pressure to 110/64
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — early bradycardia/hypotension from an unordered beta-blocker requires immediate assessment and monitoring.

opts.text: He received an anticoagulant he is not prescribed, creating a new bleeding risk even though he is not currently bleeding
opts.rat: RELEVANT — apixaban (a high-alert drug) creates a bleeding risk that mandates monitoring and baseline labs regardless of current appearance.

opts.text: There is no order for any beta-blocker or anticoagulant in his medication record
opts.rat: RELEVANT — confirms the drugs were given in error and frames what to communicate to the provider.

opts.text: Because the patient currently looks well, no assessment, notification, or documentation is needed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. An error that reached the patient always requires assessment, provider notification, monitoring, and documentation — harm can be delayed.

opts.text: The first priority is to complete the incident report before doing anything else at the bedside
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The patient comes first — assess and stabilize, then notify; paperwork (and the separate occurrence report) follows patient safety.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: An unordered beta-blocker dose can cause bradycardia and hypotension, so the patient needs telemetry, frequent vitals, and held rate-lowering medications
opts.rat: CORRECT — anticipates and monitors the predictable physiologic effect of the erroneous metoprolol.

opts.text: An unordered anticoagulant creates a bleeding risk; a normal INR does NOT exclude a direct oral anticoagulant's effect, and an apixaban-specific anti-Xa level is the appropriate measure
opts.rat: CORRECT — DOACs do not reliably prolong PT/INR/aPTT; monitor clinically for bleeding and use the specific assay if quantification is needed.

opts.text: This is a medication error that REACHED the patient (an adverse drug event), not a near-miss, and must be reported and disclosed
opts.rat: CORRECT — classifying the event correctly drives the reporting and disclosure obligations.

opts.text: The root cause is largely a SYSTEM/process failure (a barcode workaround with single-identifier verification), best addressed through just culture rather than blame alone
opts.rat: CORRECT — most errors are system failures; a non-punitive, system-focused response prevents recurrence and supports reporting.

opts.text: Honest disclosure to the patient is an ethical duty of veracity and is required regardless of whether harm ultimately occurs
opts.rat: CORRECT — transparency/truth-telling is owed to the patient and is increasingly mandated by policy/accreditation.

opts.text: Because no harm is yet evident, the event does not need to be reported or disclosed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Errors that reach the patient are reported and disclosed even without apparent harm; hiding them is unethical and unsafe.

opts.text: The correct organizational response is simply to discipline or fire the nurse as the sole cause
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. A blame-only response ignores system contributors and drives underreporting; just culture coaches at-risk behavior and fixes the system.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these from #1 (HIGHEST priority) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Assess the patient immediately for effects of the erroneous drugs (vitals, LOC, bradycardia/hypotension, signs of bleeding) and ensure safety
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Patient safety comes first; direct assessment guides every subsequent action.

opts.text: Notify the provider and charge nurse of the error and obtain orders (monitoring, holding meds, labs)
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Prompt notification mobilizes monitoring and treatment and is required after any error reaching the patient.

opts.text: Carry out monitoring and orders — telemetry, held antihypertensives, coagulation/CBC labs — with continued reassessment
opts.rat: #3 — Implements the plan that protects the patient while effects are active.

opts.text: Document the objective facts in the medical record and complete a separate confidential occurrence report
opts.rat: #4 — Necessary and follows patient stabilization; the chart holds facts only, the occurrence report stays separate.

opts.text: Participate in honest disclosure to the patient and contribute to the just-culture/root-cause review and prevention
opts.rat: #5 — Essential for ethics and prevention, and appropriately follows the immediate safety and documentation steps.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: Return to the patient first and assess vital signs, level of consciousness, and for bradycardia/hypotension and bleeding before any paperwork
opts.rat: Patient safety is the first priority after a medication error reaches the patient.

opts.text: Notify the provider and charge nurse promptly and carry out resulting orders (telemetry, hold rate-lowering meds, stat labs)
opts.rat: Timely notification mobilizes monitoring/treatment and is required after an error.

opts.text: Chart objective facts in the medical record: the medications actually given, time, the patient's assessment/response, notifications, and interventions
opts.rat: The legal record holds factual, objective information about the patient's care.

opts.text: Complete a separate confidential occurrence/variance report with objective facts for quality-improvement review
opts.rat: The occurrence report supports system analysis and trending and is kept out of the medical record.

opts.text: Participate in a prompt, honest, compassionate disclosure to the patient explaining what happened and the monitoring plan
opts.rat: Veracity/transparency is owed to the patient; disclosure is provider-led with the nurse participating.

opts.text: Report the barcode workaround and system gap so it can be reviewed under just culture and corrected to prevent recurrence
opts.rat: System-focused, non-punitive review fixes the latent causes and sustains a reporting culture.

opts.text: Write in the medical record that a 'medication error was made due to my carelessness and an incident report was completed'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the chart holds facts, not blame or self-judgment, and must NEVER reference that an incident report was filed.

opts.text: Say nothing and simply watch the patient, since he looks well and disclosure might upset him
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — concealment violates veracity and safety; errors reaching the patient must be reported and disclosed.

opts.text: Delay assessing the patient in order to first complete the incident-report paperwork
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — patient assessment and safety always precede paperwork.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Go to the patient and assess vital signs, level of consciousness, and for bradycardia/hypotension and any bleeding; ensure safety
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Direct patient assessment and safety take precedence over everything else.

opts.text: Notify the provider and charge nurse with an SBAR report and obtain orders (telemetry, hold rate-lowering meds, stat CBC/coags)
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Prompt notification mobilizes monitoring and treatment.

opts.text: Carry out the orders and continue frequent reassessment while the drug effects are active
opts.rat: #3 — Third. Implements the protective monitoring plan.

opts.text: Document the objective facts in the medical record and complete the separate confidential occurrence report
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Accurate factual documentation follows patient stabilization; chart and occurrence report stay separate.

opts.text: Participate in honest disclosure to the patient and contribute to the just-culture review and prevention measures
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Fulfills the ethical duty of disclosure and drives system improvement to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each nursing action or organizational response as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The nurse assessed the patient first, found HR 58 and a soft blood pressure, notified the provider, placed him on telemetry, and held the next rate-lowering dose
opts.rat: Patient-first assessment plus prompt notification and monitoring is the correct response to the error.

opts.text: Charting recorded the medications given, time, assessment and response, notifications, and interventions — without blame and without mentioning the occurrence report
opts.rat: The medical record holds objective facts only; the occurrence report is never referenced in the chart.

opts.text: A separate confidential occurrence report was completed objectively and used by the unit for a just-culture review and a fix for scanner availability
opts.rat: Correct use of the occurrence report — system analysis and improvement rather than punishment.

opts.text: The provider, with the nurse present, disclosed the error to the patient honestly and compassionately and explained the monitoring plan
opts.rat: Truthful, timely, provider-led disclosure fulfills the duty of veracity and supports the patient.

opts.text: The nurse charted 'medication error due to my carelessness; incident report completed' in the medical record
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the chart must not contain blame/self-judgment or any reference to an incident report being filed.

opts.text: Management's only action was to discipline the nurse, while the dead-scanner workaround and single-identifier practice were left unchanged
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — blame-only responses ignore system causes, suppress reporting, and allow the error to recur.

opts.text: Because the patient initially looked well, the nurse decided not to notify the provider or start any monitoring
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — errors reaching the patient require notification and monitoring; beta-blocker/anticoagulant effects can evolve.

opts.text: The unit added a required independent double-check for high-alert anticoagulants and ensured charged backup scanners with two-identifier verification
opts.rat: Targeted system fixes (double-checks, reliable BCMA, two identifiers) address the root cause and prevent recurrence.

opts.text: When the patient's heart rate briefly dropped to 44 with light-headedness, the telemetry already in place allowed prompt recognition and treatment
opts.rat: The monitoring instituted after the error enabled early detection and intervention — the purpose of the safety response.

title: Recognizing and Escalating PEDIATRIC SEPTIC SHOCK in a 3-Year-Old on the Floor (Hospital Day 2 for Pyelonephritis) Who Deteriorates with Persistent TACHYCARDIA, Tachypnea, PROLONGED Capillary Refill, Cool Mottled Extremities, and ALTERED Mental Status While Her Blood Pressure Is Still 'Normal' — Because HYPOTENSION Is a LATE, Pre-Arrest Sign in Children: Distinguishing COLD vs WARM Shock, Activating the RAPID RESPONSE/Sepsis Pathway, and LEADING the Bedside Team Through the First-Hour Pediatric Surviving Sepsis Bundle (High-Flow O2, Rapid IV/IO Access, Blood Culture + Broad-Spectrum ANTIBIOTICS Within an Hour, Weight-Based 20 mL/kg PUSH Fluid Boluses REASSESSED for Response AND Overload, Correcting HYPOGLYCEMIA/Hypocalcemia, and EPINEPHRINE for Fluid-Refractory Shock with PICU Transfer) — with CLOSED-LOOP Role Assignment, SBAR, and Appropriate DELEGATION
subtitle: PEDIATRIC SEPTIC SHOCK is recognized DIFFERENTLY than in adults: children have tremendous cardiovascular reserve and COMPENSATE by raising heart rate and systemic vascular resistance, so they can be in shock with a NORMAL blood pressure — HYPOTENSION is a LATE, ominous, near-arrest finding, NOT the trigger to act. This case follows M. Abara, a 3-year-old girl (≈14 kg) admitted 2 days ago for pyelonephritis on IV antibiotics, who deteriorates on the floor with PERSISTENT tachycardia (HR 184), tachypnea (RR 50), a rising fever, PROLONGED capillary refill (4–5 seconds), cool/mottled extremities with weak peripheral pulses, decreased urine output (fewer wet diapers), and ALTERED mental status (difficult to rouse) — classic COMPENSATED (cold) septic shock while her systolic pressure is still ~88–90 (above the pediatric hypotension threshold of SBP < 70 + 2×age, i.e., < 76 mmHg for a 3-year-old). The nurse must RECOGNIZE the trend EARLY and not be falsely reassured by the 'normal' blood pressure, then ESCALATE immediately by activating the RAPID RESPONSE TEAM / sepsis pathway, and LEAD the bedside team through the pediatric SURVIVING SEPSIS CAMPAIGN first-hour bundle: apply HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN; obtain rapid IV access and place an INTRAOSSEOUS (IO) line within minutes if peripheral access fails; draw a BLOOD CULTURE and a point-of-care GLUCOSE and LACTATE; give BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS within the first hour (do NOT delay antibiotics for cultures if access is difficult); deliver rapid ISOTONIC fluid BOLUSES of 20 mL/kg PUSHED by syringe or pressure bag (gravity is too slow in a small child), REASSESSING after EACH bolus for both response and signs of FLUID OVERLOAD (new crackles, hepatomegaly, increased work of breathing) — escalating toward 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour as tolerated; CORRECT HYPOGLYCEMIA and HYPOCALCEMIA (children are prone to both, and they impair cardiac function); and for FLUID-REFRACTORY shock, start a vasoactive infusion — EPINEPHRINE for cold shock (the common pediatric pattern of low output/high SVR) or NOREPINEPHRINE for warm shock (vasodilated, bounding pulses, flash capillary refill, wide pulse pressure) — running it via peripheral/IO access if needed while arranging PICU transfer. Throughout, the case emphasizes LEADERSHIP and DELEGATION: recognizing and escalating without delay, ASSEMBLING and DIRECTING the team until the provider arrives, assigning CLOSED-LOOP roles (airway/oxygen, two people for IV/IO access + labs/cultures, a dedicated person to PUSH weight-based boluses and keep a timer, a medication/antibiotic nurse, a recorder, and a family liaison), communicating with SBAR, and delegating appropriately (the UAP can obtain vitals, bring the sepsis cart/IO kit, and serve as a runner; the RN retains the initial assessment, fluid-titration decisions, vasoactive management, and overall leadership). This is DISTINCT from the adult Surviving Sepsis bundle/anastomotic-leak septic shock case ([[case-091]]), adult urosepsis septic shock ([[case-033]]), the adult frail-elder rapid-response early-warning case ([[case-150]]), and the pediatric epiglottitis airway-team leadership case ([[case-111]]) — here the focus is pediatric shock physiology and the first-hour sepsis bundle led at the bedside. Step-6 evaluates whether each finding/response reflects the child IMPROVING, WORSENING, or remaining UNCHANGED.

This morning she became increasingly fussy then progressively sleepy, with rising fever, fast hard breathing, fewer wet diapers, and cool mottled legs — a deterioration over a few hours that the nurse recognizes as evolving septic shock despite a still-'normal' blood pressure.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + WHY pediatric shock is recognized differently (hypotension is LATE)
labs.v: 3 y/o girl (~14 kg), hospital day 2 for pyelonephritis, deteriorating with HR 184, RR 50, T 39.4, capillary refill 4–5 sec, cool mottled extremities, weak pulses, decreased urine output, and altered mental status — yet SBP still ~88–90. KEY PRINCIPLE: children COMPENSATE with tachycardia + vasoconstriction and maintain blood pressure until late, so HYPOTENSION is a LATE, near-arrest sign — do NOT wait for it. Pediatric hypotension threshold = SBP < 70 + (2 × age in years) = < 76 mmHg for a 3-year-old; her BP is above that = COMPENSATED shock. Recognize the TREND (persistent tachycardia out of proportion, tachypnea, fever/hypothermia, altered mental status/poor feeding, prolonged or flash capillary refill, mottling, decreased urine output) and ACT EARLY. Distinct from adult sepsis bundles ([[case-091]], [[case-033]]), adult RRT early-warning ([[case-150]]), and pediatric epiglottitis airway leadership ([[case-111]]).
labs.r: Kids COMPENSATE (tachycardia + vasoconstriction) and keep BP normal until LATE → hypotension = near-arrest, not the trigger. Peds hypotension = SBP < 70 + 2×age (< 76 for a 3yo). Recognize the TREND early: persistent tachycardia, tachypnea, fever/hypothermia, altered mental status/poor feeding, prolonged/flash cap refill, mottling, low urine output. ACT before the pressure falls.

labs.n: COLD vs WARM septic shock + the first-hour PEDIATRIC bundle
labs.v: COLD shock (most common in children) = low cardiac output + HIGH systemic vascular resistance: cool/mottled extremities, capillary refill > 2–3 sec, weak/thready pulses, narrow pulse pressure → vasoactive of choice is EPINEPHRINE. WARM shock = vasodilation: FLASH capillary refill, bounding pulses, warm extremities, wide pulse pressure → NOREPINEPHRINE. PEDIATRIC SURVIVING SEPSIS first-hour bundle: (1) recognize + activate the sepsis pathway/RRT; (2) high-flow OXYGEN; (3) rapid IV access — place an INTRAOSSEOUS (IO) line within minutes if peripheral access fails; (4) draw BLOOD CULTURE + point-of-care GLUCOSE + LACTATE; (5) BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS within 1 hour (do NOT delay antibiotics for cultures if access is hard); (6) isotonic fluid BOLUS 20 mL/kg PUSHED by syringe or pressure bag (gravity is too slow in a small child), REASSESS after EACH bolus for response AND fluid overload (new crackles, hepatomegaly, increased work of breathing), titrating toward 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour as tolerated; (7) CORRECT HYPOGLYCEMIA and HYPOCALCEMIA; (8) for FLUID-REFRACTORY shock start a vasoactive (epinephrine/norepinephrine) via peripheral/IO and transfer to PICU.
labs.r: COLD shock (common in kids): cold/mottled, slow cap refill, weak pulses, narrow pulse pressure → EPINEPHRINE. WARM shock: flash refill, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure → NOREPINEPHRINE. First-hour bundle: activate pathway/RRT → high-flow O2 → IV/IO access (IO fast if needed) → blood culture + POC glucose + lactate → ANTIBIOTICS within 1 hr (don't delay for cultures) → 20 mL/kg PUSH boluses, REASSESS each for response + overload (crackles/hepatomegaly) toward 40–60 mL/kg → fix glucose/calcium → vasoactive + PICU for fluid-refractory shock.

labs.n: Weight-based PUSH fluids, glucose/calcium, and avoiding fluid overload
labs.v: Fluids in pediatric shock are WEIGHT-BASED and given RAPIDLY: 20 mL/kg per bolus (≈280 mL for this 14-kg child) PUSHED with a syringe or a pressure bag because a free-flowing maintenance drip is far too slow to reverse shock. After EVERY bolus, REASSESS perfusion (HR, capillary refill, mental status, urine output) AND screen for FLUID OVERLOAD — new pulmonary crackles, HEPATOMEGALY (a sensitive pediatric sign), and increased work of breathing — and STOP/slow fluids and move to vasoactives if overload appears or shock is fluid-refractory after ~40–60 mL/kg. Children have limited glycogen stores and are prone to HYPOGLYCEMIA, and ionized HYPOCALCEMIA also depresses cardiac function — both are checked early and corrected (dextrose for hypoglycemia, calcium for documented hypocalcemia). Antibiotics should not be delayed by access problems; if a peripheral line cannot be obtained quickly, use the IO route for fluids, antibiotics, and even vasoactive infusions.
labs.r: Peds fluids = 20 mL/kg PUSHED (syringe/pressure bag; drip is too slow); REASSESS after each bolus for response AND overload (crackles, HEPATOMEGALY, ↑WOB); titrate to ~40–60 mL/kg then vasoactive if refractory. CHECK + correct GLUCOSE (kids hypoglycemia-prone) and ionized CALCIUM (both depress cardiac function). Don't let access delay antibiotics — use IO for fluids/abx/pressors.

labs.n: LEADERSHIP, escalation, and DELEGATION at the bedside + PERTINENT NEGATIVES
labs.v: The nurse RECOGNIZES the deterioration and ESCALATES without delay — activating the rapid response/sepsis pathway rather than waiting or managing alone — then ASSEMBLES and LEADS the bedside team until the provider arrives. CLOSED-LOOP role assignment: airway/oxygen; TWO people for IV/IO access plus labs/cultures; a dedicated person to PUSH the weight-based boluses and keep a timer; a medication/antibiotic nurse; a RECORDER documenting times (recognition, antibiotic, each bolus); and a FAMILY LIAISON to support the mother. Communicate with SBAR and use closed-loop, read-back communication. DELEGATION within scope: the UAP can take/repeat vital signs, bring the sepsis cart/IO kit and warmed fluids, and act as a runner; the RN RETAINS the initial and ongoing assessment, fluid-titration and vasoactive decisions, and overall leadership (these are NOT delegated). PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT dismiss compensated shock because the BP was 'normal'; did NOT wait for hypotension to escalate; did NOT give slow maintenance fluids instead of rapid pushes; did NOT delay antibiotics for culture/IV access; did NOT keep bolusing without reassessing for overload; and did NOT attempt to manage the crisis single-handedly without activating the team.
labs.r: LEADERSHIP: recognize + ESCALATE early (activate RRT/sepsis pathway, don't go it alone), assemble + lead the team, CLOSED-LOOP roles (airway/O2, 2× IV-IO + labs, dedicated bolus-pusher + timer, antibiotic nurse, recorder, family liaison), SBAR + read-back. DELEGATE to UAP: vitals, fetch sepsis cart/IO kit/fluids, runner — NOT assessment/titration/leadership. NEGATIVES: don't be reassured by 'normal' BP, don't wait for hypotension, don't run slow maintenance fluids, don't delay antibiotics, don't over-bolus without reassessing, don't manage alone.
