nursesNote: 1000 — Pediatrics, hospital day 2 for pyelonephritis. 3 y/o girl (~14 kg) deteriorated over a few hours: HR 184, RR 50, T 39.4, SpO2 93% RA, capillary refill 4–5 sec with cool MOTTLED legs and weak peripheral pulses, difficult to rouse, fewer wet diapers — COMPENSATED (cold) septic shock. BP 90/54 is still above the < 76 mmHg hypotension threshold for age, so I am NOT reassured by a 'normal' pressure — hypotension would be a late, pre-arrest sign. Activated the rapid response/sepsis pathway immediately and led the bedside team until the provider arrived: high-flow O2 applied; after a failed peripheral attempt placed an IO line within minutes; drew blood culture + POC glucose (52 = low) + lactate (4.2 = high) + ionized calcium (0.95 = low) + VBG (pH 7.28); broad-spectrum antibiotics obtained and given within the first hour; began 20 mL/kg (~280 mL) isotonic boluses PUSHED by syringe, reassessing after EACH for response and for overload (lungs clear, no hepatomegaly, no increased WOB). Corrected hypoglycemia with weight-based dextrose; calcium replacement per orders. Assigned closed-loop roles (airway/O2, two for IO + labs, a bolus-pusher with a timer, antibiotic nurse, recorder, family liaison for mom) and used SBAR with read-back. Delegated to UAP: repeat vitals, bring the sepsis cart/IO kit and warmed fluids, runner. After ~60 mL/kg she remained tachycardic with borderline perfusion = fluid-refractory → peripheral/IO EPINEPHRINE infusion started for cold shock; PICU accepting with SBAR handoff (times of recognition, antibiotic, each bolus, labs). Did NOT dismiss compensated shock for a normal BP, did NOT wait for hypotension, did NOT give slow maintenance fluids, did NOT delay antibiotics for cultures/access, did NOT over-bolus without reassessing, did NOT manage alone. Mother at bedside and updated.
providerOrders: RECOGNIZE + ESCALATE: activate the pediatric rapid response/sepsis pathway for compensated septic shock; do NOT wait for hypotension (a late sign in children); nurse to lead the bedside team and provide SBAR until the provider arrives
OXYGEN: apply high-flow oxygen and continuous pulse oximetry; place on cardiorespiratory monitor
ACCESS: obtain IV access immediately; if not achieved within minutes, place an INTRAOSSEOUS (IO) line — use it for fluids, antibiotics, and vasoactive infusions as needed
LABS/CULTURES: draw BLOOD CULTURE and point-of-care GLUCOSE, LACTATE, ionized CALCIUM, and a venous blood gas/CBC; recheck lactate to gauge resuscitation
ANTIBIOTICS: administer weight-based BROAD-SPECTRUM antibiotics within the FIRST HOUR; do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for cultures or difficult access

FLUIDS: give isotonic crystalloid 20 mL/kg (~280 mL for 14 kg) as a RAPID PUSH (syringe or pressure bag); REASSESS perfusion AND for fluid overload (new crackles, hepatomegaly, increased work of breathing) after EACH bolus; titrate toward 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour as tolerated
GLUCOSE/CALCIUM: correct hypoglycemia with weight-based dextrose and replace ionized calcium per protocol

FLUID-REFRACTORY SHOCK: if shock persists after adequate fluids, start a vasoactive infusion — EPINEPHRINE for cold shock (cool/mottled, slow capillary refill, weak pulses) or NOREPINEPHRINE for warm shock (flash refill, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure) — peripheral/IO acceptable until central access; transfer to PICU

TEAM/DELEGATION: assign closed-loop roles (airway/oxygen, IV-IO + labs, dedicated bolus administration with a timer, medications/antibiotics, recorder, family liaison); delegate vital-sign monitoring, equipment retrieval, and runner tasks to the UAP; RN retains assessment, titration, and leadership
FAMILY + DOCUMENTATION: keep the mother informed and supported; document times of recognition, antibiotic administration, each fluid bolus, and reassessments; SBAR handoff to PICU

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What signals shock in this child?
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically significant cues.

opts.text: Persistent tachycardia (HR 184) and tachypnea (RR 50) out of proportion, with a rising fever
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — sustained tachycardia/tachypnea are early compensatory signs of pediatric shock and should not be dismissed as fever alone.

opts.text: Capillary refill of 4–5 seconds with cool, mottled extremities and weak peripheral pulses
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — delayed refill, mottling, and weak pulses indicate poor perfusion and the cold-shock pattern common in children.

opts.text: Altered mental status — she is now difficult to rouse
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a change in mental status reflects cerebral hypoperfusion and is an ominous sign of worsening shock.

opts.text: Decreased urine output (fewer wet diapers)
opts.rat: RELEVANT — reduced urine output signals end-organ hypoperfusion in shock.

opts.text: A known infectious source (pyelonephritis) with a rising lactate and a low glucose
opts.rat: RELEVANT — an identified source plus elevated lactate and hypoglycemia support evolving septic shock requiring the sepsis bundle.

opts.text: Because her systolic blood pressure is still ~90, she is not in shock and can be reassessed in a couple of hours
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Children maintain BP until late — a 'normal' pressure does NOT exclude shock; hypotension is a late, near-arrest sign.

opts.text: The findings are expected on day 2 of antibiotics and require no escalation
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Worsening perfusion and mental status on therapy signal deterioration and demand immediate escalation, not watchful waiting.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: This is COMPENSATED septic shock — perfusion is failing while blood pressure is maintained — so it must be treated now, before hypotension develops
opts.rat: CORRECT — recognizing compensated shock and acting early is the central pediatric principle.

opts.text: Cool, mottled extremities with delayed capillary refill and weak pulses indicate COLD shock (low output, high SVR), for which epinephrine is the preferred vasoactive
opts.rat: CORRECT — the cold-shock pattern is most common in children and guides epinephrine selection if fluid-refractory.

opts.text: She needs rapid weight-based fluid boluses and broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour, with blood cultures drawn first if it does not delay antibiotics
opts.rat: CORRECT — the first-hour bundle: cultures, early antibiotics, and rapid fluid resuscitation.

opts.text: Hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia must be checked and corrected because they worsen cardiac function in pediatric shock
opts.rat: CORRECT — children are prone to both, and each depresses contractility.

opts.text: Early escalation by activating the rapid response/sepsis pathway and leading a coordinated team is required — this is not a one-person task
opts.rat: CORRECT — timely escalation and team leadership are essential to deliver the bundle quickly.

opts.text: Slow maintenance-rate IV fluids are sufficient and safer than rapid boluses in a child this size
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Shock requires rapid PUSH boluses (syringe/pressure bag); maintenance drips are far too slow to restore perfusion.

opts.text: Antibiotics should be withheld until the blood culture results return
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are given within the first hour; do not wait for culture results.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these actions from #1 (HIGHEST priority) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Recognize compensated septic shock and activate the rapid response/sepsis pathway, assembling and leading the team
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. Early recognition and escalation mobilize the resources and people needed to deliver the bundle on time.

opts.text: Establish access (IV, or IO within minutes if peripheral fails), apply high-flow oxygen, and draw cultures/glucose/lactate
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Access and oxygen enable resuscitation; obtaining cultures/labs sets up antibiotics and monitoring.

opts.text: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour and begin 20 mL/kg push fluid boluses, reassessing after each
opts.rat: #3 — The core therapeutic interventions of the first-hour bundle.

opts.text: Correct hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia and continue reassessing perfusion and for fluid overload
opts.rat: #4 — Supports cardiac function and prevents over-resuscitation while therapy proceeds.

opts.text: For fluid-refractory shock, start epinephrine and arrange PICU transfer with SBAR handoff
opts.rat: #5 — Escalation for shock not reversed by fluids, with safe transfer to a higher level of care.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Activate the rapid response/sepsis pathway now and lead the bedside team with closed-loop role assignment and SBAR
opts.rat: Timely escalation and coordinated leadership deliver the bundle quickly and safely.

opts.text: Place an IO line within minutes if a peripheral IV cannot be obtained, and use it for fluids, antibiotics, and pressors
opts.rat: IO access prevents delays in resuscitation when peripheral access fails.

opts.text: Draw a blood culture and give broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour without letting access difficulties delay them
opts.rat: Early antibiotics improve outcomes; cultures first only if they do not delay the antibiotic.

opts.text: Give 20 mL/kg isotonic boluses by rapid push, reassessing after each for perfusion response and for fluid overload (crackles, hepatomegaly)
opts.rat: Weight-based rapid boluses with reassessment are the cornerstone of pediatric shock resuscitation.

opts.text: Check and correct hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia
opts.rat: Both impair myocardial function and are common in pediatric sepsis.

opts.text: Delegate repeat vital signs, retrieval of the sepsis cart/IO kit, and runner tasks to the UAP
opts.rat: Appropriate delegation of non-assessment tasks frees the RN to lead and perform skilled interventions.

opts.text: Hold antibiotics and fluids until the blood pressure actually drops below normal
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — waiting for hypotension (a late sign) delays life-saving treatment in compensated shock.

opts.text: Run fluids at a slow maintenance rate by gravity instead of rapid push boluses
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — maintenance drips are too slow to reverse shock; use syringe/pressure-bag push boluses.

opts.text: Have the nurse manage the entire resuscitation alone rather than activating the team
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — a coordinated team is required to deliver the time-sensitive bundle; failure to escalate risks the child.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Recognize the deterioration, activate the rapid response/sepsis pathway, and begin leading the bedside team
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Escalation brings the people and resources needed and starts the clock on the bundle.

opts.text: Apply high-flow oxygen, obtain IV/IO access, and draw blood culture, glucose, and lactate
opts.rat: #2 — Second. Oxygen and access enable everything that follows and set up antibiotics/monitoring.

opts.text: Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour and start 20 mL/kg push boluses, reassessing after each
opts.rat: #3 — Third. The central therapies — early antibiotics and rapid, reassessed fluid resuscitation.

opts.text: Correct hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia and continue reassessing perfusion and for fluid overload
opts.rat: #4 — Fourth. Optimizes cardiac function and guards against over-resuscitation.

opts.text: Start epinephrine for fluid-refractory shock and hand off to the PICU with SBAR
opts.rat: #5 — Closing. Escalates therapy for persistent shock and transfers safely to higher-level care.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as the child IMPROVING, WORSENING, or UNCHANGED.

opts.text: After two fluid boluses and antibiotics, capillary refill improves to ~3 seconds and she becomes more responsive
opts.rat: Better perfusion and mental status indicate the resuscitation is reversing shock.

opts.text: In the PICU on titrated epinephrine her heart rate falls toward 140, urine output returns, and lactate clears
opts.rat: Falling heart rate, restored urine output, and lactate clearance are reassuring markers of resolving shock.

opts.text: Her corrected glucose is now 92 mg/dL after weight-based dextrose
opts.rat: Correcting hypoglycemia removes a factor that was depressing cardiac function.

opts.text: During the third bolus she develops new crackles, a palpable enlarging liver, and increased work of breathing
opts.rat: ⚠️ Signs of FLUID OVERLOAD — slow/stop the bolus, reassess, and move toward vasoactive support.

opts.text: Her systolic blood pressure now drops to 68 mmHg with a thready pulse
opts.rat: ⚠️ Hypotension is a late, near-arrest sign — decompensated shock requiring immediate escalation of vasoactive support and PICU-level care.

opts.text: She becomes unresponsive with gasping respirations
opts.rat: ⚠️ Impending cardiopulmonary arrest — call for help/initiate PALS resuscitation immediately.

opts.text: Immediately after the first bolus her heart rate and capillary refill are essentially the same as before
opts.rat: A single bolus may not yet change perfusion — continue the bundle and reassess after the next bolus.

opts.text: Her temperature remains 39.4°C shortly after antibiotics are started
opts.rat: Fever does not resolve immediately after the first antibiotic dose; perfusion markers, not temperature, gauge early response.

opts.text: After full resuscitation and PICU transfer she is alert with warm extremities and capillary refill < 2 seconds
opts.rat: Normalized perfusion and mental status confirm the shock has been effectively treated.

title: LACTATIONAL MASTITIS and Continued BREASTFEEDING SUPPORT in a 29-Year-Old First-Time Mother 16 Days Postpartum Who Presents with a Unilateral, Wedge-Shaped, Red, Warm, Painful Area of the Right Breast Plus Fever 38.9°C, Chills, and Flu-Like Body Aches After Milk Stasis (a Missed Overnight Feeding + a Tight Bra) and a Cracked Nipple: Recognizing INFECTIOUS Mastitis vs ENGORGEMENT vs a PLUGGED DUCT vs a BREAST ABSCESS vs Inflammatory Breast Cancer, the CORNERSTONE of EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL (CONTINUE Breastfeeding — the Milk Is SAFE for the Baby — Nurse Frequently q2–3h, Warm Compress/Shower BEFORE Feeds to Aid Letdown and COLD Compress AFTER for Pain), NSAIDs + Acetaminophen + Rest + Hydration, an S. AUREUS-Directed Antibiotic (Dicloxacillin/Cephalexin × 10–14 Days — Complete the FULL Course; Clindamycin/TMP-SMX if MRSA or Penicillin-Allergic), CORRECTING the Underlying Cause (Latch/Positioning, Avoiding Tight Bras and Skipped Feeds), Recognizing the ABSCESS Complication (Fluctuant Mass + Persistent Fever Despite 48–72h of Antibiotics → Ultrasound + Drainage), and NON-JUDGMENTAL Emotional Support with a LACTATION-CONSULTANT Referral — Because Telling Her to STOP Breastfeeding or WEAN Worsens Stasis and Drives Abscess Formation
subtitle: LACTATIONAL MASTITIS is an inflammation, usually with infection, of the breast that classically appears in the 2nd–3rd week postpartum when MILK STASIS (a missed/skipped feeding, oversupply, a tight bra, abrupt weaning, or poor latch) combines with bacterial entry through a CRACKED NIPPLE — Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism. This case follows L. Okonkwo, a 29-year-old G1P1 who is 16 days postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding, presenting with one day of FEVER (38.9°C), CHILLS, and FLU-LIKE MYALGIAS/MALAISE plus a UNILATERAL, localized, WEDGE-SHAPED area of the right breast that is RED, WARM, FIRM, and TENDER — after her baby slept through an overnight feeding and she wore a too-tight bra, on a background of a cracked right nipple. The nurse must RECOGNIZE the pattern and DISTINGUISH it from look-alikes: ENGORGEMENT is bilateral, generalized, and early (no/low-grade fever); a PLUGGED DUCT is a localized lump WITHOUT systemic symptoms; MASTITIS is localized PLUS systemic fever/flu-like illness; a BREAST ABSCESS is a fluctuant, well-defined tender mass with persistent fever despite 48–72h of antibiotics (needs ultrasound + drainage); and INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER (rare, with peau d'orange and no response to antibiotics) is considered only if it does not resolve. The CORNERSTONE of treatment is EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL — the mother should CONTINUE BREASTFEEDING because the milk is SAFE for the baby; she nurses FREQUENTLY (every 2–3 hours), often STARTING on the affected side, applies a WARM compress or takes a warm shower BEFORE feeds to aid letdown, and uses a COLD compress AFTER feeds for pain/swelling; she pumps only if the baby cannot empty the breast. Comfort and anti-inflammatory measures include IBUPROFEN (compatible with breastfeeding) and acetaminophen, plus REST and HYDRATION. Because she is systemically ill, an S. AUREUS-directed ANTIBIOTIC is started — DICLOXACILLIN or CEPHALEXIN for 10–14 days (CLINDAMYCIN or TMP-SMX if MRSA is suspected or she is penicillin-allergic; avoid TMP-SMX with a jaundiced/ill/G6PD-deficient or <1-month-old infant) — and she is taught to COMPLETE THE FULL COURSE even once she feels better. The UNDERLYING CAUSE is corrected: a lactation consultant evaluates LATCH and POSITIONING, treats the nipple trauma, and counsels against tight bras, skipped feeds, and abrupt weaning. Critically, telling a mother to STOP breastfeeding or to WEAN is WRONG — it worsens stasis and promotes abscess formation — and she needs NON-JUDGMENTAL emotional support and reassurance that breastfeeding can and should continue. Step-6 evaluates whether each later finding reflects the mother IMPROVING, WORSENING (e.g., a fluctuant abscess or sepsis), or remaining UNCHANGED.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + WHY mastitis happens (milk stasis + a portal of entry)
labs.v: 29 y/o, 16 days postpartum, exclusively breastfeeding, with a unilateral WEDGE-SHAPED red/warm/firm/tender right breast PLUS fever 38.9°C, chills, and flu-like myalgias after a MISSED overnight feeding and a tight bra, on a background of a CRACKED nipple. KEY PRINCIPLE: lactational mastitis = MILK STASIS (skipped/missed feeds, oversupply, tight bra/underwire, abrupt weaning, poor latch, fatigue) + bacterial entry through a CRACKED/fissured nipple. Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is the most common organism. It typically appears in the 2nd–3rd postpartum week. Recognize it as UNILATERAL + LOCALIZED + SYSTEMIC (fever/flu-like) — distinct from bilateral engorgement and from a plugged duct without systemic symptoms.
labs.r: Mastitis = MILK STASIS (missed feeds, oversupply, tight bra, abrupt weaning, poor latch) + bacteria entering via a CRACKED nipple; most common organism S. aureus; classic in postpartum week 2–3; pattern is UNILATERAL + LOCALIZED wedge of redness/warmth/tenderness PLUS systemic fever/chills/body aches.

labs.n: DISTINGUISHING engorgement vs plugged duct vs mastitis vs abscess vs inflammatory cancer
labs.v: ENGORGEMENT: BILATERAL, generalized firmness/swelling, early (days 2–5), NO or low-grade fever — managed with frequent feeding, comfort measures, and reverse-pressure softening. PLUGGED (BLOCKED) DUCT: a LOCALIZED tender lump, often with a white bleb on the nipple, NO systemic symptoms or only low-grade — relieved by frequent feeding, warmth, massage toward the nipple, and varied positions. MASTITIS: a LOCALIZED wedge of redness/warmth/tenderness PLUS SYSTEMIC fever ≥38.5°C, chills, and flu-like aches — the case here. BREAST ABSCESS: a FLUCTUANT, well-defined, exquisitely tender mass with PERSISTENT fever despite 48–72h of appropriate antibiotics — needs ULTRASOUND and DRAINAGE (needle aspiration or incision & drainage); breastfeeding can usually continue. INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER: rare, with peau d'orange, skin thickening/dimpling, and NO response to antibiotics — consider/refer if the 'mastitis' does not resolve.
labs.r: ENGORGEMENT = bilateral/generalized, early, little/no fever. PLUGGED DUCT = localized lump, NO systemic symptoms. MASTITIS = localized redness + SYSTEMIC fever/flu-like. ABSCESS = fluctuant mass + persistent fever despite 48–72h antibiotics → US + drainage. INFLAMMATORY CANCER = peau d'orange, no antibiotic response → refer if not resolving.

labs.n: CORNERSTONE — EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL: KEEP breastfeeding (the milk is SAFE)
labs.v: The single most important treatment is EFFECTIVE, FREQUENT MILK REMOVAL to relieve stasis. The mother should CONTINUE BREASTFEEDING — the milk is SAFE for the baby and stopping makes mastitis WORSE and promotes abscess formation. Nurse FREQUENTLY (every 2–3 hours and on demand), often STARTING on the affected breast (or alternating to ensure it drains), ensure the breast is well emptied, and pump/hand-express only if the infant cannot empty it. Apply a WARM compress or take a warm shower BEFORE feeding to aid letdown and flow, gently massage the firm area toward the nipple during the feed, vary positions to drain all ducts, and use a COLD compress AFTER feeding to reduce pain and swelling. AVOID tight bras/underwires and abrupt weaning. This is teaching that an RN or LVN can reinforce in stable postpartum care.
labs.r: EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL is the cornerstone: CONTINUE breastfeeding (milk is SAFE; stopping worsens it/causes abscess), nurse q2–3h often starting on the affected side, fully empty the breast (pump only if baby can't), WARM compress/shower BEFORE to aid letdown + gentle massage toward the nipple + varied positions, COLD compress AFTER for pain; avoid tight bras and abrupt weaning.

labs.n: ANTIBIOTICS, analgesia, supportive care, and CORRECTING the cause
labs.v: Because she is SYSTEMICALLY ill (fever, chills, myalgias) and has localized findings, start an S. AUREUS-directed oral antibiotic: DICLOXACILLIN or CEPHALEXIN for 10–14 days; if MRSA is suspected or she is penicillin-allergic, use CLINDAMYCIN or TMP-SMX (AVOID TMP-SMX if the infant is <1 month old, jaundiced/ill, or G6PD-deficient). Teach her to COMPLETE THE FULL COURSE even once she feels better. For pain/inflammation/fever use IBUPROFEN (an NSAID, compatible with breastfeeding and helpful for inflammation) and/or ACETAMINOPHEN. Support with REST, increased FLUIDS, and help at home. CORRECT THE UNDERLYING CAUSE with a LACTATION CONSULTANT: fix LATCH and POSITIONING, treat nipple trauma, and address oversupply, tight bras, and skipped feeds. Reassess in 24–48h; if no improvement or a fluctuant mass develops, evaluate for an ABSCESS (ultrasound + drainage).
labs.r: Systemic illness → S. aureus-directed antibiotic: DICLOXACILLIN or CEPHALEXIN ×10–14d (CLINDAMYCIN/TMP-SMX if MRSA or PCN-allergic; avoid TMP-SMX with a young/jaundiced/G6PD infant) — COMPLETE the full course. IBUPROFEN ± acetaminophen for pain/fever; REST + fluids. Fix the CAUSE via lactation consult (latch, positioning, nipple care). Reassess 24–48h; no improvement/fluctuant mass → abscess workup (US + drainage).

labs.n: EMOTIONAL SUPPORT, RED FLAGS, and PERTINENT NEGATIVES (what NOT to do)
labs.v: Provide NON-JUDGMENTAL emotional support — many mothers feel guilt or consider quitting; reassure her that mastitis is common, treatable, and that breastfeeding can and SHOULD continue. Teach RED FLAGS to report: worsening or spreading redness, a fluctuant lump, no improvement after 24–48h of antibiotics, high persistent fever, or the baby refusing to feed. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice — these are WRONG): do NOT tell her to STOP breastfeeding or WEAN (worsens stasis → abscess); do NOT 'pump and dump' or discard the milk as unsafe; do NOT advise tight binding of the breasts to 'dry up' the milk; do NOT apply only cold and stop emptying the breast; do NOT withhold antibiotics in a systemically ill mother or tell her to stop them once she feels better; and do NOT skip correcting the latch/positioning that caused the nipple trauma.
labs.r: Give NON-JUDGMENTAL support; reassure breastfeeding can/should continue. RED FLAGS: spreading redness, fluctuant lump, no improvement in 24–48h, persistent high fever, baby not feeding. NEGATIVES (WRONG): don't tell her to stop/wean, don't call the milk unsafe or pump-and-dump, don't tightly bind to dry up milk, don't stop emptying the breast, don't withhold/prematurely stop antibiotics, don't ignore the latch.

labs.v: 13.2 x10^9/L with mild neutrophilia (modest leukocytosis consistent with a localized bacterial infection; mastitis is a clinical diagnosis — labs are not required in a typical outpatient case)
38.9°C (102.0°F) — meets the systemic-illness threshold (≥38.5°C) that, with localized breast findings, defines mastitis rather than a simple plugged duct
Mildly elevated (supports an inflammatory/infectious process; not routinely needed but can be drawn if the diagnosis is unclear)
11.6 g/dL (mild postpartum anemia; pertinent to fatigue but not the cause of mastitis)

labs.n: Breast-milk / abscess culture (only if not responding or recurrent)
labs.v: Not obtained at this routine visit; reserved for severe, hospital-acquired, recurrent, or non-responding cases, or to identify MRSA and guide antibiotics — would be sent with any abscess drainage (pending if/when collected)

nursesNote: Clinic — 16 days postpartum, G1P1, exclusively breastfeeding. Presents with 1 day of fever 38.9°C, chills, and flu-like body aches plus a UNILATERAL wedge-shaped RED/WARM/FIRM/TENDER area of the RIGHT upper-outer breast; cracked right nipple; left breast soft. History of a MISSED overnight feeding and a tight underwire bra (milk stasis) with a shallow latch — classic LACTATIONAL MASTITIS, not bilateral engorgement and not a symptom-free plugged duct. On exam NO fluctuant mass and no peau d'orange (no abscess/inflammatory-cancer features today). Taught the cornerstone — EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL: CONTINUE breastfeeding because the milk is SAFE; nurse every 2–3 hours, often starting on the affected side and fully emptying the breast; WARM compress/shower BEFORE feeds to aid letdown with gentle massage toward the nipple and varied positions; COLD compress AFTER feeds for pain; avoid tight bras and abrupt weaning. Reinforced IBUPROFEN (compatible with breastfeeding) ± acetaminophen, REST, and increased fluids. Provider started dicloxacillin for 10–14 days (cephalexin alternative; clindamycin/TMP-SMX if MRSA or penicillin-allergic, avoiding TMP-SMX with a young/jaundiced/G6PD infant) — taught to COMPLETE the full course even when feeling better. Lactation consultant engaged to correct latch/positioning and treat the nipple trauma. Provided non-judgmental support and reassurance that breastfeeding should continue, and taught RED FLAGS to report: spreading redness, a fluctuant lump, no improvement in 24–48h, persistent high fever, or the baby refusing to feed. Did NOT advise stopping/weaning, did NOT call the milk unsafe or recommend pump-and-dump, did NOT advise tight binding, and did NOT stop emptying the breast. Will reassess in 24–48h; a fluctuant mass with persistent fever would prompt ultrasound + drainage for a breast abscess.
providerOrders: DIAGNOSIS: lactational mastitis of the right breast — clinical diagnosis; routine labs/imaging not required in an uncomplicated outpatient case

CONTINUE BREASTFEEDING: the milk is safe for the infant; nurse frequently (every 2–3 hours), often starting on the affected side, and ensure the breast is well emptied (pump/hand-express only if the infant cannot empty it)

COMFORT/MILK FLOW: warm compress or warm shower BEFORE feeds to aid letdown with gentle massage toward the nipple and varied feeding positions; COLD compress AFTER feeds for pain and swelling; avoid tight bras/underwires and abrupt weaning

ANTIBIOTIC: dicloxacillin or cephalexin PO for 10–14 days (S. aureus coverage); clindamycin or TMP-SMX if MRSA suspected or penicillin-allergic — avoid TMP-SMX if the infant is <1 month old, jaundiced/ill, or G6PD-deficient; complete the FULL course
ANALGESIA/ANTIPYRETIC: ibuprofen (NSAID, breastfeeding-compatible, anti-inflammatory) and/or acetaminophen for pain and fever
SUPPORTIVE CARE: rest, increased oral fluids, and help with home/infant care
LACTATION CONSULT: evaluate and correct latch and positioning, treat nipple trauma, and counsel on preventing milk stasis (avoid skipped feeds, tight bras, oversupply, abrupt weaning)

FOLLOW-UP/ESCALATION: reassess in 24–48 hours; if no improvement, worsening/spreading erythema, or a fluctuant mass with persistent fever after 48–72h of antibiotics, obtain a BREAST ULTRASOUND and arrange DRAINAGE (needle aspiration or incision & drainage) with culture

EDUCATION/RED FLAGS: report spreading redness, a fluctuant lump, no improvement after 24–48h, persistent high fever, or the baby refusing to feed; provide non-judgmental reassurance that breastfeeding can and should continue

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically significant cues.

opts.text: A unilateral, wedge-shaped, RED, WARM, FIRM, TENDER area of the right breast
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a localized, unilateral wedge of inflammation is the hallmark of mastitis (versus bilateral, generalized engorgement).

opts.text: Fever 38.9°C with chills and flu-like body aches (malaise/myalgias)
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — systemic flu-like symptoms with fever ≥38.5°C distinguish mastitis from a symptom-free plugged duct.

opts.text: A cracked right nipple from a shallow latch
opts.rat: RELEVANT — nipple fissures are the portal of entry for S. aureus and a correctable cause.

opts.text: A missed overnight feeding and a tight underwire bra (milk stasis)
opts.rat: RELEVANT — milk stasis from skipped feeds and external compression is the key precipitant of mastitis.

opts.text: Onset at 16 days postpartum (the typical 2nd–3rd week window)
opts.rat: RELEVANT — the timing fits the classic presentation of lactational mastitis.

opts.text: Both breasts are equally firm and swollen with no fever
opts.rat: ⚠️ This describes ENGORGEMENT, not mastitis — her left breast is soft and she has a unilateral, febrile, localized process.

opts.text: A fluctuant, well-defined mass with skin that has a peau d'orange (orange-peel) appearance
opts.rat: ⚠️ Not present today — a fluctuant mass suggests an abscess and peau d'orange suggests inflammatory cancer; her exam shows neither.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: This is lactational mastitis — milk stasis plus bacterial entry (usually S. aureus) through a cracked nipple, with systemic symptoms
opts.rat: CORRECT — the localized inflammation plus fever/flu-like illness and the stasis/nipple history define infectious mastitis.

opts.text: The cornerstone of treatment is EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL — she should continue breastfeeding because the milk is safe and stopping worsens it
opts.rat: CORRECT — relieving stasis with continued, frequent, effective emptying is the most important intervention.

opts.text: Because she is systemically ill, an S. aureus-directed antibiotic (e.g., dicloxacillin or cephalexin) is indicated for 10–14 days
opts.rat: CORRECT — systemic symptoms warrant antibiotics covering S. aureus, completed as a full course.

opts.text: Correcting the underlying cause (latch/positioning, avoiding tight bras and skipped feeds) helps treat and prevent recurrence
opts.rat: CORRECT — addressing nipple trauma and stasis with lactation support is essential to resolution and prevention.

opts.text: If a fluctuant mass and persistent fever develop despite 48–72h of antibiotics, a breast abscess is likely and needs ultrasound and drainage
opts.rat: CORRECT — failure to improve with a fluctuant mass signals abscess formation requiring drainage.

opts.text: She should stop breastfeeding and wean to let the breast 'rest' and heal
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Stopping or weaning increases milk stasis and promotes abscess formation — she must keep emptying the breast.

opts.text: The breast milk is unsafe for the infant during mastitis and should be pumped and discarded
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The milk is safe; continued breastfeeding is both safe and therapeutic.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these explanations from #1 (MOST likely/important now) to #5 (LEAST).

opts.text: Lactational (infectious) mastitis of the right breast
opts.rat: #1 — MOST likely: a unilateral localized wedge of inflammation PLUS fever and flu-like systemic symptoms is the defining picture.

opts.text: A plugged (blocked) milk duct
opts.rat: #2 — On the spectrum and often precedes mastitis, but a plugged duct lacks the systemic fever/flu-like illness she has.

opts.text: Breast engorgement
opts.rat: #3 — Less likely: engorgement is bilateral and generalized with little/no fever, whereas she has a unilateral febrile process.

opts.text: A breast abscess
opts.rat: #4 — A complication to watch for, but there is no fluctuant mass yet; it becomes likely only if she fails to improve.

opts.text: Inflammatory breast cancer
opts.rat: #5 — LEAST likely: rare, with peau d'orange and no antibiotic response — considered only if the 'mastitis' does not resolve.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Continue breastfeeding frequently (every 2–3 hours), often starting on the affected side, to fully empty the breast
opts.rat: Effective, frequent milk removal is the cornerstone of treatment and is safe for the infant.

opts.text: Apply a warm compress or take a warm shower before feeds, and a cold compress after feeds
opts.rat: Warmth before feeds aids letdown/flow; cold after feeds reduces pain and swelling.

opts.text: Take ibuprofen and/or acetaminophen for pain and fever
opts.rat: Both are compatible with breastfeeding; ibuprofen also helps the inflammation.

opts.text: Start an S. aureus-directed antibiotic (dicloxacillin or cephalexin) and teach her to complete the full course
opts.rat: Systemic illness warrants antibiotics; completing the course prevents relapse and resistance.

opts.text: Refer to a lactation consultant to correct latch/positioning and treat the nipple trauma, and rest/hydrate
opts.rat: Correcting the underlying cause and supporting recovery treat the current episode and prevent recurrence.

opts.text: Advise her to stop breastfeeding and wean to let the breast heal
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — stopping increases stasis and promotes abscess formation; she must keep emptying the breast.

opts.text: Tell her to pump and discard the milk because it is unsafe for the baby
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the milk is safe; direct breastfeeding is preferred and therapeutic.

opts.text: Apply a tight breast binder to suppress milk production
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — tight binding worsens stasis and pain and can precipitate an abscess.

opts.text: Reassure her the fever needs no treatment and she can stop antibiotics as soon as she feels better
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — she should complete the full antibiotic course; stopping early risks relapse and resistance.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess the breasts and vital signs and confirm the pattern of mastitis (unilateral localized inflammation + systemic fever), ruling out a fluctuant abscess
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. A focused assessment confirms the diagnosis and screens for an abscess that would change management.

opts.text: Teach and support continued frequent breastfeeding/effective milk removal with warm-before/cold-after compresses
opts.rat: #2 — The cornerstone intervention; relieving stasis is the priority therapeutic action.

opts.text: Administer/teach the prescribed S. aureus-directed antibiotic and ibuprofen/acetaminophen, emphasizing the full course
opts.rat: #3 — Treats the infection and symptoms in a systemically ill mother.

opts.text: Refer to lactation support to correct latch/positioning and treat the nipple trauma, and advise rest and hydration
opts.rat: #4 — Addresses the underlying cause to resolve this episode and prevent recurrence.

opts.text: Teach red flags and arrange 24–48h follow-up, with ultrasound/drainage if an abscess develops
opts.rat: #5 — Ensures escalation if she fails to improve or an abscess forms.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as the mother IMPROVING, WORSENING, or UNCHANGED.

opts.text: By day 2 her temperature is 37.6°C, the redness is smaller, and the body aches are resolving
opts.rat: Defervescence and shrinking erythema indicate the antibiotics plus effective milk removal are working.

opts.text: By day 4 she is afebrile, the breast is soft after feeds, and the nipple is healing with a corrected latch
opts.rat: Resolution of fever and inflammation with a healing nipple reflects successful treatment.

opts.text: She reports she is breastfeeding comfortably every 2–3 hours and emptying the breast well
opts.rat: Effective, frequent milk removal is relieving the stasis that drives mastitis.

opts.text: Despite 72 hours of antibiotics she has a persistent fever and a new fluctuant, well-defined, exquisitely tender mass
opts.rat: ⚠️ Signs of a BREAST ABSCESS — obtain an ultrasound and arrange drainage; antibiotics alone are insufficient.

opts.text: The redness is spreading rapidly with rigors, hypotension, and tachycardia
opts.rat: ⚠️ Signs of systemic deterioration/sepsis — escalate urgently for evaluation and possible IV antibiotics.

opts.text: She stopped breastfeeding on the affected side because it hurt, and the breast is now harder and more swollen
opts.rat: ⚠️ Stopping emptying increases stasis and worsens mastitis — resume frequent effective milk removal.

opts.text: A few hours after the first antibiotic dose her temperature is still 38.7°C
opts.rat: Fever does not break immediately; expect clinical improvement over 24–48 hours, so this is not yet a change.

opts.text: The localized tenderness is about the same on the evening of day 1
opts.rat: Early in treatment, stable findings are expected; continue therapy and reassess at 24–48 hours.

opts.text: At the 2-week follow-up the mastitis has resolved and breastfeeding is well established and comfortable
opts.rat: Full resolution with continued comfortable breastfeeding confirms effective treatment and prevention of recurrence.

title: TARDIVE DYSKINESIA Recognized at a Routine Community-Mental-Health Visit in a 63-Year-Old Woman with Long-Standing Schizophrenia on ~20 Years of a First-Generation Antipsychotic (Haloperidol) Plus Type 2 Diabetes — New, Persistent, INVOLUNTARY Orofacial-Buccolingual Movements (Lip Smacking, Puckering, Tongue Protrusion/Writhing, Facial Grimacing) and Choreoathetoid Finger Movements She Is Largely UNAWARE Of: DISTINGUISHING the Four Antipsychotic Movement Syndromes by TIMING (ACUTE DYSTONIA in Hours–Days, AKATHISIA in Days–Weeks, Drug-Induced PSEUDOPARKINSONISM in Weeks–Months, and TARDIVE DYSKINESIA After MONTHS–YEARS of Dopamine Blockade — Often PERSISTENT/Irreversible), QUANTIFYING with the AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) and Ruling Out Mimics, NOTIFYING Psychiatry to Re-Evaluate/Minimize or SWITCH the Antipsychotic (NEVER an Abrupt Stop — Withdrawal-Emergent Dyskinesia + Relapse) and Start an FDA-Approved VMAT2 INHIBITOR (VALBENAZINE or DEUTETRABENAZINE) with QTc/Somnolence/Mood Monitoring, the Classic Test Point that ANTICHOLINERGICS (Benztropine/Diphenhydramine) WORSEN TD (They Treat Dystonia/Pseudoparkinsonism, NOT TD), and Swallowing/Safety + Non-Judgmental Psychosocial Support for a Stigmatizing, Quality-of-Life-Limiting Condition
subtitle: TARDIVE DYSKINESIA (TD) is a LATE ('tardive' = delayed) movement disorder caused by MONTHS-TO-YEARS of dopamine D2-receptor blockade (chronic antipsychotics — especially FIRST-GENERATION agents like haloperidol, but also second-generation agents and dopamine-blocking antiemetics such as metoclopramide/prochlorperazine), thought to arise from D2-receptor up-regulation/supersensitivity; it is frequently PERSISTENT and may be IRREVERSIBLE, so early recognition matters. This case follows B. Aldridge, a 63-year-old woman with long-standing schizophrenia maintained on haloperidol for about 20 years (with type 2 diabetes — older age, female sex, diabetes, mood disorder, and prior extrapyramidal symptoms all raise TD risk), seen for a routine long-acting injection when the nurse notices NEW, repetitive, INVOLUNTARY OROFACIAL-BUCCOLINGUAL-MASTICATORY movements (lip smacking and puckering, tongue protrusion/writhing, chewing, facial grimacing) plus slow CHOREOATHETOID finger/hand movements — present at rest, worse with distraction, absent in sleep, and movements the patient is largely UNAWARE of. The nurse must DISTINGUISH the four antipsychotic-associated movement syndromes by their TIMING and features: ACUTE DYSTONIA (hours–days; sustained spasms — torticollis, oculogyric crisis, laryngospasm = airway emergency) responds to an ANTICHOLINERGIC (benztropine) or diphenhydramine; AKATHISIA (days–weeks; subjective inner restlessness/inability to sit still) responds to dose reduction, a beta-blocker (propranolol), or a benzodiazepine; drug-induced PSEUDOPARKINSONISM (weeks–months; bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, masked facies) responds to dose reduction/switch or an anticholinergic; and TARDIVE DYSKINESIA (months–years; the picture here) is treated very differently. The nurse QUANTIFIES the movements with the AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) — the standardized tool done at antipsychotic initiation and then periodically (more often with high-risk/first-generation agents) — and helps rule out mimics (Huntington disease, primary dystonias, stereotypies, ill-fitting dentures, metoclopramide exposure, withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia). MANAGEMENT: NOTIFY psychiatry to re-evaluate the ongoing need for and DOSE of the antipsychotic and consider SWITCHING to a lower-TD-risk agent — but NEVER abruptly STOP it (abrupt withdrawal can cause withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia and psychotic relapse; changes are tapered/adjusted by the prescriber) — and START an FDA-approved VMAT2 INHIBITOR (VALBENAZINE [Ingrezza] or DEUTETRABENAZINE [Austedo]), which reduce presynaptic dopamine release and are first-line for TD, monitoring for somnolence, QTc prolongation, parkinsonism, and mood/suicidality. A CLASSIC NCLEX TEST POINT: ANTICHOLINERGICS (benztropine, diphenhydramine, trihexyphenidyl) and simply INCREASING the antipsychotic do NOT help TD and can WORSEN or merely MASK it — anticholinergics are for acute dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism, not TD. The nurse also assesses SWALLOWING/aspiration and gait safety as movements can impair function, and provides NON-JUDGMENTAL psychosocial support for a stigmatizing, distressing, quality-of-life-limiting condition while reinforcing adherence and follow-up. Step-6 evaluates whether each later finding reflects the patient IMPROVING, WORSENING, or remaining UNCHANGED.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + WHY tardive dyskinesia happens (late, from chronic dopamine blockade)
labs.v: 63 y/o woman, ~20 years on haloperidol (a first-generation antipsychotic) plus type 2 diabetes, with NEW persistent INVOLUNTARY orofacial-buccolingual-masticatory movements (lip smacking/puckering, tongue protrusion/writhing, chewing, facial grimacing) and choreoathetoid finger movements — present at rest, worse with distraction, absent in sleep, and she is largely UNAWARE of them. KEY PRINCIPLE: TARDIVE DYSKINESIA is a LATE complication ('tardive' = delayed) of MONTHS-TO-YEARS of dopamine D2-receptor BLOCKADE, attributed to D2-receptor up-regulation/supersensitivity; it is often PERSISTENT and may be IRREVERSIBLE. RISK FACTORS: longer cumulative dose/DURATION of dopamine-blocking drugs (first-generation antipsychotics highest, but also second-generation agents and antiemetics like METOCLOPRAMIDE/prochlorperazine), OLDER age, FEMALE sex, DIABETES, mood disorder, and prior extrapyramidal symptoms.
labs.r: TD = LATE (months–years) involuntary movements from chronic D2 blockade → receptor supersensitivity; often persistent/irreversible. Classic = orofacial-buccolingual (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, grimacing) + choreoathetoid limbs. Risk: long duration of antipsychotics (first-gen highest; also metoclopramide), older age, female, diabetes, mood disorder, prior EPS.

labs.n: DISTINGUISHING the FOUR antipsychotic movement syndromes by TIMING
labs.v: ACUTE DYSTONIA: onset HOURS–DAYS; sustained, painful muscle contractions — torticollis, oculogyric crisis, trismus, and LARYNGOSPASM (an airway EMERGENCY) → treat with an ANTICHOLINERGIC (benztropine) or DIPHENHYDRAMINE IM/IV. AKATHISIA: DAYS–WEEKS; subjective INNER RESTLESSNESS with inability to sit still, pacing, fidgeting → reduce dose, a BETA-BLOCKER (propranolol), or a benzodiazepine. Drug-induced PSEUDOPARKINSONISM: WEEKS–MONTHS; BRADYKINESIA, cogwheel RIGIDITY, resting TREMOR, masked facies, shuffling gait → reduce dose/switch agent or add an ANTICHOLINERGIC. TARDIVE DYSKINESIA: MONTHS–YEARS; repetitive, involuntary CHOREOATHETOID movements, classically OROFACIAL — managed entirely differently (VMAT2 inhibitor; anticholinergics WORSEN it). Recognizing the TIME COURSE is what separates a benztropine-responsive syndrome from TD.
labs.r: By TIMING: ACUTE DYSTONIA (hrs–days; spasms/oculogyric/laryngospasm → anticholinergic/diphenhydramine); AKATHISIA (days–wks; inner restlessness → dose↓/propranolol/benzo); PSEUDOPARKINSONISM (wks–mos; bradykinesia/rigidity/tremor → dose↓/switch/anticholinergic); TARDIVE DYSKINESIA (mos–yrs; orofacial choreoathetoid → VMAT2 inhibitor; anticholinergics WORSEN).

labs.n: AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) + screening schedule + ruling out mimics
labs.v: The AIMS is the standardized 12-item exam used to detect and QUANTIFY abnormal movements: facial/oral (muscles of facial expression, lips/perioral, jaw, tongue), extremities (upper and lower), trunk, plus global severity, incapacitation, and the patient's AWARENESS/distress, with items on dental/denture status. Best practice: perform AIMS at antipsychotic INITIATION (baseline) and then PERIODICALLY (e.g., every 6–12 months — MORE often with high-risk patients or first-generation agents) and whenever new movements appear, so emerging TD is caught early when intervention is most useful. RULE OUT MIMICS before attributing to TD: Huntington disease and other primary movement disorders, idiopathic dystonias, stereotypies, ill-fitting dentures/edentulous mouthing, dopamine-blocking ANTIEMETIC exposure (metoclopramide), and WITHDRAWAL-EMERGENT dyskinesia after a recent antipsychotic reduction/stop.
labs.r: AIMS = standardized 12-item scale (face/oral, extremities, trunk + severity/incapacitation/awareness) to detect + quantify movements; do at BASELINE then periodically (q6–12 mo, more often if high-risk/first-gen) and when new movements appear. Rule out mimics: Huntington, primary dystonia, stereotypies, dentures, metoclopramide, withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia.

labs.n: MANAGEMENT — re-evaluate/minimize or SWITCH the antipsychotic (NEVER abrupt stop) + VMAT2 INHIBITORS
labs.v: Steps once TD is identified and quantified: (1) NOTIFY the prescriber/psychiatry and re-evaluate the ongoing NEED and DOSE of the antipsychotic — use the LOWEST effective dose and consider SWITCHING to a lower-TD-risk agent (e.g., a second-generation agent; clozapine has the lowest risk). (2) Do NOT abruptly STOP the antipsychotic — abrupt withdrawal can cause WITHDRAWAL-EMERGENT dyskinesia and PSYCHOTIC RELAPSE; any taper/change is made by the prescriber while monitoring mental status. (3) START an FDA-approved VMAT2 INHIBITOR — VALBENAZINE (Ingrezza, once daily) or DEUTETRABENAZINE (Austedo) — which deplete/reduce presynaptic dopamine release and are FIRST-LINE, evidence-based treatment for TD; monitor for SOMNOLENCE, QTc PROLONGATION, parkinsonism, and DEPRESSION/suicidality (a particular concern with older tetrabenazine, classically used in Huntington chorea). Reassess response with serial AIMS scores.
labs.r: Manage TD: notify psychiatry → minimize dose / SWITCH to a lower-risk antipsychotic (clozapine lowest), but NEVER abruptly stop (withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia + relapse). START a VMAT2 INHIBITOR (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) = first-line; monitor somnolence, QTc, parkinsonism, mood/suicidality. Track response with serial AIMS.

labs.n: ANTICHOLINERGICS WORSEN TD + swallowing/safety + psychosocial support + PERTINENT NEGATIVES
labs.v: CLASSIC TEST POINT: ANTICHOLINERGICS (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, diphenhydramine) treat acute DYSTONIA and PSEUDOPARKINSONISM but do NOT help TD and can WORSEN it — they should be reviewed and often REDUCED/STOPPED in TD. Likewise, simply INCREASING the antipsychotic may transiently MASK movements but worsens the underlying disorder and is not the answer. The nurse assesses FUNCTION/SAFETY: SWALLOWING (orofacial/tongue movements can impair chewing/swallowing → aspiration risk and weight loss) and gait/dexterity, and provides NON-JUDGMENTAL psychosocial support because TD is visible, STIGMATIZING, and distressing and can harm self-esteem and treatment adherence. Educate on the VMAT2 medication and the importance of NOT stopping the antipsychotic on her own, and maintain regular AIMS follow-up. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice — these are WRONG): do NOT give benztropine/diphenhydramine for TD; do NOT abruptly stop the antipsychotic; do NOT increase the antipsychotic to suppress the movements; do NOT dismiss the movements as a 'habit' or 'just old age'; and do NOT skip AIMS screening on patients receiving antipsychotics.
labs.r: ANTICHOLINERGICS (benztropine/diphenhydramine) WORSEN TD (they're for dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism) → review/stop them; don't just ↑ the antipsychotic (masks, worsens). Assess SWALLOWING/aspiration + gait safety; give NON-JUDGMENTAL support (stigmatizing/distressing). NEGATIVES: don't give anticholinergics, don't abrupt-stop the antipsychotic, don't ↑ it to suppress movements, don't dismiss as habit/aging, don't skip AIMS.

labs.v: 14 (moderate-to-severe — orofacial items prominent with mild extremity involvement; used as a baseline to track response to the VMAT2 inhibitor)
7.8% (elevated — her type 2 diabetes is both a comorbidity to manage and a recognized risk factor for tardive dyskinesia)
438 ms (within normal limits — checked before/while starting a VMAT2 inhibitor, which can prolong the QT; monitor with other QT-prolonging drugs)

labs.n: TSH (screening to exclude a contributing/mimicking cause)

nursesNote: Community mental-health clinic — routine LAI visit. 63 y/o woman, schizophrenia ~20 years on haloperidol, plus type 2 diabetes. Observed NEW persistent involuntary orofacial movements (lip smacking/puckering, tongue protrusion/writhing, facial grimacing) and slow choreoathetoid finger movements — present at rest, worse with distraction, absent in sleep, and she is largely unaware of them; her sister reports they began a few months ago. Recognized this as TARDIVE DYSKINESIA, a late complication of chronic dopamine blockade — NOT acute dystonia (no sustained spasm/oculogyric crisis), NOT akathisia (no inner restlessness/pacing), and NOT pseudoparkinsonism (no bradykinesia/cogwheel rigidity/resting tremor/masked facies). Completed an AIMS (score 14, moderate-to-severe, orofacial predominant) for a baseline and to track response; screened swallowing (intact today) and gait safety. Helped rule out mimics (no metoclopramide use, no recent antipsychotic stop to suggest withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia, TSH normal). Notified psychiatry: plan to minimize the antipsychotic dose and consider switching to a lower-TD-risk agent WITHOUT abruptly stopping it (to avoid withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia and relapse) and to start a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine) with QTc/somnolence/mood monitoring (baseline QTc 438 ms). Did NOT give benztropine or diphenhydramine (anticholinergics worsen TD), did NOT increase the antipsychotic to suppress the movements, and did NOT dismiss the movements as a habit or aging. Provided non-judgmental support regarding a visible, stigmatizing condition, taught the VMAT2 medication and the importance of not stopping the antipsychotic on her own, and arranged ongoing AIMS follow-up. Sister included with the patient's consent.
providerOrders: DIAGNOSIS/ASSESSMENT: tardive dyskinesia attributed to long-term antipsychotic (dopamine D2-blockade) therapy; perform and document an AIMS for baseline severity and to track response

RULE OUT MIMICS: review for dopamine-blocking antiemetic use (metoclopramide/prochlorperazine), recent antipsychotic reduction/stop (withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia), primary movement disorders, and ill-fitting dentures; TSH and glucose as indicated

ANTIPSYCHOTIC RE-EVALUATION: psychiatry to use the lowest effective dose and consider switching to a lower-TD-risk agent (e.g., a second-generation antipsychotic; clozapine lowest risk) — do NOT abruptly discontinue (risk of withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia and psychotic relapse)
VMAT2 INHIBITOR: start valbenazine (or deutetrabenazine) as first-line treatment for tardive dyskinesia; monitor for somnolence, QTc prolongation, parkinsonism, and depression/suicidality

AVOID ANTICHOLINERGICS: do NOT use benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, or diphenhydramine for tardive dyskinesia (these worsen it; they are for acute dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism); review and reduce/stop any current anticholinergic
QTc/MONITORING: baseline and periodic ECG QTc while on a VMAT2 inhibitor; review concurrent QT-prolonging medications
FUNCTION/SAFETY: assess swallowing/aspiration risk and gait/dexterity; dietitian/speech referral if swallowing is affected; monitor weight
DIABETES/METABOLIC: continue diabetes management and routine metabolic monitoring on antipsychotic therapy (A1c, glucose, lipids, weight)

EDUCATION/SUPPORT: provide non-judgmental psychosocial support for a stigmatizing condition, teach the VMAT2 medication, reinforce NOT stopping the antipsychotic independently, and maintain regular AIMS follow-up and care coordination

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically significant cues.

opts.text: Repetitive involuntary lip smacking/puckering, tongue protrusion/writhing, and facial grimacing
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — orofacial-buccolingual-masticatory movements are the classic presentation of tardive dyskinesia.

opts.text: Slow, writhing (choreoathetoid) involuntary finger and hand movements
opts.rat: RELEVANT — extremity choreoathetoid movements are part of the TD picture and are scored on the AIMS.

opts.text: About 20 years of continuous first-generation antipsychotic (haloperidol) therapy
opts.rat: RELEVANT — long cumulative duration of dopamine blockade, especially with a first-generation agent, is the key risk factor.

opts.text: The movements are present at rest, worsen with distraction, and disappear during sleep, and she is largely unaware of them
opts.rat: RELEVANT — this pattern (and limited awareness) is characteristic of TD and helps distinguish it from voluntary or anxious movements.

opts.text: Risk factors of older age, female sex, and type 2 diabetes
opts.rat: RELEVANT — these increase the likelihood of TD and support the diagnosis.

opts.text: Sustained painful neck spasm with the eyes rolling upward (oculogyric crisis)
opts.rat: ⚠️ This describes ACUTE DYSTONIA (hours–days), not TD — she has none of these sustained spasms.

opts.text: Subjective inner restlessness with constant pacing and inability to sit still
opts.rat: ⚠️ This describes AKATHISIA, a different syndrome — she does not report restlessness or pace.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: This is tardive dyskinesia — a late complication of months-to-years of dopamine blockade that may be persistent or irreversible
opts.rat: CORRECT — the late onset, orofacial choreoathetoid pattern, and chronic antipsychotic exposure define TD.

opts.text: It is distinguished from acute dystonia, akathisia, and pseudoparkinsonism largely by its TIMING (months–years) and movement pattern
opts.rat: CORRECT — recognizing the time course separates TD from the earlier, often anticholinergic-responsive syndromes.

opts.text: An AIMS should be done to quantify severity and track response, and mimics (e.g., Huntington, metoclopramide, withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia) ruled out
opts.rat: CORRECT — standardized assessment and excluding mimics guide diagnosis and monitoring.

opts.text: Management includes notifying psychiatry to minimize/switch the antipsychotic (without abruptly stopping it) and starting a VMAT2 inhibitor
opts.rat: CORRECT — these are the evidence-based steps for TD.

opts.text: Anticholinergics such as benztropine or diphenhydramine would not help and could worsen the movements
opts.rat: CORRECT — anticholinergics treat dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism, not TD, and can aggravate it.

opts.text: Giving benztropine now is the priority treatment for these movements
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Anticholinergics worsen TD; they are indicated for acute dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism, not tardive dyskinesia.

opts.text: Increasing the haloperidol dose is the best way to control the movements
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Raising the antipsychotic may transiently mask TD but worsens the underlying disorder.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these explanations from #1 (MOST likely) to #5 (LEAST).

opts.text: Tardive dyskinesia from long-term antipsychotic (dopamine-blockade) therapy
opts.rat: #1 — MOST likely: late-onset orofacial choreoathetoid movements after ~20 years of antipsychotics are classic TD.

opts.text: Drug-induced pseudoparkinsonism
opts.rat: #2 — On the antipsychotic-EPS differential, but she lacks bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, and masked facies.

opts.text: Akathisia
opts.rat: #3 — Also antipsychotic-related, but she has no subjective restlessness or inability to sit still.

opts.text: Acute dystonic reaction
opts.rat: #4 — Unlikely: dystonia is an early (hours–days) sustained spasm, not chronic choreoathetoid movements.

opts.text: A primary neurologic movement disorder such as Huntington disease
opts.rat: #5 — LEAST likely given the clear long-term antipsychotic exposure, but worth excluding as a mimic.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Perform and document an AIMS to quantify severity and establish a baseline for tracking response
opts.rat: Standardized assessment is essential to diagnose, grade, and monitor tardive dyskinesia.

opts.text: Notify psychiatry to re-evaluate and minimize the antipsychotic dose or switch to a lower-TD-risk agent
opts.rat: Reducing dopamine-blockade exposure with a lower-risk agent is a core management step.

opts.text: Start an FDA-approved VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) with appropriate monitoring
opts.rat: VMAT2 inhibitors are first-line, evidence-based treatment for TD.

opts.text: Assess swallowing/aspiration risk and gait safety, and provide non-judgmental psychosocial support
opts.rat: Orofacial movements can impair swallowing and TD is stigmatizing; safety and support are part of care.

opts.text: Rule out mimics (metoclopramide use, withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia, primary movement disorders, dentures)
opts.rat: Excluding other causes confirms the diagnosis and avoids mismanagement.

opts.text: Administer benztropine or diphenhydramine to treat the movements
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — anticholinergics worsen TD; they are for acute dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism.

opts.text: Increase the haloperidol dose to suppress the movements
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — raising the antipsychotic only masks TD transiently and worsens the underlying disorder.

opts.text: Abruptly stop the antipsychotic today to remove the cause
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — abrupt withdrawal can cause withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia and psychotic relapse; changes are tapered by the prescriber.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Recognize the movements as possible TD and complete an AIMS, distinguishing it from dystonia/akathisia/pseudoparkinsonism and ruling out mimics
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Accurate recognition and a baseline AIMS drive correct, safe management.

opts.text: Notify psychiatry/the prescriber with the findings and AIMS score
opts.rat: #2 — Escalation enables medication decisions (dose change/switch, starting a VMAT2 inhibitor).

opts.text: Carry out the plan to minimize/switch the antipsychotic without abruptly stopping it and start the prescribed VMAT2 inhibitor
opts.rat: #3 — The definitive interventions, done safely to avoid relapse and withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia.

opts.text: Assess swallowing/aspiration and gait safety and provide education and non-judgmental support
opts.rat: #4 — Protects function and supports adherence and coping with a visible condition.

opts.text: Arrange ongoing AIMS monitoring and follow-up with metabolic/QTc surveillance
opts.rat: #5 — Ensures the response is tracked and the VMAT2 inhibitor/antipsychotic are monitored over time.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as the patient IMPROVING, WORSENING, or UNCHANGED.

opts.text: Six weeks after the antipsychotic was minimized and valbenazine started, her orofacial movements are noticeably less frequent and she eats more comfortably
opts.rat: Reduced movements and better function indicate the VMAT2 inhibitor and dose optimization are working.

opts.text: At three months her AIMS score is substantially lower with no psychotic relapse on the optimized regimen
opts.rat: A falling AIMS score with maintained psychiatric stability is the goal of treatment.

opts.text: She tolerates the VMAT2 inhibitor without excess sedation, new parkinsonism, or QTc prolongation
opts.rat: Good tolerability supports continuing effective therapy.

opts.text: After benztropine was added for the movements, the orofacial dyskinesia is now worse
opts.rat: ⚠️ Anticholinergics worsen TD — stop the benztropine; it is not a treatment for tardive dyskinesia.

opts.text: After the antipsychotic was abruptly discontinued, the dyskinesia intensified and psychotic symptoms re-emerged
opts.rat: ⚠️ Abrupt withdrawal caused withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia and relapse — changes must be tapered by the prescriber.

opts.text: The tongue and mouth movements now interfere with chewing and she coughs while drinking
opts.rat: ⚠️ Swallowing is now impaired with aspiration risk — assess swallow/airway and involve speech/dietitian.

opts.text: Two weeks into the VMAT2 inhibitor her AIMS score is about the same as baseline
opts.rat: Benefit may take several weeks; continue therapy and reassess at the next interval.

opts.text: Her psychiatric symptoms remain stable and well controlled on the optimized regimen
opts.rat: Stable mental status is the desired baseline to maintain while treating the TD.

opts.text: At six months the movements are markedly improved and she is engaged in care with regular AIMS monitoring
opts.rat: Sustained reduction in movements with ongoing monitoring confirms effective, safe management.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: ARTERIOVENOUS (AV) FISTULA CARE and CHRONIC HEMODIALYSIS SELF-MANAGEMENT in a 58-Year-Old Man with ESRD from Diabetic Nephropathy ~3 Months Into Maintenance Hemodialysis via a Tunneled CATHETER Who Has a NEW LEFT-FOREARM AV FISTULA (Created 8 Weeks Ago, Now Maturing) Being Evaluated for First Cannulation: WHY a FISTULA Is Preferred Over a Graft Over a CATHETER ('Fistula First' — Lowest Infection/Clot Risk), Assessing PATENCY (a Palpable THRILL + an Audible BRUIT) and MATURATION, the High-Yield ACCESS-ARM PRECAUTIONS (NO Blood Pressure, NO Venipuncture/IV/Blood Draws, NO Tight Clothing/Jewelry, Don't Sleep On It or Carry Heavy Loads — and Daily Self-Check of the Thrill), Recognizing COMPLICATIONS (LOSS of Thrill/Bruit = THROMBOSIS Emergency, Infection, STEAL Syndrome with a Cold/Painful Hand, Aneurysm/Pseudoaneurysm, Prolonged Post-Dialysis Bleeding), and INTERDIALYTIC SELF-CARE (Fluid + Sodium + POTASSIUM + PHOSPHORUS Restriction, PHOSPHATE BINDERS WITH Meals, an Interdialytic Weight-Gain Target, Holding Antihypertensives/Giving Dialyzable Meds AFTER Dialysis, Anemia/ESA + Iron, and NEVER Skipping Sessions) — Plus the CATHETER Infection Risk That Makes Transitioning to the Fistula a Priority
subtitle: For a patient with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on maintenance HEMODIALYSIS, the vascular ACCESS is a lifeline, and the order of preference is 'FISTULA FIRST': an arteriovenous (AV) FISTULA (a surgically created artery-to-vein anastomosis, usually in the non-dominant forearm) has the LOWEST risk of infection and clotting and the best long-term patency, followed by an AV GRAFT (a synthetic conduit, usable sooner but higher clot/infection risk), with a tunneled central CATHETER LAST because it carries the HIGHEST infection (CLABSI/sepsis) and thrombosis risk. This case follows C. Ramos, a 58-year-old man with ESRD from diabetic nephropathy who began maintenance hemodialysis about 3 months ago through a tunneled catheter and had a LEFT-FOREARM AV FISTULA created 8 weeks ago; it is now MATURING (a fistula typically needs ~6–12 weeks before first cannulation while the vein 'arterializes' — enlarges and toughens) and is being evaluated for first use so the higher-risk catheter can be removed. The nurse ASSESSES the access for patency at every encounter — a palpable THRILL (a continuous buzzing/vibration) and an audible BRUIT (a continuous swooshing sound on auscultation) confirm flow — and checks for maturation (a well-developed, easily palpable vein). The nurse teaches the high-yield ACCESS-ARM PRECAUTIONS that protect the fistula: NO blood pressure measurements, NO venipuncture/IV starts/blood draws, and NO injections in that arm; avoid tight clothing, jewelry, watches, or a name band on that wrist; don't sleep on the arm, carry heavy bags on it, or let it be compressed; and CHECK THE THRILL DAILY (report any loss). The patient is taught to recognize COMPLICATIONS: LOSS of the thrill/bruit signals THROMBOSIS (a surgical emergency — notify immediately to attempt salvage); redness/warmth/drainage/fever = INFECTION; a cold, pale, painful, numb hand = vascular STEAL syndrome; a bulging pulsatile area = aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm; and bleeding that won't stop after dialysis needs firm pressure and escalation. Between treatments, SELF-MANAGEMENT is central: restrict FLUID and SODIUM (to limit interdialytic weight gain, targeting roughly ≤1–1.5 kg/day or per the renal team), restrict POTASSIUM (avoid high-K foods — oranges, bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, salt substitutes) and PHOSPHORUS, take PHOSPHATE BINDERS WITH meals (to bind dietary phosphate in the gut, not between meals), follow the renal diet with adequate protein for dialysis patients, take ERYTHROPOIESIS-STIMULATING AGENTS and iron for anemia and active vitamin D/binders for mineral-bone disease, generally HOLD antihypertensives before a session and give DIALYZABLE medications AFTER dialysis (per protocol), and NEVER skip dialysis sessions (missed sessions cause dangerous fluid overload and HYPERKALEMIA). Step-6 evaluates whether each later finding reflects the patient IMPROVING, WORSENING, or remaining UNCHANGED.

labs.n: PRESENTATION + WHY 'FISTULA FIRST' (access types, ranking, and maturation)
labs.v: 58 y/o man, ESRD from diabetic nephropathy, ~3 months on maintenance HD via a tunneled CATHETER, with a NEW left-forearm AV fistula (8 weeks old) now maturing and being evaluated for first cannulation so the catheter can be removed. KEY PRINCIPLE — 'FISTULA FIRST': vascular-access preference is AV FISTULA (artery-to-vein anastomosis; lowest infection + clot risk, best long-term patency, but needs ~6–12 weeks to MATURE before use as the vein 'arterializes') > AV GRAFT (synthetic conduit; usable sooner ~2–4 weeks but higher clot/infection risk) > CENTRAL CATHETER (tunneled; usable immediately but the HIGHEST infection [CLABSI/sepsis] and thrombosis risk) — so transitioning OFF the catheter onto the fistula is a safety priority. Maturation is promoted by hand-exercise (e.g., squeezing a ball) per the surgeon and protected by avoiding any compression of the arm.
labs.r: FISTULA FIRST: AV fistula (lowest infection/clot risk, best patency; matures ~6–12 wks) > AV graft (usable ~2–4 wks, higher clot/infection risk) > catheter (immediate but HIGHEST infection/thrombosis risk). Get off the catheter onto the fistula ASAP. Maturation needs weeks of arterialization + hand exercises; protect the arm from compression.

labs.v: ASSESS PATENCY every shift/encounter: PALPATE for a continuous THRILL (a buzzing vibration) and AUSCULTATE for a continuous BRUIT (a swooshing sound) — both present = flowing/patent. PROTECT the access arm (teach the patient): NO blood pressure cuff, NO venipuncture/IV starts/blood draws, NO injections in that arm; NO tight clothing, jewelry, watch, or wristband on that side; do NOT sleep on the arm, carry heavy bags, or otherwise compress it; keep it clean. The patient should CHECK THE THRILL DAILY (feel for the buzz) and report any change immediately. Post-dialysis, hold the cannulation sites with gentle firm pressure until hemostasis (don't occlude flow), and keep the dressing dry.
labs.r: Patency = palpable THRILL + audible BRUIT (check every encounter; teach DAILY self-check). ACCESS-ARM PRECAUTIONS: NO BP, NO venipuncture/IV/blood draw/injection in that arm; no tight clothing/jewelry/wristband; don't sleep on it, compress it, or carry heavy loads. Post-HD: firm (not occlusive) pressure to sites until hemostasis.

labs.v: THROMBOSIS/clotting: LOSS of the thrill and bruit (no buzz/swoosh) = the access is clotting — a SURGICAL EMERGENCY; notify immediately for possible thrombectomy/declotting to salvage it. INFECTION: redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or fever at the site (catheters are especially high risk → CLABSI/sepsis) → cultures + antibiotics. VASCULAR 'STEAL' SYNDROME: the fistula diverts arterial flow from the hand → a COLD, PALE, PAINFUL, NUMB hand with weak distal pulse → report (may need flow-limiting surgery). ANEURYSM/PSEUDOANEURYSM: a bulging, pulsatile area from repeated cannulation → protect and monitor; rapid enlargement/thinning skin/bleeding is urgent. PROLONGED BLEEDING after dialysis (heparin + repeated punctures): apply firm pressure and escalate if it won't stop. HIGH-OUTPUT cardiac strain is a rarer late complication.
labs.r: Red flags: NO thrill/bruit = THROMBOSIS (emergency — notify to salvage); redness/warmth/drainage/fever = INFECTION (catheters worst); cold/pale/painful/numb hand = STEAL syndrome; pulsatile bulge = aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm; won't-stop post-HD bleeding = firm pressure + escalate.

labs.n: INTERDIALYTIC SELF-MANAGEMENT — fluid, diet, binders, meds, schedule
labs.v: FLUID + SODIUM restriction limits interdialytic weight gain (target roughly ≤1–1.5 kg/day or per the team) and pre-dialysis hypertension/edema; weigh daily and track. POTASSIUM restriction (AVOID high-K foods — oranges, bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, melons, dried fruit, and SALT SUBSTITUTES [KCl]) prevents life-threatening hyperkalemia between runs. PHOSPHORUS restriction (limit dairy, nuts, cola, processed foods) plus PHOSPHATE BINDERS taken WITH meals (binders work in the gut on food phosphate — NOT between meals) controls mineral-bone disease; active vitamin D as prescribed. Adequate PROTEIN is needed for dialysis patients (dialysis removes protein — this is NOT the protein-restricted pre-dialysis CKD diet). ANEMIA of CKD: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (epoetin/darbepoetin) + iron. MEDS: generally HOLD antihypertensives before a session (to avoid intradialytic hypotension) and give DIALYZABLE drugs (many water-soluble agents, some antibiotics) AFTER dialysis — per protocol. NEVER skip sessions: missed dialysis → fluid overload, pulmonary edema, and dangerous HYPERKALEMIA.
labs.r: Restrict FLUID + Na (weight gain ≤~1–1.5 kg/day), K (no oranges/bananas/potatoes/tomatoes/salt substitutes), and PHOSPHORUS; PHOSPHATE BINDERS WITH meals; ADEQUATE protein (dialysis removes it — not the pre-dialysis low-protein diet); ESA + iron for anemia; HOLD antihypertensives pre-HD + give dialyzable meds AFTER; daily weights; NEVER skip sessions (→ overload + hyperkalemia).

labs.n: CATHETER risk, transition to the fistula, and PERTINENT NEGATIVES (what NOT to do)
labs.v: The tunneled CATHETER carries the highest infection and clotting risk, so converting to the maturing fistula and removing the catheter is a priority once the fistula is reliably usable; meanwhile use strict aseptic catheter care, keep the dressing dry/intact, and NEVER use the dialysis catheter for routine blood draws or IV fluids unless specifically authorized. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice — these are WRONG): do NOT take blood pressures, draw blood, start IVs, or give injections in the fistula arm; do NOT apply tight bands, BP cuffs, or restrictive jewelry to that arm; do NOT ignore a lost thrill/bruit (it is an emergency, not 'wait and see'); do NOT keep the catheter longer than necessary 'because it works'; do NOT take phosphate binders between meals (they must be taken WITH food); do NOT put the patient on a protein-restricted diet (that is for pre-dialysis CKD); and do NOT let the patient skip dialysis sessions.
labs.r: Catheter = highest infection/clot risk → transition to fistula + remove catheter ASAP; aseptic catheter care, dressing dry, don't use it for routine draws/IV. NEGATIVES: no BP/venipuncture/IV/injection/tight band on the fistula arm; don't ignore a lost thrill/bruit (emergency); don't keep the catheter unnecessarily; don't take binders between meals; don't protein-restrict a dialysis patient; don't skip sessions.

6.2 mg/dL (elevated — inadequate phosphate binding/dietary phosphorus; reinforce binders WITH meals and phosphorus-restricted diet to prevent renal osteodystrophy and vascular calcification)
