nursesNote: Outpatient hemodialysis unit — ESRD (diabetic nephropathy), ~3 months on HD via a right IJ tunneled catheter, with a new left-forearm AV fistula (8 weeks old) maturing and being evaluated for first cannulation. Pre-dialysis BP 168/92 (taken in the RIGHT arm — never the fistula arm), up 2.6 kg since last session with mild pedal edema and bibasilar crackles (interdialytic fluid/sodium excess — had soup and a banana over the weekend). Left-forearm fistula with a palpable continuous THRILL and audible BRUIT, vein developing well; hand warm/pink with strong pulse and brisk refill (no steal); no redness/drainage/aneurysm; catheter exit site clean/dry/intact. Reinforced ACCESS-ARM PRECAUTIONS: no BP, venipuncture, IV, or injections in the left arm; no tight clothing/jewelry/wristband; don't sleep on it or carry heavy loads; CHECK THE THRILL DAILY and report any loss; do hand exercises to promote maturation. Taught complication red flags: loss of thrill/bruit = thrombosis emergency; redness/warmth/drainage/fever = infection; cold/pale/painful/numb hand = steal; pulsatile bulge = aneurysm; won't-stop bleeding after dialysis = firm pressure + escalate. Reviewed interdialytic self-care: fluid/sodium restriction with daily weights (target ≤~1–1.5 kg/day gain), potassium restriction (avoid oranges/bananas/potatoes/tomatoes/salt substitutes — pre-HD K 5.8), phosphorus restriction with PHOSPHATE BINDERS taken WITH meals (phosphorus 6.2), adequate protein (dialysis patient — NOT the pre-dialysis low-protein diet), ESA + iron for anemia (Hgb 9.5), hold the morning antihypertensive before the session and take dialyzable meds after, and NEVER skip sessions. Post-dialysis at target dry weight, BP 138/82, edema/crackles improved, fistula thrill/bruit intact. Plan to cannulate the fistula and remove the catheter once reliably usable. Wife included in teaching with teach-back.
providerOrders: ACCESS ASSESSMENT: assess the AV fistula every encounter for a palpable thrill and audible bruit, maturation, and signs of infection/steal/aneurysm; document patency
ACCESS-ARM PROTECTION: NO blood pressure, venipuncture, IV starts, or injections in the left (fistula) arm; place a limb-alert band on the OPPOSITE arm; avoid constriction of the access arm

FISTULA-FIRST TRANSITION: evaluate the maturing fistula for cannulation and remove the tunneled catheter once the fistula is reliably usable; until then, strict aseptic catheter care, keep the dressing dry/intact, and do not use the dialysis catheter for routine draws/IV unless authorized
DIALYSIS PRESCRIPTION: hemodialysis per schedule (M/W/F) to estimated dry weight; monitor for intradialytic hypotension/cramping; pre- and post-dialysis weights and vital signs

MEDICATIONS: hold antihypertensives before dialysis per protocol; administer dialyzable medications after dialysis; ESA (epoetin/darbepoetin) + iron for anemia of CKD; active vitamin D and phosphate binders WITH meals
DIET/FLUID: renal diet — fluid and sodium restriction (limit interdialytic weight gain), potassium restriction, phosphorus restriction, and adequate protein for a dialysis patient; daily weights
LABS: monitor potassium, phosphorus, calcium, bicarbonate, hemoglobin/iron studies, and Kt/V adequacy per protocol

COMPLICATION ESCALATION: report immediately any loss of thrill/bruit (possible thrombosis — emergency), access infection signs, a cold/painful/numb hand (steal), an enlarging pulsatile bulge, or bleeding that does not stop with firm pressure

EDUCATION: teach access-arm precautions, daily thrill self-check, complication red flags, phosphate-binder timing with meals, fluid/potassium/phosphorus control, and the importance of never skipping dialysis sessions; verify with teach-back

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically significant cues.

opts.text: A palpable continuous thrill and audible continuous bruit over the maturing left-forearm fistula
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — a thrill and bruit confirm the access is patent and flowing; their presence is exactly what to verify.

opts.text: Interdialytic weight gain of 2.6 kg with pedal edema, bibasilar crackles, and pre-dialysis BP 168/92
opts.rat: RELEVANT — excess fluid/sodium intake between sessions causes volume overload and hypertension to address with dialysis and teaching.

opts.text: He is still dialyzing through a tunneled catheter while the fistula matures
opts.rat: RELEVANT — the catheter is the highest-infection access; transitioning to the fistula and removing it is a priority.

opts.text: A warm, pink hand with a strong distal pulse and brisk capillary refill on the access side
opts.rat: RELEVANT — normal distal perfusion indicates no vascular steal, a reassuring assessment finding to confirm and document.

opts.text: Pre-dialysis potassium 5.8 mmol/L after eating a banana and soup over the weekend
opts.rat: RELEVANT — hyperkalemia between sessions is dangerous and signals a need to reinforce potassium-restriction teaching.

opts.text: His blood pressure was measured in the right (non-access) arm
opts.rat: This is CORRECT practice, not a problem — BP must never be taken in the fistula arm, so this is reassuring, not a concerning cue.

opts.text: He took a multivitamin with breakfast this morning
opts.rat: Not clinically significant to the access or today's priorities (renal vitamins are commonly prescribed).

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: A patent fistula shows a thrill and bruit; loss of either would suggest thrombosis and is an emergency
opts.rat: CORRECT — thrill/bruit indicate flow; their loss means the access is clotting and requires immediate escalation.

opts.text: The fistula is preferred over the catheter because it has lower infection and clotting risk; the catheter should be removed once the fistula is usable
opts.rat: CORRECT — 'fistula first': transitioning off the catheter reduces infection/sepsis and thrombosis risk.

opts.text: The access arm must be protected — no BP, venipuncture, IV, injections, or constriction
opts.rat: CORRECT — these protect flow and prevent damage/thrombosis of the fistula.

opts.text: The weight gain, edema, crackles, and hypertension reflect interdialytic fluid/sodium excess to manage with dialysis and diet teaching
opts.rat: CORRECT — volume overload between sessions is driven by fluid and sodium intake.

opts.text: Phosphate binders should be taken WITH meals, and potassium-rich foods/salt substitutes should be avoided
opts.rat: CORRECT — binders act on dietary phosphate in the gut; potassium restriction prevents dangerous hyperkalemia.

opts.text: Because dialysis removes wastes, he should follow a strict low-protein diet like a pre-dialysis CKD patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Dialysis removes protein, so dialysis patients need ADEQUATE protein — not the pre-dialysis protein restriction.

opts.text: It is fine to keep using the tunneled catheter long term since it is working
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The catheter carries the highest infection/clot risk; convert to the fistula and remove it as soon as feasible.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these nursing priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Assess and protect the vascular access (confirm thrill/bruit, enforce access-arm precautions)
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. The access is the lifeline; verifying patency and preventing damage/thrombosis comes first.

opts.text: Address fluid overload and hyperkalemia through dialysis and reinforce fluid/sodium/potassium limits
opts.rat: #2 — HIGH. Volume overload and hyperkalemia are immediate physiologic risks corrected by dialysis and diet.

opts.text: Plan the transition from the catheter to the maturing fistula and minimize catheter infection risk
opts.rat: #3 — Reduces the largest ongoing infection/thrombosis risk once the fistula is reliably usable.

opts.text: Reinforce mineral-bone management (phosphate binders with meals, phosphorus restriction) and anemia therapy
opts.rat: #4 — Important chronic-management targets that prevent long-term complications.

opts.text: Provide ongoing education and teach-back on the overall self-care plan and never skipping sessions
opts.rat: #5 — Consolidates safe self-management once the immediate priorities are addressed.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Palpate for a thrill and auscultate for a bruit over the fistula and teach a daily self-check
opts.rat: Confirms patency and empowers the patient to detect thrombosis early.

opts.text: Place a limb-alert band and take blood pressures only in the non-access (right) arm
opts.rat: Protects the fistula from compression/damage that could cause thrombosis.

opts.text: Teach phosphate binders WITH meals, potassium restriction, and fluid/sodium limits with daily weights
opts.rat: Correct timing and dietary control prevent hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia, and volume overload.

opts.text: Use strict aseptic technique for the catheter and plan to remove it once the fistula is usable
opts.rat: Minimizes the catheter's high infection risk and supports the fistula-first transition.

opts.text: Hold the antihypertensive before dialysis and give dialyzable medications after the session per protocol
opts.rat: Prevents intradialytic hypotension and avoids dialyzing off the medication.

opts.text: Use the fistula arm for the next IV antibiotic and a blood draw since it has good access
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — never cannulate, draw from, or infuse into the fistula arm outside of dialysis; it risks the access.

opts.text: Apply a blood pressure cuff to the left (fistula) arm for trending
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — BP cuffs compress and can thrombose the fistula; use the opposite arm.

opts.text: Place the patient on a strict low-protein diet and have him take binders between meals
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — dialysis patients need adequate protein, and binders must be taken WITH meals to work.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess the fistula (thrill/bruit, distal perfusion, signs of infection) and ensure the access arm is protected
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Confirming a functioning, protected access is the foundational priority.

opts.text: Measure pre-dialysis weight and vitals (BP in the non-access arm) and review the pre-dialysis potassium
opts.rat: #2 — Establishes fluid status and identifies hyperkalemia to be corrected by dialysis.

opts.text: Carry out the dialysis treatment to target dry weight, holding the antihypertensive beforehand per protocol
opts.rat: #3 — Removes excess fluid and potassium and corrects acidosis while avoiding intradialytic hypotension.

opts.text: Reinforce diet/fluid, phosphate-binder timing, and access-arm precautions with teach-back
opts.rat: #4 — Targets the behaviors that caused the overload/hyperkalemia and protect the access.

opts.text: Coordinate cannulating the maturing fistula and removing the catheter once it is reliably usable
opts.rat: #5 — Completes the fistula-first transition to eliminate the catheter's infection risk.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as the situation IMPROVING, WORSENING, or UNCHANGED.

opts.text: After dialysis he is at dry weight with BP 138/82, edema reduced, and the fistula thrill/bruit intact
opts.rat: Fluid removed to target with a preserved, patent access is the desired outcome.

opts.text: At two weeks his interdialytic weight gains are smaller (~1.3 kg) and he takes binders with meals
opts.rat: Better fluid/sodium control and correct binder timing reflect effective self-management teaching.

opts.text: The fistula is successfully cannulated and the tunneled catheter is removed
opts.rat: Completing the fistula-first transition eliminates the catheter's high infection risk.

opts.text: After a BP cuff was repeatedly used on the fistula arm, the thrill and bruit are now absent and the area is firm
opts.rat: ⚠️ Loss of thrill/bruit indicates THROMBOSIS — a surgical emergency; notify immediately to attempt salvage.

opts.text: The catheter exit site is red with purulent drainage and he is febrile to 38.4°C
opts.rat: ⚠️ Signs of a catheter-related bloodstream infection — obtain cultures and escalate for antibiotics/line management.

opts.text: He reports the access hand is now cold, pale, painful, and numb
opts.rat: ⚠️ Vascular steal syndrome — the fistula is diverting arterial flow from the hand; report for possible intervention.

opts.text: Immediately after teaching, his understanding of which foods are high in potassium is still incomplete
opts.rat: Learning is in progress; continue reinforcement and re-evaluate understanding at the next visit.

opts.text: His hemoglobin remains 9.5 g/dL one week after the ESA dose
opts.rat: ESAs raise hemoglobin gradually over weeks; a stable value at one week is expected, not a treatment failure.

opts.text: At follow-up the mature fistula is reliably used each session and his potassium/phosphorus are controlled
opts.rat: A durable, well-functioning access with controlled labs confirms effective, safe long-term management.

title: WITHDRAWAL OF LIFE-SUSTAINING TREATMENT and TERMINAL EXTUBATION in the ICU for a 74-Year-Old Man with DEVASTATING ANOXIC BRAIN INJURY After a Prolonged Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Who Is NOT Brain Dead and Has NO Written Advance Directive, with a FAMILY CONFLICT Between His Spouse-Surrogate and Adult Son: Confirming the Legal SURROGATE Hierarchy, Deciding by SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (What the Patient Would Want) Rather Than the Family's Wishes, Distinguishing Withdrawal of TREATMENT From Euthanasia (Withholding = Withdrawing; Allowing Natural Death; Doctrine of Double Effect), Using the ETHICS COMMITTEE for Conflict and Medical Futility, and Carrying Out a COMFORT-FOCUSED Terminal Extubation (DNR, Stop Nonbeneficial Interventions, Titrated Opioids/Benzodiazepines + Antisecretory Agents, Family Presence, Chaplaincy, Bereavement, and OPO Referral) WITHOUT Coercion or Patient Abandonment
subtitle: End-of-life decision-making in the ICU is one of the highest-stakes ETHICAL and LEGAL scenarios a nurse navigates. This case follows H. Whitfield, a 74-year-old man who suffered an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with a prolonged (~25-minute) downtime and is now ICU Day 7 after completing targeted temperature management and rewarming. MULTIMODAL NEUROPROGNOSTICATION performed at least 72 hours after rewarming shows DEVASTATING ANOXIC BRAIN INJURY — absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, status myoclonus, bilaterally absent N20 responses on somatosensory evoked potentials, a malignant EEG pattern, and a markedly elevated neuron-specific enolase — indicating an extremely poor neurologic prognosis. CRITICALLY, he is NOT BRAIN DEAD: he retains some brainstem function and intermittently over-breathes the ventilator, so this is a VALUES-BASED GOALS-OF-CARE decision, NOT a declaration of death (distinct from the brain-death/organ-donation case [[case-107]] and the post-arrest neuroprognostication case [[case-083]]). He remains on escalating norepinephrine and continuous renal replacement therapy for acute kidney injury, with multiorgan failure and no purposeful response. He has NO written advance directive, but he repeatedly told his wife over the years that he 'never wanted to be kept alive on machines with no chance of recovery.' His wife (his legal surrogate as spouse) believes he would want to be allowed to die naturally, while their adult son insists the team 'do everything.' The nurse must (1) CONFIRM DECISION-MAKING AUTHORITY — the patient lacks capacity, so the legally recognized SURROGATE HIERARCHY applies (a healthcare agent/POA if one exists, otherwise spouse, then adult children, then parents, then siblings per state law) and the surrogate speaks FOR the patient, not for themselves; (2) anchor the decision in SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT — what WOULD this patient choose, based on his known values and prior statements — using the BEST-INTERESTS standard only when wishes are truly unknown; (3) understand that WITHDRAWING life-sustaining treatment is ethically and legally permissible, that WITHHOLDING and WITHDRAWING are ethically equivalent, and that this ALLOWS THE UNDERLYING DISEASE to cause death — it is NOT euthanasia or physician-assisted death (the intent is comfort and the cause is the disease), and that titrating comfort medications under the DOCTRINE OF DOUBLE EFFECT is appropriate even if a foreseen-but-unintended side effect is a hastened death; (4) use the ETHICS COMMITTEE to help resolve the family conflict and clarify MEDICAL FUTILITY rather than allowing any one clinician to decide unilaterally; and (5) once a comfort-focused goal is agreed, carry out a COMFORT-FOCUSED TERMINAL EXTUBATION — change code status to DNR, discontinue nonbeneficial interventions (vasopressors, CRRT, routine labs, vital-sign checks, and alarms; stop tube feeds per goals), PRE-MEDICATE for comfort with titrated opioids and benzodiazepines and an antisecretory agent (glycopyrrolate/scopolamine) for terminal secretions, provide family presence, chaplaincy, and bereavement support, and make an organ/tissue-donation referral to the OPO per policy. Throughout, the nurse ADVOCATES and supports the surrogate WITHOUT imposing personal values or coercing the family, never frames the plan as 'withdrawing care' or 'nothing more we can do' (we withdraw nonbeneficial TREATMENT while intensifying COMFORT), and may exercise CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION to participating but must NOT abandon the patient and must ensure continuity of care. Step-6 evaluates whether each action is APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

vitals.spo2: not applicable; died comfortably ~3.5 hours after extubation with no signs of distress; comfort goal met; family supported by chaplain and bereavement services; death pronounced and post-mortem care + bereavement follow-up arranged; tissue-donation eligibility had been screened with the OPO

labs.n: WHO decides — capacity, the healthcare agent, and the legal SURROGATE hierarchy
labs.v: Because Mr. Whitfield lacks decision-making CAPACITY (he cannot understand, appreciate, reason, or communicate a choice), someone must decide FOR him. The order is: (1) the patient's own contemporaneous wishes if he had capacity; (2) a healthcare AGENT named in a durable power of attorney for healthcare / healthcare proxy, if one exists; (3) absent a named agent, the DEFAULT SURROGATE HIERARCHY set by state law — typically SPOUSE first, then ADULT CHILDREN, then PARENTS, then SIBLINGS. He has NO written advance directive and no named agent, so his WIFE is the legal surrogate. A surrogate's job is to speak FOR THE PATIENT — to convey what HE would choose — not to substitute the surrogate's own preferences. The adult son does NOT outrank the spouse in the hierarchy and cannot unilaterally override her (unless state law or a valid document says otherwise).
labs.r: Capacity assessed (understand/appreciate/reason/communicate); decisional patient decides → else healthcare AGENT/POA → else default surrogate hierarchy (spouse → adult children → parents → siblings) per state law. The surrogate speaks FOR the patient, not for themselves.

labs.n: SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT vs the BEST-INTERESTS standard; resolving family conflict
labs.v: For an adult who once HAD capacity, the primary standard is SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT: decide as the PATIENT would have decided, using his known values, beliefs, and prior statements — here, his repeated, consistent statements that he 'never wanted to be kept alive on machines with no chance of recovery.' Those statements are strong evidence and should ANCHOR the decision. The BEST-INTERESTS standard (weighing benefits/burdens from a reasonable-person view) is used ONLY when the patient's wishes are genuinely unknown. When the wife and son disagree, the nurse refocuses the conversation away from 'what do YOU want for him' toward 'what would HE have wanted' — and offers an ETHICS CONSULTATION to mediate. The son's distress is real and deserves support, but his wish to 'do everything' cannot override the patient's own clearly expressed values conveyed by the legal surrogate.
labs.r: Substituted judgment (what the PATIENT would choose, from his values/prior statements) is primary for a once-capacitated adult; best-interests only when wishes are unknown. Anchor on his consistent statements; mediate family conflict by refocusing on HIS values + offering an ethics consult.

labs.n: Withdrawal of TREATMENT is NOT euthanasia — withholding = withdrawing; allowing natural death; DOUBLE EFFECT
labs.v: Withdrawing (or withholding) life-sustaining treatment from a patient — or a surrogate acting on his behalf — who would not want it is ETHICALLY AND LEGALLY PERMISSIBLE and is recognized as such by professional codes and case law. WITHHOLDING and WITHDRAWING are ethically EQUIVALENT (it is no more permissible to never start a therapy than to stop one that is not achieving the patient's goals). Stopping the ventilator/pressors ALLOWS THE UNDERLYING DISEASE to cause death — this is ALLOWING NATURAL DEATH, NOT killing. It is categorically DIFFERENT from EUTHANASIA or physician-assisted death: in withdrawal the INTENT is to relieve suffering and honor wishes and the CAUSE of death is the disease, whereas in euthanasia the intent and cause are to end life. The DOCTRINE OF DOUBLE EFFECT permits giving opioids/benzodiazepines in the doses needed to relieve dyspnea and agitation even if a FORESEEN-but-UNINTENDED effect might be a hastened death — because the intent is comfort, the act (symptom relief) is good, and the good effect is not achieved BY MEANS of the bad one. There is no arbitrary dose 'ceiling' when titrating to genuine symptoms.
labs.r: Withdrawing/withholding LST a patient wouldn't want is permissible; withholding = withdrawing; stopping support ALLOWS the disease to cause death (not killing) and is NOT euthanasia/PAD (intent + causation differ). Double effect: titrate opioids/benzos to comfort even if death may be hastened — intent is symptom relief, no artificial ceiling.

labs.n: MEDICAL FUTILITY, the ETHICS COMMITTEE, and the NURSE'S role (advocacy, conscientious objection, NO abandonment)
labs.v: MEDICAL FUTILITY should be used carefully: PHYSIOLOGIC/quantitative futility (an intervention cannot achieve its physiologic aim) is distinct from VALUE-LADEN 'qualitative' judgments about whether an outcome is 'worth it' — the latter belong to the patient/surrogate, not to clinicians alone. Persistent conflicts (clinician–family or family–family) are referred to the ETHICS COMMITTEE / consultation service for a fair, transparent process — NOT settled by any single clinician unilaterally stopping treatment. The NURSE's role: ADVOCATE for the patient's voice and values; ensure the surrogate's decision is INFORMED (prognosis, options, what each choice involves); coordinate and support the interdisciplinary family meeting; provide honest, compassionate, consistent information; and support the family emotionally and spiritually. A nurse who has a moral objection to participating in withdrawal may exercise CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION and withdraw from PARTICIPATION — but must do so transparently and IN ADVANCE, arrange a competent replacement, ensure CONTINUITY of care, and NEVER ABANDON the patient or stop comfort care.
labs.r: Distinguish physiologic futility from value judgments (the latter belong to patient/surrogate); send conflicts to the ETHICS COMMITTEE, not unilateral clinician action. Nurse: advocate, ensure informed decision, coordinate + support the meeting. Conscientious objection allowed only with advance notice + replacement + continuity — never abandonment.

labs.n: HOW comfort-focused TERMINAL EXTUBATION is carried out + PERTINENT NEGATIVES (what NOT to do)
labs.v: Once a comfort-focused goal is agreed: change code status to DNR; DISCONTINUE nonbeneficial interventions (vasopressors, CRRT/dialysis, routine labs and vital-sign checks, monitors and ALARMS; stop artificial nutrition/tube feeds per the agreed goals). PRE-MEDICATE for comfort BEFORE and during withdrawal — titrated OPIOIDS (e.g., morphine) for dyspnea/pain and BENZODIAZEPINES (e.g., midazolam) for agitation/anxiety, plus an ANTISECRETORY agent (glycopyrrolate or scopolamine) for terminal secretions ('death rattle'); have PRN boluses ready and titrate to the relief of distress (air hunger, grimacing, tachypnea, accessory-muscle use). Either TERMINAL WEANING (gradual reduction) or one-step extubation may be used; remove the tube, provide suction and mouth care, and position for comfort. Maximize FAMILY PRESENCE, offer CHAPLAINCY and cultural/spiritual rituals, and provide BEREAVEMENT support; make an ORGAN/TISSUE-donation referral to the OPO per policy (notification only — clinicians do NOT make suitability judgments and the OPO approaches the family separately). PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT say 'we are withdrawing CARE' or 'there is nothing more we can do' (we withdraw nonbeneficial TREATMENT and intensify COMFORT, hygiene, and presence); did NOT equate withdrawal with euthanasia; did NOT withhold ordered opioids out of fear of hastening death; did NOT continue futile labs, vitals, or alarms; did NOT let the son override the legal surrogate and the patient's known wishes; did NOT coerce or guilt the family; and did NOT abandon the patient.
labs.r: DNR + stop nonbeneficial interventions (pressors, CRRT, labs/vitals/alarms, tube feeds per goals). Premedicate + titrate opioids/benzos + antisecretory before/around extubation; terminal weaning or one-step; family presence, chaplaincy, bereavement, OPO referral. NEGATIVES: never 'withdrawing care'/'nothing more,' never equate with euthanasia, never withhold comfort meds, never continue futile monitoring, never override the surrogate, never coerce or abandon.

labs.n: Multimodal neuroprognostication (≥72 h post-rewarming) — basis for the poor prognosis (NOT brain death)
labs.v: GCS 3 (E1 VT M1) off sedation; ABSENT pupillary and corneal reflexes; STATUS MYOCLONUS within 24 h; bilaterally ABSENT N20 cortical responses on somatosensory evoked potentials; MALIGNANT EEG pattern (suppression/burst-suppression); markedly elevated neuron-specific enolase. These CONCORDANT findings on multimodal testing performed ≥72 h after rewarming indicate devastating anoxic-ischemic brain injury and an extremely poor neurologic prognosis. IMPORTANTLY, he intermittently over-breathes the ventilator and retains some brainstem reflex activity on serial exam, so he does NOT meet BRAIN-DEATH criteria — this is a poor-prognosis, value-based goals-of-care decision, not a declaration of death.
labs.r: Concordant poor-prognosis markers (absent brainstem reflexes, status myoclonus, absent N20 SSEP, malignant EEG, high NSE) at ≥72 h; intact reflexes/purposeful response = good. He is NOT brain dead (spontaneous respiratory effort + some brainstem function) → goals-of-care decision, not death determination.

labs.v: 95 mcg/L (markedly elevated — supports severe anoxic neuronal injury; interpreted only as part of MULTIMODAL prognostication, never in isolation, and after excluding hemolysis)
4.5 mmol/L (elevated — ongoing hypoperfusion/shock with escalating vasopressor requirement)
3.8 mg/dL (elevated — anuric acute kidney injury requiring CRRT; one component of his multiorgan failure)
7.22 (metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion/multiorgan failure despite maximal support)

nursesNote: ICU Day 7, 1530 — 74 y/o man, ICU Day 7 after a prolonged out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, intubated on norepinephrine 0.24 mcg/kg/min and CRRT for anuric AKI with multiorgan failure. Multimodal neuroprognostication ≥72 h after rewarming shows devastating anoxic brain injury (GCS 3 off sedation, absent pupillary/corneal reflexes, status myoclonus, bilaterally absent N20 SSEP, malignant EEG, NSE 95) — extremely poor prognosis. He is NOT brain dead: he intermittently over-breathes the ventilator and retains some brainstem function, so this is a values-based goals-of-care decision, not a declaration of death. No written advance directive; wife is the legal surrogate (spouse). She states he repeatedly said he 'never wanted to be kept alive on machines with no chance of recovery'; their adult son wants the team to 'do everything.' Confirmed the patient lacks capacity and identified the wife as legal surrogate per the hierarchy (no POA on file). Coordinated an interdisciplinary family meeting (intensivist, RN, chaplain, social work); prognosis shared compassionately; conversation refocused on what HE would want (substituted judgment), not on the family's preferences. Offered an ethics consultation for the wife–son conflict and to address futility. With support, the family reached a comfort-focused decision consistent with his prior statements: code status changed to DNR and a comfort-care/withdrawal plan with anticipatory opioid, benzodiazepine, and antisecretory orders was written. Plan for terminal extubation Day 8: stop norepinephrine, CRRT, routine labs/vitals, monitors and alarms; premedicate and titrate morphine + midazolam to comfort (double effect) with glycopyrrolate for secretions; family presence, chaplaincy, and bereavement support; tissue-donation eligibility screened with the OPO per policy. Explained we are withdrawing nonbeneficial TREATMENT while intensifying COMFORT — not 'withdrawing care.' Did NOT coerce the family, did NOT equate withdrawal with euthanasia, did NOT withhold comfort medication for fear of hastening death, did NOT continue futile monitoring, did NOT let the son override the legal surrogate and the patient's known wishes, and did NOT abandon the patient. Wife and son supported and updated.
providerOrders: GOALS OF CARE: confirm the patient lacks decision-making capacity; identify the legal surrogate (healthcare agent/POA if any, otherwise spouse per the default hierarchy); decisions to be made by SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT based on the patient's known values and prior statements

FAMILY MEETING: convene an interdisciplinary family conference (intensivist, bedside RN, chaplain, social work, ± palliative care) to share prognosis and elicit the patient's values; offer an ETHICS COMMITTEE consultation to help resolve the family conflict and address questions of medical futility
PROGNOSIS: communicate the multimodal neuroprognostication findings honestly and compassionately; clarify that the patient is NOT brain dead and that this is a values-based goals-of-care decision
CODE STATUS: upon a comfort-focused decision, change code status to DNR/DNAR and document the comfort-care/withdrawal plan
DISCONTINUE NONBENEFICIAL INTERVENTIONS: stop vasopressors and CRRT; discontinue routine labs, vital-sign checks, monitors, and alarms; stop artificial nutrition/tube feeds per the agreed goals

COMFORT MEDICATIONS: titrated OPIOID (morphine) for dyspnea/pain and BENZODIAZEPINE (midazolam) for agitation, with PRN boluses; titrate to relief of distress (air hunger, grimacing, tachypnea) under the doctrine of double effect — no arbitrary dose ceiling when symptoms warrant; ANTISECRETORY agent (glycopyrrolate or scopolamine) for terminal secretions

TERMINAL EXTUBATION: premedicate for comfort, then perform terminal weaning or one-step extubation; provide suction, mouth care, and comfort positioning; reassess and re-dose comfort medications continuously
FAMILY + SPIRITUAL SUPPORT: maximize family presence at the bedside; offer chaplaincy and culturally appropriate rituals; provide bereavement support before and after death

ORGAN/TISSUE DONATION: make a timely referral to the Organ Procurement Organization (OPO) per policy (notification only; do not make suitability judgments; the OPO approaches the family separately after decoupling)

STAFF SUPPORT: honor any conscientious objection to participation only with advance notice, a competent replacement, and assured continuity of care — the patient is never to be abandoned; offer team debrief after the death

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically and ethically significant cues.

opts.text: Multimodal neuroprognostication ≥72 h after rewarming shows devastating anoxic brain injury (absent pupillary/corneal reflexes, status myoclonus, bilaterally absent N20 SSEP, malignant EEG, NSE 95) with an extremely poor prognosis
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — concordant multimodal findings at the appropriate time establish the poor prognosis that frames the goals-of-care conversation.

opts.text: He is NOT brain dead — he intermittently over-breathes the ventilator and retains some brainstem function — so this is a values-based goals-of-care decision, not a declaration of death
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — distinguishing a poor-prognosis decision from brain death (a separate legal determination) is essential to framing the ethics correctly.

opts.text: He has NO written advance directive, and his wife (spouse) and adult son disagree about what he would want
opts.rat: RELEVANT — the absence of a document plus family conflict makes identifying the surrogate and applying substituted judgment central.

opts.text: He repeatedly told his wife he 'never wanted to be kept alive on machines with no chance of recovery'
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — consistent prior statements are strong evidence of his wishes and anchor a substituted-judgment decision.

opts.text: He remains on escalating norepinephrine and CRRT with multiorgan failure and no purposeful response on ICU Day 7
opts.rat: RELEVANT — the trajectory of multiorgan failure despite maximal support informs prognosis and the benefit/burden discussion.

opts.text: Because he is not brain dead, treatment must legally continue indefinitely until he meets brain-death criteria
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. A non-brain-dead patient with a poor prognosis can have life-sustaining treatment withdrawn based on his wishes/surrogate decision — survival to brain death is not required.

opts.text: Because the wife and son disagree, the nurse should pick whichever option seems best and proceed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. The nurse does not decide; the legal surrogate decides using substituted judgment, and persistent conflict goes to the ethics committee.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: What do these facts mean ethically and legally?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: This is a values-based goals-of-care decision for an incapacitated adult — the surrogate decides by SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT (what HE would choose), not by her own preferences
opts.rat: CORRECT — substituted judgment is the primary standard for an adult who once had capacity.

opts.text: The legal surrogate hierarchy applies (spouse first, then adult children) — the son does not override the wife unless state law or a valid document says otherwise
opts.rat: CORRECT — default surrogate hierarchies rank the spouse ahead of adult children absent a named agent or contrary law.

opts.text: Withdrawing life-sustaining treatment is ethically and legally permissible and is NOT euthanasia — it allows the underlying disease to cause death
opts.rat: CORRECT — withdrawal allows natural death; intent and causation differ from euthanasia/physician-assisted death.

opts.text: An ethics consultation is appropriate to help resolve the family conflict and clarify futility, rather than a unilateral decision by any one clinician
opts.rat: CORRECT — ethics committees provide a fair, transparent process for intractable conflict.

opts.text: Titrating opioids/benzodiazepines to relieve dyspnea and agitation is appropriate even if a foreseen, unintended effect could be a hastened death (doctrine of double effect)
opts.rat: CORRECT — the intent is symptom relief; comfort is the duty and there is no arbitrary dose ceiling when symptoms warrant.

opts.text: Since he can't speak for himself, the team should decide based purely on the clinicians' view of futility, disregarding his prior statements
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. His known values and prior statements govern via substituted judgment; value judgments about a 'worthwhile' outcome belong to the patient/surrogate, not clinicians alone.

opts.text: Withdrawing the ventilator is the same as actively euthanizing the patient and is illegal
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Withdrawal of unwanted treatment is legal and ethically distinct from euthanasia; withholding and withdrawing are ethically equivalent.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these steps from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Confirm the patient lacks capacity and identify the legal surrogate (healthcare agent/POA if any, otherwise spouse per the hierarchy)
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Establishing who is authorized to decide is the foundation for everything that follows.

opts.text: Convene an interdisciplinary family meeting to share prognosis compassionately and elicit the patient's values
opts.rat: #2 — Bring the team and family together to inform the decision and surface what HE would want.

opts.text: Apply substituted judgment using his prior statements; offer an ethics consultation if the family conflict persists
opts.rat: #3 — Reach a values-based decision, using the ethics committee to mediate intractable conflict.

opts.text: Once a comfort-focused plan is chosen, change code status to DNR and write the comfort-care/withdrawal plan with anticipatory symptom orders
opts.rat: #4 — Operationalize the decision with the orders needed for a safe, comfortable withdrawal.

opts.text: Carry out the comfort-focused terminal extubation with family present and ongoing bereavement support
opts.rat: #5 — Execute the plan, prioritizing comfort, presence, and support.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Support the wife as legal surrogate to voice what HER HUSBAND would want, using his prior statements (substituted judgment)
opts.rat: Keeps the decision anchored in the patient's values and respects the surrogate's proper role.

opts.text: Offer an ethics committee consultation to help resolve the disagreement between the wife and son and address futility
opts.rat: A fair, transparent process for conflict rather than unilateral clinician action.

opts.text: Pre-medicate with titrated opioids ± benzodiazepines and an antisecretory agent before and during extubation to ensure comfort
opts.rat: Anticipatory, titrated comfort medication prevents and relieves dyspnea, agitation, and secretions (double effect).

opts.text: Discontinue nonbeneficial interventions per the comfort plan — vasopressors, CRRT, routine labs, vital-sign checks, and alarms — and stop tube feeds per goals
opts.rat: Removing nonbeneficial, burdensome interventions aligns care with the comfort-focused goal.

opts.text: Provide chaplaincy, family presence, and bereavement support, and make an organ/tissue-donation referral to the OPO per policy
opts.rat: Holistic end-of-life care includes spiritual/emotional support and the legally required donation referral (notification only).

opts.text: Tell the family the team is 'withdrawing care' and there is 'nothing more we can do'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — we withdraw nonbeneficial TREATMENT while intensifying COMFORT; this language abandons the family and is inaccurate.

opts.text: Withhold ordered opioids during terminal extubation out of fear of hastening death
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — under the doctrine of double effect, comfort is the duty; withholding indicated symptom relief causes needless suffering.

opts.text: Let the son unilaterally overrule the wife and demand continued aggressive treatment the patient would not have wanted
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the son does not outrank the spouse-surrogate, and the patient's known wishes govern.

opts.text: Pressure or guilt the surrogate toward a particular choice to speed the decision
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — coercion violates autonomy; the nurse informs and supports without imposing a choice.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Establish the legal surrogate and ensure the prognosis is communicated clearly and compassionately
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Identify who decides and make sure the decision will be informed.

opts.text: Facilitate the interdisciplinary family meeting, reframe around HIS values (substituted judgment), and offer an ethics consult for the conflict
opts.rat: #2 — Bring the team and family together, focus on the patient's wishes, and mediate disagreement.

opts.text: Once a comfort-focused goal is agreed, obtain DNR and comfort-care/withdrawal orders with anticipatory symptom-management medications
opts.rat: #3 — Translate the decision into the orders required for a safe, comfortable withdrawal.

opts.text: Prepare for terminal extubation: stop vasopressors/CRRT/labs/alarms, premedicate for comfort, manage secretions, position the patient, and bring the family to the bedside
opts.rat: #4 — Set up the environment and the patient for a comfortable, dignified withdrawal with family present.

opts.text: Perform the terminal extubation, titrate comfort medications to relieve any distress (double effect), and provide continuous presence and bereavement support
opts.rat: #5 — Execute the withdrawal with comfort as the priority and sustained support for the family.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action or outcome as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

opts.text: The nurse helps the wife voice what HER HUSBAND would have wanted, keeping the focus on his values rather than the family's preferences
opts.rat: This is substituted judgment applied correctly — the surrogate speaks for the patient.

opts.text: An ethics consult is offered when the son and wife remain in conflict, rather than one clinician deciding unilaterally
opts.rat: The ethics committee provides a fair process for intractable conflict and futility questions.

opts.text: Before extubation the patient receives titrated morphine and an antisecretory agent and appears calm with no air hunger or distress
opts.rat: Anticipatory, titrated comfort medication achieving symptom control is the goal of a comfort-focused withdrawal.

opts.text: The team explains they are withdrawing nonbeneficial TREATMENTS while intensifying COMFORT, and continues to bathe, reposition, and attend to the patient
opts.rat: Care is never withdrawn — only nonbeneficial treatment; comfort, hygiene, and presence continue.

opts.text: The nurse withholds ordered opioids during extubation because she worries they might hasten death, and the patient develops visible air hunger and grimacing
opts.rat: ⚠️ Under the doctrine of double effect, comfort is the duty; withholding indicated symptom relief causes needless suffering.

opts.text: The team proceeds with aggressive treatment the patient explicitly never wanted because the son insists, overriding the wife and his known wishes
opts.rat: ⚠️ The son does not outrank the spouse-surrogate, and the patient's known wishes govern the decision.

opts.text: Staff tell the family 'there's nothing more we can do' and stop comfort medications and routine hygiene
opts.rat: ⚠️ Abandoning comfort care and using hopeless language violates the duty to care; only nonbeneficial treatment is withdrawn.

opts.text: A nurse with a conscientious objection quietly leaves without arranging coverage, briefly leaving the patient unattended during the withdrawal
opts.rat: ⚠️ Conscientious objection requires advance notice, a competent replacement, and continuity of care — never abandonment.

opts.text: After extubation the patient dies peacefully within hours with family present, no signs of distress, and bereavement support provided
opts.rat: A comfortable, dignified death consistent with the patient's wishes, with the family supported, reflects the goal of care being met.

title: DELEGATION and SUPERVISION in a SKILLED NURSING FACILITY (Long-Term Care): A Day-Shift Charge RN Applies the FIVE RIGHTS OF DELEGATION and the RN-vs-LVN/LPN-vs-UAP/CNA SCOPE Matrix Across a Resident Assignment (1 LVN + 2 CNAs) When a NEW ADMISSION Arrives From the Hospital AND a Previously Stable Resident ACUTELY DETERIORATES (New Fever, Confusion, Falling SpO2, and a CNA Report of Poor Intake + Coughing With Thin Liquids) — Deciding What Can and CANNOT Be Delegated (NEVER Assessment, the Initial Teaching, Evaluation, Nursing Judgment, or the Care of an UNSTABLE Resident), Understanding That Delegating a TASK Does NOT Transfer ACCOUNTABILITY, Matching RIGHT TASK / RIGHT CIRCUMSTANCE / RIGHT PERSON / RIGHT DIRECTION-COMMUNICATION / RIGHT SUPERVISION, Acting on a UAP's Abnormal Report, and Following Up to Supervise and Evaluate Outcomes
subtitle: Safe DELEGATION is a core RN leadership competency and a heavily tested NCLEX topic. This case puts T. Nguyen, RN, in charge of a long-term-care/skilled-nursing unit on day shift with one LVN/LPN and two CNAs (UAPs) and ~20 residents, when two demands collide: a NEW ADMISSION is arriving from the hospital (post-op hip, stable) and needs an admission assessment, medication reconciliation, and initial teaching, AND a previously stable resident (Mr. Ellison) ACUTELY DETERIORATES with a new fever, new confusion, a falling SpO2, and a CNA report that he ate less than 25% of his meals for two days and now COUGHS with thin liquids (a dysphagia/aspiration red flag). The RN must apply the FIVE RIGHTS OF DELEGATION — RIGHT TASK (a routine, standardized task with a predictable outcome), RIGHT CIRCUMSTANCE (a STABLE resident), RIGHT PERSON (matched to verified competence and scope), RIGHT DIRECTION/COMMUNICATION (clear, specific instructions including what and when to report back and the expected outcome, with confirmed understanding), and RIGHT SUPERVISION/EVALUATION (monitoring, follow-up, and evaluating the outcome) — and the RN/LVN/UAP SCOPE MATRIX: a UAP/CNA performs ADLs, hygiene, feeding (only when there is NO dysphagia), ambulation, repositioning, routine vital signs and weights on STABLE residents, intake/output, and point-of-care glucose per policy — collecting DATA to REPORT to the nurse, but NEVER assessing, interpreting, teaching, or (in most settings) administering medications; an LVN/LPN may administer most PO/IM/SQ medications, reinforce teaching, perform routine ostomy/wound/tube-feeding care, gather data, and monitor STABLE residents with predictable outcomes, all under the RN's direction; and the RN RETAINS the initial and ongoing ASSESSMENT, care PLANNING, the INITIAL teaching, EVALUATION of outcomes, clinical JUDGMENT, IV push/titration and the care of UNSTABLE residents. Two principles anchor the case: (1) delegating a TASK does NOT transfer ACCOUNTABILITY — the RN remains accountable for the delegation decision and for supervising it; and (2) a task that is normally delegable becomes NON-delegable when the resident is UNSTABLE or the outcome is UNPREDICTABLE (so the deteriorating resident's vital signs and assessment must be done by the RN, not a CNA). The RN therefore assesses Mr. Ellison personally, acts on the dysphagia report (hold PO, position upright, oxygen as needed, notify provider, arrange swallow evaluation), performs the new admission's RN assessment/med reconciliation/initial teaching, delegates the right STABLE-resident tasks to the LVN (scheduled meds, reinforce established teaching) and the CNAs (ADLs, routine vitals, I&O, glucose) with clear direction, and SUPERVISES and FOLLOWS UP on every delegated task — never dismissing the CNA's abnormal report, never assigning out-of-scope work (e.g., an LVN pushing/titrating an IV medication on an unstable resident or a CNA performing an admission assessment or initial teaching), and never assuming accountability ended when the task was handed off. This is DISTINCT from the acute-care charge-RN shift-assignment/triage case ([[case-078]]) and the various rapid-response/code leadership cases ([[case-079]], [[case-091]], [[case-150]], [[case-131]]): the focus here is the Five Rights and the long-term-care RN/LVN/UAP scope matrix. Step-6 evaluates whether each action is APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE.

vitals.spo2: 97% RA; T 36.8°C; alert at baseline, no dysphagia; needs bath, ambulation, morning vital signs, I&O, and a point-of-care glucose per policy — appropriate to DELEGATE to a CNA with clear direction

vitals.time: Resident B — NEW ADMISSION arriving from hospital (post-op Day 3 R hip ORIF)
vitals.spo2: 96% RA; T 37.0°C; stable but requires the RN ADMISSION ASSESSMENT, medication reconciliation (incl. enoxaparin), skin/fall-risk evaluation, and INITIAL teaching — RN responsibilities that are NOT delegable; CNA may assist with ADLs/vitals once stable

vitals.time: Resident C (Mr. Ellison) — previously stable, now ACUTELY DETERIORATING

vitals.time: Resident E — stable, established daily dressing change
vitals.spo2: 97% RA; T 37.1°C; a healing pressure injury with an ESTABLISHED, routine dressing order (predictable, stable) may be delegated to the LVN; a NEW wound or change would require the RN's assessment first; a CNA cannot perform wound care

vitals.time: Team/assignment snapshot — re-prioritizing after the deterioration + admission
vitals.spo2: Team = RN + 1 LVN/LPN + 2 CNAs. RN re-prioritizes: personally assess the unstable resident first, act on the aspiration risk, perform the admission, and delegate stable-resident tasks with clear direction and supervision — accountability for the delegation stays with the RN

labs.v: Delegation = transferring authority to perform a selected TASK to a competent person, while the RN retains ACCOUNTABILITY. The five rights: (1) RIGHT TASK — a routine, standardized task with a predictable outcome and minimal judgment; (2) RIGHT CIRCUMSTANCE — a STABLE resident with a predictable course (an unstable/unpredictable situation is NOT delegable); (3) RIGHT PERSON — matched to the delegatee's legal scope AND verified competence; (4) RIGHT DIRECTION/COMMUNICATION — clear, specific instructions (what to do, how, by when, exactly WHAT and WHEN to report back, and the expected outcome), with confirmed understanding; (5) RIGHT SUPERVISION/EVALUATION — the RN monitors, is available, follows up, intervenes as needed, and EVALUATES the outcome.
labs.r: Right TASK (routine, predictable) + Right CIRCUMSTANCE (stable resident) + Right PERSON (scope + competence) + Right DIRECTION (clear, specific, with report-back parameters + confirmed understanding) + Right SUPERVISION/EVALUATION (monitor, follow up, evaluate).

labs.n: What the RN can NEVER delegate + accountability is NOT transferred
labs.v: The RN may NOT delegate the steps of the nursing process that require professional JUDGMENT: the initial and ongoing ASSESSMENT, NURSING DIAGNOSIS/care PLANNING, the INITIAL patient TEACHING, and the EVALUATION of outcomes — nor the care of an UNSTABLE or unpredictable resident. (An LVN/LPN may REINFORCE teaching the RN began, but the initial teaching and its evaluation remain the RN's.) A useful memory aid is that you cannot delegate what requires assessment, teaching, evaluation, or judgment. Critically, delegating a TASK does NOT transfer ACCOUNTABILITY: the RN remains accountable for the DECISION to delegate, for delegating within the delegatee's scope/competence, and for supervising and evaluating the result. The delegatee is responsible for performing the task correctly and reporting back.
labs.r: Never delegate ASSESSMENT, care PLANNING, INITIAL teaching, EVALUATION, clinical JUDGMENT, or the UNSTABLE resident. Delegating a task does NOT transfer accountability — the RN stays accountable for the delegation + supervision; the delegatee is responsible for correct performance + reporting.

labs.n: SCOPE MATRIX — RN vs LVN/LPN vs UAP/CNA
labs.v: UAP/CNA (unlicensed): ADLs, bathing/hygiene, FEEDING residents who have NO dysphagia/aspiration risk, ambulation/transfers, repositioning, routine VITAL SIGNS and weights on STABLE residents, intake/output, specimen collection, and point-of-care glucose per facility policy — they COLLECT DATA and REPORT to the nurse but do NOT assess, interpret, teach, or (in most settings) administer medications. LVN/LPN: administers most PO/IM/SQ medications, REINFORCES teaching, performs routine/established wound, ostomy, and tube-feeding care, gathers data, and monitors STABLE residents with predictable outcomes — all under the RN's direction; LVNs generally do NOT do IV-push medications, blood administration, titration, the initial admission assessment, or the care of unstable residents. RN: initial + ongoing ASSESSMENT, care PLANNING, INITIAL teaching, EVALUATION, clinical judgment, IV push/blood/titration, and the care of UNSTABLE residents.
labs.r: UAP/CNA: ADLs, hygiene, feeding (no dysphagia), ambulation, repositioning, routine vitals/weights/I&O/glucose on STABLE residents — data collection + reporting only. LVN/LPN: PO/IM/SQ meds, reinforce teaching, routine wound/ostomy/tube care, monitor STABLE residents under RN. RN: assessment, planning, initial teaching, evaluation, judgment, IV push/blood/titration, UNSTABLE residents.

labs.n: When a normally delegable task becomes NON-delegable (Right Circumstance/Right Person)
labs.v: Stability and predictability decide. A task that is routinely delegated to a CNA (e.g., taking vital signs) becomes NON-delegable when the resident is UNSTABLE or the result will require assessment/judgment to interpret — so the DETERIORATING resident's vital signs and assessment are done BY THE RN. The RN also matches the task to the delegatee's VERIFIED competence (not just the job title) and the resident's needs, then gives Right Direction: state the specific task, how and when to do it, the data to report and the parameters that require IMMEDIATE notification (e.g., 'tell me right away if his temperature is over 38, his oxygen is under 94%, or he coughs while eating/drinking'), and the expected outcome — and confirm the delegatee understands.
labs.r: Delegability depends on STABILITY + predictability: an unstable resident's vitals/assessment = RN, even if vitals are 'normally' a CNA task. Match to verified competence (not title alone); give specific direction with report-back parameters + immediate-notification thresholds + expected outcome; confirm understanding.

labs.n: SUPERVISION, follow-up, acting on a UAP report + PERTINENT NEGATIVES
labs.v: After delegating, the RN SUPERVISES — remains available, checks in, follows up that tasks were done correctly and on time, intervenes if needed, and EVALUATES the outcome and the resident's response. A UAP's report of an abnormal finding (here, poor intake + coughing with thin liquids, plus new confusion) is DATA the RN must act on: hold oral intake, keep the resident upright, provide oxygen as needed, ASSESS, notify the provider, and arrange a swallow evaluation — never dismiss it. PERTINENT NEGATIVES (correct practice): did NOT delegate the unstable resident's assessment or vital-sign interpretation to a CNA; did NOT ask a CNA to perform the new admission's assessment or initial teaching; did NOT direct the LVN to push/titrate an IV medication on an unstable resident; did NOT feed or allow PO intake for a resident coughing with liquids; did NOT ignore the CNA's report because the resident 'looked fine'; did NOT assume accountability ended when the task was handed off; and did NOT fail to follow up/supervise.
labs.r: Supervise: stay available, follow up, evaluate outcomes + resident response. A UAP's abnormal report = act on it (hold PO, upright, O2, ASSESS, notify, swallow eval) — never dismiss. NEGATIVES: don't delegate unstable-resident assessment, admission assessment/initial teaching, or out-of-scope tasks (LVN IV push/titration on unstable); don't ignore UAP reports; don't assume accountability transferred; always follow up.

labs.n: Resident C (Mr. Ellison) — RN focused assessment of the deterioration
labs.v: T 38.6°C, HR 104, RR 24, SpO2 92% on room air, NEW confusion from baseline; lungs with possible crackles at the right base; coughs with thin liquids — concerning for ASPIRATION/pneumonia, with UTI/delirium also on the differential in an older adult. Unstable + judgment-dependent → the RN performs and interprets this assessment.
labs.r: Stable baseline; afebrile; SpO2 ≥ 94%; at-baseline cognition; no cough with intake. New fever + confusion + hypoxia + cough with liquids = unstable, RN assessment required.

labs.r: Eats ≥ most of meals; no coughing/choking with food or liquids. Poor intake + coughing with thin liquids = aspiration red flag → RN action.

labs.r: Admission assessment + med reconciliation + initial teaching completed by the RN; ADLs delegable to a CNA once stable.

nursesNote: 0715 — Skilled-nursing unit, day shift; RN charge with 1 LVN/LPN + 2 CNAs and ~20 residents. Two competing demands this hour: a new admission (post-op Day 3 R hip ORIF, stable) is arriving and needs the RN admission assessment, med reconciliation, and initial teaching; and Mr. Ellison (Resident C), previously stable, has deteriorated — T 38.6, HR 104, RR 24, SpO2 92% RA, NEW confusion, and a CNA report that he ate <25% of meals × 2 days and now coughs with thin liquids (aspiration red flag). Recognized Mr. Ellison as UNSTABLE: went to him and performed the focused assessment myself (did NOT delegate the assessment or vital-sign interpretation to a CNA). Acted on the dysphagia report — held PO intake, kept him upright, applied oxygen, notified the provider, and requested a swallow evaluation and workup (possible aspiration pneumonia vs UTI/delirium). Applied the Five Rights of Delegation: delegated stable-resident ADLs, ambulation, routine vitals, I&O, and point-of-care glucose to the CNAs with clear direction and explicit report-back parameters (notify me immediately for T >38, SpO2 <94%, or coughing with intake); assigned the LVN/LPN to administer stable residents' scheduled PO/SQ meds, reinforce established teaching, and perform Resident E's established routine dressing under my supervision (a NEW wound or change would require my assessment first). Completed the new admission's RN assessment, medication reconciliation, skin/fall-risk evaluation, and initial teaching myself. Will supervise and follow up on all delegated tasks and evaluate outcomes — accountability for the delegation decisions remains mine. Did NOT delegate the unstable resident or the admission assessment/initial teaching to unlicensed staff, did NOT direct the LVN to push/titrate IV medication on an unstable resident, did NOT allow PO intake while he was coughing with liquids, did NOT dismiss the CNA's report, and did NOT assume accountability ended at hand-off.
providerOrders: DELEGATION FRAMEWORK: charge RN to apply the Five Rights of Delegation (right task, right circumstance, right person, right direction/communication, right supervision/evaluation) and the RN/LVN/UAP scope matrix across the assignment
UNSTABLE RESIDENT (Mr. Ellison): RN to perform and interpret the focused assessment (not delegable); obtain vital signs, oxygen saturation, lung sounds, and mental-status exam personally

ASPIRATION/DYSPHAGIA PRECAUTIONS: hold oral intake, keep upright, provide oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 94%, notify provider, and arrange a swallow/dysphagia evaluation before further PO intake; obtain ordered workup (e.g., chest imaging, urinalysis/cultures, labs) for the new fever + confusion

NEW ADMISSION (post-op hip): RN to complete the admission assessment, medication reconciliation (including enoxaparin), skin and fall-risk evaluation, and initial teaching; delegate stable ADLs to a CNA once stable

DELEGATE TO CNAs/UAPs: ADLs, hygiene, ambulation, repositioning, routine vital signs and weights on STABLE residents, intake/output, and point-of-care glucose per policy — with clear direction, report-back parameters, and immediate-notification thresholds (data collection only; no assessment/teaching/medication administration)

ASSIGN TO LVN/LPN: administer stable residents' scheduled PO/IM/SQ medications, reinforce established teaching, and perform routine/established wound, ostomy, and tube-feeding care for STABLE residents under RN direction (no IV push, titration, blood administration, admission assessment, or unstable-resident care)
SUPERVISION/EVALUATION: RN to monitor, remain available, follow up on all delegated tasks, evaluate outcomes and resident responses, and re-prioritize the assignment as conditions change
ESCALATION OF UAP REPORTS: any UAP-reported abnormal finding (poor intake, coughing with intake, new symptoms, out-of-range vitals) is to be reported to and assessed by the RN promptly

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What requires the charge RN's attention?
steps.inst: Select ALL clinically and managerially significant cues.

opts.text: Mr. Ellison (Resident C) has a new fever, new confusion, a falling SpO2 (92%), and tachypnea — a previously stable resident who is now UNSTABLE
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — an acutely deteriorating, unstable resident requires RN assessment and clinical judgment and cannot be delegated.

opts.text: The CNA reports he ate <25% of meals × 2 days and now coughs with thin liquids — a dysphagia/aspiration red flag that must be assessed
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — this UAP-collected data signals aspiration risk and must be acted on by the RN, not dismissed.

opts.text: A new admission is arriving from the hospital and needs an admission assessment, medication reconciliation, and initial teaching
opts.rat: RELEVANT — admission assessment and initial teaching are RN responsibilities and must be planned into the workload.

opts.text: Routine tasks remain due for stable residents — morning vital signs, ADLs, ambulation, point-of-care glucose, and scheduled established medications
opts.rat: RELEVANT — these predictable, standardized tasks for stable residents are candidates for appropriate delegation.

opts.text: The RN has one LVN/LPN and two CNAs to coordinate across the assignment
opts.rat: RELEVANT — knowing the team's scope and competence is the basis for matching tasks to the right person.

opts.text: Because the unit is busy, the CNA can complete the new admission's assessment and teaching to save time
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Admission assessment and initial teaching require nursing judgment and are RN responsibilities — never delegated to a UAP.

opts.text: The deteriorating resident's vital signs can be delegated to the CNA and interpreted later
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. On an unstable resident, vital signs and assessment are done by the RN — the circumstance is no longer right for delegation.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: What do these facts mean for delegation?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate interpretations.

opts.text: The unstable, deteriorating resident requires RN assessment and clinical judgment — this cannot be delegated
opts.rat: CORRECT — assessment and care of an unstable resident are RN-only responsibilities.

opts.text: The CNA's report of poor intake and coughing with liquids is data the RN must act on — hold PO, position upright, assess, notify the provider, and arrange a swallow evaluation
opts.rat: CORRECT — UAPs collect and report data; acting on it (and the assessment) is the RN's role.

opts.text: The admission assessment and initial teaching are RN responsibilities; the CNA may assist with ADLs and routine vitals once the resident is stable
opts.rat: CORRECT — initial assessment/teaching stay with the RN, while stable ADLs/vitals are delegable.

opts.text: Stable residents' ADLs, hygiene, ambulation, routine vitals, I&O, and point-of-care glucose are appropriate to delegate to the CNAs
opts.rat: CORRECT — these are routine, predictable tasks within UAP scope for stable residents.

opts.text: The LVN/LPN may administer stable residents' scheduled PO/SQ medications and reinforce established teaching under the RN's direction
opts.rat: CORRECT — within LVN scope for stable residents with predictable outcomes, under RN supervision.

opts.text: Delegating these tasks transfers the RN's accountability for them to the LVN and CNAs
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Delegating a task does not transfer accountability — the RN remains accountable for the delegation and its supervision.

opts.text: Because the CNA already took his vital signs, no further nursing assessment of the deteriorating resident is needed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Vital-sign numbers are data; the RN must still assess and interpret the unstable resident's full picture.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these actions from #1 (HIGHEST priority) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Personally assess the deteriorating, unstable resident (Mr. Ellison) — airway/breathing, oxygenation, mental status, and vital signs
opts.rat: #1 — HIGHEST. The unstable resident needs immediate RN assessment and judgment.

opts.text: Act on the aspiration risk — hold PO intake, keep him upright, provide oxygen, notify the provider, and arrange a swallow evaluation
opts.rat: #2 — Protect the airway and start the workup once the deterioration is recognized.

opts.text: Complete the new admission's RN assessment, medication reconciliation, and initial teaching
opts.rat: #3 — A required RN responsibility for the incoming resident, performed after the unstable resident is addressed.

opts.text: Delegate stable residents' ADLs, routine vitals, and glucose checks to the CNAs and scheduled meds to the LVN, with clear direction
opts.rat: #4 — Distribute routine, predictable work to the right team members so care continues.

opts.text: Follow up on and supervise all delegated tasks and evaluate the outcomes
opts.rat: #5 — Supervision and evaluation complete the delegation process and remain the RN's accountability.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH action, classify as INDICATED or NOT INDICATED.

opts.text: Assess Mr. Ellison personally; do not delegate the unstable resident's assessment
opts.rat: Assessment and care of an unstable resident are RN-only.

opts.text: Hold his oral intake, keep him upright, provide oxygen, notify the provider, and arrange a swallow evaluation after the coughing-with-liquids report
opts.rat: Protects the airway and initiates appropriate workup for aspiration risk.

opts.text: Delegate stable residents' bathing, ambulation, routine vitals, I&O, and glucose checks to the CNAs with clear direction and report-back parameters
opts.rat: Routine, predictable tasks within UAP scope, delegated with the right direction.

opts.text: Assign the LVN/LPN to administer stable residents' scheduled PO/SQ meds, reinforce established teaching, and do Resident E's established routine dressing under RN supervision
opts.rat: Within LVN scope for stable residents with predictable outcomes, under RN direction.

opts.text: Perform the new admission's RN assessment, medication reconciliation, and initial teaching yourself, then delegate stable follow-up ADLs to a CNA
opts.rat: Initial assessment and teaching are RN responsibilities; routine ADLs are delegable once stable.

opts.text: Ask a CNA to perform the new admission's assessment and initial teaching because the unit is short-staffed
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — assessment and initial teaching require nursing judgment and are never delegated to a UAP.

opts.text: Delegate the deteriorating resident's vital-sign monitoring and interpretation to the CNA and check back at end of shift
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — the unstable resident requires RN assessment and ongoing judgment, not end-of-shift follow-up.

opts.text: Direct the LVN to push and titrate an IV medication on the acutely unstable resident
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — IV push/titration and unstable-resident management are outside typical LVN scope and are RN responsibilities.

opts.text: Dismiss the CNA's report of decreased intake and coughing because the resident 'looks okay'
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — UAP-reported abnormal data must be assessed and acted upon, not dismissed.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Go to and assess the deteriorating resident (airway, breathing, oxygenation, mental status, vital signs) using clinical judgment
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. The unstable resident takes priority and requires RN assessment.

opts.text: Hold PO, position upright, provide oxygen, notify the provider, and arrange a swallow evaluation/workup
opts.rat: #2 — Protect the airway and start the diagnostic workup for the new fever and confusion.

opts.text: Delegate clear, specific tasks to the LVN (scheduled meds, reinforce teaching, established dressing) and the CNAs (ADLs, routine vitals, I&O, glucose), stating what and when to report
opts.rat: #3 — Distribute routine work with the right direction so the rest of the unit is covered.

opts.text: Complete the new admission's RN assessment, medication reconciliation, and initial teaching
opts.rat: #4 — Fulfill the RN-only responsibilities for the incoming resident.

opts.text: Supervise, remain available, follow up on delegated tasks, and evaluate outcomes; re-prioritize as conditions change
opts.rat: #5 — Supervision and evaluation close the loop and remain the RN's accountability.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action as APPROPRIATE or INAPPROPRIATE delegation/supervision.

opts.text: The RN assessed Mr. Ellison herself rather than delegating the unstable resident's assessment
opts.rat: Assessment and care of an unstable resident are RN responsibilities.

opts.text: The CNA's report of low intake and coughing prompted the RN to hold PO and arrange a swallow evaluation
opts.rat: Acting on UAP-reported data to protect the airway is correct nursing judgment.

opts.text: Stable residents' ADLs, routine vitals, and glucose checks were delegated to the CNAs with clear direction and a report-back plan
opts.rat: Routine tasks for stable residents delegated with the Five Rights satisfied.

opts.text: The LVN administered stable residents' scheduled medications and reinforced established teaching under RN supervision
opts.rat: Within LVN scope for stable residents under the RN's direction.

opts.text: The RN delegated the new admission's full assessment and initial teaching to a CNA to save time
opts.rat: ⚠️ Assessment and initial teaching require nursing judgment and are never delegated to a UAP.

opts.text: The RN told the CNA to monitor the deteriorating resident's vitals and report only at end of shift, with no RN assessment
opts.rat: ⚠️ The unstable resident needs prompt RN assessment and judgment, not deferred UAP monitoring.

opts.text: The LVN was directed to push and titrate an IV medication on the acutely unstable resident
opts.rat: ⚠️ IV push/titration and unstable-resident care are RN responsibilities outside typical LVN scope.

opts.text: After delegating tasks, the RN followed up, verified completion, and evaluated outcomes, knowing accountability for the delegation remained with her
opts.rat: Supervision and evaluation complete the delegation process; accountability stays with the RN.

opts.text: The CNA's report of a new abnormal finding was dismissed because the resident 'looked fine'
opts.rat: ⚠️ Abnormal UAP-reported data must be assessed and acted upon, not dismissed.

title: Safe Intravenous PHENYTOIN Loading and NARROW-THERAPEUTIC-INDEX Monitoring in a 27-Year-Old Woman with Epilepsy Admitted After a Breakthrough Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizure from Medication Nonadherence: NEVER Mix in Dextrose (Saline + Inline Filter Only), Slow Rate with Continuous Cardiac/BP Monitoring, Purple-Glove and Extravasation Vigilance, Free-Phenytoin Interpretation in Hypoalbuminemia, and Adverse-Effect + Enzyme-Inducer Drug-Interaction Teaching
subtitle: PHENYTOIN is a first-line antiseizure (anticonvulsant) medication with a NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX (NTI) — the gap between an effective and a toxic dose is small, so it requires careful DOSING and serum-LEVEL MONITORING. The therapeutic TOTAL serum level is about 10-20 mcg/mL (free/unbound ~1-2 mcg/mL). TOXICITY is dose-related and progresses predictably with rising levels: NYSTAGMUS appears first (often >20), then ATAXIA, slurred speech, and DIPLOPIA (~>30), then confusion, lethargy, and ultimately coma/seizures at very high levels (~>40). A crucial interpretation point: phenytoin is HIGHLY PROTEIN-BOUND (to albumin), and only the FREE (unbound) fraction is active. In HYPOALBUMINEMIA (or renal failure/uremia, or with displacing drugs), the TOTAL level UNDER-ESTIMATES the active free drug — a patient can be clinically TOXIC despite a 'normal' total level — so obtain a FREE phenytoin level or use a correction (e.g., Sheiner-Tozer) when albumin is low. INTRAVENOUS phenytoin is HIGH-RISK to administer: it is INCOMPATIBLE WITH DEXTROSE (it PRECIPITATES in dextrose-containing fluids and forms crystals/microemboli), so it is diluted/flushed with NORMAL SALINE ONLY and given through an INLINE FILTER. It must be infused SLOWLY — NOT faster than 50 mg/min in adults (and ≤25 mg/min in older adults or those with cardiac disease) — because rapid infusion causes HYPOTENSION, BRADYCARDIA, heart block, and asystole (largely from the propylene-glycol diluent). Continuous CARDIAC and BLOOD-PRESSURE MONITORING is required during loading; the rate is slowed or stopped for hypotension/bradycardia. Phenytoin is a vesicant: extravasation/infiltration can cause 'PURPLE GLOVE SYNDROME' (limb edema, discoloration, and ischemia), so use a PATENT, large-bore IV in a LARGE vein (avoid small hand/wrist veins), verify blood return, and never IV-push undiluted phenytoin into a small line. FOSPHENYTOIN (a water-soluble prodrug, dosed in 'phenytoin-equivalents'/PE) is often preferred because it is better tolerated, can be given faster and IM, is compatible with saline AND dextrose, and causes less site irritation. CHRONIC/oral adverse effects to teach: GINGIVAL HYPERPLASIA (overgrowth of the gums — meticulous oral hygiene, soft toothbrush, regular dental care), HIRSUTISM and coarsening of facial features, RASH that may herald STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME / DRESS (a serious rash → STOP the drug and notify the provider immediately), folate/vitamin-D/calcium effects (megaloblastic anemia; osteomalacia/osteoporosis with long-term use), and gait/balance changes if levels rise. DRUG INTERACTIONS: phenytoin is a potent hepatic ENZYME INDUCER (CYP450) that REDUCES the effectiveness of many drugs — notably HORMONAL CONTRACEPTIVES (use an ADDITIONAL/backup nonhormonal method), warfarin, and others — and its own level is changed by many drugs (e.g., some antibiotics and antifungals raise it). It is a known TERATOGEN (fetal hydantoin syndrome), so women of childbearing potential need contraception counseling and preconception planning with FOLIC ACID. ADHERENCE is critical: abrupt discontinuation can precipitate status epilepticus, so the drug is NEVER stopped suddenly; missed doses and drug interactions (here, a recent interacting course plus running out of medication) are common precipitants of breakthrough seizures. NURSING ROLE: ensure post-ictal airway/safety and seizure precautions; recognize the breakthrough seizure and the subtherapeutic level; administer IV phenytoin SAFELY (saline only — NEVER dextrose; inline filter; slow rate ≤50 mg/min with continuous cardiac/BP monitoring; large patent vein with extravasation/purple-glove vigilance; consider fosphenytoin); MONITOR serum levels and interpret them in light of ALBUMIN (free level when low); watch for dose-related toxicity (nystagmus → ataxia → confusion) and for serious rash; and TEACH adverse effects (gingival hyperplasia/oral care, report rash), drug interactions (enzyme inducer — additional contraception, warfarin), teratogenicity/folic acid, and strict ADHERENCE (never stop abruptly; consistent levels; follow-up labs).

patient.admitDate: A 27-year-old woman with a known seizure disorder (generalized epilepsy) maintained on oral PHENYTOIN is brought in by EMS after a witnessed GENERALIZED TONIC-CLONIC SEIZURE at work. She reports she RAN OUT of her phenytoin a week ago and recently finished an antibiotic course; she is now postictal — drowsy and confused but protecting her airway. Her serum phenytoin level is SUBTHERAPEUTIC at 6.2 mcg/mL (therapeutic ~10-20) and her serum albumin is LOW at 2.8 g/dL (which means the total level under-represents the active free drug). The provider orders an IV phenytoin/fosphenytoin LOADING dose and resumption of oral maintenance. The nurse must give this NTI medication SAFELY — saline only (NEVER dextrose), inline filter, slow rate (≤50 mg/min) with continuous cardiac and blood-pressure monitoring, a large patent vein with purple-glove/extravasation vigilance — then monitor levels (free level given low albumin), watch for dose-related toxicity, and provide thorough teaching.
