title: Charge-Nurse ASSIGNMENT-MAKING, DELEGATION, and BEHAVIORAL-ESCALATION Leadership on a 20-Bed Adult Inpatient PSYCHIATRIC Unit: Matching Patient Acuity to Staff SCOPE (RN vs LPN/LVN vs UAP/Psych Tech), the FIVE RIGHTS of Delegation, What the RN CANNOT Delegate (Assessment, Evaluation, Initial Teaching, Unstable Patients), Leading VERBAL DE-ESCALATION FIRST with the Least-Restrictive Continuum (Oral PRN Before IM, Restraint/Seclusion LAST), and Staff/Environmental Safety During a Behavioral Emergency
subtitle: This is a LEADERSHIP, DELEGATION, and SAFE-ASSIGNMENT case (distinct from cases that teach the clinical care of a single psychiatric diagnosis). A day-shift CHARGE RN on a 20-bed adult inpatient psychiatric unit (census 18) leads a team of one additional staff RN, one LPN/LVN, and two psychiatric technicians (UAP) across a varied-acuity board — a newly admitted patient on 1:1 CONSTANT OBSERVATION for active suicidal ideation with a plan, a patient in ACUTE MANIA (bipolar I) who is escalating, a patient with first-episode psychosis responding to internal stimuli, a patient with borderline personality disorder testing limits, a patient in alcohol withdrawal on CIWA monitoring, and several stable patients pending discharge. The two intertwined competencies are SAFE DELEGATION/ASSIGNMENT and BEHAVIORAL DE-ESCALATION LEADERSHIP. DELEGATION follows the FIVE RIGHTS — the RIGHT TASK, under the RIGHT CIRCUMSTANCES, to the RIGHT PERSON, with the RIGHT DIRECTION/COMMUNICATION, and the RIGHT SUPERVISION/EVALUATION — and the RN ALWAYS retains ACCOUNTABILITY for the outcome even when a task is delegated. SCOPE OF PRACTICE governs who may do what: the RN performs and is solely responsible for ASSESSMENT, ANALYSIS, care PLANNING, EVALUATION of responses, INITIAL patient teaching, and the care of UNSTABLE or unpredictable patients and any task requiring clinical JUDGMENT — these are NEVER delegated; the LPN/LVN may administer most routine PO/IM/SQ medications, REINFORCE previously taught content, collect/REPORT data, and care for STABLE patients with predictable outcomes, under RN supervision; the UAP/psychiatric technician may perform CONSTANT 1:1 OBSERVATION (with clear parameters and RN oversight), obtain VITAL SIGNS, assist with ADLs/hygiene, transport, and help maintain a calm MILIEU, but never assessment, teaching, evaluation, or medication titration. SAFE ASSIGNMENT-MAKING matches ACUITY to COMPETENCY: the RN keeps the highest-acuity/least-predictable patients (the new 1:1 suicidal patient's risk assessment and safety plan, the escalating manic patient, the first-episode-psychosis assessment) and delegates stable, predictable work appropriately. BEHAVIORAL DE-ESCALATION uses the LEAST-RESTRICTIVE continuum: recognize the ESCALATION cycle (triggering → escalation → crisis) EARLY; lead VERBAL DE-ESCALATION FIRST — a single calm spokesperson, respect personal space, lower environmental stimulation, listen and validate, set clear limits, and offer realistic CHOICES including an ORAL PRN medication (oral is less restrictive than IM); ensure STAFF and ENVIRONMENTAL SAFETY (summon help/a behavioral response, keep your own egress and do NOT corner the patient, remove other patients and dangerous objects, never confront alone); escalate to IM emergency medication ONLY when oral is refused and danger is imminent (with monitoring of sedation/airway/EPS); and reserve SECLUSION/RESTRAINT as the absolute LAST resort, requiring a time-limited, non-PRN provider order, continuous monitoring, and a post-event debrief. The charge nurse uses CLOSED-LOOP communication, supervises and EVALUATES delegated work, reassesses assignments after the event, and leads a post-incident DEBRIEF and documentation. NURSING (CHARGE) ROLE: make safe, scope-appropriate assignments; delegate by the five rights while retaining accountability; protect the highest-acuity patients personally; lead least-restrictive behavioral de-escalation; safeguard staff and the milieu; and supervise, evaluate, debrief, and document.

labs.n: SCOPE OF PRACTICE — RN vs LPN/LVN vs UAP/psychiatric technician
labs.v: Safe delegation begins with SCOPE OF PRACTICE — knowing what each team member may legally and competently do. The REGISTERED NURSE (RN) performs and is solely responsible for ASSESSMENT, ANALYSIS/clinical judgment, care PLANNING, EVALUATION of patient responses, INITIAL patient teaching, and the care of UNSTABLE, complex, or unpredictable patients (e.g., a newly admitted actively suicidal patient, an escalating manic patient, a first-episode-psychosis assessment) — these are NEVER delegated. The LICENSED PRACTICAL/VOCATIONAL NURSE (LPN/LVN) works under RN supervision and may administer most routine PO/IM/SQ medications, REINFORCE teaching the RN already initiated, perform ongoing data COLLECTION and REPORTING, and care for STABLE patients with PREDICTABLE outcomes (LPN/LVN scope generally excludes initial assessment, IV-push high-risk meds in many states, care planning, and patient teaching of new content). The UNLICENSED ASSISTIVE PERSONNEL (UAP)/PSYCHIATRIC TECHNICIAN may perform CONSTANT 1:1 OBSERVATION (with clear parameters and RN oversight), obtain VITAL SIGNS, assist with ADLs/hygiene/meals, transport, and help maintain a calm MILIEU — but NEVER assessment, evaluation, teaching, clinical judgment, or medication titration. Matching the right task to the right scope is the foundation of every safe assignment.
labs.r: RN ONLY: assessment, analysis/judgment, planning, EVALUATION, INITIAL teaching, UNSTABLE/complex patients — NEVER delegated. LPN/LVN (under RN): routine PO/IM/SQ meds, REINFORCE teaching, data collection/reporting, STABLE/PREDICTABLE patients. UAP/tech: 1:1 observation (with parameters + RN oversight), vitals, ADLs, transport, milieu — NO assessment/teaching/evaluation/judgment/titration. Charge role: match task to scope.

labs.n: THE FIVE RIGHTS OF DELEGATION (+ RN retains accountability)
labs.v: Delegation is the transfer of responsibility for performing a TASK to another team member while the RN RETAINS ACCOUNTABILITY for the OUTCOME. It is guided by the FIVE RIGHTS: (1) RIGHT TASK — a routine, predictable task within the delegatee's scope/competency; (2) RIGHT CIRCUMSTANCE — an appropriate, stable setting/patient; (3) RIGHT PERSON — the delegatee is competent and trained for THIS task with THIS patient; (4) RIGHT DIRECTION/COMMUNICATION — a clear, specific description of the task, expected outcome, limits, and what/when to report (closed-loop); and (5) RIGHT SUPERVISION/EVALUATION — the RN monitors performance, intervenes as needed, and EVALUATES the result. Crucially, delegating a task does NOT transfer accountability: if the RN delegates 1:1 observation to a technician, the RN remains accountable for the patient's safety and must give clear parameters and follow up. Tasks involving the nursing PROCESS (assessment, analysis, planning, evaluation), INITIAL teaching, clinical JUDGMENT, or UNSTABLE patients CANNOT be delegated regardless of how busy the unit is.
labs.r: FIVE RIGHTS: right TASK, right CIRCUMSTANCE, right PERSON, right DIRECTION/communication (clear + closed-loop), right SUPERVISION/EVALUATION. RN RETAINS ACCOUNTABILITY even after delegating. CANNOT delegate: assessment, analysis, planning, EVALUATION, INITIAL teaching, judgment, UNSTABLE patients. Being busy never justifies unsafe delegation. Charge role: delegate by the five rights + supervise/evaluate.

labs.n: SAFE ASSIGNMENT-MAKING — match ACUITY to COMPETENCY
labs.v: Making assignments is delegation at the unit level. The charge nurse matches each patient's ACUITY, predictability, and care needs to the team member's SCOPE and demonstrated COMPETENCY. The RN keeps for licensed-RN care the HIGHEST-acuity and LEAST-predictable patients: the newly admitted actively suicidal patient (initial risk assessment + safety plan), the escalating manic patient (active de-escalation + medication decisions), and the first-episode-psychosis patient (assessment of a changing/guarded presentation). STABLE, predictable patients (e.g., those pending discharge, the cooperative patient on maintenance medications) can be assigned to the LPN/LVN within scope, with the RN remaining available for assessment/teaching/evaluation. Continuous OBSERVATION, vitals, ADLs, and milieu support can be assigned to the psychiatric technicians with clear parameters. The charge nurse also balances workload, avoids assigning two highly demanding patients to one person, considers continuity, and stays free enough to respond to emergencies and supervise the team. Assignments are reassessed as acuity changes (e.g., after Mr. D's escalation).
labs.r: Assignment = unit-level delegation. Match ACUITY/predictability to SCOPE + COMPETENCY. RN keeps the high-acuity/unpredictable (new SI risk assessment, escalating mania, first-episode-psychosis assessment). LPN/LVN: stable/predictable within scope. UAP: observation/vitals/ADLs/milieu with parameters. Balance workload, keep charge available to supervise + respond, REASSESS as acuity changes. Charge role: safe acuity-to-competency matching.

labs.v: A high-yield safety principle: certain responsibilities CANNOT be delegated to an LPN/LVN or UAP because they require the RN's education and clinical JUDGMENT. These include the steps of the NURSING PROCESS that require judgment — ASSESSMENT (including the initial and any focused/changing assessment), ANALYSIS/nursing diagnosis, care PLANNING, and EVALUATION of the patient's response to interventions — as well as INITIAL patient/family TEACHING of new content, the care of UNSTABLE or unpredictable patients, and decisions requiring clinical judgment (e.g., titrating a CIWA-based benzodiazepine, deciding to administer an emergency medication, judging suicide risk). An LPN/LVN may REINFORCE teaching the RN already provided and collect/report data, but the RN interprets that data and makes the clinical decisions. A UAP may report observations (e.g., 'he's pacing and yelling') but does NOT assess, interpret, or decide. When a task is unstable, evaluative, judgment-laden, or involves initial teaching — the RN does it.
labs.r: RN CANNOT delegate: ASSESSMENT (initial/focused/changing), ANALYSIS/diagnosis, PLANNING, EVALUATION of response, INITIAL teaching, UNSTABLE-patient care, and JUDGMENT calls (med titration, emergency-med decision, suicide-risk determination). LPN/LVN may REINFORCE teaching + collect/report data; UAP may REPORT observations — neither assesses/interprets/decides. Charge role: keep judgment + assessment + evaluation + initial teaching as RN work.

labs.v: The newly admitted patient with active suicidal ideation and a PLAN is on 1:1 CONSTANT OBSERVATION — continuous, arm's-length, line-of-sight supervision that is never interrupted, including in the bathroom, with environmental safety measures (remove ligature points, cords, sharps, belts/shoelaces, glass, and other means; search belongings per policy). The RN performs the SUICIDE-RISK ASSESSMENT and develops the SAFETY PLAN (these are RN-only). The continuous OBSERVATION itself CAN be delegated to a trained UAP/psychiatric technician — but only with the RIGHT DIRECTION (explicit parameters: never leave the patient, maintain constant visual contact, what behaviors/statements to report immediately, no distractions/phones) and the RIGHT SUPERVISION (the RN checks in, ensures relief for breaks without leaving the patient unobserved, and remains ACCOUNTABLE for the patient's safety). The observer reports observations; the RN interprets them and re-assesses risk. Continuity of the 1:1 must be protected even during a unit emergency — coverage is reassigned, never abandoned.
labs.r: 1:1 constant observation = continuous arm's-length/line-of-sight, even in the bathroom + means-restriction (remove ligatures/cords/sharps/belts). RN does the suicide-risk ASSESSMENT + SAFETY PLAN (RN-only). The OBSERVATION may be delegated to a trained UAP with explicit parameters + RN supervision; RN stays ACCOUNTABLE. Observer REPORTS; RN interprets/re-assesses. Never break 1:1 coverage — reassign during emergencies. Charge role: protect 1:1 continuity.

labs.n: THE AGGRESSION/ESCALATION CYCLE + VERBAL DE-ESCALATION FIRST
labs.v: Behavioral emergencies follow a recognizable ESCALATION CYCLE — a TRIGGERING phase, an ESCALATION phase (rising agitation: pacing, loud/pressured speech, intrusiveness, clenched fists, refusing redirection — Mr. D's current state), a CRISIS/peak, and a recovery/post-crisis phase. The goal is to intervene EARLY, during escalation, with the LEAST-RESTRICTIVE intervention: VERBAL DE-ESCALATION. Key techniques: designate ONE calm spokesperson (avoid multiple voices/crowding); maintain a calm, low tone and non-threatening posture; RESPECT personal space (stay outside arm's reach, at an angle, hands visible); LISTEN and acknowledge the patient's feelings/concerns; LOWER environmental stimulation (reduce noise, move other patients away, dim the area); set CLEAR, simple LIMITS without arguing or power-struggling; and offer realistic CHOICES, including an ORAL PRN medication and a quieter space. De-escalation preserves dignity and the therapeutic relationship and frequently prevents the need for any chemical or physical restraint.
labs.r: Escalation cycle: triggering → ESCALATION (pacing, loud/pressured speech, intrusive, clenched fists) → crisis → recovery. Intervene EARLY with VERBAL DE-ESCALATION (least restrictive): ONE calm spokesperson, low tone, RESPECT personal space (outside arm's reach, hands visible), LISTEN/validate, LOWER stimulation, set clear limits without arguing, offer CHOICES (oral PRN, quiet space). Preserves dignity + often prevents restraint. Charge role: lead verbal de-escalation first.

labs.n: STAFF + ENVIRONMENTAL SAFETY during a behavioral emergency
labs.v: While de-escalating, the charge nurse simultaneously safeguards staff, the patient, and other patients. SUMMON HELP early — activate the unit's behavioral-response procedure so adequate trained staff are present (a show of organized, calm support; never confront an escalating patient ALONE). Position for SAFETY: keep your OWN clear path to an exit, do NOT corner or block the patient's egress (a cornered patient is more likely to strike out), stand at an angle outside arm's reach, and avoid turning your back. Reduce the ENVIRONMENT's danger: quietly move OTHER patients away from the area (their safety and dignity, and removal of an audience that can fuel escalation), and remove or secure objects that could be used as weapons. Assign clear roles (who speaks, who moves patients, who retrieves medication, who calls the provider) using closed-loop communication. Continuous 1:1 and other high-acuity coverage must be maintained throughout — reassign, do not abandon.
labs.r: During escalation: SUMMON HELP/behavioral response early — never confront alone. Keep YOUR exit path; do NOT corner the patient (cornering provokes striking out); stand at an angle, outside arm's reach, don't turn your back. Move OTHER patients away + remove possible weapons. Assign clear roles (speaker, mover, med, provider call) with closed-loop communication. Maintain 1:1/high-acuity coverage — reassign, never abandon. Charge role: staff + environmental safety.

labs.n: PRN / EMERGENCY MEDICATION — least-restrictive route first
labs.v: Medication during agitation follows the LEAST-RESTRICTIVE principle. OFFER an ORAL (PO) PRN medication FIRST when the patient can still participate — oral administration is LESS restrictive than intramuscular and preserves autonomy (e.g., oral olanzapine or another ordered agent; oral concentrate/ODT options aid acceptance). IM EMERGENCY MEDICATION is reserved for when oral is REFUSED AND the patient poses an IMMINENT danger to self or others that verbal de-escalation has not controlled; common regimens include an antipsychotic (e.g., haloperidol) ± a benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam) ± an anticholinergic (e.g., diphenhydramine or benztropine to prevent dystonia) — NOTE: avoid combining IM olanzapine with IM benzodiazepine (excess sedation/cardiorespiratory depression). After ANY sedating medication, MONITOR sedation level, airway/respirations, vital signs, and for extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia/akathisia), and DOCUMENT the indication, attempts at less-restrictive measures, the drug/dose/route, and the response. The RN (not the UAP) decides on, administers/oversees, and evaluates emergency medication.
labs.r: Least-restrictive ROUTE: ORAL PRN FIRST while the patient can participate (oral < IM). IM emergency meds ONLY when oral refused AND imminent danger persists despite de-escalation — antipsychotic (haloperidol) ± benzo (lorazepam) ± anticholinergic (diphenhydramine/benztropine); AVOID IM olanzapine + IM benzo (sedation/cardioresp risk). After sedation: monitor LOC/airway/VS/EPS + document indication, lesser measures tried, drug/dose/route, response. RN decides/evaluates, not UAP. Charge role: oral before IM.

labs.n: SECLUSION / RESTRAINT — the absolute LAST resort
labs.v: Seclusion and physical restraint are the MOST restrictive interventions and are used ONLY as a LAST resort, when the patient poses an imminent danger to self or others and ALL less-restrictive measures (verbal de-escalation, environmental changes, offered oral medication) have failed or are clearly inadequate. Requirements (CMS/Joint Commission): a PROVIDER ORDER that is NOT PRN/standing and is TIME-LIMITED (adult restraint orders generally up to 4 hours, with renewal and required in-person evaluation within set timeframes); the LEAST restrictive effective method; CONTINUOUS or very frequent monitoring of safety, circulation, respiration, hydration, toileting, and behavior; ongoing assessment of readiness for the EARLIEST possible discontinuation (release criteria, not the clock); and a POST-EVENT DEBRIEF with the patient and staff. Restraint is NOT a behavior-management or staffing convenience and is never the first response to pacing or a raised voice. (See the dedicated restraint-safety case for the full standard.) On a psychiatric unit, the emphasis is preventing the need for restraint through early de-escalation.
labs.r: Seclusion/restraint = MOST restrictive = LAST resort: only for imminent danger AFTER less-restrictive measures fail. Needs a TIME-LIMITED, NON-PRN provider order; least-restrictive method; CONTINUOUS monitoring (safety/circulation/respiration/hydration/toileting); release at the EARLIEST safe point (criteria, not clock); post-event DEBRIEF. NOT for convenience and never the first response to pacing/raised voice. Charge role: exhaust least-restrictive first; restraint last.

labs.v: Throughout, the charge nurse leads with CLOSED-LOOP communication (give a clear directive, have it read back, confirm completion), supervises and EVALUATES delegated work (e.g., verifies the technician maintained the 1:1 with the correct parameters; confirms the LPN/LVN gave scheduled medications and reported the CIWA findings for the RN to interpret), and stays available to respond and re-prioritize. After the event, the charge nurse REASSESSES assignments and 1:1 coverage for the changed acuity, leads a POST-INCIDENT DEBRIEF with staff (what triggered it, what worked, lessons, emotional support/countertransference) and, when ready, with the patient (collaborative review and prevention planning), and ensures accurate, objective DOCUMENTATION of the escalation, the least-restrictive measures used, medications, monitoring, and outcomes. PROTECTIVE PRACTICES demonstrated: scope-appropriate assignments; delegation by the five rights with retained accountability; protecting the highest-acuity patients personally; early least-restrictive de-escalation (oral before IM, restraint avoided); staff/environmental safety; uninterrupted 1:1 coverage; and supervision, evaluation, debrief, and documentation. EXPECTED OUTCOME: the manic patient regains control without restraint, no one is injured, the suicidal patient remains safely observed, delegated tasks are completed correctly, and the team debriefs and adjusts.
labs.r: Charge leadership: CLOSED-LOOP communication, SUPERVISE + EVALUATE delegated work (verify 1:1 parameters, confirm LPN meds + reported data for RN to interpret), stay available to re-prioritize. Post-event: REASSESS assignments/1:1, lead a DEBRIEF (staff + patient) + objective DOCUMENTATION. PROTECTIVE: scope-appropriate assignments, five-rights delegation with retained accountability, RN keeps high-acuity, early least-restrictive de-escalation, staff/milieu safety, unbroken 1:1, supervision/evaluation/debrief. Charge role: lead, supervise, debrief, document.

providerOrders: SETTING: 20-bed adult inpatient psychiatric unit; charge RN leads RN + LPN/LVN + 2 psychiatric techs (UAP); make safe scope-appropriate assignments and supervise the team

1:1 CONSTANT OBSERVATION (Bed 4): continuous arm's-length/line-of-sight suicide precautions including bathroom; environmental means-restriction (remove ligatures/cords/sharps/belts/glass); RN performs suicide-risk assessment and safety plan; observation may be delegated to a trained technician with explicit parameters and RN supervision; never interrupt coverage

DELEGATION: follow the five rights (right task, circumstance, person, direction/communication, supervision/evaluation); RN retains accountability; do NOT delegate assessment, analysis, planning, evaluation, initial teaching, unstable-patient care, or judgment (e.g., CIWA-based benzodiazepine titration, emergency-medication decisions)

BEHAVIORAL ESCALATION (Bed 7, acute mania): recognize escalation early; lead VERBAL DE-ESCALATION first (single calm spokesperson, respect personal space, lower stimulation, listen, set clear limits, offer choices including an oral PRN); least-restrictive continuum

SAFETY: activate the behavioral-response procedure; never confront alone; maintain staff egress and do not corner the patient; move other patients away and remove possible weapons; assign roles with closed-loop communication

PRN/EMERGENCY MEDICATION: offer ORAL PRN first (e.g., olanzapine) while the patient can participate; reserve IM emergency medication (antipsychotic ± benzodiazepine ± anticholinergic; avoid IM olanzapine + IM benzodiazepine) for refused oral with imminent danger; monitor sedation/airway/VS/EPS and document

SECLUSION/RESTRAINT: last resort only for imminent danger after less-restrictive measures fail; requires a time-limited, non-PRN provider order, continuous monitoring, earliest safe discontinuation, and a post-event debrief

ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL (Bed 15): CIWA-Ar monitoring; the technician may obtain vitals and report findings, the LPN/LVN may collect data and administer ordered medications within scope, but the RN interprets CIWA scores and directs symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing

SUPERVISION/EVALUATION: charge RN supervises and evaluates all delegated tasks (verify 1:1 parameters maintained; confirm scheduled medications given and data reported for RN interpretation); stay available to respond and re-prioritize

POST-EVENT: reassess assignments and 1:1 coverage for changed acuity; lead a post-incident debrief with staff and (when ready) the patient; ensure accurate, objective documentation of the escalation, least-restrictive measures, medications, monitoring, and outcomes

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for safe assignments and the escalating patient?
steps.inst: Select ALL findings/considerations that are clinically significant.

opts.text: Mr. D (acute mania) is escalating — pacing, loud pressured speech, intrusiveness, clenched fists, rising HR/BP — the escalation phase calling for early verbal de-escalation
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — recognizing escalation early allows the least-restrictive intervention before crisis. Charge role: lead de-escalation now.

opts.text: The newly admitted patient with active suicidal ideation and a plan requires continuous 1:1 observation and a safe environment, with RN risk assessment and safety planning
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the highest-acuity safety need; the RN performs the assessment/plan while observation may be delegated with parameters. Charge role: protect 1:1 coverage.

opts.text: The staff mix (charge RN, staff RN, LPN/LVN, 2 psychiatric techs) and the varied patient acuity must be matched in scope-appropriate assignments
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — assignment-making matches acuity to competency. Charge role: safe assignments.

opts.text: Delegation must follow scope of practice and the five rights, and the RN remains accountable for delegated tasks
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the framework for every safe delegation. Charge role: delegate by the five rights, retain accountability.

opts.text: Verbal de-escalation and least-restrictive measures (including an offered oral PRN) come before any IM medication or restraint
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — the least-restrictive continuum guides the behavioral response. Charge role: verbal/oral before IM/restraint.

opts.text: Staff and environmental safety — summoning help, keeping exits, removing other patients and dangerous objects — is essential during escalation
opts.rat: PRIORITY CUE — protecting staff, the patient, and peers is concurrent with de-escalation. Charge role: ensure safety.

opts.text: Immediately place Mr. D in physical restraints and give an IM injection as the first response to his pacing and loud voice
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Restraint is a last resort; pacing and a raised voice call for early verbal de-escalation and an offered oral PRN, not a first-line restraint.

opts.text: Delegate the initial suicide-risk assessment of the new patient and the assessment of Mr. D's escalation to a psychiatric technician
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Assessment and clinical judgment cannot be delegated to a UAP; the RN performs risk assessment and evaluates the escalating patient.

opts.text: Have the unlicensed technician independently interpret CIWA-Ar scores and titrate the alcohol-withdrawal patient's benzodiazepine dose
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Interpreting CIWA and titrating medication require nursing judgment and are outside UAP scope; the RN directs dosing (the tech may obtain vitals and report).

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: What delegation, scope, and de-escalation principles apply?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: The RN cannot delegate assessment, analysis, planning, evaluation, initial teaching, or care of unstable patients — these require nursing judgment
opts.rat: CORRECT — defines RN-only responsibilities. Foundation for safe assignment.

opts.text: The five rights of delegation (right task, circumstance, person, direction/communication, supervision/evaluation) guide delegation, and the RN keeps accountability
opts.rat: CORRECT — the delegation framework with retained accountability. Foundation for safe delegation.

opts.text: A trained UAP/psychiatric technician can perform constant 1:1 observation, obtain vital signs, assist with ADLs, and transport — with clear parameters and RN oversight
opts.rat: CORRECT — UAP scope with direction and supervision. Foundation for appropriate task assignment.

opts.text: An LPN/LVN can administer most routine PO/IM/SQ medications, reinforce previously taught content, and collect/report data for stable patients under RN supervision
opts.rat: CORRECT — LPN/LVN scope. Foundation for matching stable, predictable work.

opts.text: Verbal de-escalation (one calm spokesperson, respect personal space, lower stimulation, set limits, offer choices) is first-line; restraint/seclusion is last resort
opts.rat: CORRECT — least-restrictive de-escalation continuum. Foundation for the behavioral response.

opts.text: Offering an oral medication is less restrictive than IM; seclusion/restraint requires a time-limited, non-PRN provider order and continuous monitoring
opts.rat: CORRECT — least-restrictive route and the restraint standard. Foundation for safe, lawful intervention.

opts.text: Because the unit is busy, the charge nurse may delegate patient assessments and clinical judgment to the UAP to save time
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Workload never authorizes delegating assessment or judgment; these remain RN responsibilities regardless of how busy the unit is.

opts.text: Physical restraint is the appropriate first intervention whenever a psychiatric patient raises their voice or paces the hall
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG. Restraint is a last resort for imminent danger after less-restrictive measures fail; early agitation calls for verbal de-escalation.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank these priorities from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Ensure immediate safety — lead de-escalation of the escalating manic patient and protect him, other patients, and staff
opts.rat: #1 — An escalating patient is an imminent danger to self and others; de-escalation and safety come first. Charge role: immediate safety.

opts.text: Maintain uninterrupted, safe 1:1 observation of the actively suicidal patient throughout the event
opts.rat: #2 — The highest standing safety need; coverage must never lapse, even during the escalation. Charge role: protect 1:1.

opts.text: Make and adjust assignments that match each team member's scope and competency to patient acuity
opts.rat: #3 — Safe assignments structure the whole shift and free the RN to respond. Charge role: acuity-to-competency matching.

opts.text: Delegate appropriate tasks to the LPN/LVN and technicians with clear direction and ongoing supervision
opts.rat: #4 — Appropriate delegation extends safe care, but follows the higher-priority safety and assignment decisions. Charge role: delegate + supervise.

opts.text: Document the event and lead a post-incident debrief with staff and the patient
opts.rat: #5 — Essential follow-through, performed after the immediate situation is safe. Charge role: debrief + document.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: For EACH task, classify the MOST appropriate team member: RN Only, LPN/LVN, or UAP/Tech.

opts.text: Perform the suicide-risk assessment of the newly admitted patient and develop the safety plan
opts.rat: Assessment and care planning require nursing judgment — RN-only. Charge role: keep risk assessment as RN work.

opts.text: Lead verbal de-escalation of the escalating manic patient and decide on PRN/emergency medication
opts.rat: Real-time judgment, assessment of danger, and medication decisions are RN responsibilities. Charge role: lead de-escalation.

opts.text: Evaluate the patient's response to a PRN medication and revise the plan of care
opts.rat: Evaluation of response and revising the plan require nursing judgment — RN-only. Charge role: evaluate outcomes.

opts.text: Provide initial teaching to a newly admitted patient about the unit, the safety plan, and new medications
opts.rat: Initial teaching of new content is RN-only; an LPN/LVN may later reinforce it. Charge role: initial teaching.

opts.text: Administer the scheduled oral mood stabilizer and a routine ordered IM antipsychotic to a stable patient
opts.rat: Routine medication administration to a stable patient is within LPN/LVN scope under RN supervision.

opts.text: Reinforce previously taught coping skills and collect/report self-reported symptom data for the RN to interpret
opts.rat: Reinforcing prior teaching and collecting/reporting data are within LPN/LVN scope; the RN interprets the data.

opts.text: Perform the CIWA-Ar symptom checklist on the alcohol-withdrawal patient and report the findings to the RN
opts.rat: Structured data collection and reporting are within LPN/LVN scope; the RN interprets the score and directs dosing.

opts.text: Provide continuous 1:1 line-of-sight observation of the suicidal patient and report any concerning statements or behavior
opts.rat: Constant observation with clear parameters and reporting is within UAP scope, with RN oversight and retained accountability.

opts.text: Obtain and record routine vital signs and assist patients with ADLs and hygiene
opts.rat: Vital-sign measurement and ADL assistance are routine tasks within UAP scope.

opts.text: Accompany a stable patient to the activity room and help maintain a calm, low-stimulation milieu
opts.rat: Escort, supervision of stable patients, and milieu support are within UAP scope.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: Sequence the response to the escalation
steps.inst: Rank the order of the charge nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Summon help/activate the behavioral response and ensure safety — keep exits clear, do not corner the patient, and move other patients and dangerous objects away
opts.rat: #1 — FIRST. Adequate staff and a safe environment must be in place before anything else; never confront alone. Charge role: safety setup.

opts.text: Lead verbal de-escalation — one calm spokesperson, respect personal space, lower stimulation, listen, and set clear limits
opts.rat: #2 — The least-restrictive intervention; frequently resolves the escalation. Charge role: verbal de-escalation.

opts.text: Offer an oral PRN medication and a quiet, low-stimulation space to help him regain control
opts.rat: #3 — Oral medication is less restrictive than IM and is offered while the patient can still participate. Charge role: oral PRN + quiet space.

opts.text: If he refuses oral medication and danger is imminent, administer the ordered IM emergency medication with monitoring
opts.rat: #4 — Escalate to IM only when oral is refused and danger persists; then monitor sedation/airway/VS/EPS. Charge role: IM if needed.

opts.text: Reserve seclusion/restraint for last resort with a time-limited order, then reassess assignments, debrief, and document
opts.rat: #5 — Restraint is the final option for imminent danger after all else fails; follow with reassessment, debrief, and documentation. Charge role: last resort + follow-through.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: For each action/outcome, classify the charge nurse's practice.

opts.text: The charge nurse kept the new patient's suicide-risk assessment, safety planning, and the de-escalation/medication decisions as RN responsibilities
opts.rat: Assessment, planning, evaluation, and judgment are RN-only and were correctly retained. Appropriate practice.

opts.text: Verbal de-escalation plus an offered oral PRN and a quiet space helped Mr. D regain control without IM medication or restraint
opts.rat: The least-restrictive continuum succeeded — the ideal outcome. Appropriate practice.

opts.text: The technician was assigned continuous 1:1 observation with explicit parameters and RN oversight, and reported behaviors for the RN to interpret
opts.rat: Observation is delegable to a trained UAP with direction and supervision; the RN retains accountability and interprets. Appropriate practice.

opts.text: The LPN/LVN administered the scheduled oral mood stabilizer, reinforced coping skills, and reported CIWA findings within scope
opts.rat: Routine medications, reinforcing teaching, and data reporting are within LPN/LVN scope under RN supervision. Appropriate practice.

opts.text: After the event, the charge nurse reassessed assignments and 1:1 coverage and led a debrief with staff and the patient
opts.rat: Reassessment, supervision, and debrief are core charge-nurse follow-through. Appropriate practice.

opts.text: The charge nurse delegated the newly admitted suicidal patient's risk assessment to a psychiatric technician
opts.rat: ⚠️ Assessment and clinical judgment cannot be delegated to a UAP; this is unsafe and outside scope. Inappropriate practice.

opts.text: Mr. D was placed in restraints and given an IM injection immediately for pacing and a raised voice, skipping verbal de-escalation
opts.rat: ⚠️ Restraint is a last resort; early agitation warrants verbal de-escalation and an offered oral PRN first. Inappropriate practice.

opts.text: The technician was told to independently interpret CIWA scores and adjust the alcohol-withdrawal patient's benzodiazepine dose
opts.rat: ⚠️ Interpreting CIWA and titrating medication require nursing judgment and exceed UAP scope. Inappropriate practice.

opts.text: The charge nurse delegated tasks without giving clear direction, parameters, or any follow-up supervision
opts.rat: ⚠️ Violates the right direction/communication and supervision/evaluation; delegation without clear direction and oversight is unsafe. Inappropriate practice.

opts.text: Other patients were left in the dayroom near the escalating patient with no plan for their safety or removal
opts.rat: ⚠️ Failing to safeguard other patients during a behavioral emergency endangers them and can fuel escalation. Inappropriate practice.

title: SBAR Hand-off and Safe Transfer of Care: Shift-Change Report on a Stable Post-Op Patient
subtitle: Hand-off (shift report / transfer of care) is a high-risk moment when communication gaps cause errors. SBAR — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation — gives a clear, complete, structured report. This case follows a routine shift-change hand-off of a stable post-op day 1 patient: organizing the report into SBAR, including the essentials (allergies, code status, IV access, pending results), using read-back, and avoiding subjective labels and interruptions.

patient.name: Ronald Mercer
patient.code: Full code; stable post-op day 1 — routine end-of-shift SBAR hand-off to the oncoming nurse
patient.admitDate: Post-op day 1 after an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He is stable, comfortable (pain 3/10), tolerating sips, voiding, and ambulating with assistance. History of type 2 diabetes and hypertension. The off-going nurse is giving a shift-change hand-off using SBAR.
patient.room: Med-surg unit; saline-lock IV left forearm; sliding-scale insulin; pending evening blood culture result

vitals.temp: 37.2°C; reported incisional pain 6/10, medicated with effect
37.0°C; ambulated in hall with assist, tolerated well
36.9°C; incisions clean and dry, voiding without difficulty
37.0°C; stable and comfortable at end of shift
37.0°C; both nurses verify the patient, IV site, and orders together

labs.v: 11.2 g/dL — mildly low post-op but stable, no signs of bleeding.
labs.r: Report as part of Assessment; flag the trend, not just the number.
Normal; no infection concern at hand-off.
Mention in Recommendation as a possible recheck.

labs.v: 142 mg/dL — mildly elevated, on sliding-scale insulin.
labs.r: Report current value and the insulin plan.

labs.v: Situation (who/why now), Background (relevant history/context), Assessment (current findings/concerns), Recommendation (what to do/follow up).
labs.r: SBAR keeps hand-off clear, complete, and prioritized.

labs.v: Always include identity/diagnosis, code status, allergies, IV access, current status, meds/pending results, and active concerns.
labs.r: Omitting code status, allergies, or pending results is a classic hand-off error.

labs.v: Use read-back of key items, clarify questions, and ideally hand off at the bedside verifying the patient and lines.
labs.r: Read-back and bedside verification catch errors before they reach the patient.

labs.v: Avoid subjective labels ('difficult'), gossip, and giving report where it can be overheard (privacy).
labs.r: Report objective, relevant, confidential information only.

labs.v: Evening blood culture result still pending at hand-off.
labs.r: Pending results MUST be communicated so follow-up is not lost.

nursesNote: Ronald Mercer, 68, post-op day 1 after uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy; stable, pain 3/10, ambulating with assist, voiding, incisions clean/dry. PMH type 2 diabetes, HTN. Allergy penicillin (rash). Full code. Saline-lock IV left forearm; sliding-scale insulin. Labs: Hgb 11.2 (low-stable), K 3.6, glucose 142; evening blood culture PENDING. End-of-shift hand-off using SBAR — include identity/diagnosis, code status, allergies, IV access, status, meds, pending culture, and concerns; use read-back and bedside verification; keep it objective and confidential.
providerOrders: Routine post-op day 1 care; advance diet and activity as tolerated
Sliding-scale insulin per protocol; recheck morning glucose
Continue saline-lock; normal saline if needed
Pain management; monitor incisions for bleeding/infection
Follow up pending evening blood culture result

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for a safe hand-off?
steps.inst: Select ALL items that should be communicated or considered.

opts.text: Identity, diagnosis, and that he is post-op day 1 and stable
opts.rat: Core Situation information for the oncoming nurse.

opts.text: Code status (full code) and allergy to penicillin
opts.rat: Safety essentials that must never be omitted.

opts.text: IV access, current meds (sliding-scale insulin), and the pending blood culture
opts.rat: Access, meds, and pending results must be handed off so follow-up is not lost.

opts.text: Current status — stable vitals, pain 3/10, ambulating, incisions clean/dry
opts.rat: The Assessment the oncoming nurse needs as a baseline.

opts.text: Recommendations — recheck glucose and possibly potassium, monitor incision, follow up culture
opts.rat: Clear next steps complete the SBAR report.

opts.text: A subjective label that he is a 'difficult, needy' patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ Subjective labels bias care and are inappropriate in hand-off.

opts.text: Skip report and let the oncoming nurse read the chart to save time
opts.rat: ⚠️ A verbal structured hand-off is the standard; chart-only is unsafe.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: SBAR organizes report into Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
opts.rat: Correct — the structure that keeps hand-off complete.

opts.text: Code status, allergies, and pending results are essential hand-off elements
opts.rat: Correct — omitting them is a classic, dangerous error.

opts.text: Read-back and bedside verification reduce hand-off errors
opts.rat: Correct — confirming key items catches mistakes early.

opts.text: Report should be objective, relevant, and confidential
opts.rat: Correct — avoid labels, gossip, and being overheard.

opts.text: Pending results can be left out since the next shift will see them eventually
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — unspoken pending results are a leading cause of lost follow-up.

opts.text: A complete hand-off is unnecessary for a stable patient
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — stable patients still require a structured hand-off.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Identify the patient, diagnosis, and current situation
opts.rat: #1 — Situation orients the oncoming nurse first.

opts.text: Communicate safety essentials — code status and allergies
opts.rat: #2 — Critical safety data given early.

opts.text: Give the current assessment and stability
opts.rat: #3 — Baseline status for the next shift.

opts.text: Hand off meds, IV access, and pending results
opts.rat: #4 — Ongoing care and follow-up items.

opts.text: State recommendations and confirm with read-back
opts.rat: #5 — Close the loop with next steps and verification.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.sub: Sort each statement into its SBAR component
steps.inst: Classify each item as Situation, Background, Assessment, or Recommendation.

opts.text: 'This is Ronald Mercer, 68, post-op day 1 after a lap cholecystectomy; I'm handing off his care.'
opts.rat: Who the patient is and why we are reporting now.

opts.text: 'Right now he is stable and comfortable, pain 3/10.'
opts.rat: The immediate situation/status snapshot.

opts.text: 'He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension; surgery was uncomplicated.'
opts.rat: Relevant history/context.

opts.text: 'He is allergic to penicillin and is a full code.'
opts.rat: Essential background safety data.

opts.text: 'He has a saline-lock IV in the left forearm with a normal-saline order if needed.'
opts.rat: Access and standing orders are background.

opts.text: 'Vitals are stable; morning glucose was 142 and potassium 3.6.'
opts.rat: Current findings/data.

opts.text: 'Lungs clear, incisions clean and dry, voiding, ambulating with assist.'
opts.rat: Current objective assessment.

opts.text: 'Hgb is 11.2, slightly low post-op but stable with no signs of bleeding.'
opts.rat: Current finding with interpretation.

opts.text: 'Please continue the sliding-scale insulin and recheck a morning glucose; potassium may need rechecking.'
opts.rat: What to do next.

opts.text: 'Monitor the incision and pain, encourage ambulation, and follow up the pending blood culture this evening.'
opts.rat: Follow-up actions to complete the hand-off.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: State the Situation — patient, diagnosis, current status
opts.rat: #1 — Orient the oncoming nurse.

opts.text: Give the Background — history, allergies, code status, access
opts.rat: #2 — Provide essential context and safety data.

opts.text: Report the Assessment — vitals, labs, current findings
opts.rat: #3 — Share the baseline and any concerns.

opts.text: Make Recommendations — meds, pending results, follow-up
opts.rat: #4 — Define next steps.

opts.text: Verify at the bedside and use read-back to confirm
opts.rat: #5 — Close the loop and catch errors.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each hand-off practice.

opts.text: The nurse used SBAR and included code status, allergies, and the pending culture
opts.rat: Complete, structured, safe hand-off.

opts.text: The nurses verified the patient, IV site, and orders together at the bedside
opts.rat: Bedside verification reduces errors.

opts.text: The oncoming nurse read back the insulin plan and pending follow-up
opts.rat: Read-back confirms shared understanding.

opts.text: Report was given objectively without labels and in a private area
opts.rat: Objective and confidential — correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse skipped code status and allergies because the patient is stable
opts.rat: ⚠️ These are always essential, regardless of stability.

opts.text: The pending blood culture was not mentioned
opts.rat: ⚠️ Unspoken pending results lead to lost follow-up.

opts.text: The nurse described the patient as 'difficult and needy' instead of objective findings
opts.rat: ⚠️ Subjective labels bias care and are unprofessional.

opts.text: Report was given loudly in the hallway where visitors could hear
opts.rat: ⚠️ Violates patient privacy/confidentiality.

title: Honoring a Valid DNR Order During ICU Deterioration: DNR Does NOT Mean Do-Not-Treat
subtitle: A DNR (Do Not Resuscitate) order means no CPR — no chest compressions, defibrillation, or intubation — IF the patient arrests. It does NOT mean 'do not treat.' Patients who are DNR still receive active care consistent with their goals: oxygen, suctioning, antibiotics, IV fluids, comfort, and ICU monitoring. This case follows an ICU patient with a valid DNR (full treatment otherwise) who deteriorates from sepsis — the nurse must treat the reversible problem, verify the order's scope, support the family, and never abandon care.

patient.name: Eleanor Voss
patient.code: DNR/DNI (no CPR, defibrillation, or intubation at arrest) — FULL active treatment otherwise; valid signed POLST reflecting her own wishes
patient.admitDate: ICU admission for severe community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis. She has a valid, current DNR/DNI order and POLST that she completed herself while capacitated, specifying no resuscitation but full medical treatment otherwise. She now deteriorates — increasing work of breathing and falling oxygen saturation. The nurse must escalate appropriate treatment while honoring the DNR.

vitals.spo2: 86% — increased work of breathing, accessory muscle use
92% on high-flow O2 after airway suctioning
vitals.temp: 38.4°C; treated actively within DNR goals (no intubation)
37.9°C; family and patient reaffirm DNR with full non-resuscitative treatment
37.3°C; resting comfortably, care continued per goals

labs.r: Active infection still treated despite DNR.
Guides fluids/treatment within goals of care.

labs.v: Low with hypoxemia on the ABG.
labs.r: Treat with oxygen/suction; DNR does not bar oxygen.

labs.v: DNR = no CPR (compressions, defibrillation, intubation) at arrest. It is NOT 'do not treat.'
labs.r: Reversible problems are still treated per the patient's goals.

labs.v: Confirm the DNR is current, properly ordered, and matches the patient's wishes/POLST.
DNR is not the same as comfort-care-only; this patient has full treatment otherwise.
labs.r: Do not assume DNR means withdraw active care.

labs.v: Honoring a DNR is not abandonment — keep assessing, treating within goals, and supporting the family.
labs.r: The nurse continues full nursing care.

labs.v: The patient (or surrogate) may rescind the DNR at any time; reassess goals with changes.
labs.r: Document deterioration, interventions, and DNR status.

nursesNote: Eleanor Voss, 80, ICU for severe pneumonia + sepsis. Valid current DNR/DNI + POLST she completed herself: no CPR/defibrillation/intubation at arrest, but FULL active treatment otherwise. Deteriorating — RR 30, SpO2 86%, increased work of breathing. DNR ≠ do-not-treat: continue oxygen, suction, antibiotics, IV fluids, comfort, monitoring per goals; only resuscitation at arrest is withheld. Verify the order is current and clarify scope; treat the reversible problem; manage dyspnea; support and update the family; the patient may rescind anytime; document. Honoring DNR is not abandonment.

Titrate oxygen for hypoxia; suction airway PRN
Continue IV antibiotics for sepsis; IV fluids per protocol
Treat dyspnea/pain for comfort; continue ICU monitoring
Family updates; reaffirm goals of care; document deterioration and interventions

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What matters for this DNR patient's deterioration?
steps.inst: Select ALL items that are clinically significant.

opts.text: The DNR/POLST is valid, current, and reflects her own wishes
opts.rat: A verified order guides care.

opts.text: She is DNR but ordered full treatment otherwise (oxygen, antibiotics, fluids, ICU care)
opts.rat: DNR limits only resuscitation, not active treatment.

opts.text: She is deteriorating from sepsis — falling SpO2, rising RR, increased work of breathing
opts.rat: A reversible problem to treat within her goals.

opts.text: DNR applies only at arrest (no CPR/defibrillation/intubation), not to ongoing treatment
opts.rat: The core distinction guiding care.

opts.text: She may rescind the DNR at any time, and goals should be reassessed
opts.rat: Patient autonomy is ongoing.

opts.text: DNR means withhold oxygen, antibiotics, and fluids and stop monitoring
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — DNR does not mean do-not-treat.

opts.text: Because she is DNR, transfer her out of the ICU and give only comfort care
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — she has full treatment otherwise; DNR ≠ comfort-care-only.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: DNR means no CPR, defibrillation, or intubation if the patient arrests
opts.rat: Correct definition of the order.

opts.text: DNR does not mean 'do not treat'; reversible problems are still treated per goals
opts.rat: Correct — the key teaching point.

opts.text: A valid DNR must be verified as current and consistent with the patient's wishes
opts.rat: Correct — always confirm scope.

opts.text: The patient retains the right to rescind the DNR at any time
opts.rat: Correct — autonomy is ongoing.

opts.text: Honoring a DNR is not abandonment; the nurse keeps treating and supporting
opts.rat: Correct — continue full nursing care.

opts.text: A DNR order authorizes withholding antibiotics, oxygen, and routine care
opts.rat: ⚠️ WRONG — those treatments continue per goals.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Treat the reversible deterioration within goals — oxygen, suction, antibiotics, fluids
opts.rat: #1 — She is not arrested; treat the hypoxia/sepsis now.

opts.text: Verify the DNR order is current and clarify its resuscitation scope
opts.rat: #2 — Confirm what is and isn't withheld.

opts.text: Manage symptoms and comfort (dyspnea, pain)
opts.rat: #3 — Relieve distress alongside treatment.

opts.text: Communicate with the patient/family and reaffirm goals of care
opts.rat: #4 — Keep them informed and aligned.

opts.text: Document the deterioration, interventions, and DNR status
opts.rat: #5 — Record care and decisions.

opts.rat: Part of ongoing care — provided.

opts.text: Begin chest compressions if she arrests
opts.rat: CPR is withheld under the DNR.

opts.text: Defibrillate/cardiovert a pulseless arrest
opts.rat: Resuscitation is withheld under the DNR.

opts.text: Intubate and mechanically ventilate at arrest
opts.rat: Withheld under the DNR/DNI order.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of the nurse's actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Stay with the patient and assess airway, breathing, and circulation
opts.rat: #1 — Rapid assessment of the deterioration.

opts.text: Apply oxygen, suction, and deliver ordered treatments
opts.rat: #2 — Treat the reversible problem within goals.

opts.text: Verify the DNR order and clarify resuscitation scope with the team
opts.rat: #3 — Confirm what is withheld at arrest.

opts.text: Update and support the family and reaffirm goals of care
opts.rat: #4 — Keep them informed and aligned.

opts.text: Document findings, interventions, and DNR status
opts.rat: #5 — Record the care and decisions.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each practice.

opts.text: The nurse gave oxygen, suctioned, and continued antibiotics/fluids while honoring the DNR
opts.rat: Active treatment within goals — correct.

opts.text: The nurse verified the DNR was current and clarified the DNR/DNI scope
opts.rat: Confirming scope is correct practice.

opts.text: The nurse treated her dyspnea, stayed with her, and supported the family
opts.rat: Comfort and presence — correct.

opts.text: The nurse documented the deterioration, interventions, and that CPR would be withheld at arrest
opts.rat: Accurate documentation — correct.

opts.text: The nurse withheld oxygen and antibiotics because the patient was DNR
opts.rat: ⚠️ DNR does not mean do-not-treat.

opts.text: The nurse called a full code and began compressions when she arrested
opts.rat: ⚠️ Violates the valid DNR order.

opts.text: The nurse stopped all monitoring and assessment because 'she's DNR'
opts.rat: ⚠️ Care continues; this is abandonment.

opts.text: The nurse assumed DNR meant comfort-care-only and moved her out of the ICU without discussion
opts.rat: ⚠️ DNR is not comfort-care-only; she has full treatment otherwise.

title: Dysphagia & Aspiration Precautions in an Older Adult with Parkinson's Disease
subtitle: A 79-year-old man with Parkinson's disease was admitted with aspiration pneumonia and is now improving. The nurse must recognize dysphagia, keep him safe until a swallow evaluation, and apply correct aspiration precautions during feeding.

patient.name: Walter Briggs
patient.admitDate: Admitted 3 days ago with aspiration pneumonia. Parkinson's disease for 8 years. Now afebrile-trending and improving on IV antibiotics. Reports food 'sticking' and coughs with thin liquids. Awaiting swallow evaluation before resuming oral intake.
patient.room: Med-surg; HOB elevated, on 2 L nasal cannula, IV antibiotics

vitals.time: Today — trial sips of thin water
vitals.spo2: dipped to 90% with wet, gurgly voice and coughing

vitals.temp: Pain 2/10; alert, no distress at rest

labs.v: FAILED — cough and wet voice with thin liquids.
labs.r: Keep NPO; obtain formal SLP evaluation.

labs.v: Pharyngeal-phase delay; silent aspiration of thin liquids.

nursesNote: Walter Briggs, 79, Parkinson's disease, day 3 for aspiration pneumonia and improving. Coughs and has a wet, gurgly voice with thin liquids; reports food sticking; chews slowly and pockets food. Bedside swallow screen failed. Currently NPO pending SLP evaluation. HOB up, suction at bedside.
providerOrders: NPO until swallow evaluation completed
Consult Speech-Language Pathology for swallow evaluation
Aspiration precautions; HOB elevated; suction available at bedside
Continue IV antibiotics and IV fluids
Advance diet per SLP recommendations; oral care every shift

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What signals dysphagia and aspiration risk?
steps.inst: Select ALL items that suggest dysphagia or aspiration risk.

opts.text: Coughing or throat-clearing during/after swallowing thin liquids
opts.rat: Classic sign of unsafe swallow.

opts.text: Wet, 'gurgly' voice quality after swallowing
opts.rat: Suggests residue/penetration in the airway.

opts.text: Pocketing food in the cheeks; slow, effortful chewing
opts.rat: Impaired oral phase, common in Parkinson's.

opts.text: A present gag reflex confirms the swallow is safe
opts.rat: Gag reflex does NOT predict swallow safety.

opts.text: Drooling and trouble managing oral secretions
opts.rat: Reflects poor oral/pharyngeal control.

opts.text: Multiple swallows per bite and very long mealtimes
opts.rat: Indicates swallowing difficulty.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Parkinson's disease impairs the oral and pharyngeal swallow phases
opts.rat: A leading neurologic cause of dysphagia.

opts.text: Silent aspiration can occur with NO cough; clear lungs don't rule it out
opts.rat: Absence of coughing is not reassuring.

opts.text: The right-lower-lobe infiltrate fits an aspiration event
opts.rat: Aspirate commonly tracks to the RLL.

opts.text: Dysphagia is a normal part of aging and needs no workup
opts.rat: Dysphagia is never 'normal aging' — evaluate it.

opts.text: Low albumin and high BUN point to poor intake / dehydration risk
opts.rat: Nutrition and hydration are at risk.

opts.text: A formal swallow evaluation is needed before oral intake resumes
opts.rat: Keep NPO until cleared.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Keep him NPO until a swallow screen/evaluation is completed
opts.rat: #1 — Prevent further aspiration first.

opts.text: Position fully upright (90°) and ensure suction is at the bedside
opts.rat: #2 — Safe positioning and airway backup.

opts.text: Notify the provider and request an SLP swallow evaluation
opts.rat: #3 — Get the formal assessment ordered.

opts.text: Provide oral care to reduce oral bacterial load
opts.rat: #4 — Lowers aspiration-pneumonia risk.

opts.text: Plan diet texture and feeding teaching per SLP results
opts.rat: #5 — Follows evaluation findings.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Classify each aspiration-precaution measure as Recommended or Avoid.

opts.text: Sit fully upright (90°) for meals and 30–60 min after
opts.rat: Gravity protects the airway.

opts.text: Thickened liquids and modified textures as the SLP recommends
opts.rat: Slows flow, reduces aspiration.

opts.text: Small bites, slow pace, chin-tuck, single sips
opts.rat: Safer swallow mechanics.

opts.text: Alternate solids and liquids; check the mouth for pocketing
opts.rat: Clears residue between bites.

opts.text: Oral care before and after every meal
opts.rat: Lowers oral bacterial load.

opts.text: Minimize distractions; no talking with food in the mouth
opts.rat: Focus reduces mis-swallows.

opts.text: Feed him while reclined, drowsy, or lying flat
opts.rat: High aspiration risk.

opts.text: Give thin water or juice when thickened liquids are ordered
opts.rat: Thin liquids are aspirated silently.

opts.text: Rush feeding with large or stacked spoonfuls
opts.rat: Overwhelms a slow swallow.

opts.text: Lay him flat immediately after eating
opts.rat: Promotes reflux and aspiration.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: SLP cleared a nectar-thick, mechanical-soft diet — sequence the feeding
steps.inst: Rank the order of safe-feeding actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Confirm he is awake/alert and verify the current diet order
opts.rat: #1 — Never feed a drowsy patient or wrong texture.

opts.text: Position him fully upright at 90° with suction ready
opts.rat: #2 — Set up a safe swallow.

opts.text: Offer small bites at a slow pace using a chin-tuck
opts.rat: #3 — Controlled, protected swallow.

opts.text: Check the mouth for pocketing before the next bite
opts.rat: #4 — Prevents accumulation and aspiration.

opts.text: Provide oral care and keep him upright 30–60 min after
opts.rat: #5 — Reduces post-meal aspiration.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action or observation.

opts.text: The UAP kept him upright for 45 minutes after lunch
opts.rat: Correct post-meal positioning.

opts.text: The nurse stopped feeding and reported a new wet, gurgly voice
opts.rat: Recognized and escalated a danger sign.

opts.text: Liquids were thickened to nectar consistency as ordered
opts.rat: Followed the SLP plan.

opts.text: Feeding was slow with rest breaks and pocketing checks
opts.rat: Safe technique.

opts.text: Oral care was given after the meal
opts.rat: Reduces aspiration-pneumonia risk.

opts.text: The UAP laid him flat right after eating
opts.rat: Promotes reflux/aspiration.

opts.text: Family gave sips of plain water 'because he was thirsty'
opts.rat: Thin liquids are contraindicated here.

opts.text: The tray was left for him to self-feed while drowsy, unsupervised
opts.rat: Unsafe — requires supervision.

opts.text: Coughing during sips was ignored and feeding continued
opts.rat: A clear stop-and-reassess signal.

title: Safe Administration of a HIGH-ALERT Continuous IV Heparin Infusion
subtitle: A 64-year-old man with an acute pulmonary embolism is started on a weight-based IV unfractionated heparin infusion. The nurse must run this high-alert drug safely: independent double-checks, protocol-based aPTT titration, bleeding and HIT surveillance.

patient.name: Raymond Hill
patient.admitDate: Admitted today with acute submassive pulmonary embolism. Started on a weight-based IV unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusion per the institutional nomogram. Hemodynamically stable on 2 L nasal cannula. No active bleeding.
patient.room: Telemetry; smart-pump heparin infusion, labs per protocol

labs.r: Hold/decrease per protocol; bleeding risk up.

nursesNote: Raymond Hill, 64, acute submassive PE, started on weight-based IV unfractionated heparin per nomogram. Stable on 2 L. Smart-pump infusion. 6-hour aPTT is 95 sec (goal 60–80) — supratherapeutic. No active bleeding. Platelets and Hgb being trended; protamine available as reversal agent.
providerOrders: IV unfractionated heparin per weight-based nomogram; titrate to aPTT goal 60–80 sec
aPTT every 6 hours until therapeutic ×2, then daily; CBC/platelets daily
Independent double-check by 2 RNs for initiation and every rate change
Bleeding precautions; protamine sulfate available as antidote
Notify provider for active bleeding or platelet drop ≥50%

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What does safe high-alert heparin require?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements about starting this infusion safely.

opts.text: Heparin is a HIGH-ALERT drug needing an independent double-check of pump settings
opts.rat: Standard for high-alert infusions.

opts.text: The dose is WEIGHT-BASED per the institutional protocol/nomogram
opts.rat: Bolus and rate follow the nomogram.

opts.text: aPTT (or anti-Xa) guides titration of the infusion
opts.rat: Lab values drive rate changes.

opts.text: Baseline aPTT, PT/INR, platelets, and Hgb are drawn before starting
opts.rat: Establishes safe baselines.

opts.text: A single-nurse check is enough because heparin is low-risk
opts.rat: False — it is high-alert; two-nurse verify.

opts.text: 'Units' labels and concentrations must be verified to avoid an insulin/heparin mix-up
opts.rat: Both dose in units — verify carefully.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: An aPTT of 95 sec (goal 60–80) is supratherapeutic and raises bleeding risk
opts.rat: Above the target window.

opts.text: Per protocol, hold or decrease the infusion and recheck the aPTT
opts.rat: Standard nomogram response.

opts.text: A ~40–50% platelet drop around day 4–10 raises concern for HIT
opts.rat: Classic HIT timing/magnitude.

opts.text: A supratherapeutic aPTT alone means give protamine routinely
opts.rat: Protamine is for significant bleeding/overdose, not a high aPTT alone.

opts.text: A falling hemoglobin could signal occult bleeding
opts.rat: Trend Hgb and assess sources.

opts.text: Continue the same rate regardless of the aPTT result
opts.rat: False — titrate to the result.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: The 6-hour aPTT is critically high at 95 sec
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (HIGHEST) to #5 (LOWEST).

opts.text: Assess the patient for active bleeding (neuro, GI, urine, skin, vitals)
opts.rat: #1 — Patient safety first.

opts.text: Hold or decrease the infusion per the protocol/nomogram
opts.rat: #2 — Reduce the excess anticoagulation.

opts.text: Notify the provider and verify the corrected rate with a double-check
opts.rat: #3 — Communicate and confirm.

opts.text: Recheck the aPTT at the protocol-specified interval
opts.rat: #4 — Confirm the response.

opts.text: Document the event and the rate change
opts.rat: #5 — Record after acting.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Classify each heparin-infusion practice as Safe or Unsafe.

opts.text: Independent double-check of the bag, concentration, and pump rate
opts.rat: Required for high-alert drugs.

opts.text: Use a smart pump with dose-error-reduction limits
opts.rat: Reduces programming errors.

opts.text: Titrate strictly per the weight-based protocol and aPTT/anti-Xa
opts.rat: Evidence-based dosing.

opts.text: Keep protamine sulfate available as the reversal agent
opts.rat: Antidote ready for emergencies.

opts.text: Monitor platelets for HIT and hemoglobin for bleeding
opts.rat: Detects complications early.

opts.text: Teach bleeding precautions and to report any bleeding
opts.rat: Engages the patient in safety.

opts.text: Adjust the rate from memory without the protocol
opts.rat: Bypasses the nomogram safeguard.

opts.text: Give a heparin IV push to 'catch up' a subtherapeutic level
opts.rat: Not ordered; dangerous bolus.

opts.text: Skip the second-nurse verification because the unit is busy
opts.rat: Removes a key high-alert check.

opts.text: Confuse the 'units' with insulin or use the wrong concentration
opts.rat: Classic fatal medication error.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: Provider increases the rate after a subtherapeutic aPTT — sequence it
steps.inst: Rank the order of safe actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Verify the new order against the weight-based protocol
opts.rat: #1 — Confirm the dose is correct.

opts.text: Obtain an independent double-check of the new setting with a second nurse
opts.rat: #2 — High-alert verification.

opts.text: Reprogram the smart pump and confirm concentration and rate
opts.rat: #3 — Set and confirm the pump.

opts.text: Reassess the patient and document the change
opts.rat: #4 — Check status and record.

opts.text: Recheck the aPTT at the protocol interval
opts.rat: #5 — Confirm the new rate's effect.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: Two nurses independently verified the bag and pump rate before the change
opts.rat: Correct high-alert practice.

opts.text: The nurse held the infusion for the supratherapeutic aPTT per protocol
opts.rat: Followed the nomogram.

opts.text: Platelets were trended and the provider notified of a ~40% drop
opts.rat: Appropriate HIT surveillance.

opts.text: Bleeding precautions were taught and the patient verbalized them
opts.rat: Effective safety teaching.

opts.text: The aPTT was rechecked at the ordered interval
opts.rat: Confirms therapeutic response.

opts.text: The nurse gave a heparin bolus from memory to reach goal faster
opts.rat: Unordered, dangerous.

opts.text: The second-nurse check was skipped 'to save time'
opts.rat: Omits a required safeguard.

opts.text: A supratherapeutic aPTT was ignored and the rate left unchanged
opts.rat: Increases bleeding risk.

opts.text: Protamine was given routinely for a high aPTT without bleeding
opts.rat: Reversal is not indicated here.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Principles of Surgical Asepsis and a Sterile Dressing Change
subtitle: A 58-year-old man is postoperative day 2 from abdominal surgery with a clean, intact midline incision that needs a sterile dressing change. The nurse must apply surgical asepsis correctly, keep the sterile field intact, and watch for early surgical-site infection.

patient.name: Carl Donovan
patient.admitDate: Postoperative day 2 after open abdominal surgery. Midline incision is clean, dry, and well-approximated. A sterile dressing change is ordered. Afebrile-trending; incisional pain controlled. No signs of infection at this time.
patient.room: Surgical floor; sterile dressing-change supplies at bedside

vitals.temp: Edges approximated, no drainage, mild expected tenderness

labs.r: Hyperglycemia raises SSI risk; optimize control.
Poor nutrition impairs healing/raises SSI risk.

labs.v: Edges approximated; no erythema or drainage.

nursesNote: Carl Donovan, 58, POD2 open abdominal surgery. Midline incision clean, dry, well-approximated; sterile dressing change ordered. Afebrile, pain controlled, no drainage. Glucose 185 and albumin 3.0 noted as healing/SSI-risk factors. Sterile supplies set up at bedside.
providerOrders: Sterile dressing change daily and PRN using surgical aseptic technique
Assess incision each shift; notify provider for erythema, purulent drainage, fever, or dehiscence
Optimize glycemic control; nutrition consult for low albumin
Incentive spirometry and early ambulation
Hand hygiene and standard precautions

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What does a sterile dressing change require?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: A sterile field is required for the surgical-aseptic dressing change
opts.rat: Sterile technique protects the incision.

opts.text: Hand hygiene is done before and after; clean gloves remove the old dressing
opts.rat: Clean gloves for the soiled dressing.

opts.text: Sterile gloves are donned for the sterile portion of the procedure
opts.rat: Sterile-to-sterile contact only.

opts.text: Items below the waist or table level are considered contaminated
opts.rat: Out of sight/below waist = contaminated.

opts.text: A 1-inch (2.5 cm) border around the sterile field is contaminated
opts.rat: Standard sterile-field rule.

opts.text: Once set up, a sterile field stays sterile even if left unattended
opts.rat: False — an unattended field is contaminated.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: What maintains or breaks sterility — and the SSI risk?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Reaching ACROSS the sterile field contaminates it
opts.rat: Never reach over a sterile field.

opts.text: Moisture wicking (strikethrough) from a wet field contaminates it
opts.rat: Wet field draws up microbes.

opts.text: Turning your back on the sterile field contaminates it
opts.rat: Keep the field in view at all times.

opts.text: A clean, approximated incision with no drainage shows no current SSI
opts.rat: Reassuring assessment.

opts.text: Hyperglycemia and low albumin increase surgical-site-infection risk
opts.rat: Both impair healing/immunity.

opts.text: A set-up sterile field can be re-used for the next patient
opts.rat: False — never re-use a sterile field.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Order the steps to BEGIN the dressing change
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Verify the order, gather supplies, and check the patient and allergies
opts.rat: #1 — Prepare and confirm.

opts.text: Hand hygiene; explain the procedure; provide privacy and time analgesia
opts.rat: #2 — Patient prep and comfort.

opts.text: Don clean gloves; remove and discard the soiled dressing; assess the wound
opts.rat: #3 — Clean gloves for the old dressing.

opts.text: Perform hand hygiene again and set up the sterile field
opts.rat: #4 — Re-clean hands, then sterile setup.

opts.text: Don sterile gloves and apply the sterile dressing
opts.rat: #5 — Sterile portion last.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: Keep all sterile items within the field and above waist level
opts.rat: Core sterile-field rule.

opts.text: Open the first package flap away from you, then the sides, then toward you
opts.rat: Prevents reaching over contents.

opts.text: Keep sterile items in front of you and in view
opts.rat: Out of sight = contaminated.

opts.text: Add sterile solution without splashing or soaking the field
opts.rat: Avoids strikethrough.

opts.text: Use sterile-to-sterile contact only
opts.rat: Keeps the field sterile.

opts.text: Don sterile gloves before touching sterile supplies or the wound
opts.rat: Sterile hands for sterile items.

opts.text: Reach over the sterile field with an ungloved arm
opts.rat: Contaminates the field.

opts.text: Set a sterile package on a wet surface
opts.rat: Strikethrough contamination.

opts.text: Turn away from the field to chart
opts.rat: Unwitnessed field is contaminated.

opts.text: Let the outer wrapper edge touch the sterile inner contents
opts.rat: Edge/border is contaminated.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: Field is set and the wound is exposed — sequence the sterile application
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Don sterile gloves
opts.rat: #1 — Sterile hands before sterile work.

opts.text: Clean the incision per order, one stroke per swab, clean-to-dirty
opts.rat: #2 — Aseptic cleaning technique.

opts.text: Apply the new sterile dressing without touching the wound-contact surface
opts.rat: #3 — Keep the contact layer sterile.

opts.text: Secure the dressing and ensure patient comfort
opts.rat: #4 — Finish and position the patient.

opts.text: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and document the wound
opts.rat: #5 — Clean up and record findings.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: Hand hygiene was performed before and after the procedure
opts.rat: Standard practice.

opts.text: The nurse kept sterile items above the waist and in view
opts.rat: Maintained the sterile field.

opts.text: A strikethrough-soaked field was discarded and restarted
opts.rat: Correctly recognized contamination.

opts.text: The incision was cleaned clean-to-dirty with a new swab each stroke
opts.rat: Prevents reintroducing microbes.

opts.text: Wound appearance and patient tolerance were documented
opts.rat: Completes the assessment.

opts.text: The nurse reached across the sterile field to grab tape
opts.rat: Contaminated the field.

opts.text: The soiled dressing was removed with the sterile gloves meant for the new one
opts.rat: Use clean gloves for the old dressing.

opts.text: A dropped sterile gauze (below the waist) was used anyway
opts.rat: Below-waist items are contaminated.

opts.text: The sterile field was left unattended, then used
opts.rat: Unattended field is not sterile.
