title: Childhood Immunization Visit: Schedule, True vs False Contraindications & Vaccine Hesitancy
subtitle: A healthy 15-month-old is at a well-child visit and is due for vaccines. She has mild rhinorrhea and a low-grade temp, and her parent voices hesitancy. The nurse must screen for true contraindications, vaccinate safely, and counsel the parent.

patient.name: Mia Sandoval
patient.admitDate: Well-child visit. Active, playful, thriving. Mild rhinorrhea and low-grade temp (37.8°C) from a cold. Due for 12–15-month vaccines (MMR, varicella, Hib and PCV boosters, hepatitis A, DTaP catch-up). Parent worried about a 'link between MMR and autism.'

vitals.temp: Mild fussiness, low-grade temp, sore thigh

labs.v: Behind one DTaP — catch-up due today.

nursesNote: Mia Sandoval, 15 months, healthy and thriving at a well-child visit; due for 12–15-month vaccines plus a DTaP catch-up. Mild cold with low-grade temp 37.8°C. Parent voices concern about MMR and autism. No anaphylaxis to prior doses; not immunocompromised. VIS sheets ready; epinephrine available.
providerOrders: Administer due 12–15-month vaccines, including DTaP catch-up
Provide Vaccine Information Statements before administration
Observe 15 minutes post-vaccination for immediate reactions
Iron-deficiency follow-up for hemoglobin 10.8
Anticipatory guidance and routine well-child counseling

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What applies to vaccinating this toddler today?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: A mild cold with low-grade fever is NOT a contraindication — vaccinate today
opts.rat: Minor illness does not delay vaccines.

opts.text: Verify the immunization record and which vaccines are due
opts.rat: Confirm the catch-up needs.

opts.text: Provide the Vaccine Information Statement (VIS) before administering
opts.rat: Required before each vaccine.

opts.text: Confirm there was no anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component
opts.rat: Anaphylaxis is a true contraindication.

opts.text: Current antibiotic use for an ear infection means delay all vaccines
opts.rat: False — antibiotic use is not a contraindication.

opts.text: Screen for true contraindications to LIVE vaccines (severe immunocompromise)
opts.rat: Relevant for MMR and varicella.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Anaphylaxis to a vaccine or component is a true contraindication
opts.rat: Do not give that vaccine.

opts.text: Mild illness, antibiotic use, and prematurity are FALSE contraindications
opts.rat: Still vaccinate; use chronological age.

opts.text: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
opts.rat: MMR/varicella precautions.

opts.text: A family history of vaccine reactions means skip the vaccine
opts.rat: False — not a contraindication.

opts.text: Encephalopathy within 7 days of a prior pertussis dose contraindicates further DTaP
opts.rat: A true pertussis-specific contraindication.

opts.text: A mild local reaction to a prior dose means stop that series
opts.rat: False — minor local reactions are expected.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Order the steps to safely give today's vaccines
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Review the record, confirm due vaccines, and screen for true contraindications
opts.rat: #1 — Safety screening first.

opts.text: Provide the VIS and address the parent's questions and hesitancy
opts.rat: #2 — Informed parent before giving.

opts.text: Prepare the correct vaccines, doses, sites, and routes
opts.rat: #3 — Right drug/dose/route/site.

opts.text: Administer with correct technique and comfort measures
opts.rat: #4 — Give the vaccines.

opts.text: Observe ~15 minutes for an immediate reaction and document
opts.rat: #5 — Watch for anaphylaxis, then record.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: Give multiple due vaccines at the same visit in different sites
opts.rat: Simultaneous administration is recommended.

opts.text: Use the vastus lateralis for IM injections in this toddler
opts.rat: Preferred site at this age.

opts.text: Give MMR and varicella subcutaneously
opts.rat: These live vaccines are SQ.

opts.text: Have epinephrine ready and observe for anaphylaxis
opts.rat: Emergency readiness.

opts.text: Use comfort measures (positioning, distraction, breastfeeding)
opts.rat: Reduces distress and pain.

opts.text: Document lot number, site, route, and VIS date
opts.rat: Required vaccine documentation.

opts.text: Delay vaccines because of a mild cold and low-grade fever
opts.rat: Minor illness is not a reason to delay.

opts.text: Withhold a vaccine for current antibiotic use
opts.rat: Not a contraindication.

opts.text: Routinely give acetaminophen before vaccinating to prevent fever
opts.rat: Prophylactic antipyretics are not recommended.

opts.text: Skip the 15-minute post-vaccine observation
opts.rat: Needed to catch immediate reactions.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: Parent says 'I heard MMR causes autism' — sequence your response
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Listen and acknowledge the concern without judgment
opts.rat: #1 — Build trust first.

opts.text: Provide clear, accurate information (no MMR–autism link; disease risks)
opts.rat: #2 — Correct the misinformation.

opts.text: Give a strong, presumptive recommendation and answer questions
opts.rat: #3 — Recommend vaccination clearly.

opts.text: Respect the decision; if still declining, document informed refusal
opts.rat: #4 — Honor autonomy, document.

opts.text: Schedule follow-up and keep the door open to vaccinate later
opts.rat: #5 — Maintain the relationship.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: The nurse vaccinated despite the mild cold and explained why

title: Maternal Cardiac Arrest (Code Blue) in Pregnancy: Team Leadership and Pregnancy-Modified Resuscitation
subtitle: A 34-year-old at 36 weeks collapses on the antepartum unit and is pulseless. The nurse must lead a code with pregnancy modifications — continuous manual left uterine displacement, standard ACLS, and readiness for a perimortem cesarean if there is no ROSC.

patient.name: Renata Cole
patient.admitDate: G1 at 36 weeks, admitted for observation. Witnessed sudden collapse — unresponsive, apneic, pulseless. Suspected pulmonary/amniotic-fluid embolism. The nurse activates a code and leads resuscitation with pregnancy modifications while OB, anesthesia, and neonatal teams are summoned.

title: Care Coordination & Safe Discharge Planning After Inpatient Psychiatric Hospitalization

patient.name: Daniel Okafor
patient.admitDate: Inpatient psychiatry day 10 after major depressive disorder with a suicide attempt. Stabilized on sertraline, engaged in care, future-oriented, denies current suicidal ideation, sleeping/eating better. Discharge planned today; outpatient follow-up and safety plan being finalized.

title: Against-Medical-Advice (AMA) Discharge: Honoring a Capable Patient's Informed Refusal
subtitle: A 52-year-old man admitted with leg cellulitis and early sepsis is improving on IV antibiotics but wants to leave AMA after one day for work and childcare reasons. He is alert and decisional. The nurse must protect his rights, avoid coercion, and reduce harm.

patient.name: Marcus Webb
patient.admitDate: Admitted ~18 hours ago with lower-leg cellulitis and early sepsis; started on IV antibiotics and fluids. Clinically improving but IV course incomplete. Alert, oriented, decisional. States he must leave today for work and childcare; verbalizes he understands he is leaving against advice.

vitals.temp: Calm; adamant about leaving for work/childcare

labs.v: Understands risks/benefits/alternatives; reasons; states a choice.
Risks explained; provider notified; form offered.

nursesNote: Marcus Webb, 52, ~18 h into treatment for leg cellulitis with early sepsis; improving on IV antibiotics but IV course incomplete. Alert, oriented, decisional; wants to leave AMA today for work/childcare. No coercion used. Risks/benefits explained, provider notified, barriers explored, harm-reduction (oral antibiotics, follow-up, return precautions) arranged.
providerOrders: Continue IV antibiotics and fluids for cellulitis/early sepsis
If patient elects to leave: assess capacity and document informed refusal
Provide oral antibiotic prescription, follow-up, and return precautions
Notify provider of any decision to leave against medical advice
Do not coerce or physically detain a capable, decisional patient

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: A capable patient is requesting an AMA discharge — what applies?

opts.text: You may physically restrain him to prevent leaving

opts.text: Explore and try to address his reasons (work, childcare, cost)
opts.rat: Barriers may be solvable.

steps.sub: What is true about capacity and AMA?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Capacity = understands info, appreciates consequences, reasons, states a choice

opts.text: Leaving AMA does not forfeit discharge teaching, prescriptions, or follow-up

opts.text: Refusing to sign the AMA form does not void his right to leave

opts.text: Coercion, threats, or shaming are inappropriate
opts.rat: Undermines autonomy and trust.

opts.text: Because he is leaving AMA, no return precautions are needed
opts.rat: False — harm-reduction still applies.

opts.text: An incomplete IV course risks worsening cellulitis, abscess, or sepsis

title: Hypertensive Emergency: Controlled IV Blood-Pressure Reduction in the ICU
subtitle: A 58-year-old man arrives with BP 226/128, severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion after running out of his antihypertensives. Labs show acute end-organ damage. The nurse must support a CONTROLLED IV blood-pressure reduction and avoid dropping it too fast.

patient.name: Gregory Tan
patient.admitDate: ED then ICU for hypertensive emergency. BP 226/128 with severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion (hypertensive encephalopathy). Ran out of antihypertensives ~1 week ago. End-organ damage on labs. Started on IV nicardipine with an arterial line for continuous monitoring.

nursesNote: Gregory Tan, 58, hypertensive emergency: BP 226/128 with headache, blurred vision, confusion (encephalopathy) and end-organ damage (rising creatinine, troponin, papilledema). Med nonadherence ~1 week. ICU; IV nicardipine titrating with an arterial line. Goal is a controlled reduction, not abrupt normalization.
providerOrders: Admit to ICU; continuous arterial-line BP monitoring and cardiac monitor
IV nicardipine titration; lower MAP by ~10–20% in the first hour
Then target ~160/100 over the next 2–6 hours; avoid abrupt drops
Serial neuro, cardiac, and urine-output assessments
Identify precipitant; resume/optimize oral antihypertensives per orders

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What marks a hypertensive EMERGENCY needing ICU/IV therapy?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: BP >180/120 WITH acute end-organ damage is a hypertensive emergency
opts.rat: Defines the emergency.

opts.text: Headache, blurred vision, and confusion suggest hypertensive encephalopathy
opts.rat: CNS end-organ effect.

opts.text: Rising creatinine, troponin, and papilledema indicate end-organ damage
opts.rat: Renal/cardiac/ocular injury.

opts.text: This requires ICU admission and IV titratable antihypertensives
opts.rat: Controlled IV therapy.

opts.text: Severely high BP with NO end-organ damage is the same as an emergency
opts.rat: False — that is urgency.

opts.text: An arterial line gives continuous, accurate BP during titration
opts.rat: Beat-to-beat monitoring.

steps.sub: How fast — and how far — should the BP come down?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Emergency (end-organ damage) needs IV therapy; urgency uses gradual oral meds
opts.rat: Different pathways.

opts.text: Lower the BP in a CONTROLLED way, not abruptly to normal
opts.rat: Protect perfusion.

opts.text: Reduce MAP ~10–20% in the first hour, then toward ~160/100 over hours
opts.rat: Standard targets.

opts.text: Dropping BP too fast risks cerebral, coronary, and renal hypoperfusion
opts.rat: Ischemia from over-correction.

opts.text: The goal is to normalize BP completely within the first hour
opts.rat: False — controlled, not normalized.

opts.text: Aortic dissection is an exception — lower BP and HR more rapidly
opts.rat: Reduce aortic shear fast.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Order the management of the hypertensive emergency
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Recognize end-organ damage and identify a hypertensive emergency
opts.rat: #1 — Frame the problem.

opts.text: Admit to ICU; establish IV access and continuous BP monitoring
opts.rat: #2 — Set up safe titration.

opts.text: Start the ordered IV titratable antihypertensive
opts.rat: #3 — Begin therapy.

opts.text: Titrate to a controlled reduction (~10–20% MAP in hour 1); reassess
opts.rat: #4 — Controlled lowering.

opts.text: Watch for too-rapid drop/hypoperfusion and document the response
opts.rat: #5 — Monitor and record.

opts.rat: Tracks end-organ response.

opts.text: Identify the precipitant and resume oral meds as ordered
opts.rat: Treats the cause.

opts.text: Keep the patient on a cardiac monitor in the ICU
opts.rat: Detects ischemia/arrhythmia.

opts.text: Give a rapid IV bolus to drop BP to normal immediately
opts.rat: Causes hypoperfusion.

opts.text: Use sublingual immediate-release nifedipine to crash the BP

opts.text: Rely on intermittent cuff readings while titrating a fast IV vasodilator
opts.rat: Continuous monitoring needed.

title: Acute Delirium in a Hospitalized Older Adult: Recognize It, Find the Cause
subtitle: An 82-year-old woman on POD2 after hip-fracture repair develops sudden, fluctuating confusion and inattention. Family says she was sharp at home. The nurse must recognize delirium, hunt for reversible causes, and manage it without restraints or benzodiazepines.

patient.name: Eleanor Pruitt
patient.admitDate: POD2 after left hip-fracture repair. New acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention overnight. Baseline (per daughter) alert and oriented, lives independently. On scheduled oxycodone + PRN diphenhydramine for sleep; has not voided well; low-grade fever.

vitals.temp: Hip pain; not voided; on opioid + diphenhydramine

labs.v: Sharp and independent at home per family.
labs.r: This is an ACUTE change, not dementia.

nursesNote: Eleanor Pruitt, 82, POD2 hip repair with new overnight confusion that comes and goes, plus inattention and disorganized thinking. Baseline alert/oriented per daughter. Low-grade fever with a positive UA, 600 mL bladder retention, Na 129, SpO2 93%, and deliriogenic meds (opioid, diphenhydramine, PRN lorazepam). CAM positive. Plan: confirm delirium, treat reversible causes, non-pharmacologic management, avoid restraints/benzodiazepines.
providerOrders: Confirm acute mental-status change with CAM; rule out reversible causes
Treat UTI per orders; relieve urinary retention; supplemental O2 for hypoxia
Review and minimize deliriogenic meds (diphenhydramine, PRN benzodiazepine)
Non-pharmacologic delirium bundle: reorient, sensory aids, sleep-wake support, mobilize
Reserve low-dose antipsychotic for severe agitation threatening safety only; reassess mental status each shift

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What points to acute delirium rather than baseline dementia?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Confusion of sudden onset that FLUCTUATES over hours suggests delirium
opts.rat: Acute + fluctuating.

opts.text: Inattention — can't sustain or follow attention — is a core feature
opts.rat: Hallmark of delirium.

opts.text: Disorganized thinking and altered consciousness support the diagnosis
opts.rat: CAM features.

opts.text: Family report that she was sharp at home means this is an ACUTE change
opts.rat: Baseline matters.

opts.text: A gradual, stable memory decline over years with intact attention is delirium
opts.rat: False — that is dementia.

opts.text: Look for a reversible trigger: infection, drugs, hypoxia, pain, retention
opts.rat: Delirium has a cause.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: How do you confirm and interpret it?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: CAM: acute/fluctuating + inattention + (disorganized thinking OR altered LOC) = positive
opts.rat: CAM algorithm.

opts.text: Delirium is often the FIRST or only sign of a new medical problem in elders
opts.rat: Watch for it.

opts.text: Quiet, withdrawn (hypoactive) delirium is common and easily missed
opts.rat: Not always agitated.

opts.text: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and opioids can precipitate delirium
opts.rat: Deliriogenic drugs.

opts.text: New confusion in an older adult is normal aging and needs no workup
opts.rat: False — always evaluate.

opts.text: Urinary retention, constipation, and hypoxia are reversible contributors
opts.rat: Treat the cause.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Recognize the acute change and confirm delirium with CAM
opts.rat: #1 — Name the problem.

opts.text: Find and treat reversible causes (UTI, retention, hypoxia, meds)
opts.rat: #2 — Fix the trigger.

opts.text: Provide non-pharmacologic management and a safe environment
opts.rat: #3 — First-line care.

opts.text: Reserve low-dose medication only for severe, unsafe agitation
opts.rat: #4 — Last resort.

opts.text: Reassess mental status and document the response
opts.rat: #5 — Track the trend.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Classify each feature.

opts.text: Acute onset over hours-to-days with a fluctuating course
opts.rat: Sudden, waxing/waning.

opts.text: Prominent inattention and altered level of consciousness
opts.rat: Core features.

opts.text: Often reversible once the underlying cause is treated
opts.rat: Treat the cause.

opts.text: Gradual, progressive memory loss over years; attention preserved early
opts.rat: Slow and chronic.

opts.text: Chronic and largely irreversible; consciousness usually normal
opts.rat: Stable baseline decline.

opts.text: Weeks of low mood and anhedonia with frequent "I don't know" answers
opts.rat: Mood-driven.

opts.text: Sad affect with sleep/appetite change; attention largely intact
opts.rat: Pseudodementia picture.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess and confirm the acute mental-status change (CAM)
opts.rat: #1 — Establish delirium.

opts.text: Address reversible causes: treat UTI, relieve retention, give O2, manage pain, review meds
opts.rat: #2 — Remove triggers.

opts.text: Reorient; provide glasses/hearing aids, family presence, day-night cues
opts.rat: #3 — Non-pharm bundle.

opts.text: Keep her safe with least-restrictive measures; avoid restraints and benzodiazepines
opts.rat: #4 — Do no harm.

opts.text: Reassess frequently and document the trend
opts.rat: #5 — Monitor response.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each outcome.

opts.text: After the UTI is treated and retention relieved, her attention returns
opts.rat: Cause corrected.

opts.text: She recognizes family and follows simple commands again
opts.rat: Mentation recovering.

opts.text: Sleep-wake cycle normalizes and agitation settles without sedatives
opts.rat: Non-pharm working.

opts.text: Mental status returns to her baseline over the next few days
opts.rat: Delirium resolving.

opts.text: She is placed in wrist restraints and becomes more agitated
opts.rat: Restraints worsen delirium.

opts.text: A benzodiazepine is given for agitation and she grows more confused
opts.rat: Benzos are deliriogenic.

opts.text: The confusion is dismissed as dementia and the UTI goes untreated
opts.rat: Missed reversible cause.

opts.text: She stays in bed for days, deconditions, and develops a pressure injury
opts.rat: Immobility harms.

title: Starting Long-Term Oral Corticosteroids: Prednisone Therapy & Self-Management Teaching
subtitle: A 64-year-old woman is started on long-term prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica. The nurse teaches safe corticosteroid use — never stopping abruptly, sick-day stress dosing, glucose and infection monitoring, and bone protection.

patient.name: Margaret Boyd
patient.admitDate: Rheumatology clinic. New polymyalgia rheumatica started on prednisone 20 mg daily with a planned slow taper. PMH borderline glucose intolerance, HTN, osteopenia. Here for medication teaching before going home.

labs.r: Watch GI bleeding, esp. with NSAIDs.

nursesNote: Margaret Boyd, 64, starting long-term prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica with a planned taper. Early effects: glucose 168, K 3.3, BP rising with +2 kg and mild edema; osteopenia on DEXA. Chronic use suppresses the HPA axis. Teaching focus: never stop abruptly, take in the morning with food, sick-day stress dosing, infection precautions, glucose/BP/weight monitoring, bone protection, no live vaccines, and a medical-alert ID.
providerOrders: Prednisone per taper schedule; do NOT discontinue abruptly
Monitor glucose, BP, weight, and potassium
Start calcium + vitamin D; bone-protection per guidelines
Teach infection precautions, sick-day stress dosing, and medical-alert ID
Avoid live vaccines; review and limit concurrent NSAIDs

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What must the patient understand about long-term steroids?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Long-term corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis — never stop them abruptly
opts.rat: Adrenal suppression.

opts.text: Abrupt withdrawal can trigger adrenal crisis (hypotension, weakness, nausea)
opts.rat: Life-threatening.

opts.text: Steroids raise blood glucose and can cause hyperglycemia
opts.rat: Expected effect.

opts.text: They increase infection risk and can MASK fever and other signs
opts.rat: Blunted response.

opts.text: It is fine to stop prednisone as soon as she feels better
opts.rat: False — must taper.

opts.text: Long-term use risks osteoporosis, weight gain, and mood/sleep changes
opts.rat: Cumulative effects.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: How should the drug be taken and monitored?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Take the dose in the MORNING with food to mimic cortisol rhythm and ease GI upset
opts.rat: Timing + protection.

opts.text: Doses must be TAPERED, never stopped suddenly
opts.rat: Prevents crisis.

opts.text: During illness or surgery the body needs MORE steroid (stress dosing)
opts.rat: Higher demand.

opts.text: Hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, fluid retention, and rising BP are expected effects
opts.rat: Monitor these.

opts.text: A live vaccine is preferred while taking immunosuppressive steroids
opts.rat: False — avoid live vaccines.

opts.text: New black, tarry stools could mean GI bleeding and must be reported
opts.rat: GI risk.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Order the teaching and monitoring priorities
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Confirm she understands NEVER to stop the steroid abruptly
opts.rat: #1 — Prevent crisis.

opts.text: Teach correct dosing: morning, with food, exactly per the taper
opts.rat: #2 — Safe use.

opts.text: Teach infection precautions, sick-day stress dosing, and when to call
opts.rat: #3 — Anticipate illness.

opts.text: Set up monitoring (glucose, BP, weight, K) and bone protection
opts.rat: #4 — Manage effects.

opts.text: Reinforce a medical-alert ID and follow-up labs
opts.rat: #5 — Safety net.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.sub: Does the patient's statement show correct understanding?
steps.inst: Classify each statement.

opts.text: "I'll take it in the morning with breakfast."
opts.rat: Right timing.

opts.text: "I won't stop it suddenly — I'll follow the taper."
opts.rat: Prevents crisis.

opts.text: "I'll call if I get a fever or feel ill, and ask about a higher dose when sick."
opts.rat: Infection + stress dosing.

opts.text: "I'll take calcium and vitamin D and keep my bone-density follow-up."
opts.rat: Bone protection.

opts.text: "I'll wear a medical-alert bracelet."
opts.rat: Flags steroid use.

opts.text: "Once my pain is gone I'll just quit the pills."
opts.rat: Abrupt stop = crisis.

opts.text: "I should get the live shingles/MMR vaccine now while on steroids."
opts.rat: Avoid live vaccines.

opts.text: "I'll add a couple of ibuprofen daily for extra relief."
opts.rat: Compounds GI-bleed risk.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Verify the exact taper schedule and have her state it back
opts.rat: #1 — Confirm plan.

opts.text: Teach administration: morning, with food, never skip or stop abruptly
opts.rat: #2 — Core safety.

opts.text: Review infection precautions, sick-day stress dosing, and when to call
opts.rat: #3 — Illness plan.

opts.text: Arrange monitoring (glucose, BP, weight, K) and bone-protective measures
opts.rat: #4 — Manage effects.

opts.text: Provide a medical-alert ID and schedule follow-up
opts.rat: #5 — Safety net.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each outcome.

opts.text: She follows the taper and her PMR symptoms stay controlled
opts.rat: Therapy working.

opts.text: Glucose and BP are monitored and managed with no infection
opts.rat: Effects controlled.

opts.text: She reports a fever promptly and gets early treatment
opts.rat: Caught masked infection.

opts.text: She takes calcium/vitamin D and keeps her bone-density follow-up
opts.rat: Bone protected.

opts.text: She stops prednisone on her own and becomes hypotensive, weak, and nauseated
opts.rat: Adrenal crisis.

opts.text: An infection is missed because steroids blunted her fever
opts.rat: Masked signs.

opts.text: She develops a bleeding ulcer after adding daily NSAIDs
opts.rat: GI hemorrhage.

opts.text: Unmonitored glucose climbs and she develops hyperglycemia symptoms
opts.rat: Uncontrolled effect.

title: Internal Radiation (Sealed-Source Brachytherapy) Safety: Protecting the Patient and Staff
subtitle: A 54-year-old woman has a sealed intracavitary implant placed for cervical cancer and is on strict bedrest. The nurse applies ALARA — time, distance, and shielding — and knows exactly what to do if the source dislodges.

patient.name: Diane Foster
patient.admitDate: Oncology unit for low-dose-rate intracavitary brachytherapy (tandem and ovoids) for cervical cancer. Sealed source in place; strict bedrest with a Foley and low-residue diet. Private room with radiation signage; lead container and long-handled forceps at the bedside.

vitals.temp: Source found on linens — exposure risk

labs.r: Lead container + long forceps at bedside.

nursesNote: Diane Foster, 54, with a sealed intracavitary brachytherapy implant for cervical cancer; strict bedrest, Foley, low-residue diet in a private room with radiation signage, a lead container, and long-handled forceps at the bedside. Sealed source means her body fluids are NOT radioactive. Care follows ALARA — minimize time, maximize distance, use shielding — with dosimetry badges, visitor screening, and a clear dislodged-source protocol.
providerOrders: Strict bedrest with Foley; low-residue diet while implant is in place
Private room with radiation warning signage; staff wear dosimetry badges
Apply ALARA: minimize time, maximize distance, use shielding; rotate staff
Keep lead-lined container and long-handled forceps in the room
If source dislodges: secure with forceps into the container and notify the radiation safety officer

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What does a sealed implant require?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Radiation comes from the source — apply time, distance, and shielding (ALARA)
opts.rat: Core principle.

opts.text: The patient is on strict bedrest to keep the implant from dislodging
opts.rat: Prevents displacement.

opts.text: A private room with a radiation warning sign is required
opts.rat: Controls access.

opts.text: Pregnant staff and children should not enter the room
opts.rat: Highest-risk groups.

opts.text: It is fine to spend long, unhurried periods at the bedside
opts.rat: False — minimize time.

opts.text: Keep a lead-lined container and long-handled forceps in the room
opts.rat: For a dislodged source.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: How is exposure minimized and tracked?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: ALARA = keep staff exposure As Low As Reasonably Achievable
opts.rat: Safety standard.

opts.text: Minimizing time, maximizing distance, and shielding all reduce exposure
opts.rat: The three levers.

opts.text: Staff wear a dosimetry (film) badge to track cumulative exposure
opts.rat: Monitors dose.

opts.text: A dislodged source is handled only with long forceps — never with hands
opts.rat: No direct contact.

opts.text: With a SEALED source, the patient's urine and linens are highly radioactive
opts.rat: False — sealed ≠ radioactive fluids.

opts.text: Check linens, bedpans, and dressings for a dislodged source before disposal
opts.rat: Don't discard the source.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: The source is found dislodged on the bed — order the actions
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Do NOT touch it; grasp it with the long-handled forceps
opts.rat: #1 — No bare hands.

opts.text: Place the source into the lead-lined container in the room
opts.rat: #2 — Shield it.

opts.text: Notify the radiation safety officer/physician immediately
opts.rat: #3 — Expert response.

opts.text: Keep everyone back; limit time and proximity to the source
opts.rat: #4 — Reduce exposure.

opts.text: Document the event and how long the source was unsecured
opts.rat: #5 — Record it.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.sub: Which ALARA principle does each action use?
steps.inst: Classify each protective action.

opts.text: Plan and organize care to spend the fewest minutes at the bedside
opts.rat: Less time = less dose.

opts.text: Rotate the patient's care among several nurses each shift
opts.rat: Spreads/limits time.

opts.text: Gather all supplies before entering so tasks are done quickly
opts.rat: Shortens exposure.

opts.text: Stand at the foot of the bed or doorway when not giving direct care
opts.rat: Farther = less dose.

opts.text: Ask visitors to stay several feet away and keep visits brief
opts.rat: Increase separation.

opts.text: Use the bedside lead shield while providing care
opts.rat: Lead blocks radiation.

opts.text: Place a dislodged source into the lead-lined container
opts.rat: Contains emission.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Confirm the private room, warning signage, and dosimetry badge
opts.rat: #1 — Set up safely.

opts.text: Organize care to minimize time and maximize distance at the bedside
opts.rat: #2 — Apply ALARA.

opts.text: Provide bedrest care and check linens/bedpan for a dislodged source
opts.rat: #3 — Guard the source.

opts.text: Screen visitors: no pregnant staff/children, brief visits at a distance
opts.rat: #4 — Protect others.

opts.text: Document care and reinforce the plan with the patient
opts.rat: #5 — Record/educate.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: The nurse clusters care and spends minimal time at the bedside
opts.rat: Limits exposure.

opts.text: A dislodged source is secured with forceps into the lead container
opts.rat: Correct protocol.

opts.text: Staff wear dosimetry badges and exposure stays within limits
opts.rat: Monitored safety.

opts.text: Visitors are screened and kept at a distance for brief visits
opts.rat: Protects others.

opts.text: A pregnant nurse is assigned to give the patient's direct care
opts.rat: High-risk to fetus.

opts.text: The nurse picks up a dislodged source with gloved hands
opts.rat: Use forceps only.

opts.text: The patient is allowed up to ambulate freely in the hall
opts.rat: Dislodges + exposes others.

opts.text: Linens are discarded without checking for a dislodged source
opts.rat: Could discard the source.

title: Pediatric Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Crisis: Pain, Hydration, and Comfort
subtitle: An 8-year-old boy with sickle cell disease (HbSS) arrives with severe pain in his back and legs after a cold swim and poor fluid intake. The nurse manages the crisis with around-the-clock analgesia, hydration, oxygen, and warmth — and watches for life-threatening complications.

patient.name: Marcus Bell
patient.admitDate: Pediatric unit for an acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis. Known HbSS sickle cell disease. Severe pain (9/10) in back and legs after a cold pool and two days of poor intake; low-grade fever. On scheduled IV opioids, IV fluids, and oxygen; penicillin prophylaxis at home.

vitals.temp: Severe pain 9/10 back/legs after cold swim
Dry mucous membranes; poor intake x2 days

nursesNote: Marcus Bell, 8, HbSS sickle cell disease in an acute vaso-occlusive crisis: severe back/leg pain (9/10) after a cold swim and poor intake, low-grade fever, SpO2 94%, Hgb 7.8. On scheduled IV opioids, IV fluids, and oxygen. Care = prompt around-the-clock analgesia, hydration, oxygen, and WARMTH (never cold). Monitor closely for acute chest syndrome and splenic sequestration; reinforce trigger avoidance and the fever-emergency rule.
providerOrders: Around-the-clock IV opioid analgesia with a pediatric pain scale; reassess often
IV isotonic fluids; encourage oral intake
Oxygen to keep SpO2 within target
Warm compresses, rest, treat infection; continue penicillin prophylaxis
Monitor for acute chest syndrome and splenic sequestration; daily hemoglobin

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What is happening in a vaso-occlusive crisis?
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Sickled cells block small vessels → tissue ischemia and severe pain
opts.rat: Vaso-occlusion.

opts.text: Common triggers include dehydration, infection, cold, hypoxia, and stress
opts.rat: Precipitants.

opts.text: Severe pain in the back, legs, and abdomen is typical
opts.rat: Classic crisis.

opts.text: Fever can signal infection — a serious risk in sickle cell disease
opts.rat: Asplenia risk.

opts.text: Crisis pain is usually mild and needs no opioids
opts.rat: False — often severe.

opts.text: These children have functional asplenia and high infection risk
opts.rat: Encapsulated organisms.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Treat pain promptly with scheduled (around-the-clock) analgesia, often opioids
opts.rat: Don't undertreat.

opts.text: Hydration (IV and oral) helps reduce sickling
opts.rat: Improves flow.

opts.text: Give oxygen if the child is hypoxic
opts.rat: Limits sickling.

opts.text: Use WARMTH (warm compresses) — never cold, which worsens vasoconstriction
opts.rat: Cold harms.

opts.text: Fluids should be restricted during a crisis
opts.rat: False — hydrate.

opts.text: Watch for acute chest syndrome and splenic sequestration — both emergencies
opts.rat: Life-threatening.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Order the management of the crisis
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Assess pain, airway/breathing, and oxygenation
opts.rat: #1 — Baseline.

opts.text: Start prompt around-the-clock analgesia for severe pain
opts.rat: #2 — Relieve pain.

opts.text: Provide IV/oral hydration and oxygen as needed
opts.rat: #3 — Reduce sickling.

opts.text: Apply warmth, promote rest, and treat any infection
opts.rat: #4 — Support.

opts.text: Monitor for complications (acute chest, sequestration) and document
opts.rat: #5 — Surveillance.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.sub: Indicated or contraindicated in a crisis?
steps.inst: Classify each action.

opts.text: Around-the-clock opioids guided by a pain scale
opts.rat: Adequate analgesia.

opts.text: Generous IV and oral fluids
opts.rat: Reduces sickling.

opts.text: Supplemental oxygen for hypoxia
opts.rat: Limits sickling.

opts.text: Warm compresses to painful areas
opts.rat: Promotes flow.

opts.text: Encourage rest and treat infection promptly
opts.rat: Supports recovery.

opts.text: Cold/ice packs to painful joints
opts.rat: Vasoconstriction worsens crisis.

opts.text: Restricting fluids to "rest the gut"
opts.rat: Dehydration worsens sickling.

opts.text: Withholding opioids over addiction fears in a true crisis
opts.rat: Undertreats real pain.

opts.text: Using meperidine (Demerol) as the routine analgesic
opts.rat: Metabolite risks seizures.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Assess pain and respiratory status with the right tools
opts.rat: #1 — Evaluate.

opts.text: Give the ordered around-the-clock analgesia and reassess effect
opts.rat: #2 — Treat pain.

opts.text: Begin IV/oral hydration and oxygen as needed
opts.rat: #3 — Reduce sickling.

opts.text: Apply warmth, position for comfort, and promote rest
opts.rat: #4 — Comfort.

opts.text: Monitor for acute chest/sequestration and teach trigger avoidance
opts.rat: #5 — Safety + teaching.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each outcome.

opts.text: Pain score drops and the child rests comfortably
opts.rat: Analgesia working.

opts.text: Hydration restored; mucous membranes moist with good urine output
opts.rat: Volume restored.

opts.text: SpO2 stays at/above 95% with no chest symptoms
opts.rat: No ACS.

opts.text: Parents can name triggers and the fever-emergency rule
opts.rat: Effective teaching.

opts.text: New chest pain and fever with a falling SpO2 and infiltrate
opts.rat: Acute chest syndrome.

opts.text: Rapid spleen enlargement with falling hemoglobin and shock
opts.rat: Splenic sequestration.

opts.text: Pain stays severe because doses are skipped or delayed
opts.rat: Undertreated pain.

opts.text: Cold packs are applied and the pain intensifies
opts.rat: Cold worsens sickling.

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage from Uterine Atony: Rapid Team Response
subtitle: One hour after a vaginal birth of a large baby following a long, oxytocin-augmented labor, a 29-year-old G3P3 is saturating pads with a soft, boggy uterus. The nurse must recognize postpartum hemorrhage, act on the 4 T's, and lead the team response.

patient.name: Tasha Greene
patient.admitDate: Postpartum unit, ~1 hour after a vaginal delivery of a 4.2 kg infant following prolonged labor with oxytocin augmentation. Now saturating perineal pads with a soft, boggy, displaced fundus and a rising pulse. Hemorrhage protocol activated.

vitals.temp: Pulse rising, BP falling — early shock

labs.r: Avoid Methergine in HTN, carboprost in asthma.

nursesNote: Tasha Greene, 29 (G3P3), ~1 hour after a vaginal birth of a 4.2 kg infant following prolonged oxytocin-augmented labor — all atony risk factors. Saturating pads, soft/boggy fundus displaced by a full bladder, EBL ~1200 mL, pulse rising and BP trending down. Hemorrhage protocol activated. Priorities: firm fundal massage, empty the bladder, oxytocin and ordered uterotonics (check contraindications), fluids/blood, quantify loss, and lead the team with closed-loop communication.
providerOrders: Activate the obstetric hemorrhage protocol; call for help
Firm fundal massage; ensure the bladder is empty (straight cath/Foley)
Two large-bore IVs, isotonic fluids; type and crossmatch; CBC and coags
Uterotonics: oxytocin first-line; methylergonovine (avoid if hypertensive); carboprost (avoid if asthma); misoprostol; tranexamic acid per orders
Quantify blood loss; transfuse as ordered; prepare for bimanual compression/OR if uncontrolled

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: A soft, boggy uterus suggests atony — the leading cause of early PPH
opts.rat: Tone problem.

opts.text: Saturating a pad in ≤15 minutes or a steady trickle of blood is abnormal
opts.rat: Excess loss.

opts.text: Tachycardia often appears BEFORE the blood pressure drops
opts.rat: Early shock sign.

opts.text: A full bladder can displace the uterus and prevent it from contracting
opts.rat: Empty it.

opts.text: Heavy postpartum bleeding is normal and needs no intervention
opts.rat: False — act now.

opts.text: Prolonged labor, a large baby, and oxytocin augmentation raise the risk
opts.rat: Atony risk factors.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select ALL accurate statements.

opts.text: Atony (TONE) is the most common cause — assess fundal tone first
opts.rat: Start there.

opts.text: The 4 T's are Tone, Trauma, Tissue, and Thrombin
opts.rat: The differential.

opts.text: Firm fundal massage and emptying the bladder are immediate measures
opts.rat: First steps.

opts.text: Oxytocin is first-line; add other uterotonics per orders
opts.rat: Restore tone.

opts.text: Methylergonovine (Methergine) is safe to give in severe hypertension
opts.rat: False — contraindicated.

opts.text: Call for help early and activate the hemorrhage protocol
opts.rat: Mobilize the team.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Order the management of the hemorrhage
steps.inst: Rank from #1 (FIRST) to #5 (LAST).

opts.text: Massage the fundus and empty the bladder
opts.rat: #1 — Restore tone.

opts.text: Call for help and activate the hemorrhage protocol
opts.rat: #2 — Get the team.

opts.text: Ensure large-bore IV access, fluids, and ordered uterotonics
opts.rat: #3 — Resuscitate + treat.

opts.text: Quantify blood loss, monitor vitals, and give blood products as ordered
opts.rat: #4 — Track + replace.

opts.text: Prepare for escalation (bimanual compression/OR) and document
opts.rat: #5 — Next level.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.sub: Which of the 4 T's does each finding point to?
steps.inst: Classify each finding.

opts.text: Soft, boggy uterus that firms up with massage
opts.rat: Atony.

opts.text: Fundus boggy and displaced upward by a full bladder
opts.rat: Distention prevents contraction.

opts.text: Firm uterus but steady bright-red bleeding from a vaginal/cervical tear
opts.rat: Laceration.

opts.text: A swollen, painful, bluish bulge in the perineum
opts.rat: Hematoma.

opts.text: Bleeding continues despite a firm, well-contracted, empty uterus
opts.rat: Look for a tear.

opts.text: Placenta delivered incomplete with fragments retained
opts.rat: Retained products.

opts.text: Missing cotyledons/membranes on placental inspection
opts.rat: Retained tissue.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.sub: Sequence the bedside and team actions
steps.inst: Rank the order of actions. #1 = FIRST.

opts.text: Stay with the patient and massage the fundus while calling for help
opts.rat: #1 — Don't leave.

opts.text: Assign clear roles with closed-loop communication (meds, IV/labs, recorder)
opts.rat: #2 — Lead the team.

opts.text: Give ordered uterotonics after checking contraindications
opts.rat: #3 — Safe meds.

opts.text: Give fluids/blood and continuously monitor the response
opts.rat: #4 — Resuscitate.

opts.text: Escalate to the provider/OR if bleeding continues; SBAR handoff
opts.rat: #5 — Escalate.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each outcome.

opts.text: The uterus firms and bleeding slows after massage and oxytocin
opts.rat: Tone restored.

opts.text: Vital signs stabilize and the pad count decreases
opts.rat: Bleeding controlled.

opts.text: Bladder emptied; fundus firm and midline

title: Psychiatric Patient Rights: The Right to Refuse Medication on an Involuntary Hold
subtitle: A 34-year-old man on a 72-hour involuntary hold for psychosis is now calm and organized but refuses his oral antipsychotic. The nurse must respect retained civil rights, recognize the narrow exceptions for involuntary medication, and avoid coercion.

nursesNote: Daniel Hayes, 34, on a 72-hour involuntary hold for psychosis, now calm/organized and not currently dangerous, refusing his oral risperidone with intact understanding. title: Autonomic Dysreflexia: A Spinal Cord Injury Emergency
subtitle: A 38-year-old man with a T4 spinal cord injury suddenly develops a pounding headache and a blood pressure of 210/110 — far above his usual low baseline. The nurse must recognize autonomic dysreflexia, sit him up, and find and remove the trigger fast.

patient.name: Andre Coleman
patient.admitDate: Rehab unit, T4 spinal cord injury 8 months ago (paraplegia). Sudden severe pounding headache with BP 210/110 (usual baseline ~96/60), flushing and sweating above the injury, and a distended bladder with a kinked indwelling catheter. Treated for autonomic dysreflexia.

AD occurs with injuries at/above T6 from a noxious stimulus below the level. Priorities: SIT UPRIGHT, loosen constrictive items, find and remove the trigger (bladder first, then bowel with anesthetic lubricant), monitor BP every 2-5 min, give a rapid antihypertensive if it stays high, and reinforce prevention.

title: ARDS: Lung-Protective Ventilation and Coordinated ICU Care

patient.name: Victor Hale
patient.admitDate: Medical ICU, intubated for ARDS from severe bacterial pneumonia. Bilateral infiltrates with refractory hypoxemia (SpO2 86% on FiO2 100%) and a low PaO2/FiO2 ratio. On lung-protective ventilation; team coordinating prone positioning.

title: Insulin Therapy: Types, Administration, and High-Alert Safety
subtitle: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is on NPH plus regular insulin with a rapid-acting correction scale. The nurse applies high-alert safety — correct mixing order, an independent double-check, careful meal timing — and manages hypoglycemia at the insulin's peak.

patient.name: Frank Delgado
patient.admitDate: Medical unit, type 2 diabetes requiring insulin. Orders for NPH plus regular insulin before meals and a rapid-acting correction scale. Pre-breakfast glucose 210. Later developed hypoglycemia (58) near the NPH peak.

vitals.temp: Regular+NPH drawn correctly; rapid with tray

nursesNote: Frank Delgado, 58, type 2 diabetes on NPH + regular insulin with a rapid-acting correction scale; pre-meal glucose 210, later 58 near the NPH peak. Insulin is a high-alert drug: verify order/glucose/concentration, perform an independent double-check, write "units" (not "U"), and use a U-100 syringe. When mixing, draw REGULAR (clear) before NPH (cloudy); never mix long-acting basal insulin; only regular insulin may be given IV. Give rapid-acting insulin with the meal; hold/adjust if NPO. Manage hypoglycemia with the Rule of 15 (IV dextrose/IM glucagon if unable to take PO).

Rotate injection sites; store insulin properly

title: Hygiene and Skin Care for a Dependent Patient: Comfort and Infection Prevention
subtitle: A 76-year-old woman who is dependent and incontinent after a stroke needs total hygiene care. The nurse provides bathing, perineal, and oral care that protects her skin, prevents infection, and preserves her comfort and dignity.

patient.name: Estelle Moreau
patient.admitDate: Rehab unit after a stroke; dependent for all ADLs and incontinent of urine and stool. Sacral and perineal skin reddened from moisture. Requires total hygiene care, frequent skin protection, and oral care.

vitals.temp: Skin breakdown, foul odor, new fever

nursesNote: Estelle Moreau, 76, dependent and incontinent after a stroke, with perineal/sacral redness from moisture. Hygiene care protects comfort, dignity, skin integrity, and prevents infection. Key practices: hand hygiene before/after care; clean-to-dirty bathing; perineal care FRONT TO BACK after each incontinence episode with a moisture barrier; oral care every shift (even if NPO) with aspiration precautions; reposition at least q2h keeping skin clean and dry; distinguish incontinence-associated dermatitis from a pressure injury; and safe linen handling. Avoid scrubbing bony prominences, hot water, leaving skin damp, and placing soiled linens on the floor.

Perineal care front to back after each incontinence episode; apply moisture barrier
Oral care every shift (side-lying with suction if decreased consciousness)
Reposition at least every 2 hours; keep skin clean and dry; contain soiled linens

title: Pediatric Cardiac Arrest (PALS): Leading the Code on a Child
subtitle: A 3-year-old in severe respiratory distress deteriorates to bradycardia and poor perfusion, then arrest. The nurse must lead the pediatric code — prioritizing oxygenation and ventilation, applying PALS, and coordinating the team with weight-based dosing.

patient.name: Mateo Rivas
patient.admitDate: Pediatric unit for severe pneumonia and respiratory distress. Despite oxygen, he becomes lethargic and mottled with bradycardia and poor perfusion, then apneic and pulseless. Pediatric code team activated; nurse leading the resuscitation.

vitals.temp: HR <60 with poor perfusion — start CPR

nursesNote: Mateo Rivas, 3, with severe pneumonia and respiratory distress decompensating to bradycardia (HR 50) with poor perfusion, then apnea and pulselessness — a respiratory/hypoxic arrest, the typical pediatric pathway. Pediatric code activated. Priorities: prioritize airway, oxygenation, and ventilation; start CPR for HR <60 with poor perfusion (depth ~1/3 chest, 15:2 with two rescuers, rotate q2min); give weight-based medications using the length-based (Broselow) tape; defibrillate VF/pVT at 2 then 4 J/kg; treat reversible causes (hypoxia first). Lead with one designated leader, clear role assignment, and closed-loop communication.

Prioritize airway, oxygenation, and bag-mask ventilation
Start CPR if HR <60 with poor perfusion; depth ~1/3 chest, 15:2 with two rescuers

Defibrillate VF/pVT at 2 J/kg then 4 J/kg; treat reversible causes; transfer to PICU

title: Newborn Prophylaxis: Parental Informed Consent and Refusal
subtitle: Healthy newborn parents decline the IM vitamin K injection and question the eye ointment and hepatitis B vaccine. The nurse educates without coercion, respects informed parental decisions, documents, and knows when a refusal must be escalated.

patient.name: Baby Girl Larsen
patient.admitDate: Term newborn, vigorous, feeding well; mother HBsAg-negative. Parents decline the routine IM vitamin K injection and have questions about erythromycin eye ointment and the hepatitis B birth dose. Nurse providing education and informed-consent counseling.

vitals.temp: Educated on VKDB risk; considering oral vitamin K

labs.r: Hep B birth dose not time-critical.
HBIG + vaccine ≤12 h if mother HBsAg+.

nursesNote: Baby Girl Larsen, term newborn, vigorous and feeding; mother HBsAg-negative. Parents decline the IM vitamin K injection (asking about oral vitamin K) and have questions about eye ointment and hepatitis B. Parents are the newborn's surrogate decision-makers; informed consent applies. The nurse gives accurate, non-coercive education (benefits/risks/alternatives), uses teach-back, respects an informed decision for non-emergent prophylaxis, documents objectively, and notifies the pediatrician. Refusal of clearly life-saving emergency care — or care whose absence causes serious imminent harm (medical neglect) — exceeds parental authority and is escalated (provider/ethics/social work/CPS).

Obtain informed consent; document acceptance or informed refusal
If mother is HBsAg-positive: hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours
Notify the pediatrician of any refusal; arrange follow-up
Do not coerce or administer declined interventions covertly

title: Schizophrenia: Community Care Coordination and Relapse Prevention
subtitle: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia comes to the community clinic with early warning signs after missing doses for two weeks. The nurse coordinates care — adherence support, a long-acting injectable, interdisciplinary follow-up — to prevent relapse.

title: Heart Failure Self-Management: Daily Weights, Sodium, and Medication Adherence
subtitle: A 68-year-old man with reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure is stable and ready for discharge after a decompensation. The nurse teaches daily weights, a low-sodium diet, medication adherence, and the warning signs that should prompt an early call.

patient.name: Clyde Bennett
patient.admitDate: Cardiology unit, recovering from an acute heart-failure decompensation (HFrEF). Now euvolemic and stable on guideline-directed therapy. Here for discharge self-management teaching: daily weights, low-sodium diet, medication adherence, and symptom monitoring.

vitals.temp: Dry weight set; daily weights taught
Mild exertional dyspnea; cardiac rehab planned
Weight up 6 lb, dyspnea, crackles — readmission

nursesNote: Clyde Bennett, 68, HFrEF, stable and euvolemic after a decompensation, ready for discharge teaching. Self-management priorities: daily morning weights (same time/scale, after voiding) and report a gain >2-3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week; low-sodium diet (~2 g/day, avoid canned/processed/restaurant foods) with fluid restriction if ordered; take all medications consistently (diuretic in the morning) and AVOID NSAIDs; monitor for increasing dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, and edema; balance activity with rest and attend cardiac rehab; update vaccines; keep follow-up; and know when to call vs seek emergency care.
providerOrders: Heart-failure discharge teaching: daily weights, low-sodium diet, fluid restriction if ordered
Medication reconciliation; reinforce adherence; avoid NSAIDs
Teach weight-gain thresholds and worsening-symptom warning signs
Refer to cardiac rehabilitation; update influenza/pneumococcal vaccines

title: Preventing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia: The Vent Bundle

title: Urinary Incontinence in the Older Adult: Types and Behavioral Management
subtitle: A 78-year-old woman reports leaking urine and frequent urgency, with mild perineal skin redness. The nurse identifies the type of incontinence, starts first-line behavioral therapy, and protects skin and dignity — without restricting fluids or rushing to a catheter.

patient.name: Marjorie Flynn

vitals.temp: Uses walker; bathroom far; nocturia x3

nursesNote: Marjorie Flynn, 78, with mixed symptoms — urge leakage plus occasional stress leakage — compounded by limited mobility (walker, distant bathroom) and mild perineal redness. Incontinence is common but NOT normal aging and is treatable. Plan: screen for reversible causes (UTI, meds, constipation), identify the type with a bladder diary and post-void residual, and start first-line behavioral therapy (timed/prompted voiding, pelvic floor exercises, bladder training). Optimize fluids (adequate intake, limit caffeine/evening fluids — do not restrict), protect the skin, ensure easy toilet access and dignity, and avoid an indwelling catheter except as a last resort.

title: Medication Administration: Scope of Practice and Safe Delegation
subtitle: During a busy med pass, the RN leads a team with an LPN/LVN and a UAP. She must match each medication task to the correct scope of practice, apply the five rights of delegation, and keep RN-only tasks with the RN.

patient.name: Day-Shift Med Pass (RN, LPN, UAP)
patient.admitDate: Medical unit. The charge/primary RN organizes the medication pass across the team: a stable patient due for routine oral meds, a new admission needing a first-dose IV antibiotic, a patient on a heparin drip needing titration, and a patient with new pain needing a PRN decision.

labs.v: Being busy is not an excuse.

nursesNote: Day-shift medication pass led by the RN with an LPN/LVN and a UAP. The RN matches tasks to scope: she personally gives IV push meds, titrated drips, first doses, and blood products and makes PRN judgments for new/complex symptoms; the LPN/LVN gives routine scheduled oral/SubQ/IM meds to stable patients and reinforces teaching under supervision; the UAP supports (reminders, water, vitals) and reports but does NOT administer medications. Delegation follows the five rights (task/circumstance/person/direction/supervision), the RN retains accountability, and 'being busy' never justifies delegating outside scope.

title: When an Error Happens: Disclosure, Incident Reporting, and Just Culture
subtitle: A patient mistakenly received a double dose of her beta-blocker. She is stable but mildly bradycardic. The nurse must protect the patient, disclose the error honestly, document factually, and report it through a just-culture system.

nursesNote: Beatrice Holloway, 70, received a duplicate dose of metoprolol from a process breakdown, caught shortly after; asymptomatic with mild bradycardia, on telemetry, provider notified and next dose held. title: Prenatal Care and a Healthy Pregnancy: First-Visit Teaching
subtitle: A healthy 27-year-old at about 10 weeks comes in for her first prenatal visit. The nurse teaches folic acid, nutrition, vaccines, substances and foods to avoid, and the danger signs that need prompt reporting.

nursesNote: Hana Okada, 27, G1 at ~10 weeks, healthy, here for her first prenatal visit. Teaching: take a daily prenatal vitamin with folic acid (prevents neural tube defects); eat a balanced diet with adequate protein/iron/calcium and appropriate weight gain; get the inactivated influenza vaccine and Tdap while AVOIDING live vaccines (MMR/varicella); avoid alcohol (no safe amount), tobacco, and listeria foods (unpasteurized dairy, deli meats unless heated, raw/undercooked items); avoid cat litter (toxoplasmosis); exercise moderately. title: Suicide Precautions: Maintaining a Safe Environment
subtitle: A 32-year-old is admitted to inpatient psychiatry with active suicidal ideation and a plan. The nurse establishes suicide precautions — the right observation level, means restriction, a ligature-safe room, and a searched environment.

patient.name: Jordan Wells
patient.admitDate: Inpatient psychiatry for active suicidal ideation with a plan and a hopeless affect. Placed on suicide precautions: continuous 1:1 observation, means restriction, ligature-safe room, and a searched environment.

vitals.temp: Active SI with a plan; hopeless affect

nursesNote: Jordan Wells, 32, admitted with active suicidal ideation and a plan; placed on suicide precautions. Environmental safety is central: maintain the ordered observation level (continuous 1:1 = arm's-length, including the bathroom), restrict means, and make the room ligature-safe (remove cords/belts/shoelaces/drawstrings). Search belongings and secure contraband (sharps, medications, glass, lighters); supervise meals with plastic utensils. Perform safety checks at random, unpredictable intervals; never leave a 1:1 patient alone. Ask directly about ideation/plan/means (it does not plant the idea), engage the patient in a safety plan, and reassess risk regularly and at every hand-off. A 'no-suicide contract' does not replace monitoring.

title: Postoperative Pain Management: Assessment and Multimodal Comfort
subtitle: A 55-year-old on the first day after abdominal surgery rates his incisional pain 8/10 and is splinting and reluctant to cough. The nurse assesses the pain, provides multimodal analgesia, and monitors for opioid side effects.

patient.name: Carl Whitman
patient.admitDate: Surgical unit, POD1 after open abdominal surgery (bowel resection). Reports 8/10 incisional pain with guarding, reluctant to cough or deep breathe. On scheduled non-opioid analgesia with opioid for breakthrough pain.

labs.r: Pain is what the patient says.

nursesNote: Carl Whitman, 55, POD1 open abdominal surgery, rating incisional pain 8/10 with guarding and reluctant to cough/deep breathe (atelectasis risk). Pain is subjective — the patient's self-report is the most reliable indicator; normal vital signs do not rule out pain. Provide multimodal analgesia (scheduled non-opioid + opioid for breakthrough, around-the-clock for constant pain) plus non-pharmacologic measures (positioning, splinting the incision, ice/heat, relaxation). Start a bowel regimen with opioids and monitor sedation level and respiratory rate (sedation precedes respiratory depression). Do not undertreat over addiction fears; reassess pain and function after each intervention and document.

title: Recognizing Deterioration: Rapid Response and the Chain of Command
subtitle: A 67-year-old on the floor with pneumonia develops a rising respiratory rate, falling oxygen, hypotension, and new confusion. The nurse must recognize the deterioration, activate the rapid response team, and escalate to rescue the patient before arrest.

patient.name: Gerald Stack
patient.admitDate: Medical unit, admitted with pneumonia. Over the last hour: respiratory rate climbing, SpO2 dropping, blood pressure falling, and new acute confusion with low urine output — meeting rapid-response criteria. Nurse recognizing deterioration and activating the team.

vitals.temp: O2 applied; IV access; RRT at bedside
Stabilizing; transfer to higher level of care
Progressed to arrest — failure to rescue

labs.v: RR, SpO2, BP, mental status, UOP.

nursesNote: Gerald Stack, 67, admitted with pneumonia, now deteriorating: RR 30+, SpO2 88%, BP 86/54, HR 118, new confusion, and low urine output — meeting rapid-response criteria. Subtle changes (especially a rising respiratory rate) often precede arrest by hours; early recognition enables rescue. Activate the rapid response team WITHOUT delay (don't wait to 'see if it improves'); stay with the patient and support ABCs (oxygen, positioning, monitor, IV access). Communicate with SBAR and coordinate roles with closed-loop communication. If a provider is unresponsive or the plan is inadequate, escalate up the chain of command to prevent failure to rescue. Document and reassess.

title: Advance Directives and Advance Care Planning
subtitle: A capacitated 74-year-old with chronic illness wants to complete her advance directives on admission. The nurse explains the document types, facilitates her choices, names a proxy, and ensures the directive is honored.

nursesNote: Frances Whitaker, 74, capacitated, completing advance directives on admission. Advance directives generally take effect only when the patient loses decision-making capacity (except a POLST/DNR, which are active provider orders). A living will states which life-sustaining treatments she wants or refuses; a durable power of attorney for healthcare (healthcare proxy) names a surrogate who uses substituted judgment. title: Medication Reconciliation Across Care Transitions
subtitle: A 72-year-old is admitted on 11 medications from several prescribers and pharmacies. The nurse performs medication reconciliation — building a complete list, comparing it to new orders, and resolving discrepancies to prevent errors.

patient.name: Arthur Benson
patient.admitDate: Medical unit, admitted with a heart-failure exacerbation. Takes 11 medications prescribed by several providers and filled at two pharmacies, plus an over-the-counter supplement. Nurse performing admission medication reconciliation.

nursesNote: Arthur Benson, 72, admitted with a heart-failure exacerbation on 11 medications from several prescribers and two pharmacies, plus an OTC supplement. Medication reconciliation (a National Patient Safety Goal) builds the most accurate list of ALL medications (prescription, OTC, herbal, supplements, drops, inhalers, patches) from multiple sources (patient/family, pill bottles, pharmacy, records) and compares it to new orders at EVERY transition (admission, transfer, discharge) to find and resolve discrepancies — omissions, duplications, wrong dose/frequency, interactions. Found: an omitted home levothyroxine, a duplicate antihypertensive, and an unreported herbal supplement. Resolve with the provider/pharmacist, then give the patient an updated list with teach-back at discharge and communicate it to the next provider/pharmacy.

Identify and resolve discrepancies with the provider and pharmacist
Provide an updated reconciled list with teach-back; communicate to the next provider/pharmacy

title: Antibiotic Stewardship: Teaching Appropriate Use and Preventing Resistance
subtitle: A 40-year-old with a 3-day viral cold asks for antibiotics. The nurse teaches that antibiotics don't treat viruses, explains antimicrobial resistance, provides symptom self-care, and reinforces infection prevention.

patient.name: Denise Carver
patient.admitDate: Primary-care clinic with 3 days of cough, congestion, and sore throat consistent with a viral upper respiratory infection. No signs of a bacterial infection. Requesting antibiotics; here for assessment and teaching.

vitals.temp: Cough, congestion, sore throat x3 days (viral)
No bacterial signs; viral URI likely
C. diff diarrhea / future resistant infection

nursesNote: Denise Carver, 40, with a 3-day viral upper respiratory infection requesting antibiotics. Antibiotics treat bacterial — not viral — infections; taking them for a cold is ineffective and contributes to antimicrobial resistance, a major public-health threat. Teaching: reserve antibiotics for bacterial infections and take them exactly as prescribed (complete the course, don't skip doses); never share or save leftover antibiotics; don't demand them for viral illness. Manage the cold with rest, fluids, and OTC symptom care. Prevent infections (and antibiotic need) with vaccines, hand hygiene, and food safety. Note antibiotics can disrupt normal flora and cause C. difficile diarrhea — report severe or bloody diarrhea. Provide return precautions.

title: Childhood Injury Prevention: Age-Appropriate Safety Teaching
subtitle: A curious, newly walking 15-month-old comes in for a well visit. The nurse provides injury-prevention anticipatory guidance — car seats, choking, poisoning, water, burns, and falls — matched to the child's developmental stage.

patient.name: Mia Torres
patient.admitDate: Pediatric clinic for a 15-month well visit. Healthy and thriving; walking, climbing, and mouthing objects. Parents report the home is not yet fully childproofed. Visit focused on injury-prevention anticipatory guidance.

nursesNote: Mia Torres, 15 months, healthy and thriving — walking, climbing, and mouthing objects; home not fully childproofed. Unintentional injury is a leading cause of death in children, and prevention is matched to the developmental stage. Teaching: rear-facing car seat in the back seat; lock medications and chemicals up and out of reach (keep the Poison Control number, do NOT induce vomiting/give ipecac); avoid choking hazards (whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, hot dogs — cut foods small); constant supervision near water (never leave a child alone in the tub/pool); set the water heater to a safe temperature and turn pot handles inward; use stair gates and window guards and lower the crib mattress; store firearms locked and unloaded, separate from ammunition. Childproofing does not replace supervision.

Teach car-seat safety (rear-facing, back seat), safe sleep, and supervision
Teach safe storage of medications/chemicals and choking-hazard avoidance
Provide the Poison Control number; advise against inducing vomiting
Address home hazards (water, burns, falls, firearms); reassess at follow-up

title: Comfort Measures in Labor: Nonpharmacologic Support
subtitle: A 26-year-old in active labor with back pain wants to cope without medication for now. The nurse uses position changes, hydrotherapy, counterpressure, breathing, and continuous support to ease discomfort and aid labor.

patient.name: Aisha Bello
patient.admitDate: Labor and delivery, G1 in active labor with contractions every 3 minutes and reassuring fetal heart tones. Reports back pain (suspected occiput-posterior). Prefers nonpharmacologic comfort measures for now.

nursesNote: Aisha Bello, 26, G1 in active labor (contractions q3min, reassuring FHR) with back pain from a suspected occiput-posterior position; prefers nonpharmacologic comfort for now. Comfort measures: frequent position changes and upright positions/ambulation; side-lying to avoid supine hypotension; hydrotherapy (warm shower/tub); sacral counterpressure for back labor; coached paced breathing and relaxation; massage; a calm environment with continuous labor support (partner/doula reduces interventions); and regular bladder emptying (a full bladder impedes progress and comfort). These complement — not replace — pharmacologic options (epidural, IV opioid, nitrous) the patient may choose.
providerOrders: Provide nonpharmacologic comfort measures per the patient's preferences
Encourage frequent position changes, upright positions, and ambulation as appropriate
Offer hydrotherapy, counterpressure, massage, and breathing/relaxation coaching
Encourage regular bladder emptying; avoid prolonged supine positioning
Offer pharmacologic options (epidural/IV/nitrous) as desired; provide continuous support

title: Behavioral Emergency: Leading the Team Response to an Escalating Patient
subtitle: A 38-year-old on the unit is pacing, shouting, and threatening with clenched fists. The nurse must lead a coordinated team response — ensuring safety, de-escalating with one calm voice, and using restraint only as a last resort.

title: Patient Confidentiality and HIPAA: Protecting Health Information
subtitle: Across one shift the nurse faces a phone caller, family at the desk, hallway conversations, and a social-media temptation. The nurse must protect every patient's information while still sharing what the care team legitimately needs.

patient.name: R. Castillo

nursesNote: R. Castillo, 57, is stable on a medical unit. During the shift several people request her information: a caller on the phone, family members at the desk, and staff chatting in the hallway. The nurse protects confidentiality by sharing protected health information (PHI) only with those involved in the patient's care and only the minimum necessary. Before releasing any information to a caller or visitor, the nurse verifies identity and confirms the patient's consent (or the designated code word). PHI is not discussed in public areas, devices are kept logged off, and nothing about any patient is posted on social media. The nurse knows the limited permitted disclosures (such as mandatory abuse reporting and certain communicable diseases) and reports any suspected breach promptly per facility policy.

title: Floating to an Unfamiliar Unit: Accepting a Safe Assignment
subtitle: A med-surg RN is floated to a busy telemetry unit. The nurse must accept the assignment safely — communicating competencies, getting oriented, taking patients and tasks within scope, and getting help for unfamiliar ones — without committing patient abandonment.

patient.name: Float Assignment
patient.admitDate: Med-surg RN floated to a telemetry unit for the shift. Must accept a safe assignment, work within competence, and get help for unfamiliar tasks — without abandoning patients.

vitals.temp: Floating is a legal staffing practice

nursesNote: A med-surg RN is floated to a telemetry unit. Floating is a legal, common staffing practice; an assignment cannot be refused for unfamiliarity alone. The nurse reports to the unit, notifies the charge nurse of clinical background and any limitations, and requests a brief orientation (layout, equipment, emergency supplies, codes, where to get help). The nurse accepts the more stable patients and tasks within competence, and asks that unfamiliar high-risk tasks — such as titrating a vasoactive drip the nurse has never managed — be reassigned or performed with help. A buddy-system pairing and the chain of command support safe care; concerns are documented through proper channels. The nurse keeps patient safety first and does not abandon patients: declining must happen before accepting report, and walking off after taking report constitutes patient abandonment.

Obtain a brief orientation to layout, equipment, emergency supplies, and codes
Accept stable patients and tasks within competence

title: Osteoporosis Prevention and Bone Health in the Older Adult
subtitle: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman with a DEXA showing osteopenia attends a wellness visit. The nurse teaches bone-protective habits — calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall-proofing, and safe bisphosphonate use — to prevent fragility fractures.

patient.name: G. Bennett
patient.admitDate: Outpatient wellness visit. Postmenopausal (menopause at 51), maternal history of hip fracture, sedentary, low dairy intake, former smoker. DEXA shows osteopenia. Here for bone-health teaching.

labs.r: Act before more bone is lost.

labs.v: Remove rugs; add lighting + grab bars.

labs.r: Empty stomach, full glass of water.

nursesNote: G. Bennett, 62, is postmenopausal with several osteoporosis risk factors (menopause at 51, maternal hip fracture, sedentary lifestyle, low dairy intake, former smoker). Her DEXA shows osteopenia (T-score -2.0). At this wellness visit the nurse teaches bone-protective habits: aim for about 1200 mg of calcium per day from food first plus roughly 800-1000 IU of vitamin D; perform regular weight-bearing and resistance exercise; and fall-proof the home (remove loose rugs, improve lighting, add grab bars) since most fragility fractures follow a fall. The nurse reviews smoking and alcohol moderation, the role of DEXA screening and T-score interpretation, and, if a bisphosphonate is prescribed, safe administration: take it in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes. Teaching is confirmed with teach-back before the visit ends.

The nurse wears the correct PPE (two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves and an impervious gown, plus face/eye protection if splashing is possible and respiratory protection if aerosolization is a risk), uses pharmacy-prepared doses with a closed-system transfer device, and keeps tubing primed by pharmacy with non-drug fluid. Doses are transported in sealed, labeled containers (never the pneumatic tube). A chemotherapy spill kit is kept accessible: for a spill, the nurse dons kit PPE, contains and cleans the area per policy, and disposes of all material in designated hazardous-waste containers. Because the drug is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, PPE is worn when handling urine, stool, emesis, and linens. After any skin contact the nurse washes immediately with soap and water (eyes flushed 15 minutes at the eyewash), reports the exposure, and seeks evaluation. Staff who are pregnant or lactating follow facility reproductive-risk policy.

title: Atraumatic Care: Nonpharmacologic Comfort for the Hospitalized Child
subtitle: A frightened 4-year-old needs an IV start. The nurse minimizes physical and emotional distress with honest preparation, parental presence, comfort positioning, topical anesthetic, and distraction — using a treatment room and saving the bed and playroom as safe spaces.

patient.name: L. Tran
patient.admitDate: Pediatric unit. A 4-year-old needs an IV start and blood draw. Frightened and clinging to a parent. Nurse applying atraumatic-care principles to reduce distress and pain.

nursesNote: L. Tran, 4, needs an IV start and blood draw and is frightened and clinging to her parent. The nurse applies atraumatic care to minimize physical and emotional distress: keep the parent present as a comforter, give an honest and simple age-appropriate explanation (avoiding words with double meanings and false reassurance), and perform the painful procedure in the treatment room so the child's bed and the playroom stay safe. Comfort measures include a comfort position (upright in the parent's lap or chest-to-chest rather than lying flat and being held down), a topical numbing cream before the needlestick when time allows, and age-appropriate distraction such as bubbles, a video, or guided breathing. For infants, nonnutritive sucking, swaddling, oral sucrose, facilitated tucking, skin-to-skin, or breastfeeding help. Therapeutic play lets the child handle equipment and gain a sense of control. Afterward the nurse comforts and praises the child, offers a comfort item, and never threatens or shames.

Prepare the child honestly with simple, age-appropriate language
Perform painful procedures in the treatment room, not the bed or playroom
Use comfort positioning, topical anesthetic, and age-appropriate distraction
Comfort and praise the child afterward; provide a comfort item and rest

title: Questioning an Unsafe Provider Order: The Duty to Clarify and the Chain of Command
subtitle: A med-surg nurse receives an order for digoxin 2.5 mg IV — about ten times the usual dose — for a 79-year-old in new atrial fibrillation. The nurse must hold the dose, clarify with the prescriber, and use the chain of command rather than carry out an unsafe order.

patient.name: M. Foster
patient.admitDate: Med-surg unit, new atrial fibrillation with rapid rate. A new order reads 'digoxin 2.5 mg IV now' — about ten times the usual dose. Nurse must clarify before acting.

vitals.temp: Do NOT give; call the prescriber

nursesNote: M. Foster, 79, is on the med-surg unit in new atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate. A new order reads 'digoxin 2.5 mg IV now' — roughly ten times the usual dose (about 0.125-0.25 mg), a classic tenfold/decimal error. The nurse has a legal and ethical duty NOT to carry out an order believed to be unsafe: the dose is held and not administered. The nurse rechecks the order, the usual safe dose range, and the patient (allergies, weight, renal function, current rhythm), then contacts the prescriber directly to clarify dose, route, and frequency. If the prescriber insists and the nurse still believes the order is unsafe, the nurse does not give it and escalates up the chain of command (charge nurse, nursing supervisor, pharmacy, and the medical chain). The nurse never alters the order independently and never silently omits it. Once a corrected, safe order is confirmed, it is carried out, and the clarification and resolution are documented objectively (who was contacted, when, what was discussed, and the outcome).

title: Truth-Telling and the Right to Know: When Family Asks to Withhold a Diagnosis
subtitle: A 76-year-old woman has newly diagnosed metastatic cancer, and her adult children ask the team not to tell her. The patient is alert and competent and is asking about her results. The nurse must protect her right to know without dismissing the family.

patient.name: R. Adeyemi

nursesNote: R. Adeyemi, 76, has newly diagnosed metastatic cancer. Her adult children, citing protection and cultural reasons, ask the team not to tell her. She is alert and competent and has been asking about her results. A competent adult has the ethical and legal right to know her own diagnosis and to make informed decisions (autonomy and veracity); the information belongs to the patient, and the nurse must not lie to her or deceive her. At the same time, the nurse asks the patient directly how much she wants to know and whom she wants involved, because a patient may choose to receive less information or designate a family member to hear details — that is the patient's choice, not the family's. The nurse explores the family's concerns with empathy and cultural humility rather than dismissing them, and coordinates a provider-led family meeting where the diagnosis can be disclosed compassionately with support (chaplain, social work, interpreter as needed). If conflict persists, the nurse involves the ethics committee and documents the discussions objectively.

title: Setting Priorities: Deciding Which Patient to See First
subtitle: An RN starts the shift with four patients and must decide who to assess first. Using ABCs, Maslow, and unstable-before-stable, the nurse prioritizes a hypoxic COPD patient over routine and stable needs.

patient.name: Shift-Start Prioritization
patient.admitDate: RN receives report on four patients and must decide which to assess first, applying prioritization frameworks (ABCs, Maslow, acute/unstable before chronic/stable).
