nursesNote: An RN takes report on four med-surg patients and must decide who to assess first. Patient A has COPD with a new SpO2 of 88%, rising respiratory rate, increasing dyspnea, and restlessness — an airway/breathing problem in an unstable patient. Patient B is post-op day 1 and is requesting a PRN pain medication; the need is real but the patient is stable. Patient C is stable and awaiting discharge teaching. Patient D has a scheduled 0900 oral medication that can be timed within its window. Applying ABCs, Maslow's hierarchy, and the principle that unstable/acute patients are seen before stable/chronic ones, the nurse assesses Patient A first, then addresses the stable pain need, gives the time-sensitive medication, and provides discharge teaching last. Priorities are reassessed continuously, since a sudden, unexpected change outranks an expected finding.

nursesNote: A 52-year-old woman presents for a wellness visit. She is average risk for most cancers, is a former smoker (20 pack-years, quit 5 years ago), and has a sister with breast cancer. The nurse reviews age-appropriate cancer screening: colorectal screening begins at age 45 (colonoscopy every 10 years, or an annual FIT, or stool-DNA every 3 years); mammography is recommended for women roughly 40–74; cervical screening uses a Pap and/or HPV test and usually stops around age 65; and because of her smoking history, annual low-dose CT lung screening is indicated for ages 50–80 with at least a 20 pack-year history. The nurse emphasizes that screening detects cancer before symptoms appear, that a positive screening test requires diagnostic follow-up, and that family history may warrant earlier or more frequent screening.

title: Seizure Precautions: Keeping the Patient Safe
subtitle: A 24-year-old man with a seizure disorder is admitted after a breakthrough seizure. The nurse sets up bedside seizure precautions and provides safe care during and after a tonic-clonic seizure — protecting the airway and never restraining or placing anything in the mouth.

patient.name: Seizure Precautions
patient.admitDate: 24M with epilepsy admitted after a breakthrough tonic-clonic seizure (missed doses). On seizure precautions for monitoring and medication adjustment.

vitals.temp: Padded rails up, bed low + locked

nursesNote: A 24-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is admitted after a breakthrough tonic-clonic seizure following missed medication doses. The nurse places him on seizure precautions: padded side rails kept up, bed in the lowest position with wheels locked, and functioning suction, oxygen, and a bag-valve mask set up at the bedside. The nurse teaches that during a seizure the priority is to stay with the patient, call for help, protect the head, turn the patient to the side to protect the airway, loosen tight clothing, and time the event — while NEVER restraining the limbs or placing anything in the mouth. A seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes is status epilepticus and requires an ordered IV benzodiazepine. Afterward, the nurse keeps the patient side-lying, suctions as needed, reorients, assesses for injury, and documents the onset, duration, characteristics, and postictal state.

title: Managing Constipation: Bowel Elimination and Comfort
subtitle: A 70-year-old man on around-the-clock opioids for pain, with low mobility, has not had a bowel movement in 3 days. The nurse manages constipation with fluids, fiber, activity, a toileting routine, and an appropriate bowel regimen.

patient.name: Constipation Management

nursesNote: A 70-year-old man on scheduled opioids for pain, with limited mobility and low fluid and fiber intake, has not had a bowel movement in 3 days and reports bloating and straining. Constipation means hard, infrequent, or difficult-to-pass stools; a daily bowel movement is not required for everyone. Opioids are a leading cause, so a bowel regimen should accompany opioid therapy. The nurse promotes first-line measures — increased fluids, dietary fiber, activity, privacy, an upright position with a footstool, and responding promptly to the urge — and gives ordered laxatives, favoring a stimulant (senna) with or without an osmotic agent (polyethylene glycol) for opioid-induced constipation; bulk-forming agents alone are not effective for opioids and require adequate fluid. New abdominal distension with no stool, nausea, and vomiting suggests impaction or obstruction and must be evaluated before further laxatives.

Encourage fluids, dietary fiber, activity, and a toileting routine
Start a prophylactic bowel regimen with opioid therapy

title: The Impaired Colleague: Duty to Report and Patient Safety
subtitle: A nurse notices a coworker with slurred speech and an unsteady gait, frequent narcotic-count discrepancies, and patients reporting unrelieved pain. Patient safety comes first: remove the nurse from care, report up the chain, and support recovery — never cover it up.

patient.name: Impaired Colleague
patient.admitDate: A nurse suspects a coworker is impaired/diverting on shift: slurred speech, unsteady gait, count discrepancies, excessive PRN waste, and patients with unrelieved pain. The nurse must act to protect patients.

labs.v: Remove the nurse from patient care.

nursesNote: A nurse notices that a coworker has slurred speech, an unsteady gait, and frequent unexplained absences from the unit, along with repeated narcotic-count discrepancies, excessive PRN waste and overrides, and several patients reporting unrelieved pain. These are warning signs of possible impairment and drug diversion. Patient safety is the first priority: the impaired nurse must be removed from patient care. The nurse reports the concern to the charge nurse or supervisor through the chain of command per facility policy, documents specific objective observations factually, and does not cover for the colleague, ignore the signs, or confront and accuse them publicly. The colleague's safety is also protected (not driving impaired). Reporting to the Board of Nursing may be required by state law. Substance use disorder is a treatable disease, and many states offer nondisciplinary peer-assistance or alternative-to-discipline recovery programs.

title: Professional Boundaries in the Nurse–Patient Relationship
subtitle: Over a long admission, a patient offers the nurse an expensive gift, asks for a personal phone number, and wants to connect on social media. The nurse keeps the relationship patient-centered and professional — declining personal contact and avoiding boundary violations.

patient.name: Professional Boundaries
patient.admitDate: During a prolonged admission a patient offers gifts, requests the nurse's personal phone number, and asks to be social-media friends. The nurse must maintain a therapeutic, professional relationship.

labs.r: Helps the patient, not the nurse.

labs.v: Only if it benefits the patient.

nursesNote: Over a prolonged admission, a patient offers the nurse an expensive gift, asks for the nurse's personal phone number to stay in touch, and requests to be social-media friends. The nurse-patient relationship is therapeutic: patient-centered, goal-directed, professional, and time-limited, ending at discharge. The nurse keeps interactions focused on the patient's care goals, limits self-disclosure to what benefits the patient, and recognizes warning signs of over-involvement (off-duty contact, secret-keeping, accepting money or expensive gifts) as well as under-involvement (neglect, disinterest). The nurse politely declines the gift and personal contact, does not friend, follow, post about, or photograph patients on social media, and never enters a romantic or sexual relationship with a patient. If objectivity becomes compromised, the nurse consults the supervisor, considers transferring care, and documents appropriately.
providerOrders: Keep the relationship patient-centered, professional, and goal-directed
Decline money or expensive gifts and personal/social-media contact
Limit self-disclosure to what benefits the patient
Recognize over- or under-involvement and consult the supervisor
Protect confidentiality; never form a romantic relationship with a patient

title: Therapeutic Communication: Building the Nurse-Patient Relationship
subtitle: A patient newly diagnosed with a serious illness becomes tearful and withdrawn. The nurse uses therapeutic communication — open-ended questions, active listening, silence, and empathy — while avoiding nontherapeutic blocks like false reassurance and 'why' questions.

patient.name: Therapeutic Communication
patient.admitDate: A patient newly diagnosed with a serious illness becomes tearful and quiet. The nurse uses therapeutic techniques to build trust and explore feelings while avoiding communication blocks.

nursesNote: A patient newly diagnosed with a serious illness becomes tearful, quiet, and withdrawn. Therapeutic communication is patient-centered and goal-directed: the nurse sits down, gives full attention, and uses open-ended questions, active listening, silence, reflection, and empathy to help the patient express feelings. The nurse clarifies and validates understanding and provides honest information without false reassurance. The nurse avoids communication blocks — clichés, false reassurance, giving personal advice, judgmental 'why' questions, and changing the subject — and stays alert to cultural needs and privacy. When the patient voices hopelessness, the nurse calmly and directly assesses for suicidal thoughts, ensures safety, notifies the provider, and documents.

Directly assess safety if the patient expresses hopelessness; notify provider and document

title: Oxygen Therapy: Safe Delivery and Device Selection
subtitle: A patient on the medical unit becomes short of breath with a falling SpO2. The nurse selects the correct oxygen device, titrates to the target saturation, and applies oxygen-safety precautions while watching for hypoxia.

patient.name: Oxygen Therapy
patient.admitDate: A hospitalized patient becomes dyspneic with a falling oxygen saturation. The nurse chooses the right delivery device, titrates to target SpO2, and enforces oxygen-safety precautions.

labs.v: Add for higher flow / long use.

nursesNote: A patient on the medical unit becomes increasingly short of breath with a falling SpO2. Oxygen is a drug: the nurse gives the lowest effective dose to correct hypoxemia and titrates to the ordered target saturation. Device choice matches the need — a nasal cannula (1-6 L/min) for low-flow needs, a simple face mask (run at least 5 L/min to flush CO2), a Venturi mask for a precise FiO2, and a non-rebreather (10-15 L/min, reservoir bag kept inflated) for the highest concentration in emergencies. The nurse adds humidification for higher flows, checks the nares/ears for skin breakdown, and monitors pulse oximetry and work of breathing. In a COPD CO2 retainer the target is ~88-92% — oxygen is never withheld from a hypoxic patient. Oxygen supports combustion, so the nurse keeps flames, sparks, smoking, and petroleum products away and posts an 'Oxygen in Use' sign. Restlessness, tachypnea, and tachycardia are early hypoxia; cyanosis and bradycardia are late.

Match the device to the need (cannula, simple/Venturi mask, or non-rebreather)

Add humidification for higher flows; monitor SpO2 and skin integrity
Enforce oxygen fire safety; never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic COPD patient

title: Safe Patient Handling and Body Mechanics
subtitle: A nurse must reposition and transfer a weak, partially dependent patient. Using proper body mechanics and safe-handling equipment protects both the patient and the nurse from injury.

patient.name: Safe Patient Handling
patient.admitDate: A weak, partially dependent patient must be repositioned in bed and transferred to a chair. The nurse applies proper body mechanics and safe-handling equipment to prevent injury.

vitals.temp: Protect patient AND nurse from injury
Lifts, slings, draw sheet, gait belt

labs.v: Lift with legs, not the back.

nursesNote: A weak, partially dependent patient needs repositioning in bed and a transfer to the chair. Safe handling protects the patient and the nurse: the nurse first assesses the patient's weight, strength, and ability to assist, then uses mechanical lifts, friction-reducing draw sheets, slings, or a gait belt as needed and gets adequate help. Good body mechanics include a wide base of support (feet shoulder-width apart), bending at the knees and hips with the back straight, keeping the load close, pushing or rolling rather than lifting, and pivoting the whole body instead of twisting the spine. The nurse raises the bed to waist height, locks the wheels of the bed and chair, applies a gait belt over clothing, and moves on a count. The nurse never lifts a heavy patient alone or lifts with the back.

Use mechanical lifts and assistive devices for heavy or dependent patients
Lock the wheels and raise the bed to waist height before transfers

title: Safe Blood Transfusion Administration
subtitle: A patient is ordered one unit of packed red blood cells. The nurse verifies the unit safely, starts it correctly, monitors closely for the first 15 minutes, and knows exactly what to do if a transfusion reaction develops.

patient.name: Blood Transfusion
patient.admitDate: A patient is ordered one unit of packed red blood cells. The nurse safely verifies, administers, and monitors the transfusion and responds correctly to any reaction.

vitals.temp: ID + blood type + unit # at bedside

labs.v: Stop; NS via new line; notify.

nursesNote: A patient is ordered one unit of packed red blood cells. Before starting, the nurse confirms the provider order and informed consent, ensures large-bore IV access (18-20 gauge), obtains baseline vital signs, and performs a two-person bedside verification of patient identity, blood type, and unit number. Blood is administered through Y-type tubing with an in-line filter primed with 0.9% normal saline only — never dextrose or lactated Ringer's. The nurse starts the transfusion slowly, stays with the patient for the first 15 minutes (when most reactions appear), rechecks vital signs, and completes the unit within 4 hours. At the first sign of a reaction (fever, chills, flank/back pain, hypotension, dyspnea), the nurse STOPS the transfusion, keeps the line open with normal saline through new tubing, and notifies the provider and blood bank.

title: Peripheral IV Complications: Infiltration, Phlebitis, and Extravasation
subtitle: A nurse monitoring peripheral IV sites must recognize infiltration, phlebitis, extravasation, and infection early, then stop the infusion and respond correctly to protect the patient's tissue and vein.

patient.name: Peripheral IV Complications
patient.admitDate: A nurse assesses peripheral IV sites and must recognize and respond to infiltration, phlebitis, extravasation, and infection.

vitals.temp: Cool, swollen, pale, no blood return

nursesNote: The nurse routinely assesses each peripheral IV site (every 1-2 hours) to catch complications early. Infiltration is leakage of a non-vesicant solution into the tissue — cool, pale, taut swelling with a slowed infusion and no blood return. Extravasation is the same leak with a vesicant drug and can cause blistering and tissue necrosis. Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein — redness, warmth, pain, and a palpable cord along its path. Infection shows purulent drainage, redness, and fever. For any of these the nurse first STOPS the infusion. Infiltration and phlebitis: remove the catheter, elevate, apply the appropriate warm or cool compress, and restart elsewhere. Vesicant extravasation: stop, leave the catheter to follow the extravasation protocol/antidote, and notify the provider. Prevention includes good vein selection (avoiding joints and areas of flexion), secure dressing, and frequent assessment.

Recognize infiltration, phlebitis, extravasation, and infection early
Stop the infusion at the first sign of any complication
Remove the catheter for infiltration/phlebitis; follow protocol for vesicant extravasation
Elevate the limb, apply the appropriate compress, and document

title: Hypoglycemia: Recognition and the Rule of 15
subtitle: A patient on insulin becomes shaky, sweaty, and confused with a low blood glucose. The nurse recognizes hypoglycemia, treats with the Rule of 15, and knows how care changes if the patient cannot swallow.

patient.name: Hypoglycemia
patient.admitDate: A patient on insulin develops shakiness, sweating, and confusion with a low blood glucose. The nurse recognizes and treats hypoglycemia.

nursesNote: A patient on insulin becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and confused. The nurse confirms a blood glucose below 70 mg/dL and recognizes hypoglycemia — adrenergic signs (shakiness, sweating, palpitations, hunger, anxiety) and neuroglycopenic signs (confusion, irritability, slurred speech, seizures). For a conscious patient who can swallow, the nurse follows the Rule of 15: give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (4 oz juice, glucose tablets/gel, or regular soda), recheck the glucose in 15 minutes, and repeat if still below 70; once normalized, provide a complex-carbohydrate snack or meal. High-fat foods (chocolate, nuts, peanut butter) are avoided initially because fat slows sugar absorption. If the patient is unconscious or cannot swallow safely, the nurse gives NOTHING by mouth and treats with IV dextrose (when access exists) or IM/SQ glucagon, then rechecks. Prevention teaching includes carrying a fast carb source and not skipping meals.

Conscious patient: 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if needed
Follow normalized glucose with a complex-carbohydrate snack or meal
Unconscious or unable to swallow: nothing by mouth; give IV dextrose or glucagon
Teach prevention: carry fast carbs and avoid skipping meals

title: Patient Teaching and Health Literacy: The Teach-Back Method
subtitle: A nurse teaches a patient a new self-care skill and medication plan. Using plain language, assessing barriers, and confirming understanding with teach-back ensures the patient can safely manage care at home.

patient.name: Patient Teaching
patient.admitDate: A nurse teaches a patient a new self-care skill and medication plan, using health-literacy principles and teach-back to confirm understanding.

nursesNote: The nurse teaches a patient a new self-care skill and medication plan. Effective teaching starts by assessing readiness to learn, prior knowledge, and barriers (pain, anxiety, language, low health literacy, sensory deficits). The nurse uses plain everyday language instead of jargon, presents information in small prioritized chunks, and uses teach-back — asking the patient to explain instructions in their own words or to give a return demonstration — rather than a yes/no 'Do you understand?'. Written materials are provided at about a 5th-6th grade reading level, and a professional interpreter (not a family member or child) is used for limited-English-proficiency patients. Pain and anxiety are addressed before teaching, the caregiver is involved, and goals are realistic. When teach-back reveals a gap, the nurse re-explains more simply and checks again.

Use plain language and present information in small, prioritized chunks
Confirm understanding with teach-back and return demonstration
Use a professional interpreter for limited-English patients; involve the caregiver
Provide written materials at an appropriate reading level and re-teach gaps

title: Standard Precautions and Hand Hygiene
subtitle: Across a multi-patient assignment, the nurse applies standard precautions to every patient — hand hygiene, the right PPE for the anticipated exposure, and safe sharps practices — and knows when soap and water are required over an alcohol rub.

patient.name: Standard Precautions
patient.admitDate: The nurse applies standard precautions to every patient: hand hygiene, PPE matched to exposure, and safe sharps handling.

vitals.temp: No recapping; sharps box at point of use

nursesNote: The nurse applies standard precautions to every patient regardless of diagnosis, treating all blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes as potentially infectious. Hand hygiene is performed before and after patient contact, before an aseptic task, and after exposure to body fluids or the patient's surroundings. An alcohol-based hand rub is preferred when hands are not visibly soiled; soap and water are used when hands are soiled or when caring for a patient with C. difficile or norovirus (spores/viruses resist alcohol). PPE is selected for the anticipated exposure: gloves for body fluids or non-intact skin, a gown if clothing may be soiled, and a mask with eye protection when splashes or sprays are likely. Gloves never replace hand hygiene. Safe injection and sharps practices apply — never recap needles two-handed, and dispose of sharps in a puncture-resistant container at the point of use. PPE is removed in order (gloves, goggles, gown, mask) followed by hand hygiene.

Perform hand hygiene before and after patient contact and aseptic tasks
Use soap and water for visibly soiled hands, C. difficile, or norovirus
Select PPE based on the anticipated exposure to body fluids
Never recap needles two-handed; dispose of sharps at the point of use

title: Therapeutic Diets: Matching Nutrition to the Condition
subtitle: Across an assignment the nurse matches the right therapeutic diet to each patient — clear vs full liquid, texture-modified for dysphagia, low-sodium, renal, carbohydrate-consistent, and low-residue — and advances diets safely.

patient.name: Therapeutic Diets
patient.admitDate: The nurse matches each patient to the correct therapeutic diet and advances diets safely as tolerated.

nursesNote: The nurse matches each patient to the correct therapeutic diet. A clear liquid diet (broth, apple juice, plain gelatin, tea, clear ice pops) is see-through and used short-term around procedures; a full liquid diet adds milk, pudding, and cream soups as a transition. A mechanical soft or pureed diet with thickened liquids reduces aspiration risk in dysphagia. A low-sodium diet (~2 g/day) is used for heart failure, hypertension, and cirrhosis with ascites; a renal diet limits potassium and phosphorus in CKD/ESRD; a carbohydrate-consistent diet supports glucose control in diabetes; a low-residue (low-fiber) diet rests the bowel during an acute diverticulitis or IBD flare, while a high-fiber diet treats constipation and diverticulosis. NPO is maintained before surgery or with aspiration risk. Diets are advanced gradually (clear -> full -> soft -> regular) after bowel function returns and per order.
providerOrders: Match the therapeutic diet to each patient's condition
Use texture-modified foods and thickened liquids for dysphagia
Provide low-sodium for HF/HTN and a renal diet (low K/phosphorus) for CKD
Keep NPO patients without food or fluids before surgery or with aspiration risk
Advance diet gradually (clear -> full -> soft -> regular) as tolerated and ordered

title: Hazards of Immobility: Complications and Prevention
subtitle: An immobile, bedbound patient is at risk for complications in every body system. The nurse recognizes the hazards of immobility and applies prevention measures, then mobilizes the patient safely.

patient.name: Hazards of Immobility
patient.admitDate: A bedbound, immobile patient is at risk for system-wide complications. The nurse applies prevention measures and mobilizes safely.

nursesNote: An immobile, bedbound patient is at risk for complications in every body system. Respiratory: pooled secretions cause atelectasis and pneumonia. Cardiovascular: venous stasis causes deep vein thrombosis, and deconditioning causes orthostatic hypotension. Integumentary: pressure injuries form over bony prominences. Musculoskeletal: muscle atrophy, contractures, foot drop, and disuse osteoporosis. GI: constipation from slowed peristalsis. GU: urinary stasis with calculi and infection. The nurse prevents these by repositioning every 2 hours with skin assessment, encouraging incentive spirometry and deep breathing, applying sequential compression devices with ordered VTE prophylaxis, performing range-of-motion exercises, maintaining hydration and fiber, and — most importantly — mobilizing the patient as early and progressively as the condition allows. Position changes are made slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension and falls.
providerOrders: Reposition every 2 hours and assess the skin
Encourage incentive spirometry and deep breathing while awake
Apply sequential compression devices and give ordered VTE prophylaxis
Perform range-of-motion exercises and maintain hydration and fiber
Mobilize early and progressively; change positions slowly to prevent orthostasis

title: Wound Healing and Dressing Selection
subtitle: The nurse assesses a healing wound, distinguishes normal healing from infection, and selects the right dressing while changing it with aseptic technique to support moist wound healing.

patient.name: Wound Healing
patient.admitDate: The nurse assesses a healing wound, distinguishes healthy healing from infection, and selects and changes the appropriate dressing.

vitals.temp: Protein, vit C, zinc, glucose control

nursesNote: The nurse assesses a healing wound through the phases of healing: hemostasis, inflammatory (mild redness, warmth, and edema in the first 1-3 days is normal), proliferative (red granulation tissue and epithelialization), and maturation. A clean surgical incision with approximated edges heals by primary intention; an open wound left to granulate heals by secondary intention with more scarring. Drainage is described as serous (clear), serosanguineous (thin pink), sanguineous (bloody), or purulent (thick, colored, foul — a sign of infection). Healthy granulation is red and moist; yellow slough and black eschar are nonviable. The nurse keeps the wound bed moist (moist wound healing speeds epithelialization), selects a dressing matched to exudate, and changes it with aseptic technique. Increasing pain, spreading redness, purulent drainage, and fever signal infection and are reported. Adequate protein, vitamin C, zinc, perfusion, and glucose control support healing.

Distinguish normal inflammation/granulation from signs of infection
Maintain moist wound healing and match the dressing to the exudate
Change dressings using aseptic technique; obtain cultures as ordered
Optimize protein, vitamin C, zinc, and glucose control; report infection

title: Cast Care and Neurovascular Assessment
subtitle: A patient with a new extremity cast needs neurovascular monitoring and cast care. The nurse performs the checks (the P's), recognizes compartment syndrome early, and responds to this limb-threatening emergency.

patient.name: Cast & Neurovascular Care
patient.admitDate: A patient has a newly applied extremity cast. The nurse performs neurovascular checks, provides cast care, and recognizes compartment syndrome.

vitals.temp: Color, temp, pulse, refill, move, sense

nursesNote: A patient has a newly applied extremity cast. The nurse performs neurovascular checks distal to the cast — assessing the P's: Pain, Pallor (color/temperature), Pulselessness (pulses and capillary refill < 3 seconds), Paresthesia (sensation), and Paralysis (movement) — and compares the casted limb to the opposite side. In the first 24-48 hours the limb is elevated with ice to reduce swelling, and a plaster cast is left open to air and handled with the palms (no fingertip pressure that dents it). The nurse does not insert objects to scratch inside the cast, petals rough edges, and keeps it clean and dry. Severe pain unrelieved by opioids and worsened by passive stretch, tense swelling, and paresthesia signal compartment syndrome, a limb-threatening emergency — the nurse keeps the limb at heart level (not elevated), loosens constriction, and notifies the provider STAT for cast bivalving and possible fasciotomy. Pulselessness, pallor, and paralysis are late signs. Hot spots, foul odor, or drainage suggest infection or skin breakdown under the cast.
providerOrders: Perform neurovascular checks distal to the cast and compare both limbs
Elevate with ice in the first 24-48 hours to reduce swelling
Keep the cast clean and dry; do not insert objects inside it
Report pain unrelieved by opioids, paresthesia, or a tense, swollen limb
For suspected compartment syndrome, keep limb at heart level and notify STAT

title: Nasogastric Tube: Insertion, Placement Verification, and Decompression
subtitle: A patient needs a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression. The nurse inserts it safely, verifies placement correctly (not by auscultation), manages low intermittent suction, and prevents complications.

patient.name: Nasogastric Tube
patient.admitDate: A patient needs a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression. The nurse inserts, verifies, and manages it safely.

vitals.temp: Keep blue pigtail up; don't clamp

nursesNote: A patient with a bowel obstruction needs a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression. The nurse positions the patient in high Fowler's, measures the tube nose-to-earlobe-to-xiphoid, lubricates it with a water-soluble lubricant, and inserts it while the patient flexes the chin toward the chest and swallows sips of water. If the patient coughs, chokes, or becomes cyanotic, the nurse withdraws the tube and reassesses the airway. Placement is confirmed by X-ray before any use; a gastric aspirate pH of 5 or less supports gastric placement, and the external length is marked and checked each shift. Auscultation of an air bolus is NOT reliable. For a Salem sump, low intermittent suction is used and the blue air-vent pigtail is kept above stomach level and never clamped. The nurse keeps the head of bed elevated to reduce aspiration, provides oral and nasal care, irrigates with normal saline for patency, and monitors output, intake/output, and electrolytes (prolonged suction can cause hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis).

Confirm placement by X-ray before use; check pH and external length
Use low intermittent suction; keep the Salem sump air vent open and elevated
Keep the head of bed elevated; provide oral/nasal care and irrigate for patency
Monitor output, intake/output, and electrolytes during gastric suction

title: Specimen Collection: Urine, Stool, Sputum, and Blood Cultures
subtitle: The nurse collects diagnostic specimens correctly — clean-catch urine, stool, sputum, and blood cultures — using the right technique, timing, and labeling to keep results accurate.

patient.name: Specimen Collection
patient.admitDate: The nurse collects urine, stool, sputum, and blood-culture specimens using correct technique, timing, and labeling.

nursesNote: The nurse collects diagnostic specimens using standard precautions and correct technique. A clean-catch midstream urine is obtained after cleaning the meatus (front to back), beginning the stream, then catching the midstream in a sterile container; a 24-hour urine collection starts after discarding the first void and keeps the container on ice. Stool specimens go into a clean container without urine or toilet-water contamination; liquid stool is used for C. difficile testing. Sputum is collected early in the morning with a deep cough (not saliva) after rinsing the mouth with water, not mouthwash. Blood cultures are drawn aseptically from two different sites and BEFORE antibiotics are started. The nurse uses two identifiers, labels every specimen at the bedside, and transports it promptly to preserve accuracy.

Draw two blood-culture sets aseptically from separate sites before antibiotics
Collect an early-morning deep-cough sputum, not saliva
Avoid urine/toilet-water contamination of stool specimens
Use two identifiers, label at the bedside, and transport promptly

title: Tracheostomy Care and Suctioning
subtitle: The nurse suctions and cares for a tracheostomy safely — suctioning only when needed, hyperoxygenating, using sterile technique, limiting each pass, and keeping emergency equipment at the bedside.

patient.name: Tracheostomy Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse suctions and cares for a tracheostomy using correct technique, oxygenation, and emergency readiness.

vitals.temp: Suction PRN, not by the clock
100% O2 before and after each pass
No suction going in; suction on withdrawal

labs.v: Audible secretions, ↑ work of breathing, desat.

nursesNote: The nurse provides tracheostomy care and suctions only when secretions are present (audible gurgling, increased work of breathing, or desaturation) rather than on a fixed schedule. Before and after each suction pass the patient is hyperoxygenated with 100% oxygen. Using sterile technique, the nurse inserts the suction catheter without applying suction until resistance or the premeasured depth is met, then applies intermittent suction while rotating and withdrawing, limiting each pass to 10-15 seconds and allowing recovery between passes. Adult wall suction is set to 100-150 mmHg, and normal saline is not routinely instilled. The nurse monitors SpO2 and heart rate, stopping to reoxygenate if the patient becomes bradycardic or desaturates. Trach ties are secured to a two-finger tightness, and the obturator plus a spare tube (same size and one smaller) stay at the bedside for emergency reinsertion.

Hyperoxygenate with 100% O2 before and after suctioning
Use sterile technique; limit each pass to 10-15 seconds
Keep the obturator and a spare tracheostomy tube at the bedside

title: Indwelling Urinary Catheter: Insertion, Maintenance, and Removal
subtitle: The nurse inserts, maintains, and removes an indwelling urinary catheter safely — sterile insertion, inflating the balloon only after urine return, dependent closed drainage, and early removal to prevent CAUTI.

patient.name: Urinary Catheter Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse inserts, maintains, and removes an indwelling urinary catheter using sterile technique and CAUTI-prevention principles.

labs.v: Front to back; hold labia apart.
Hold penis upright; advance to bifurcation.

nursesNote: The nurse inserts an indwelling urinary catheter only when clinically indicated, using sterile technique. After positioning the patient and setting up the sterile field, the meatus is cleaned with antiseptic (female: front to back with the labia held apart; male: penis held upright). The catheter is advanced until urine returns and then slightly further before the balloon is inflated with sterile water from the prefilled syringe — never before urine is seen. The catheter is secured to the thigh to prevent traction, the closed drainage bag is hung below the level of the bladder and kept off the floor, and the tubing is kept free of kinks and dependent loops. Daily meatal care is done with soap and water, specimens are drawn from the sampling port (not the bag), and the catheter is removed as early as possible to prevent CAUTI. On removal, the balloon is fully deflated and the nurse monitors for the first spontaneous void within 6-8 hours.

Review daily and remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed

title: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN): Safe Administration and Monitoring
subtitle: The nurse safely administers TPN — a hypertonic, high-alert solution given through a central line, run on a pump, never stopped abruptly, with close glucose and infection monitoring.

patient.name: TPN Administration
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers and monitors total parenteral nutrition using central access, an infusion pump, and aseptic technique.

vitals.temp: No other meds/blood in TPN lumen

labs.v: Run at the ordered rate only.
labs.r: No speeding up to catch up.

nursesNote: The nurse administers total parenteral nutrition as a high-alert therapy. Because the solution is hypertonic and high in dextrose, it is given only through a central venous catheter and run on an infusion pump at the exact ordered rate — the rate is never sped up to 'catch up' or slowed down. Before hanging, the nurse verifies the order and additives with a second nurse per policy, inspects the bag for cloudiness, precipitate, or oil separation, and uses strict aseptic technique at a dedicated lumen that is not used for other medications, blood, or CVP readings. TPN is never stopped abruptly; if the next bag is delayed, 10% dextrose (D10W) is hung to prevent rebound hypoglycemia. The nurse checks blood glucose every 4-6 hours, changes the bag and tubing every 24 hours, and monitors daily weight, intake and output, and electrolytes (watching for refeeding syndrome in malnourished patients) along with signs of infection.

Do not stop TPN abruptly; hang D10W if the next bag is delayed

Change the bag and tubing every 24 hours using aseptic technique

title: Intramuscular and Subcutaneous Injection Technique
subtitle: The nurse gives IM and subcutaneous injections safely — correct site, angle, needle, and volume, the Z-track method for irritating IM meds, no aspiration/massage for subQ heparin, and safe sharps disposal.

patient.name: Injection Technique
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers intramuscular and subcutaneous injections using the correct site, angle, needle, volume, and sharps safety.

nursesNote: The nurse administers intramuscular and subcutaneous injections using correct technique. For IM injections the ventrogluteal site is preferred (away from major nerves and vessels) and the dorsogluteal site is avoided due to sciatic nerve risk; the deltoid is used for small volumes and vaccines and the vastus lateralis for infants. IM injections are given at a 90-degree angle, and the Z-track method (pull the skin laterally, inject, wait about 10 seconds, withdraw, then release without massaging) is used for irritating medications to prevent leakage and tissue staining. Subcutaneous injections are given at a 45-90 degree angle with a short, small-gauge needle into the abdomen, upper arm, or thigh, avoiding the area around the umbilicus and rotating sites. Subcutaneous heparin is not aspirated or massaged. The nurse lets the antiseptic dry before injecting, never recaps a used needle, and disposes of all sharps in the proper container.

Give IM injections at 90 degrees and subcutaneous at 45-90 degrees
Use the Z-track method for irritating IM medications
Do not aspirate or massage after subcutaneous heparin; rotate sites
Never recap a used needle; dispose of sharps in the proper container

title: Assistive Devices: Safe Use of Canes, Walkers, and Crutches
subtitle: The nurse teaches safe use of canes, walkers, and crutches — cane on the strong side, weight on the hands (not the armpits) with crutches, and 'up with the good, down with the bad' on stairs.

patient.name: Assistive Devices
patient.admitDate: The nurse teaches safe, fall-preventing use of canes, walkers, and crutches.

vitals.temp: Up with good, down with bad

labs.v: Advance ~a step; weak then strong leg.
Nonskid shoes, intact tips, clear path.

nursesNote: The nurse teaches safe use of mobility aids. A cane is held on the strong (unaffected) side, advanced together with the weak leg, then the strong leg follows; the handle reaches the wrist crease with the elbow flexed about 15-30 degrees. With a walker, all four legs are placed on the floor before the patient steps, the device is advanced about a step's length, and the weak leg moves before the strong one while the patient stays inside the frame. Crutch weight is borne on the hands, never the axillae, with the pads about two finger-widths below the armpits to avoid nerve injury. On stairs the rule is 'up with the good, down with the bad': the strong leg leads going up, and the crutches with the weak leg lead going down. The nurse reinforces nonskid shoes, intact rubber tips, and a clear, clutter-free path to prevent falls.

Bear crutch weight on the hands, not the axillae
Place all walker legs on the floor before stepping

Check footwear, rubber tips, and a clear path before ambulating

title: Intake and Output and Fluid Balance Monitoring
subtitle: The nurse measures intake and output accurately, uses daily weights as the best fluid indicator, and recognizes fluid overload versus deficit — reporting urine output under 30 mL/hr.

patient.name: Intake & Output
patient.admitDate: The nurse measures and records intake and output and monitors fluid balance.

vitals.temp: PO, IV, tube feeds, ice chips

labs.v: Dry mucosa, poor turgor, low BP.

nursesNote: The nurse measures intake and output to assess fluid balance and hydration. Intake includes oral fluids, IV fluids, tube feedings, and foods that are liquid at room temperature (gelatin, popsicles, broth); ice chips are counted as about half their volume. Output includes urine, emesis, liquid stool, and drainage from tubes or wounds, all measured in a graduated container read at eye level. Daily weights — taken at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing — are the most sensitive indicator of fluid status, where about 1 kg of change equals roughly 1 liter of fluid. The nurse recognizes fluid overload (edema, crackles, weight gain, distended neck veins) versus deficit (dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, hypotension, concentrated urine) and reports a urine output under 30 mL/hr.

Count ice chips as about half their volume
Obtain daily weights at the same time on the same scale
Report urine output less than 30 mL/hr
Monitor for signs of fluid overload or deficit

title: Eye, Ear, and Nasal Medication Administration
subtitle: The nurse instills eye, ear, and nasal medications correctly — drops into the conjunctival sac, room-temperature ear drops with the right pinna pull, and a blown nose before nasal sprays.

patient.name: Eye/Ear/Nasal Meds
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers ophthalmic, otic, and nasal medications using correct technique.

nursesNote: The nurse administers ophthalmic, otic, and nasal medications safely. Eye drops are placed into the lower conjunctival sac (never directly on the cornea) without touching the dropper to the eye or lashes; gentle pressure on the inner canthus for 30-60 seconds reduces systemic absorption, and when two drops are ordered the nurse waits about 5 minutes between them and gives drops before ointment. Ear drops are warmed to room temperature to avoid vertigo, and the pinna is pulled up and back in adults (down and back in children under 3) before instilling along the side of the canal, with the patient staying side-lying for a few minutes. Before a nasal spray the patient blows the nose and then sniffs gently during instillation. The nurse verifies the rights, performs hand hygiene, and avoids contaminating any dropper or tip.

Apply pressure to the inner canthus after eye drops
Warm ear drops to room temperature before instilling
Pull the pinna up and back (adults) or down and back (young children)
Have the patient blow the nose before a nasal spray

title: Heat and Cold Therapy Application
subtitle: The nurse applies heat and cold safely — cold for acute injury and swelling, heat for chronic stiffness, always with a skin barrier, a 15-20 minute limit, and frequent skin checks.

patient.name: Heat & Cold Therapy
patient.admitDate: The nurse applies heat and cold therapy using correct indications, barriers, timing, and skin monitoring.

labs.v: No higher temp to rush it.

nursesNote: The nurse applies heat and cold therapy safely and for the correct indication. Cold causes vasoconstriction and is used for acute injuries, swelling, inflammation, and bleeding (especially the first 24-48 hours), while heat causes vasodilation and relieves chronic muscle stiffness and spasm by increasing blood flow. A cloth or towel barrier is always placed between the pack and the skin, application is limited to about 15-20 minutes with recovery time between, and the skin is checked frequently for redness, pallor, blistering, or numbness. Patients with impaired sensation, poor circulation, cognitive impairment, or extremes of age are at higher risk for burns or frostbite. Heat is avoided on a fresh, swollen, or bleeding injury, and the nurse never raises the temperature to speed the effect or lets a patient lie directly on a heating device.

Check the skin frequently for redness, pallor, or numbness
Avoid heat on a fresh or bleeding injury

title: Therapeutic Patient Positioning
subtitle: The nurse matches position to purpose — high-Fowler's for breathing, eating, and tube feeding; side-lying to protect the airway and offload the sacrum — while keeping alignment and repositioning every 2 hours.

patient.name: Patient Positioning
patient.admitDate: The nurse positions patients therapeutically for breathing, safety, comfort, and skin protection.

nursesNote: The nurse positions patients to match the clinical purpose. High-Fowler's (60-90 degrees) eases breathing and is used for eating and during and after tube feedings to prevent aspiration, while semi-Fowler's (30-45 degrees) provides comfort and reduces reflux. A side-lying (lateral) position offloads the sacrum and protects the airway of an unconscious or drowsy patient by letting secretions drain, and the Sims position is used for enemas and recovery. Prone positioning can improve oxygenation in severe respiratory failure, and the orthopneic position (sitting and leaning over a table) relieves severe dyspnea. The nurse keeps the body in neutral alignment, supports joints and pressure points with pillows, repositions immobile patients about every 2 hours, and lifts rather than drags the patient to prevent shear and skin injury.

Use a side-lying position to protect the airway of a drowsy patient
Keep the head of bed elevated during and after tube feedings
Reposition immobile patients about every 2 hours
Maintain body alignment and lift rather than drag the patient

title: Range of Motion (ROM) Exercises
subtitle: The nurse performs and teaches ROM exercises to prevent contractures — supporting the joint above and below, moving slowly to the point of resistance (never past pain), and encouraging active ROM when able.

patient.name: Range of Motion
patient.admitDate: The nurse performs and teaches range-of-motion exercises to maintain mobility and prevent contractures.

nursesNote: The nurse performs and teaches range-of-motion exercises to maintain joint mobility, preserve muscle tone, promote circulation, and prevent contractures. Active ROM, in which the patient moves independently, is encouraged whenever possible and can be built into bathing and dressing; active-assisted ROM is used when the patient has partial ability, and passive ROM is performed by the nurse for a patient who cannot move the joint. During the exercises the nurse supports the joint above and below, moves it slowly and smoothly through its full available range, and stops at the point of resistance — never forcing past pain. Each movement is repeated several times and done at least twice a day. The nurse does not force a contracted joint, stops if pain or spasm occurs, and reports any new or worsening limitation.

Encourage active ROM when the patient is able

Move each joint to the point of resistance, not past pain
Report any new pain, swelling, or loss of range

title: Vital Signs: Measurement and Normal Adult Ranges
subtitle: The nurse measures vital signs accurately and knows the normal adult ranges — correct cuff size, an apical pulse for irregular rhythms, discreet respiratory counts, and reporting out-of-range values.

patient.name: Vital Signs
patient.admitDate: The nurse measures temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation accurately.

nursesNote: The nurse measures vital signs accurately and recognizes normal adult ranges: heart rate 60-100 bpm, respirations 12-20/min, blood pressure below 120/80, oxygen saturation 95-100%, and temperature around 37°C (98.6°F), with pain assessed on a 0-10 scale. Blood pressure requires the correct cuff size (a cuff that is too small reads falsely high), the arm supported at heart level, and the patient rested; the nurse avoids the arm with an IV, a dialysis fistula, or on the mastectomy side. An apical pulse is counted for a full minute when the rhythm is irregular or before giving digoxin (which is held for a rate under 60). Respirations are counted discreetly so the patient does not alter their breathing. For orthostatic vital signs the nurse measures lying, sitting, and standing, where a systolic drop of 20 mmHg or a diastolic drop of 10 mmHg suggests orthostatic hypotension. Out-of-range values are reported.
providerOrders: Measure temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and SpO2
Use the correct cuff size and avoid arms with IV/fistula/mastectomy
Count an apical pulse for one minute when the rhythm is irregular
Hold digoxin and notify the provider for an apical rate under 60
Report any vital sign outside the normal range

title: Enema Administration
subtitle: The nurse gives an enema safely — left lateral Sims position, warmed solution, gentle 3-4 inch insertion, slow instillation from 12-18 inches above, and stopping for cramping, severe pain, or bleeding.

patient.name: Enema Administration
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers a cleansing enema using correct position, technique, and safety monitoring.

nursesNote: The nurse administers an enema using correct technique and safety monitoring. The patient is placed in the left lateral Sims position to follow the natural curve of the colon, and the solution is warmed to about body temperature because cold solution causes cramping. After lubricating the tip, the nurse inserts the tube about 3-4 inches in an adult, aiming toward the umbilicus, and instills the solution slowly from a bag hung 12-18 inches above the anus — hanging it higher increases flow and pressure and triggers cramping. If the patient cramps, the nurse lowers the bag, slows or pauses the flow, and has the patient breathe slowly. The tube is never forced against resistance, and the nurse stops and notifies the provider for severe pain, bleeding, or a rigid abdomen. The patient is encouraged to retain the solution before expelling, and no more than about three cleansing enemas are given without notifying the provider.

Warm the solution and insert the tube 3-4 inches toward the umbilicus
Hang the bag 12-18 inches above the anus and instill slowly
Slow or stop the flow if the patient cramps
Stop and notify the provider for severe pain, bleeding, or rigid abdomen

title: Postmortem Care
subtitle: The nurse provides dignified care of the body after death and supports the grieving family — leaving tubes in place for medical-examiner cases, positioning before rigor, and honoring cultural and religious wishes.

patient.name: Postmortem Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse provides dignified postmortem care and supports the family after a patient's death.

nursesNote: After the death is pronounced and the time noted, the nurse provides postmortem care with dignity and respect. Before doing anything, the nurse confirms whether the death is a medical-examiner/autopsy case or involves organ or tissue donation — in those situations all tubes, lines, and devices are left in place. The body is cleaned, soiled dressings are replaced, and drainage pads are applied; the eyes are closed and dentures inserted to maintain facial appearance, and the body is positioned supine with the head slightly elevated to prevent facial discoloration. Because rigor mortis begins within 2-4 hours, the nurse positions the body before it sets in and applies identification tags per policy. Throughout, the nurse honors the family's cultural and religious practices, provides a private space for viewing and goodbyes, offers chaplaincy and bereavement resources, and documents belongings released to the family.

Leave all tubes and lines in place for a medical-examiner, autopsy, or donation case
Position the body supine with the head slightly elevated before rigor sets in
Apply identification tags and document belongings per policy
Honor the family's cultural and religious wishes and offer support

title: Preoperative Care and Teaching
subtitle: The nurse prepares a patient for surgery — confirming the surgeon-obtained consent before sedation, NPO status, the preop checklist, and teaching coughing, deep breathing, splinting, and early ambulation.

patient.name: Preoperative Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse prepares a patient for surgery with consent verification, the preop checklist, and preoperative teaching.

nursesNote: The nurse prepares the patient for surgery. The surgeon explains the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives and obtains the informed consent; the nurse witnesses the signature, confirms the patient understands, and notifies the surgeon if the patient has questions or seems unsure — and the consent must be signed before any sedating preop medication. The nurse verifies NPO status to reduce aspiration risk, completes the preop checklist (baseline vitals, labs, allergies, ID band), and has the patient remove dentures, jewelry, contacts, and nail polish. The patient voids before transfer, and ordered preop medications and VTE prophylaxis (sequential compression devices or stockings) are applied. Preoperative teaching covers coughing and deep breathing, incentive spirometer use, splinting the incision, early ambulation, and leg exercises to prevent postoperative pneumonia, atelectasis, and blood clots.

Verify NPO status and complete the preoperative checklist
Have the patient remove jewelry, dentures, and nail polish and void
Apply VTE prophylaxis and give preop medications as ordered

title: Postoperative Care
subtitle: The nurse cares for the patient after surgery — airway and breathing first, monitoring vitals and the surgical site, recognizing hemorrhage and shock, and preventing atelectasis, clots, ileus, and urinary retention.

patient.name: Postoperative Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse provides postoperative care, prioritizing the airway and monitoring for complications.

nursesNote: The nurse provides postoperative care, always prioritizing the airway and breathing first, then circulation. On arrival the nurse assesses airway patency, respirations, oxygen saturation, vital signs, and level of consciousness, then checks the surgical site, dressing, and drains and assesses pain. A rapid, weak pulse with a falling blood pressure and cool, pale skin can signal hemorrhage or shock, and a saturated dressing with bright red blood is reported and reinforced. To prevent complications the nurse promotes coughing, deep breathing, and incentive spirometry (atelectasis and pneumonia), early ambulation and leg exercises with sequential compression devices (blood clots), monitors bowel sounds for return of function (ileus), and ensures the patient voids within about 6-8 hours (urinary retention). Nausea and vomiting after anesthesia are treated while protecting the airway, and pain is managed to support recovery.
providerOrders: Assess airway, breathing, and circulation first on arrival
Monitor vital signs, level of consciousness, and the surgical site
Reinforce the dressing and report bright red bleeding or shock signs
Promote coughing, deep breathing, spirometry, and early ambulation
Ensure the patient voids within 6-8 hours and monitor bowel sounds

title: Pulse Oximetry
subtitle: The nurse measures SpO2 accurately — choosing a warm, well-perfused site, recognizing what lowers accuracy (poor perfusion, motion, dark polish), knowing CO poisoning reads falsely high, and always correlating with the patient.

patient.name: Pulse Oximetry
patient.admitDate: The nurse measures and interprets oxygen saturation accurately.

nursesNote: The nurse uses pulse oximetry to measure oxygen saturation, where a normal value is about 95-100%. An accurate reading requires a warm, well-perfused site (finger, toe, earlobe, or forehead) and a good pulse waveform; poor perfusion from a cold extremity, hypotension, or peripheral vascular disease, along with motion, shivering, dark nail polish, artificial nails, and bright ambient light, all reduce accuracy. The nurse knows that carbon monoxide poisoning can produce a falsely HIGH reading because the device cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxygenated hemoglobin, and that severe anemia may read a normal percent despite low total oxygen content. The probe site is rotated to prevent skin breakdown. Above all, the nurse correlates the number with the patient's clinical status — color, work of breathing, and level of consciousness — rather than trusting the value alone, and checks the probe before acting on a low reading.

title: Ostomy Care: Colostomy and Ileostomy
subtitle: The nurse cares for an ostomy — assessing a healthy pink, moist stoma, emptying the pouch at 1/3-1/2 full, cutting the wafer to fit, protecting peristomal skin, and reporting a dusky or black stoma.

patient.name: Ostomy Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse assesses the stoma, changes the appliance, and protects peristomal skin.

nursesNote: The nurse provides ostomy care and teaching. A healthy stoma is pink to red, moist, and slightly raised; mild bleeding when cleaning is normal, but a dusky, purple, or black stoma signals impaired circulation and is reported promptly, as is retraction or excoriated, weeping peristomal skin. The pouch is emptied when it is about one-third to one-half full to prevent leaks, and the appliance is changed every 3-7 days or when leaking, ideally when output is least. The nurse measures the stoma and cuts the wafer about 1/8 inch larger so it protects the skin without constricting the stoma, and re-measures over the first 6-8 weeks as the stoma shrinks. Peristomal skin is cleaned with water and patted dry, since skin breakdown is the most common complication. Ileostomy output is liquid and enzyme-rich (higher dehydration and skin-injury risk), while a distal colostomy produces more formed stool. The nurse encourages self-care and supports body image.

Empty the pouch when it is 1/3 to 1/2 full
Measure the stoma and cut the wafer ~1/8 inch larger
Protect and monitor the peristomal skin
Monitor ileostomy output for dehydration and teach self-care

title: Sleep and Rest Promotion
subtitle: The nurse promotes sleep and rest — a dark, quiet, cool room, clustered care, a consistent bedtime routine, and nonpharmacologic measures before sleep medications.

patient.name: Sleep & Rest
patient.admitDate: The nurse promotes adequate sleep and rest using sleep hygiene and nonpharmacologic measures.

nursesNote: The nurse promotes sleep and rest by supporting good sleep hygiene and reducing barriers. A dark, quiet, cool room, a consistent sleep schedule, and a calming bedtime routine all help, while caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, large evening meals, screens, and long daytime naps interfere with sleep. In the hospital the nurse clusters care to allow uninterrupted rest, dims lights, lowers noise at night, manages pain, and offers toileting before bed. Daytime activity and relaxation measures (warm milk, quiet music, deep breathing) support nighttime sleep. The nurse assesses the cause of any insomnia — pain, anxiety, environment, or nocturia — and addresses it first, trying nonpharmacologic measures before giving a prescribed sleep aid. Sleep medications are used short-term because long-term use increases fall risk, especially in older adults, who normally have lighter sleep and more awakenings.

title: Point-of-Care Blood Glucose Monitoring
subtitle: The nurse performs a fingerstick glucose correctly — side of the fingertip, alcohol dried first, no hard squeezing, a checked meter and in-date strips — and acts on a value under 70 mg/dL.

patient.name: Glucose Monitoring
patient.admitDate: The nurse obtains and acts on a point-of-care fingerstick blood glucose.

nursesNote: The nurse performs point-of-care glucose monitoring accurately. After hand hygiene and checking that the meter is coded and the strips are in date (with quality control done per policy), the nurse warms or dangles the hand to improve blood flow and cleanses the site, letting alcohol dry completely because residual alcohol can affect the reading. The puncture is made on the side of the fingertip rather than the center pad to reduce pain, and sites are rotated; the nurse avoids squeezing the finger hard, which dilutes the sample with tissue fluid and gives an inaccurate value. An adequate drop is applied to the strip, and alternate sites such as the forearm are avoided when glucose is changing rapidly. The result is documented and acted on — a value under 70 mg/dL signals hypoglycemia and is treated promptly with a fast-acting carbohydrate, then rechecked.

Use the side of the fingertip and let alcohol dry before puncture
Verify the meter is coded and the strips are in date

Treat a glucose under 70 mg/dL and recheck

title: Safe Medication Administration: The Rights and Three Checks
subtitle: The nurse gives medications safely — the rights of administration, three label checks, two identifiers, checking allergies, staying until the dose is taken, and clarifying unclear orders.

patient.name: Medication Safety
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers medications safely using the rights, three checks, and two identifiers.

nursesNote: The nurse administers medications safely using the rights of administration — right patient, drug, dose, route, and time, plus right reason, documentation, response, and the patient's right to refuse. The label is checked three times: when taking it from storage, when preparing it, and at the bedside before giving it. The patient is verified with two identifiers (name and date of birth or medical record number, not the room number), and allergies are checked first. The nurse gives only medications they personally prepared, does not leave doses at the bedside, and stays until the patient takes the medication. Extended-release and enteric-coated tablets are not crushed; a liquid form is used when needed. Any unclear, illegible, or unsafe order is held and clarified with the prescriber before administration, high-alert drugs receive an independent double-check, and documentation is done after the dose is given. Medication errors are reported and the patient is monitored.

Document after administration and report any error

title: IV Piggyback (Secondary Infusion) Administration
subtitle: The nurse runs an IV piggyback safely — hanging the secondary bag higher than the primary, checking compatibility, back-priming, assessing the IV site, and stopping for infiltration.

patient.name: IV Piggyback
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers an intermittent IV piggyback medication through a primary line.

nursesNote: The nurse administers an IV piggyback (secondary) medication safely. A piggyback is a small-volume bag of intermittent medication that connects to the primary line; it is hung higher than the primary bag so the pressure difference lets it infuse first, with the primary lowered on an extender hook. Before connecting, the nurse verifies the medication rights and confirms the drug is compatible with the primary fluid — if incompatible, the line is flushed or a separate line is used. The secondary set is connected at the upper Y-port and back-primed to clear air, and the pump is set for the secondary volume and rate so the primary resumes when it finishes. The IV site is assessed for patency before infusing, and the nurse monitors for reactions. Burning, swelling, coolness, or a slowed rate at the site suggests infiltration, while redness, warmth, and pain along the vein suggest phlebitis — both require stopping the infusion and addressing the site.
providerOrders: Verify the medication rights and compatibility with the primary fluid
Hang the secondary bag higher than the primary bag
Connect at the upper Y-port and back-prime the tubing
Assess the IV site for patency before infusing
Stop the infusion for signs of infiltration or phlebitis

title: Surgical Wound Drains: JP, Hemovac, and Penrose
subtitle: The nurse manages wound drains — restoring suction by compressing and capping a JP or Hemovac, recognizing the open Penrose drain, measuring each drain's output, and reporting bright red or foul drainage.

patient.name: Wound Drains
patient.admitDate: The nurse empties, measures, and maintains surgical wound drains.

nursesNote: The nurse manages surgical wound drains. Jackson-Pratt and Hemovac drains are closed systems that use gentle suction; to restore suction the nurse empties the device, then compresses it and replaces the plug while it stays collapsed, which creates the negative pressure that pulls fluid out. A Penrose drain is an open drain that uses no suction, draining onto the dressing and held in place by a safety pin, so the dressing is kept clean and changed often. Drains are emptied when about half to two-thirds full, and each drain's output is measured and recorded separately by amount and color; drainage normally progresses from sanguineous (red) to serosanguineous to serous over days. The nurse secures the drain to prevent tension or dislodgement, assesses the site for infection, and uses aseptic technique. A sudden increase in bright red drainage, foul or purulent output, or a sudden stop with swelling is reported to the surgeon.

Secure the drain to prevent tension or dislodgement
Report bright red, foul, or suddenly stopped drainage

title: VTE Prevention: Sequential Compression Devices and Antiembolism Stockings
subtitle: The nurse uses mechanical VTE prophylaxis safely — applying SCDs and graduated stockings correctly, checking skin each shift, encouraging early ambulation, and withholding compression for a suspected DVT.

patient.name: VTE Prophylaxis
patient.admitDate: The nurse applies sequential compression devices and antiembolism stockings to prevent venous thromboembolism.

labs.v: Two fingers fit under the sleeve.

nursesNote: The nurse provides mechanical VTE prophylaxis. Immobility causes venous stasis, which raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis; sequential compression devices (SCDs) gently inflate and deflate to push blood back toward the heart, and graduated antiembolism stockings (TED hose) apply pressure that is greatest at the ankle to improve venous return. Stockings are measured for the correct size and applied before the patient rises, with the legs elevated and before edema develops; they are smoothed so there are no wrinkles, since a rolled or bunched stocking acts like a tourniquet. SCD sleeves are kept on continuously except while the patient walks or bathes and are then reapplied. Each shift the nurse removes the device to inspect the skin and check color, warmth, and sensation. Early ambulation, ankle pumps, and hydration are the most effective prevention. Compression is withheld for an active or suspected DVT, severe peripheral arterial disease or leg ischemia, or open skin, and a newly swollen, warm, painful calf is reported without massaging the leg.

Measure for and apply graduated antiembolism stockings before the patient rises

Withhold compression and report a suspected DVT or leg ischemia

title: Incentive Spirometry and Postoperative Breathing Exercises
subtitle: The nurse coaches lung expansion to prevent atelectasis — positioning upright, teaching a slow deep inhalation with a breath hold, splinting the incision to cough, and using the spirometer about 10 times per hour.

patient.name: Incentive Spirometry
patient.admitDate: The nurse teaches incentive spirometry and deep-breathing exercises to prevent postoperative atelectasis.

vitals.temp: Splint with a pillow to cough

nursesNote: The nurse teaches incentive spirometry and postoperative breathing exercises to prevent atelectasis and pneumonia. After surgery, shallow breathing from pain and immobility lets alveoli collapse, so deep lung expansion is encouraged. The patient sits upright in high-Fowler's, exhales normally, then seals the lips tightly around the mouthpiece and inhales slowly and deeply to raise the piston to the goal marker, holds the breath for about 3-5 seconds, and exhales. This is repeated about 10 times each hour while awake. The patient is taught to cough afterward to clear secretions and to splint the incision with a pillow to reduce pain. A common error is blowing out forcefully into the device or taking quick shallow breaths; the device is for slow, sustained inhalation. The spirometer does not replace turning and early ambulation. The nurse reports fever, crackles or decreased breath sounds, a productive cough, or a falling oxygen saturation, which can signal atelectasis or pneumonia.

title: Wound Irrigation and Cleansing
subtitle: The nurse irrigates a wound safely — using warmed normal saline, sterile technique for a surgical wound, cleaning from the cleanest to the dirtiest area at safe pressure until the return runs clear, then assessing the wound.

patient.name: Wound Irrigation
patient.admitDate: The nurse cleanses a wound by irrigation to remove debris and promote healing.

nursesNote: The nurse irrigates a wound to remove debris, exudate, and bacteria and to promote healing. Warmed normal saline is the standard irrigant because it is isotonic and does not harm healthy tissue; warming improves comfort and avoids cooling the wound bed. Sterile technique is used for a fresh surgical wound, while clean technique may be used for a chronic wound. After hand hygiene and donning gloves, gown, and goggles, the nurse positions the patient so the solution flows from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest and drains into a basin. A 30-35 mL syringe with a 19-gauge catheter delivers a safe irrigation pressure (about 4-15 psi) that cleans the wound without driving bacteria deeper or damaging tissue; the tip is held about an inch above the bed and not touched to the wound. Irrigation continues until the return solution runs clear, then the nurse pats the area dry, assesses the wound bed for size, color, drainage, odor, and tunneling, and applies the ordered dressing. Foul odor, increasing redness, or purulent drainage is reported.

Use sterile technique for the surgical wound and don PPE
Cleanse from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest until the return is clear
Use a 30-35 mL syringe with a 19-gauge catheter for safe pressure
Assess and document the wound; report signs of infection

title: Central Venous Access Device (CVAD) Care and Maintenance
subtitle: The nurse maintains a central line safely — using sterile technique for dressing changes, scrubbing the hub before access, flushing with saline, clamping to prevent air embolism, and recognizing a line infection.

patient.name: Central Line Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a central venous access device, including dressing changes and flushing.

nursesNote: The nurse maintains a central venous access device (CVAD) such as a PICC, tunneled catheter, or implanted port, which ends in a large central vein for long-term therapy. Strict sterile technique is used for dressing changes, with a mask on both the nurse and the patient; the skin is cleansed with chlorhexidine using friction and allowed to dry before the new dressing is applied. A transparent dressing is changed about every 7 days (gauze every 2 days) and immediately if it is loose, soiled, or damp. Before every access the nurse scrubs the hub with alcohol or chlorhexidine for about 15 seconds and lets it dry, then flushes with normal saline using positive pressure to keep the line patent; resistance is never forced, since that can dislodge a clot. The line is kept clamped or capped when not in use and tubing is primed to prevent an air embolism. PICC tip placement is confirmed by X-ray before first use. The nurse assesses the site for redness, swelling, drainage, or tenderness and reports fever, which can signal a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI); the catheter is removed as soon as it is no longer needed.
providerOrders: Use sterile technique with masks for central line dressing changes
Cleanse with chlorhexidine and allow it to dry
Scrub the hub before each access and flush with normal saline
Keep the line clamped or capped when not in use
Assess the site and report signs of a CLABSI; remove the line when no longer needed

title: Chest Tube and Closed Chest Drainage Care
subtitle: The nurse manages a closed chest drainage system — keeping it upright below the chest, recognizing normal tidaling versus an air leak, never routinely clamping, and responding when the tube disconnects or is dislodged.

patient.name: Chest Tube Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a patient with a chest tube and closed chest drainage system.

labs.v: Place tube end in sterile water.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a chest tube connected to a closed drainage system, which removes air, fluid, or blood from the pleural space and helps the lung re-expand. The system is kept upright and below the level of the chest so gravity aids drainage, and the tubing is kept free of kinks and dependent loops. In the water-seal chamber, tidaling (fluctuation with breathing) shows the tube is patent and stops when the lung re-expands or the tube is blocked; brief bubbling when the patient coughs is expected with a pneumothorax, but continuous bubbling suggests an air leak and the connections are checked. Suction-control bubbling should be gentle. The nurse does not routinely clamp, strip, or milk the tube, since clamping can cause a tension pneumothorax. Sterile water and an occlusive dressing are kept at the bedside: if the tube disconnects from the system, the end is placed in sterile water to restore the seal, and if the tube is pulled out of the chest, the site is covered with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides and the provider is notified. Drainage over 100 mL/hr, sudden bright-red output, increasing shortness of breath, or crepitus is reported.
providerOrders: Keep the drainage system upright and below the level of the chest
Monitor the water seal for tidaling and report continuous bubbling
Keep tubing free of kinks; do not routinely clamp, strip, or milk it
Keep sterile water and an occlusive dressing at the bedside
Report drainage over 100 mL/hr, bright-red output, or respiratory distress

title: Peritoneal Dialysis Care
subtitle: The nurse performs a peritoneal dialysis exchange safely — warming the dialysate, using sterile technique, timing inflow/dwell/outflow, recognizing cloudy effluent as peritonitis, and troubleshooting poor drainage.

patient.name: Peritoneal Dialysis
patient.admitDate: The nurse manages peritoneal dialysis exchanges through an abdominal catheter.

labs.r: Slight pink early may be ok.

nursesNote: The nurse manages peritoneal dialysis (PD), which uses the patient's peritoneal membrane as the filter: warmed dialysate is instilled through an abdominal catheter (inflow), allowed to dwell for the ordered time so wastes and fluid move into it, then drained out (outflow). The dialysate is warmed to body temperature with dry heat and never microwaved, which improves comfort and the exchange. Because peritonitis is the major complication, strict aseptic technique is used when connecting the bags. Normal drained effluent is clear and pale yellow; a slight pink tinge can occur in the first few exchanges after catheter placement, but cloudy effluent with abdominal pain and fever is the hallmark of peritonitis and is reported, with a sample sent for culture. Outflow should roughly equal or exceed inflow; sluggish drainage is troubleshooted by repositioning the patient, checking for tubing kinks, keeping the drain bag below the abdomen, and treating constipation. The nurse monitors daily weight, intake and output, and blood glucose (the dextrose in dialysate can raise it), and assesses the catheter exit site for redness or drainage.

Use strict aseptic technique to connect the dialysis bags
Instill, dwell, and drain per the ordered volumes and times
Inspect and document the effluent; report cloudy returns
Monitor daily weight, intake/output, and blood glucose

title: Assisting with Thoracentesis and Paracentesis
subtitle: The nurse assists with fluid-removal taps — verifying consent, positioning the patient, coaching stillness, and watching for pneumothorax after thoracentesis and hypotension after large-volume paracentesis.

patient.name: Thoracentesis / Paracentesis
patient.admitDate: The nurse assists the provider with a thoracentesis or paracentesis and monitors for complications.

nursesNote: The nurse assists the provider with a thoracentesis (pleural fluid removal) or paracentesis (ascitic fluid removal). Before either, the nurse confirms informed consent and performs a time-out, gathers supplies, and explains the procedure. For a thoracentesis the patient sits upright leaning forward over a bedside table with arms supported, and is coached to stay still and avoid coughing or deep breathing while the needle is in; the main complication is a pneumothorax, so respiratory status is watched and a chest X-ray is obtained afterward, and no more than about 1000-1500 mL is removed at once to avoid re-expansion pulmonary edema. For a paracentesis the patient empties the bladder first to prevent bladder puncture and sits upright or in high-Fowler's so fluid settles to the lower abdomen; abdominal girth and weight are measured before and after, and after large-volume removal the nurse watches for hypotension from fluid shifts (albumin may be ordered). Throughout, vital signs are monitored, specimens are labeled, the site is checked for leakage, and findings are documented.

Position the patient: upright over a table for thoracentesis; voided and upright for paracentesis
Coach the patient to stay still and not cough during needle insertion
Monitor vital signs and watch for pneumothorax or hypotension

title: Topical, Transdermal, and Rectal Medication Administration
subtitle: The nurse gives medications by skin and rectal routes safely — wearing gloves for topicals, removing the old patch before a new one and never cutting it, and positioning in Sims' for a retained suppository.

patient.name: Topical / Patch / Rectal Meds
patient.admitDate: The nurse administers topical, transdermal, and rectal medications safely.

nursesNote: The nurse administers medications by the topical, transdermal, and rectal routes after verifying the medication rights. Gloves are worn for topical agents, which are applied in a thin, even layer to clean skin. For a transdermal patch the nurse always removes the previous patch before applying a new one to prevent a double dose, chooses a clean, dry, hairless site, rotates sites to reduce irritation, and never cuts the patch because that alters the dose; the new patch is dated, timed, and initialed, and the old one is folded sticky-sides together and discarded safely. For a rectal suppository the patient is placed in the left lateral (Sims') position; the lubricated suppository is inserted past the internal anal sphincter along the rectal wall and not into a mass of stool, and the patient stays lying for about 15-20 minutes and avoids bearing down so the medication is retained. The nurse documents the removal of the old patch as well as each medication given.

Wear gloves for topical and transdermal medications
