title: Assisting with a Lumbar Puncture
subtitle: The nurse assists with a lumbar puncture safely — verifying consent, curling the patient into the fetal position, keeping them still and sterile, labeling CSF tubes, and lying the patient flat afterward to prevent a spinal headache.

patient.name: Lumbar Puncture
patient.admitDate: The nurse assists the provider with a lumbar puncture and provides post-procedure care.

nursesNote: The nurse assists the provider with a lumbar puncture, which collects cerebrospinal fluid, measures pressure, or delivers medication; the needle is placed below the end of the spinal cord (around L3-L4/L4-L5) to avoid cord injury. After confirming informed consent and a time-out, the nurse has the patient empty the bladder and positions them side-lying with the knees drawn to the chest (fetal position) or sitting and leaning forward over a table, which widens the spaces between the vertebrae. A sterile field is maintained to prevent meningitis, and the nurse helps the patient stay still during insertion. The CSF tubes are labeled in order of collection and sent promptly. Afterward the patient lies flat for the ordered time and increases fluids to help replace CSF and prevent a post-LP (spinal) headache, which is positional and worse when sitting or standing. The nurse monitors neurologic status and leg movement/sensation, checks the site for CSF leakage, and reports a severe headache, numbness or tingling, fever, or drainage.

Position the patient side-lying with knees to the chest (or sitting, leaning forward)
Maintain a sterile field and help the patient hold still
Label CSF tubes in order of collection and send them promptly
Keep the patient flat per order, encourage fluids, and report a severe headache

title: Choking and Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction Response
subtitle: The nurse responds to choking — letting a person with a mild block keep coughing, giving abdominal thrusts to an adult or child with a severe block, using back blows and chest thrusts for an infant, and starting CPR if they collapse.

patient.name: Choking Response
patient.admitDate: The nurse recognizes and responds to a foreign-body airway obstruction.

labs.v: No air; weak or no cough.

nursesNote: The nurse recognizes and responds to a foreign-body airway obstruction. The universal sign of choking is clutching the throat; the key is distinguishing a mild from a severe obstruction. With a mild (partial) obstruction the person can still cough, speak, or breathe, so the nurse encourages forceful coughing, stays with them, and does not interfere. With a severe obstruction the person cannot speak, cough, or breathe and may turn blue, so the nurse acts at once: for a responsive adult or child, abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) are given just above the navel with quick inward and upward motions; chest thrusts are used instead for a pregnant or very obese person. For a choking infant under one year, the nurse alternates 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts and never uses abdominal thrusts because of organ-injury risk. Thrusts continue until the object is expelled or the person becomes unconscious. If the victim collapses, the nurse lowers them, calls for help, begins CPR, and looks in the mouth before breaths, removing an object only if it is visible (no blind finger sweep). After relief, the person is assessed and may need evaluation for injury from the thrusts.

Give abdominal thrusts to a responsive adult or child with a severe obstruction
Use chest thrusts for a pregnant or very obese person

Call for help and begin CPR if the victim becomes unconscious

title: Continuous Bladder Irrigation (CBI)
subtitle: The nurse manages CBI through a three-way catheter — using sterile saline, titrating the rate to keep urine pink and clear, subtracting irrigant to find true urine output, and recognizing an obstructing clot.

patient.name: Bladder Irrigation
patient.admitDate: The nurse manages continuous bladder irrigation through a three-way catheter, often after prostate surgery.

labs.r: Faster if red, slower if clear.

nursesNote: The nurse manages continuous bladder irrigation (CBI), which runs sterile normal saline through a three-way (triple-lumen) catheter to flush clots and keep the catheter patent, most often after a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). The irrigation rate is titrated to the urine color: it is increased when drainage is bright red or has clots and slowed as the urine clears toward light pink. Drainage output always exceeds the irrigant infused, so the nurse subtracts the volume of irrigant from the total output to record true urine output. Pink-tinged urine that gradually clears, with a few small clots early, is expected. A sudden drop or absence of output with a distended, painful bladder and spasms suggests an obstructing clot; the nurse checks the tubing for kinks and clots, increases the rate or performs manual irrigation per order, and notifies the provider if output does not return. The CBI is not stopped when the urine turns bloody; instead the rate is increased. The bag is kept below the bladder, a closed sterile system is maintained, and bladder spasms are treated with prescribed antispasmodics.

Titrate the rate to keep the urine light pink and clear
Record true urine output by subtracting the irrigant volume
Keep output greater than input; report no output with bladder distension
Increase the rate for bright-red drainage; do not stop the CBI

title: Traction and Skeletal Pin Care
subtitle: The nurse maintains traction safely — keeping weights hanging freely, ropes running in the pulleys, the patient in alignment with counter-traction, and assessing pin sites and neurovascular status.

patient.name: Traction Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a patient in traction with skeletal pins.

labs.r: Pain, pallor, pulse, paresthesia, paralysis, temp.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient in traction, which aligns and immobilizes a fracture and reduces muscle spasm. Skin traction (such as Buck's) uses a boot or straps with lighter weight and is usually temporary, while skeletal traction uses pins or wires inserted into the bone with heavier weights and must be maintained continuously and never interrupted. The weights are kept hanging freely off the floor and are not lifted or removed; the ropes run freely in the pulleys with secure, unfrayed knots; and the patient is kept in proper alignment with counter-traction so they do not slide down in bed. Pin sites are assessed for infection (redness, drainage, odor, or loosening) and cleaned per protocol. The nurse performs neurovascular checks distal to the injury using the 6 Ps (pain, pallor, pulse, paresthesia, paralysis, and temperature) and inspects the skin over pressure points. Because of immobility, the patient is encouraged to exercise unaffected limbs and is monitored for DVT, pneumonia, and constipation.

Keep ropes in the pulleys with secure knots and the patient in alignment
Perform pin-site care per protocol and monitor for infection

title: Ear and Eye Irrigation
subtitle: The nurse irrigates safely — warming ear solution and pulling the pinna up and back, withholding for a perforated eardrum, and flushing the eye from inner to outer canthus, copiously and at once for a chemical splash.

patient.name: Ear / Eye Irrigation
patient.admitDate: The nurse performs ear and eye irrigation to remove cerumen, debris, or a chemical.

vitals.temp: No ear irrigation if TM perforated

labs.v: Toward the side of the canal.

nursesNote: The nurse performs ear and eye irrigation. Ear irrigation removes cerumen or debris; the solution is warmed to body temperature because cold or hot fluid against the eardrum causes dizziness, vertigo, and nausea. The pinna is pulled up and back in an adult (down and back in a child under three) to straighten the canal, and the stream is directed toward the side of the canal rather than at the eardrum, with the return allowed to flow out into a basin. Ear irrigation is withheld if the tympanic membrane is perforated or an ear infection is suspected. Eye irrigation flushes a foreign body or chemical from the eye; for a chemical splash the eye is flushed immediately and copiously with sterile normal saline (at least 15 minutes) before other care. The head is turned toward the affected side so fluid flows from the inner to the outer canthus into a basin, away from the unaffected eye, and the stream is aimed onto the conjunctiva, not directly on the cornea. The nurse stops either irrigation for new pain, dizziness, or nausea, then assesses and documents.

title: High-Alert Medications: Safe Handling
subtitle: The nurse safely handles high-alert drugs — doing independent two-nurse checks for insulin and heparin, never giving concentrated potassium IV push, separating look-alike drugs, and writing 'units' in full.

patient.name: High-Alert Medications
patient.admitDate: The nurse applies extra safeguards when giving high-alert medications.

vitals.temp: High harm if an error occurs

labs.v: Anticoag, K+, Insulin, Narcotics, Chemo, Heparin.

nursesNote: The nurse applies extra safeguards to high-alert medications, which carry a heightened risk of serious harm when given in error. Common classes are remembered as A-PINCH: Anticoagulants, Potassium and other concentrated electrolytes, Insulin, Narcotics (opioids), Chemotherapy, and Heparin. For drugs like insulin and heparin the nurse performs an independent double-check with a second nurse (verifying the drug, dose, concentration, pump settings, and patient) and writes 'units' out in full rather than 'U,' which can be misread as a zero and cause a tenfold overdose. Concentrated potassium chloride is NEVER given by IV push because it can cause fatal arrhythmias; it is diluted and infused slowly by pump (generally no more than 10 mEq/hr peripherally) with cardiac monitoring and IV-site assessment. Concentrated electrolytes are removed from floor stock, look-alike/sound-alike drugs are separated and labeled (Tall Man lettering), and error-prone abbreviations are avoided. The standard rights and three checks still apply on top of these measures.

title: IV Flow Rate & Dosage Calculation
subtitle: The nurse safely calculates IV drip rates and drug doses — using the formula method, checking the drop factor, verifying a safe dose, and double-checking high-risk math.

patient.name: IV Flow Rate & Dosage
patient.admitDate: The nurse calculates and verifies IV rates and drug doses before giving them.

labs.r: mg vs g, kg vs lb.

nursesNote: The nurse calculates and verifies every IV rate and drug dose before administration. For an infusion pump the rate is programmed in mL/hr (total volume divided by total hours). For gravity tubing the nurse calculates gtt/min using the formula (volume in mL x the drop factor) / time in minutes, and the drop factor is found on the tubing package — macrodrip sets deliver 10-20 gtt/mL and microdrip (mini-drip) sets deliver 60 gtt/mL. Drug doses use the formula Desired dose / dose on Hand x Quantity, and all units must be converted to match (for example mg to g, or pounds to kilograms) before calculating. For weight-based and pediatric drugs the nurse confirms the ordered mg/kg dose falls within the safe reference range. Answers to gtt/min are rounded to whole drops because a partial drop cannot be delivered. The nurse always sanity-checks that the result is reasonable to catch tenfold errors, and performs an independent two-nurse check for high-alert medications such as insulin and heparin and for pediatric doses.

title: Grief and Loss: Supporting the Grieving Patient
subtitle: The nurse supports a grieving patient — recognizing types and stages of grief, using therapeutic presence, allowing the person to express feelings, and spotting complicated grief that needs referral.

patient.name: Grief and Loss
patient.admitDate: The nurse provides supportive care to a patient experiencing grief and loss.

nursesNote: The nurse provides supportive, individualized care to a patient experiencing grief, the normal emotional response to a loss, while mourning is the outward, often culturally shaped expression of that grief. Grief takes several forms: anticipatory grief occurs before an expected loss (as in terminal illness), disenfranchised grief is a loss that is not openly acknowledged by others (such as a miscarriage or the death of a pet), and complicated grief is prolonged, intense, and disabling and requires referral. The Kubler-Ross stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) are a common framework, but people do not move through them in a fixed order and may revisit stages. The nurse's role is therapeutic presence: sitting with the patient, allowing silence, using open-ended questions, and encouraging the person to express feelings without judging, rushing, or offering false reassurance. Cultural and spiritual rituals are respected and a chaplain or support resources are offered. The nurse watches for red flags such as suicidal ideation or an inability to function and refers or escalates when grief becomes complicated or unsafe.

Assess the type and stage of grief the patient is experiencing
Respect cultural and spiritual mourning practices

title: Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA): Safe Use
subtitle: The nurse manages a PCA pump — teaching that ONLY the patient presses the button, doing a two-nurse setup check, monitoring sedation and respirations, and keeping naloxone ready.

patient.name: Patient-Controlled Analgesia
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely manages a patient using a PCA pump for pain control.

vitals.temp: ONLY the patient presses the button

labs.v: Press when in pain, before activity.
labs.r: Do not wait for severe pain.

nursesNote: The nurse safely manages a patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump, which lets the patient self-administer a preset IV opioid dose by pressing a button for steadier pain control. The single most important safety rule is that ONLY the patient presses the button: 'PCA by proxy,' where a family member or nurse pushes it, can cause overdose and is not permitted, and the patient must be alert and able to understand the device. Because the opioid is a high-alert medication, two nurses perform an independent check at setup and shift change, verifying the drug, concentration, demand dose, lockout interval, and any continuous (basal) rate against the order. The lockout interval limits how often a dose can be delivered. The nurse monitors sedation level and respiratory status closely, because increasing sedation appears before respiratory depression and is the best early warning sign; a low respiratory rate or oversedation means holding doses, stimulating the patient, and being ready to give naloxone, the opioid antidote kept available. Common opioid effects such as constipation, nausea, and pruritus are managed, and the patient is taught to press the button when pain begins and before activity rather than waiting until pain is severe.

Perform an independent two-nurse check of the PCA settings
Monitor sedation level, respiratory rate, and SpO2 closely
Keep naloxone available for opioid-induced respiratory depression
Manage constipation, nausea, and pruritus from the opioid

title: Therapeutic Communication Techniques
subtitle: The nurse uses therapeutic communication — open-ended questions, reflection, silence, and clarifying — while avoiding blocks like false reassurance, giving advice, 'why' questions, and changing the subject.

patient.name: Therapeutic Communication
patient.admitDate: The nurse uses therapeutic communication to build trust and support the patient.

nursesNote: The nurse uses therapeutic communication to build trust and keep the interaction patient-centered. Helpful techniques include open-ended questions that invite the patient to share ('Tell me more about how you're feeling'), reflection that restates the feeling the patient expressed to show active listening, clarifying to confirm understanding ('What do you mean by that?'), purposeful silence that gives the patient time to think without being rushed, and offering self to convey presence ('I'll stay with you a while'). The nurse keeps the focus on the patient's feelings rather than on facts or the nurse's own opinions. Common communication blocks are avoided: false reassurance ('Everything will be fine') dismisses real concerns, giving advice ('If I were you...') removes the patient's autonomy, 'why' questions can sound accusing and put the patient on the defensive, and changing the subject signals that the topic is unwelcome and shuts down sharing. Closed-ended questions have a place for specific data but should not dominate an emotional conversation.

Reflect and restate the patient's feelings to show listening
Use silence to give the patient time to process
Avoid false reassurance, giving advice, and 'why' questions
Keep the focus on the patient's feelings and concerns

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers medications through an enteral feeding tube (NG or PEG). Tube placement is verified before anything is instilled, and the head of the bed is kept elevated 30-45 degrees to reduce aspiration risk. Liquid forms are used whenever available because they clog the tube less; when only tablets exist, the nurse crushes immediate-release tablets to a fine powder and dissolves them in water, but NEVER crushes extended-release (SR/XL/CR), enteric-coated, or sublingual products, since crushing destroys the delivery mechanism and can cause a dangerous dose dump or gastric irritation. Each medication is given separately, one at a time, with a water flush before, between, and after the medications (commonly about 15-30 mL) to keep the tube patent and prevent drug interactions. Medications are not added to the feeding bag. Certain drugs (such as phenytoin) require the tube feeding to be held before and after the dose to ensure absorption. If the tube clogs, warm water and gentle pressure are used; the tube is never forced. The standard rights and three checks still apply.

title: Anticoagulant Therapy: Heparin and Warfarin
subtitle: The nurse manages anticoagulants — monitoring aPTT for heparin (antidote protamine) and INR for warfarin (antidote vitamin K), teaching bleeding precautions, and watching for signs of bleeding.

patient.name: Anticoagulant Therapy
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely manages a patient receiving anticoagulant therapy.

nursesNote: The nurse safely manages anticoagulant therapy, which prevents clot formation and extension but raises bleeding risk. Heparin acts quickly (IV or SQ) and is monitored with the aPTT (therapeutic about 1.5-2.5 times baseline; anti-Xa may also be used); its antidote is protamine sulfate. Warfarin is oral with a slow onset over several days and is monitored with the INR (usual goal 2-3; an INR above 4 signals high bleeding risk); its antidote is vitamin K, so the patient keeps dietary vitamin K (leafy greens) steady rather than suddenly bingeing or avoiding it. Low-molecular-weight heparin such as enoxaparin is given SQ and usually needs no routine lab monitoring. The nurse watches for any signs of bleeding (bruising, bleeding gums, blood in urine or stool, prolonged bleeding) and monitors platelets for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), stopping heparin if it develops. Bleeding precautions are taught: a soft toothbrush, an electric razor, avoiding aspirin/NSAIDs unless ordered, fall prevention, and reporting bleeding. Two anticoagulants are high-alert drugs requiring an independent double-check, and IM injections are generally avoided.
providerOrders: Monitor aPTT for heparin and keep protamine available
Monitor INR for warfarin and keep vitamin K available
Teach the patient to keep dietary vitamin K intake steady
Assess for bleeding and report bruising, blood in urine/stool, or bleeding gums
Teach bleeding precautions: soft toothbrush, electric razor, avoid NSAIDs

title: Anxiety: Levels and Management
subtitle: The nurse cares for an anxious patient — recognizing mild, moderate, severe, and panic levels, staying with the patient, using a calm voice and simple directions, and teaching coping skills.

patient.name: Anxiety
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient experiencing anxiety.

nursesNote: The nurse supports a patient experiencing anxiety, a vague feeling of dread that activates the body's stress response. Anxiety occurs on a continuum. Mild anxiety sharpens awareness and is the best time to teach, since the patient is alert and learns well. Moderate anxiety narrows the perceptual field, so the patient needs help focusing and benefits from redirection. Severe anxiety leaves the patient unable to focus or solve problems, so teaching is deferred. Panic is a loss of control with possible disorganized behavior or fleeing, making safety the priority. The nurse stays with an anxious patient rather than leaving, uses a calm, low voice with short and simple directions, and reduces stimulation. As anxiety eases, the nurse guides slow, deep breathing and teaches coping and grounding skills, helping the patient name the feeling and identify triggers. A PRN anxiolytic may be given for severe or panic-level anxiety if ordered. The nurse avoids false reassurance and instead acknowledges the feeling and provides steady, supportive presence.
providerOrders: Assess the patient's level of anxiety (mild, moderate, severe, panic)
Stay with the patient and provide a calm, low-stimulation environment
Use a calm voice with short, simple directions
Teach slow breathing and coping skills as anxiety eases
Give a PRN anxiolytic for severe or panic-level anxiety if ordered

title: Digoxin Therapy and Toxicity
subtitle: The nurse manages digoxin — checking the apical pulse for a full minute, holding for a rate under 60, watching potassium and a narrow therapeutic level, and recognizing toxicity (nausea, visual halos, bradycardia).

patient.name: Digoxin
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers and monitors digoxin.

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers digoxin, a cardiac glycoside that slows the heart rate and strengthens contraction, used in heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Before each dose the nurse counts the apical pulse for one full minute and holds the dose, then notifies the provider, if an adult's rate is below 60 (or below 70 in a child). Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic range (about 0.5-2 ng/mL), so levels are monitored. Low potassium increases the risk of toxicity, so the nurse watches the potassium level, especially in patients also taking potassium-wasting diuretics. Early signs of toxicity are gastrointestinal, including anorexia, nausea, and vomiting; visual changes such as blurred vision and yellow-green halos are classic; and cardiac effects include bradycardia and dysrhythmias. If toxicity is suspected, the nurse holds the drug, checks the digoxin and potassium levels, monitors the heart rhythm, and notifies the provider. Severe toxicity is treated with digoxin immune Fab. The nurse teaches the patient to check the pulse, report nausea or visual halos, maintain potassium-rich intake as advised, and not double up on missed doses.

Hold digoxin and notify the provider if the adult pulse is under 60
Monitor the digoxin level and the serum potassium
Assess for toxicity: nausea, visual halos, and bradycardia
Keep digoxin immune Fab available for severe toxicity

title: Ego Defense Mechanisms
subtitle: The nurse recognizes defense mechanisms — unconscious ways people cope with stress and anxiety, such as denial, projection, displacement, and rationalization — and knows when they become unhealthy.

patient.name: Defense Mechanisms
patient.admitDate: The nurse identifies how a patient copes with stress and anxiety.

vitals.temp: Shifting feelings to a safe target

labs.v: Shifting emotion to a safe target.
Offsetting a weakness with a strength.

nursesNote: The nurse recognizes ego defense mechanisms, the unconscious mental strategies people use to reduce anxiety and protect the self from stress. Common examples include denial (refusing to accept a painful reality, such as ignoring a new diagnosis), projection (attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else), displacement (shifting an emotion from its source onto a safer target, like snapping at family instead of a boss), rationalization (offering a logical-sounding excuse for behavior), regression (returning to an earlier developmental behavior, common during illness or in children), repression (unconsciously blocking a distressing memory), compensation (offsetting a perceived weakness by excelling in another area), and sublimation (channeling an unacceptable urge into a socially acceptable activity). Defense mechanisms are normal and can be adaptive when used briefly to get through stress; sublimation is generally the healthiest. They become unhealthy when overused, when they distort reality, or when they block problem-solving and daily function. The nurse identifies the mechanism without judging, builds trust, and gently helps the patient develop healthier coping, referring for counseling when defenses interfere with care or safety.
providerOrders: Identify the defense mechanism the patient is using
Build trust and avoid confronting denial harshly early on
Assess whether the mechanism is helping or blocking coping
Support healthier coping skills as the patient is ready
Refer for counseling when defenses impair function or safety

title: Corticosteroid Therapy
subtitle: The nurse manages corticosteroids — never stopping them abruptly, giving with food, and watching for high glucose, infection risk, fluid retention, and Cushingoid effects.

patient.name: Corticosteroids
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers and monitors corticosteroid therapy.

labs.v: Moon face, buffalo hump, weight gain.
Mood changes, slow healing, GI ulcer.

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers corticosteroids (such as prednisone, hydrocortisone, methylprednisolone), which reduce inflammation and suppress the immune response across many conditions. The most critical teaching is to never stop the drug abruptly: long-term use suppresses the adrenal glands, and sudden withdrawal can trigger acute adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis), so the dose is tapered slowly. The drug is given with food or milk to protect the stomach, since it raises the risk of GI ulcers. Corticosteroids raise blood glucose, so the nurse monitors sugar levels, especially in patients with diabetes, and they suppress immunity and can mask the usual signs of infection (including fever), so infection risk is high and sick contacts are avoided. Sodium and water retention can cause weight gain, edema, and higher blood pressure, while potassium tends to fall. Long-term effects include osteoporosis (calcium and vitamin D are encouraged), and Cushingoid changes such as a moon face, buffalo hump, and central weight gain. The nurse also watches for mood changes, delayed wound healing, and bruising, teaches the patient to carry medical identification, and reports signs of infection promptly.
providerOrders: Teach the patient to never stop corticosteroids abruptly and to taper as ordered
Give the dose with food or milk to protect the stomach
Monitor blood glucose, especially in patients with diabetes
Assess for infection and teach the patient to avoid sick contacts
Monitor weight, edema, blood pressure, and potassium

title: De-escalating the Agitated Patient
subtitle: The nurse calms an escalating patient — keeping everyone safe, using a calm voice and personal space, setting clear limits, and saving restraints as a last resort.

patient.name: Agitation / De-escalation
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely de-escalates an agitated patient.

nursesNote: The nurse safely de-escalates an agitated patient, keeping the safety of the patient, staff, and others as the top priority. The nurse watches for early warning signs of escalation, such as pacing, a loud or rising voice, clenched fists, and a tense posture, and intervenes early. The approach matters: the nurse maintains a calm, non-threatening stance with hands visible, respects the patient's personal space, keeps a clear path to the exit, and does not corner the patient or turn their back. A low, slow voice with short and simple words helps, and the nurse reduces stimulation by lowering noise and removing an audience. The nurse listens, acknowledges the patient's concern, and offers reasonable choices to restore a sense of control, while setting clear, firm limits without threats or arguing. Help is called early, and the nurse does not face an escalating patient alone. A PRN medication may be offered or given if ordered. Restraints and seclusion are a last resort, used only when less restrictive measures fail and the patient is a danger; they require a provider order, the least restrictive type, and close, frequent monitoring. The nurse documents the behaviors, interventions, and the patient's response.

title: Diuretic Therapy
subtitle: The nurse manages diuretics — watching potassium (loop/thiazide lower it, potassium-sparing raise it), weighing the patient daily, and timing doses in the morning.

patient.name: Diuretics
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers and monitors diuretic therapy.

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers diuretics, which remove excess fluid and sodium and are used for heart failure, edema, and hypertension. The main classes differ in how they affect potassium. Loop diuretics such as furosemide are strong and fast-acting and waste potassium; thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide are milder and also lower potassium; potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone retain potassium and can cause it to rise. The nurse monitors the potassium level closely (low with loop and thiazide, high with potassium-sparing) and watches for signs of low potassium such as muscle weakness, cramps, and an irregular heartbeat. Patients on loop or thiazide diuretics are encouraged to eat potassium-rich foods or take supplements as ordered, while patients on potassium-sparing diuretics avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes. The nurse weighs the patient daily at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing, since weight is the best measure of fluid change, and tracks intake and output and blood pressure while watching for dehydration. Doses are given in the morning to avoid waking at night to void. The nurse teaches the patient to rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness and to follow the diet appropriate to their diuretic type.

Weigh the patient daily at the same time and scale

Assess for signs of low potassium and dehydration
Teach diet and safety based on the diuretic type

title: Suicide Risk and Safety
subtitle: The nurse keeps a suicidal patient safe — asking directly about suicide, taking a plan with means seriously, never leaving a high-risk patient alone, and removing dangerous items.

patient.name: Suicide Risk / Safety
patient.admitDate: The nurse maintains safety for a patient at risk for suicide.

labs.v: Asking does not plant the idea.
No-harm contract is not a safeguard.

nursesNote: The nurse maintains safety for a patient at risk for suicide. The nurse asks directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts; asking about suicide does not plant the idea and is essential to assess risk. The nurse explores whether the patient has a plan and access to the means to carry it out, since a specific plan with available means (such as a firearm or stockpiled pills) and a history of a prior attempt indicate the highest risk. For a high-risk patient, safety comes first: the patient is placed on close or one-to-one observation and is never left alone, including in the bathroom. The environment is made safe by removing dangerous items such as sharps, glass, cords, belts, and medications. The nurse stays with the patient, listens without judging, and conveys hope while taking every statement seriously, including indirect comments like giving away possessions. A sudden, unexplained calm or improvement in a previously distressed patient can be a warning that a decision to act has been made and warrants increased vigilance. No-harm or no-suicide contracts are not reliable safeguards and do not replace observation and a safe environment. The nurse notifies the provider, documents the risk assessment and interventions, and ensures continuity of safety measures.

title: Inhaled Respiratory Medications
subtitle: The nurse teaches inhaler use — a fast-acting rescue inhaler for sudden symptoms, a daily maintenance inhaler for prevention, using a spacer, and rinsing the mouth after a steroid inhaler.

patient.name: Inhalers
patient.admitDate: The nurse teaches safe and correct use of inhaled medications.

labs.v: Steroid inhaler is not a rescue.

nursesNote: The nurse teaches correct use of inhaled respiratory medications. A short-acting bronchodilator (rescue inhaler) such as albuterol works quickly to relieve sudden symptoms like wheezing or shortness of breath and is used as needed. A maintenance (controller) inhaler, such as an inhaled corticosteroid or a long-acting bronchodilator, is taken daily to prevent attacks and does not relieve an acute attack, so it is never used as a rescue. When both a bronchodilator and a steroid inhaler are scheduled together, the bronchodilator is used first to open the airways, then the steroid, and the patient waits about a minute between puffs of the same inhaler. A spacer used with a metered-dose inhaler improves delivery to the lungs and reduces medication left in the mouth. Good technique includes a slow, deep breath coordinated with the puff and holding the breath for about ten seconds. After using a steroid inhaler, the patient rinses the mouth and spits to prevent oral thrush and hoarseness. Mild tremor and a faster heart rate are expected effects of a short-acting bronchodilator. Needing the rescue inhaler more often than usual signals poor control and should be reported to the provider.

Teach correct technique and use of a spacer

title: Opioid Analgesics and Naloxone
subtitle: The nurse gives opioids safely — watching for sedation before respiratory depression, holding for a slow respiratory rate, preventing constipation, and keeping naloxone ready.

patient.name: Opioid Analgesics
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers and monitors opioid pain medication.

labs.v: Hold if RR < 12 or very drowsy.

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers opioid analgesics (such as morphine, hydromorphone, oxycodone, fentanyl) for moderate to severe pain. Because opioids are central nervous system depressants, the nurse assesses the respiratory rate and the level of sedation before each dose and holds the dose, then notifies the provider, if the respiratory rate is below 12 or the patient is overly sedated and hard to arouse. The key safety principle is that increasing sedation comes before respiratory depression, so a rising sedation level is the early warning sign to act on, not just a low respiratory rate. The most serious adverse effect is respiratory depression (slow, shallow breathing), and the antidote naloxone is kept readily available; the nurse should know that naloxone is short-acting, so the opioid effect and pain can return and repeat doses and continued monitoring may be needed. Constipation is very common, does not improve with continued use, and is prevented with a scheduled bowel regimen, fluids, and fiber. Nausea and itching are common early and usually ease, while dizziness and orthostatic hypotension call for fall precautions. The nurse reassesses pain after giving the medication, uses the lowest effective dose, and teaches the patient and family about safe use, sedation warning signs, and not combining opioids with alcohol or other sedatives.

Hold the dose and notify the provider if the respiratory rate is under 12
Keep naloxone available for opioid-induced respiratory depression
Start a bowel regimen to prevent constipation
Use fall precautions and reassess pain after the dose

title: Immunizations and Vaccine Safety
subtitle: The nurse gives vaccines safely — knowing live vaccines from inactivated, screening for contraindications, handling true reactions, and teaching the schedule and aftercare.

patient.name: Immunizations
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers vaccines and teaches immunization.

labs.v: Flu shot, Tdap, hep B, pneumo.

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers vaccines, which provide active immunity by prompting the body to build its own antibodies. Live attenuated vaccines (such as MMR, varicella, and the intranasal flu vaccine) contain a weakened germ and are generally avoided in pregnancy and in immunocompromised patients. Inactivated and component vaccines (such as the flu shot, Tdap, hepatitis B, and pneumococcal) do not contain a live germ and are safer in those groups. Before giving a vaccine the nurse screens for true contraindications, the most important being anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component, and provides the Vaccine Information Statement and obtains consent. A mild illness, a low-grade fever, current antibiotics, or a family history of reactions are not reasons to withhold a vaccine. Expected effects include a sore arm or injection-site redness, a mild fever, and fussiness in children, which are self-limited and managed with a cool compress and acetaminophen as needed. The nurse stays alert for a rare true allergic reaction (anaphylaxis with hives, swelling, or wheezing), keeps epinephrine available, and treats it as an emergency. The nurse documents the site, route, lot number, the Vaccine Information Statement given, and follows the recommended immunization schedule across the lifespan.

title: Antibiotic Therapy
subtitle: The nurse manages antibiotics — screening for allergy, drawing cultures before the first dose, teaching the patient to finish the full course, and watching for C. diff and superinfection.

patient.name: Antibiotics
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers and monitors antibiotic therapy.

nursesNote: The nurse safely administers antibiotics, which treat bacterial infections. Before the first dose the nurse screens for drug allergies, since the most serious risk is an allergic reaction up to anaphylaxis, and asks what reaction occurred. When ordered, cultures (such as blood, urine, or wound) are drawn before the first dose so the organism can be identified, though antibiotics for sepsis are not delayed waiting on cultures. The nurse teaches the patient to take the entire prescribed course even after feeling better, because stopping early promotes antibiotic resistance, and to take doses on time and evenly spaced to keep a steady blood level. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset and the loss of normal flora, which can lead to a superinfection such as oral thrush or a vaginal yeast infection; new watery, foul-smelling diarrhea suggests Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) and requires stopping the drug if indicated and placing the patient on contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene. Some antibiotics need level monitoring, such as vancomycin (peak and trough levels; nephrotoxic and ototoxic), which is infused slowly to avoid 'red man' flushing. The nurse checks food and interaction rules for each drug, watches for an allergic reaction, keeps epinephrine available, and reports rash, swelling, wheezing, or severe diarrhea.

title: Transmission-Based Precautions
subtitle: The nurse applies isolation precautions — airborne (N95, negative-pressure room), droplet (surgical mask), and contact (gown and gloves) — on top of standard precautions.

patient.name: Isolation Precautions
patient.admitDate: The nurse selects the correct transmission-based precautions.

nursesNote: The nurse applies transmission-based precautions, which are added on top of standard precautions (hand hygiene and PPE used for every patient) when a specific spread route is known or suspected. Airborne precautions are for tiny droplet nuclei that stay suspended in the air, used for tuberculosis, measles, and varicella; the patient is in a private negative-pressure room with the door closed and staff wear an N95 respirator. Droplet precautions are for larger respiratory droplets spread at close range, used for influenza, pertussis, meningitis, mumps, and rubella; staff wear a surgical mask, and the patient is in a private room. Contact precautions are for organisms spread by direct or indirect touch, used for MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, and RSV; staff wear a gown and gloves and use dedicated equipment. For C. difficile, hands are washed with soap and water because alcohol gel does not kill the spores. PPE is applied before entering and removed carefully on exit (gloves are usually removed first and the mask last), with hand hygiene before and after. The patient stays in the room when possible, and if transport is needed the patient wears a mask. The nurse teaches the patient and visitors and ensures the correct signage is posted.

title: Psychosis and Schizophrenia Care
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient with psychosis — telling positive from negative symptoms, not arguing with delusions, presenting reality calmly, and checking command hallucinations for safety.

patient.name: Psychosis / Schizophrenia
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient experiencing psychosis.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient with psychosis, a loss of contact with reality seen in schizophrenia. Symptoms are grouped as positive (added experiences such as hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized speech or behavior) and negative (a loss of normal function such as flat affect, lack of motivation or pleasure, poverty of speech, and social withdrawal); positive symptoms generally respond better to medication, while negative symptoms are harder to treat. Delusions are fixed false beliefs: the nurse neither argues with nor agrees with them, but acknowledges the underlying feeling and calmly presents reality. Hallucinations are false sensory experiences, most often auditory; the nurse asks about their content and specifically assesses for command hallucinations telling the patient to harm self or others, because these are a safety priority. The nurse uses a calm, simple, consistent approach to build trust, avoids reinforcing the hallucination by pretending to see or hear it, and reduces stimulation. Antipsychotic medications reduce symptoms, must be taken consistently, and should not be stopped abruptly; the nurse watches for extrapyramidal side effects (tremor, rigidity, restlessness, acute dystonia) and for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (high fever, severe rigidity, altered mental status, unstable vital signs), which is a medical emergency. The nurse promotes safety, medication adherence, and connection to ongoing support.

title: Substance Use and Alcohol Withdrawal
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient withdrawing from alcohol — using a nonjudgmental approach, giving thiamine before glucose, treating with scheduled assessment and benzodiazepines, and watching for seizures and delirium tremens.

patient.name: Alcohol Withdrawal
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely supports a patient in alcohol withdrawal.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient withdrawing from alcohol using a calm, nonjudgmental approach, treating substance use disorder as a chronic, treatable disease. Early withdrawal (about 6 to 24 hours after the last drink) brings tremors, anxiety, nausea, sweating, and autonomic arousal such as a fast heart rate, high blood pressure, and a low-grade fever. Withdrawal seizures can occur roughly 12 to 48 hours out, and delirium tremens (DTs) typically appear at 48 to 72 hours or later with confusion, agitation, hallucinations, and dangerously unstable vital signs; DTs are a medical emergency that can be fatal. A standardized scale such as CIWA-Ar guides symptom-triggered dosing. Benzodiazepines (for example lorazepam or diazepam) are first-line to ease withdrawal and prevent seizures and are tapered as symptoms settle. Thiamine (vitamin B1) is given, and importantly before any glucose, to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy; folate and fluids are also provided. The nurse maintains seizure and fall precautions, provides a calm, quiet, well-lit environment, and reorients the patient frequently. Vital signs and mental status are monitored closely. As the patient stabilizes, the nurse reinforces hope, avoids shaming, and connects the patient to counseling, recovery programs, and ongoing support.

title: Bipolar Disorder and Mania
subtitle: The nurse cares for a manic patient — keeping them safe, lowering stimulation, setting firm limits, offering portable high-calorie foods, and monitoring lithium levels and toxicity.

patient.name: Bipolar Disorder / Mania
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely supports a patient in a manic episode.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient with bipolar disorder, a chronic but treatable mood disorder with swings between mania and depression. In a manic episode the patient shows an elevated or irritable mood, a decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, rapid or pressured speech, racing ideas, distractibility, and impulsive, risky behavior such as overspending or hypersexuality with poor judgment. Safety is the priority: the nurse sets firm, consistent limits, reduces environmental stimulation, provides structure, and protects the patient from harmful impulses. Because a manic patient is often too busy and distracted to sit and eat, the nurse offers portable, high-calorie, high-protein finger foods and fluids to prevent weight loss and dehydration, and promotes rest. Lithium is a common mood stabilizer with a narrow therapeutic range (about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L); the nurse monitors blood levels and watches for toxicity (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fine then coarse tremor, confusion, and ataxia), holding the dose and notifying the provider if toxicity is suspected. The patient is taught to keep sodium and fluid intake steady, since low sodium or dehydration raises the lithium level, and to avoid abrupt sodium or fluid changes. Lithium takes one to two weeks to work, so an antipsychotic or benzodiazepine may be used to manage acute mania in the meantime. The nurse supports adherence and follow-up.

Provide a calm, low-stimulation, structured environment
Offer portable high-calorie finger foods and fluids
Monitor lithium levels and assess for toxicity
Teach steady sodium and fluid intake and medication adherence

title: Major Depression and Antidepressants
subtitle: The nurse cares for a depressed patient — assessing suicide risk (highest as energy returns), spending time without false cheer, and teaching that antidepressants take weeks and have key safety rules.

patient.name: Major Depression
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with major depressive disorder.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient with major depressive disorder, a treatable illness marked by persistent low mood and loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) along with changes in sleep and appetite, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, and possible thoughts of death or suicide. The priority is safety: the nurse asks directly about suicidal thoughts and a plan, knowing that suicide risk is highest early in treatment as energy begins to return, because the patient may still feel hopeless but now has the energy to act. The nurse spends unhurried time with the patient, uses a calm and accepting manner, avoids false cheerfulness or telling the patient to simply 'snap out of it,' offers simple choices, and gently encourages small, achievable activities to rebuild a sense of success. Antidepressants such as SSRIs are first-line and take about two to four weeks or longer for full effect, so the patient is taught not to stop early and not to discontinue abruptly. The nurse watches for serotonin syndrome (agitation, high fever, tremor, sweating, and rapid heart rate), especially when serotonergic drugs are combined, and teaches patients on MAOIs to avoid tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured or smoked meats, and certain wines) to prevent a hypertensive crisis. The nurse supports medication adherence, therapy, and follow-up.

Increase observation as energy returns early in treatment
Spend time with the patient and avoid false reassurance
Teach that antidepressants take weeks and should not be stopped abruptly
Teach SSRI and MAOI safety, including tyramine avoidance

title: Eating Disorders: Anorexia and Bulimia
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient with an eating disorder — telling anorexia from bulimia, supervising meals, monitoring electrolytes and heart rhythm, and watching for refeeding syndrome.

patient.name: Eating Disorders
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with an eating disorder.

labs.v: Binge then purge; often normal weight.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient with an eating disorder. Anorexia nervosa is marked by food restriction, an intense fear of gaining weight, a very low body weight, and a distorted body image; medical effects include bradycardia, low blood pressure and temperature, amenorrhea, fine downy hair (lanugo), and electrolyte and bone problems. Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binge eating followed by purging (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, or excessive exercise), often at a near-normal weight, with signs such as dental enamel erosion, calluses on the knuckles (Russell's sign), and swollen parotid glands. Both disorders can cause dangerous electrolyte imbalances, especially low potassium from purging, which raises the risk of cardiac dysrhythmias, so the nurse monitors electrolytes and heart rhythm. Mealtimes are supervised: the nurse stays with the patient during meals and for about an hour afterward to discourage purging or hiding food, and weighs the patient consistently (same time, in a gown, after voiding) while watching for hidden weights or water-loading. A calm, firm, consistent approach with clear limits avoids power struggles over food. Care also addresses the underlying feelings, control issues, and body-image distortion through therapy and support, not just intake. When a severely malnourished patient is refed, the nurse watches for refeeding syndrome (dangerous drops in phosphate, potassium, and magnesium), advancing nutrition slowly with close monitoring.

Monitor electrolytes (especially potassium) and heart rhythm
Supervise meals and stay with the patient after eating
Weigh the patient consistently and watch for hidden weights
Advance nutrition slowly and monitor for refeeding syndrome

title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
subtitle: The nurse supports a patient with PTSD — building safety and trust, helping ground them during a flashback, identifying triggers, and avoiding anything that re-traumatizes.

patient.name: PTSD
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with post-traumatic stress disorder.

nursesNote: The nurse supports a patient with post-traumatic stress disorder, a reaction that can follow exposure to a traumatic event, with symptoms lasting more than a month. Core symptoms fall into groups: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares, and distressing memories that feel like reliving the event), avoidance (staying away from people, places, or reminders, with emotional numbing), negative changes in mood and thinking, and hyperarousal (hypervigilance, an exaggerated startle response, irritability, and poor sleep). The foundation of care is physical and emotional safety and trust: the nurse keeps the environment calm, predictable, and consistent, and explains actions before doing them. During a flashback the nurse stays calm, helps the patient ground to the here-and-now by orienting them (stating who and where they are, naming objects in the room) and guiding slow breathing, and reassures them they are safe. The nurse helps the patient identify personal triggers but does not force the patient to recount trauma details before they are ready, letting the patient lead. Sudden touch, approaching from behind, cornering, or loud, chaotic settings are avoided because they can re-traumatize. Effective treatment includes trauma-focused therapy (such as CBT or EMDR) and medications like SSRIs. The nurse also watches for co-occurring depression, substance use, and suicide risk, and connects the patient to ongoing support.

Maintain a calm, predictable environment and explain actions first
Help the patient ground to the present during flashbacks
Help identify triggers without forcing trauma disclosure
Refer to trauma-focused therapy and monitor for depression, SUD, and suicide risk

title: Personality Disorders
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient with a personality disorder — recognizing the clusters, setting consistent limits, keeping the team unified against splitting, and protecting against self-harm.

patient.name: Personality Disorders
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a patient with a personality disorder.

labs.v: Sees people as all good or all bad.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a patient with a personality disorder, an enduring, rigid, and maladaptive pattern of thinking and behaving that disrupts relationships and functioning. Disorders are grouped into three clusters: Cluster A is odd or eccentric (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal); Cluster B is dramatic, emotional, or erratic (borderline, antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic); and Cluster C is anxious or fearful (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive personality). Borderline personality disorder is high-yield: it features unstable mood, relationships, and self-image, an intense fear of abandonment, impulsivity, and recurrent self-harm or suicidal gestures, so assessing and protecting safety is a priority. A hallmark is splitting, viewing people as all good or all bad and pitting staff against each other; the team counters this by communicating and applying the same clear, firm, and consistent limits, so no one is idealized or devalued. The nurse stays matter-of-fact and non-defensive, does not take idealization or devaluation personally, avoids power struggles, and reinforces the patient's responsibility for behavior. Antisocial personality disorder involves manipulation, disregard for others, and a lack of remorse, requiring firm limits and consistent consequences. Care is long-term and largely therapy-based (such as dialectical behavior therapy for borderline), with medications used mainly for co-occurring symptoms; the nurse promotes consistency, safety, and connection to ongoing treatment.

Set clear, firm, consistent limits across the whole team
Communicate among staff to prevent splitting
Assess and protect against self-harm, especially in borderline PD
Stay matter-of-fact and reinforce the patient's responsibility

title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
subtitle: The nurse supports a patient with OCD — obsessions cause anxiety, compulsions (rituals) relieve it. Allow time for rituals at first, set gentle limits, and never punish.

patient.name: OCD
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with OCD.

nursesNote: OCD involves obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts that cause anxiety) and compulsions (rituals done to relieve that anxiety). Because rituals consume time, the nurse watches basic needs (skin from washing, eating, and rest), teaches other coping skills, and supports treatment with SSRIs and exposure (ERP) therapy.

title: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) Care
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient having ECT for severe depression. Ensure consent and NPO before; reorient and watch for confusion after.

patient.name: ECT
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient receiving ECT.

nursesNote: ECT sends a brief electrical current to trigger a short seizure under anesthesia, used for severe or treatment-resistant depression. title: Opioid Withdrawal and MAT
subtitle: The nurse supports a patient in opioid withdrawal — uncomfortable but rarely deadly. Use a nonjudgmental approach and treat with MAT (methadone, buprenorphine, clonidine).

patient.name: Opioid Withdrawal
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient in opioid withdrawal.

nursesNote: Opioid withdrawal is very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening, unlike alcohol withdrawal. Early signs are flu-like (anxiety, yawning, tearing, runny nose), followed by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, dilated pupils, sweating, and gooseflesh; the COWS scale rates severity. The nurse uses a calm, nonjudgmental approach, supports comfort and hydration, and gives medication-assisted treatment (methadone or buprenorphine; clonidine for autonomic symptoms). Naloxone reverses an opioid overdose.

Rate withdrawal severity (e.g., COWS) on a schedule
Support comfort, hydration, and rest
Give MAT as ordered: methadone, buprenorphine, or clonidine
Keep naloxone available for opioid overdose

title: Restraint and Seclusion Safety
subtitle: The nurse uses restraints only as a last resort for danger — needs a provider order, is time-limited, and requires close monitoring. Never for punishment or convenience.

patient.name: Restraint / Seclusion
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely manages restraint and seclusion.

nursesNote: Restraints and seclusion are a last resort, used only to prevent a patient from harming self or others after less restrictive measures (de-escalation, redirection) have failed. They require a provider order and are time-limited (about 4 hours for adults, shorter for children) and may never be used for punishment, staff convenience, or as a standing PRN order. The nurse uses the least restrictive effective type, monitors the patient frequently or continuously, and provides circulation, skin, toileting, hydration, and range-of-motion care. Quick-release knots are tied to the bed frame, and restraints are removed as soon as the patient meets release criteria.

Apply the least restrictive effective type
Monitor frequently and provide skin, circulation, and toileting care
Reassess and release as soon as criteria are met

title: Panic Disorder and Phobias
subtitle: The nurse helps a patient with panic attacks and phobias. Stay with the patient, use a calm voice and slow breathing; phobias improve with gradual exposure.

patient.name: Panic / Phobias
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with panic disorder or a phobia.

nursesNote: A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear with physical symptoms (palpitations, chest tightness, shortness of breath) that can mimic a heart attack and usually peaks within about 10 minutes. The nurse stays with the patient, uses a calm low voice with short directions, reduces stimulation, guides slow breathing, and reassures that they are safe. A phobia is an intense, persistent fear of a specific object or situation that leads to avoidance; it is treated with gradual exposure (desensitization), sometimes with SSRIs. The nurse teaches coping and relaxation skills once the patient is calmer.

Use a calm voice and reduce stimulation
Guide slow, deep breathing and reassure safety
Support gradual exposure for phobias
Teach coping and relaxation skills once calmer

title: Delirium vs. Dementia
subtitle: The nurse tells delirium (sudden, reversible) from dementia (gradual, chronic). Find and treat delirium's cause; keep both patients safe, oriented, and calm.

patient.name: Delirium / Dementia
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a patient with confusion.

nursesNote: Delirium is a sudden, fluctuating confusion that is usually reversible and signals an underlying problem (infection, medications, dehydration, low oxygen), so the nurse looks for and treats the cause. Dementia (such as Alzheimer's) is a gradual, chronic, progressive decline that is not reversible, with recent memory lost first. For both, the nurse keeps the patient safe (fall and wandering risk), uses simple, calm, one-step communication, reorients or redirects, and provides a consistent routine with low stimulation. Restraints and overstimulation are avoided; confusion that worsens in the evening (sundowning) is eased with light and reassurance.

Keep the patient safe from falls and wandering
Use simple, calm, one-step communication and reorient
Provide a consistent routine with low stimulation
Avoid restraints and overstimulation

title: Therapeutic Milieu
subtitle: The nurse maintains a therapeutic milieu — a safe, structured environment where the unit itself, daily routine, and group activities support healing.

patient.name: Therapeutic Milieu
patient.admitDate: The nurse maintains a therapeutic milieu.

nursesNote: A therapeutic milieu is a planned, structured environment in which the unit itself, the daily routine, and group activities all support healing, not just medications and individual therapy. Safety, both physical and emotional, is the top priority. The nurse provides a predictable routine with clear, consistent limits applied the same way by all staff, offers groups and activities to practice coping and social skills, and treats every interaction as therapeutic by role-modeling calm, respectful behavior. Patients share in decisions (community meetings) and are treated with dignity and respect. Consistency across the team builds trust and a sense of safety.
providerOrders: Maintain physical and emotional safety on the unit
Provide a predictable routine with consistent limits
Offer groups and activities to build coping and social skills
Treat every interaction as therapeutic and role-model behavior
Involve patients in their care and decisions

title: Crisis Intervention
subtitle: The nurse helps a patient in crisis — an acute, time-limited state when usual coping fails. Focus on safety, the here-and-now problem, and returning to baseline.

patient.name: Crisis Intervention
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient in crisis.

nursesNote: A crisis is an acute, time-limited state (usually resolving in about 4 to 6 weeks) that occurs when a person's usual coping is overwhelmed; anyone can experience one. Types include maturational (developmental changes like marriage or retirement), situational (external events like job loss or illness), and adventitious (disasters or violence). title: Postpartum Mood Disorders
subtitle: The nurse tells baby blues (mild, brief) from postpartum depression (needs treatment) and postpartum psychosis (an emergency with risk to mother and baby).

patient.name: Postpartum Mood Disorders
patient.admitDate: The nurse assesses a new mother's mood and safety.

nursesNote: The nurse distinguishes three postpartum mood states. Baby blues are mild mood swings and tearfulness starting days 2-3 that resolve within about two weeks and need only support and reassurance. Postpartum depression is deeper and lasts more than two weeks, with sadness, guilt, and trouble caring for self or baby; it needs treatment (therapy and often SSRIs) and bonding is assessed. Postpartum psychosis is rare but a psychiatric emergency, with delusions or hallucinations and a real risk of harm to the mother or infant, so the mother is never left alone with the baby and usually needs hospitalization. The nurse screens mood, asks directly about thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby, ensures safety, and refers for treatment.

title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
subtitle: The nurse supports a patient with GAD — chronic, excessive worry most days for 6+ months. Teach coping and relaxation; treat with therapy and SSRIs or buspirone.

patient.name: GAD
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with generalized anxiety disorder.

nursesNote: Generalized anxiety disorder is chronic, excessive worry occurring most days for at least six months that is hard to control and disrupts daily life, often with muscle tension, restlessness, fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, and sleep problems. The nurse builds trust, helps the patient name worries, and teaches coping and relaxation skills (slow breathing, exercise, limiting caffeine). First-line treatment is therapy (CBT) and SSRIs or SNRIs, which take a few weeks to work; buspirone is a non-addictive option that is taken daily (not PRN) and also has a slow onset. Benzodiazepines work fast but are addictive, so they are used only short-term.

Teach coping and relaxation skills and limit caffeine
Support therapy (CBT) and SSRIs/SNRIs or buspirone
Use benzodiazepines only short-term

title: Somatic Symptom and Conversion Disorders
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient with physical symptoms that have no medical cause. The symptoms are real to the patient — don't confront, but don't reinforce them.

patient.name: Somatic / Conversion
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with somatic symptom disorder.

vitals.temp: Confront or say 'it's in your head'

nursesNote: In somatic symptom disorder the patient has real, distressing physical symptoms along with excessive thoughts and anxiety about them; in conversion disorder there is a loss of function (such as paralysis, blindness, or pseudo-seizures) with no medical explanation, sometimes with surprising calm about the deficit (la belle indifference). These symptoms are not intentionally produced, unlike malingering (faking for external gain) or factitious disorder (faking for the sick role). The nurse first ensures a medical cause has been ruled out, then acknowledges that the symptoms feel real and never confronts the patient or says it is 'all in your head.' The nurse avoids reinforcing the symptoms with excessive attention or secondary gain, stays matter-of-fact, and gently redirects to feelings, stress, and coping skills.

Acknowledge the symptoms are real to the patient
Do not confront or say the symptoms are imagined
Avoid reinforcing symptoms or secondary gain

title: ADHD and Stimulant Therapy
subtitle: The nurse supports a child with ADHD — inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity. Give stimulants in the morning, after meals, and monitor growth, appetite, and sleep.

patient.name: ADHD
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a child with ADHD.

labs.v: Give in morning, not late afternoon.

nursesNote: ADHD is a childhood-onset disorder of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Stimulants such as methylphenidate or amphetamine are first-line and work well, but the nurse times them in the morning and not in the late afternoon to prevent insomnia, gives them after meals to reduce appetite loss, and monitors growth, weight, and appetite along with heart rate and blood pressure. A non-stimulant such as atomoxetine is an option. Behavioral care uses a consistent routine, clear and simple expectations, fewer distractions, short tasks broken into steps, and praise for success; the nurse teaches the family and supports a school plan.

title: Dissociative Disorders
subtitle: The nurse supports a patient who disconnects from memory, identity, or reality — often after trauma. Ensure safety, build trust, and use grounding.

patient.name: Dissociative Disorders
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with a dissociative disorder.

nursesNote: Dissociative disorders involve a disconnection from memory, identity, or reality, usually as a way of coping with past trauma or abuse. Dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important information, often around a traumatic event; dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identities with gaps in memory; and depersonalization/derealization is feeling detached from oneself or that surroundings are unreal. The nurse first ensures safety, since self-harm and suicide risk can be high, then builds trust with a calm, consistent, predictable approach. During an episode the nurse helps the patient ground to the here-and-now and does not force recall of traumatic memories, letting the patient lead. Care supports trauma-focused therapy over time.

Build trust with a calm, consistent approach
Use grounding to orient the patient during episodes
Do not force recall of traumatic memories
Support trauma-focused therapy over time

title: Therapeutic Relationship Phases
subtitle: The nurse uses the phases of the nurse-patient relationship — orientation, working, and termination — while keeping professional boundaries.

patient.name: Therapeutic Relationship
patient.admitDate: The nurse builds a therapeutic relationship.

nursesNote: The therapeutic nurse-patient relationship moves through phases. In pre-orientation the nurse gathers information and examines personal feelings before meeting the patient. In orientation the nurse builds trust and rapport, sets goals and boundaries, and explains confidentiality and its limits. In the working phase the nurse helps the patient identify and explore problems, express feelings, and make changes. In termination the nurse summarizes, evaluates whether goals were met, and prepares for the ending; planning for termination begins early and feelings of loss are addressed. Throughout, the nurse keeps clear professional boundaries: the relationship is goal-directed and patient-focused, not a friendship, with limited self-disclosure and no gifts or social contact, while staying aware of transference and countertransference.

Build trust and set goals and boundaries in orientation
Explore problems and promote change in the working phase
Summarize and plan for termination early
Maintain professional boundaries throughout

title: Autism Spectrum Disorder
subtitle: The nurse cares for a child with autism — keep routines consistent, use simple concrete communication, reduce sensory overload, and involve caregivers.

patient.name: Autism Spectrum
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a child with autism spectrum disorder.

nursesNote: Autism spectrum disorder is a developmental condition with deficits in social communication and interaction along with restricted, repetitive behaviors; it varies widely (a spectrum). A child may have delayed or atypical speech, poor eye contact, repetitive behaviors (stimming), fixed interests, a strong preference for routine and sameness, and sensory sensitivities. The nurse keeps routines consistent, prepares the child before any change, and uses simple, concrete, literal communication with visual aids. Reducing sensory overload (noise, lights) helps, and a familiar comfort item eases anxiety. The nurse ensures safety (wandering, self-injury), individualizes care, and works closely with caregivers who know the child best.

Use simple, concrete communication and visual aids
Reduce sensory overload (noise and bright lights)
Ensure safety from wandering and self-injury
Involve caregivers and individualize care

title: Oppositional Defiant and Conduct Disorder
subtitle: The nurse cares for a child with disruptive behavior — ODD is defiance toward authority; conduct disorder violates others' rights. Use firm, consistent limits.

patient.name: ODD / Conduct Disorder
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a child with disruptive behavior.

nursesNote: These are disruptive behavior disorders of childhood and adolescence. Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is a pattern of angry or irritable mood and argumentative, defiant behavior toward authority figures, sometimes with vindictiveness, but without seriously violating the basic rights of others. Conduct disorder is more serious and involves repeatedly violating the rights of others or major rules: aggression toward people or animals, destruction of property, deceit or theft, and serious rule-breaking; it can progress to antisocial personality disorder, so early help matters. The nurse uses firm, clear, consistent limits with predictable consequences and follows through (no empty threats), reinforces positive behavior with praise and behavior contracts, maintains a structured routine, watches for aggression to protect safety, and supports therapy and parent training.

Apply predictable consequences and follow through
Reinforce positive behavior with praise and contracts
Maintain safety and watch for aggression
Support therapy and parent training

title: Antipsychotic Medication Safety
subtitle: The nurse gives antipsychotics and watches for side effects — EPS, tardive dyskinesia, metabolic changes, and the emergency of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

patient.name: Antipsychotics
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely administers antipsychotic medication.

nursesNote: Antipsychotics treat psychosis and schizophrenia. Typical agents (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) cause more extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): acute dystonia (sudden muscle spasm needing benztropine or diphenhydramine right away), akathisia (inner restlessness), and pseudoparkinsonism (tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait). Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect of involuntary face and tongue movements that may be permanent, so the nurse watches for early signs. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (high fever, severe rigidity, altered mental status, unstable vital signs) is a medical emergency: stop the drug and get help. Atypical agents (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine) cause more metabolic effects (weight gain, high glucose and lipids), so the nurse monitors weight and labs. Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, requiring regular WBC/ANC monitoring. Antipsychotics take weeks to work fully and should not be stopped abruptly.
providerOrders: Assess for EPS, including acute dystonia and akathisia
Watch for tardive dyskinesia and report early signs
Treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome as an emergency: stop the drug
Monitor weight, glucose, and lipids on atypicals
Monitor WBC/ANC for patients on clozapine

title: Mood Stabilizers (Non-Lithium)
subtitle: The nurse manages anticonvulsant mood stabilizers for bipolar — valproate (liver), carbamazepine (blood counts), and lamotrigine (serious rash).

patient.name: Mood Stabilizers
patient.admitDate: The nurse manages non-lithium mood stabilizers.

nursesNote: Several anticonvulsants are used as mood stabilizers in bipolar disorder when lithium is not ideal. Valproate (divalproex/valproic acid) can be hepatotoxic and lower platelets, so the nurse monitors liver function, platelet counts, and drug levels. Carbamazepine can suppress blood cell counts (agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia) and cause a severe rash, so the nurse monitors the CBC and watches for rash. Lamotrigine carries a risk of a serious rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), so it is titrated slowly and any rash is reported immediately. For all of these, the patient takes the drug daily and does not stop abruptly, has regular labs, and is counseled that these drugs are teratogenic. The nurse teaches the patient to report any rash, easy bruising or bleeding, yellowing of the skin, or fever.

Monitor the CBC on carbamazepine
Report any rash immediately on lamotrigine and titrate slowly
Teach daily adherence and not stopping abruptly
Counsel about teratogenic risk and report rash, bruising, or jaundice

title: Insomnia and Sleep Hygiene
subtitle: The nurse helps a patient with insomnia — teach sleep hygiene first, treat causes, and use sleep medications short-term and cautiously.

patient.name: Insomnia
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports a patient with insomnia.

nursesNote: Insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep that causes daytime tiredness and poor function. The nurse first looks for and treats causes such as anxiety, depression, pain, caffeine, or medications. Sleep hygiene is the first-line treatment: a consistent sleep and wake schedule, using the bed only for sleep (and getting up if not sleepy), limiting caffeine, alcohol, and screens in the evening, a relaxing wind-down routine in a dark, quiet room, daytime exercise (not late), and avoiding long naps. Sleep medications are used short-term at the lowest effective dose because of dependence and next-day sedation; the nurse uses fall precautions, especially in older adults.
providerOrders: Assess and treat causes of insomnia
Teach sleep hygiene as the first-line approach
Encourage a consistent sleep and wake schedule
Limit caffeine, alcohol, screens, and long naps
Use sleep medication short-term with fall precautions

title: Group Therapy
subtitle: The nurse co-leads a therapy group — set clear norms, encourage participation, manage members who monopolize or stay silent, and protect confidentiality.

patient.name: Group Therapy
patient.admitDate: The nurse co-leads a therapy group.

vitals.temp: Respect; one speaks at a time

labs.v: Guide, keep on task, ensure safety.

nursesNote: In group therapy several members meet with a leader to work on shared concerns. Benefits (therapeutic factors) include universality (realizing one is not alone), instillation of hope (seeing others improve), altruism (helping fellow members), sharing information, catharsis, and cohesion (belonging). The leader sets clear norms early (respect, one person speaks at a time, confidentiality that stays within the group), keeps the group on task, encourages participation, and ensures safety. The nurse gently redirects a member who monopolizes so others can share, and invites a silent member to contribute without forcing them. Confidentiality and a supportive, nonjudgmental atmosphere build the trust that makes the group work.
providerOrders: Set clear group norms and confidentiality early
Encourage participation from all members
Gently redirect a member who monopolizes
Invite quiet members without forcing them
Keep the group on task and maintain safety

title: Intellectual Disability Care
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient with an intellectual disability — communicate at their level, promote independence, keep routines, and treat them with age-appropriate respect.

patient.name: Intellectual Disability
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a patient with an intellectual disability.

nursesNote: Intellectual disability involves deficits in intellectual functioning and adaptive (everyday) skills that begin in childhood and range from mild to profound. The nurse communicates at the person's developmental level using simple, concrete, one-step instructions and demonstrations, and promotes maximum independence by encouraging the activities of daily living the person can do rather than over-helping. Tasks are broken into small steps with repetition and praise. A consistent routine reduces confusion, the environment is adapted for safety with supervision as needed, and the person is treated with age-appropriate dignity (not talked to as a young child if they are an adult). The nurse positively reinforces effort and success and works with caregivers, who know the patient best, to plan care.

Keep a consistent routine and adapt the environment for safety

title: Anger and Aggression Management
subtitle: The nurse helps a patient handle anger — a normal feeling — in healthy, assertive ways, spotting escalation early and teaching coping before it becomes aggression.

patient.name: Anger / Aggression
patient.admitDate: The nurse helps a patient manage anger.

nursesNote: Anger is a normal emotion; the problem is aggression, the harmful expression of anger through words or actions. The goal is to help the patient express anger in a healthy, assertive way (respectful 'I' statements) rather than aggressively or passively. The nurse recognizes early escalation cues (pacing, a louder voice, clenched fists, a tense posture) and intervenes early with a calm voice, respect for personal space, and offered choices, while encouraging the patient to name and talk through feelings before acting out. Teaching focuses on identifying triggers and using coping skills such as taking a time-out, physical activity, and relaxation. The nurse sets clear limits on behavior (not on the feeling itself) and protects safety, using medication or restraint only as a last resort.
