Intervene early with a calm voice and offered choices
Encourage the patient to verbalize feelings
Teach triggers and coping skills (time-out, activity, relaxation)
Set clear limits on behavior and ensure safety

title: Antihypertensive Therapy
subtitle: The nurse manages blood pressure medications — beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and calcium channel blockers. Watch for low pulse, dry cough, and orthostatic dizziness.

patient.name: Antihypertensives
patient.admitDate: The nurse safely manages antihypertensive therapy.

labs.v: Hold if HR < 60 or low BP.

nursesNote: Antihypertensives lower blood pressure to prevent complications. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) lower heart rate and blood pressure, so the nurse checks the apical pulse and blood pressure first and holds the dose for a pulse under 60 or low blood pressure; they are not stopped abruptly (rebound) and can mask low-blood-sugar signs. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril) can cause a dry cough and raise potassium; facial or throat swelling (angioedema) is an emergency requiring the drug to be stopped. ARBs (losartan) are similar with less cough. Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) can cause ankle edema, and grapefruit juice is avoided. For all of these, the patient rises slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness, keeps taking the medication even when feeling well, and monitors blood pressure at home.

Do not stop beta-blockers abruptly
Monitor for ACE inhibitor dry cough and high potassium
Treat angioedema as an emergency and stop the drug
Teach rising slowly and continued adherence with home BP checks

title: Fire Safety: RACE and PASS
subtitle: The nurse responds to a fire using RACE — Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish/Evacuate — and uses an extinguisher with PASS.

patient.name: Fire Safety
patient.admitDate: The nurse responds safely to a fire.

nursesNote: In a fire the nurse follows RACE in order: Rescue anyone in immediate danger first, sound the Alarm (pull the alarm and call the code), Confine the fire by closing doors and windows, and then Extinguish a small fire or Evacuate. Oxygen sources are turned off because oxygen fuels fire, and patients on oxygen are protected. During evacuation, ambulatory patients are moved first, then those needing more help, using stairs rather than elevators. To use a fire extinguisher the nurse uses PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep side to side. Exits are kept clear and staff know the fire plan ahead of time.

Rescue patients in immediate danger first
Turn off oxygen sources and protect oxygen-dependent patients

Use PASS to operate a fire extinguisher

title: Growth and Development Milestones
subtitle: The nurse uses developmental milestones to assess a child and teach age-appropriate safety, knowing some variation is normal.

patient.name: Development
patient.admitDate: The nurse assesses a child's development.

labs.v: First steps, says a few words.

nursesNote: The nurse uses developmental milestones to assess a child's progress, knowing some variation is normal. By about 2 months an infant has a social smile and lifts the head; by 6 months rolls over and sits with support; by 9 months sits alone, crawls, and develops a pincer grasp with stranger anxiety; by 12 months takes first steps and says a few words; by 2 years runs and uses 2-word phrases with parallel play; by 3 years rides a tricycle and speaks in short sentences; and by 4-5 years hops or skips, draws, and dresses. The nurse tracks milestones over time and refers for evaluation if a child loses skills or misses major milestones. Safety teaching is matched to age and skills: choking and aspiration risks in infants, falls and poisoning in mobile toddlers, and age-appropriate car seats throughout.

title: Dysthymia and Seasonal Affective Disorder
subtitle: The nurse supports chronic low-grade depression (dysthymia) and seasonal depression (SAD) — still assess suicide risk, and teach light therapy for SAD.

patient.name: Dysthymia / SAD

nursesNote: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is a chronic, milder depression with a low mood most days for at least two years; the person usually keeps functioning but feels persistently down. Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is depression in a seasonal pattern, usually fall and winter, with fatigue, oversleeping, carbohydrate craving, and weight gain. title: Medication Adherence and Relapse Prevention
subtitle: The nurse helps a patient stay on psychiatric medication — the main way to prevent relapse. Address barriers and teach early warning signs.

patient.name: Adherence / Relapse
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports medication adherence and relapse prevention.

nursesNote: Staying on prescribed psychiatric medication is the main way to prevent relapse and rehospitalization, so the nurse teaches the patient not to stop the medication even when feeling better, because the medication is what keeps symptoms away. The nurse addresses common barriers to adherence: bothersome side effects, cost, poor insight or denial of illness, complex regimens, and substance use. Strategies include simplifying the regimen, considering a long-acting injectable (depot) form, managing side effects rather than ignoring them, and building trust. The nurse teaches the patient and family to recognize early warning signs of relapse (changes in sleep, social withdrawal, stopping medication, or returning symptoms) and to follow a relapse plan that includes who to call. Family support and consistent follow-up reinforce adherence.

title: Behavior Modification and Token Economy
subtitle: The nurse uses behavior modification — reinforcing wanted behavior and not rewarding unwanted behavior — with consistency. A token economy rewards target behaviors.

patient.name: Behavior Modification
patient.admitDate: The nurse uses behavior modification techniques.

nursesNote: Behavior modification changes behavior through its consequences (operant conditioning). Positive reinforcement adds a reward (praise, a token) to increase a wanted behavior, and negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant stimulus to increase a behavior. Punishment adds a consequence to reduce a behavior, while extinction withholds the usual reward to decrease a behavior (for example, not giving attention to attention-seeking acts). A token economy lets patients earn tokens for clearly defined target behaviors that can be exchanged for privileges. Success depends on clear expectations, consistency across all staff, immediate reinforcement, and a focus on rewarding positive behavior rather than power struggles. The nurse individualizes the plan and reinforces progress.

title: Family Therapy and Dynamics
subtitle: The nurse supports family therapy — treating the family as a unit, staying neutral, and improving communication and boundaries.

patient.name: Family Therapy
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports family therapy.

nursesNote: Family therapy treats the family as a system, viewing a member's problem in the context of how the family functions. Goals include improving communication, clarifying roles, resolving conflict, and setting healthy boundaries. The nurse or therapist stays neutral, does not take sides, and encourages every member to speak so patterns become clear. Unhealthy patterns include enmeshment (over-involvement with blurred boundaries), disengagement (too much distance), scapegoating (blaming one member for the family's problems), and triangulation (pulling in a third person to avoid direct conflict). Families often resist change (homeostasis), which is expected. The nurse supports open, respectful communication and healthier roles and boundaries.

Identify unhealthy patterns like scapegoating and triangulation

title: Abuse and Intimate Partner Violence
subtitle: The nurse cares for a possible abuse survivor — ensure safety, interview privately, stay nonjudgmental, document objectively, and report when required.

patient.name: Abuse / IPV
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a possible abuse survivor.

nursesNote: The nurse cares for a possible abuse survivor (physical, emotional, sexual, neglect, or financial). Red flags include injuries that do not match the story, injuries in various stages of healing, delayed care, and a partner who answers for the patient or refuses to leave the room. Safety comes first. The nurse interviews the patient privately and alone (without the suspected abuser), stays nonjudgmental, believes and validates the patient, and documents objectively using the patient's exact words and photos when appropriate, since records may become evidence. Abuse of children and of elders or vulnerable adults must be reported (mandatory reporting). For a competent adult experiencing intimate partner violence, the nurse respects the person's autonomy and cannot force them to leave, but provides a safety plan and resources such as a hotline. The nurse offers help without pressuring and ensures follow-up.

nursesNote: Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone in hypothyroidism. The nurse teaches the patient to take it on an empty stomach in the morning at the same time daily, separate from calcium, iron, and antacids that reduce absorption, and to continue it lifelong without stopping; it takes weeks for full effect. Signs of too much (tachycardia, weight loss, nervousness, insomnia) should be reported, especially chest pain or palpitations, while too little causes fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. Antithyroid drugs (methimazole, PTU) treat hyperthyroidism by lowering hormone production and also take weeks to work; the major risk is agranulocytosis, so the patient reports a sore throat or fever right away. The nurse monitors TSH and symptoms to guide dosing.

title: Cultural and Spiritual Care
subtitle: The nurse provides culturally and spiritually sensitive psychiatric care — assess beliefs, stay nonjudgmental, use interpreters, and tell cultural beliefs from symptoms.

patient.name: Cultural / Spiritual Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse provides culturally sensitive care.

nursesNote: The nurse provides culturally and spiritually sensitive psychiatric care. The nurse assesses the patient's beliefs and practices rather than assuming, individualizes care, and avoids stereotyping. A nonjudgmental approach that does not impose the nurse's own values is essential, along with respecting dietary needs, prayer, rituals, and modesty. A professional interpreter is used for language barriers, not family members or children. Importantly, the nurse distinguishes culturally normal beliefs or spiritual experiences from psychiatric symptoms, since what is normal in one culture (for example, certain spiritual practices or beliefs) is not a delusion; the nurse clarifies with the patient and family when unsure. Spiritual support such as a chaplain is offered when the patient wishes. The nurse stays self-aware of personal biases and treats every patient with dignity to build trust.

title: Coping and Stress Management
subtitle: The nurse helps a patient manage stress — assess stressors and coping, teach healthy coping skills, and replace maladaptive ones.

patient.name: Coping / Stress
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports stress management.

nursesNote: Stress is the body and mind's response to demands; some stress is normal, and coping is how a person manages it. The nurse assesses the patient's stressors and current coping. Adaptive (healthy) coping includes problem-solving, exercise, relaxation and deep breathing, mindfulness, talking with support, and time management. Maladaptive coping such as substance use, avoidance, denial, aggression, isolation, or overeating may relieve stress briefly but is harmful over time. The nurse teaches and helps the patient practice healthy coping skills, encourages social support, and works to replace maladaptive patterns with adaptive ones. Care is individualized, and the patient is supported in building skills they can use long-term.

title: Discharge Planning and Community Resources

patient.admitDate: The nurse plans a safe psychiatric discharge.

nursesNote: Discharge planning for a psychiatric patient begins at admission to ensure a smooth, safe transition. The nurse confirms a clear medication plan and how the patient will obtain medications, sets up outpatient follow-up appointments, and connects the patient to community resources such as case management (or an assertive community treatment team for severe illness), support and peer groups, and step-down levels of care like partial hospitalization (PHP) or intensive outpatient (IOP). title: Milieu Safety: Observation and Contraband
subtitle: The nurse keeps the psychiatric unit safe — using the right observation level, removing contraband, and documenting safety checks.

patient.name: Milieu Safety
patient.admitDate: The nurse maintains psychiatric unit safety.

nursesNote: The nurse keeps the psychiatric milieu safe by matching the observation level to the patient's risk: routine checks for low risk, close observation (often every 15 minutes) for higher risk, and one-to-one constant observation at arm's length for the highest risk (such as active suicidal ideation), keeping the patient in view even in the bathroom and never leaving them alone. Contraband that could be used for self-harm is removed: sharps, glass, cords, belts, shoelaces, lighters, and outside medications or substances. Belongings are searched on admission per policy, and items brought by visitors are monitored. Environmental safety includes ligature-resistant fixtures and counting sharps and utensils. The nurse documents all safety checks for accountability and adjusts the observation level as the patient's risk changes.

title: Reminiscence and Validation Therapy
subtitle: The nurse uses reminiscence (recalling past memories) and validation (accepting the person's feelings and reality) — helpful for older adults and dementia.

patient.name: Reminiscence / Validation
patient.admitDate: The nurse uses reminiscence and validation therapy.

nursesNote: Reminiscence therapy encourages a person to recall and share past memories (life review) and can lift mood, strengthen identity, and build connection, especially in older adults; the nurse uses photos, music, familiar objects, and open-ended prompts. Validation therapy is used with people who have dementia: instead of arguing, correcting, or forcing reality (reality orientation), the nurse acknowledges the person's feelings and their experienced reality and responds to the emotion behind the words, which reduces agitation and distress. Reality orientation is more helpful in delirium or early confusion but can increase distress in advanced dementia. The nurse uses a calm, patient, empathetic, nonjudgmental approach and individualizes the technique using the person's life history.

nursesNote: Relaxation techniques lower physiologic arousal and help with anxiety, stress, pain, and insomnia. Deep diaphragmatic breathing uses slow, deep breaths to calm the body. Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) tenses then releases muscle groups to release tension. Guided imagery has the patient picture a peaceful, calming scene, and mindfulness focuses attention on the present moment. The nurse teaches in a quiet, comfortable setting and has the patient practice regularly so the skill is ready when needed. These skills are best learned when the patient is calm or only mildly anxious, not in the middle of a panic attack. They are safe, nondrug, low-risk options used alongside other care.

title: Sexual Assault Survivor Care
subtitle: The nurse cares for a sexual assault survivor — ensure safety, stay nonjudgmental, preserve evidence, and respect the survivor's choices.

patient.name: Sexual Assault Care
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a sexual assault survivor.

nursesNote: The nurse provides trauma-informed care to a sexual assault survivor, who may show acute disorganization (shock, fear, guilt, numbness) followed later by a reorganization phase. Safety and emotional support come first: the nurse stays with the survivor, provides a calm private space, believes them, and never blames. Evidence is preserved when possible by advising the survivor not to bathe, shower, change clothes, eat, drink, or urinate before the exam, and a forensic (SANE) exam is done only with consent, maintaining chain of custody. The survivor consents to each step, which helps restore a sense of control. For a competent adult, the decision to report to police is the survivor's choice and the nurse respects that autonomy. The nurse offers STI prophylaxis and emergency contraception, connects the survivor to an advocate, counseling, and follow-up, and does not pressure them.

Stay nonjudgmental; believe and never blame the survivor
Preserve evidence: advise not to bathe, change, or eat before the exam
Obtain consent for a forensic (SANE) exam and each step
Respect the survivor's choice about reporting and offer resources

title: Self-Esteem and Body-Image Disturbance
subtitle: The nurse supports a patient with low self-esteem or a changed body image — encourage expressing feelings, give genuine feedback, and rebuild confidence.

patient.name: Self-Esteem / Body Image
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports self-esteem and body image.

labs.v: Look at/care for the change slowly.

nursesNote: Low self-esteem and disturbed body image can follow surgery (such as mastectomy, amputation, or an ostomy), chronic illness, eating disorders, or depression. Signs include negative self-talk, social withdrawal, avoiding looking at or touching a changed body part, and refusing to take part in care. The nurse builds a trusting relationship, accepts the patient's feelings, and encourages the patient to express feelings and grieve the change. The patient is gently encouraged to look at and care for the changed body part at their own pace. Feedback should be genuine and specific rather than false praise, which the patient will not believe. The nurse sets realistic, achievable goals to build success, focuses on the patient's strengths and abilities, promotes independence, involves the patient in care and decisions, and connects them to support groups.
providerOrders: Build trust and accept the patient's feelings
Encourage expression of feelings and grieving
Encourage gradual viewing and care of the changed body part
Give genuine, specific feedback (not false praise)
Set realistic goals and focus on strengths

title: Assertiveness Training
subtitle: The nurse teaches assertive communication — expressing needs directly and respectfully with 'I' statements, instead of passive, aggressive, or passive-aggressive styles.

patient.name: Assertiveness Training
patient.admitDate: The nurse teaches assertive communication.

nursesNote: Assertiveness training helps a patient express needs and feelings directly and respectfully while honoring both their own and others' rights, which is the healthiest communication style. It contrasts with passive communication (suppressing one's needs and avoiding conflict), aggressive communication (hostile, blaming, 'you' statements that violate others' rights), and passive-aggressive communication (indirect resistance, sarcasm, or the silent treatment). The nurse teaches 'I' statements (for example, 'I feel ___ when ___, and I need ___'), calm tone, eye contact, confident posture, and how to set boundaries and say no respectfully. The nurse uses role-play and practice to build the skill. Assertive communication lowers conflict and stress and improves relationships and self-esteem.

Model and teach 'I' statements
Encourage calm tone, eye contact, and confident posture
Practice setting boundaries and saying no respectfully
Use role-play to build the skill

title: Motivational Interviewing
subtitle: The nurse uses motivational interviewing to support change — collaborative and nonjudgmental, drawing out the patient's own reasons rather than lecturing.

patient.name: Motivational Interviewing
patient.admitDate: The nurse uses motivational interviewing.

nursesNote: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative, patient-centered way to strengthen a person's own motivation and commitment to change, useful in substance use and other behavior change. The nurse expresses empathy nonjudgmentally, helps the patient see the discrepancy between current behavior and their own goals, rolls with resistance instead of arguing or confronting, and supports self-efficacy (the belief they can change). Core skills are OARS: Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, and Summarizing. The nurse draws out the patient's own reasons for change (change talk) rather than lecturing or jumping in to fix the problem (the 'righting reflex'). The patient's autonomy is respected: the patient decides, and the nurse guides without forcing. This approach lowers defensiveness and increases readiness to change.

Express empathy and support self-efficacy
Help the patient see discrepancy with their own goals
Roll with resistance; do not argue or lecture
Use OARS and draw out the patient's own reasons to change

title: Stages of Change
subtitle: The nurse matches support to the patient's stage of change — precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance.

patient.name: Stages of Change
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports behavior change by stage.

labs.v: Fit the intervention to the stage.

nursesNote: The transtheoretical model describes behavior change in stages, and the nurse matches support to the patient's current stage. In precontemplation the patient is not yet considering change, so the nurse raises awareness gently without pushing. In contemplation the patient is ambivalent and weighing it, so the nurse explores pros and cons. In preparation the patient is getting ready and planning, so the nurse helps set realistic goals and a plan. In action the patient is actively changing, so the nurse provides support and reinforcement. In maintenance the patient is sustaining the change, so the nurse focuses on preventing relapse. Relapse can occur and is treated as a normal part of change, not a failure: the patient is encouraged to resume without shame. The key principle is to meet the patient where they are and not force action before they are ready.
providerOrders: Assess the patient's current stage of change
Match the intervention to the stage
Avoid pushing action before the patient is ready
Support and reinforce the action stage
Treat relapse as normal and help the patient resume

subtitle: The nurse supports families of patients with mental illness — educate about the illness, reduce blame, connect to resources, and address caregiver burnout.

patient.name: Caregiver Support
patient.admitDate: The nurse supports the patient's family and caregivers.

labs.v: Mental illness affects the whole family.

nursesNote: Mental illness affects the whole family, who often experience stress, grief, and caregiver burden. With the patient's consent (respecting confidentiality), the nurse educates the family about the illness and treatment, teaches how to communicate and respond to symptoms calmly and supportively, and teaches the warning signs of relapse so they can act early. The nurse reduces stigma and blame, reassuring the family that the illness is not their fault. Families are connected to support groups (such as NAMI), respite care, and community resources, and are involved in the care and discharge plan. The nurse assesses for caregiver burden and burnout (stress, exhaustion, isolation) and encourages caregiver self-care so support is sustainable.

Teach how to respond to symptoms and warning signs of relapse
Reduce stigma and reassure the family it is not their fault
Connect to support groups, respite, and resources
Assess caregiver burden and encourage self-care

title: Communicating During Hallucinations
subtitle: The nurse talks with a patient who is hallucinating — acknowledge their experience without reinforcing it, present reality calmly, and check for command hallucinations.

patient.name: Hallucination Communication
patient.admitDate: The nurse communicates with a hallucinating patient.

labs.v: Validate the feeling, not the content.
Don't act like you hear it.
'I don't hear it, but you seem scared.'

nursesNote: When a patient is hallucinating (a false sensory experience, most often hearing voices), the nurse first asks what the voices are saying to assess for command hallucinations that tell the patient to harm self or others, which is a safety priority. The nurse acknowledges the patient's experience and the feelings behind it (the experience is real to them) without reinforcing the hallucination: the nurse does not pretend to see or hear it and does not argue about whether it is real, since both increase distress. Reality is presented calmly and simply, for example, 'I don't hear any voices, but I can see you feel frightened.' The nurse reduces environmental stimulation, speaks in short, calm sentences, and redirects the patient to reality-based activities or conversation. Escalating distress is monitored and the nurse stays with the patient as needed.

Acknowledge the patient's feelings without reinforcing the hallucination
Do not pretend to see or hear it, and do not argue
Calmly present reality in simple terms
Reduce stimulation and redirect to reality-based activity

title: Physical Health in Mental Illness
subtitle: The nurse protects the physical health of psychiatric patients — monitor metabolic effects, ensure screenings, and never blame all symptoms on mental illness.

patient.name: Physical Health / SMI
patient.admitDate: The nurse coordinates physical health care.

labs.v: SMI = more physical illness, shorter life.
Blaming all symptoms on mental illness.

nursesNote: Patients with serious mental illness have higher rates of physical illness and a shorter lifespan, due to medication side effects, poor access to care, lifestyle factors, and neglected health. The nurse monitors metabolic effects (weight, glucose, lipids, blood pressure), especially on antipsychotics, and ensures routine screenings, vaccines, and dental care are not skipped. Smoking cessation, healthy nutrition, and activity are encouraged. A critical risk is diagnostic overshadowing, wrongly attributing physical symptoms to the patient's mental illness; the nurse takes physical complaints seriously and investigates them rather than dismissing them. The nurse coordinates with primary and medical care for whole-person treatment and advocates so the patient receives the same quality of physical care as anyone else.
providerOrders: Monitor metabolic effects (weight, glucose, lipids, BP)
Ensure routine screenings, vaccines, and dental care
Encourage smoking cessation, nutrition, and activity
Take physical complaints seriously (avoid diagnostic overshadowing)
Coordinate with primary and medical care

title: Oral Antidiabetic Medications
subtitle: The nurse manages non-insulin diabetes drugs — metformin (first-line, hold before contrast) and sulfonylureas (can cause hypoglycemia).

patient.name: Oral Antidiabetics
patient.admitDate: The nurse manages oral antidiabetic medications.

nursesNote: Metformin is the first-line oral drug for type 2 diabetes; it lowers glucose production and does not cause hypoglycemia by itself, but can cause GI upset (take with food) and must be held before and after iodinated contrast dye because of the risk of lactic acidosis and kidney injury. Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide) stimulate insulin release and CAN cause hypoglycemia, so the patient should not skip meals and should recognize low-blood-sugar signs (shaky, sweaty, confused, fast heart rate) and treat with a fast-acting carbohydrate. Other agents include GLP-1 agonists (names ending in -tide; weight loss, GI effects) and SGLT2 inhibitors (ending in -flozin; spill glucose in urine, raising UTI and genital infection risk). Lifestyle (diet, activity, weight) remains core therapy, and the nurse monitors blood glucose and A1C.
providerOrders: Give metformin with food and hold it before contrast dye
Monitor for hypoglycemia with sulfonylureas
Teach not to skip meals and to recognize low-blood-sugar signs
Watch for UTI/genital infection with SGLT2 inhibitors
Monitor blood glucose and A1C

title: Psychiatric Patient Rights
subtitle: The nurse protects the rights of psychiatric patients — voluntary vs involuntary admission, the right to refuse treatment, least restrictive care, and duty to warn.

patient.name: Patient Rights
patient.admitDate: The nurse protects psychiatric patient rights.

nursesNote: The nurse protects psychiatric patients' rights. Voluntary patients admit themselves and may request discharge (though a brief evaluation may delay release if they become a danger). Involuntary (committed) patients are admitted against their will because they are a danger to self or others or are gravely disabled. Importantly, committed patients keep their rights, including dignity, communication, confidentiality, informed consent, and usually the right to refuse medication, unless there is an emergency or a court order. Care uses the least restrictive option, with seclusion or restraint only as a last resort. Confidentiality is protected, with a key exception: the duty to warn an identifiable person whom the patient has seriously threatened. In an emergency, the nurse may treat to prevent imminent harm and then document. The nurse advocates for patients and reports any rights violations.
providerOrders: Distinguish voluntary from involuntary status
Ensure committed patients keep their rights
Honor the right to refuse treatment unless an emergency or court order applies
Use the least restrictive care option
Maintain confidentiality but follow the duty to warn

title: Mental Status Examination
subtitle: The nurse performs a mental status exam — appearance, behavior, mood and affect, thought, perception, cognition, insight, and judgment.

patient.name: Mental Status Exam
patient.admitDate: The nurse performs a mental status exam.

nursesNote: The mental status examination is an objective snapshot of a patient's current mental state. The nurse assesses appearance (grooming, hygiene, dress), behavior (motor activity, eye contact), and speech (rate, volume, amount, such as pressured or poverty of speech). Mood is what the patient reports feeling, while affect is the emotion the nurse observes; the two may not match. Thought process is how thoughts flow (for example tangential or flight of ideas), and thought content includes delusions and suicidal or homicidal ideation, which the nurse assesses directly for safety. Perception covers hallucinations and illusions. Cognition includes orientation, memory, and attention. Insight is the patient's awareness of their illness, and judgment is their ability to make sound decisions. The nurse documents findings objectively and uses them to guide safety and the plan of care.
providerOrders: Assess appearance, behavior, and speech
Distinguish mood (reported) from affect (observed)
Assess thought content for suicidal/homicidal ideation and delusions
Assess perception, cognition, insight, and judgment
Document findings objectively and act on safety risks

title: Psychiatric Medication Emergencies
subtitle: The nurse recognizes psych-med emergencies — neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, and MAOI hypertensive crisis. Stop the drug and get help.

patient.name: Psych Med Emergencies
patient.admitDate: The nurse recognizes psychiatric medication emergencies.

labs.v: High fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered LOC.

nursesNote: Several psychiatric medications can cause emergencies the nurse must recognize fast. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) comes from antipsychotics: high fever, severe 'lead-pipe' rigidity, altered consciousness, and unstable vital signs, developing over days. Serotonin syndrome comes from serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, especially combined): agitation, high fever, tremor, hyperreflexia or clonus, and sweating, with a rapid onset. Lithium toxicity (narrow therapeutic range) causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, a coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion, often triggered by low sodium or dehydration. MAOI hypertensive crisis follows eating tyramine-rich foods: severe high blood pressure and a pounding headache. Anticholinergic toxicity causes hot, dry, red skin, confusion, and urinary retention. In any of these the nurse stops the offending drug, calls for help, supports the airway and vital signs, provides cooling and fluids as needed, and monitors closely; prevention includes monitoring levels and teaching diet and early warning signs.
providerOrders: Recognize NMS, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, and MAOI crisis
Stop the offending medication immediately
Call for help and support airway and vital signs
Provide cooling and fluids as needed
Prevent by monitoring levels and teaching diet/early signs

title: Care After a Suicide Attempt
subtitle: The nurse cares for a patient after a suicide attempt — risk stays high, so keep close observation, stay nonjudgmental, and assess ongoing risk.

patient.name: Post-Suicide Attempt
patient.admitDate: The nurse cares for a patient after a suicide attempt.

labs.v: A past attempt is a top risk factor.

nursesNote: After a suicide attempt the patient's risk stays high, since a prior attempt is one of the strongest predictors of future suicide. The nurse maintains close or one-to-one observation, never leaves the patient alone, and keeps the environment free of dangerous items. The approach is calm and nonjudgmental, without anger or shame, and the nurse does not minimize the attempt as merely 'a cry for help.' The nurse directly assesses current suicidal ideation, plan, and intent, and stays alert for a sudden, unexplained calm, which can signal that a decision to act has been made. Care addresses the underlying problem (such as depression or substance use) with medication and therapy, involves family and support, and builds a safety plan with follow-up. No-harm contracts are not reliable safeguards and do not replace observation and a safe environment.
providerOrders: Maintain close or one-to-one observation; never leave alone
Keep the environment free of dangerous items
Use a nonjudgmental approach and do not minimize the attempt
Assess ongoing ideation, plan, and intent
Treat the underlying cause and build a safety plan

title: Developmental Disabilities — Core Care & Behavior (Set 1)
subtitle: Autism, Down syndrome, seizures, communication & positive behavior support
scenario: Care of clients with intellectual and developmental disabilities: communication, safety, behavior support, and recognizing unmet physical needs.

steps.q: A client with autism spectrum disorder becomes highly distressed when the unit's daily schedule is changed without warning. The BEST approach is to:

opts.text: Maintain a consistent routine and prepare the client in advance for any change
opts.rat: Predictable routine and advance preparation (including visual supports) reduce anxiety for clients with autism.

opts.text: Change routines frequently so the client learns to adapt
opts.rat: Frequent unpredictable change increases anxiety and behavioral escalation in autism.

opts.text: Insist the client join every new activity immediately
opts.rat: Forcing sudden participation increases distress and resistance.

opts.text: Withhold information about changes to avoid upsetting the client
opts.rat: Lack of preparation makes transitions harder; advance, concrete notice helps.

steps.q: When assisting a client with Down syndrome, the technician should be aware of the increased risk of atlantoaxial instability, which means avoiding:

opts.text: All ambulation
opts.rat: Mobility is encouraged; only extreme cervical movement/positioning is a concern.

opts.text: Extreme flexion or hyperextension of the neck
opts.rat: Down syndrome is associated with atlantoaxial instability; extreme neck movement can injure the spinal cord.

opts.text: Use of eyeglasses
opts.rat: This is unrelated to atlantoaxial instability.

opts.text: Oral fluids with meals
opts.rat: This has no relationship to cervical spine safety.

steps.q: A nonverbal client with a severe intellectual disability suddenly begins rocking, grimacing, and guarding the abdomen. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Assume the behavior is attention-seeking and ignore it
opts.rat: Dismissing behavior risks missing a serious physical problem.

opts.text: Apply restraints to stop the rocking
opts.rat: Restraint does not address the underlying cause and may worsen distress.

opts.text: Assess for a physical cause such as pain, constipation, or illness and report findings
opts.rat: In nonverbal clients, new behavior often signals pain or an unmet physical need; assessment and reporting come first.

opts.text: Withhold the next meal as a consequence
opts.rat: This is punitive and ignores a possible medical emergency.

steps.q: The technician is teaching a client with an intellectual disability to brush his teeth. Breaking the skill into small sequential steps is called:

opts.text: Diagnostic overshadowing
opts.rat: That refers to attributing symptoms to the disability and missing another condition.

opts.text: Seclusion
opts.rat: Seclusion is a restrictive intervention, not a teaching method.

opts.text: Reality orientation
opts.rat: Reality orientation is used in confusion/dementia, not skill training.

opts.text: Task analysis
opts.rat: Task analysis breaks a skill into small, teachable steps, supporting learning and independence.

steps.q: In a positive behavior support approach, the FIRST step in managing a client's challenging behavior is to:

opts.text: Identify the function of the behavior and its antecedents/triggers
opts.rat: Understanding what triggers and maintains a behavior guides effective, individualized interventions and replacement skills.

opts.text: Punish the behavior each time it occurs
opts.rat: Punishment does not teach replacement behavior and can escalate problems.

opts.text: Immediately medicate the client
opts.rat: Medication is not the first-line behavioral strategy and does not address the cause.

opts.text: Ignore all behaviors regardless of safety
opts.rat: Safety must always be ensured; blanket ignoring is inappropriate for harmful behavior.

steps.q: A client with a developmental disability engages in head-banging (self-injurious behavior). The technician's PRIORITY is to:

opts.text: Give the client extra attention and treats during the behavior
opts.rat: Providing reinforcement during the behavior can strengthen it.

opts.text: Protect the client from injury while assessing for triggers or an unmet need
opts.rat: Safety is the priority; protecting the client and identifying the behavior's function (pain, communication, sensory) guide care.

opts.text: Leave the client alone until the behavior stops
opts.rat: Leaving a self-injuring client risks serious harm.

opts.text: Tell the client the behavior is 'bad' and walk away
opts.rat: This neither ensures safety nor addresses the cause.

steps.q: Attributing a client's new symptoms of depression solely to their intellectual disability, and therefore missing a treatable mental illness, is known as:

opts.text: Normalization
opts.rat: Normalization means providing life patterns as close to typical as possible.

opts.text: Task analysis
opts.rat: Task analysis is a teaching method.

opts.text: Diagnostic overshadowing
opts.rat: Diagnostic overshadowing occurs when symptoms are wrongly attributed to the disability, causing a co-occurring illness to be overlooked.

opts.text: Reinforcement
opts.rat: Reinforcement is a behavioral technique, not a diagnostic error.

steps.q: A client with cerebral palsy has dysphagia. To reduce aspiration risk during meals, the technician should:

opts.text: Feed the client quickly while reclined
opts.rat: Reclining and rushing increase aspiration risk.

opts.text: Give only thin liquids to make swallowing easier
opts.rat: Thin liquids are often the highest aspiration risk in dysphagia; thickening is commonly ordered.

opts.text: Encourage the client to talk while eating to relax
opts.rat: Talking while eating increases aspiration risk.

opts.text: Position the client upright and follow the ordered diet/thickened-liquid plan
opts.rat: Upright positioning and prescribed diet modifications reduce aspiration risk in dysphagia.

steps.q: When giving directions to an adult client with a moderate intellectual disability, the technician should:

opts.text: Use simple, concrete, one-step directions and allow time to respond
opts.rat: Clear, concrete, single-step directions with extra processing time promote understanding and success.

opts.text: Use long, detailed explanations with abstract terms
opts.rat: Abstract, lengthy instructions are difficult to process.

opts.text: Speak in a childlike, exaggerated tone
opts.rat: Adults deserve age-appropriate, respectful communication.

opts.text: Give several instructions at once to save time
opts.rat: Multiple simultaneous instructions overwhelm and confuse the client.

steps.q: The principle of 'normalization' in developmental disability services means:

opts.text: Making the client behave exactly like everyone else
opts.rat: Normalization is about life conditions and opportunities, not forcing conformity.

opts.text: Providing living patterns and daily routines as close as possible to those of the general community
opts.rat: Normalization promotes typical, valued life experiences and the least restrictive environment.

opts.text: Keeping clients in institutions for their safety
opts.rat: This is the opposite of normalization and least-restrictive care.

opts.text: Removing all choices to reduce confusion
opts.rat: Choice and self-determination are central to normalization.

steps.q: Many clients with developmental disabilities and limited mobility are at high risk for which common, preventable problem?

opts.text: Hyperthyroidism
opts.rat: This is not a mobility-related problem.

opts.text: Excessive height gain
opts.rat: Not a relevant clinical concern here.

opts.text: Constipation
opts.rat: Reduced mobility, medication effects, and low fluid/fiber intake make constipation common; monitoring bowel patterns is important.

opts.text: Tyramine reaction
opts.rat: Tyramine reactions relate to MAOIs and diet, not immobility.

steps.q: A client with a seizure disorder begins a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Place an object between the client's teeth
opts.rat: Never put anything in the mouth; it can cause injury or airway obstruction.

opts.text: Restrain the client's limbs to stop the movements
opts.rat: Restraining a seizing client can cause injury and does not stop the seizure.

opts.text: Leave to find help and return later
opts.rat: The client should not be left unattended during an active seizure.

opts.text: Protect the head, clear the area, and turn the client to the side when possible
opts.rat: Preventing injury, protecting the airway, and side positioning are the priorities during a seizure.

steps.q: An adult client with a severe intellectual disability lacks the capacity to consent to a medical procedure. Consent should be obtained from:

opts.text: The legally appointed conservator or guardian
opts.rat: When a client lacks capacity, the legally authorized conservator/guardian provides informed consent.

opts.text: The technician on duty
opts.rat: Direct-care staff do not provide substitute consent.

opts.text: Another client on the unit
opts.rat: Peers have no legal authority to consent.

opts.text: No one; consent is not needed
opts.rat: Consent is always required, obtained through the legally authorized decision-maker.

steps.q: A client with cerebral palsy has spasticity and is at risk for contractures. An appropriate technician intervention is to:

opts.text: Keep the client in one position for long periods
opts.rat: Prolonged single positioning promotes contractures and skin breakdown.

opts.text: Assist with prescribed range-of-motion and proper positioning/repositioning
opts.rat: Range-of-motion and correct, changing positioning help prevent contractures and maintain function.

opts.text: Discourage all movement to prevent injury
opts.rat: Immobility worsens contractures and overall health.

opts.text: Apply heat to the spastic muscles without an order
opts.rat: Interventions require an order and assessment; unordered heat can harm.

steps.q: A client with autism becomes overwhelmed in a loud, crowded dayroom and covers his ears, rocking. The BEST intervention is to:

opts.text: Increase the stimulation to help him habituate
opts.rat: More stimulation worsens sensory overload.

opts.text: Insist he remain to finish the group activity
opts.rat: Forcing continued exposure escalates distress.

opts.text: Guide the client to a quieter, low-stimulation area
opts.rat: Reducing sensory input by moving to a calmer space helps a client experiencing sensory overload.

opts.text: Turn up the television to distract him
opts.rat: Additional noise intensifies the overload.

steps.q: To reduce a client's disruptive behavior, the care plan focuses on teaching and rewarding an appropriate alternative behavior. This strategy is:

opts.text: Seclusion
opts.rat: Seclusion is a restrictive intervention, not skill-building.

opts.text: Chemical restraint
opts.rat: Medicating to control behavior is not a teaching strategy and is tightly regulated.

opts.text: Diagnostic overshadowing
opts.rat: That is a diagnostic error, not an intervention.

opts.text: Positive reinforcement of a replacement behavior
opts.rat: Teaching and reinforcing a functional replacement behavior is a core positive behavior support strategy.

steps.q: Which developmental disability is caused by prenatal alcohol exposure and is preventable?

opts.text: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder
opts.rat: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder results from prenatal alcohol exposure and is entirely preventable by avoiding alcohol in pregnancy.

opts.text: Down syndrome
opts.rat: Down syndrome is a chromosomal condition (trisomy 21), not caused by alcohol.

opts.text: Fragile X syndrome
opts.rat: Fragile X is an inherited genetic condition.

opts.text: Cerebral palsy from birth injury
opts.rat: This example is not alcohol-related.

steps.q: A client consistently becomes aggressive right before lunch each day. The MOST helpful first action is to:

opts.text: Place the client in seclusion each morning to prevent it
opts.rat: Preemptive seclusion is restrictive, punitive, and does not address the cause.

opts.text: Document the pattern and assess for a trigger such as hunger or a schedule stressor
opts.rat: Identifying the antecedent (e.g., hunger, transition) allows a proactive, individualized intervention.

opts.text: Skip the client's lunch
opts.rat: Withholding food is harmful and may worsen the behavior.

opts.text: Assume the client is simply manipulative
opts.rat: Labeling the client ignores a likely identifiable, addressable trigger.

steps.q: An aging adult with Down syndrome shows increased memory loss and functional decline. The technician recognizes that adults with Down syndrome have an increased risk of:

opts.text: Complete immunity to cognitive change
opts.rat: This is inaccurate; risk is increased, not absent.

opts.text: Improved memory with age
opts.rat: Cognitive decline, not improvement, is the concern.

opts.text: Early-onset Alzheimer-type dementia
opts.rat: Adults with Down syndrome have a substantially increased and earlier risk of Alzheimer-type dementia; changes should be assessed and reported.

opts.text: Spontaneous resolution of the disability
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are lifelong.

steps.q: Clients with developmental disabilities are at increased risk for abuse. If a technician suspects a client has been abused, they must:

opts.text: Investigate fully and only report if certain
opts.rat: Staff are not required to prove abuse before reporting; suspicion triggers the duty to report.

opts.text: Keep it confidential at the client's request
opts.rat: Safety and legal reporting duties override a request for secrecy.

opts.text: Wait for the family to address it
opts.rat: Reporting cannot be delegated or delayed; the reporter must act.

opts.text: Report the suspicion promptly per mandated-reporting requirements
opts.rat: Technicians are mandated reporters; reasonable suspicion of abuse of a dependent adult must be reported without delay.

title: Developmental Disabilities — ID Levels, Genetic Conditions & Services (Set 2)
subtitle: Intellectual disability, syndromes, health maintenance, regional centers & rights
scenario: Understanding intellectual disability, common genetic and metabolic conditions, health maintenance, and the California service system for people with developmental disabilities.

steps.q: Most people with an intellectual disability fall into which severity level, and are able to gain considerable independence with support?

opts.text: Mild
opts.rat: The majority of people with intellectual disability have MILD severity and, with appropriate support, can achieve substantial independence in daily living and work.

opts.text: Profound
opts.rat: Profound intellectual disability is the least common and involves the greatest support needs.

opts.text: Severe
opts.rat: Severe intellectual disability is less common and involves extensive support needs.

opts.text: There are no severity levels
opts.rat: Intellectual disability is described by severity levels based on adaptive functioning.

steps.q: Severity of intellectual disability is determined primarily by the person's:

opts.text: Chronological age
opts.rat: Age does not determine the severity level.

opts.text: Adaptive functioning across conceptual, social, and practical skills
opts.rat: Current criteria base severity mainly on adaptive functioning (conceptual, social, and practical domains), not IQ score alone.

opts.text: Physical height and weight
opts.rat: Physical size is unrelated to severity classification.

opts.text: Number of siblings
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to intellectual disability severity.

steps.q: Which condition is the MOST common inherited cause of intellectual disability?

opts.text: A broken bone in childhood
opts.rat: This is not a cause of intellectual disability.

opts.text: Seasonal allergies
opts.rat: Allergies do not cause intellectual disability.

opts.text: Fragile X syndrome
opts.rat: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited (genetic) cause of intellectual disability.

opts.text: Nearsightedness
opts.rat: Refractive error is unrelated to intellectual disability.

steps.q: A client with Down syndrome is admitted. The technician knows this condition is commonly associated with:

opts.text: Immunity to all infections
opts.rat: People with Down syndrome are not immune to infection; they may be more susceptible.

opts.text: Unusually tall stature
opts.rat: Short stature, not tall, is typical.

opts.text: Accelerated wound healing
opts.rat: This is not a feature of Down syndrome.

opts.text: Congenital heart defects
opts.rat: Congenital heart defects occur in a large proportion of people with Down syndrome and require monitoring.

steps.q: Clients with Down syndrome should be periodically screened for which common endocrine problem?

opts.text: Hypothyroidism
opts.rat: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome, so periodic thyroid screening is recommended.

opts.text: Gigantism
opts.rat: This is not associated with Down syndrome.

opts.text: Excessive growth hormone
opts.rat: This is not a typical concern in Down syndrome.

opts.text: No endocrine problems occur
opts.rat: Thyroid disease is notably more common in Down syndrome.

steps.q: A client with Prader-Willi syndrome has an insatiable appetite (hyperphagia). A key management strategy is to:

opts.text: Provide unlimited access to snacks
opts.rat: Unlimited food access is dangerous in Prader-Willi syndrome.

opts.text: Supervise and limit access to food to prevent life-threatening overeating
opts.rat: Prader-Willi syndrome causes uncontrolled appetite; structured food access and supervision are essential to prevent dangerous obesity and complications.

opts.text: Ignore the eating behavior entirely
opts.rat: The overeating must be actively managed for safety.

opts.text: Withhold all meals
opts.rat: Withholding meals is harmful; structured, controlled portions are used.

steps.q: A client with phenylketonuria (PKU) requires which dietary management?

opts.text: A high-protein, unrestricted diet
opts.rat: High protein provides phenylalanine, which is harmful in PKU.

opts.text: Extra aspartame-sweetened drinks
opts.rat: Aspartame contains phenylalanine and must be avoided.

opts.text: A diet low in phenylalanine, avoiding aspartame and high-protein foods
opts.rat: PKU requires restricting phenylalanine; aspartame and high-protein foods contain phenylalanine and must be limited to prevent neurologic damage.

opts.text: No dietary changes at all
opts.rat: Dietary management is essential in PKU.

steps.q: Why is EARLY intervention important for a child with a developmental disability?

opts.text: It cures the disability completely
opts.rat: Early intervention improves outcomes but does not cure a developmental disability.

opts.text: It is only useful after adulthood
opts.rat: Intervention is most effective early, not delayed to adulthood.

opts.text: It has no measurable benefit
opts.rat: Early intervention has well-documented benefits.

opts.text: It maximizes developmental progress and functional outcomes
opts.rat: Early intervention takes advantage of developmental plasticity and improves long-term functional outcomes.

steps.q: To promote independence for a client with a developmental disability, the technician should:

opts.text: Provide adaptive equipment and support the client in doing tasks themselves
opts.rat: Adaptive equipment and supported practice let the client perform tasks as independently as possible, promoting dignity and skill.

opts.text: Complete all tasks for the client
opts.rat: Doing everything for the client fosters dependence.

opts.text: Discourage the client from trying new skills
opts.rat: Discouraging skill-building limits growth and independence.

opts.text: Remove all choices from daily routines
opts.rat: Removing choice undermines self-determination.

steps.q: In California, which agencies coordinate and fund services for people with developmental disabilities?

opts.text: The local fire department
opts.rat: Fire departments do not coordinate developmental-disability services.

opts.text: Regional centers
opts.rat: California regional centers coordinate assessment, planning, and services for people with developmental disabilities.

opts.text: Public libraries
opts.rat: Libraries are not the service-coordination agency.

opts.text: The post office
opts.rat: This is unrelated to developmental-disability services.

steps.q: The Individual Program Plan (IPP) for a client with a developmental disability should be:

opts.text: Written by one staff member without any input
opts.rat: The plan must involve the individual and team, not be made unilaterally.

opts.text: Identical for every client
opts.rat: Plans are individualized, not standardized.

opts.text: Person-centered and developed with the client and their family/team
opts.rat: The IPP is a person-centered plan created with the individual and their support team to reflect their goals and needs.

opts.text: Kept secret from the client
opts.rat: The individual participates in and knows their own plan.

steps.q: According to the least-restrictive-environment principle, an adult with a mild developmental disability who can live with support should ideally reside in:

opts.text: A locked institution regardless of ability
opts.rat: Institutionalizing someone who can live in the community violates least-restrictive principles.

opts.text: Isolation from the community
opts.rat: Community integration, not isolation, is the goal.

opts.text: A hospital indefinitely
opts.rat: Indefinite hospitalization is not appropriate for stable community living needs.

opts.text: A community setting such as a group home or supported apartment
opts.rat: Least-restrictive care favors community living (e.g., group homes, supported apartments) over institutionalization when the person can be safely supported there.

steps.q: When supporting an adult with a developmental disability in making decisions, the BEST approach is to:

opts.text: Offer information in an understandable way and support the person's own choices
opts.rat: Supported decision-making provides accessible information and honors the person's right to make their own choices whenever possible.

opts.text: Make all decisions for them without asking
opts.rat: Making all decisions removes autonomy and self-determination.

opts.text: Assume they cannot understand anything
opts.rat: Assuming incapacity is disrespectful and often inaccurate.

opts.text: Pressure them into the staff's preferred choice
opts.rat: Coercion violates the person's rights.

steps.q: People with developmental disabilities often have unmet health needs. The technician should promote:

opts.text: Care only when a crisis occurs
opts.rat: Waiting for crises leads to preventable complications.

opts.text: Routine preventive care and regular health screenings
opts.rat: People with developmental disabilities are at risk for overlooked health problems; routine preventive care and screenings help catch issues early.

opts.text: Avoiding all medical visits
opts.rat: Avoiding care worsens health outcomes.

opts.text: Skipping vaccinations and dental care
opts.rat: Preventive services including vaccines and dental care are important.

steps.q: Dental care deserves special attention in clients with developmental disabilities because they:

opts.text: Never develop cavities
opts.rat: They are not immune to dental disease; risk is often higher.

opts.text: Do not need oral care
opts.rat: Oral care is essential for all clients.

opts.text: Often have higher rates of oral health problems and may need extra support with hygiene
opts.rat: Clients with developmental disabilities frequently have more dental/oral health problems and may need assistance and adapted approaches for oral hygiene.

opts.text: Should avoid brushing entirely
opts.rat: Avoiding brushing worsens oral health.

steps.q: As adults with developmental disabilities age, the technician should be aware that they may:

opts.text: Become immune to all illness with age
opts.rat: Aging does not confer immunity to illness.

opts.text: No longer require any health monitoring
opts.rat: Ongoing monitoring remains important.

opts.text: Reverse their disability as they age
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are lifelong.

opts.text: Experience some age-related health changes earlier than the general population
opts.rat: Some adults with developmental disabilities experience age-related conditions earlier, so monitoring for changes in health and function is important.

steps.q: Promoting self-determination for a client with a developmental disability means:

opts.text: Offering meaningful choices and respecting the client's preferences
opts.rat: Self-determination means supporting the person to make choices about their own life and honoring their preferences.

opts.text: Removing all opportunities to choose
opts.rat: Removing choice is the opposite of self-determination.

opts.text: Making every decision for the client
opts.rat: Deciding everything for the client removes autonomy.

opts.text: Ignoring the client's stated wishes
opts.rat: Ignoring wishes disrespects the person's rights.

steps.q: Supported employment for adults with developmental disabilities aims to:

opts.text: Keep the person from ever working
opts.rat: The goal is to enable, not prevent, employment.

opts.text: Help the person work in the community with individualized supports
opts.rat: Supported employment provides individualized assistance so the person can work successfully in a community/integrated setting.

opts.text: Isolate the person from coworkers
opts.rat: Integration with coworkers is a goal, not isolation.

opts.text: Provide work without any support
opts.rat: The model specifically provides individualized supports.

steps.q: Regarding relationships and sexuality, adults with developmental disabilities have the right to:

opts.text: No information on the topic at all
opts.rat: Withholding all education is not respectful of their rights or safety.

opts.text: Be treated as if they have no feelings
opts.rat: This is disrespectful and inaccurate.

opts.text: Age-appropriate education and respect for their rights, with support for safety
opts.rat: Adults with developmental disabilities have rights to relationships and to appropriate education, delivered with respect and attention to safety and consent.

opts.text: Be punished for expressing affection
opts.rat: Punishing normal expression violates their rights.

steps.q: The exhausted family caregiver of an adult with a developmental disability could BEST be supported by:

opts.text: Telling the caregiver to simply cope alone
opts.rat: Dismissing the caregiver's needs is not supportive.

opts.text: Discouraging any outside help
opts.rat: Outside support is beneficial, not something to discourage.

opts.text: Ignoring signs of caregiver burnout
opts.rat: Caregiver burnout should be recognized and addressed.

opts.text: Sharing information about respite care and support resources with the team
opts.rat: Connecting families to respite care and support resources helps sustain caregivers and benefits the client.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Developmental Disabilities. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Developmental Disabilities — Communication, Behavior Techniques & Dual Diagnosis (Set 3)
subtitle: AAC, functional behavior assessment, teaching methods & mental illness in DD
scenario: Supporting communication, using behavior-support and teaching techniques, and recognizing co-occurring mental illness in people with developmental disabilities.

steps.q: A nonverbal client uses a picture board and a speech-generating device to communicate. These are examples of:

opts.text: Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC)
opts.rat: Picture boards and speech-generating devices are augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) tools that support people with limited or no speech.

opts.text: Physical restraint
opts.rat: These are communication supports, not restraints.

opts.text: A form of punishment
opts.rat: AAC supports communication; it is not punitive.

opts.text: Chemical sedation
opts.rat: AAC has nothing to do with medication.

steps.q: A visual (picture) schedule benefits many clients with developmental disabilities by:

opts.text: Confusing them with too much information
opts.rat: Visual schedules are designed to clarify, not confuse.

opts.text: Helping them anticipate the day and reducing anxiety around transitions
opts.rat: Visual schedules make routines predictable, support understanding, and reduce anxiety around transitions.

opts.text: Replacing the need for any staff support
opts.rat: They support—rather than replace—staff interaction and care.

opts.text: Serving as a disciplinary tool
opts.rat: A schedule is a support, not a punishment.

steps.q: A functional behavior assessment is used to determine:

opts.text: The client's favorite color
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to behavior assessment.

opts.text: How to punish the behavior fastest
opts.rat: The goal is understanding function to guide support, not punishment.

opts.text: The purpose (function) a behavior serves for the client
opts.rat: A functional behavior assessment identifies why a behavior occurs—its function, such as gaining attention, escaping a demand, sensory input, or obtaining a tangible item.

opts.text: The client's shoe size
opts.rat: This has nothing to do with behavior function.

steps.q: Common FUNCTIONS of a challenging behavior include gaining attention, obtaining an item, sensory input, and:

opts.text: Improving the weather
opts.rat: This is not a behavioral function.

opts.text: Changing the client's height
opts.rat: This is unrelated to behavior.

opts.text: Predicting the future
opts.rat: This is not a function of behavior.

opts.text: Escaping or avoiding a demand or situation
opts.rat: Behaviors often function to escape/avoid a task or situation, alongside attention, tangible, and sensory functions.

steps.q: When staff record the Antecedent, Behavior, and Consequence (ABC) of an event, the ANTECEDENT is:

opts.text: What happened right before the behavior
opts.rat: The antecedent is what occurred immediately before the behavior; ABC data helps identify triggers and patterns.

opts.text: The reward given afterward
opts.rat: That is the consequence, not the antecedent.

opts.text: The behavior itself
opts.rat: The antecedent precedes the behavior.

opts.text: The client's diagnosis
opts.rat: The antecedent is the immediate preceding event, not a diagnosis.

steps.q: Teaching a new skill by reinforcing small steps that get closer and closer to the goal behavior is called:

opts.text: Seclusion
opts.rat: Seclusion is a restrictive intervention, not a teaching method.

opts.text: Shaping
opts.rat: Shaping reinforces successive approximations—progressively closer attempts—until the target skill is achieved.

opts.text: Extinction
opts.rat: Extinction is withholding reinforcement, not building a skill in steps.

opts.text: Restraint
opts.rat: Restraint is not a teaching technique.

steps.q: Gradually reducing the cues given to a client as they master a skill is known as:

opts.text: Prompt increasing forever
opts.rat: The goal is to reduce prompts, promoting independence, not increase them.

opts.text: Physical restraint
opts.rat: This is unrelated to fading.

opts.text: Prompt fading
opts.rat: Fading gradually removes prompts/cues as the client becomes able to perform the skill independently.

opts.text: Punishment
opts.rat: Fading is a teaching support, not punishment.

steps.q: In a token economy, a client:

opts.text: Is fined money for existing
opts.rat: A token economy rewards desired behavior; it is not a punishment system for existing.

opts.text: Is secluded for earning tokens
opts.rat: Tokens are earned for and exchanged toward reinforcers, not seclusion.

opts.text: Receives medication for each token
opts.rat: Tokens are not linked to medication.

opts.text: Earns tokens for desired behaviors that can be exchanged for reinforcers
opts.rat: A token economy reinforces desired behaviors with tokens the client later exchanges for preferred items or activities.

steps.q: When a previously reinforced behavior is placed on extinction (reinforcement withheld), the technician should expect:

opts.text: A temporary increase in the behavior (extinction burst) before it decreases
opts.rat: An extinction burst—a temporary increase in the behavior—commonly occurs before the behavior decreases; consistency is essential.

opts.text: The behavior to vanish instantly with no change
opts.rat: Behaviors on extinction often briefly increase first, rather than vanishing instantly.

opts.text: The client to develop a new physical illness
opts.rat: Extinction is a behavioral process, not a cause of illness.

opts.text: Immediate permanent improvement in all areas
opts.rat: Extinction affects the targeted behavior, not all behaviors instantly.

steps.q: For a behavior-support plan to be effective, all staff across shifts and settings should:

opts.text: Each use their own personal approach
opts.rat: Inconsistent approaches confuse the client and weaken the plan.

opts.text: Apply the plan consistently the same way
opts.rat: Consistency across all staff and settings is essential; inconsistent responses undermine behavior-support plans.

opts.text: Ignore the plan when busy
opts.rat: Skipping the plan breaks the consistency it depends on.

opts.text: Change the plan daily without documentation
opts.rat: Undocumented, constant changes make the plan ineffective.

steps.q: 'Generalization' of a newly learned skill means the client can:

opts.text: Only perform it in the exact training room
opts.rat: That is the opposite of generalization.

opts.text: Forget the skill entirely
opts.rat: Generalization involves retaining and transferring the skill.

opts.text: Use the skill in different settings and with different people
opts.rat: Generalization is applying a learned skill across various settings, people, and situations, not just where it was taught.

opts.text: Perform it only for one specific staff member
opts.rat: Generalization means the skill transfers across people, not just one.

steps.q: Accurate data collection on a client's behavior is important because it:

opts.text: Is only busywork with no purpose
opts.rat: Data directly informs effective care decisions.

opts.text: Should be based on guesses
opts.rat: Data must be objective and accurate, not guessed.

opts.text: Replaces the need to observe the client
opts.rat: Data comes from careful observation; it does not replace it.

opts.text: Guides and evaluates the behavior-support plan objectively
opts.rat: Objective data reveals patterns, guides the plan, and shows whether interventions are working.

steps.q: A 'dual diagnosis' in this population refers to a person who has:

opts.text: Both a developmental disability and a co-occurring mental illness
opts.rat: Dual diagnosis here means a developmental disability plus a co-occurring mental illness; both are real and treatable.

opts.text: Two different favorite foods
opts.rat: This is not a clinical concept.

opts.text: A developmental disability that cannot coexist with mental illness
opts.rat: Mental illness can and does co-occur with developmental disability.

opts.text: No conditions at all
opts.rat: Dual diagnosis means two coexisting conditions.

steps.q: A client with a developmental disability shows a marked change from their usual behavior—new withdrawal and loss of interest. The technician should:

opts.text: Assume it is simply part of the disability and ignore it
opts.rat: Attributing new symptoms solely to the disability (diagnostic overshadowing) can miss treatable illness.

opts.text: Report the change, considering a possible mental or physical illness
opts.rat: A change from baseline may signal a treatable mental illness or medical problem; it should be assessed and reported rather than assumed to be 'just the disability.'

opts.text: Withhold meals as a consequence
opts.rat: This is punitive and ignores a possible illness.

opts.text: Tell the client to cheer up and move on
opts.rat: This dismisses a potentially serious change.

steps.q: When a psychotropic medication is prescribed for a client with a developmental disability, the technician should:

opts.text: Assume side effects never occur
opts.rat: Side effects can and do occur and must be monitored.

opts.text: Give extra doses to keep the client quiet
opts.rat: Extra dosing for convenience is chemical restraint and is prohibited.

opts.text: Monitor for both therapeutic effects and side effects and report changes
opts.rat: Psychotropics in this population are used carefully at the lowest effective dose; monitoring for benefit and adverse effects and reporting changes is essential.

opts.text: Stop reporting once the client is calm
opts.rat: Ongoing monitoring and reporting are always required.

steps.q: Using a sedating medication mainly to make a client with a developmental disability easier to manage, rather than to treat a condition, is:

opts.text: A recommended routine practice
opts.rat: This is not acceptable practice.

opts.text: Required for all clients
opts.rat: It is never a required or appropriate routine.

opts.text: The least restrictive option
opts.rat: Sedating for convenience is highly restrictive, not least restrictive.

opts.text: Chemical restraint, which is not acceptable
opts.rat: Medicating for staff convenience rather than a legitimate treatment purpose is chemical restraint and is prohibited and tightly regulated.

steps.q: To prevent a behavioral crisis, the technician should:

opts.text: Recognize early signs of escalation and intervene calmly and early
opts.rat: Noticing early warning signs and intervening early with calm, supportive strategies helps prevent a full behavioral crisis.

opts.text: Wait until the behavior is severe before acting
opts.rat: Waiting for severe behavior misses the chance to prevent escalation.

opts.text: Ignore all early warning signs
opts.rat: Ignoring warning signs allows crises to develop.

opts.text: Immediately use restraint at the first sign
opts.rat: Restraint is a last resort, not a first response to early signs.

steps.q: When choosing an intervention for challenging behavior, the technician should first use:

opts.text: The most restrictive option available
opts.rat: Starting with the most restrictive option violates least-restrictive principles.

opts.text: The least restrictive effective strategy
opts.rat: Behavior interventions follow the least-restrictive principle—positive, supportive strategies first, with restrictive measures only as a last resort for safety.

opts.text: Seclusion for any behavior
opts.rat: Seclusion is a last resort, not a first-line intervention.

opts.text: Whatever is fastest for staff
opts.rat: Convenience does not justify restrictive interventions.

steps.q: Which reflects respectful, person-first language?

opts.text: 'The retard in room 4'
opts.rat: This is a slur and is disrespectful and unacceptable.

opts.text: 'The disabled one'
opts.rat: Defining a person by their disability is not person-first or respectful.

opts.text: 'A person with an intellectual disability'
opts.rat: Person-first language ('a person with an intellectual disability') puts the individual before the condition and conveys respect.

opts.text: 'That difficult case'
opts.rat: This is dehumanizing and disrespectful.

steps.q: Teaching a client with a developmental disability functional life skills (such as dressing or making a simple meal) primarily promotes:

opts.text: Increased dependence on staff
opts.rat: The goal is independence, not dependence.

opts.text: Punishment for poor behavior
opts.rat: Skill-building is supportive, not punitive.

opts.text: Isolation from the community
opts.rat: Life skills support community participation, not isolation.

opts.text: Greater independence and quality of life
opts.rat: Functional life-skills training increases independence, self-esteem, and quality of life.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Developmental Disabilities. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Developmental Disabilities — Physical Health, Seizure & Swallowing Safety (Set 4)
subtitle: Cerebral palsy, seizure care, dysphagia & aspiration, choking, pain in nonverbal clients, skin & aging
scenario: Protecting the physical health and safety of people with developmental disabilities—recognizing and responding to seizures, swallowing and aspiration risk, choking, pain in nonverbal clients, and skin, mobility, and aging needs.

steps.q: Cerebral palsy is best described as:

opts.text: A disorder of movement and posture caused by early, non-progressive brain injury
opts.rat: Cerebral palsy results from injury to the developing brain that affects movement, muscle tone, and posture. It is non-progressive (the brain injury does not worsen) and is not contagious.

opts.text: A contagious infection spread between clients
opts.rat: Cerebral palsy is not an infection and is not contagious.

opts.text: A progressive disease that always worsens over time
opts.rat: The underlying brain injury in cerebral palsy is non-progressive, though secondary problems like contractures can develop without good care.

opts.text: A temporary condition that resolves in childhood
opts.rat: Cerebral palsy is a lifelong condition, not a temporary one.

steps.q: For a client with cerebral palsy and muscle spasticity, careful positioning and range-of-motion primarily help to:

opts.text: Cure the cerebral palsy
opts.rat: Positioning and range-of-motion support function and comfort; they do not cure cerebral palsy.

opts.text: Prevent contractures and maintain comfort and function
opts.rat: Good positioning and regular range-of-motion help prevent contractures (permanent tightening of muscles/joints), reduce pain, and preserve function.

opts.text: Replace the need for any staff assistance
opts.rat: These measures support the client but do not remove the need for care and assistance.

opts.text: Allow the client to skip all other care
opts.rat: Positioning is one part of overall care, not a substitute for it.

steps.q: A client has a generalized seizure and falls to the floor with jerking movements. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Hold the client's arms and legs still to stop the movements
opts.rat: Restraining the limbs during a seizure can cause injury and does not stop the seizure.

opts.text: Place a padded object between the client's teeth
opts.rat: Nothing should be placed in the mouth; it can break teeth, block the airway, or injure the client and staff.

opts.text: Protect the client from injury, ease them to the floor, and turn them on their side
opts.rat: Priorities are safety and airway: protect the head, clear nearby hazards, do not restrain, and position the client on their side to help keep the airway clear. Time the seizure.

opts.text: Leave the client alone and document later
opts.rat: The client must be protected and monitored throughout the seizure, not left unattended.

steps.q: During a seizure, which action should the technician AVOID?

opts.text: Moving nearby furniture or hazards away
opts.rat: Clearing hazards is appropriate and protects the client.

opts.text: Cushioning the head with something soft
opts.rat: Protecting the head from injury is appropriate.

opts.text: Noting the time the seizure started and how long it lasts
opts.rat: Timing the seizure is important information to report.

opts.text: Forcing objects into the mouth or restraining the limbs
opts.rat: Nothing should be placed in the mouth and the limbs should not be held down; both can cause serious injury. Let the seizure run its course while keeping the client safe.

steps.q: In the postictal period (right after a seizure), the client is often confused and sleepy. The technician should:

opts.text: Stay with the client, check for injuries, offer calm reassurance, and allow rest
opts.rat: After a seizure the client may be drowsy, confused, or embarrassed. Provide a calm environment, check for injury, reorient gently, and allow rest while monitoring.

opts.text: Insist the client return to full activity immediately
opts.rat: Pushing the client to resume activity too soon ignores the normal postictal recovery period.

opts.text: Scold the client for having a seizure
opts.rat: A seizure is not the client's fault; scolding is inappropriate and harmful.

opts.text: Leave the confused client unsupervised
opts.rat: A confused client is at risk for falls or injury and needs supervision.

steps.q: Which seizure situation is a medical EMERGENCY requiring immediate emergency response?

opts.text: A brief seizure after which the client recovers and returns to baseline
opts.rat: A single brief seizure with recovery is monitored and reported per the client's plan, but is not by itself the emergency described here.
