opts.text: Personally administer the insulin and due medications and reinforce the hip-precaution teaching
opts.rat: These require nursing knowledge and are correctly kept by the LVN.

opts.text: Report the low hemoglobin/hematocrit and the increased incisional pain to the RN, and have the RN initiate the ordered blood transfusion
opts.rat: Escalating out-of-scope and clinically significant findings to the RN is the correct action.

opts.text: Ask the CNA to give the insulin and reinforce the teaching so the LVN can chart
opts.rat: Medication administration and teaching are not delegated to a CNA, regardless of charting workload.

opts.text: Start the blood transfusion independently to save the RN time
opts.rat: Initiating blood is outside the California LVN's scope; the RN starts and monitors it.

opts.text: Tell the CNA to assess the incision and decide whether it needs attention
opts.rat: Assessing and clinically judging a surgical incision is a nursing task, not delegated to a CNA.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Assess the client's incisional pain and dressing and check for bleeding
opts.rat: FIRST — directly evaluate the new symptom and possible bleeding; current data is needed before escalating and acting.

opts.text: Report the findings and the low hemoglobin/hematocrit to the RN using SBAR
opts.rat: SECOND — timely escalation lets the RN initiate the ordered transfusion and reassess the plan.

opts.text: Give the CNA clear directions for the delegated routine care so the whole assignment stays safe
opts.rat: THIRD — delegating routine care frees the LVN for nursing tasks while keeping the assignment covered.

opts.text: Administer the due insulin and medications and reinforce hip-precaution teaching
opts.rat: FOURTH — carry out the retained nursing tasks after the acute concern is handled and routine care is delegated.

opts.text: Document the assessment, delegation, medications, and communication, and follow up on the CNA's reported results
opts.rat: LAST — documentation and follow-up on delegated tasks maintain accountability and continuity.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Later in the shift, classify each finding.

opts.text: The CNA obtained the routine vital signs and reported them to the LVN, and completed the client's ADLs
opts.rat: Appropriate delegation with report-back kept the assignment safe — effective coordination.

opts.text: After the LVN's SBAR report, the RN initiated the blood transfusion and the LVN assists with monitoring within scope
opts.rat: Correct escalation and role division: the RN starts the blood; the LVN supports monitoring within scope.

opts.text: The LVN finds the CNA about to administer the client's insulin
opts.rat: Medication administration is outside the CNA's scope; the LVN must stop this immediately, give the insulin, and re-clarify the delegation.

opts.text: The client's incisional pain is controlled after intervention and the dressing is dry and intact
opts.rat: The acute concern resolved and there is no sign of active bleeding — a good outcome.

opts.text: The CNA reports that the client felt dizzy during ambulation, so the CNA stopped and notified the LVN
opts.rat: The CNA correctly recognized a limit and reported promptly — appropriate delegation and communication in action.

opts.text: The LVN charted the delegated tasks but never checked whether they were actually completed
opts.rat: Failing to follow up is an accountability/supervision lapse; the LVN must verify delegated tasks were done and the results.

opts.text: Teaching was reinforced and the client correctly restates two hip precautions; a follow-up glucose is being rechecked per order
opts.rat: Correct teach-back and ordered follow-up monitoring indicate the retained nursing tasks are working.

opts.text: The client's daughter asks the LVN to explain the overall plan of care; the LVN refers the question to the RN
opts.rat: Referring a plan-of-care explanation to the RN is appropriate handling within scope — neither deterioration nor a clinical change.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Coordinated Care (the app's 'Management of Care' grouping), using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Coordinated Care is 18-24% of the NCLEX-PN exam). Scope statements reflect the California LVN scope of practice under the Board of Vocational Nursing and Psychiatric Technicians (BVNPT): the California LVN practices under the direction of an RN/NP/physician; delegates only tasks within a CDPH-certified CNA's scope while retaining accountability and supervising; keeps medication administration, teaching, and assessment as nursing tasks; and does NOT perform the initial/independent assessment, develop the nursing care plan, give IV push medications, or initiate blood/blood-product transfusions (these are RN functions). The 5 rights of delegation are right task, right circumstance, right person, right direction/communication, and right supervision. Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation. Pending faculty review by Joseph Ongongo, LPT / RN reviewer.

title: Advance Directives, Code Status & the Consent Role (California LVN Scope)
subtitle: 82 y/o male, metastatic cancer with a DNR and an advance directive — the LVN must uphold the client's wishes, keep the consent process in the provider's hands, and know that DNR is not 'do not treat'
nursesNote: 1000 - 82 y/o male, skilled-nursing facility, metastatic cancer, comfort-focused (palliative) plan of care. Alert and oriented x4 with intact decision-making capacity. Chart contains a current California Advance Health Care Directive naming his daughter as health care agent, and a POLST/DNR order (Do Not Resuscitate) reflecting the client's stated wishes. He is scheduled for a paracentesis today to relieve symptomatic ascites; the consent form is at the desk but the provider has not yet spoken with the client about the procedure. This morning the client asked the LVN to 'explain the risks' before he signs. His adult son arrived, is upset, and is demanding staff 'do everything and ignore that DNR.' The client continues on scheduled antibiotics for a UTI and routine pain medication. The daughter (health care agent) is reachable by phone. LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider.

patient.name: H. Nakamura
patient.admitDate: SNF, palliative/comfort-focused plan

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: What needs the LVN's correct action
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that MOST require the LVN to respond correctly regarding directives, code status, and consent.

opts.text: The client, who is alert with intact capacity, asks the LVN to explain the risks and benefits of the paracentesis before he signs the consent
opts.rat: Explaining the procedure's risks/benefits is the provider's role; the client's request means the provider must speak with him before consent — the LVN must respond correctly, not explain it.

opts.text: The son is demanding staff 'do everything and ignore the DNR,' contrary to the client's documented wishes
opts.rat: A family demand that conflicts with a competent client's directive/DNR is a legal-ethical issue the LVN must handle correctly and report.

opts.text: The consent form is unsigned and the provider has not yet discussed the procedure with the client
opts.rat: Consent must follow the provider's discussion; an unsigned form with no provider conversation means the informed-consent process is not complete.

opts.text: A current advance health care directive naming the daughter as agent is on the chart
opts.rat: A current directive on the chart is a reassuring, correct finding — not a problem to fix.

opts.text: The client is receiving his scheduled antibiotics and routine pain medication
opts.rat: Continuing ordered treatment and comfort care is appropriate for a DNR client — a correct finding, not a concern.

opts.text: The client ate breakfast and is resting comfortably
opts.rat: A comfortable, stable client is a reassuring finding, not a priority cue.

opts.text: The POLST/DNR order is documented and matches the client's stated wishes
opts.rat: A documented order matching the client's wishes is correct — not a problem requiring action.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect the law, ethics, and the LVN's role.

opts.text: Obtaining informed consent — explaining risks, benefits, and alternatives — is the PROVIDER's responsibility; the LVN notifies the provider of the client's questions and, per facility policy, may witness the voluntary signature, but does not explain the procedure or obtain consent
opts.rat: Informed consent is a provider duty. The nurse's role is to ensure the client's questions reach the provider and to witness that the signature is voluntary, not to provide the medical explanation.

opts.text: A competent client's own wishes and a valid advance directive/DNR take precedence over family demands; the health care agent (daughter) makes decisions only if and when the client loses capacity
opts.rat: While the client has capacity, he decides; the agent's authority activates only upon loss of capacity, and family cannot override a competent client's valid directive.

opts.text: A DNR order means no CPR; it does NOT mean withholding other treatment — antibiotics, pain control, and comfort care continue
opts.rat: DNR limits resuscitation only. All other ordered and comfort care continues; DNR is not 'do not treat.'

opts.text: The LVN should explain the procedure's risks and benefits and have the client sign the consent form
opts.rat: Explaining and obtaining informed consent is the provider's responsibility, not the LVN's.

opts.text: The son can override the client's DNR because he is family and is present
opts.rat: Family presence does not grant authority to override a competent client's valid directive.

opts.text: A DNR order means the client should receive no further medications or treatment
opts.rat: This is a common, dangerous misconception; DNR restricts only CPR, not other care.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.sub: Rank the LVN's actions by priority
steps.inst: Drag to rank these actions from HIGHEST priority (1) to LOWEST (5).

opts.text: Hold the consent process and notify the provider that the client has questions and needs the procedure explained before signing
opts.rat: Protecting the client's right to informed consent comes first — no signature until the provider has explained and answered questions.

opts.text: Reaffirm that the documented DNR reflects the competent client's wishes and report the son's demand to the RN
opts.rat: Upholding the valid code status and escalating the family conflict prevents an inappropriate override and guides the team's response.

opts.text: Continue the client's ordered treatments and comfort care (antibiotics, pain control)
opts.rat: Ongoing treatment and comfort continue for a DNR client and are maintained while the other issues are handled.

opts.text: Provide support to the client and family and refer their questions to the RN/provider/social work as needed
opts.rat: Emotional support and appropriate referral help the family but rank below the direct consent and code-status actions.

opts.text: Confirm the advance directive and health-care-agent designation are documented and accessible on the chart
opts.rat: Verifying documentation is important housekeeping but the lowest-urgency of these actions since it is already on the chart.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's role.

opts.text: Notify the provider that the client has questions and needs the risks, benefits, and alternatives explained before any consent is signed
opts.rat: Routing the client's questions to the provider protects the informed-consent process and stays within the LVN's role.

opts.text: Reassure that the DNR reflects the client's wishes, continue ordered treatments and comfort care, and report the son's demand to the RN
opts.rat: Upholding the directive, maintaining care, and escalating the conflict are all correct.

opts.text: Document the client's stated wishes and the family interaction objectively and keep the advance directive accessible on the chart
opts.rat: Objective documentation and keeping the directive available support continuity and the client's rights.

opts.text: Explain the procedure's risks yourself and obtain the client's signature on the consent form
opts.rat: Explaining and obtaining informed consent is the provider's role, not the LVN's.

opts.text: Change the code status to full code because the son insists
opts.rat: Code status is not changed on a family member's demand; it reflects the competent client's wishes and requires the provider process.

opts.text: Stop the client's antibiotics and pain medication because he is a DNR
opts.rat: DNR does not mean withholding treatment; stopping ordered care would be incorrect and harmful.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Hold the consent and notify the provider that the client has questions to be answered before signing
opts.rat: FIRST — the consent process pauses until the provider explains the procedure and answers questions.

opts.text: Reaffirm the DNR with the client as appropriate and report the son's demand and the situation to the RN
opts.rat: SECOND — uphold the valid code status and escalate the family conflict to the RN promptly.

opts.text: Continue the ordered treatments and comfort care
opts.rat: THIRD — maintain antibiotics, pain control, and comfort measures throughout.

opts.text: Support the client and family and refer their questions to the RN/provider/social work
opts.rat: FOURTH — provide emotional support and route deeper questions to the appropriate team members.

opts.text: Document the client's wishes, the family interaction, and the notifications objectively
opts.rat: LAST — accurate documentation preserves the record and continuity of care.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Later in the shift, classify each finding.

opts.text: The provider met with the client, explained the paracentesis and answered his questions, and the client gave informed consent; the LVN witnessed the voluntary signature per policy
opts.rat: Informed consent was completed correctly by the provider with the LVN in the appropriate witnessing role.

opts.text: The RN and provider met with the son, who now understands the DNR reflects his father's wishes; the DNR remains in place
opts.rat: The conflict was resolved through the team while honoring the competent client's directive.

opts.text: The LVN is found preparing to explain the procedure's surgical risks and obtain the consent signature independently
opts.rat: This is outside the LVN's role; obtaining informed consent is the provider's duty and must be stopped and corrected.

opts.text: The client continues to receive scheduled antibiotics and pain control and reports being comfortable
opts.rat: Maintaining ordered treatment and comfort for a DNR client is correct and effective.

opts.text: Staff withheld the client's pain medication because he is a DNR
opts.rat: DNR does not justify withholding pain medication; this misconception must be corrected and the medication given as ordered.

opts.text: The advance directive and health-care-agent designation are confirmed current and accessible on the chart
opts.rat: Verified, accessible documentation supports the client's rights and continuity of care.

opts.text: The client remains clear and firm about his wishes and says he feels heard by the staff
opts.rat: The client's decisions and capacity are consistent; being heard is appropriate care, with no clinical change.

opts.text: The daughter (agent) asks to start making decisions for her father; the team clarifies she acts only if he loses capacity, which he currently retains
opts.rat: The decision-maker is unchanged: while the client has capacity, he decides; the agent's authority is not yet active.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Coordinated Care (the app's 'Management of Care' grouping) — advance directives, informed consent, and client rights — using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Coordinated Care is 18-24% of the NCLEX-PN exam). Scope and rights statements reflect standard nursing practice and the California context: informed consent (explaining risks/benefits/alternatives) is the provider's responsibility, while the nurse notifies the provider of client questions and, per facility policy, may witness the voluntary signature; a competent adult client's own wishes and a valid advance directive (California Advance Health Care Directive) / POLST-DNR order take precedence over family demands; the designated health care agent's authority activates only when the client loses decision-making capacity; and a DNR order limits CPR only and does not mean withholding treatment or comfort care. The California LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider and does not obtain informed consent, change code status, or override a valid directive independently. Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation. Pending faculty review by Joseph Ongongo, LPT / RN reviewer.

title: SBAR, Reporting a Change & Hand-off Continuity (LVN Scope)
subtitle: 74 y/o female, post-op day 2, trending toward a complication — the LVN must report the change to the RN using SBAR, use read-back for orders, and give a complete hand-off
nursesNote: 1500 - 74 y/o female, skilled-nursing/med-surg, post-op day 2 following exploratory laparotomy with bowel resection. Alert and oriented. Over this shift her temperature has climbed, heart rate has risen, blood pressure has trended down, and urine output has fallen to less than 30 mL/hour over the last 2 hours. She now reports feeling weak and nauseated and appears pale. Post-op dressing is dry and intact; pain is controlled on scheduled medication. Pending: a scheduled antibiotic dose is due, a STAT CBC was ordered and is still pending, and a dressing change is scheduled for the evening. It is near shift change. The LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider.

patient.name: E. Torres
patient.admitDate: Post-op day 2 (exploratory laparotomy, bowel resection)

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that represent a significant change the LVN must report to the RN.

opts.text: Temperature has risen (37.2 → 38.6°C) with heart rate up (82 → 108) and blood pressure trending down (118/72 → 100/60)
opts.rat: A trend of rising fever and heart rate with falling blood pressure is a significant change that may signal a developing complication and must be reported.

opts.text: Urine output has fallen to less than 30 mL/hour over the last 2 hours
opts.rat: Falling urine output can indicate hypovolemia or worsening perfusion and is a key finding to report.

opts.text: The client now reports feeling weak and nauseated and appears pale
opts.rat: New subjective and objective signs of feeling unwell accompany the vital-sign changes and belong in the report.

opts.text: The post-op dressing is dry and intact
opts.rat: A dry, intact dressing is a reassuring, unchanged finding, not a change to escalate.

opts.text: The client has NKDA documented
opts.rat: Allergy status is important background but not a new change requiring escalation.

opts.text: The client ambulated once this morning with assist
opts.rat: Expected post-op activity, not a change.

opts.text: The client's pain is controlled on scheduled medication
opts.rat: Controlled pain is a stable, reassuring finding.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect good communication, continuity, and LVN scope.

opts.text: The trending changes (fever, rising heart rate, falling blood pressure, low urine output) suggest a developing complication and must be reported to the RN promptly; the LVN collects and communicates data while the RN assesses and adjusts the plan with the provider
opts.rat: Recognizing and escalating a change is the LVN's role; assessment and plan changes belong to the RN/provider.

opts.text: A structured SBAR report — Situation, Background, Assessment/observations, Recommendation/request — communicates the change clearly and reduces errors and omissions
opts.rat: SBAR standardizes hand-off and change-of-condition communication, improving clarity and safety.

opts.text: A complete hand-off at shift change includes the change in condition, pending tasks (due antibiotic, pending STAT CBC, scheduled dressing change), and safety information, to maintain continuity of care
opts.rat: Complete hand-off with pending items and safety information prevents gaps in care.

opts.text: Because it is near shift change, the LVN should wait and let the oncoming nurse report the changes
opts.rat: A change in condition is reported promptly; delaying to the next shift risks harm.

opts.text: The LVN should independently diagnose the client with sepsis and start new treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosing and initiating new treatment is outside the LVN's scope; the LVN reports to the RN/provider.

opts.text: The hand-off can safely omit pending labs and tasks to keep the report brief
opts.rat: Omitting pending labs and tasks breaks continuity and risks missed care.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.sub: Put the report in SBAR order
steps.inst: Drag the parts of the LVN's report to the RN into the correct SBAR order (1 = stated first).

opts.text: Situation — 'I'm calling about Mrs. Torres in 210; her vital signs have changed and her urine output has dropped.'
opts.rat: SITUATION comes first: a concise statement of who the client is and what is happening now.

opts.text: Background — 'She's post-op day 2 from a bowel resection, full code, on scheduled antibiotics, NKDA.'
opts.rat: BACKGROUND provides the relevant context and history the RN needs to interpret the situation.

opts.text: Assessment/observations — 'Temp is up to 38.6, heart rate 108, BP down to 100/60, urine under 30 mL/hr, and she feels weak, nauseated, and looks pale.'
opts.rat: ASSESSMENT/observations share the LVN's current findings and the data behind the concern.

opts.text: Recommendation/request — 'I'm concerned she may be developing a complication — can you come assess her and advise on orders?'
opts.rat: RECOMMENDATION/request states what the LVN needs from the RN, closing the loop of the SBAR report.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Report the change to the RN promptly using SBAR, including the vital-sign trend, urine output, and observations
opts.rat: Prompt, structured SBAR reporting of the change is the correct action.

opts.text: If the RN or provider gives a verbal or telephone order, use read-back — repeat the order back to confirm it — before carrying it out
opts.rat: Read-back verification of verbal/telephone orders prevents errors.

opts.text: Give a complete end-of-shift hand-off that includes the change in condition, the pending STAT CBC and due antibiotic, and safety information, and document the report
opts.rat: A complete, documented hand-off maintains continuity of care.

opts.text: Delay reporting until the end of shift so the oncoming nurse can handle it
opts.rat: A change in condition is reported promptly, not deferred to the next shift.

opts.text: Independently start IV fluids and antibiotics beyond what is ordered
opts.rat: Initiating treatment beyond orders is outside the LVN's scope; report to the RN/provider.

opts.text: Keep the hand-off brief by leaving out the pending labs and tasks
opts.rat: Omitting pending items breaks continuity and risks missed care.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Recheck the client and gather current data (vital signs, urine output, appearance, symptoms)
opts.rat: FIRST — obtain current data so the report is accurate and complete.

opts.text: Report the change to the RN promptly using SBAR
opts.rat: SECOND — escalate the change so the RN can assess and involve the provider.

opts.text: Carry out any new orders within scope, using read-back for verbal or telephone orders
opts.rat: THIRD — implement ordered interventions correctly, verifying verbal orders with read-back.

opts.text: Give a complete hand-off to the oncoming nurse including the change and all pending tasks
opts.rat: FOURTH — transfer care with a complete hand-off so nothing is dropped.

opts.text: Document the assessment findings, the SBAR report, actions taken, and the hand-off
opts.rat: LAST — accurate, timely documentation preserves the record and continuity.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding.

opts.text: The RN assessed the client after the SBAR report and started ordered interventions, which the LVN carried out within scope
opts.rat: Timely escalation led to prompt assessment and treatment — effective communication and coordination.

opts.text: The LVN repeated a telephone order back to the provider to confirm it before giving the medication
opts.rat: Read-back verification is correct practice and prevents order errors.

opts.text: The oncoming nurse was not told about the pending STAT CBC or the due antibiotic
opts.rat: An incomplete hand-off creates a continuity gap; the LVN must communicate all pending items.

opts.text: The end-of-shift hand-off included the change in condition, pending labs and tasks, and safety information, and the oncoming nurse verbalized understanding
opts.rat: A complete hand-off with confirmed understanding maintains continuity of care.

opts.text: The LVN documented the change, the SBAR report, and the actions objectively and in a timely manner
opts.rat: Timely, objective documentation supports the record and continuity.

opts.text: The change in condition was not reported until the very end of the shift, delaying the RN's assessment
opts.rat: Delayed reporting postpones needed assessment and treatment — a communication failure to correct.

opts.text: After the initial ordered interventions, the client's vital signs and symptoms are unchanged and continue to be monitored
opts.rat: No change yet after early interventions; continued monitoring and reassessment are appropriate.

opts.text: The post-op dressing remains dry and intact and pain stays controlled
opts.rat: A stable, reassuring finding with no change — requires no new action.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Coordinated Care (the app's 'Management of Care' grouping) — communication, hand-off, and continuity of care — using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Coordinated Care is 18-24% of the NCLEX-PN exam). Concepts reflect standard nursing practice at LVN scope: recognizing and promptly reporting a change in condition to the RN (the LVN collects and communicates data; the RN assesses and adjusts the plan with the provider); the SBAR structure (Situation, Background, Assessment/observations, Recommendation/request); read-back verification of verbal/telephone orders; and complete shift-change hand-off including change in condition, pending tasks/labs, and safety information to maintain continuity. Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation. Pending faculty review by Joseph Ongongo, LPT / RN reviewer.

title: Prioritizing a Multi-Client Assignment (LVN Scope)
subtitle: LVN receives report on 5 clients on a med-surg hall — who is seen first? Applying ABCs, safety, and time-critical needs, then delegating and coordinating the rest
nursesNote: 0700 shift report - The LVN receives report on a 5-client assignment (med-surg hall) and works with one CNA. Room 1 (chart shown): 72 y/o male, COPD with community-acquired pneumonia, day 3; over the last 30 minutes his shortness of breath has increased, oxygen saturation has fallen to 89% on his usual 2 L nasal cannula, he is using accessory muscles, and he appears anxious. Room 2: 84 y/o female, high fall risk (recent hip-fracture history), restless and repeatedly trying to climb out of bed unassisted; the bed alarm is sounding. Room 3: 66 y/o male, type 2 diabetes; scheduled rapid-acting insulin is due now as his breakfast tray arrives. Room 4: 58 y/o female, post-op day 1, requesting pain medication for moderate, stable incisional pain; ordered analgesic is available. Room 5: 70 y/o male, stable and awaiting discharge later today; his family has questions about the discharge paperwork. LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider.

patient.name: W. Osei (Room 1)
patient.admitDate: Day 3 (COPD exacerbation + community-acquired pneumonia)

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: Which client needs are most urgent
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that represent the MOST urgent client needs on this assignment.

opts.text: Room 1: increasing shortness of breath with oxygen saturation falling to 89% on oxygen and use of accessory muscles
opts.rat: A worsening airway/breathing problem with falling oxygen is the most urgent, life-threatening need (ABC).

opts.text: Room 2: high-fall-risk client restless and repeatedly trying to climb out of bed with the alarm sounding
opts.rat: An imminent fall/injury is a high-priority safety threat requiring prompt intervention.

opts.text: Room 3: scheduled rapid-acting insulin is due now as the breakfast tray arrives
opts.rat: Rapid-acting insulin must be timed with food; it is a time-critical task that cannot be arbitrarily delayed.

opts.text: Room 4: post-op client requesting pain medication for moderate, stable incisional pain
opts.rat: Pain relief is a real need, but stable moderate pain ranks below life-threat, imminent-safety, and time-critical needs.

opts.text: Room 5: family has questions about discharge paperwork
opts.rat: Non-urgent family questions are a low priority that can be acknowledged and addressed after urgent needs.

opts.text: Room 5: client is stable and comfortable awaiting discharge
opts.rat: A stable, comfortable client is a reassuring finding, not an urgent need.

opts.text: Room 4: client's vital signs are stable and within normal limits
opts.rat: Stable vital signs are reassuring and do not indicate an urgent need.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect sound prioritization.

opts.text: Airway and breathing problems take top priority, so Room 1's worsening respiratory distress with falling oxygen is seen first (ABC framework)
opts.rat: Life-threatening airway/breathing needs are the highest priority.

opts.text: After life-threatening needs, imminent safety threats are prioritized, so Room 2's client actively trying to climb out of bed needs prompt intervention
opts.rat: Preventing an imminent fall/injury is the next priority after ABCs.

opts.text: Time-critical medications tied to an event (rapid-acting insulin with a meal) are prioritized over comfort and routine requests, but after life-threat and imminent-safety needs
opts.rat: Event-timed medications are time-critical yet still rank below life-threat and imminent safety.

opts.text: Comfort requests such as pain medication and family questions always come before airway problems
opts.rat: Airway/breathing emergencies outrank comfort and informational requests.

opts.text: Clients should always be seen strictly in room-number order
opts.rat: Room order does not reflect clinical urgency; priority is by acuity and safety.

opts.text: Because the Room 5 client is being discharged, his family's paperwork questions are the top priority
opts.rat: Discharge paperwork is not urgent compared with the acute clinical and safety needs.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.sub: Rank the clients — who is seen first
steps.inst: Drag to rank the clients from FIRST seen (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Room 1 — worsening shortness of breath with oxygen saturation falling to 89%
opts.rat: FIRST — an airway/breathing problem with falling oxygen is the top (life-threat) priority.

opts.text: Room 2 — high-fall-risk client trying to climb out of bed
opts.rat: SECOND — imminent fall/injury is the next priority (safety) after ABCs.

opts.text: Room 3 — scheduled insulin due with the arriving meal tray
opts.rat: THIRD — a time-critical medication tied to the meal, prioritized over comfort and routine needs.

opts.text: Room 4 — post-op client requesting pain medication for moderate pain
opts.rat: FOURTH — a real comfort need, addressed after the acute and time-critical priorities.

opts.text: Room 5 — family with discharge-paperwork questions
opts.rat: LAST — a non-urgent request that is acknowledged and addressed after the priority needs.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Go to Room 1 first, assess breathing and oxygen, position the client upright and ensure oxygen is delivered as ordered, and report the change to the RN
opts.rat: Attending the airway/breathing priority and escalating to the RN is the correct first action.

opts.text: Direct the CNA to stay with and assist the restless fall-risk client in Room 2 and to help with the breakfast trays, while the LVN handles the clinical priorities and retains accountability
opts.rat: Delegating safe, in-scope supervision/assistance to the CNA — while the LVN keeps accountability — helps cover the assignment safely.

opts.text: Coordinate timing so the Room 3 insulin is given with the meal, and keep the team and oncoming staff informed of pending needs
opts.rat: Coordinating time-critical medication with the meal and communicating pending needs maintains safe, continuous care.

opts.text: See all clients strictly in room-number order regardless of urgency
opts.rat: Room order ignores acuity; priority is by clinical urgency and safety.

opts.text: Ask the CNA to assess the Room 1 client's breathing and decide what to do
opts.rat: Assessing and clinically judging a client's breathing is a nursing task, not delegated to a CNA.

opts.text: Ignore the Room 5 family entirely until the end of the shift
opts.rat: Low-priority needs are deferred but still acknowledged; the family is told the LVN will return, not ignored.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: For the Room 1 respiratory client, drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Go to the client, assess airway and breathing and oxygen saturation, and ensure the airway is patent
opts.rat: FIRST — assess airway/breathing and obtain current data.

opts.text: Position the client upright and ensure oxygen is being delivered as ordered
opts.rat: SECOND — within-scope interventions that support breathing immediately.

opts.text: Report the change to the RN using SBAR
opts.rat: THIRD — escalate so the RN can assess and involve the provider.

opts.text: Carry out new orders within scope (e.g., adjust oxygen per order, monitor closely), using read-back for any verbal order
opts.rat: FOURTH — implement ordered interventions correctly and keep monitoring.

opts.text: Document the assessment, interventions, and communication, and coordinate the rest of the assignment by delegating and supervising the CNA
opts.rat: LAST — document and coordinate the remaining assignment so all clients stay safe.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding.

opts.text: After the LVN positioned the Room 1 client upright and ensured oxygen, and the RN assessed and adjusted the plan, the client's oxygen saturation improved and work of breathing eased
opts.rat: Prompt prioritization and escalation improved the client's breathing — the correct outcome.

opts.text: The CNA stayed with and assisted the Room 2 fall-risk client, and no fall occurred
opts.rat: Appropriate delegation kept the at-risk client safe.

opts.text: The Room 3 client received the scheduled insulin timed with the meal
opts.rat: Coordinating the time-critical medication with food was done correctly.

opts.text: The Room 4 client's pain was relieved after the ordered medication was given
opts.rat: The comfort need was met after the higher priorities — an appropriate outcome.

opts.text: The LVN saw clients strictly in room-number order, and the Room 1 client's oxygen fell further before being seen
opts.rat: Ignoring acuity delayed care for the airway priority — a prioritization error to correct.

opts.text: The Room 2 client was left alone and got up unassisted, resulting in a near-fall
opts.rat: Failing to cover the imminent-safety need led to a near-fall — must be corrected.

opts.text: The Room 5 discharge and family questions are still pending, but the family was acknowledged and told the LVN will return
opts.rat: A low-priority need appropriately deferred with acknowledgment — no change and no harm.

opts.text: The Room 4 client's vital signs remain stable and within normal limits
opts.rat: A stable client with no change — expected and requires no new action.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Coordinated Care (the app's 'Management of Care' grouping) — establishing priorities across an assignment — using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Coordinated Care is 18-24% of the NCLEX-PN exam). Concepts reflect standard prioritization frameworks at LVN scope: life-threatening airway/breathing/circulation needs first (ABCs), then imminent safety threats, then time-critical tasks (e.g., rapid-acting insulin timed with a meal), then comfort needs, then routine/informational requests; assessment and clinical judgment stay with the nurse (not delegated to a CNA), while safe, routine, predictable tasks and supervision/assistance may be delegated to a CDPH-certified CNA with the LVN retaining accountability; and changes in condition are escalated to the RN using SBAR. Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation. Pending faculty review by Joseph Ongongo, LPT / RN reviewer.

title: Recognizing & Responding to Respiratory Deterioration (LVN Scope)
subtitle: 68 y/o female, community-acquired pneumonia, worsening oxygenation — the LVN must recognize early vs late hypoxia, intervene within scope, and escalate to the RN
nursesNote: 1000 - 68 y/o female, hospital day 2 for community-acquired pneumonia, on scheduled IV antibiotics. Earlier this morning she was resting comfortably. Over the last hour her breathing has become more labored: she is now using accessory muscles, her respiratory rate and heart rate have risen, and her oxygen saturation has fallen on room air. She appears restless and anxious and says 'I feel like I can't catch my breath.' Lung auscultation reveals crackles in the right lower lobe with diminished breath sounds. Productive cough with yellow sputum. Pain controlled; afebrile-range temperature elevated consistent with infection. The LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider.

patient.name: L. Bennett
patient.admitDate: Hospital day 2 (community-acquired pneumonia)

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that BEST indicate the client's respiratory status is worsening.

opts.text: Respiratory rate has risen to 28 with accessory-muscle use and oxygen saturation falling to 89% on room air
opts.rat: Rising respiratory rate, accessory-muscle use, and falling oxygen saturation are direct signs of worsening oxygenation and increased work of breathing.

opts.text: New restlessness and anxiety with the client saying she 'can't catch her breath'
opts.rat: Restlessness and anxiety are EARLY signs of hypoxia and are key cues to act on before the client deteriorates further.

opts.text: Heart rate has increased to 110 (tachycardia)
opts.rat: Tachycardia commonly accompanies hypoxia as the body tries to compensate — a sign of worsening status.

opts.text: Temperature is elevated consistent with the pneumonia
opts.rat: Fever is expected with pneumonia and is being treated; it is not the specific sign of respiratory deterioration here.

opts.text: The client's pain is controlled
opts.rat: Controlled pain is a reassuring finding, not a sign of deterioration.

opts.text: Bowel sounds are present in all quadrants
opts.rat: Normal bowel sounds are unrelated to the respiratory concern.

opts.text: The client ate most of her breakfast earlier
opts.rat: Adequate intake earlier is reassuring and not a current respiratory cue.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect the physiology and the LVN's response.

opts.text: Restlessness, anxiety, tachypnea, and tachycardia are EARLY signs of hypoxia, while cyanosis and a decreased level of consciousness are LATE signs — recognizing the early signs allows intervention before further deterioration
opts.rat: Early recognition of subtle hypoxia (restlessness, anxiety, increased rate) is critical; waiting for cyanosis or altered mental status means the client is already severely compromised.

opts.text: Worsening oxygenation and increased work of breathing indicate deterioration that must be reported to the RN; the LVN provides within-scope interventions (positioning, oxygen as ordered) and monitors closely
opts.rat: The LVN recognizes and escalates the change while providing supportive within-scope care; the RN assesses and the provider adjusts the plan.

opts.text: Placing the client upright (high-Fowler's) and ensuring oxygen is delivered as ordered support oxygenation and ease the work of breathing
opts.rat: Upright positioning improves lung expansion, and oxygen per order supports saturation — appropriate first interventions.

opts.text: Cyanosis and a decreased level of consciousness are the EARLIEST signs of hypoxia
opts.rat: These are LATE signs; relying on them delays recognition until the client is severely hypoxic.

opts.text: The client should be laid flat to help her rest
opts.rat: Lying flat worsens the work of breathing; an upright position is preferred for respiratory distress.

opts.text: Oxygen should be withheld until the client becomes cyanotic
opts.rat: Oxygen is provided for hypoxia per order/protocol; waiting for cyanosis is dangerous.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.inst: Drag these possible respiratory findings from MOST concerning (1) to LEAST (5).

opts.text: The client becomes difficult to arouse / develops a decreased level of consciousness
opts.rat: A falling level of consciousness is a LATE, ominous sign of severe hypoxia/impending respiratory failure — the most concerning.

opts.text: Oxygen saturation 88% with accessory-muscle use and nasal flaring
opts.rat: Significant hypoxia with markedly increased work of breathing signals serious deterioration.

opts.text: Respiratory rate 30 and shallow
opts.rat: Marked tachypnea reflects respiratory compromise and is concerning, though it ranks below altered LOC and severe hypoxia.

opts.text: Restlessness and anxiety
opts.rat: An important EARLY sign of hypoxia to catch, but less immediately dangerous than the findings above.

opts.text: Productive cough with sputum
opts.rat: Expected with pneumonia and the least acutely concerning of these findings.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Position the client upright (high-Fowler's) and ensure oxygen is delivered as ordered
opts.rat: Upright positioning and ordered oxygen support oxygenation and ease breathing.

opts.text: Encourage effective coughing and deep breathing (and incentive spirometry) as tolerated to help clear secretions and expand the lungs
opts.rat: Coughing, deep breathing, and incentive spirometry help mobilize secretions and improve ventilation.

opts.text: Report the worsening respiratory status to the RN promptly using SBAR and continue close monitoring
opts.rat: Prompt escalation and monitoring are correct; the RN assesses and the provider adjusts the plan.

opts.text: Lay the client flat and discourage coughing so she can rest
opts.rat: Lying flat and suppressing cough worsen oxygenation and secretion clearance.

opts.text: Independently increase the oxygen well above the ordered flow rate
opts.rat: Oxygen is titrated per order/protocol; making large independent changes is outside the LVN's scope — report and act per order.

opts.text: Wait to report the change until the next scheduled check
opts.rat: A worsening respiratory status is reported promptly, not deferred.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Assess airway and breathing, lung sounds, oxygen saturation, and level of consciousness
opts.rat: FIRST — gather current respiratory data and check the airway.

opts.text: Position the client upright and ensure oxygen is delivered as ordered
opts.rat: SECOND — immediate within-scope interventions that support breathing.

opts.text: Encourage coughing and deep breathing as tolerated
opts.rat: THIRD — help clear secretions and expand the lungs once positioned and oxygenated.

opts.text: Report the worsening status to the RN using SBAR and carry out new orders within scope, using read-back for verbal orders
opts.rat: FOURTH — escalate and implement ordered interventions correctly.

opts.text: Document the assessment, interventions, and communication, and continue close monitoring and reassessment
opts.rat: LAST — document and keep reassessing the client's response.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding.

opts.text: After upright positioning and ordered oxygen, the client's oxygen saturation rose and her work of breathing eased
opts.rat: Improved saturation and reduced work of breathing show the interventions are working.

opts.text: The client becomes more restless, oxygen saturation falls further, and she is now lethargic
opts.rat: Increasing distress with a falling level of consciousness is deterioration toward respiratory failure — escalate to the RN immediately.

opts.text: The client coughed up sputum and reports her breathing feels easier
opts.rat: Effective secretion clearance with subjective improvement is a positive response.

opts.text: The RN assessed the client and the provider ordered a chest x-ray and titrated oxygen; the LVN carried out the orders within scope
opts.rat: Appropriate escalation led to assessment and orders that the LVN implemented correctly.

opts.text: Staff laid the client flat and discouraged coughing so she could rest
opts.rat: This worsens oxygenation and secretion clearance and must be corrected — keep the client upright and encourage coughing.

opts.text: The client's temperature remains elevated consistent with pneumonia and is being treated with ordered antibiotics
opts.rat: The fever is expected and already being treated — no acute change in the respiratory concern.

opts.text: Right-lower-lobe crackles persist but are no worse, and oxygen saturation is stable on the titrated oxygen
opts.rat: Stable findings on the adjusted oxygen indicate the client is holding steady — continue monitoring.

opts.text: The client's oxygen saturation is maintained and she rests comfortably in high-Fowler's position
opts.rat: Maintained oxygenation with comfort in the upright position reflects an effective response.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation (respiratory alterations/oxygenation) using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Physiological Adaptation is 7-13% of the NCLEX-PN exam and is currently thin in the app). Concepts reflect standard nursing practice at LVN scope: early signs of hypoxia (restlessness, anxiety, tachypnea, tachycardia) versus late signs (cyanosis, decreased level of consciousness); upright (high-Fowler's) positioning and oxygen administration per order/protocol; encouraging coughing, deep breathing, and incentive spirometry to clear secretions and expand the lungs; and prompt escalation of a worsening respiratory status to the RN via SBAR, with the LVN collecting data and providing within-scope interventions while the RN assesses and the provider adjusts the plan (diagnosis, oxygen titration beyond protocol, and advanced airway management are not independent LVN functions). Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation. Pending faculty review by Joseph Ongongo, LPT / RN reviewer.

title: Mental Health — Suicide Risk, Crisis & Depression (Set 1)
subtitle: Suicide risk assessment, safety, crisis intervention & mood disorders
scenario: Assessing and protecting clients at risk for suicide, intervening in crisis, and caring for clients with depressive and mood disorders.

steps.q: A 29-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder tells the technician she has saved her pills and plans to take them 'this weekend.' Which factor makes this the HIGHEST acute risk?

opts.text: A specific plan, available means, and a defined time frame
opts.rat: Ideation combined with a specific plan, accessible means, and a set time frame indicates high, imminent risk requiring immediate protection.

opts.text: She has a diagnosis of depression
opts.rat: A diagnosis alone does not establish imminent risk the way plan, means, and timeline do.

opts.text: She is a young adult
opts.rat: Age is one risk factor but is far less predictive than a specific plan with means and timing.

opts.text: She is currently hospitalized
opts.rat: Hospitalization is protective; it is not what makes the risk high.

steps.q: Asking a client directly, 'Are you thinking about killing yourself?' will most likely:

opts.text: Plant the idea and increase the risk
opts.rat: This is a myth; direct questioning does not create suicidal thoughts.

opts.text: Open honest discussion without increasing risk
opts.rat: Direct, matter-of-fact questioning conveys concern and allows accurate assessment; it does not increase risk.

opts.text: Cause the client to become violent
opts.rat: Asking about suicide does not provoke violence.

opts.text: Violate the client's confidentiality
opts.rat: Assessing safety is appropriate and within the technician's role.

steps.q: A client with active suicidal ideation and a plan is admitted. The technician's PRIORITY intervention is to:

opts.text: Have the client sign a no-suicide contract and continue routine rounds
opts.rat: No-suicide contracts do not ensure safety and cannot substitute for observation.

opts.text: Place the client in a private room alone to reduce stimulation
opts.rat: Isolating a suicidal client removes protective observation and increases risk.

opts.text: Initiate close/continuous observation and remove available means of self-harm
opts.rat: Protecting the client through close observation and removing means (belts, sharps, cords) is the immediate safety priority.

opts.text: Reassure the client that everything will be fine
opts.rat: False reassurance dismisses the client's distress and does not address safety.

steps.q: A severely depressed client who has been withdrawn suddenly appears calm and cheerful and begins giving away belongings. The technician should:

opts.text: Conclude the client has fully recovered
opts.rat: Sudden calm after severe depression can be an ominous sign, not proof of recovery.

opts.text: Reduce the level of observation as a reward
opts.rat: Lowering observation at this point could be dangerous.

opts.text: Encourage the client to give away more items
opts.rat: This ignores a potential warning sign.

opts.text: Recognize a possible warning sign of suicide and increase observation
opts.rat: A sudden lift in mood and giving away possessions may signal the client has decided to act on a plan; vigilance must increase.

steps.q: The single strongest predictor of future suicide risk is:

opts.text: A previous suicide attempt
opts.rat: A prior attempt is the strongest known predictor of future suicide; it must always be assessed and taken seriously.

opts.text: Being employed full-time
opts.rat: Employment is generally protective, not a strong risk predictor.

opts.text: Having many close friends
opts.rat: Strong social support is protective.

opts.text: A single episode of sadness
opts.rat: Transient sadness is far less predictive than a history of attempts.

steps.q: A client is placed on one-to-one suicide precautions. This means the technician must:

opts.text: Check the client every 30 minutes
opts.rat: Intermittent checks are a lower level of observation, not one-to-one.

opts.text: Maintain constant, arm's-length visual contact at all times, including toileting
opts.rat: One-to-one precautions require continuous, close visual observation at all times, including in the bathroom, to prevent self-harm.

opts.text: Observe the client only during the day shift
opts.rat: Continuous observation applies around the clock.

opts.text: Allow the client to be alone if calm
opts.rat: Constant observation cannot be interrupted based on apparent calm.

steps.q: To make the environment safe for a suicidal client, the technician should:

opts.text: Allow the client to keep all personal items unchecked
opts.rat: Unchecked belongings may contain means of self-harm.

opts.text: Provide a glass drinking cup and metal utensils
opts.rat: Glass and sharp utensils can be used for self-harm.

opts.text: Remove potentially harmful items such as belts, shoelaces, sharps, and cords
opts.rat: Removing means of self-harm from the environment is a core safety intervention for suicidal clients.

opts.text: Leave the client alone in a locked private room
opts.rat: Isolation removes observation and increases risk.

steps.q: A depressed client starting an antidepressant begins to have more energy but still voices hopelessness. This period is important because:

opts.text: The client is now at no risk
opts.rat: Increased energy with persistent hopelessness is a higher-risk period, not a safe one.

opts.text: Observation can safely be discontinued
opts.rat: This is precisely when vigilance should be maintained.

opts.text: The medication has clearly failed
opts.rat: Energy returning first is an expected pattern, not treatment failure.

opts.text: Suicide risk may increase when energy returns before mood improves
opts.rat: Returning energy can precede mood improvement, giving a still-hopeless client the ability to act on suicidal thoughts; observation must continue.

steps.q: A client says, 'Everyone would be better off without me.' The BEST response by the technician is to:

opts.text: Ask directly, 'Are you thinking about killing yourself?'
opts.rat: A statement implying worthlessness warrants a direct, caring suicide-risk assessment.

opts.text: Say, 'Don't talk like that.'
opts.rat: This shuts down communication and dismisses the client's feelings.

opts.text: Say, 'Everyone feels that way sometimes.'
opts.rat: This minimizes a potentially serious disclosure.

opts.text: Change the subject to something positive
opts.rat: Avoiding the statement neglects a possible safety concern.

steps.q: The MOST therapeutic response to a client who says, 'Nobody cares whether I live or die,' is:

opts.text: 'Of course people care about you.'
opts.rat: This is false reassurance that dismisses the feeling.

opts.text: 'You sound like you're feeling very alone right now.'
opts.rat: Reflecting the client's feeling acknowledges their experience and invites them to share more.

opts.text: 'Why would you say something like that?'
opts.rat: 'Why' questions can sound confrontational and block communication.

opts.text: 'You have so much to live for.'
opts.rat: This minimizes distress and is non-therapeutic.

steps.q: The focus of crisis intervention is BEST described as:

opts.text: Long-term personality change
opts.rat: Crisis intervention is short-term, not focused on restructuring personality.

opts.text: Exploring early childhood in depth
opts.rat: In-depth exploration is not the goal during an acute crisis.

opts.text: Short-term help focused on the immediate problem and coping/safety
opts.rat: Crisis intervention is time-limited and directed at resolving the immediate problem, restoring coping, and ensuring safety.

opts.text: Waiting for the crisis to resolve on its own
opts.rat: Active, supportive intervention is provided, not passive waiting.

steps.q: Which cluster of findings is most consistent with major depression?

opts.text: Elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, and rapid speech
opts.rat: These describe mania, not depression.

opts.text: Hallucinations and disorganized speech only
opts.rat: These are psychotic features, not the defining features of depression.

opts.text: Excessive goal-directed activity and grandiosity
opts.rat: These are manic symptoms.

opts.text: Depressed mood, loss of interest, appetite and sleep changes, and fatigue
opts.rat: Depressed mood, anhedonia, appetite/sleep disturbance, low energy, and worthlessness are core features of major depression.

steps.q: A client with severe depression has marked psychomotor retardation. The BEST approach to activities of daily living is to:

opts.text: Allow extra time with simple, step-by-step encouragement
opts.rat: Depression slows thinking and movement; extra time and gentle, structured guidance support functioning without frustration.

opts.text: Do everything for the client to conserve their energy
opts.rat: Doing everything fosters dependence and does not support recovery.

opts.text: Insist the client complete tasks quickly
opts.rat: Pressuring a slowed client increases frustration and failure.

opts.text: Withhold help entirely to force independence
opts.rat: Abruptly withholding support can overwhelm a severely depressed client.

steps.q: A withdrawn, depressed client refuses to get out of bed or attend meals. The technician should:

opts.text: Allow the client to remain isolated indefinitely
opts.rat: Prolonged isolation worsens depression.

opts.text: Provide consistent, gentle encouragement and structure for participation
opts.rat: Consistent, non-punitive encouragement with structure supports a withdrawn client without forcing or abandoning them.

opts.text: Demand immediate compliance
opts.rat: Demands are non-therapeutic and may increase resistance.

opts.text: Withdraw all attention until the client complies
opts.rat: Withdrawing attention is punitive and harmful.

steps.q: When teaching a client about a newly prescribed SSRI antidepressant, the technician should explain that:

opts.text: It works fully within 24 hours
opts.rat: Antidepressant effect is delayed, not immediate.

opts.text: It should be stopped as soon as mood improves
opts.rat: Stopping early risks relapse and discontinuation symptoms.

opts.text: Full effect may take 2–4 weeks or longer, and it should not be stopped abruptly
opts.rat: SSRIs have a delayed onset of 2–4+ weeks; clients should continue as prescribed and avoid abrupt discontinuation.

opts.text: It causes immediate dependence like a sedative
opts.rat: SSRIs do not cause the dependence associated with sedatives.

steps.q: A 20-year-old client is starting an antidepressant. The technician monitors closely because the black box warning notes an increased risk of:

opts.text: Immediate hair loss
opts.rat: This is not the black box concern.

opts.text: Permanent memory loss
opts.rat: This is not associated with SSRIs.

opts.text: Hyperthyroidism
opts.rat: This is unrelated to the warning.

opts.text: Suicidal thinking in those under 25, especially early in treatment
opts.rat: Antidepressants carry a black box warning for increased suicidality in children, adolescents, and young adults under 25, particularly when starting or changing the dose.

steps.q: A client grieving the recent death of a spouse says, 'I just can't believe he's gone.' The technician recognizes this as:

opts.text: A normal early grief reaction
opts.rat: Disbelief and denial are common, normal early responses in grief; supportive presence and listening are appropriate.

opts.text: A psychotic delusion requiring medication
opts.rat: Normal grief is not psychosis.

opts.text: Evidence of malingering
opts.rat: There is no basis to label normal grief as feigning.

opts.text: A sign the client needs restraint
opts.rat: Grief is not a reason for restraint.

steps.q: Which response by the technician is therapeutic for a grieving client?

opts.text: 'You need to move on with your life.'
opts.rat: This dismisses the client's grief and rushes the process.

opts.text: 'Tell me about your husband.'
opts.rat: Inviting the client to talk about the deceased facilitates healthy grieving and shows genuine interest.

opts.text: 'At least he is no longer suffering.'
opts.rat: This minimizes the loss and offers premature reassurance.

opts.text: 'You are still young and will find someone else.'
opts.rat: This dismisses the current loss.

steps.q: A woman 11 days postpartum reports hearing voices telling her the baby is 'evil.' The technician recognizes postpartum psychosis and knows the PRIORITY is to:

opts.text: Reassure her the thoughts will pass and let her rest with the baby
opts.rat: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency; leaving mother and infant together unsupervised is unsafe.

opts.text: Encourage more alone bonding time
opts.rat: Unsupervised time increases danger during postpartum psychosis.

opts.text: Ensure the safety of the mother and infant and never leave them alone together
opts.rat: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with real infant-harm risk; ensuring safety, direct supervision, and urgent escalation are the priority.

opts.text: Document the finding and reassess in the morning
opts.rat: This is an emergency requiring immediate action, not delayed reassessment.

steps.q: Which change suggests a depressed client is beginning to improve?

opts.text: Increasing social withdrawal
opts.rat: Greater withdrawal suggests worsening, not improvement.

opts.text: Refusing to speak with anyone
opts.rat: This indicates continued or worsening depression.

opts.text: Giving away personal possessions
opts.rat: This can be a warning sign of suicide, not improvement.

opts.text: Improved grooming, appetite, and participation in activities
opts.rat: Return of self-care, appetite, and engagement are signs of improving depression.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Mental Health — Schizophrenia, Psychosis & Communication (Set 2)
subtitle: Positive/negative symptoms, hallucinations, delusions & therapeutic communication
scenario: Caring for clients experiencing psychosis: recognizing symptoms, ensuring safety, and using therapeutic communication.

steps.q: Which are considered POSITIVE symptoms of schizophrenia?

opts.text: Hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized speech
opts.rat: Positive symptoms are an excess or distortion of normal function—hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized speech/behavior.

opts.text: Flat affect and social withdrawal
opts.rat: These are negative symptoms (a loss of normal function).

opts.text: Lack of motivation (avolition)
opts.rat: Avolition is a negative symptom.

opts.text: Poverty of speech (alogia)
opts.rat: Alogia is a negative symptom.

steps.q: A client sits alone, shows little facial expression, speaks minimally, and has stopped participating in activities. These NEGATIVE symptoms include:

opts.text: Hallucinations and paranoia
opts.rat: These are positive symptoms, not negative.

opts.text: Flat affect, alogia, and avolition
opts.rat: Flat affect, poverty of speech (alogia), and lack of motivation (avolition) are negative symptoms reflecting a loss of normal function.

opts.text: Grandiose delusions
opts.rat: A delusion is a positive symptom.

opts.text: Rapid, pressured speech
opts.rat: This suggests mania, not negative symptoms.

steps.q: A client states that voices are telling him to hurt another client. The technician's PRIORITY is to:

opts.text: Tell the client the voices are not real
opts.rat: Arguing about the voices does not address the immediate danger.

opts.text: Leave the client alone to reduce stimulation
opts.rat: Leaving a client with harmful command hallucinations is unsafe.

opts.text: Ensure safety, stay with the client, and notify the nurse while increasing observation
opts.rat: Command hallucinations to harm are a safety emergency; ensuring safety, staying with the client, and escalating are the priority.

opts.text: Encourage the client to act out the feelings
opts.rat: This could lead to harm and is inappropriate.

steps.q: When a client is experiencing auditory hallucinations, the BEST assessment question is:

opts.text: 'The voices aren't real, are they?'
opts.rat: This is leading and dismissive, and does not assess content.

opts.text: 'Why are you making this up?'
opts.rat: This is accusatory and non-therapeutic.

opts.text: 'Just ignore the voices and they'll stop.'
opts.rat: This dismisses the client's experience and offers no assessment.

opts.text: 'What are the voices saying to you right now?'
opts.rat: Assessing the content of hallucinations—especially command hallucinations—is essential for safety.

steps.q: A client firmly believes the government has implanted a tracking chip in his arm. The MOST therapeutic response is:

opts.text: 'I don't share that belief, but I can see you feel frightened.'
opts.rat: The technician neither argues with nor reinforces the delusion, but acknowledges the underlying feeling to maintain trust.

opts.text: 'That's not true; there is no chip.'
opts.rat: Directly arguing against a delusion tends to increase defensiveness.

opts.text: 'Show me where they put the chip.'
opts.rat: This reinforces and validates the delusion.

opts.text: 'You're being paranoid.'
opts.rat: Labeling the client is dismissive and non-therapeutic.

steps.q: A client insists the television news anchor is sending him secret personal messages. This is an example of a(n):

opts.text: Illusion
opts.rat: An illusion is a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus, not a belief about personal messages.

opts.text: Idea of reference
opts.rat: An idea of reference is the false belief that neutral external events have special personal meaning directed at the client.

opts.text: Neologism
opts.rat: A neologism is a made-up word.

opts.text: Echolalia
opts.rat: Echolalia is repeating another person's words.

steps.q: A client uses invented words that have meaning only to himself, such as 'the flibbergast is coming.' This is called:

opts.text: Clang association
opts.rat: Clang associations are based on rhyming sounds.

opts.text: Echopraxia
opts.rat: Echopraxia is imitating another's movements.

opts.text: Neologism
opts.rat: Neologisms are newly invented words with private meaning, seen in psychosis.

opts.text: Flight of ideas
opts.rat: Flight of ideas is rapid shifting between topics, typical of mania.

steps.q: The difference between a hallucination and an illusion is that a hallucination:

opts.text: Is a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus
opts.rat: That describes an illusion, not a hallucination.

opts.text: Is always a false fixed belief
opts.rat: That describes a delusion.

opts.text: Only occurs in dementia
opts.rat: Hallucinations occur in many conditions, not only dementia.

opts.text: Is a false sensory perception with no external stimulus present
opts.rat: A hallucination is a sensory perception (hearing, seeing) that occurs without any real external stimulus; an illusion misinterprets a real one.

steps.q: When approaching a client with paranoid ideation, the technician should:

opts.text: Approach calmly, maintain interpersonal space, and be honest and consistent
opts.rat: A calm, non-intrusive, honest, and consistent approach with adequate personal space builds trust and reduces suspicion.

opts.text: Use frequent touch to convey warmth
opts.rat: Unexpected touch can be perceived as threatening by a paranoid client.

opts.text: Whisper with coworkers near the client
opts.rat: Whispering nearby increases suspicion and mistrust.

opts.text: Make many promises quickly to gain trust
opts.rat: Unkept promises damage trust; consistency matters more than promises.

steps.q: A suspicious client refuses meals, convinced the food is poisoned. The BEST intervention is to:

opts.text: Insist the client eat the plated hospital tray
opts.rat: Insisting increases fear and resistance.

opts.text: Offer sealed, packaged foods the client opens himself
opts.rat: Intact, sealed foods the client opens reduce fear of tampering and support nutrition without confrontation.

opts.text: Tell the client the food is safe and walk away
opts.rat: This does not address the client's fear or ensure intake.

opts.text: Withhold food until the client trusts staff
opts.rat: Withholding nutrition is harmful.

steps.q: A stable client with schizophrenia says he wants to stop his antipsychotic because he 'feels fine now.' The BEST teaching is:

opts.text: 'You can stop once your symptoms are gone.'
opts.rat: Stopping when symptoms resolve commonly leads to relapse.

opts.text: 'The medicine is only needed while you're in the hospital.'
opts.rat: Maintenance therapy usually continues after discharge.

opts.text: 'Continuing the medication as prescribed helps prevent your symptoms from returning.'
opts.rat: Maintenance antipsychotic therapy prevents relapse even when the client feels well; abrupt discontinuation often causes recurrence.

opts.text: 'Take it only when you hear voices.'
opts.rat: Antipsychotics are taken consistently, not as needed for symptoms.

steps.q: Which is an example of a therapeutic communication technique?

opts.text: Offering false reassurance
opts.rat: False reassurance blocks communication.

opts.text: Giving personal advice
opts.rat: Giving advice discourages the client's own problem-solving.

opts.text: Changing the subject when topics are difficult
opts.rat: Changing the subject avoids the client's concerns and blocks communication.

opts.text: Using open-ended questions and reflecting the client's feelings
opts.rat: Open-ended questions and reflection encourage the client to express thoughts and feelings.

steps.q: Which statement by the technician is a NON-therapeutic communication block?

opts.text: 'Why do you always do that?'
opts.rat: 'Why' questions can feel accusatory and defensive, blocking communication.

opts.text: 'Tell me more about what that was like for you.'
opts.rat: This is an open-ended, therapeutic invitation to share.

opts.text: 'I'll sit here with you for a while.'
opts.rat: Offering self is therapeutic.

opts.text: 'You seem upset right now.'
opts.rat: Reflecting an observed feeling is therapeutic.

steps.q: The therapeutic use of silence during a conversation with a client allows the client to:

opts.text: Feel ignored and rejected
opts.rat: Purposeful silence conveys acceptance, not rejection.

opts.text: Gather thoughts and take the lead in what to share
opts.rat: Purposeful silence gives the client time to reflect and encourages them to continue at their own pace.

opts.text: Realize the technician is not interested
opts.rat: Silence, used therapeutically, communicates attentiveness.

opts.text: End the interaction as quickly as possible
opts.rat: The goal is to support reflection, not rush the client.

steps.q: A client's speech jumps between unrelated ideas with no logical connection, making it hard to follow. This is BEST described as:

opts.text: Flat affect
opts.rat: Flat affect refers to reduced emotional expression, not thought disorganization.

opts.text: Anhedonia
opts.rat: Anhedonia is the inability to feel pleasure.

opts.text: Loose associations (disorganized thinking)
opts.rat: Loose associations are a disorganized thought pattern in which ideas shift with little or no logical connection.

opts.text: Waxy flexibility
opts.rat: Waxy flexibility is a motor sign in catatonia.

steps.q: A client with psychosis appears to be responding to internal stimuli during a conversation. The technician should:

opts.text: Play along with what the voices might be saying
opts.rat: Reinforcing hallucinations is not therapeutic.

opts.text: Speak in long, complex sentences
opts.rat: Complex speech is hard to process during psychosis.

opts.text: Stop all communication until the client is medicated
opts.rat: Supportive communication should continue.

opts.text: Speak clearly and simply, and gently refocus the client on the present conversation
opts.rat: Clear, simple communication and reorienting the client to reality and the present interaction are helpful during active hallucinations.

steps.q: A client with schizophrenia stopped his medication and relapsed, and he does not believe he is ill. This lack of awareness of illness is called:

opts.text: Anosognosia (lack of insight)
opts.rat: Anosognosia is a lack of awareness/insight into one's own illness, a common cause of nonadherence in schizophrenia.

opts.text: Malingering
opts.rat: Malingering is intentionally faking illness for gain, not lack of insight.

opts.text: Confabulation
opts.rat: Confabulation is filling memory gaps with invented information.

opts.text: Tangentiality
opts.rat: Tangentiality is a speech pattern that wanders off point.

steps.q: A client with disorganized thinking is overwhelmed on a busy unit. A helpful environmental intervention is to:

opts.text: Increase noise and activity to keep the client engaged
opts.rat: Overstimulation worsens disorganization and agitation.

opts.text: Provide a calm, low-stimulation environment and simple, clear communication
opts.rat: A calm, structured, low-stimulation setting with simple communication helps a client with disorganized thinking.

opts.text: Enroll the client in several groups at once
opts.rat: Multiple simultaneous demands increase overwhelm.

opts.text: Leave the television and radio on loudly
opts.rat: Loud, competing stimuli increase distress.

steps.q: The technician notices a client 'cheeking' (hiding) medication in the side of the mouth. The BEST action is to:

opts.text: Ignore it if the client seems calm
opts.rat: Cheeking risks nonadherence or later overdose and must be addressed.

opts.text: Give a double dose next time
opts.rat: Altering the dose is outside the technician's authority and unsafe.

opts.text: Check the mouth after administration and report the cheeking to the nurse
opts.rat: Verifying the medication was swallowed (mouth check) and reporting cheeking ensures the client is treated and safe.

opts.text: Let the client save the pills for later
opts.rat: Allowing saved pills risks a dangerous overdose.

steps.q: Which approach BEST helps build trust with a withdrawn client who has schizophrenia?

opts.text: Demand that the client immediately join a large group
opts.rat: Forcing group participation can overwhelm a withdrawn client.

opts.text: Avoid the client entirely until they approach staff
opts.rat: Avoidance does not build a therapeutic relationship.

opts.text: Share personal problems to seem relatable
opts.rat: Self-disclosure of personal problems is not therapeutic and blurs boundaries.

opts.text: Make brief, consistent, low-pressure contacts and follow through on what you say
opts.rat: Short, regular, reliable interactions and dependable follow-through gradually build trust with a withdrawn client.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Mental Health — Bipolar Disorder & Mood Stabilizers (Set 3)
subtitle: Mania safety, lithium toxicity/monitoring, valproate, carbamazepine & lamotrigine
scenario: Caring for clients with bipolar disorder during mania and depression, and safely monitoring mood-stabilizing medications.

steps.q: A client with bipolar I disorder has not slept in three days, speaks rapidly, and plans to 'buy five businesses today.' These findings are consistent with:

opts.text: A manic episode
opts.rat: Decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, and impaired judgment are hallmark features of a manic episode.

opts.text: Major depression
opts.rat: Depression involves low mood and energy, not grandiosity and hyperactivity.

opts.text: Catatonia
opts.rat: Catatonia involves marked immobility or purposeless motor activity, not grandiose planning.

opts.text: Generalized anxiety disorder
opts.rat: GAD features chronic worry, not grandiosity and decreased need for sleep.

steps.q: A key safety concern during an acute manic episode is:

opts.text: Excessive sleeping
opts.rat: Mania involves decreased, not increased, sleep.

opts.text: Impulsivity and poor judgment leading to harm or exhaustion
opts.rat: Mania brings impulsivity, poor judgment, and hyperactivity, increasing risk of injury, risky behavior, and physical exhaustion/dehydration.

opts.text: Social withdrawal and isolation
opts.rat: Withdrawal is more typical of depression.

opts.text: Slowed movements
opts.rat: Mania features increased activity, not psychomotor slowing.

steps.q: A manic client cannot sit still long enough to eat a meal. The BEST intervention is to provide:

opts.text: A large multi-course meal in the dining room
opts.rat: A hyperactive, distractible client cannot sit to eat a full meal.

opts.text: Only meals eaten while seated quietly
opts.rat: Requiring the client to sit quietly is unrealistic during acute mania.

opts.text: High-calorie finger foods and fluids the client can carry
opts.rat: Portable high-calorie finger foods and fluids maintain nutrition and hydration without requiring the client to sit.

opts.text: Caffeinated drinks to keep energy up
opts.rat: Caffeine increases agitation and hyperactivity.

steps.q: The environment for a client in acute mania should be:

opts.text: Brightly lit with competitive group games
opts.rat: Stimulating, competitive activities escalate mania.

opts.text: Crowded to encourage socializing
opts.rat: Crowding and overstimulation worsen mania.

opts.text: Full of loud music to match the client's energy
opts.rat: Loud stimulation increases agitation.

opts.text: Calm with reduced stimulation
opts.rat: A calm, low-stimulation environment helps prevent escalation of hyperactivity and irritability.

steps.q: The therapeutic serum lithium level for maintenance is approximately:

opts.rat: Maintenance lithium is 0.6–1.2 mEq/L; levels above 1.5 mEq/L are toxic.
This is below the therapeutic range and unlikely to be effective.
This range indicates toxicity.
This is a dangerously toxic level.
