Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level and stated conceptually, marked for faculty confirmation: the priority hierarchy (life-threats via airway-breathing-circulation, then imminent safety, including active suicidality/violence in the psychiatric setting); unstable-before-stable and unexpected-before-expected; a needs-based framework (physiological and safety needs before higher-level needs); applied who-comes-first judgment across psychiatric and medical scenarios (chest pain over a routine conversation, choking over emotional needs, a fall-risk toileting need over restocking, an acute change over a chronic stable condition, an emergency over a routine activity); appropriate delegation to the technician (routine, predictable, in-scope tasks with stable clients and known outcomes) versus tasks requiring nursing judgment that are not delegated (initial assessment of an unstable client, care planning, initial teaching for a new diagnosis, evaluating/revising the plan); declining and communicating when a task is untrained or out of scope; the conditions for safe delegation (right task, clear direction, appropriate supervision, ability to clarify); prompt escalation of a new change in condition; never skipping required safety measures (such as ordered close observation); efficient, reassessed time management; and structured communication of priority concerns via SBAR. This management-of-care application set complements, without duplicating, the legal scope-of-practice, supervision, delegation-criteria, and accountability content in legal-core-04, and uses the SBAR hand-off introduced in bnc-core-15. No specific numeric values are asserted. Pending faculty review.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
subtitle: 22 y/o male with type 1 diabetes, hyperglycemia and deep breathing
nursesNote: 1200 - 22 y/o male with type 1 diabetes brought to the ED by a friend. He ran out of insulin 3 days ago and has had a flu-like illness. He reports increasing thirst, frequent urination, nausea, and abdominal pain, and is now drowsy and confused. Breathing is deep and rapid, and the friend notes a 'fruity' smell to his breath. Mucous membranes are dry and skin turgor is poor. Fingerstick glucose reads 'HIGH'; the laboratory glucose is 540 mg/dL.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate diabetic ketoacidosis.

opts.text: Glucose 540 mg/dL with positive ketones
opts.rat: Marked hyperglycemia with elevated ketones is the biochemical hallmark of DKA.

opts.text: Deep, rapid (Kussmaul) respirations and a fruity breath odor
opts.rat: Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2 to compensate for metabolic acidosis, and the fruity odor reflects ketones.

opts.text: Low pH (7.18) and low bicarbonate (12)
opts.rat: A low pH with low bicarbonate confirms the metabolic acidosis of DKA.

opts.text: Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, and low blood pressure
opts.rat: These reflect the significant dehydration from osmotic diuresis in DKA.

opts.text: Oxygen saturation of 98%
opts.rat: A normal oxygen saturation is reassuring but is not a sign of DKA.

opts.text: He is 22 years old
opts.rat: Age is background information, not a clinical cue for DKA.

opts.text: He has a friend at the bedside
opts.rat: This is not a clinical finding relevant to DKA.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: Insulin deficiency caused hyperglycemia and fat breakdown into ketones, producing the acidosis
opts.rat: Without insulin, the body breaks down fat for fuel, generating ketoacids that cause the metabolic acidosis of DKA.

opts.text: The potassium may look normal or high now but total body potassium is depleted, and it will fall as insulin is given
opts.rat: Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells, so serum potassium can be high despite total-body depletion; insulin drives it back in, dropping serum levels-so potassium must be watched closely.

opts.text: Fluid replacement is a first priority because the client is severely dehydrated
opts.rat: Osmotic diuresis causes large fluid losses; IV isotonic fluids are started early to restore volume and perfusion.

opts.text: The best initial treatment is a single dose of subcutaneous long-acting insulin
opts.rat: Acute DKA is treated with IV fluids and a continuous IV regular insulin infusion, not a single dose of long-acting subcutaneous insulin.

opts.text: The deep, rapid breathing should be suppressed with sedation
opts.rat: Kussmaul respirations are a compensatory response to acidosis and must not be suppressed; treating the DKA resolves them.

opts.text: Fluids should be restricted to avoid overload
opts.rat: The client is volume-depleted; restricting fluids would worsen dehydration and perfusion.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis from missed insulin and illness
opts.rat: Missed insulin plus infection, with hyperglycemia, ketosis, and acidosis, makes DKA the clear diagnosis.

opts.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
opts.rat: A key differential, but HHS typically occurs in older type 2 clients with very high glucose and minimal ketones/acidosis-this client has marked ketoacidosis.

opts.text: Sepsis from the recent flu-like illness
opts.rat: Infection can precipitate DKA and must be evaluated, but it does not by itself explain the ketoacidosis picture.

opts.text: Hypoglycemia
opts.rat: The glucose is very high, not low, so hypoglycemia does not fit.

opts.text: A primary respiratory disorder causing the fast breathing
opts.rat: Least likely: the rapid breathing is compensating for a metabolic acidosis, not a primary lung problem.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions.

opts.text: Start IV isotonic fluid (0.9% normal saline) to restore volume
opts.rat: IV isotonic fluid resuscitation is a first priority to correct the severe dehydration in DKA.

opts.text: Begin a continuous IV regular insulin infusion per protocol
opts.rat: Regular insulin by continuous IV infusion lowers glucose and stops ketone production; only regular insulin is given IV.

opts.text: Monitor potassium closely and replace it as ordered as insulin is given
opts.rat: Because insulin drives potassium into cells, potassium must be monitored and replaced to prevent dangerous hypokalemia.

opts.text: Monitor glucose, electrolytes, and acid-base, and add dextrose to fluids when glucose approaches 200-250
opts.rat: Frequent monitoring guides therapy, and dextrose is added as glucose falls so the insulin infusion can continue clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Give a large IV push of regular insulin without starting fluids
opts.rat: Fluids are prioritized, and insulin is given by controlled infusion; a large push without fluids is unsafe.

opts.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate routinely to all DKA clients
opts.rat: Bicarbonate is not given routinely; the acidosis resolves as fluids and insulin correct the underlying process.

opts.text: Withhold potassium entirely because the level is currently high
opts.rat: The level will fall with insulin; potassium is monitored and replaced rather than ignored.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Establish IV access and begin isotonic fluid resuscitation
opts.rat: FIRST-restoring circulating volume addresses the immediate threat of dehydration and poor perfusion.

opts.text: Verify the potassium level before/as the insulin infusion is started
opts.rat: SECOND-potassium must be checked because insulin is held if potassium is dangerously low until it is replaced.

opts.text: Start the continuous IV regular insulin infusion per protocol
opts.rat: THIRD-insulin lowers glucose and halts ketogenesis once fluids are running and potassium is addressed.

opts.text: Monitor glucose, potassium, and acid-base frequently and add dextrose as glucose falls
opts.rat: FOURTH-frequent monitoring and adding dextrose prevent hypoglycemia and hypokalemia during treatment.

opts.text: Provide diabetes teaching (sick-day rules, not stopping insulin) before discharge
opts.rat: LAST-education prevents recurrence once the client is stabilized.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: During treatment, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Glucose falls steadily toward 250 and the pH rises toward normal
opts.rat: A controlled fall in glucose with a rising pH shows the DKA is resolving with treatment.

opts.text: Mental status clears and the Kussmaul breathing slows to a normal rate
opts.rat: Improving consciousness and normalizing respirations indicate the acidosis is correcting.

opts.text: Skin turgor and blood pressure normalize with fluids
opts.rat: Restored perfusion and turgor reflect successful volume replacement.

opts.text: Potassium drops to 2.9 mEq/L during the insulin infusion with new ECG changes
opts.rat: Hypokalemia developing as insulin drives potassium into cells is dangerous and requires holding insulin per protocol and replacing potassium.

opts.text: Glucose falls to 55 mg/dL because dextrose was not added to the fluids
opts.rat: Hypoglycemia from continuing insulin without adding dextrose is a preventable complication needing immediate treatment.

opts.text: The client develops a severe headache and decreasing responsiveness after rapid correction
opts.rat: New headache and declining consciousness raise concern for cerebral edema, a serious complication of overly rapid correction requiring urgent evaluation.

opts.text: Heart rate remains 118 early in resuscitation before much fluid has been given
opts.rat: A persistently elevated heart rate early in treatment reflects ongoing dehydration that has not yet been corrected.

opts.text: Oxygen saturation stays at 98%
opts.rat: A stable, normal oxygen saturation is neither an improvement nor a decline in this context.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction
subtitle: 58 y/o male, 10 minutes into a PRBC transfusion
nursesNote: 1410 - 58 y/o male, post-op day 1 after partial colectomy, ordered 1 unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) for symptomatic anemia (Hgb 6.8). Two-RN verification of client ID, blood type, and unit completed; transfusion started at 1400 via a Y-tubing filter set with 0.9% normal saline. At 1410 (about 10 minutes in) the client becomes anxious, reports chills, low back/flank pain, and a 'sense of doom.' Temperature has risen from 98.6F to 101.8F. He reports the infusion site 'burns.' Approximately 40 mL has infused.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: Identify signs of a transfusion reaction
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate an acute transfusion reaction.

opts.text: Chills and a temperature rise to 101.8F within 10 minutes of starting the unit
opts.rat: Fever and chills occurring soon after starting a transfusion are hallmark early signs of a transfusion reaction and require immediate attention.

opts.text: Low back/flank pain and burning at the infusion site
opts.rat: Flank/back pain and infusion-site burning are classic signs of acute hemolytic reaction from red-cell destruction.

opts.text: New hypotension (90/52) with tachycardia (HR 120)
opts.rat: A sudden drop in blood pressure with tachycardia signals a severe systemic reaction and hemodynamic compromise.

opts.text: Anxiety and a reported 'sense of doom'
opts.rat: A sense of impending doom and acute anxiety frequently accompany an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

opts.text: Pre-transfusion hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL
opts.rat: The low hemoglobin is the reason for the transfusion, not a sign of a reaction.

opts.text: Baseline blood pressure 126/74 at 1400
opts.rat: This is a normal pre-transfusion baseline, not a reaction cue.

opts.text: Two-RN verification was completed before starting
opts.rat: Correct verification is a safety step, not a clinical sign of a reaction.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: Link findings to the type of reaction
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret these findings.

opts.text: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, and burning at the site together suggest an acute HEMOLYTIC reaction
opts.rat: This cluster—fever, flank/back pain, hypotension, and infusion-site pain—is characteristic of acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, usually from ABO incompatibility.

opts.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of transfused red cells can lead to hemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury
opts.rat: Hemolysis releases free hemoglobin that can turn urine dark and damage the kidneys; severe cases can trigger DIC.

opts.text: The reaction is severe and requires the transfusion to be stopped immediately
opts.rat: Signs of hemolysis with hemodynamic instability are an emergency; the transfusion must be stopped at once.

opts.text: These findings most likely represent a mild allergic (urticarial) reaction that needs only an antihistamine
opts.rat: A mild allergic reaction causes hives/itching without fever, flank pain, or hypotension; this presentation is far more serious.

opts.text: The findings indicate simple circulatory overload (TACO) and should be treated with a diuretic while continuing the unit
opts.rat: TACO causes fluid overload (hypertension, crackles, dyspnea), not fever with flank pain and hypotension; continuing the unit would be dangerous here.

opts.text: The client is simply anxious and the transfusion can continue at a slower rate
opts.rat: Attributing hemolytic signs to anxiety and continuing the transfusion could be fatal.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO incompatibility)
opts.rat: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, site burning, and doom within minutes make acute hemolytic reaction most likely.

opts.text: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction
opts.rat: Common and causes fever/chills, but does not typically cause flank pain, hypotension, and infusion-site burning.

opts.text: Allergic (urticarial) reaction
opts.rat: Causes hives/itching; would not explain fever with flank pain and hypotension.

opts.text: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)
opts.rat: Causes dyspnea, hypertension, and crackles from volume overload—not this hemolytic picture, and only 40 mL has infused.

opts.text: Anxiety unrelated to the transfusion
opts.rat: Least likely: the objective fever, hypotension, and flank pain point to a true reaction, not anxiety alone.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate immediate interventions.

opts.text: STOP the transfusion immediately
opts.rat: Stopping the transfusion at the first sign of a serious reaction is the single most important action to limit hemolysis.

opts.text: Keep the IV line open with 0.9% normal saline using NEW tubing (not the blood set)
opts.rat: Maintaining IV access with normal saline through new tubing preserves the line for treatment and supports blood pressure/renal perfusion without infusing more blood.

opts.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank
opts.rat: The provider directs treatment and the blood bank must investigate the reaction and re-check compatibility.

opts.text: Stay with the client, monitor vital signs closely, and reassess frequently
opts.rat: Close monitoring detects worsening hemodynamics or airway compromise so care can be escalated quickly.

opts.text: Slow the transfusion and continue observing the client
opts.rat: The transfusion must be stopped, not slowed; continuing to infuse incompatible blood worsens hemolysis.

opts.text: Flush the remaining blood in the tubing into the client to avoid waste
opts.rat: Flushing residual blood into the client delivers more incompatible cells and is dangerous.

opts.text: Discard the blood bag and tubing in the trash
opts.rat: The blood bag and tubing must be saved and returned to the blood bank for investigation, not discarded.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the transfusion
opts.rat: FIRST—immediately halting the infusion stops delivery of incompatible blood.

opts.text: Disconnect the blood tubing and keep the line open with 0.9% normal saline via new tubing
opts.rat: SECOND—maintains IV access and supports perfusion without infusing more blood.

opts.text: Assess vital signs and airway, and stay with the client
opts.rat: THIRD—rapid reassessment guides how urgently care must be escalated.

opts.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank
opts.rat: FOURTH—the provider orders treatment and the blood bank begins the reaction workup.

opts.text: Send the blood bag, tubing, and required blood/urine specimens to the blood bank/lab
opts.rat: LAST of these steps—returning the unit and specimens allows compatibility re-testing and hemolysis workup.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After initial management, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Blood pressure rises to 118/70 after normal saline and the chills resolve
opts.rat: Recovering blood pressure and resolving symptoms indicate the client is stabilizing after the transfusion was stopped.

opts.text: Urine output is clear yellow and adequate (about 40 mL/hr)
opts.rat: Clear, adequate urine suggests the kidneys are being protected from hemoglobin-related injury.

opts.text: Client passes dark, tea-colored (red-brown) urine
opts.rat: Dark urine reflects hemoglobinuria from ongoing hemolysis and a risk of acute kidney injury—escalate care.

opts.text: Blood pressure continues to fall to 78/40 despite normal saline
opts.rat: Persistent, worsening hypotension signals a severe reaction requiring emergency intervention.

opts.text: Temperature returns to 98.8F and the client reports feeling calm
opts.rat: Resolving fever and anxiety indicate the reaction is settling after prompt management.

opts.text: New oozing of blood from the IV site and gums appears
opts.rat: New bleeding from multiple sites suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a serious complication of hemolytic reaction.

opts.text: Heart rate remains 118 with no change after the first liter of saline
opts.rat: A persistently elevated heart rate that has not changed reflects ongoing instability rather than improvement.

opts.text: Oxygen saturation stays at 93% on room air
opts.rat: An unchanged, borderline saturation shows the client has neither improved nor deteriorated on this measure and needs continued monitoring.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: IV Heparin Over-Anticoagulation
subtitle: 62 y/o female on a heparin drip with a supratherapeutic aPTT
nursesNote: 0600 - 62 y/o female admitted 2 days ago with a pulmonary embolism, on a weight-based continuous IV unfractionated heparin infusion. The 0600 aPTT resulted at 118 seconds (therapeutic goal 60-80 seconds). Over the past hour the client reports gums bleeding when brushing, has passed pink-tinged urine, and has a new large bruise on the left forearm without known trauma. She reports feeling lightheaded. She is scheduled to transition to warfarin. Platelet count is within normal limits and this is day 2 of heparin.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate the client is over-anticoagulated and bleeding.

opts.text: aPTT 118 seconds (therapeutic goal 60-80)
opts.rat: An aPTT well above the therapeutic range indicates excessive anticoagulation and a high bleeding risk on heparin.

opts.text: Bleeding gums and pink-tinged (blood-tinged) urine
opts.rat: Bleeding from the gums and hematuria are signs of active bleeding from over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: New large bruise (ecchymosis) without trauma
opts.rat: Spontaneous bruising reflects impaired clotting from excess heparin effect.

opts.text: Falling hemoglobin/hematocrit with new tachycardia and lower blood pressure
opts.rat: A dropping H&H with rising heart rate and falling blood pressure suggests ongoing blood loss.

opts.text: History of pulmonary embolism (the reason for heparin)
opts.rat: The PE is the indication for anticoagulation, not a sign of over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: Platelet count 205 K/uL
opts.rat: A normal platelet count is reassuring and is not a sign of over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
opts.rat: Normal renal function is not a sign of bleeding or over-anticoagulation.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret these findings.

opts.text: The aPTT above the therapeutic range means the client is receiving too much anticoagulation
opts.rat: Heparin is titrated to keep the aPTT in the therapeutic window; a value well above it indicates over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: Bleeding from several sites points to a systemic over-anticoagulation effect, not a single local injury
opts.rat: Simultaneous bleeding from gums, urine, and skin reflects a body-wide clotting problem from excess heparin.

opts.text: Protamine sulfate is the antidote if heparin reversal is needed for serious bleeding
opts.rat: Protamine sulfate reverses heparin and may be ordered for significant bleeding or a dangerously high aPTT.

opts.text: An aPTT of 118 is therapeutic and no change is needed
opts.rat: 118 seconds is well above the 60-80 goal; this is supratherapeutic, not therapeutic.

opts.text: Vitamin K is the antidote that should be given to reverse the heparin
opts.rat: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; the heparin antidote is protamine sulfate.

opts.text: Bleeding is an expected effect of heparin and requires no intervention
opts.rat: Active bleeding with a supratherapeutic aPTT is a complication that must be acted on, not ignored.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Heparin over-anticoagulation causing systemic bleeding
opts.rat: A supratherapeutic aPTT with multi-site bleeding makes over-anticoagulation the most likely explanation.

opts.text: An ongoing bleeding source (e.g., GI) worsened by anticoagulation
opts.rat: The falling H&H and hemodynamic changes suggest a bleeding source amplified by the excess heparin effect.

opts.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
opts.rat: Possible with heparin, but less likely here: platelets are normal and HIT typically develops around days 5-10, not day 2, and causes clotting rather than this bleeding picture.

opts.text: Subtherapeutic heparin with clot extension
opts.rat: The aPTT is high, not low, so under-anticoagulation does not fit.

opts.text: Anxiety unrelated to the medication
opts.rat: Least likely: objective bleeding, a high aPTT, and a falling H&H point to a real complication.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate immediate interventions.

opts.text: Stop (hold) the heparin infusion
opts.rat: Stopping the heparin halts further anticoagulation and is the priority when a client is over-anticoagulated and bleeding.

opts.text: Notify the provider immediately
opts.rat: The provider must be informed to order reversal, adjust therapy, and investigate the bleeding.

opts.text: Anticipate administering protamine sulfate per order for serious bleeding
opts.rat: Protamine sulfate is the heparin antidote and may be ordered for significant bleeding or a dangerously high aPTT.

opts.text: Institute bleeding precautions and monitor vital signs, sites, and H&H closely
opts.rat: Bleeding precautions and close monitoring help control blood loss and detect deterioration early.

opts.text: Increase the heparin infusion rate to reach a higher aPTT
opts.rat: Increasing heparin would worsen the over-anticoagulation and bleeding; the rate must be stopped or reduced.

opts.text: Administer vitamin K to reverse the heparin
opts.rat: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; it would not correct the heparin effect.

opts.text: Give aspirin to the client for comfort
opts.rat: Aspirin further impairs clotting and would increase bleeding; it is contraindicated here.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the heparin infusion
opts.rat: FIRST-halting the drug stops ongoing over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: Assess vital signs, bleeding sites, and the client's overall status
opts.rat: SECOND-rapid assessment gauges how severe the bleeding is and how urgently to escalate.

opts.text: Notify the provider of the aPTT and bleeding
opts.rat: THIRD-the provider directs reversal and further orders.

opts.text: Prepare and administer protamine sulfate as ordered
opts.rat: FOURTH-the antidote is given per order once the situation is communicated.

opts.text: Recheck the aPTT, hemoglobin/hematocrit, and platelets
opts.rat: LAST-repeat labs confirm whether the reversal and dose changes are working.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After initial management, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Repeat aPTT returns to 70 seconds after holding heparin and giving protamine
opts.rat: An aPTT back within the 60-80 goal shows the over-anticoagulation is corrected.

opts.text: Gum bleeding and hematuria have stopped
opts.rat: Resolution of bleeding indicates the reversal and holding of heparin were effective.

opts.text: Blood pressure returns to 122/74 and heart rate to 82
opts.rat: Normalizing vital signs suggest bleeding has slowed and the client is stabilizing.

opts.text: New sudden severe headache with confusion
opts.rat: Sudden headache with confusion may signal intracranial hemorrhage-a life-threatening bleeding complication requiring emergency care.

opts.text: Hemoglobin falls further from 9.6 to 7.4 g/dL with black, tarry stool
opts.rat: A further drop in hemoglobin with melena indicates continued GI blood loss.

opts.text: Platelet count drops from 205 to 95 K/uL with a new leg clot
opts.rat: A large platelet drop with new clotting raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), which requires stopping all heparin.

opts.text: Small forearm bruise remains the same size with no new bruising
opts.rat: A stable, non-expanding bruise shows no new bleeding at that site-neither better nor worse.

opts.text: aPTT remains 116 seconds one hour later
opts.rat: A persistently high aPTT shows the over-anticoagulation has not yet corrected and continued management is needed.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Warfarin Over-Anticoagulation
subtitle: 71 y/o male on warfarin with an elevated INR after antibiotics
nursesNote: 0900 - 71 y/o male on chronic warfarin for atrial fibrillation (target INR 2-3). He completed a 7-day course of an oral antibiotic for a urinary tract infection 3 days ago and reports taking over-the-counter aspirin 'a few times' for a headache. Today he has bleeding gums, a nosebleed this morning, several new bruises, and blood-tinged urine. Today's INR is 6.5. He is alert, denies dizziness, and his vital signs are near his baseline. He states, 'I take my warfarin the same time every day and never miss it.'

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate the client is over-anticoagulated on warfarin.

opts.text: INR of 6.5 (target 2-3)
opts.rat: An INR far above the therapeutic goal indicates excessive warfarin effect and a high bleeding risk.

opts.text: Bleeding gums and a nosebleed
opts.rat: Mucosal bleeding (gums, nose) is a sign of active bleeding from over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: Several new bruises (ecchymoses)
opts.rat: New spontaneous bruising reflects impaired clotting from too much warfarin effect.

opts.text: Blood-tinged (pink) urine
opts.rat: Hematuria is another sign of bleeding related to the elevated INR.

opts.text: Atrial fibrillation (the reason for warfarin)
opts.rat: AFib is the indication for anticoagulation, not a sign of over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: Platelet count 230 K/uL
opts.rat: A normal platelet count is reassuring and not a sign of warfarin excess.

opts.text: Blood pressure 128/76 near baseline
opts.rat: A near-baseline blood pressure is a stable finding, not a cue of over-anticoagulation.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret these findings.

opts.text: The recent antibiotic and the aspirin can raise the INR and bleeding risk when combined with warfarin
opts.rat: Many antibiotics potentiate warfarin (raising the INR), and aspirin adds bleeding risk-both help explain the elevated INR and bleeding.

opts.text: An INR of 6.5 means the client is over-anticoagulated, not therapeutic
opts.rat: The therapeutic INR for AFib is 2-3; 6.5 is markedly supratherapeutic.

opts.text: Vitamin K (phytonadione) is the antidote used to reverse warfarin
opts.rat: Vitamin K reverses warfarin; for serious/major bleeding, prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma may be used for faster reversal.

opts.text: Protamine sulfate should be given to reverse the warfarin
opts.rat: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin; warfarin is reversed with vitamin K.

opts.text: The client's perfect adherence rules out any medication cause
opts.rat: Even with perfect adherence, drug and dietary interactions (like the antibiotic and aspirin) can raise the INR.

opts.text: The bleeding is expected and needs no intervention
opts.rat: Active bleeding with an INR of 6.5 is a complication that must be treated.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Drug interaction (antibiotic + aspirin) potentiating warfarin, causing a high INR and bleeding
opts.rat: The timing of the antibiotic and aspirin with a jump in INR and new bleeding makes an interaction the most likely cause.

opts.text: A change in dietary vitamin K intake altering the INR
opts.rat: Diet affects warfarin, but a major swing to 6.5 with bleeding is more consistent with the drug interactions reported.

opts.text: An accidental extra dose of warfarin
opts.rat: Possible, but the client reports consistent, non-missed dosing; interactions better explain the picture.

opts.text: Subtherapeutic warfarin with new clotting
opts.rat: The INR is high, not low, so under-anticoagulation does not fit.

opts.text: Laboratory error with a normal true INR
opts.rat: Least likely: the elevated INR matches the clinical bleeding, so it is unlikely to be a lab error.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions.

opts.text: Hold the warfarin dose and notify the provider of the INR and bleeding
opts.rat: Holding warfarin and reporting to the provider are the priorities for a high INR with bleeding.

opts.text: Anticipate administering vitamin K (phytonadione) per order
opts.rat: Vitamin K is the antidote and is commonly ordered for a markedly elevated INR with bleeding.

opts.text: Institute bleeding precautions and monitor for further bleeding
opts.rat: Bleeding precautions (soft toothbrush, no NSAIDs, monitor sites/output) help limit and detect blood loss.

opts.text: Teach the client to avoid aspirin/NSAIDs and to report all new medications, including antibiotics
opts.rat: Education on avoiding interacting drugs and reporting new prescriptions helps prevent recurrence.

opts.text: Encourage the client to take an extra warfarin dose to 'balance it out'
opts.rat: An extra dose would raise the INR further and worsen bleeding.

opts.text: Administer protamine sulfate to reverse the warfarin
opts.rat: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin; vitamin K is the correct antidote.

opts.text: Tell the client to completely stop eating all green vegetables from now on
opts.rat: The teaching is to keep vitamin K intake CONSISTENT, not to eliminate it, which could destabilize the INR.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Hold the warfarin dose
opts.rat: FIRST-stop adding warfarin effect while the INR is dangerously high.

opts.text: Assess vital signs and all bleeding sites
opts.rat: SECOND-determine how significant the bleeding is and whether the client is stable.

opts.text: Notify the provider of the INR of 6.5 and the bleeding
opts.rat: THIRD-the provider orders reversal and dose adjustment.

opts.text: Administer vitamin K as ordered
opts.rat: FOURTH-the antidote is given per order to bring the INR down.

opts.text: Recheck the INR and reinforce medication/diet teaching
opts.rat: LAST-repeat INR confirms reversal, and teaching helps prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: At follow-up, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Repeat INR is 2.6 after holding warfarin and giving vitamin K
opts.rat: An INR back within the 2-3 goal shows the over-anticoagulation is corrected.

opts.text: Gum bleeding, nosebleed, and hematuria have resolved
opts.rat: Resolution of bleeding indicates the reversal was effective.

opts.text: The client correctly explains he will avoid aspirin and report new antibiotics to his provider
opts.rat: Accurate teach-back shows improved understanding that lowers the risk of recurrence.

opts.text: The client develops black, tarry stools and a further hemoglobin drop
opts.rat: Melena with a falling hemoglobin indicates continued GI bleeding requiring urgent care.

opts.text: New confusion and a severe headache develop
opts.rat: These may indicate intracranial hemorrhage, a life-threatening bleeding complication.

opts.text: Repeat INR remains 6.2 several hours later
opts.rat: A persistently high INR shows the anticoagulation has not yet corrected and further management is needed.

opts.text: An existing small bruise is the same size with no new bruising
opts.rat: A stable, non-expanding bruise indicates no new bleeding at that site.

opts.text: The client states he plans to stop all warfarin permanently on his own
opts.rat: Stopping warfarin without provider guidance would leave his atrial fibrillation unprotected and raise stroke risk-this reflects a knowledge gap needing correction.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Insulin-Induced Hypoglycemia
subtitle: 48 y/o male given rapid-acting insulin with a delayed meal tray
nursesNote: 0745 - 48 y/o male with type 2 diabetes admitted for cellulitis. At 0700 the nurse administered the ordered rapid-acting insulin (lispro) for a pre-breakfast glucose of 168, but the breakfast tray was delayed and has not yet arrived. At 0745 the client becomes diaphoretic and shaky, reports feeling anxious and 'suddenly very hungry,' and has mild difficulty concentrating. A repeat fingerstick glucose is 52 mg/dL. He is awake, alert, and able to swallow.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate the client is hypoglycemic.

opts.text: Fingerstick glucose 52 mg/dL
opts.rat: A glucose below 70 mg/dL confirms hypoglycemia; 52 mg/dL requires prompt treatment.

opts.text: Diaphoresis and shakiness (tremor)
opts.rat: Sweating and tremor are classic adrenergic (early) signs of hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Heart rate rising to 106 with anxiety
opts.rat: Tachycardia and anxiety are sympathetic responses to a falling blood glucose.

opts.text: Sudden hunger and difficulty concentrating
opts.rat: Hunger and impaired concentration are common neuroglycopenic/adrenergic signs of hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Hemoglobin A1C of 8.4%
opts.rat: The A1C reflects long-term glucose control, not the acute hypoglycemic event.

opts.text: The client has diabetes and received insulin
opts.rat: These are background facts/indication, not the clinical signs of hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Pre-insulin glucose of 168 mg/dL at 0700
opts.rat: The earlier elevated glucose was the reason for the insulin, not a sign of the current low.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret these findings.

opts.text: Rapid-acting insulin was given but the meal was delayed, so the insulin lowered glucose without food to balance it
opts.rat: Rapid-acting insulin (lispro) acts within about 15 minutes and peaks around 1 hour; giving it without the expected meal causes hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Because the client is awake and can swallow, treatment with a fast-acting oral carbohydrate is appropriate
opts.rat: For a conscious client who can swallow, 15 grams of a fast-acting carbohydrate is the correct first treatment.

opts.text: Untreated hypoglycemia can progress to confusion, seizures, and loss of consciousness
opts.rat: As glucose falls further, neuroglycopenic symptoms worsen, making prompt treatment essential.

opts.text: The client should receive additional insulin to correct the situation
opts.rat: More insulin would drop the glucose further; insulin is held during hypoglycemia.

opts.text: These findings indicate hyperglycemia (too much sugar)
opts.rat: A glucose of 52 mg/dL is hypoglycemia (too little sugar), not hyperglycemia.

opts.text: The safest immediate treatment is a high-fat, high-protein meal alone
opts.rat: Fat and protein raise glucose too slowly; a fast-acting carbohydrate is needed first to correct the acute low.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Hypoglycemia from rapid-acting insulin given without the expected meal
opts.rat: The timing of insulin peak with a missed/delayed meal and a glucose of 52 makes this the clear explanation.

opts.text: Increased metabolic demand from the cellulitis/infection contributing to the low glucose
opts.rat: Illness can affect glucose, but the insulin-meal mismatch is the dominant cause here.

opts.text: Anxiety alone causing the symptoms
opts.rat: Anxiety can mimic adrenergic symptoms, but the measured glucose of 52 confirms true hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Hyperglycemia / diabetic ketoacidosis
opts.rat: The glucose is low, not high, so a hyperglycemic crisis does not fit.

opts.text: An acute cardiac event as the primary cause
opts.rat: Least likely: the tachycardia is explained by hypoglycemia, which should be corrected first.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions for this conscious client.

opts.text: Give about 15 grams of a fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g., 4 oz juice or glucose tablets)
opts.rat: Fifteen grams of a fast-acting carbohydrate is the standard first treatment for hypoglycemia in a client who can swallow.

opts.text: Recheck the blood glucose in about 15 minutes and repeat carbohydrate if still below 70
opts.rat: The 'rule of 15' guides rechecking in 15 minutes and re-treating until glucose is above 70 mg/dL.

opts.text: Hold further rapid-acting insulin and ensure the meal is provided once glucose normalizes
opts.rat: Additional insulin is held during hypoglycemia, and a meal or complex carbohydrate follows to prevent recurrence.

opts.text: Stay with the client and notify the provider of the hypoglycemic event
opts.rat: Staying with the client ensures safety, and the provider should be informed of the event and insulin timing.

opts.text: Administer an extra dose of rapid-acting insulin
opts.rat: Giving more insulin during hypoglycemia is dangerous and would lower glucose further.

opts.text: Have the client walk laps in the hallway to feel better
opts.rat: Exercise increases glucose use and would worsen hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Withhold all food and simply observe
opts.rat: Withholding carbohydrate leaves the hypoglycemia untreated and allows it to worsen.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Confirm the low glucose and give 15 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate
opts.rat: FIRST-treating the confirmed hypoglycemia promptly is the priority.

opts.text: Stay with the client and monitor for worsening symptoms
opts.rat: SECOND-continuous observation ensures safety in case the client deteriorates.

opts.text: Recheck the blood glucose in 15 minutes
opts.rat: THIRD-the recheck determines whether more carbohydrate is needed.

opts.text: Provide the meal or a complex carbohydrate once glucose is above 70
opts.rat: FOURTH-a longer-acting carbohydrate/meal prevents the glucose from dropping again.

opts.text: Notify the provider and document the event and insulin/meal timing
opts.rat: LAST-communication and documentation support follow-up and prevention.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After treatment, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Repeat glucose after 15 minutes is 96 mg/dL
opts.rat: A glucose back above 70 shows the fast-acting carbohydrate corrected the hypoglycemia.

opts.text: Diaphoresis, tremor, and hunger have resolved
opts.rat: Resolution of the adrenergic symptoms confirms the low glucose has been treated.

opts.text: The client eats the delayed breakfast and heart rate returns to 80
opts.rat: Eating a complex carbohydrate/meal and normalizing heart rate indicate stability.

opts.text: The client becomes confused and difficult to arouse
opts.rat: Decreasing level of consciousness signals worsening hypoglycemia-if unable to swallow, treat with IM glucagon or IV dextrose.

opts.text: Repeat glucose is 58 mg/dL and symptoms persist
opts.rat: A still-low glucose with continued symptoms means the hypoglycemia is not yet corrected and requires repeat carbohydrate.

opts.text: The client verbalizes that insulin timing should match meal delivery
opts.rat: Correct teach-back reduces the risk of another insulin-meal mismatch.

opts.text: Blood pressure remains 132/82 with no other change
opts.rat: A stable blood pressure with no other change is neither improvement nor deterioration.

opts.text: The client asks whether he should skip his next insulin dose entirely on his own
opts.rat: This reflects a knowledge gap that has not yet been corrected-insulin changes are made with the provider, and teaching is still needed.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Hypokalemia & IV Potassium Replacement
subtitle: 70 y/o male on a loop diuretic with a potassium of 2.9
nursesNote: 0800 - 70 y/o male admitted with a heart failure exacerbation, on IV furosemide and oral digoxin. He reports generalized weakness, tired legs, and muscle cramps since yesterday. The morning basic metabolic panel shows a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. Telemetry shows frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and flattened T waves with U waves. The provider orders IV potassium chloride (KCl) replacement. Urine output has been about 45 mL/hr.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate hypokalemia.

opts.text: Potassium 2.9 mEq/L
opts.rat: A potassium below 3.5 mEq/L confirms hypokalemia; 2.9 is significantly low and affects the heart and muscles.

opts.text: Generalized weakness and muscle cramps
opts.rat: Muscle weakness and cramps are classic neuromuscular signs of hypokalemia.

opts.text: Flattened T waves with U waves on telemetry
opts.rat: Flattened T waves and the appearance of U waves are characteristic ECG changes of hypokalemia.

opts.text: Frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)
opts.rat: Low potassium increases cardiac irritability and can cause PVCs and other dysrhythmias.

opts.text: Digoxin level 1.4 ng/mL
opts.rat: The digoxin level is within range; it is not itself a sign of hypokalemia (though hypokalemia raises digoxin-toxicity risk).

opts.text: Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
opts.rat: Normal renal function is reassuring for replacement, but it is not a sign of hypokalemia.

opts.text: Urine output about 45 mL/hr
opts.rat: Adequate urine output is a safety check before giving potassium, not a hypokalemia sign.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: Interpret the findings and the risk
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret the situation.

opts.text: The loop diuretic (furosemide) is a likely cause of the potassium loss
opts.rat: Loop diuretics increase renal potassium excretion and commonly cause hypokalemia.

opts.text: IV potassium must be DILUTED and infused slowly-never given by IV push
opts.rat: IV potassium given undiluted or by rapid push can cause fatal cardiac arrest; it is always diluted and infused slowly via a pump with monitoring.

opts.text: The low magnesium can make the hypokalemia harder to correct until it is also treated
opts.rat: Hypomagnesemia promotes ongoing potassium loss; potassium is often refractory until magnesium is replaced.

opts.text: IV potassium can safely be given by rapid IV push to correct the level quickly
opts.rat: This is dangerous and false-rapid IV push of potassium can cause cardiac arrest and death.

opts.text: Hypokalemia has no effect on a client taking digoxin
opts.rat: Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity, so it is especially important to correct.

opts.text: These ECG changes and the weakness require no action
opts.rat: The dysrhythmias and neuromuscular symptoms of hypokalemia require prompt, careful correction.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Most likely explanation for the low potassium
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Potassium loss from the loop diuretic (with contributing low magnesium)
opts.rat: A loop diuretic plus low magnesium best explains ongoing potassium loss and the current level of 2.9.

opts.text: Inadequate dietary potassium intake
opts.rat: Poor intake can contribute, but the diuretic is the dominant driver here.

opts.text: Gastrointestinal losses (vomiting/diarrhea)
opts.rat: A possible cause of hypokalemia, but none are reported in this client.

opts.text: Acute kidney injury causing potassium retention
opts.rat: Kidney injury tends to RAISE potassium; the creatinine is normal, so this does not fit.

opts.text: Laboratory error with a truly normal potassium
opts.rat: Least likely: the ECG changes and symptoms match the low value, so it is unlikely to be a lab error.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions for safe IV potassium replacement.

opts.text: Administer the KCl DILUTED in IV fluid, infused slowly via an infusion pump-never by IV push
opts.rat: Diluting the potassium and infusing it slowly on a pump is the mandatory safe method; IV push is never done.

opts.text: Keep the client on continuous cardiac (telemetry) monitoring during replacement
opts.rat: Cardiac monitoring detects dysrhythmias from either the hypokalemia or too-rapid correction.

opts.text: Confirm adequate urine output / renal function before and during the infusion
opts.rat: Verifying kidney function and urine output prevents dangerous potassium accumulation (hyperkalemia).

opts.text: Monitor the IV site for pain/irritation and recheck the potassium (and magnesium) level
opts.rat: IV potassium irritates veins, and rechecking levels confirms the correction is working and not overshooting.

opts.text: Give the potassium by rapid IV push to raise the level quickly
opts.rat: Rapid IV push of potassium can cause fatal cardiac arrest and is never done.

opts.text: Administer concentrated undiluted KCl directly into the vein
opts.rat: Undiluted concentrated potassium is extremely dangerous and prohibited; it must be diluted.

opts.text: Increase the furosemide dose to help the client feel better
opts.rat: More diuretic would worsen the potassium loss.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Verify the order, the diluted premixed concentration, and adequate urine output/renal function
opts.rat: FIRST-confirming a safe, diluted preparation and kidney function prevents a dangerous error before anything is infused.

opts.text: Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
opts.rat: SECOND-monitoring must be in place before and during potassium replacement.

opts.text: Start the diluted KCl infusion on an infusion pump at the ordered controlled rate
opts.rat: THIRD-the infusion is delivered slowly and precisely by pump, never pushed.

opts.text: Monitor the IV site, ECG, and the client's symptoms during the infusion
opts.rat: FOURTH-ongoing monitoring detects site irritation or cardiac changes early.

opts.text: Recheck the potassium and magnesium levels after the infusion
opts.rat: LAST-repeat labs confirm the correction and guide any further replacement.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After replacement, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Repeat potassium is 4.0 mEq/L
opts.rat: A potassium back within 3.5-5.0 shows the replacement corrected the deficit.

opts.text: T waves normalize and the PVCs resolve on telemetry
opts.rat: Resolution of the ECG changes reflects correction of the hypokalemia.

opts.text: Muscle strength returns and cramps resolve
opts.rat: Improved neuromuscular symptoms indicate the potassium level is restored.

opts.text: Repeat potassium is 6.2 mEq/L with new peaked (tall, tented) T waves
opts.rat: Over-correction to hyperkalemia with peaked T waves is dangerous and requires stopping potassium and treating the high level.

opts.text: New bradycardia with a widening QRS complex develops
opts.rat: Bradycardia and a widening QRS suggest hyperkalemia affecting cardiac conduction-a medical emergency.

opts.text: The IV site becomes red, swollen, and painful
opts.rat: Redness, swelling, and pain indicate phlebitis/infiltration from the irritating infusion, requiring the site to be changed.

opts.text: Repeat potassium remains 3.0 mEq/L and magnesium is still low
opts.rat: A persistently low potassium with untreated low magnesium shows the deficit has not corrected-magnesium must also be replaced.

opts.text: Blood pressure remains 120/70 as before
opts.rat: A stable, unchanged blood pressure is neither an improvement nor a decline.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Opioid Oversedation & Naloxone
subtitle: 54 y/o female post-op on a morphine PCA, now difficult to arouse
nursesNote: 0300 - 54 y/o female, post-op day 0 after abdominal surgery, using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump for pain. On rounds the nurse finds her difficult to arouse, responding only to vigorous stimulation. Respirations are slow and shallow at 7/min, SpO2 has fallen to 88% on room air, and her pupils are pinpoint. Her adult daughter at the bedside states, 'She was hurting, so I kept pressing the button for her while she slept.'

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate opioid-induced respiratory depression.

opts.text: Respiratory rate of 7/min, slow and shallow
opts.rat: A low respiratory rate with shallow breathing is the hallmark of opioid-induced respiratory depression.

opts.text: Difficult to arouse, responding only to vigorous stimulation
opts.rat: Excessive sedation-a decreased level of consciousness-precedes and accompanies opioid respiratory depression.

opts.text: Pinpoint (constricted) pupils
opts.rat: Miosis (pinpoint pupils) is a classic sign of opioid effect.

opts.text: SpO2 fallen to 88%
opts.rat: A falling oxygen saturation reflects hypoventilation from the opioid effect.

opts.text: Blood pressure 112/68
opts.rat: This blood pressure is near baseline and not the key sign of opioid oversedation.

opts.text: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL
opts.rat: A mildly low hemoglobin from surgery is not a sign of opioid respiratory depression.

opts.text: Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
opts.rat: Normal renal function is not a sign of oversedation.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret the situation.

opts.text: The daughter pressing the PCA button ('PCA by proxy') has delivered extra opioid the client did not self-administer
opts.rat: Only the client should press the PCA button; dosing by family or staff bypasses the built-in safety of self-administration and can cause overdose.

opts.text: The ABG (low pH, high PaCO2) shows respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation
opts.rat: Opioid-induced hypoventilation retains CO2, producing a respiratory acidosis (low pH, high PaCO2).

opts.text: Naloxone is the opioid antagonist that can reverse the respiratory depression
opts.rat: Naloxone reverses opioid effects and is used for significant opioid-induced respiratory depression.

opts.text: The safest response is to press the PCA button more to keep her comfortable
opts.rat: Giving more opioid would deepen the respiratory depression; the opioid must be stopped, not increased.

opts.text: Pinpoint pupils suggest a stimulant overdose
opts.rat: Stimulants dilate pupils; pinpoint pupils point to opioids.

opts.text: These findings are expected and need no intervention
opts.rat: A respiratory rate of 7 with an SpO2 of 88% is dangerous and requires immediate action.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Opioid-induced respiratory depression from excess PCA dosing (by proxy)
opts.rat: Slow breathing, sedation, pinpoint pupils, and the reported proxy dosing make opioid oversedation the clear cause.

opts.text: Postoperative hypoventilation worsened by the opioid
opts.rat: Post-op splinting/atelectasis can contribute, but the opioid effect is the dominant, reversible cause here.

opts.text: Oversedation compounded by the client's own drowsiness during sleep
opts.rat: Sleep lowers respiratory drive somewhat, but the opioid excess is the key issue.

opts.text: Acute stroke as the primary cause
opts.rat: Pinpoint pupils with reversible opioid signs make stroke much less likely; treat the opioid effect first.

opts.text: Simple normal post-op sleep
opts.rat: Least likely: an RR of 7 and SpO2 of 88% are not normal sleep and require intervention.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate immediate interventions.

opts.text: Stop the PCA opioid and stimulate the client while assessing airway and breathing
opts.rat: Stopping the opioid and stimulating the client, with airway/breathing support, are the immediate priorities.

opts.text: Apply oxygen and support ventilation as needed
opts.rat: Oxygen and ventilatory support correct the hypoxemia while the opioid effect is addressed.

opts.text: Call for help and administer naloxone per order/protocol
opts.rat: Naloxone reverses the opioid-induced respiratory depression and is given per order for significant depression.

opts.text: Teach the family that only the client may press the PCA button, and monitor for re-sedation
opts.rat: Educating the family prevents recurrence, and monitoring is needed because naloxone is short-acting and re-sedation can occur.

opts.text: Press the PCA button to give another dose for pain
opts.rat: Additional opioid would worsen the respiratory depression.

opts.text: Place the client flat and leave the room to get supplies
opts.rat: Leaving a client with RR 7 and SpO2 88% is unsafe; stay and call for help.

opts.text: Administer a large single dose of naloxone to fully reverse all opioid effect at once
opts.rat: Naloxone is titrated to restore adequate breathing; a large abrupt dose can precipitate severe pain and acute withdrawal.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the PCA and stimulate the client while checking airway/breathing
opts.rat: FIRST-stopping the opioid and assessing/stimulating addresses the immediate threat.

opts.text: Apply oxygen and support ventilation
opts.rat: SECOND-oxygenation is restored while further help is summoned.

opts.text: Call for help and notify the provider
opts.rat: THIRD-additional responders and orders (including naloxone) are mobilized.

opts.text: Administer naloxone titrated to restore adequate respirations
opts.rat: FOURTH-the antagonist reverses the respiratory depression, titrated to effect.

opts.text: Continue close monitoring for re-sedation and educate the family about PCA use
opts.rat: LAST-ongoing monitoring catches re-sedation, and teaching prevents recurrence.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After naloxone and supportive care, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Respiratory rate rises to 16 and SpO2 improves to 96%
opts.rat: A normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation show the opioid effect has been reversed.

opts.text: The client becomes easily arousable and oriented
opts.rat: Returning alertness indicates the respiratory depression and oversedation have resolved.

opts.text: The family verbalizes that only the client may press the PCA button
opts.rat: Correct understanding reduces the risk of another proxy-dosing event.

opts.text: Thirty minutes later the client becomes drowsy again with an RR of 8
opts.rat: Re-sedation is expected because naloxone is shorter-acting than the opioid; repeat naloxone/monitoring is needed.

opts.text: SpO2 falls again to 85% with shallow breathing
opts.rat: A falling oxygen saturation with shallow breathing signals recurring respiratory depression requiring re-intervention.

opts.text: The client reports pain of 7/10 but is breathing 16/min with SpO2 97%
opts.rat: Adequate breathing with pain reflects the expected trade-off after reversal; pain is managed with safer, monitored analgesia-neither a decline nor full resolution of comfort.

opts.text: Blood pressure remains 114/70 with no change
opts.rat: A stable blood pressure is neither an improvement nor a worsening in this situation.

opts.text: Pupils remain pinpoint with no return of alertness
opts.rat: Persistent pinpoint pupils and unchanged sedation indicate the opioid effect has not yet been reversed and further naloxone is needed.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Unsafe Dose Order & High-Alert Medication Safety
subtitle: 5 y/o, 20 kg — an ordered dose that exceeds the safe range
nursesNote: 1300 - 5 y/o child weighing 20 kg (44 lb) admitted with a febrile illness. A new order reads: 'acetaminophen 600 mg PO now.' The unit's pediatric medication reference lists the recommended acetaminophen dose as 10-15 mg/kg per dose. The nurse notes the order was entered shortly after a verbal handoff and that the same prescriber's earlier orders used a trailing zero (e.g., '1.0 mg'). The child has no known liver disease and normal baseline liver enzymes. The nurse has not yet administered the dose.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: Identify what makes this order unsafe
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that indicate this order should NOT be given as written.

opts.text: The safe range for this 20 kg child is 200-300 mg per dose (10-15 mg/kg)
opts.rat: Multiplying 10-15 mg/kg by 20 kg gives a safe single dose of 200-300 mg-the reference the nurse must check the order against.

opts.text: The ordered 600 mg equals 30 mg/kg, about double the maximum safe single dose
opts.rat: 600 mg divided by 20 kg is 30 mg/kg, well above the 10-15 mg/kg range-an unsafe dose that must be questioned.

opts.text: The order followed a verbal handoff and the prescriber uses trailing zeros, both error-prone practices
opts.rat: Verbal orders and trailing zeros ('1.0 mg' misread as '10 mg') are recognized sources of tenfold medication errors, raising suspicion of a transcription error.

opts.text: The child has a temperature of 102.4F
opts.rat: The fever is the indication for the medication, not evidence that the dose is unsafe.

opts.text: Baseline ALT and AST are within normal limits
opts.rat: Normal liver enzymes are reassuring, but they do not make an excessive dose safe.

opts.text: Heart rate of 124 in a febrile 5-year-old
opts.rat: Tachycardia is expected with fever in a young child; it is not a cue about the dose.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: Interpret the risk and the safeguards
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: Acetaminophen given above recommended limits risks liver (hepatic) injury
opts.rat: Exceeding recommended acetaminophen dosing is a well-established cause of hepatotoxicity, which is why the safe range matters.

opts.text: The nurse is accountable for verifying a dose is safe before administering it, even when a prescriber ordered it
opts.rat: Administering a medication is an independent nursing responsibility; a nurse who gives a clearly unsafe dose shares accountability for the harm.

opts.text: Error-prone abbreviations such as 'U' for units, trailing zeros, and missing leading zeros should be avoided in orders
opts.rat: These notations are on 'do not use' lists precisely because they cause tenfold dosing errors; orders using them should be clarified.

opts.text: The nurse should give the dose as written because the prescriber is responsible for the order
opts.rat: Following a clearly unsafe order does not transfer accountability; the nurse must clarify before administering.

opts.text: A dose only needs to be checked if the medication is on the high-alert list
opts.rat: Every dose is verified; high-alert medications simply add an extra independent double-check requirement.

opts.text: Weight-based dosing is unnecessary in children if the child looks average sized
opts.rat: Pediatric doses must be calculated from an accurate measured weight, never estimated by appearance.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.sub: Most likely explanation for the discrepancy
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: A transcription/decimal error during order entry after the verbal handoff
opts.rat: A dose that is a clean multiple of the safe dose, entered after a verbal handoff by a prescriber using error-prone notation, most suggests a transcription error.

opts.text: The order was intended as a total daily amount rather than a single dose
opts.rat: Confusing a daily total with a single dose is another common ordering error worth clarifying.

opts.text: The dose was calculated from an incorrect (adult or estimated) weight
opts.rat: Using a wrong weight is a plausible source of pediatric dosing error and should be checked.

opts.text: The prescriber deliberately intends a dose above the standard range
opts.rat: Unlikely for routine fever management, and it would still require explicit clarification before administering.

opts.text: The pediatric reference range in the unit manual is wrong
opts.rat: Least likely: standard references are well established, so the order-not the reference-is the thing to question.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate actions.

opts.text: Hold the dose and do not administer it as written
opts.rat: A dose outside the safe range is withheld until it is clarified; giving it first and asking later risks harm.

opts.text: Recalculate using the child's documented weight and the reference range
opts.rat: Independently recalculating confirms the discrepancy before the prescriber is contacted.

opts.text: Contact the prescriber to clarify and obtain a corrected written order
opts.rat: Clarifying with the prescriber and getting a corrected, clearly written order resolves the problem at its source.

opts.text: Ask a second nurse for an independent double-check of the calculation
opts.rat: An independent double-check-standard for high-alert medications and useful for any questionable dose-catches calculation errors.

opts.text: Give half the ordered dose so it falls closer to the safe range
opts.rat: Nurses do not unilaterally alter a prescribed dose; the order must be clarified and rewritten.

opts.text: Administer the 600 mg and document that the order seemed high
opts.rat: Giving a known unsafe dose and documenting concern afterward does not protect the child.

opts.text: Accept a verbal correction without a read-back or a written order
opts.rat: Verbal orders require read-back verification and prompt written entry; accepting one without either repeats the original error risk.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Hold the medication and do not administer
opts.rat: FIRST-withholding the unsafe dose immediately protects the child.

opts.text: Verify the child's documented weight and recalculate the safe dose range
opts.rat: SECOND-confirming the weight and math establishes the discrepancy on solid ground.

opts.text: Obtain an independent double-check from a second nurse
opts.rat: THIRD-a second verifier confirms the calculation before escalating.

opts.text: Contact the prescriber and obtain a corrected written order with read-back
opts.rat: FOURTH-the corrected order is obtained and verified to prevent the same error recurring.

opts.text: Administer the corrected dose and document the clarification per policy
opts.rat: LAST-the safe dose is given and the near-miss documented/reported so the system can learn from it.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each outcome as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: The prescriber rewrites the order as 300 mg PO, within the 200-300 mg safe range
opts.rat: A corrected order inside the calculated safe range resolves the original hazard.

opts.text: The child's temperature falls to 99.2F after the corrected dose, with no adverse effects
opts.rat: Fever reduction without adverse effects shows the corrected dose was both safe and effective.

opts.text: A near-miss report is filed and the unit removes trailing zeros from its order sets
opts.rat: System-level change from a reported near miss reduces the chance of the same error reaching another child.

opts.text: A colleague states she gave the 600 mg to a similar child earlier without questioning it
opts.rat: Another child has already received an excessive dose-that child needs assessment and the event needs immediate reporting.

opts.text: The child develops nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain with rising ALT/AST
opts.rat: These are early signs of acetaminophen-related liver injury and require urgent evaluation and treatment.

opts.text: The prescriber verbally insists the 600 mg is correct but will not enter a written order
opts.rat: An unresolved unsafe order with no written clarification is still a hazard; the nurse should escalate through the chain of command.

opts.text: The child's temperature remains 102.2F one hour after the corrected dose
opts.rat: The fever has not yet responded; this warrants continued monitoring but is not itself a sign of harm.

opts.text: Heart rate remains 122 with the child alert and drinking fluids
opts.rat: A stable heart rate in an alert, hydrated febrile child is neither improvement nor deterioration.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Norepinephrine Drip & Extravasation
subtitle: 66 y/o male in septic shock on a peripheral vasopressor
nursesNote: 0230 - 66 y/o male in the ICU with septic shock. He remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation, so a norepinephrine infusion was started 3 hours ago and titrated per protocol to a MAP goal of at least 65 mmHg. The drip is currently running through a 20-gauge peripheral IV in the left forearm while central access is pending. At 0230 the nurse notes the left forearm around the IV site is pale, cool, and swollen, and the client reports burning pain at the site. The infusion pump shows no occlusion alarm.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that BEST indicate extravasation of the vasopressor.

opts.text: The forearm around the IV site is pale and cool
opts.rat: Blanching and coolness reflect intense local vasoconstriction from norepinephrine leaking into the tissue, threatening tissue perfusion.

opts.text: Swelling at and around the insertion site
opts.rat: Localized swelling indicates the vesicant medication is infiltrating the surrounding tissue rather than entering the vein.

opts.text: The client reports burning pain at the IV site
opts.rat: Burning or pain at the site is an early hallmark of extravasation of a vesicant such as norepinephrine.

opts.text: Lactate of 3.8 mmol/L
opts.rat: An elevated lactate reflects the underlying septic shock, not the IV-site complication.

opts.text: WBC of 18.6 K/uL
opts.rat: Leukocytosis is part of the sepsis picture, not evidence of extravasation.

opts.text: The pump has not sounded an occlusion alarm
opts.rat: A silent pump is falsely reassuring-extravasation frequently occurs without any alarm, so it is not a cue that extravasation is happening.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: Norepinephrine is a potent vasoconstrictor and a vesicant; extravasation can cause tissue ischemia and necrosis
opts.rat: Local vasoconstriction from extravasated norepinephrine can produce severe ischemic tissue injury, which is why prompt recognition matters.

opts.text: Vasopressors are preferentially given through central access; peripheral use should be short-term with close site monitoring
opts.rat: Central administration reduces extravasation risk; when peripheral access is used temporarily, the site must be checked frequently.

opts.text: The falling blood pressure suggests the client is no longer receiving the intended vasopressor dose
opts.rat: If drug is leaking into tissue rather than the circulation, the hemodynamic effect is lost and the MAP falls despite the pump running.

opts.text: The absence of a pump occlusion alarm rules out extravasation
opts.rat: Infusion pumps often continue without alarming during extravasation; assessment of the site-not the pump-detects it.

opts.text: The infusion should simply be increased to restore the blood pressure
opts.rat: Increasing the rate through a compromised site delivers more vesicant into the tissue and worsens the injury.

opts.text: Norepinephrine extravasation is harmless and needs only a warm compress
opts.rat: It is a serious complication; management typically involves stopping the infusion and specific measures per protocol, not casual treatment.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Extravasation of the norepinephrine into the surrounding tissue
opts.rat: Pallor, coolness, swelling, and burning pain at the site of a peripheral vasopressor is the classic extravasation picture.

opts.text: Worsening septic shock with progressive hypotension
opts.rat: The sepsis is certainly worsening the picture, and lost drug delivery plus disease progression can occur together.

opts.text: Phlebitis or local infection at the IV site
opts.rat: Phlebitis typically causes redness, warmth, and a palpable cord-not the pallor and coolness seen here.

opts.text: Arterial occlusion of the limb from an unrelated cause
opts.rat: Possible but far less likely than extravasation given the timing and the infusion running at that exact site.

opts.text: Normal expected response to vasopressor therapy
opts.rat: Least likely: a painful, pale, swollen infusion site is never an expected or acceptable finding.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate immediate interventions.

opts.text: Stop the infusion at that site immediately while leaving the catheter in place initially to aspirate residual drug per protocol
opts.rat: Stopping delivery halts further tissue injury; the catheter is typically left briefly to aspirate residual vesicant before removal, per policy.

opts.text: Notify the provider urgently and obtain orders for extravasation management
opts.rat: Extravasation of a vasopressor requires prompt provider notification; specific antidote therapy (e.g., phentolamine) may be ordered per protocol.

opts.text: Restart the norepinephrine at a different, preferably central, access site to maintain the MAP goal
opts.rat: The client remains in shock and still needs vasopressor support, so the infusion must be re-established through appropriate access without delay.

opts.text: Elevate the affected extremity and mark/assess the area, documenting the event
opts.rat: Elevation, serial assessment with the area marked, and documentation guide treatment and track whether tissue injury progresses.

opts.text: Increase the infusion rate at the current site to raise the blood pressure
opts.rat: Increasing the rate through an extravasated site delivers more vesicant into the tissue and worsens ischemic injury.

opts.text: Apply firm massage to the site to disperse the medication
opts.rat: Massaging spreads the vesicant through the tissue and can enlarge the area of injury.

opts.text: Flush the line briskly with saline to clear the medication into the vein
opts.rat: Flushing an extravasated line pushes additional drug into the tissue rather than clearing it.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the norepinephrine infusion at the affected site
opts.rat: FIRST-halting delivery stops ongoing tissue injury from the vesicant.

opts.text: Re-establish the vasopressor through alternate/central access to maintain perfusion
opts.rat: SECOND-the client is in shock; vasopressor support must be restored quickly to protect organ perfusion.

opts.text: Notify the provider and obtain extravasation orders
opts.rat: THIRD-the provider directs antidote and further management of the affected limb.

opts.text: Carry out ordered extravasation treatment and elevate the extremity
opts.rat: FOURTH-specific treatment and elevation limit the extent of ischemic tissue damage.

opts.text: Document the event, mark the area, and monitor the site serially
opts.rat: LAST-documentation and serial assessment track progression and support follow-up care.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: After intervention, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: MAP rises above 65 mmHg after the drip is restarted through central access
opts.rat: Restoring the MAP goal shows the vasopressor is now reaching the circulation and perfusion is supported.

opts.text: Color, warmth, and capillary refill return to the left forearm
opts.rat: Return of normal perfusion signs indicates the local vasoconstriction is resolving without tissue loss.

opts.text: Lactate falls from 3.8 to 2.0 mmol/L over the next several hours
opts.rat: A falling lactate reflects improving tissue perfusion and response to shock management.

opts.text: The forearm develops dusky discoloration with blistering and a firm, dark area
opts.rat: Duskiness, blistering, and firm dark tissue signal progressing ischemic necrosis requiring urgent surgical/wound consultation.

opts.text: MAP remains 52 mmHg despite the restarted infusion and ordered titration
opts.rat: A persistently low MAP despite appropriate vasopressor delivery indicates deteriorating shock needing escalation.

opts.text: Urine output falls to 10 mL/hr with a rising creatinine
opts.rat: Declining urine output with rising creatinine reflects worsening organ hypoperfusion and acute kidney injury.

opts.text: Mild residual swelling remains at the old site with normal color and sensation
opts.rat: Stable residual swelling without perfusion changes is neither clear improvement nor deterioration; it warrants continued monitoring.

opts.text: Heart rate remains 110 with no other change
opts.rat: An unchanged heart rate alone does not indicate improvement or decline and must be interpreted with the other findings.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: TPN & Central Line Complications
subtitle: 59 y/o female on parenteral nutrition with a rising glucose and fever
nursesNote: 0600 - 59 y/o female, post-op day 6 after bowel resection with a prolonged ileus, receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a tunneled central venous catheter for the past 4 days. Overnight she developed a temperature of 101.6F with shaking chills, and the 0600 fingerstick glucose is 268 mg/dL (her values had been running 120-150). The central line insertion site is reddened with a small amount of purulent drainage. The current TPN bag has been hanging for 26 hours. She reports feeling 'awful' but denies chest pain or shortness of breath.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that MOST suggest a central line-associated infection.

opts.text: Temperature 101.6F with shaking chills
opts.rat: New fever with rigors in a client with a central line is a classic sign of a catheter-related bloodstream infection.

opts.text: Redness and purulent drainage at the central line insertion site
opts.rat: Local erythema with purulent drainage points directly to infection at the catheter site.

opts.text: WBC elevated at 17.4 K/uL
opts.rat: Leukocytosis supports an active infectious process.

opts.text: New tachycardia (118) with a falling blood pressure
opts.rat: Rising heart rate with a dropping blood pressure suggests a systemic inflammatory response and possible early sepsis.

opts.text: Albumin of 2.6 g/dL
opts.rat: Low albumin reflects her underlying nutritional/surgical status, not the acute infection.

opts.text: Potassium of 3.4 mEq/L
opts.rat: A mildly low potassium is a TPN electrolyte issue to correct, not a sign of catheter infection.

opts.text: She denies chest pain or shortness of breath
opts.rat: The absence of these symptoms is reassuring against other complications; it is not a cue for infection.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: TPN's high glucose concentration makes the central line a high-risk site for infection
opts.rat: The dextrose-rich solution is an excellent medium for microbial growth, which is why strict sterile technique and site care are essential with TPN.
