opts.text: The rising glucose may reflect both the TPN dextrose load and the stress of infection
opts.rat: Hyperglycemia is a known TPN complication and is worsened by the counter-regulatory hormones released during infection/sepsis.

opts.text: A TPN bag hanging 26 hours exceeds the recommended hang time and increases infection risk
opts.rat: TPN bags are generally changed within 24 hours; prolonged hang time increases the risk of microbial growth.

opts.text: The TPN should simply be stopped abruptly and no further glucose monitoring is needed
opts.rat: Abruptly stopping TPN risks rebound hypoglycemia, and glucose must continue to be monitored closely.

opts.text: Fever in a client with a central line is expected and requires no investigation
opts.rat: New fever with a central line always warrants evaluation for a catheter-related bloodstream infection.

opts.text: TPN can safely be interrupted to infuse other medications through the same lumen
opts.rat: The TPN lumen is dedicated; mixing other infusions increases contamination and incompatibility risk.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Central line-associated bloodstream infection from the TPN catheter
opts.rat: Fever with rigors, purulent site drainage, leukocytosis, and hemodynamic change in a client with a TPN central line make catheter infection most likely.

opts.text: TPN-related hyperglycemia contributing to the picture
opts.rat: Hyperglycemia is a real and expected TPN complication here, compounding infection risk, though it does not explain the fever and purulent drainage.

opts.text: Surgical site or intra-abdominal infection from the recent bowel resection
opts.rat: A plausible alternative source that must be evaluated, but the purulent central line site points more directly to the catheter.

opts.text: Postoperative atelectasis or pneumonia
opts.rat: Less likely given normal oxygen saturation and no respiratory complaints, though fever workup should remain broad.

opts.text: Air embolism from the central line
opts.rat: Least likely: air embolism presents suddenly with respiratory distress and chest pain, which she denies.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions.

opts.text: Notify the provider promptly and anticipate blood cultures (including from the line) before antibiotics
opts.rat: Prompt notification and obtaining cultures before starting antibiotics identify the organism and guide therapy.

opts.text: Continue close glucose monitoring and administer insulin coverage as ordered
opts.rat: TPN-related hyperglycemia worsened by infection requires frequent monitoring and ordered insulin coverage.

opts.text: Replace the TPN bag and tubing per policy using strict sterile technique
opts.rat: The bag has exceeded its hang time; changing bag and tubing with sterile technique removes a potential contamination source.

opts.text: Assess and care for the insertion site, and monitor vital signs closely for sepsis
opts.rat: Site assessment/care and close hemodynamic monitoring detect worsening infection and progression toward sepsis.

opts.text: Abruptly discontinue the TPN and hang nothing in its place
opts.rat: Stopping TPN abruptly can cause rebound hypoglycemia; a dextrose-containing solution is typically ordered if TPN must be interrupted.

opts.text: Use the TPN lumen to give the new IV antibiotic
opts.rat: The TPN lumen is dedicated; using it for other infusions raises contamination and incompatibility risks.

opts.text: Increase the TPN infusion rate to improve her nutrition and help her fight the infection
opts.rat: Increasing the rate would worsen the hyperglycemia and does not treat the infection.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Assess the client fully-vital signs, insertion site, and level of consciousness
opts.rat: FIRST-a focused assessment establishes how sick she is and confirms the suspected source.

opts.text: Notify the provider of the fever, purulent site, and hemodynamic changes
opts.rat: SECOND-early notification mobilizes cultures, antibiotics, and line-management decisions.

opts.text: Obtain blood cultures as ordered before antibiotics are started
opts.rat: THIRD-cultures drawn before antibiotics preserve the ability to identify the organism.

opts.text: Administer ordered antibiotics and insulin coverage
opts.rat: FOURTH-treatment proceeds once cultures are obtained and orders are in place.

opts.text: Change the TPN bag and tubing with sterile technique and document the event
opts.rat: LAST of these steps-removing the expired bag and documenting completes the immediate response.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Over the next 24 hours, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Temperature returns to 98.8F and the chills resolve after antibiotics
opts.rat: Defervescence and resolution of rigors suggest the infection is responding to treatment.

opts.text: Glucose stabilizes at 128-145 mg/dL with the ordered insulin coverage
opts.rat: Glucose returning toward her usual range shows the TPN-related hyperglycemia is being controlled.

opts.text: The insertion site is clean and dry with no drainage after line replacement
opts.rat: A clean, dry site after removing the infected catheter indicates the local source has been addressed.

opts.text: Blood pressure falls to 82/44 with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L
opts.rat: Hypotension with a rising lactate signals progression to septic shock requiring immediate escalation.

opts.text: Glucose drops to 48 mg/dL after the TPN is stopped without a dextrose replacement
opts.rat: This is rebound hypoglycemia from abrupt TPN discontinuation-a preventable complication needing immediate treatment.

opts.text: Blood cultures grow an organism and the client develops new confusion
opts.rat: Confirmed bacteremia with new altered mental status indicates worsening systemic infection.

opts.text: Potassium remains 3.4 mEq/L with no change after the TPN formula review
opts.rat: A persistently borderline potassium shows the electrolyte issue has not yet been corrected in the TPN formulation.

opts.text: Albumin remains 2.6 g/dL
opts.rat: Albumin changes slowly and would not be expected to shift meaningfully in 24 hours; it is neither better nor worse.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Vancomycin Infusion Reaction vs Anaphylaxis
subtitle: 44 y/o male flushing during a rapid vancomycin infusion
nursesNote: 1500 - 44 y/o male admitted with an MRSA wound infection, receiving IV vancomycin. The dose was started at 1445 and the pump was programmed to deliver it over 30 minutes. At 1500, about 15 minutes into the infusion, the client develops marked flushing and redness of the face, neck, and upper chest with intense itching. He is speaking in full sentences, his airway is clear, lungs are clear to auscultation with no wheezing, and there is no lip or tongue swelling. He reports feeling warm and 'itchy all over' but denies throat tightness or difficulty breathing.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: Identify the reaction and what is absent
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST characterize this reaction.

opts.text: Flushing and redness of the face, neck, and upper chest
opts.rat: Erythema over the face, neck, and upper torso during a vancomycin infusion is the characteristic distribution of a rate-related infusion reaction.

opts.text: Intense generalized itching (pruritus)
opts.rat: Pruritus accompanies the histamine release triggered by rapid vancomycin infusion.

opts.text: Symptoms began about 15 minutes into an infusion running over only 30 minutes
opts.rat: The timing during an unusually rapid infusion is the key cue linking the reaction to infusion rate.

opts.text: Clear airway and lungs with no wheezing or lip/tongue swelling
opts.rat: The ABSENCE of airway compromise, wheezing, and angioedema is a critical cue that distinguishes this from anaphylaxis.

opts.text: WBC of 15.8 K/uL
opts.rat: Leukocytosis reflects the underlying MRSA infection being treated, not the infusion reaction.

opts.text: Vancomycin trough of 8 mcg/mL
opts.rat: A subtherapeutic trough is a dosing issue to address separately; it does not characterize the acute reaction.

opts.text: Temperature of 100.8F
opts.rat: The low-grade fever is from the infection, not the infusion reaction.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: This is a rate-related vancomycin infusion reaction caused by histamine release, not an IgE-mediated allergy
opts.rat: Rapid vancomycin infusion triggers direct histamine release producing flushing and itching; it is not a true allergic (IgE) reaction.

opts.text: Infusing vancomycin over at least 60 minutes helps prevent this reaction
opts.rat: Slowing the infusion (generally at least 60 minutes, longer for larger doses) is the primary prevention for this rate-related reaction.

opts.text: True anaphylaxis would include airway compromise, wheezing, or angioedema with severe hypotension and would require epinephrine
opts.rat: Distinguishing the two matters: anaphylaxis involves airway/respiratory compromise and profound hypotension and is treated with epinephrine.

opts.text: The client should be permanently labeled allergic to vancomycin and never receive it again
opts.rat: A rate-related infusion reaction is not a true allergy; vancomycin can usually be continued with a slower rate and premedication.

opts.text: The infusion should be completed at the current rate since the airway is clear
opts.rat: Continuing at the rapid rate would worsen the histamine release; the infusion must be stopped or slowed.

opts.text: Epinephrine is the immediate first-line treatment for this presentation
opts.rat: Without airway compromise or severe hypotension, this is not anaphylaxis; epinephrine is not the first-line response here.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Rate-related vancomycin infusion reaction (histamine release)
opts.rat: Flushing of the face/neck/torso with itching during a rapid infusion, without airway involvement, is the classic picture.

opts.text: Early anaphylaxis that could still progress
opts.rat: Must remain high on the list and be monitored closely, since a reaction can evolve-but current findings lack airway or respiratory compromise.

opts.text: A drug rash from another medication
opts.rat: Possible but less likely given the tight temporal link to the vancomycin infusion.

opts.text: Fever/flushing from the underlying MRSA infection
opts.rat: The infection explains the fever and leukocytosis but not the sudden flushing and itching timed to the infusion.

opts.text: Anxiety causing the flushing
opts.rat: Least likely: anxiety would not produce this distribution of erythema and pruritus during the infusion.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions.

opts.text: Stop the infusion and assess the airway, breathing, and vital signs
opts.rat: Stopping the infusion halts further histamine release, and immediate reassessment rules out progression to anaphylaxis.

opts.text: Notify the provider and administer an antihistamine as ordered
opts.rat: Antihistamines counter the histamine-mediated flushing and itching; the provider directs treatment and the plan for resuming therapy.

opts.text: Plan to resume the vancomycin at a slower rate (at least 60 minutes) once symptoms resolve, per order
opts.rat: Because this is rate-related rather than a true allergy, the drug can usually be resumed more slowly with premedication as ordered.

opts.text: Continue monitoring for airway swelling, wheezing, or worsening hypotension
opts.rat: Ongoing monitoring is essential because a reaction can evolve into true anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine.

opts.text: Increase the infusion rate to finish the dose quickly and end the exposure
opts.rat: Speeding the infusion increases histamine release and would worsen the reaction.

opts.text: Document a permanent vancomycin allergy and cancel all future doses
opts.rat: Mislabeling a rate-related reaction as an allergy can wrongly deny the client an effective antibiotic for MRSA.

opts.text: Administer IM epinephrine immediately as the first action
opts.rat: Epinephrine is reserved for anaphylaxis with airway compromise or severe hypotension, which this client does not have.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the vancomycin infusion
opts.rat: FIRST-halting the infusion stops the trigger immediately.

opts.text: Assess airway, breathing, and vital signs to rule out anaphylaxis
opts.rat: SECOND-distinguishing infusion reaction from anaphylaxis determines whether epinephrine is needed.

opts.text: Notify the provider of the reaction and findings
opts.rat: THIRD-the provider orders treatment and directs how therapy should resume.

opts.text: Administer the ordered antihistamine and monitor the response
opts.rat: FOURTH-antihistamines relieve the histamine-mediated symptoms.

opts.text: Resume the infusion over at least 60 minutes per order and document the event accurately
opts.rat: LAST-restarting slowly completes therapy, and accurate documentation prevents a false allergy label.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Flushing and itching resolve after the antihistamine and the dose completes over 90 minutes without recurrence
opts.rat: Resolution with a slower infusion confirms the rate-related mechanism and successful management.

opts.text: Blood pressure returns to 124/74 and heart rate to 82
opts.rat: Normalizing vital signs show the reaction has settled without progression.

opts.text: A repeat trough returns at 15 mcg/mL after dose adjustment
opts.rat: A trough within the target range indicates the dosing is now therapeutic for the MRSA infection.

opts.text: The client develops stridor, lip swelling, and a blood pressure of 76/40
opts.rat: Airway compromise with severe hypotension indicates true anaphylaxis-stop the drug and give epinephrine immediately.

opts.text: Creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL over several days
opts.rat: A rising creatinine suggests vancomycin-related nephrotoxicity, requiring level and dose reassessment.

opts.text: The client reports new ringing in the ears and decreased hearing
opts.rat: Tinnitus and hearing loss suggest ototoxicity, another known vancomycin adverse effect that must be reported.

opts.text: Temperature remains 100.6F with the WBC still elevated
opts.rat: The infection markers have not yet improved; this reflects the ongoing MRSA infection rather than the infusion reaction.

opts.text: A faint residual pink flush remains on the neck with no itching or vital-sign change
opts.rat: A stable residual flush without other symptoms is neither clear improvement nor deterioration and warrants continued observation.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.

title: Digoxin Toxicity
subtitle: 78 y/o male on digoxin with nausea, yellow vision, and bradycardia
nursesNote: 0800 - 78 y/o male with chronic atrial fibrillation and heart failure, on daily digoxin and furosemide. Over the past two days he has had poor appetite, nausea, and now reports 'seeing yellow-green halos around the lights.' He feels weak and is intermittently confused. The apical pulse is 48 and irregular. The morning digoxin level is 2.8 ng/mL and potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. The 0800 digoxin dose has not yet been given.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) findings that BEST indicate digoxin toxicity.

opts.text: Digoxin level of 2.8 ng/mL
opts.rat: A level above the 0.5-2.0 ng/mL therapeutic range confirms an elevated digoxin concentration.

opts.text: Seeing yellow-green halos around lights
opts.rat: Visual disturbances such as yellow-green vision and halos are classic signs of digoxin toxicity.

opts.text: Anorexia, nausea, and weakness
opts.rat: GI upset (anorexia, nausea) and fatigue/weakness are common early signs of digoxin toxicity.

opts.text: Apical heart rate of 48 and irregular
opts.rat: Digoxin slows conduction; toxicity commonly causes bradycardia and dysrhythmias.

opts.text: Blood pressure 104/60
opts.rat: This blood pressure is not the defining cue of digoxin toxicity.

opts.text: Magnesium 1.6 mEq/L
opts.rat: This magnesium is within normal limits and is not itself a sign of toxicity.

opts.text: Respiratory rate of 18
opts.rat: A near-normal respiratory rate is not a marker of digoxin toxicity.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: The low potassium increases the risk and severity of digoxin toxicity
opts.rat: Hypokalemia potentiates digoxin's effect on the heart; the furosemide contributes to both the low potassium and the toxicity.

opts.text: Reduced kidney function (elevated creatinine/BUN) can raise digoxin levels because digoxin is renally excreted
opts.rat: Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys; impaired renal function reduces clearance and can lead to accumulation and toxicity.

opts.text: The scheduled digoxin dose should be held and the provider notified
opts.rat: With a toxic level, bradycardia, and symptoms, the dose is withheld and the provider is notified before any further digoxin is given.

opts.text: The 0800 digoxin dose should be given now to keep the level therapeutic
opts.rat: Giving more digoxin during toxicity would worsen it and is contraindicated.

opts.text: A heart rate of 48 means the nurse should give the digoxin to strengthen the heart
opts.rat: Digoxin is held for bradycardia (typically an apical rate below 60); giving it would further slow the heart.

opts.text: The visual and GI symptoms are unrelated to the digoxin
opts.rat: Yellow-green vision, halos, and GI upset are hallmark digoxin-toxicity effects, not unrelated findings.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Digoxin toxicity, worsened by hypokalemia and reduced renal clearance
opts.rat: The elevated level with classic visual/GI signs, bradycardia, low potassium, and rising creatinine make digoxin toxicity the clear explanation.

opts.text: Progression of the underlying heart failure
opts.rat: Heart failure is present, but it does not explain the yellow-green vision and the toxic digoxin level.

opts.text: A primary cardiac conduction problem unrelated to medication
opts.rat: Possible, but the toxic level and symptom cluster point squarely at digoxin as the cause of the bradycardia.

opts.text: A viral gastroenteritis causing the nausea
opts.rat: Gastroenteritis would not cause yellow-green vision, bradycardia, or a high digoxin level.

opts.text: Normal aging changes
opts.rat: Least likely: these are acute, dangerous findings, not normal aging.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate interventions.

opts.text: Hold the digoxin and notify the provider of the level, heart rate, and symptoms
opts.rat: Withholding digoxin and notifying the provider are the immediate priorities for suspected toxicity.

opts.text: Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
opts.rat: Cardiac monitoring detects the dysrhythmias that digoxin toxicity can cause.

opts.text: Check and correct the potassium level as ordered
opts.rat: Correcting hypokalemia reduces the severity of toxicity; potassium is replaced carefully per order with monitoring.

opts.text: Anticipate digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) for severe or life-threatening toxicity per order
opts.rat: Digoxin immune Fab is the antidote reserved for severe toxicity, life-threatening dysrhythmias, or very high levels.

opts.text: Administer the scheduled digoxin dose to maintain the level
opts.rat: Giving more digoxin during toxicity is dangerous and contraindicated.

opts.text: Administer IV calcium to support the heart
opts.rat: Calcium can worsen digoxin's cardiac effects and is generally avoided in digoxin toxicity.

opts.text: Increase the furosemide dose to help the heart failure
opts.rat: More furosemide would worsen the hypokalemia and further potentiate the toxicity.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Hold the digoxin dose and assess the apical pulse and rhythm
opts.rat: FIRST-withholding the drug and assessing the heart rate/rhythm prevent further harm and gauge severity.

opts.text: Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
opts.rat: SECOND-monitoring is established to catch dangerous dysrhythmias.

opts.text: Notify the provider of the digoxin level, bradycardia, and symptoms
opts.rat: THIRD-the provider directs potassium correction, antidote, and further management.

opts.text: Correct the potassium as ordered
opts.rat: FOURTH-restoring potassium reduces the severity of the toxicity.

opts.text: Administer digoxin immune Fab as ordered for severe toxicity and recheck the level
opts.rat: LAST-the antidote is given per order for severe toxicity, and levels are rechecked to confirm response.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: Repeat digoxin level falls into the therapeutic range and the halos resolve
opts.rat: A therapeutic level with resolving visual symptoms shows the toxicity is correcting.

opts.text: Apical heart rate rises to 68 with a regular rhythm
opts.rat: A return toward a normal rate and rhythm indicates the cardiac effects of toxicity are resolving.

opts.text: Potassium returns to 4.2 mEq/L and appetite improves
opts.rat: Normalizing potassium reduces toxicity risk, and returning appetite reflects resolving GI symptoms.

opts.text: The client develops a new second- or third-degree heart block with a rate of 36
opts.rat: Advancing heart block with severe bradycardia is a dangerous progression of digoxin toxicity requiring urgent intervention.

opts.text: The client becomes more confused and has a brief syncopal episode
opts.rat: Worsening confusion and syncope suggest inadequate cardiac output from the toxicity and need immediate escalation.

opts.text: Potassium continues to fall to 2.8 mEq/L
opts.rat: A further drop in potassium deepens the potentiation of digoxin toxicity and must be treated.

opts.text: Blood pressure remains 106/62 with no other change
opts.rat: A stable blood pressure with no other change is neither improvement nor deterioration.

opts.text: The digoxin dose remains held pending the next level
opts.rat: Continuing to hold the dose is appropriate management but does not itself represent a change in the client's condition.

title: Chemotherapy Safety & Vesicant Extravasation
subtitle: 51 y/o female receiving a vesicant chemotherapy through a peripheral IV
nursesNote: 1030 - 51 y/o female with breast cancer receiving IV chemotherapy with a known vesicant agent through a 22-gauge peripheral IV in the right hand (her port is not yet accessed). About 20 minutes into the infusion she reports burning and stinging at the IV site. The nurse notes swelling and redness around the insertion site, and there is no blood return when checked. She has a low neutrophil count from prior cycles. The nurse is certified in chemotherapy administration and is wearing the required personal protective equipment.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that BEST indicate vesicant extravasation.

opts.text: Burning and stinging at the IV site during the infusion
opts.rat: Pain, burning, or stinging at the site is an early warning sign of vesicant extravasation.

opts.text: Swelling and redness around the insertion site
opts.rat: Local swelling and redness suggest the vesicant is leaking into the surrounding tissue.

opts.text: No blood return from the IV
opts.rat: Loss of blood return suggests the catheter is no longer reliably in the vein, supporting extravasation.

opts.text: Absolute neutrophil count of 900
opts.rat: Neutropenia is an important chemotherapy concern (infection risk) but is not a sign of extravasation.

opts.text: Platelet count of 95 K/uL
opts.rat: Thrombocytopenia raises bleeding risk but does not indicate extravasation.

opts.text: Heart rate of 90
opts.rat: A mild rise in heart rate is nonspecific and not a defining cue of extravasation.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.sub: Interpret the findings and the safety context
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly interpret this situation.

opts.text: A vesicant that extravasates can cause severe tissue damage and necrosis, so the infusion must be stopped immediately
opts.rat: Vesicants blister and destroy tissue when they leak out of the vein; stopping the infusion is the first priority to limit injury.

opts.text: Some vesicants have a specific antidote, and the manufacturer/protocol guidance directs whether to apply warm or cold compresses
opts.rat: Management is drug-specific: certain agents have antidotes, and warm versus cold compress selection depends on the particular vesicant per protocol.

opts.text: The client's neutropenia and thrombocytopenia mean she is also at high risk for infection and bleeding
opts.rat: Chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression (low ANC and platelets) raises infection and bleeding risk, which shapes her overall care.

opts.text: Because only a little has infused, the nurse should continue and watch the site
opts.rat: Continuing a vesicant into tissue rapidly worsens the injury; it must be stopped at the first sign.

opts.text: Vesicant extravasation is minor and needs no special management
opts.rat: It is a serious complication that can require antidotes, specialist referral, and possible surgical debridement.

opts.text: The catheter should be removed immediately and the site massaged to disperse the drug
opts.rat: The catheter is typically left in place initially to aspirate residual drug/give antidote per protocol, and the site is NOT massaged, which spreads the vesicant.

steps.title: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.inst: Drag to rank the explanations from MOST likely (1) to LEAST likely (5).

opts.text: Vesicant chemotherapy extravasation into the tissue
opts.rat: Burning/stinging, swelling, redness, and loss of blood return during a vesicant infusion point clearly to extravasation.

opts.text: Chemical phlebitis/irritation along the vein
opts.rat: Irritation is possible, but the swelling and lost blood return specifically suggest the drug is leaving the vein.

opts.text: An allergic/hypersensitivity reaction to the chemotherapy
opts.rat: Possible with some agents, but hypersensitivity usually involves systemic signs (flushing, wheezing, hypotension) rather than isolated site findings.

opts.text: Simple anxiety about the infusion
opts.rat: Anxiety does not cause swelling, redness, and loss of blood return at the site.

opts.text: Normal expected sensation from the infusion
opts.rat: Least likely: burning with swelling and no blood return is never a normal, acceptable finding.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the FOUR (4) MOST appropriate immediate interventions.

opts.text: Stop the chemotherapy infusion immediately
opts.rat: Stopping the vesicant at the first sign of extravasation is the single most important action to limit tissue damage.

opts.text: Leave the catheter in place initially and aspirate residual drug/give antidote per the extravasation protocol
opts.rat: The catheter is typically left briefly to aspirate residual vesicant and instill an antidote if indicated, following the drug-specific protocol.

opts.text: Notify the provider and follow the drug-specific extravasation protocol (antidote, warm or cold compress as directed)
opts.rat: Management is agent-specific; the provider and protocol direct the antidote and whether warm or cold compresses apply.

opts.text: Elevate the extremity, mark and assess the area, and document the event thoroughly
opts.rat: Elevation, marking/serial assessment, and detailed documentation guide care and track tissue injury over time.

opts.text: Continue the infusion at a slower rate to finish the dose
opts.rat: Continuing to infuse a vesicant into the tissue rapidly worsens the injury.

opts.text: Vigorously massage the site to disperse the medication
opts.rat: Massaging spreads the vesicant through the tissue and enlarges the area of damage.

opts.text: Flush the line briskly with saline to push the drug into the vein
opts.rat: Flushing forces more vesicant into the tissue rather than clearing it.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag to rank the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the chemotherapy infusion
opts.rat: FIRST-halting the vesicant stops ongoing tissue injury.

opts.text: Leave the catheter in place and aspirate residual drug per protocol
opts.rat: SECOND-aspirating residual vesicant through the existing catheter removes some drug before further steps.

opts.text: Notify the provider and initiate the drug-specific extravasation protocol
opts.rat: THIRD-the provider and protocol direct the antidote and compress therapy.

opts.text: Apply the ordered antidote and warm or cold compress as directed, and elevate the limb
opts.rat: FOURTH-agent-specific treatment and elevation limit the extent of tissue damage.

opts.text: Mark the area, document the event, and arrange follow-up/referral
opts.rat: LAST-documentation and follow-up (including possible specialist referral) support ongoing wound management.

steps.title: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.inst: Over the following days, classify each finding as Improving, Worsening, or Unchanged.

opts.text: The site pain, redness, and swelling steadily decrease with intact skin
opts.rat: Resolving local signs with intact skin indicate the extravasation was managed before significant tissue loss.

opts.text: Chemotherapy is safely resumed through the newly accessed implanted port
opts.rat: Resuming therapy through appropriate central (port) access shows the plan is back on track with a safer route.

opts.text: The client and nurse verbalize that vesicants are preferably given through central access
opts.rat: Correct understanding reduces the risk of a future peripheral extravasation.

opts.text: The site develops blistering, then an ulcer with dark, firm (necrotic) tissue
opts.rat: Blistering progressing to ulceration and necrosis is worsening tissue injury requiring wound care and possible surgical referral.

opts.text: The client spikes a fever of 101.5F with her neutropenia (ANC 900)
opts.rat: Fever in a neutropenic client is neutropenic fever-a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and antibiotics.

opts.text: New bruising and gum bleeding appear with the low platelet count
opts.rat: Bleeding signs with thrombocytopenia indicate worsening bleeding risk needing prompt attention.

opts.text: The marked area of redness is the same size the next day with no new changes
opts.rat: A stable, non-expanding area without new changes is neither clearly improving nor worsening and warrants continued monitoring.

opts.text: Hemoglobin remains 10.4 g/dL
opts.rat: A stable hemoglobin reflects her chronic anemia and is neither better nor worse in this timeframe.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model. Written from standard nursing references. Pending faculty review.
